speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the first question, yes we will buy government debt up to the percentage that will allow a proper market price formation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one is an issuer limit, which is 33%, and another one is an issue limit, which is 25%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, we won't buy more than 25% of each issue, and not more than 33% of each issuer's debt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The 25% limit, by the way, is the one foreseen in order not to be a blocking minority in the collective action clause assemblies, basically, bond holders' assemblies, and it's the basis for us to be able to say, there is going to be pari passu.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other question, first of all let me say I was surprised that this risk-sharing issue became almost the most important thing about our monetary policy decisions today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact, it shouldn't be so, but let me explain how we reached the percentage of 20%, and what is the reasoning behind this decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, let me start by saying that each monetary policy operation always has some fiscal implication, and for the Central Bank what matters first and foremost is that monetary policy is effective, and then it takes into account these implications, but without prejudice for the monetary policy effectiveness.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Usually, these fiscal implications are dealt with easily within a one-country framework, between the central bank and the treasury.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the euro area, there is no European treasury, and each national treasury gives an implicit or explicit indemnity to its own central bank, but not the euro system as a whole.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the question on how to allocate risks in the euro area has been with the Governing Council since the very beginning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a combined ruling coming from the statutes of the ECB and from a Governing Council decision that a default mode is a full risk-sharing mode.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, the Governing Council is also free to decide what it deems more appropriate according to the circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, it is not the first time the Governing Council has used its discretion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Originally, in the early times, there were two lists of collateral, one risk-shared, the risk of which was shared, the so-called Tier 1, and one where the risk was not shared, and that's Tier 2.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The additional credit claims decision we took about, I think two years ago, was on a no-risk-sharing basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, there are other examples where we actually use the full risk-sharing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, the Dutch central bank was indemnified for some small losses based on full risk-sharing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Luxemburg central bank was indemnified for Icelandic banks when, you'll remember there was that crisis, on a full risk-sharing, and we raised the buffers on a full risk-sharing for some potential losses that Germany, the Bundesbank, might have after the Lehman crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me add, this has nothing to do with the singleness of the monetary policy, because the decisions are being taken by the Governing Council with a euro area focus, as I just said in the introductory statement, so the same is true for sovereign bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The modalities, the amounts, the rules, the limits that you just asked me about have been decided here in Frankfurt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council is the sole decision-maker, and the decisions are meant to affect monetary and financial conditions across the whole euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This way, this time, we had a situation where the programme is very large.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense, it is different from the SMP, for example.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so, on the one hand, we want to keep the principle of the risk-sharing in place, and that's why we retained the 20% share under the regime of full risk-sharing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, we want to take a decision that would mitigate the concerns that many participating countries in the euro area have about the unintended fiscal consequences of potential developments in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is risk-sharing or no risk-sharing a fundamental decision as far as the effectiveness of this decision is concerned?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that it might have some effects, but they are not relevant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me give you an example where actually it is fundamental; OMT.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In OMT full risk-sharing is fundamental for the effectiveness of that monetary policy measure and you understand why; because it's selective, it addresses specific countries, the countries are under stress, the debt sustainability is an issue and there are tail risks that could make things precipitate for certain individual countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In that case, risk-sharing is fundamental for the effectiveness of monetary policy, and by the way, to address these risks, OMT is there, ready to be acted, in case there were risks of that kind, of that nature, tail risks were to materialise, and that programme is under full risk-sharing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I think you should ask the first question to the people who have these concerns.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We took these concerns into account, and that's why this decision would mitigate these concerns, but certainly, we are not in a one-country setup.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in a multi-country setup, so the issue of potential fiscal transfers coming from our monetary policy decision is there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the first question we should ask, is it fundamental for the effectiveness of monetary policy or not?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If it's not, then we can do something to mitigate these concerns.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Do we want to abandon the principle of full risk-sharing?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Absolutely no, and as I said, the singleness of the monetary policy remains in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, we would believe that the measures taken today will be effective, will raise inflation, medium-term inflation expectations, and basically will address the economic situation in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are several channels through which these measures will be effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first is the portfolio rebalancing effect, where you basically substitute bonds with cash, and therefore banks, at that point, will have more incentive to lend to the private sector, households and companies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of recent inflation expectations, medium-term inflation expectations, dropped by something like 50 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Since our nominal interest rates are at the zero lower bound, this meant that real interest rates went up by about 50 basis points, basically nullifying the effects of our reductions of nominal interest rates, the two reductions of nominal interest rates that we had decided in the course of the year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we do expect that effect to be also important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, let me add something here, because it's actually quite important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What monetary policy can do, I've said this many times, but I think itis worthwhile repeating it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What monetary policy can do is to create the basis for growth, but for growth to pick up, you need investment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For investment you need confidence, and for confidence you need structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB has taken a further, very expansionary measure today, but it's now up to the governments to implement these structural reforms, and the more they do, the more effective will be our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's absolutely essential, as well as the fiscal consolidation side.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So structural reforms is one thing, budget and fiscal consolidation is a different issue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's very important to have in place a so-called growth-friendly fiscal consolidation for confidence strengthening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This combined with a monetary policy which is very expansionary, which has been and is even more so after our decisions today, is actually the optimal combination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But for this now, we need the actions by the governments, and we need the action also by the Commission, both in its overseeing role of fiscal policies and in its implementing the investment plan, which was launched by the President of the Commission, which was certainly welcome at the time, now has to be implemented with speed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: At the meeting today -- it's the first time that we'll have the accounts be published of this meeting, and so we have also worked out some qualifiers to indicate how the meeting proceeded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The meeting was unanimous in stating that the asset purchase programme is a true monetary policy tool in a legal sense.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's important, because it establishes the principle that this is a monetary policy tool that should be used in the right situations, but it is part of our toolbox.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, there was a large majority on the need to trigger it now, and so large that we didn't need to take a vote.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, there was a good discussion on the need, I would say a majority on the need to trigger it now, but of course there were differing views about the need to act now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And finally, there was a consensus on risk-sharing set at 20%, and 80% on a no-risk-sharing basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, unanimity on the asset purchase programme being a monetary policy tool, a large majority on the need to trigger it now, and some discussion on the need to trigger it now, in fact I say a large majority, but not unanimity, and finally, consensus on the risk-sharing set, as I've just described.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The measure of this asset purchase programme exceeds what, well it doesn't exceed really, it's in the ballgame.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You'll remember that you have two figures for the beginning/early 2012 balance sheet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is in January, the other one is in March, so this figure by and large is set in that ballgame.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second point is absolutely no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I just said, it would be a big mistake if countries were to consider that the presence of this programme might be an incentive to fiscal expansion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They would undermine the confidence, so it's not directed to monetary financing at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually, it's been designed as to avoid any monetary financing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This programme should increase the lending capacity of the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This programme, the national central banks, the ECB would buy bonds, and then banks will have this money, and this money can be used either to repay some liabilities, or it would be placed in our deposit facility, in which case they would have to pay a negative interest rate, so there is an incentive to lend to the private sector, stronger incentive than there was simply on collateralised borrowing as we used to do in the past, namely out of TLTROs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The limitation, the three-year maturity that was present in the TLTROs, in this case isn't there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The first question is yes, the maturities range between 2 and 30 years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question really shows how important you made this risk-sharing issue, because it shows a degree of sophistication in understanding what happens if.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, if we have an event, the first thing that would be drawn upon would be the buffers of the national central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, most central banks have adequate buffers, so nothing will happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, I really only read again the statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just don't want to speculate, giving horizons of dates, of deadlines.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these purchases are intended to be carried out until end September 2016, and will in any case be conducted until we see a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You might as well have asked, what is sustained adjustment?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Sustained adjustment in the path of inflation, which is consistent with our aim of achieving inflation rates below but close to 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It depends on many parameters, and at this point, certainly we wouldn't want to speculate on precise deadlines.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other question, , it's difficult to give a precise division between the precise split between the two purchases, because first of all the size of the market for ABS is relatively small, although we think it will expand in the coming months, and the covered bond programme has done quite well, much better than the other programme, but also we don't know what the market size will be next year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What you could look at is basically the past behaviour as an inference for the future behaviour of our purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why under certain circumstances, I find this discussion on risk-sharing quite futile.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I have some jokes that I could make at this point in time, but I'll just re-read the statement if you want, because that's really what we can say today, and I'd just rather avoid jokes on this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mean, the overall situation of inflation, inflation developments, doesn't allow us to make these jokes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to the first question, let me say one thing here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are obviously some conditions before we can buy Greek bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, there is a waiver that has to remain in place, has to be a program.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then there is this 33% issuer limit, which means that, if all the other conditions are in place, we could buy bonds in, I believe, July, because by then there will be some large redemptions of SMP bonds and therefore we would be within the limit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by the way, let me add, if there is a problem, if there is a waiver, all these are not exceptional rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, we monitor closely any potential instance of risk to financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There may be some local episodes of certain specific markets where prices are going up fast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But to have a bubble, besides having that, one should also identify, detect an increase, dramatic increase in leverage or in bank credit, and we don't see that now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If bubbles are of a local nature, they should be addressed by local instruments, namely macro-prudential instruments rather than by monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question, well, I would say the readings of reality differ.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In some cases the inflation developments are considered to be temporary or heavily affected by temporary factors like the fall in oil prices and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's different readings of reality, which suggest a different urgency in acting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well the answer to the second question is absolutely no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We shouldn't forget that --perhaps today is the first time I say it, usually by now I am in the fifth time-- We shouldn't forget that our mandate is price stability, price stability defined as keeping inflation rate close but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are, at this point in time, distant from that objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to give you a few ideas, the average inflation rate for 2014 was 0.4%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The five-year, the average inflation rate over the next five years is 0.3%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the inflation rate, the average inflation rate over the next 10 years at this point in time, these are market-based measures, are 0.9%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The 5y-5y inflation expectation is today, I think should be around 1.64, to be compared with an average of 2.30.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is little doubt, in our view at least, that one should act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe and are convinced and have good arguments to think that the monetary policy measures that we have decided today will contribute to lift inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You said that they are already priced in the market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some, it's hard to say how much, but certainly some of the effects have already been priced in the market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is a difference between expectation and actual announcement that things are going to be undertaken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that's, in the end, after months pass by, it's the announcements that really matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, expectations work only if there is certain credibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are showing that this credibility is deserved with today's action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have shown that all monetary policy measures have some fiscal implications.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What matters is, first and foremost, the effectiveness of the monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is geared to our mandate, which is maintaining price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These fiscal implications are usually dealt in a one-country set-up rather simply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a multi-country set-up they are dealt in a different way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I told you about the history that shows that they were dealt in various ways, I would say based on an ad-hoc consideration of the circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have told you that risk sharing or no risk sharing was not a fundamental aspect of the effect, of the effectiveness of our monetary policy measures today, while it is a fundamental component of our OMT programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And finally, given the size that this programme will have and the fact it's so broad-based all across all countries, the solution that we found seemed to be the most reasonable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On one hand you want to keep the principle of full risk sharing in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other you want to mitigate the concerns expressed by several member countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we can do so because it's not essential for the effectiveness of the monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The consensus means the following, means that everybody could either agree or not object.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The large majority means that a lot of people agreed and a few people objected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From now on I cannot say we had a fantastic majority or things like that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be either a majority or a large majority or a consensus, or unanimity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first point, the way the introductory statement reads says that both things are important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The overall amount but also the scale of these purchases, the monthly flows are quite meaningful, as is the overall amount.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question, I think the best way to answer to this is, have we seen lots of inflation since QE programmes started?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And now it's been quite a few years since they started.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our experience since we have these press conferences goes back to a little more than three years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In these three years we've lowered interest rates I don't know how many times, four or five times, six times maybe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And each time someone was saying this is going to be terribly expansionary, there will be inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some people voted against lower interest rates way back at the end of November 2013.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I'm saying is that certainly the jury's still out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also for the people who say that there will be inflation, yes, when, please?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: That is a question similar to the one that has been asked before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It says they are intended to be carried out -- they are intended -- to be carried out until the end of September 2016 and will in any case be conducted until we see a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation, which is consistent with our aim of achieving inflation rates below but close to 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'm not sure I understand the second question, but the first question is, I've said it many times, for us the exchange rate is not a policy target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's important for price stability, for growth, but it's not a policy target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The movements in the exchange rate since three years were the outcome of diverging monetary policy cycles as well as divergent economic recovery paths between major jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They were not intended, it was not an action geared to cause these exchange rate movements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can't remember, because we never comment on other central bank policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So whoever wants to ask me about Switzerland, just you should know; we never comment on other central banks' decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, this programme is meant to create a large injection of liquidity that is fungible across the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, if it starts in Germany, it can easily flow everywhere through our payment system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly where the spreads are higher, you would expect greater effectiveness, greater immediate direct effects from this policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is you said do we expect our inflation expectations to stay low after a prolonged period of time, and if we have a plan B. I say again, this is a question that's been asked before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We just present a plan A and we have a plan A.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the sentence and the wording here could be, actually says many things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'm not going to reread it, but each word has been carefully chosen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The sustained improvement, it just says what it says.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no other way to answer your first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, a material dislocation from the foreseen objective would be the criteria, but at this point in time, we see absolutely no reason to think or plan or act in any different way from what we've planned, namely the purchasing of €60 billion a month of securities until September 2016, or beyond, if needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point, a quick answer to your question is the following.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of the rules that we comply with is contained in the Treaty, and it's Article 123, and it's the prohibition of monetary financing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary financing is when the central bank of a country prints money to buy the government bonds in the primary market of that country, and it could be either direct or indirect, when banks bring collateral to the ECB in order to be financed in order to buy the sovereign debt of that country, and we are prohibited from doing that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, let me say, our monetary policy decisions have worked, and it's with a certain degree of satisfaction that the Governing Council has acknowledged this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The monetary policy decisions we are discussing today are the final set of measures of a series of decisions that have been taken starting in June last year, and we see that the objectives are gradually being attained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The market reaction to the announcement, the expectation first and the announcement second, of our asset purchase programme has also been quite effective and quite positive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We haven't even started, and a lively discussion about whether we'll actually be able to do this has developed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite interesting that until a month ago, nobody had any doubt that public debt, sovereign debt in the euro area, was actually very, very big, and now some people worry that we won't have enough bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Incidentally, I'm told that the very same statements were made when the US and the UK started their bond buying programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the bottom line of this is that there may be complexities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We observe that almost half of the euro bonds are outside the euro area and we also observe that the average weighted price of bonds in the 2 to 30-year maturity is well above par.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question assumes that the improvements we see in the financial markets will never pass through to the real economy, but that's exactly what we have not been observing over the last few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, in a more and more accelerated way, we've seen a decline, if not a steep fall, in the lending rates across the euro area, a significant decrease in dispersion in the lending rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know from previous press conferences that fragmentation on the funding side for the banking system has basically disappeared several months ago, but for quite a time, fragmentation on the lending side still remained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That has gone down a lot, and one can say now that all rates have converged quite well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are seeing now is that these benefits from a very accommodative monetary policy stance are being passed in the form of lower borrowing costs to the real economy, to non-financial companies, to households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see for example the credit flows to households have increased, and then we will see that the channels through which this asset purchase programme works will firm up, will strengthen the transmission through the usual signalling channel, confidence channel, interest rate channels, wealth effects, and exchange rate effect of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me first say something that perhaps is not entirely known.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB up to today has lent to Greece €100 billion, and more exactly has doubled its lending from €50 billion to €100 billion in the last month and a half, the last two months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The lending to Greece today is 68% of the Greek GDP, which is the highest in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense, one can really say that the ECB is the central bank of Greece, but it's also the central bank of all the other countries, and it's a rules-based institution, as I have just recalled a moment ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB is the first to wish to re-start the financing to the Greek economy, provided the conditions are in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the conditions to be in place is that a process which suggests a successful completion of the review be put in place fast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the condition, and we will certainly welcome such development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Going to your second question, right now, the ECB cannot buy Greek bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The purchase programme doesn't foresee the purchase of private bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It cannot buy Greek bonds for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the purchases are not supposed to take place for countries under a contract or a programme during the review period, so in this sense, we wouldn't be able to buy Cypriot bonds either, or Greek bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Secondly, we can only buy investment-grade bonds, and as such, the Greek bonds are below the threshold of investment-grade, so the waiver will have to be reinstated, and we are ready to do so, as soon as these conditions are in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, we have a limit of 33% per issuer's bonds, so we cannot buy more than 33% of the bonds, of the total stock of bonds issued by the same sovereign, and our current SMP holdings are such that this limit is at present overcome, so we wouldn't be able to buy these bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As soon as Greece repays the SMP bonds that are due, they're coming due I believe in July or August, and if the waiver had been reinstated of course, then we would be able to buy Greek bonds via this new asset purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what the Governing Council has decided, by €500 million.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From this viewpoint, the decision about lifting the waiver, as well as the decision not to allow monetary financing, and finally the decision about determining an ELA, are all the outcome of rules, not our political decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: ELA is a decision of the National Central Bank of Greece, to which the Governing Council may decide to object with a very special and demanding majority requirement, if certain conditions are not in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One condition is that ELA can be given to solvent banks with adequate collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Their capital levels are well above the minimum requirements, and that's positive news.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A lot has been done by Greece to strengthen its banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of the NPL, the non-performing loan problems, have been addressed so, today, the Greek banking system is solvent and is key to providing credit to the Greek economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's absolutely essential that this solvency be maintained, because that is the precondition for the ECB to be able to allow ELA, and therefore financing to the economy, financing to companies and households in Greece, and the private sector in Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is important, and I'm saying this because if there is in place a certain communication that creates volatility in the markets, this communication destroys collateral, increases the spreads and destroys collateral, undermines the solvency of the Greek banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the most important thing that we can do today, to preserve the solvency and the robustness of the Greek banking system, and also to this extent, the ECB has asked the Eurogroup members to make sure that the recapitalisation fund of something around €10 billion be readily available to face any sudden negative contingency that might materialise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some language in the last Eurogroup statement reflects this request by the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to comment on the ill feelings, but certainly, what I would suggest is you go back to the last 15-plus years and look at which countries have been in the excessive deficit procedure most often, over the last, say, 15, 16, 17 years, and then draw a conclusion from there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But to address your point, there is a sentence here that says, full and consistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Consistent implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact is key for confidence in our fiscal framework.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Georghadji: As President Draghi explained, countries like Cyprus, which are under a programme, to get benefit from the programme, they must have a positive review by the Troika, or the institutions, whatever you like.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Unfortunately, as you know, the Fifth Review of the Cyprus economy has not been concluded yet, and this is because the law for the foreclosures has not been put into effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When there is a positive review, we will be able to start immediately and get the benefit of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: According to the parameters of the programme, then the Cyprus economy can benefit up to €500 million throughout the effect of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The programme, as President Draghi said in his initial statement, will start on 9 March, and it will go at least until September 2016.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This programme will have a very beneficial impact for Cyprus, as it will suppress the interest rates, and suppress the interest rates downwards, and therefore, the Cypriot government will be able to borrow at lower rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is the big benefit from the programme, and therefore, we look forward to taking part in this programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decided to have a waiver in place at the time when there were reasonable assessments for a successful completion of the review of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, by and large, the programme was on track.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have this rule that says we can't accept as collateral bonds that are below a certain threshold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Greek bonds at the present time, and were even then, below this threshold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, if certain conditions are in place, as far as the economic policy is concerned, that would make the ECB and the Governing Council think that in some time from now these bonds will become again eligible, will be rated above the threshold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we assessed that these conditions were not in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that in mid-February when we decided this, the programme was not on track.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was not only an assessment that we were making; it was an assessment explicitly stated by the government.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, we stand ready to reinstate the waiver as soon as we are able to make a positive assessment about the likelihood of a successful completion of the review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first point, I frankly don't want to pass judgement on specific individual countries' fiscal policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I could say, however, is that the monetary policy measures that we decided in January, but also for the previous ones, to be fully effective, need first and foremost strong structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is, otherwise we can provide as much credit as possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can refinance the banking system so they can lend as much money at the lowest interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if the structural conditions are not in place, there will be little incentive to use this credit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm saying that their effectiveness is going to be lower.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And from our viewpoint, that means it's going to take longer to get to our objective of price stability, namely an inflation that is close but below 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: You rightly said, you rightly reminded us that the ECB has already lent - not liquidity - just lent 100 billion euros.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I repeat, it's 68% of Greece's GDP, and it's the highest in the whole euro zone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it has doubled this amount in the last two months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the last thing one can say is that the ECB is not supporting Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now you asked the question to what extent our decisions depend on what happens in the Eurogroup.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there is an agreement - called contract, call it whatever you want - our underlying, our background changes completely, and we would be much better in place to take favourable, more favourable, decisions for Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, once a country has a contract, then disbursements could take place, could be restored by the member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there is market access, many of our concerns about monetary financing would disappear because if the government has the capacity to finance itself on the market then the issue of having banks financing the government would disappear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the ultimate result of all this is that flexibility to the Greek government economic policy would return within the contract that the Greek government would define with the other members of the Eurogroup.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I will first answer my question, and then the governor will answer the other question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Core inflation is still low, although we noticed just today that one of our measures of inflation expectations is now back to a fairly high level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't say an all-time high, certainly not, but a three-month or four-month high, yes, I'm pretty sure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I wouldn't rely too much on point observations because as they come they also go.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we can say safely is that our monetary policy decisions, this one but also the previous ones, have stopped a decline in inflation expectations that had started at the end of July last year, and it became more and more marked by year-end.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, it is true that our projections of inflation are basically, as you said, based on oil price futures, but also there are other factors which play a role for core inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One, of course, is again our monetary policy stance and its effects on the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second one is the closing of the output gap that we foresee happening gradually between now and 2017.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Another factor is that real disposable income is being supported, again, not only by oil prices but also by our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And here the channel through which this may happen is the following.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our monetary policy decisions have significantly decreased the risk of second round effects coming from lower oil prices on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember, when we discussed the effects of lower oil prices a few months ago, we said they were a good thing, but also there was a potential negative side to that if these effects produced second round effects which could have a deflationary impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that our monetary policy decisions have avoided this risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore, we foresee a savings rate which remains what it is today, a recovery where consumption gradually strengthens and firms up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now all these factors will have an impact on core inflation as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Georghadji: The decisions were taken in March 2013, two years ago, and they were very painful for the country and for its people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, it is my view that under the then circumstances, there was no other way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We should have taken measures long before the very difficult decisions were taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Capital controls also were inevitable until the restoration of the confidence in the banking sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it was a decision taken by the minister of finance after consultation with the Governor of the Central Bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I can assure you that it is the view of the minister, of the government and of the Governor that these capital controls, the very few capital controls which are still in place, very few, only two or three measures, will be very soon lifted, before the end of the first quarter of the year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first issue, it's the same condition we have with OMT.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: During a review process, we don't want to influence the review process via conditions that are special conditions for market access of the country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it would be an element which would interfere with the negotiations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is a standard rule that we have in place, that we have in place with OMT as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, I'm not sure I know anything about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Georghadji: With regard to the first question, let me add to what President Draghi has said, that one prerequisite to participate in the programme is that you have a positive review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore, during the review period you cannot participate in the programme anyway since you need to have a positive review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: With regard to the second question concerning ELA, of course President Draghi was there in the meeting with the President.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we have to remind you that, as he said twice during his opening speech, the ECB is a rules-based institution and ELA is extended under a framework and rules of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Within these rules I can assure you that both the governor, the central bank and the government is doing the best for the country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Georghadji: We believe, we expect, we anticipate that the obstacle that exists for the completion of the fifth review, the law on foreclosures, the obstacle that exists will be lifted and we will be able to participate in the QE programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There could not be any waiver or exception to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I think the answer to your question is entirely in the hands of the Greek government.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, we approved the ELA and we'll continue to do so, extending liquidity to the Greek banks while they are solvent and they have adequate collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far, we have reached an exposure to Greece of €110 billion, which is the highest in the euro area in relation to GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from this viewpoint, we have always been and we continue to be a rules-based institution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The worries about potential scarcity of government bonds, sovereign bonds, to be bought under our purchase programme, are just a little exaggerated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All, both direct and indirect evidence, and market feedback, show that there isn't any problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And our programme is flexible enough in any event to be adjusted if circumstances were to change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, some of these worries have been motivated with the need that some banks will have to retain sovereign bonds for complying with the liquidity requirements, the regulatory liquidity requirements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also not quite clear why this should be a worry because government bonds are used for liquidity, as well as cash is used for liquidity, so if they sell bonds, they get cash.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From a regulatory perspective, it shouldn't change, unless I'm mistaken, but by and large, we believe that these worries are, to say the least, premature, certainly not supported by the current evidence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a sentence which was here, but basically, it's an explanatory sentence that gives the meaning of a sustained adjustment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we say, 'until we see a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation that is consistent with our aim of achieving inflation rates below but close to 2% over the medium term'.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sentence that you rightly identified explains what we mean by that, by sustained, by medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're not going to be judging or assessing on the basis of point-in-time observations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There has to be looking through unexpected outcomes in measured inflation in either direction if judged to be transient and to have no implication for the medium-term outlook for price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, the bank lending survey is done over 142 banks in the euro area, and this time, more strongly than on previous occasions, banks have been reporting better credit standards, better credit conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, when we look at the composition of these answers, we see that the risk aversion factor, which used to be a stronger limit to credit expansion, has lost a lot of its weight, if not all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see that the return of demand for credit is also a factor in this positive assessment that the bank lending survey gives, and we see also that the return of competition amongst banks is playing a factor in this credit expansion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you rightly said, there are countries where this is more visible, and countries where this is less visible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Spain is not the only one where this progress in credit standards is less visible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see how our monetary policy measures are finding their way through the economy; namely they're being passed through, through the banking channel to the real economy, and I will expand, if there are questions on this later on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On Spain, it's I think beyond question, the fact that the Spanish economy is experiencing a strong and an employment-rich recovery, and almost half a million jobs have been created since the end of 2013.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also unquestionable that this progress has been supported by important labour-market reforms undertaken since 2012.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To sustain these developments, enhance conditions for hiring youth and long-term unemployed and reduce, that's a key point, reduce the still elevated duality of the labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly, as you suggest, you seem to say, further action is needed on strengthening active labour-market policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, the answer to the second question is, no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's entirely depending on the conditions that will be in place, that are in place, and clearly, the answer to all these questions about ELA and further prosecution of ELA is entirely in the hands of the Greek government and the negotiations that are taking place between the Greek government and euro area members.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question is, I should re-read my introductory statement, because it says everything.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Purchases are intended, intended, to run until the end of September 2016.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of you, when I first used the word intended, rather than expected, rightly pointed out the difference between the two concepts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was at the beginning of December last year, in an introductory statement where we changed the word, and that was meant, and was accepted by markets, as being a powerful signal of changing the monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, purchases are intended to run until the end of September 2016, and in any case until we see a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation that is consistent with our aim of achieving inflation rates over etc etc, and then there is this new sentence explaining exactly what we mean by sustained and by medium-term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think it's the case now to go beyond this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm quite surprised, frankly, by the attention that a possible early exit of the programme receives, when we've been in this programme only a month, and like a colleague of ours said today, during the discussion in the Governing Council, he said, you know, he has run several marathons, it's like asking yourself, after 1 km, are we going to finish this marathon?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the second question, the haircuts on Greece were mentioned in today's Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because we decided, the Governing Council decided to carefully monitor whether conditions would warrant a change in the current schedule, taking into account the change in environment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we will come back on this issue in due time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first point, there is no change in our reaction function, not at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you meant to say that we are consistent with our previous monetary policy strategy, yes, the answer is yes, we are consistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So why have we felt the need to explain more?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because we are talking about unconventional instruments, so the more we explain, the better these instruments will be understood by you, by the markets, by public opinion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I'll quickly and readily answer the second question immediately, saying that I don't even want to contemplate that, and based on the Greek government leaders' statements, this option is not contemplated by themselves as well, so I'm not ready to discuss any possible situation like that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the waiver, let me say this once again, the ECB lifted the waiver because the conditions for a successful conclusion of the review were not there, and the precise statement that I used at that time and I've used on and on and on, and everybody has used, is that to reinstate the waiver, there must be a credible perspective, a credible perspective for a successful conclusion of the review under the current arrangements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, having said that, the Governing Council will assess the existence of this credible perspective in total independence, and of course we are ready to reinstate the waiver if the conditions are there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the second question, we are certainly aware that a protracted period of time with very low interest rates is potentially conducive to financial stability imbalances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far, we have not seen evidence of any bubble.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are certain conditions that would lead people to think there may be a bubble that we have seen before the crisis started, one of which is a serious, significant increase in leverage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we observed was an increase in debt in the banking sector, and we are not seeing that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not seeing an increase in leverage accompanied by sustained bank credit development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly, and if we were to assess that financial imbalances are forming, the first line of defence of course is the use of macro-prudential instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the extent that these imbalances are somewhat localised, that's the answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the answer is not change your monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The monetary policy stance is determined by our objective to reach price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I would say that there's one word which in a sense puts together these two questions; they're premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To ask about scarcity in the bond market is really premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also impossible to answer what would one do in case something that's not evident at all were to materialise, and it would be very difficult to answer this question now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We would have to see, what sort of scarcity, where, who's actually scarce of these bonds, but so far, frankly, we don't have any evidence that this might happen in the future, but it's always good to ask difficult questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, as I've said many times, the exchange rate is not a policy target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We view the current developments, the current and recent developments of the exchange rate, as the outcome of different monetary policy cycles in different jurisdictions, and the monetary policy cycles in turn depend on the different business cycles in the different jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, just let me add one thing about the exchange rate and its relation with inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not obvious, and that is one of the things that look more and more apparent in the analysis, it's not obvious what is the pass-through between changes in the exchange rate and the inflation rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, we are seeing that previous appreciations of the exchange rate still have an effect on current inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this pass-through will happen, pretty sure, and it is happening actually, so that right now, we are seeing two competing effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The lagged effect of previous appreciations with the incipient effect of the recent deprecations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm saying this because it's something that's not easy to assess, and it's gradual.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is no, we don't feel responsible for that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a mandate, and the only responsibility we feel is if we are not able to comply with our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, let me just read through a few data about inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just also answering previous questions about when would you assess that you are in a certain situation, so that you will change monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, it's very, very early to say anything like that, but also, let me give you an idea of what may come out in a certain amount of time from now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, we're not bound by one specific indicator.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll be using a variety of indicators about inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And second, if history and experience tells us something, it's very unlikely that the Governing Council will choose a route with clear quantitative constraints in its decision-making.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look back, and you look at our forward guidance, how that was different from the forward guidance that was stated in other monetary policy jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This will give you good hints of what may come out; it's going to be mostly a qualitative process and based on several indicators.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we go back and look at these indicators, that's very important, for a reason that I will say in a moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A one-year forward swap rate, one year ahead, the average in 2014 was 0.46 inflation expectation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's now 1.53, and as we move forward, if we go to nine-year ahead, for example, was 1.73 on January 15, now it's 1.87.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The five-year swap rate was 0.57, as an average of 2014.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The longest, to some extent the longest time-defined indicators moved up too, but less dramatically.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is very important, so that's why I spent time in reading these numbers, because that accounted for a significant decrease in real interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You may remember when last year in December, I did mention the fact that in a zero lower-bound situation, where nominal interest rates are at lower bound, what determines real rates are movements in inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In December, they were still trending down, and real rates were going up, so much so that I think they started to parallel between our most recent decisions about lowering nominal interest rates and the decrease in inflation expectations, and I did say that the recent, then recent, changes, decreases in inflation expectations, had actually nullified our monetary policy decisions taken in the previous months of lowering nominal rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we are in a completely opposite trend, and real interest rates actually declined, and that's certainly very supportive of the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why I'm saying that we start seeing a pass-through from our monetary policy decisions to the real economy, through significantly lower real interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question our metrics are essentially the inflation expectations and in the end actual inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so far developments have been on the right side, because as I said before real interest rates declined significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the second question I just take note of what you said but there are procedures for the eligibility to be a member of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are criteria that all countries have to comply with at the time of accession to the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And even recently countries that have entered the euro area had to go through this and comply with these criteria.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think if we are to run the same survey now we would probably find a better number.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's very important to understand that our expansion in monetary policy finds its natural complement in structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some people argue, and you certainly have heard them argue in this way, that accommodative monetary policy removes the incentives for governments to undertake structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary policy actually accompanies -- there is a dividend from a combined expansion of monetary policy and the right structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are good reasons for doing structural reforms without too many questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the main reason really is that we are in an area where potential output is bound to grow modestly given the demographics, the aging population, the decline in the labour force.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time European Commission figures show that there is an average structural unemployment rate in the euro area of 11%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's an average, which means that some countries and we know which, have an unemployment rate of around 20% or even above 20%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And they had this high unemployment rate even before the financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why there is no other way than undertaking the needed structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One reason why they are also important was quoted in the introductory statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to see which structural reforms we talk about because there are reforms like the change in the education system or the judiciary and so on which are completely different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the argument which we hear often is that structural reforms in the long run may produce some positive effect on output growth; in the short run they actually don't.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of the reasons why this may not be entirely correct is that good sound structural reforms actually raise expected permanent income, expected permanent income and therefore have an effect immediately on consumption for firms for households and on investments for firms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's why there shouldn't be any doubt about doing structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well to the second question I really can repeat my answer I gave before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are aware that very low interest rates for a very long time are a fertile terrain for financial stability imbalances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen that in the past and we are aware that this is a risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's why our monitoring of this aspect of our monetary policy is continuous and it's very, very careful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, we don't see at this point in time evidence of systemically large financial stability imbalances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally the first line of defence to that is use all your macro-prudential instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there is a lot of work going on as far as macro-prudential instruments are concerned both in the ECB, in the ESRB, in EBA.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All agencies are actually thinking, and national authorities of course, are thinking about this because as you know, the implementation of these macro-prudential instruments is in great part at national level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, the ECB can top-up on that and coordinate certainly all this, but it's mostly at national level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, first let me say that the revisions to previous forecasts for growth had been very significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first was the ECB revision of course, which raised from 1% for 2015 to 1.5% and for 2016 about the same from 1.5% to 1.9%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All other institutions since then have come out with revisions in the same direction, not of the same amount but in the same direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all institutions now see the prospects for a recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said the downside risks are still there, but they are diminished.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The issue now is to firm up this recovery and create conditions so that it's sustained through time that it's not only cyclical but becomes a structural recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The recovery is certainly due both to our monetary policy and that's because our monetary policy, accommodative monetary policy stance, which has been in place a long time before we actually did QE, is finally finding its route through easier credit conditions and significantly lower real interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, and here it's not clear, which is the channel of causation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly the monetary policy stance helped but there must be other factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Both consumer and business confidence have picked up creating a very positive climate for a continued recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a second aspect in which the monetary, even the recent monetary policy decisions have been important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember when we experienced this dramatic fall in oil prices there were many worries that there may not be all that pass-through into higher spending but actually the opposite could take place having negative second round effects on lower inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that our monetary policy stance avoided that risk, and it eased the pass-through of lower oil prices into higher consumption and in due time higher investment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is also another channel of course, which is the difference in monetary policy cycles between different jurisdictions, which had implications on the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these are the main drivers that one can see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of which is certainly the condition of the capital stock in the euro area where many, many years of low investment both private and public would suggest that the years ahead should see a firming up of investments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is another factor which would suggest that the pressure to de-lever should gradually ease if it's not eased already.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And finally, of course, there are going to be less headwinds coming from fiscal policy consolidation than what was in place a year ago and this because of the progress that many governments have already achieved on that front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, as I said, the current recovery is basically the outcome of two competing factors -- oil prices, actually not competing they are complementing factors -- oil prices and our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is one condition which makes a big difference that was not in place in 2012 when we first started creating conditions for the return of confidence in the financial markets; namely the banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The health check that all banks had to go through last year nowadays ensures that more accommodative monetary policy is being translated into better credit conditions, which is not something we've seen before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember in 2012 many of you were asking me this question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Were we happy after July/August 2012 about the changes in financial markets, the euro the return of confidence in the euro, the dramatic decline in sovereign spreads?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And all this however had a very hard time in being translated into better credit conditions and being translated into better credit standards for firms and households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think one very important reason often neglected is the better health of the banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That this recovery is conditional upon the full implementation of our monetary policy stance, so let's never forget that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, there are risks and I've dwelt on that but if you have any question I'll be glad to take up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the third question I think you give it to yourself I guess.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now to the first point, if I correctly remember our discussion it was not so much about certainty or uncertainty of the recovery after 2016, but it was about the cyclical nature of the recovery as it is today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary policy as such cannot have a long-lasting effect whereby potential output growth increases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why the combination of monetary policy and structural reforms is so important, because what gives the economy the resilience to carry on recovering through time are structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think the discussion was not so much about, certainly oil certainly, but about what the conditions need to be in place after say 2016 maybe in 2017 that would guarantee that the present cyclical recovery becomes a potential output growth recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question, some of your colleagues asked me the same question before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One thing that I hear people say is that our programme has been so effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way there are three moments to measure the effectiveness of our programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One was the expectations -- this thing started being expected way back last year in August --.the announcement, and the implementation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Each one of these three stages produced positive effects on the markets and in due time to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of the considerations that I heard being made quite, I would say, complimentary towards the ECB was that the design of the programme and the determination with which it was applied, implemented, produced some extra positive effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Why do you want me to change this programme now or say that it's going to be changed?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I know too little other than what you said really about this that you called the investigation, so I don't know enough to say what's going to be the consequence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all we certainly need to achieve a situation where the definitions of capital are going to be harmonized.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's one of the important aspects of having a common supervision, one supervisor.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also certainly important and desirable that we have a level playing field in the banking sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that actually holds true for all sectors of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way I've raised them myself in various hearings in Parliament about the desirability of these changes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can't go beyond this to say what is going to happen exactly, what are going to be the measures taken or agreed by the various parties in this dialogue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is one thing one reassuring thing that I assume that all these people who are actually part and parcel of these big decisions are responsible people, so I take for granted that they will not cause a banking crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well it's probably the most difficult question I got today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I can say is that the present situation of the labour market is something that should be overcome, should have been overcome many years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I hear that the level of interest rates could be an incentive or a disincentive for countries governments to change their labour markets, I ask myself, shouldn't the unemployment level be an incentive to change the labour market, especially since these levels are not the output, or not only the output of the financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They've been high, very high for many years before the financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, on top of this in the early years 2000's several countries had passed labour legislation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: With a view to increasing flexibility in the labour market, they passed legislation where the labour conditions of the ones who were already employed wouldn't change at all, but the new entrants would have very flexible terms of employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the outcome of this was a disproportionate fall of flexibility onto the young sector of the working population.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was, as you can imagine, especially unfortunate for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of which was that as soon as the financial crisis struck the first to lose their jobs were the young people, were the youth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's why we still have such high levels of youth unemployment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to eliminate this sort of dual labour market condition.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we have to make sure the flexibility as its needed falls proportionately on all segments of the labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So first restore the conditions whereby people hire, entrepreneurs, companies hire people easily.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Reduce the amount of time, if someone loses a job, reduce the amount of time he or she is unemployed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Change the educational skills, improve the educational skills because very much so today we see that more and more employment is dictated by technological skills and conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Education today is a most important factor for finding a job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from this viewpoint you are a privileged person, you and your classmates of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And especially now, that we've seemed to enter into a period of time where economic conditions are improving.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, the answer is no, because basically, and this also holds for all the other possible questions on this issue, negotiations are proceeding at this point in time, so there is no point in me commenting on different aspects of these negotiations and different proposals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Both the Greek government and the institutions have now sets of proposals that they are confronting with each other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council of the ECB wants Greece to stay in the euro, but there should be a strong agreement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And a strong agreement is one that produces growth, that has social fairness, but that is also fiscally sustainable and addresses the remaining sources or factors of financial instability in the financial sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these will be the components of a strong agreement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first is that we are certainly aware of the prerequisite and the rules that are contained in the Code of Ethics; the ethical code that governs the Executive Board Members' appearances in different sites, on different occasions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They basically amount to saying that we should avoid any situation of conflict of interests and we should not divulge non-public information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The text of the speech was meant to go live immediately, and instead went live the morning after.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is leading us now to review our rules, to revisit our rules, to make them more explicit, and we'll shortly come out with a new set of rules as far as speaking engagements are concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, on the second question, you know what the condition should be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There should be a credible perspective for a successful conclusion of the current review, which would imply a disbursement by the member countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That would be the condition for the Governing Council to consider, because, in any event, there is no automaticity for considering a lifting of the T-bills' thresholds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The current downgraded perspectives, growth perspectives, of the Greek economy should be taken into account in determining what the appropriate budget surplus figures should be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, you quite rightly pointed out there is a difference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me say, the recovery is on track, exactly according to our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, we had expected stronger figures, stronger than our projections originally, and at some point, some indicators were showing this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There has been some loss of momentum, modest I would say, mostly due to a weakening of the economies outside the euro area, emerging markets mostly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, all survey indicators and other data show that domestic demand in the euro area remains strong, so we just wanted to point out this slight loss of momentum coming from global trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, I don't want to comment on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have to examine exactly what the conditions are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The option of bundling the payments has been used by one country in the 1970s, if I'm not mistaken, and we'll see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Yes indeed, there was some reversal generally in financing conditions recently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There have been many explanations that have been given, one of which you hinted at, namely that there is an improvement, in the perspectives of growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A third explanation is actually a bunch of technical conditions present in the markets like, and here I'm going through them quickly, first, there have been one-directional investments into long-term maturities, and the turnaround has been quite abrupt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, there was strong supply pressure, in the sense that issuance had been quite significant, by various governments in the meantime.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
