text: Third is that when shorter-dated German Bunds became eligible, previously they had not been, because of their negative yields, there was less need to buy longer-dated bonds, and that produced a steepening of the curve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fourth technical condition is simply that volatility by itself generated further volatility and further selling, and a fifth is poor market liquidity because of the absence of certain significant investors during this period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, it's very difficult to distinguish between these three sets of factors, sets of conditions, so we won't speculate exactly on what explanation is the most likely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly one lesson is that we should get used to periods of higher volatility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At very low levels of interest rates, asset prices tend to show higher volatility, and in terms of the impact that this might have on our monetary policy stance, the Governing Council was unanimous in its assessment that we should look through these developments and maintain a steady monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to both questions is no and nothing, but let me also qualify this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, as I've said many times, we have a mandate, which is maintaining price stability based on the definition that we've discussed several times, and we plan to keep our course steady and unchanged, and if anything, if necessary, we'll actually add to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A long period, a protracted period of very low interest rates, causes a series of problems.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, it may increase the financial stability risk, but also it causes problems for insurance companies and for other important financial market actors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is this a good reason to change our monetary policy?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we were to undertake the wrong monetary policy to address the problems of these specific sectors, we actually would do them a disservice.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'd create in the end a more difficult situation for everybody.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is that when we see a financial stability risk, this should be addressed by the proper instruments, which are macroprudential instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, the insurance companies try to respond to this situation in a variety of ways, which I don't want to discuss, because some of them have to do with their business models, but certainly it's quite clear that certain regulatory provisions make their task of diversifying their investments into higher yield and potentially more liquid investments more difficult.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can't give you an update, a real-time report, on how the negotiations are going.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also because I'm here in Frankfurt, and the negotiations are not taking place here; but also because they are actually in a state of flux.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I've said before, there is a general will and strong determination that in the end, an agreement will be found This agreement should be a strong agreement, and the components that I've listed before are the ones towards which, certainly the ECB is working, but I can say the same as far as the European Commission and the IMF are concerned, namely strong growth, social fairness, fiscal stability and addressing the financial stability concerns.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's one mandate, formulated as pursuing price stability, which the Governing Council, in 2003 clarified that, in the pursuit of price stability, it aims at a rate of inflation of below, but close to, 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The monetary policy addresses the cyclical component of the weakness in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So for example, now our monetary policy, in pursuing price stability, addresses also the cyclical component of the slack we have in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it does good to both things, price stability and unemployment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we should not forget that the structural component of our unemployment is high, and was high even before the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I'm not mistaken, it was on the border of 9%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary policy cannot address the structural component of the weakness in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It cannot address the reasons why potential growth is low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the first question is, no we have not been surprised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Inflation came out higher than market expectations but not higher than our expectations, and this in a sense has a quite important consequence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It actually strengthened the Governing Council in its decisions, basically in its determination and its conviction that it has taken the right decision with QE, with the size and the design of QE, but not only QE, but also the monetary policy measures that had been taken previously, in the previous months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second part of your question is really how do we assess whether we have reached our objective of inflation or not, and I've said several times that we're not going to be happy with a single data point on inflation, but we'll have to look through the medium term and be convinced that the objective has been reached in a sustained fashion through time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other point, it's quite a complicated question to answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of these programmes have been implemented; some other parts have not been implemented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Why hasn't the euro area, or more generally, Europe, been able to come up with a situation which could be considered as, I would say as normal, in this situation, as an ordinary situation?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, as I said, programmes have been designed, have been agreed, and have been implemented only partly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mean, exit strategies are really a high-class problem, and we're really far from that, so we're not discussing anything about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm just wondering what makes you think and say that we are there in terms of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll have to see again at the next meeting how things are, what is the state of negotiations, what is the state of markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, how the evolution, the current evolution, affects the quality of the Greek debt, and that's the key decision we have to take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We assess that our present monetary policy stance is adequate to reach our objectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact, the reaching of the objectives in terms of inflation and growth is predicated, is conditional, on the full implementation of the monetary policy stance as it has been designed, as it has been announced, as it has been implemented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I said before is that, if need be, if there were other factors which would, for example, create an unwanted tightening of monetary policy or, when we discuss growth, we said there were downside risks to growth and price stability, then we will have to review and reconsider the size, the timing, the design of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's only to say that if needed we will add to that, but so far we frankly see no reason to do that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, the answer is at the present time - by the way we are fully aware, as I said before, that low interest rates for a protracted period of time tend to generate financial stability risk - we monitor quite closely all these developments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we don't see, so far, the emergence of these risks, even in one of the sectors that is most often quoted, like the housing market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see selected local situations where one could actually think that price movements are wide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there isn't any real financial stability risk that we can see in that market or elsewhere.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I should also add leverage, private sector leverage, because what you look at is lots of things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You don't look only at price increases but you also want to see whether these increases in prices have been accompanied by increase in leverage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we don't see that, at least in bank leverage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But having said that, I repeat what I said before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there were to be financial stability risks in the stock market, for example, they would have to be addressed by the proper instruments, which is not a change in our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: It would be difficult for me to actually identify a set of pension funds in a specific country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is quite clear, and I had that remark in mind for insurance companies, is that certain parts of the regulatory framework make diversification more difficult.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I make an example - it's not the only example by the way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the treatment that securitisation receives in the present regulatory framework makes it difficult for companies to invest in assets that are potentially illiquid and make them liquid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Securitisation is important to liquefy assets that are otherwise illiquid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, yes, we see the Greek economy as a viable economy provided, like any other economy, the right policies are being undertaken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Things that are unsustainable in a certain situation, because the policies that are being undertaken are wrong, could become sustainable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And economies that are not viable under a certain set of policies could become viable under a different set.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the judgment is certainly the economy is viable, but it has to have the right set of policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, policies that certainly favour equity but also promote growth, or, if you want, that favour growth but also promote equity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said before, growth with social fairness and fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, let me only say that we are revisiting all our rules including this change that we have announced last week.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we'll discuss when our rules have been published, then we'll discuss them again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I don't want to speculate on the likelihood of these events.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do assess how the developments in the markets affect the quality of our collateral, namely the quality of the Greek government bonds that have been posted as collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So were the conditions to change, we would certainly go through a series of things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We are a rule-based institution, and we follow, in this sense, the rules exactly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know the rules, for example, forbid monetary financing and our ELA is devised and designed to supply credit to the private sector, not to finance the government.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, the rules of collateral for ELA are different from the rules of collateral for the monetary policy instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these rules are being applied and they are being regularly reassessed as developments in the financial markets unfold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the more general issue is really, I think, we should focus now at this contingency in finding a strong agreement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all our energies should now be focused on finding an agreement that is strong, along the lines that I've illustrated before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What the Greek leaders have said, and I'm taking them at their word, is that they, the bonds, will be timely and fully paid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer is no, we are not joining that meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: People in the world generally don't comment on pronouncements by the judiciary or by courts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if we don't comment on pronouncements, you can imagine how difficult it is to form an expectation on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, we do have the opinion of the General Rapporteur, and that is the only element upon which one can form an expectation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that wouldn't suggest a redesign of the OMT programme, although it has other interesting suggestions for other functions that the ECB is currently performing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Simply said, we are not either interfering or in any way taking a stance with respect to the current negotiations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But you have to understand that there are two different sets of rules: one is for collateral posted against monetary policy instruments, and the other one is the collateral posted against ELA.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You should remember that ELA is given by the national central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from this viewpoint the set of rules is different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This difference is important, so much so, that the majority required to change Governing Council decisions about ELA is two-thirds, because when the ECB was created, the idea was that national central banks ought to retain a certain margin of discretion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we currently discuss and we assess and see whether financial market developments within that specific and different set of rules warrant a change in the collateral haircut.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: There are several main lessons that one can take, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the first that comes to mind is that...well let me step back.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The lessons that one draws from the crisis depend on what one views as the main factors, the main reasons for a crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One view is that the crisis originated in jurisdictions other than the European one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so the issue is what was the main reason for the crisis in that jurisdiction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And here there are a variety of explanations, one of which is the too expansionary monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But another which has, in our view, and I think in most members' of the Governing Council's view, more weight, is the fact that financial regulation in that jurisdiction was made much weaker in the early 2000's, basically lowering levels on leverage, lowering or cancelling indebtedness levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sub-prime crisis is mostly due to lack of supervision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So one lesson we learned is that we made our financial system stronger.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we increased more generally the resilience of the financial services industry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't know where the next crisis will come from, but at least we ought to be reasonably confident that we've done everything we could to make our financial services industry more robust, stronger and more resilient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the path is: this year we foresee inflation staying low in the months ahead and to rise towards the end of the year and further in 2016 reaching 1.5%, mostly because of base effects, namely oil prices should not continue to decline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so if you compare the latest data of the last part of last year with the data that we will have at the end of this year, under the assumption that we would have no further declines, you have a base effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also there are other forces that will drive the inflation rate back to the objective, one of which is obviously the closing of the output gap: So the increase in domestic demand, the closing in the output gap and some sort of higher inflation rate domestically generated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Strong means that it should be strong both in design and implementation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It should have the reforms that promote growth and have social fairness, and at the same time produce a macroeconomic framework that is fiscally sustainable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of the things that have been discussed in the course of the previous months are clearly fiscally unsustainable, so that is one part of the strength.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of these reforms ought to be what is called in the negotiating language prior action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A strong programme has prior action, meaning certain things are done soon rather than late.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nobody, neither the institutions nor the Eurogroup members would conceive of a programme, would define a strong programme that's not financed adequately.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The decision to raise ELA today is symmetrical to the one we took a few days ago to freeze it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, ELA goes to solvent banks with adequate collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: After the breakdown of negotiations and the likely default to the IMF, the ECB decided to freeze ELA at that level, applying what we call the proportionality criteria.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were some who were actually calling for a cut to zero, which would have caused an immediate collapse of the banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council decided to keep ELA at that level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had a series of news, with the approval of the bridge financing package, with the various votes in various parliaments - to begin with, in the Greek Parliament - which have restored the conditions for a raise in ELA.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second point is about the Grexit, whether this should be pronounced or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me tell you what I said in the course of the summit meetings that we had in Brussels last weekend.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Especially it was addressed to several observers, policy-makers, public opinion scholars who have suggested that we should have cut ELA to Greece a long time ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said basically that it's not up to the ECB to decide who's a member, who's not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB has acted within its mandate and will continue to do so, under the assumption that Greece will remain a member of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether this assumption proves right is entirely within the responsibility both of the Greek Government and of the Member States here represented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the ECB continues to act on the assumption that Greece is, it is of course, and will remain, a member of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: To your first question I should read out the Eurogroup statement on Greece that just came out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "The Eurogroup welcomes the adoption by the Greek Parliament of all the commitments specified in the Euro Summit statement of 12 July.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the basis of a positive assessment by the institutions, which concluded that the authorities have implemented the first set of four measures in a timely and overall satisfactory manner and which confirmed that the Euro Summit statement has been included in the preamble to the implementing law adopted by the Greek parliament, we reached today a decision to grant in principle a three-year ESM stability support to Greece, subject to the completion of relevant national procedures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Upon the completion of the relevant national procedures and the formal decision by the ESM Board of Governors expected by the end of this week, the institutions would be entrusted with the task of swiftly negotiating an MoU detailing the policy conditionality attached to the financial assistance facility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Eurogroup calls on the Greek authorities to swiftly adopt the second set of measures by 22 July as foreseen in the Euro Summit statement, and update the legislation related to the first set of measures consistent with the recommendations made by the institutions in their compliance report."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So several positive things have happened that would justify the increase in ELA that we approved today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We substantially accommodated the request put forward by the Bank of Greece, recalibrated over one week.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the increase would be €900 million over one week.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To your second point, let me say that the liquidity provision, according to our rules, was never meant to be unlimited and unconditional.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And let me preface this by saying that we take these sorts of criticisms very, very seriously.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to underplay the difficulty that the ECB and the Governing Council of the ECB had in the last few weeks about having to take decisions between making sure the payment system continued to work, liquidity provision, monetary policy and not to amass excessive risk for the euro system all at the same time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the payment system that some people have referred to doesn't have to do with liquidity provisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is an article in the Treaty that says that basically the ECB has the responsibility to promote the smooth functioning of the payment system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this has to do with the functioning of TARGET2, the distribution of notes, coins.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So not with the provision of liquidity, which actually is regulated by a different provision, in Article 18.1 in the ECB Statute: "In order to achieve the objectives of the ESCB, the ECB and the national central banks may conduct credit operations with credit institutions and other market participants, with lending based on adequate collateral."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But our operations were not monetary policy operations, but ELA operations, and so they are regulated by a separate agreement, which makes explicit reference to the necessity to have sufficient collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, all in all, liquidity provision has never been unconditional and unlimited.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But is it true that we did not provide enough liquidity to Greece all throughout this time?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the month with the highest deposit outflow was January 2015.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The month with the second highest deposit outflow was last month, June 2015, again associated with increased political uncertainty related to the breakdown of the negotiations and the announcement of the referendum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The increase in Eurosystem lending to the Greek banking sector was €10.3 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, as I said several times, ELA has increased from zero to almost €90 billion, and now the Eurosystem has a total exposure to Greece of about €130 billion, which makes the Eurosystem the largest depositor in Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you take the total private sector deposits in Greece, they are €120 billion, while the Eurosystem exposure to Greece now is, as I said, about €130 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I find these observations that there wasn't enough liquidity assistance, or that actually there was a bank run that was caused by the ECB, quite unwarranted, and certainly unfounded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Oh, incidentally, each time we announced an ELA operation we also said - and I think I said it explicitly in April - "and emergency lending assistance will continue, liquidity assistance will continue."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So even communication-wise, there was always quite an open stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, when the solvency and the collateral adequacy and quality prospects deteriorated, we had to calibrate the provision of liquidity according to these developments, and that's how it went, for the reasons that I mentioned before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we did it, however, as I said, always acting on the assumption that Greece will be a member of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is what makes us different from the ones who said, 'You should have cut ELA a long time ago.'

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They wanted us not to respect our mandate, deciding who should be a member of the euro area and who should not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: In response to the first question, I frankly hesitate in commenting on the programme as such.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me say one thing: for, I believe, the first time, the text that circulated at the level of heads of state was not generic, was quite specific.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It contained an impressive list of policy measures, prior actions and structural reforms, for which the Greek Parliament was asked either to take a vote on or to endorse these measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Without commenting specifically on that, let me say that the overall purpose of that document is to ensure that Greece will become a thriving economy in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Quite considerable space in that document was given to structural reforms, so it was not the usual budget-based document only.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second thing is something that I did say many times: the programme had to be a strong programme, which promotes growth, which ensures social fairness, which is also fiscally sustainable, and which addresses the financial stability problems.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I believe that by and large that programme has these features.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And finally, there is another issue that has been widely discussed: is debt relief necessary?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's uncontroversial that debt relief is necessary, and I think that nobody has ever disputed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The issue is: what is the best form of debt relief within our framework, within our legal, institutional framework?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we should focus on this point in the coming weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is about whether the simple fact of having discussed a possibility would weaken the union: well, I mean, if you phrase it this way you can see that that is not an issue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were discussions, and I think discussions by themselves don't necessarily weaken things - but they have shown, again, something that I've said many times: that this union is imperfect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And being imperfect, is fragile, is vulnerable, and doesn't deliver all the benefits that it could if it were to be completed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the future now should see decisive steps on further integration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, today we have accommodated the Bank of Greece's request, completely and fully, though scaled to one week.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is understandable because we want to see how the situation will evolve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In so doing, we have accepted the assessment of the Bank of Greece in terms of the immediate needs of liquidity that the Greek economy has.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, if things continue to proceed in a positive way, as they have done in the last two days, we will have a phase during which the Bank of Greece and the ECB, which are working very actively in monitoring the situation, will look at exactly the needs of the Greek economy: how can they be gradually satisfied?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What are the general conditions so as to make sure that we are always there, ready to provide the Greek economy with the needed liquidity, and at the same time we don't risk a bank run again?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the meantime, all these developments are improving the quality of collateral that the Greek banks can post.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because, you see, each time we have an improvement in the quality of the Greek government paper, we have an improvement in the quality of the collateral of the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And not only in that, because as you know, much of the equity, probably more than 50% of the equity of the Greek banks - or the largest Greek banks, at least - is formed by credits to the state.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the quality of these credits improves or worsens according to the overall developments and the quality of the policy dialogue between the Greek Government and the euro area Member States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point: there are two assessments which are being given of the solvency of the bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point-in-time assessment which is given by supervisor looks at the Common Equity Tier 1 at 4.5%, the total capital ratio at 8%, and the Tier 1 capital ratio at 6%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you take these numbers, Greek banks are solvent, and that's what the Chair of the Supervisory Board has said several times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, if you look at it prospectively, and just on the basis of what I said about the enormous influence that the quality of the government paper has on the solvency of the banks, well, you question their solvency in prospective terms because you look at how things go, how the policy dialogue develops, and therefore how the quality of the government paper changes according to these developments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's on the basis of this prospective assessment that looks at the quality of the government paper, but also at the quality of the overall banks' balance sheets after such a protracted recession, and therefore with a foreseeable increase in non-performing loans: it's on the basis of these two considerations - by and large; also others, but these are the two most important - that an overall envelope of €25 billion was earmarked, out of a programme of between €82 billion and €86 billion, was earmarked for the Greek banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: In a sense what I said before could be used in several ways: I'm not going to comment on politicians' statements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And our mandate is to act based on the assumption that Greece is, of course, and will be a member of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the answer to the first point: it's hard to predict.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are all aware it's clearly in the interest of the Greek economy to have these capital controls last as little as possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, the responsibility to lift capital controls, as well as to impose them, is with the Greek government.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is something that the Greek government has to decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have to be doing this in a way that we don't run the opposite risk which we were about to run before the imposition of capital controls, namely a bank run, which would leave all the depositors being, basically, hit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Capital controls have protected the depositors - which, by the way, to a great extent are now small depositors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The awareness that capital controls are hampering the recovery of the Greek economy is there, and the idea is to move as fast as we can, but also with a due degree of caution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on ELA, you're absolutely right: that was the usual - that was the past, in fact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the past, there was a certain reticence to publish the numbers of ELA, because the whole ELA concept was born to address liquidity shortages of individual banks that are solvent and have collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the situation that was addressed by the old ELA agreement was one where a bank which was solvent and with adequate collateral, in spite of this was experiencing a liquidity shortage of some kind, and would be protected by this facility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, it was quite understandable if you had that situation, and the amounts and the modalities of ELA were to be made public, this - it was thought, at least - could worsen the situation of that bank at that time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now here we are facing a completely different set-up where we are not talking about individual banks, but we are talking about countries; banking systems.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we're talking about a systemic problem, not any longer about an individual bank, an individual institution short of collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so we are in fact revising our communication about ELA, because there's absolutely no reason to keep things secret now, when we're addressing a massive systemic problem, a macroeconomic problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, on the first, about 20 July repayment, all my evidence and information leads me to say that we will be repaid, as well as the IMF, so that is off the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to speculate what are the conditions whereby countries would not receive the assistance of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are three documents that you should look at: one is the Treaty, another one is the ECB Statute, and the third is the ELA agreement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All of them make the point of solvency and availability of adequate collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then, as you've just seen in the case of Greece, the assessment of these two features is not at all simple, is not at all one-dimensional.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's point-in-time, it's dynamic, it depends on the underlying issuer of this collateral; what is the credit-worthiness of the underlying issuer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's very difficult to think about a system where you simply push a button and you decide what to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think by and large the Governing Council has shown that it is a rule-based decision-making body, even in the very difficult circumstances that have characterised our work in the last few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second point is whether we respect the decision of the politicians.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, if you phrase it this way it's hard to answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I would phrase it differently: do we respect the Treaty, as it is today, as it may become tomorrow?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had raised it before and we took no decision today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the point of further integration, well, you know, it's not so much what matters is my disappointment or not; clearly there was such a complex climate focused on what was happening in Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My understanding is the European Council is going to discuss this report at the next meeting, I believe, or the meeting after that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is important is that - I was answering before with the same words - what this experience shows is that we have to act, and we can act in different ways.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Five Presidents' report is a rather broad roadmap, but it sends three messages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is to say, establish a deposit insurance guarantee scheme and the Single Resolution Fund.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again, the modalities of this oscillate - and I don't want to get into too much detail -between a purely private-sector financed system and a purely mutualised, public-sector financed system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we'll have to decide there, but the important thing is to move now on that front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second area of action is what the European Commission has launched, namely the creation of a Capital Markets Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's very important for an area that doesn't share a common budget, or a federal budget, because a Capital Markets Union would be an extraordinary assistance in sharing risks across the Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is actually a very ambitious and complex, and very likely long undertaking, because it entails changes in legislation in several parts of the area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Mostly that, legislation that's been with national countries for ages, like bankruptcy legislation and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then the third area is, what are member countries going to do in a certain number of years as far as fiscal union, economic union and political union are concerned?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the report doesn't tell what countries should do in this area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It only urges member countries to reflect on what sort of a roadmap they want to design for themselves in these areas.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, on the first point, it's actually - technically I believe the question about whether it was unanimous or not is not well posed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The decision here is not to object to the request of the Bank of Greece, and what you need in order to object is a two-thirds majority.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So by definition, you needn't have unanimity on these decisions, because it's not really what's required.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the other thing is about what makes us confident.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that there is a financing concept that's been elaborated and it's on its way to be approved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's been elaborated by the European Commission, which I want to thank for their responsiveness, for the designs capacity, and I want to thank also all the members of the European Union that have made this possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No matter who you talk to, there are, I would say, questions about the implementation, will and capacity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so that's what I said: it will be really in the Greek Government's capacity to respond with policy decisions, with actions, that will dispel these doubts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to use other words that have been used recently, but that's certainly an issue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me ask you, would you think it is legitimate for the ECB to take its decisions based on doubts about a government's capacity to implement the measures?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The next point is about the expanding list of agencies: frankly, we have received requests.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This list is not cast in stone, as you've seen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We keep on adding members - the requirement of this is that basically they are public-sector entities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They issue bonds that have a certain rating, and therefore they are eligible for QE purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We certainly don't want to have private-sector entities, because then it would be a different programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Are you sure that sentence wasn't in a previous statement?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here we have the memory of the institution that says it was two statements ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: [2]So there isn't any specific policy decision behind having the sentence now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly we discussed it in the last two meetings, there has been a considerable increase in volatility, which has led to a rise in interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This rise in interest rates could be explained in a variety of ways, and I think we went through this last time: higher expectations of inflation, higher expected growth, or simply higher term premium.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not clear which of these explanations seems to be more robust.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Probably the higher term premium is one that receives attention.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But having said that, we don't see this as having changed the medium-term outlook for price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this sentence basically says what I've said all throughout, that if we were to see an unwarranted tightening of monetary policy, which could lead to a change in the medium-term outlook for price stability, then we would seriously think, and we have instruments to address this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then on Greece and QE: for being eligible for QE the issuer has to issue instruments that are eligible for monetary policy operations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is an issue of going back to a rating which would make Greek bonds, eligible for monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second point is the limit on how much of each country's bonds can be bought by the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As some SMP holdings will be repaid on 20 July and afterwards Greece would comply with this limit and there would be some room for doing QE.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then there is another requirement - by the way, someone hinted or suggested that all these requirements were devised for Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the third requirement is, we can't buy bonds during a review period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So much so that we're now doing QE for Cyprus.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that's more or less the response, and it describes in a sense the roadmap that we and Greece plan to follow to make Greece eligible for QE.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: The point is the following: when a country has a rating which is below the investment grade which is the minimum, then to access monetary policy operations, it has to have a waiver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the waiver is granted if there are two conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first condition is that the country must be under a programme with the EU and IMF; and second, we have to assess that there is credible compliance with such a programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's what we did on 4 February this year, when in spite of the fact that Greece was formally still under the second programme, the Governing Council assessed that there was no credible compliance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the Governing Council will have to assess, after there is a programme, at a certain moment, that there is a credible compliance with the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That may come at the end of the first review, because that would be clear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council could nevertheless decide even before that if there was credible implementation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's at the discretion of the Governing Council either to wait for the review or to do it slightly before, if indeed, there is good implementation of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these two conditions are to be fulfilled before the waiver can be reinstated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: So it says here, on the basis of and following the implementation of the steps and measures outlined in the Euro Summit statement of 12 July 2015, Greece is expected to soon enter into a three-year ESM programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Assuming that it is decided that the implementation of the referred steps and measures would be sufficient, a two-month window for PSPP (QE) purchases of Greek government bonds would open after the ESM board of governors have officially approved the first disbursement attached to the approval of the MoU.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The purchase window would be suspended upon the beginning of the first review or after two months, the earliest date.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it was not meant to be complicated for Greece only.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, it's quite clear that a drop in oil price has an effect on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the issue is whether there are going to be stable second-round effects on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we do believe that our monetary policy decisions have avoided the second-round effects of a drop in oil price in January, and will continue to do so now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So our accommodative monetary policy will avoid this risk of stably lower inflation in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point, I'm sorry, I have to contradict you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, there should be frontloading because usually people work less in August, and so there is less of a market then.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And frankly, I can't see why there should be such a drama.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's why Mr Cœuré suggested - said, actually - that there should be frontloading.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was by €3 billion in May and €3 billion in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so you can kind of figure out what's going to happen in August.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: [1]This answer has been edited to clear up confusion on a double negative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: [2]It was included in the Introductory Statement at the hearing of the European Parliament's Economic and Monetary Affairs Committee, Brussels, 15 June 2015.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We may see negative numbers of inflation in the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council tends to think that these are transitory effects, mostly due to oil price effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, as I said before, we will closely monitor all incoming information, and the Governing Council wanted to emphasise in the discussion we had today its willingness to act, its readiness to act, and its capacity to act, its ability to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There aren't special limits to the possibilities that the ECB has in gearing up monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in a sense, the decision we've taken today, in changing one of the parameters to ensure the smooth and full implementation of the programme, is exactly a sign.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me just, perhaps repeat, perhaps say it differently: I started saying that the economic recovery is expected to continue, but at a somewhat slower pace, reflecting the slowdown in emerging market economies, primarily.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said it's still premature to conclude whether these developments could have a lasting impact on output and inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, downside risks have increased and emerging market economies' challenges are unlikely to be quickly reversed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me add that the cut-off date of these projections was August 12, so the events that took place since then are a downside risk to the projections themselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Furthermore, financing conditions, especially in the last two weeks and even before, have tightened.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So lower commodity prices, a stronger euro, a somewhat lower growth, have increased the risk to a sustainable path of inflation towards 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I also said, on the other hand, that monetary conditions remain supportive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the discussion today basically converged on an assessment that the downside risks to output and inflation have increased; that we'll still monitor the risks to the outlook; and that the Governing Council emphasised, as I said a moment ago, the willingness and ability to act if warranted, by using all the instruments available within its mandate, and in particular regarding the asset purchase programme that provides by itself sufficient flexibility as far as the horizon, the size, and the parameters, as we've seen today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've said several times that the exchange rate is very important for growth, for price stability, and I've said it today as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've also said that it's not a policy target, but it's rather the effect of divergent recovery paths across the major jurisdictions; and it's the effect of divergent monetary policies across the major jurisdictions; and it's also the effect, of course, of what the market expectations are about future growth rates, future monetary policies, future interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, all countries in the G20 have several times reaffirmed their commitment to the exchange rate policies, to these policies not being used in a competitive fashion, and you know the statement of the G20.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So when we describe a situation where the exchange rate has produced certain effects, we want to give a description of what's happened.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the inflation rate, your second question, this is an increasing ­- we shouldn't forget that 10, maybe 12, 13 years ago, a quite similar discussion was taking place, whether we should look at perhaps core inflation, perhaps headline inflation, and we decided to look at headline inflation as our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Which doesn't mean that we are excluding all other definitions of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact in our analysis, both economic and monetary analysis, we use both concepts, but our mandate is defined in terms of headline inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You also said whether this, the 2% as an objective, is still reasonable or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We haven't discussed that, and in a sense it's kind of - it would test, I think, our credibility if we were to change target when it's taking more effort to achieve that target, so there hasn't been any discussion about changing target of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Yes, it's true, the ECB insisted to exclude any bail-in of depositors for the Greek banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB deemed any such measure to be counterproductive for the economic recovery and harmful for the Greek economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It would have hit not only several thousand savers, but especially also SMEs and corporations and their deposits, and the ECB viewpoint was accepted by the Eurogroup.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Similar considerations were deemed not to be applicable to senior bondholders.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the measure [depositor bail-in] is concerned, it's been excluded and will stay excluded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, for reinstating a waiver, the country has to be in a programme for financial assistance, has to comply with it, and so has to show strong ownership and consistent and significant implementation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be some milestones that will be judged and assessed in the weeks ahead and based on that assessment, the Governing Council will take a decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, once a waiver is in place, is this enough to start purchasing bonds?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is, as you know, the bond purchases cannot take place while a review is ongoing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, there are, as we've seen today moving from 25% to 33%, issue and issuers' limits that have to be respected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And finally, there has to be a debt sustainability analysis by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the ELA, you've seen that now we have open communication about ELA, and so the numbers were not discovered by your investigative capacities, but they were normally published.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so we've just one word about the terms about our ELA communication as far as the future is concerned: the Governing Council agreed in principle that in future a national central bank could, together with a request for non-objection regarding ELA, seek approval from the Governing Council to communicate related elements, including the outcome of ELA, if it sees a benefit in doing so from a financial stability perspective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, this would apply in particular if ELA addressed systemic issues, so that's what I was saying last time: if ELA is extended to a large part of a banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the details of this principle will be discussed further in the Governing Council in due course, but basically the national central bank that asks for the non-objection by the Governing Council of the ELA will communicate the decision based on the communication that's basically agreed with the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this mostly, in particular, will apply for systemic issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Christine was saying that actually, even in this case, the ELA number was gathered by you thanks to your investigative capacities because it came out before we could announce it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Lower oil prices may be lower because of demand and/or because of supply effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this present situation it's lower because of supply effects and because demand from China and possibly other emerging market economies is lower.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If it's because of supply effects, the outcome, the consequences of a lower price of oil are positive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would say unambiguously positive, if there are no second-round effects, which can come from financial stability considerations, or second-round effects that simply these lower oil prices are being transmitted into a lower inflation rate for non-energy components.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, when oil prices are lower because of demand effects, then we have to consider also the negative impact that lower growth in emerging market economies might have on the growth of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question: as I think I said in the introductory statement, a review after six months was scheduled, and we found out that the ECB could actually buy more than the 25% limit in some cases where there would be no blocking minority by the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why in those cases the limit was pushed from 25 to 33%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was meant to ensure a smooth carrying on of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in this sense, it shows the readiness of the Governing Council to basically use the flexibility of the programme so as to make sure the programme will carry out in a smooth way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So also it is a sign that technical aspects will not stop the full implementation, and the full commitment of the ECB to the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Not really, because we don't see at this point in time, concerns coming from that decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said we will look at it issue by issue and transaction by transaction and consider that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I would say that our accommodative monetary policy is being passed through to the rest of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I went through the various indicators of the monetary conditions: not only robust growth in M1, significant growth in M3, but also credit flows are now picking up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the interesting thing is that credit is also improving considerably in some of the stressed countries, like Spain and Italy, but certainly in France as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More particularly what we have is a composed lending indicator cost: it went down by 74 basis points since the announcement of the credit easing measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have a reduction in dispersion of credit flows, and also a reduction in spreads in lending costs and a reduction in spreads in lending costs to SMEs vis-à-vis other kinds of companies, large companies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, we have the rest of the world, and we have these effects that we've observed over the last few weeks - perhaps more than a few weeks; especially in the last few weeks - so we'll have to see whether these effects are transitory or are permanent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether what happened is worsening our medium-term outlook or is just a transitory effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then we'll decide whether to do more or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: What happened in the last few weeks is basically twofold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first is that we had a worsening of the situation in several emerging market economies, and it's unlikely that these challenges are going to be quickly reversed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And second, we had a tightening of financing conditions across the board, especially in the last two weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You should consider these projections assume certain stock prices, certain exchange rates, certain interest rates, which are not the stock prices, the exchange rates and the interest rates that prevail over a 10 days' average until today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So basically, much of what I've been saying is that we'll have to see whether this is actually short-term volatility or is permanent volatility, in which case you would observe an increase in risk premia.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at, for example, inflation expectations, inflation expectations have been pretty volatile.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is, as I said, the loss of growth momentum in emerging market economies; the movements in the oil prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There could also be another reason: that simply risk premium may have gone up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we'll have to assess and look through all these several factors before we can decide whether the medium-term outlook has worsened.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other question, I think that the only answer there is that really any European should be horrified by the tragic loss of life happening on our doorstep.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB simply doesn't have any democratic mandate to act in this sphere, so it's a question for our elected leaders, but this certainly shouldn't hamper our most heartfelt participation to what is happening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are designing our monetary policy on the basis of that measure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, our mandate is defined in terms of price stability: are we ignoring growth?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in the same way we are not ignoring core inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is really the causes now mainly lie with the oil price changes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we are to ask what is the main source of the revised projections, I would say the main source is the change in the oil price.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To a lesser extent it's the slower closing of the output gap, but it's to a much lesser extent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We didn't discuss the issuer limit, and our decision to change the issue limit is simply to ensure the smooth implementation of the current programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time it clearly is a sign of the readiness of the Governing Council to adapt the parameters of the programme to the situation, so as to ensure the full implementation of the programme, because we shouldn't ever forget that the inflation path that is projected to reach 1.7%, if I'm not mistaken, now after the revision, in 2017, and the growth projections, are both predicated, conditional upon the full implementation of that programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As a matter of fact, we do expect to have that, to have much more visibility than we have today, in the coming days at the G20 in Ankara.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is going to be one of the major themes of the meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, we took note of the Chinese decision, Chinese government decision, as far as the exchange rate is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: China reaffirmed several times the commitment she undertook in the G20, as far as the exchange rate is concerned, the commitment that I've said before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And at the same time certainly the Chinese government will have to continue implementing reforms so as to ensure the convertibility of the currency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually, the answer to your second question was not discussed today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, you're absolutely right: that's what I said in June, and the reference was to short-term volatility periods.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we've seen in the last few weeks, and months, actually, was basically two factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One was the weakening of the major emerging market economies; and second, we've seen an induced volatility due to this effect and to the sudden changes in the oil prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether this is short-term or long-term is what I was saying before, we'll have to assess.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And of recent, we've seen obviously some considerable tightening of financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Second question answer: no, there wasn't any discussion about changes in the size of the programme or pace.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other question, we never really comment on other jurisdictions' policies, but if this is necessary to achieve the inflation objectives and more generally, more broadly, the objectives of the Federal Reserve's monetary policy, this is a plus for the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from this viewpoint we can only wish that all jurisdictions achieve their objectives in monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just going back also to - well, it's partly related to that; going back to the previous question as well: you see, the difference in June is that in June there was no need to revise downward our projections at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Yes, you are right, I several times have commented on the imperfect nature of our integration at the present time, and how this imperfection is a source of fragility for the monetary union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are several reasons, of course: these are countries that are different nation states; they have been different for many, many years; and they have fought against each other, for centuries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the point is that all these countries, in the aftermath of the Second World War, acknowledged that European integration was not only an economic project but primarily a political project aimed at achieving permanent peace in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm quite confident that this absolute certainty still is with all Europeans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And of course the integration process is a very complicated and complex process that involves several dimensions, so it can go faster at times; at other times it can go slower.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But recently for example we had the Five Presidents' report, which was designing a path towards greater integration, and we've seen several episodes where you could see, you could be actually quite optimistic, that the process is moving forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it moves forward, like in many other situations, it moves forward by coping with challenges, and winning over them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the ECB - now, of course, I'm a biased observer here - but you would judge that the integration of monetary policies has been pretty successful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because we moved from a rules-based system that we had in the '80s and the '90s to an institution-based system where you have co-decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Co-decision in our sense, not co-decision in the way it's been used in Brussels between Parliament and different institutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a sharing of responsibility and a sharing of sovereignty within the same institution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what I've been arguing is that the same path ought to be adopted in other areas, one of which is the budgetary area, where we now coordinate our actions based on a set of rules, one of which is the Stability and Growth Pact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we think, and I certainly think, that this system is not completely satisfactory, for a variety of reasons that you've seen in the last few years, and so it would be a good thing if we were to move to a common institution also in the budgetary area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is a point that's been made in the Five Presidents' report so it's not only my own view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's shared by other people; I wouldn't say 'widely shared': it would be too ambitious, perhaps.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we are observing a weakening of the prospects for the Chinese economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is through the trade channel, weakening the economies of the rest of the world, because China by now is a large share of the world economy, and has a confidence effect, as we've seen, on stock markets and all the other financial markets, which is also operating on the negative side.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, of course, we see a lower oil price, and the rest of the world, at least certainly the euro area, would draw some benefit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To know what are the origins of this change, and especially whether this is just the beginning of a permanent lower long-term output or simply a transitory phenomenon, that's what we are going to - what we hope, at least, to know more about in Ankara in the G20.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, you're right: one of the lingering questions was, how is it possible that with all this volatility in oil prices and exchange rates and interest rates, isn't there any financial stability problem?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I can say that at least as far as the institutions that are being supervised by the ECB, we have not observed such an effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, it's true that volatility is higher so the risks are higher.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's probably true that risk premia are higher as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, we have not observed in the banking sector a substantial, significant increase in leverage, and I am deliberately very cautious in saying this, limiting our observations to what we are actually observing, namely the regulated institutions subject to our supervision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first issue, I'm really commenting only on monetary policy, and as we said in the last part of the introductory statement, monetary policy shouldn't be the only game in town, but this can be viewed in a variety of ways, one of which is the way in which our colleague actually explored in examining the situation, but there are other ways.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Like, for example, as we've said several times, the structural reforms are essential.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary policy is focused on maintaining price stability over the medium term, and its accommodative monetary stance supports economic activity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, in order to reap the full benefits of our monetary policy measures, other policy areas must contribute decisively.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So here we stress the high structural unemployment and the low potential output growth in the euro area as the main situations which we have to address.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ongoing cyclical recovery should be supported by effective structural policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there may be other points of view on this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point is that monetary policy can support and is actually supporting a cyclical economic recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to address also the structural components of this recovery, so that we can actually move from a cyclical recovery to a structural recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's not forget that even before the financial crisis, unemployment has been traditionally very high in the euro area and many of the structural weaknesses have been there before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, as you might have seen in the introductory statement, there was a very rich discussion about all monetary policy instruments that might be used if warranted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there was a thorough assessment of the situation, which I'll elaborate further following your questions, and the conclusion was that we are ready to act if needed; we will examine all incoming information and we are open to a whole menu of monetary policy instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To this extent, the Governing Council has tasked the relevant committees to work on different monetary policy instruments that could potentially be used, to examine the pros and cons of different instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, if one had to summarise what was the attitude or the stance of the Governing Council discussion today, one would say it was not "wait and see", but it was "work and assess".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me just report to you on the general lines of our discussion today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, we examined the prospects for a firming up of our recovery and we concluded that the recovery is continuing, and is projected to continue at the same pace it had in the second quarter of this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have to distinguish two components: the domestic part of this recovery and the external part.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The domestic part has shown resilience, mostly driven by consumption, and the drivers of this recovery are the lower oil prices, our monetary policy and, to some extent, the fact that many countries have achieved some progress in fiscal consolidation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the headwinds coming from fiscal policy would be lower than in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To see how important our monetary policy is, consider that real disposable income and consumption have grown at the same pace, which implies the growth rate of savings has been flat.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is so because interest rates are so low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we often complain about interest rates being low for savings, but there is also a positive side to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, we have an external demand which has shown weakness mainly for the challenges that emerging market economies are now experiencing, and more particularly China.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the inflation rate side, the picture is in a sense less sanguine.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see that headline inflation will stay low for a protracted period of time, although as I just said in the introductory statement, we expect some pick-up, due mostly to base effects and possibly projections of higher oil prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, the core inflation is basically stable at 0.9%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the expectations of inflation, which of course is a very relevant variable for our monetary policy decisions, we see that since our last meeting survey-based short-term inflation expectations have declined, but medium to long-term inflation expectations, after some decline following our last meeting, have recovered and are basically unchanged since then.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we see that the latter development is both for market-based inflation expectations and survey-based inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, we see some downside risk as far as this picture is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the downside risks come from a continuing high output gap, from the possible further fall in oil prices, from the fact that the nominal effective exchange rate has appreciated in the last three or four months, if I'm not mistaken, by almost 6%, and, finally, from the fact that we continue to observe a high degree of correlation between headline inflation and medium-term inflation expectations, which means a high degree of correlation between oil prices and inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a risk because it could lead to a de-anchoring of inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not saying that these risks are materialising, but they are present and as I observed in the course of the last meeting these risks have gone up, and we want to be vigilant, as people used to say in the old times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, we see that credit markets are improving, and we can expand on that in the coming questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the overall assessment, as I said, is not wait and see, but it's work and assess, so the Governing Council is there, ready to act if the convergence of our inflation path to 2% in the medium term is pushed back.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the interest rate on the deposit facility, I said before - I don't know whether it was the last meeting or the meeting before that when I was asked whether it was discussed, I had said it was not discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Further lowering of the deposit facility rate was indeed discussed, and it's one of the instruments of monetary policy that I referred to when I said all instruments have been discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The projections of recovery both in output and inflation are based, are conditional on the full implementation of the QE programme as announced in January and the full implementation of all the credit-easing measures that have been announced in the course of 2014.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, they were also based on a set of technical assumptions concerning exchange rates, oil prices, external demand, growth in output and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to the extent that these conditions change and possibly worsen, we will have to adjust our QE programme or in general our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On why to fight low inflation: I've discussed this many times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Low inflation on one hand has a supporting power for real disposable income.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, it increases the real value of debt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As we've seen, low interest rates promote consumption and it's essential for the recovery of growth and economic activity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But to fight low inflation doesn't mean that we want high inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We just want to be compliant with our mandate, which is to drive inflation back to below but close to 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I understand the Vice-President may want to add something on the first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because it's the second or third time that you asked that question, so let me add something.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First, let me remind you that some years ago in the US there was a commission headed by an economist called Boskin to examine the measurement of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the conclusion of the Boskin Commission was that the way inflation is measured, in particular the type of indexes that are used, Laspeyres indexes, tend to exaggerate the measurement of inflation, in the case of the US by 1.5 percentage points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, if the target would be zero, very likely we would be targeting a negative inflation rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is a measurement problem with inflation which justifies that the target for inflation should be above zero.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second point is the point that the President just reminded you about debt deflation, and when there is a situation of high indebtedness, when inflation is very low, the burden of servicing the debt increases and that is very detrimental to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third point is that with very low inflation or negative inflation, the real interest rate increases, and when the nominal rate cannot go below zero it means that the interest rate in real terms may be above the equilibrium real interest rates that would equal savings to investment at the level of full employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's another reason why negative inflation rates can be detrimental.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
