text: Then there are the deflation risks - real deflation, not what you implied in your question, because to have negative inflation for a few months is not a deflation situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A deflation situation is a situation of prolonged period, meaning more than one year, of negative inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in that case you have two phenomena: you have an increase in real wages, because there is rigidity in nominal wage growth to not go negative, so you will constrain supply, profits of firms, and you hit growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And second, there is also then in such a situation a problem of consumers postponing their expenditure, if deflation lasts long enough; when we are talking about real deflation, not just a few months of negative inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there are a host of reasons why central banks fight deflation, why they spend money, as you implied - and by the way, just reminding you, there is not just one way of central banks to spend money to fight low inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Swiss central bank purchases foreign exchange in order to defend the level of the exchange rate that they want, and they have a balance sheet which is higher than ours in relation to the respective GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, we touched lower bound but, also in this, my answer is linked to the previous question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we are at practically zero nominal rates, the real rates are being driven by the expectation of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So lower expectations of inflation imply higher real rates - and this is an answer to Brian Blackstone before, that's why we fight negative expectations of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whenever expectations of inflation become more and more negative, we have higher and higher real rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's one of the reasons why we consider other nonstandard monetary policy measures, one of which is the negative rate on the deposit facility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there we've decided a year ago that that would be the lower bound, then we've seen the experience of other countries and now we are thinking about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I should say, we've not taken any decision about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was an open discussion on all the monetary policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've discussed some other monetary policy instruments besides this one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the scarcity, I've been asked this question many times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me say that also the fact that the ECB, the Eurosystem now is a constant source of demand on the markets, this is helping market makers to show their bid prices and this by itself increases liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also we're not chasing bonds that we know are less available, so that's another thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And let's not forget that the ECB is also lending bonds to the market makers and the market participants, so it's also increasing liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I've said many times, we stand ready to adjust the design of our asset purchase programme according to the needs and when and if needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On this question I'd like to give the floor to Governor Bonnici, but first let me say one thing about the other countries, why we observe this difference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You're absolutely right, one of the most important differences is the degree of implementation of structural reforms in different parts of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are different cyclical positions; there's different exposure to external shocks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If, for example, a large export market were to experience a recession, this would reverberate in a different way according to the different countries and different exports they have to this part of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What sort of economic policies different countries have undertaken to adjust to their macroeconomic imbalances that they had before the crisis, that's also one other consideration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, probably one of the most important differences across the euro area is, the degree of indebtedness, both in the public sector and in the private sector, of different countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that a high stock of debt hampers growth, so how to get rid of this, different ways to decrease the indebtedness, also have different implications.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now I would like to give the floor to Governor Bonnici as far as the specific experience of the Maltese economy is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Bonnici: Well, as the President has said, in fact, structural change has a lot to do with the performance of an economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the Maltese economy has gone through quite a significant structural change over the years, which has enabled the economy to be much more resilient and dynamic, so new sectors develop as old sectors fall by the wayside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think also that the impact of the QE, or the asset purchase programme, has on a country that has exports of goods and services of 150% of GDP on the exchange rate is also very important for a small economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from tourism to exports of goods, these are positively influenced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And perhaps also one needs to look at the space, the fiscal space the government has.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The deficit has been coming down, the public sector debt is just above the EU average, and all these factors give you more space for an economy to be able to expand, in some ways similar to Germany too, which also has a similar scenario.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is to look at different channels of propagation of what happens in China towards the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, we look at all these channels, namely the direct trade channel or indirect trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the direct trade channel, the conclusion is the exposure of the euro area to the Chinese economy is not very significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: After all, the exports of the euro area to China are 6% of the total.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, there are some countries where such a figure is higher and reaches almost 10%, in the case of Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second is so-called indirect channels, where you have also to account for the changes in oil prices and commodity prices that a higher recession in China would imply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third channel is the financial channel and again we do not see a very significant exposure of the euro area towards China.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But then there is another channel, which is the confidence channel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We think that so far what happens to the growth in China hasn't affected confidence in the rest of the world and more specifically in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the latest meetings in Lima, the IMF confirmed the growth projections for this year as far as China is concerned, which are above 6%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So your perspective is not something that is on the screens now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, any very large surprise in a very large economy might have the potential to affect confidence worldwide, and then we would have to see in which way and how to cope with that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other dimension to this is, when we say it concerns the effect of lower oil prices on our economies in general, we've been saying several times that most of the reasons why oil prices are low have to do with supply conditions and that demand conditions play only a minor role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, recent analysis suggests that we should be more cautious about this, because to the extent that the investment in oil production had been geared in the past on the basis of projections of demand which turned out later to be less than expected, this is also a demand-induced oil price shock, and has different consequences on inflation and inflation expectations than it would if it were a shock which was supply-determined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, one of the downsides I mentioned before, one of the downside risks to our inflation projections comes from the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I've said before, the nominal effective exchange rate has been appreciating over the last few months - four, five months - to a somewhat significant level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me restate: the exchange rate is not a policy target for the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, it's significant, as I've just said, for price stability and for growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to the first question is no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was no explicit preference towards one instrument or another instrument.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me add one thing about the possible changes, possible cuts in the rate on the deposit facility: the issue there is how come we announced a year ago that that was practically the zero lower bound and now we're thinking of going into further negative territory?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, let me state quite clearly that the credibility of a central bank is measured by its ability to comply with its mandate and to this extent any instrument could be potentially used.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Given the conditions prevailing a year ago, that was the statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Today things have changed, but this doesn't necessarily imply that we are going to use this instrument.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, I would say there were a few members of the Governing Council who hinted at the possibility of acting today, but I wouldn't say it was a prevailing theme of our discussion today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, I never said that QE would not yield its benefits if there were no structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would say that structural reforms will transform what is a cyclical recovery produced, amongst other factors, by our monetary policy into a structural recovery later on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite apparent that the monetary policy measures that we've been undertaking over the last year and a half, two years, especially, but even before, have significantly improved the financial markets, the credit markets and the money markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And now it's time we see these improvements being translated into a recovery which is resilient, especially in its domestic component.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So no doubts whatsoever about the effectiveness of our monetary policy, regardless of whether structural reforms have been implemented or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also add that we shouldn't have a too negative picture of how structural reforms have been implemented, because there has been some progress in several of our countries about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So more can be done, there's room for improvement, but quite a few reforms have been undertaken in several of our euro area countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Our judgement today is that the monetary stance that has been designed with the monetary policy measures announced in January, with the credit-easing measures announced in the course of 2014, is essential for producing recovery in output and convergence of inflation towards the objective of being below but close to 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These objectives are predicated on the full implementation of this monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, if we were to see that the technical assumptions underlying these projections have worsened, or the downside risks are increasing and further on materialising, we may well change the size, the composition, the design of all our monetary policy instruments as needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But a more gentle way of saying no would be the following: uncertainty, for economics, is bad.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I think China is a very significant partner of the euro area and will remain so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if anything, will become a stronger and stronger economic partner of the euro area in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: My answer is going to be very short: it's very, very early to say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be a time when we'll have full visibility on the economic impact, but it's very, very early to say now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was very brief, because it's very, very early to say what the impact could be on the eurozone's economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are at the time when we can only make inferences, really, from standard economic thinking.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's clearly a very significant increase in labour supply; however, there's also probably a need of significant investments in this labour supply, and also to see how these public investments in knowledge, education and so on are going to be financed is also going to make a big difference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would say, as I said before on the occasion of a different question, it's very early to have full visibility on the economic consequences of this phenomenon, and even more so to know what impact this might have on our monetary policy decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The key important thing, however, is that we should be able to cope successfully with this humanitarian crisis of unprecedented size.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'm sorry to say, but I'll revert again to Governor Bonnici for an answer to this question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'm saying this not because I want to avoid the answer, but because I think he's the most fully qualified for answering this question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And also when you read the press release that we've issued about structural change and the need to have growth-friendly fiscal policy, I think it's on the right track.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is the type of fiscal policy that is reducing the debt; it's forecasted next year to be 1.1% of GDP lower, and I think that is pretty good.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time the debt burden is going down, and the expenditure is going into areas, from education to other areas that essentially improve the quality of the labour supply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, in general I think Malta's performing reasonably well for its own future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me tell you how we came to take the decisions we've taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the last Governing Council we decided to assess whether the degree of monetary accommodation that we had achieved until then was adequate or needed to be recalibrated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first is that we are witnessing a continuing recovery, gradual but continual recovery driven mostly, as I said a minute ago, by consumption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The growth rates in this year have been 0.5%, 0.4% and 0.3% over the last three quarters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The drivers to this recovery are first, our accommodative monetary policy; second, less headwinds to our fiscal policy; and third, very importantly, is the oil prices, of course, which are supporting real disposable income.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also our policies have been effective also on the inflation front, because if you observe, especially in the last month, we observe - I wouldn't say for the first time, but certainly after a long time - the correlation between our inflation expectations measures and the current inflation or the oil prices has decreased or has just disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So overall, the conclusion about our policies was that they've been effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can dwell on that later, to give you a few figures to show how effective these policies have been, in improving the credit conditions, in improving the financial markets conditions, and in supporting what we have seen so far happening in the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The question then was, have they been effective enough for us to be confident that we would reach our objectives about inflation within the horizon that we have planned?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So let me say this very clearly: we are doing more because it works, not because it fails.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, you see, we said the last macroeconomic projections implied a downward revision in inflation, very small but still there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This downward revision comes after a long series of downward revisions in inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, the projections contained the effect of our policy communications in the last month already, and in spite of that they had a downward revision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, after the cut-off date we had another other data point on inflation which was slightly lower than expected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So for a variety of reasons we decided that our monetary policy accommodation needed to be recalibrated so as to have a faster convergence of our inflation objective to our 2017 horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, we took several decisions, as I've just illustrated, but one of them comes pretty new, namely the reinvestment of principal payments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, that is a quite important measure, because it basically says that we intend to maintain the degree of monetary accommodation and favourable conditions for liquidity for a longer horizon than we have been saying so far.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Which means that the conditions of quite abundant liquidity and high excess liquidity will continue for a long, long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we shouldn't discount another fact that we have not been discussing so far: that there are a series of factors coming into play in the years ahead which tend to reduce the excess liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is the repayment of the TLTRO; another one is the demand for bank notes; another one is the bonds purchased under the SMP programme that may come due.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we counteract this reduction and we actually may do even more than offset these reductions, which means that the conditions for this liquidity will ensure that the bonds we purchased, and we are purchasing and will be purchasing, will stay on our balance sheet for a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are confident that these decisions actually are adequate to achieve our objectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decided this cut in the deposit rate: we think it's adequate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, they were not unanimous, but there was a very large majority in favour of this package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think these measures need time to be fully appreciated, and we will see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, the answer to the second question is that our inflation rate ought to go close to 2% but below 2% over the medium term, and one should certainly take into account the fact that it was well below 2% for a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, we do say, and we just said, that our QE has been quite effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The market-based financing conditions showed a fairly significant success of our policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Euro area 10-year government bond yields fell by around 120 basis points between June 2014 and now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the same - decline in yields on bonds issued by firms and by banks, and basically the declines, the cuts in the deposit facility rate have enhanced the power of our transmission channels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the most important thing is the fall in the cost of credit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The cost of credit for the euro area, for the whole of the euro area bank lending rates, fell by approximately 80 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just think about that: to achieve that under normal circumstances, one needs a reduction in interest rates by 100 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the transmission channel of this reduction to lower lending rates has been faster.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For so-called vulnerable Member States, such a reduction was up to 140 basis points, so credit has become much cheaper.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Credit volumes have become much broader and more significant for both households and firms all across the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Spreads have been going down, between large borrowers and small borrowers, and between borrowers in the vulnerable countries and in the non-vulnerable countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all in all, all these measures have had an effect on the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So let me give you a figure produced by our staff: in the absence of our measures, inflation would be at least half a percentage point lower next year, and about a third of a percentage point lower in 2017.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our measures are contributing to raise GDP by almost 1% in the years 2015 to 2017.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think we rightly claim that our policies have been effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Because in January 2015 we calibrated QE on the basis of certain conditions, and these conditions have changed through 2015 and in particular during the summertime, because of changes in the external factors: the weakening of emerging market economies, the appreciation of the exchange rate and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All this produced lower inflation and so we had to recalibrate, and we are going to do this on and on, if the external conditions will put at risk the achievement of our objectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can always adjust its horizon, its size, its design.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are not going to be hampered in doing this by technical issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, we are going to revisit or review some of the technical parameters of our programme in the spring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This time we decided that the extension of the horizon, and especially the introduction of the reinvestment, would be the right thing to do, and the new calibration that was achieved after that, would tell that we would be able, we are confident, to reach our objectives within the horizon as we planned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Which means basically we are not excluding the use of all other instruments if we were to decide that they were the right ones to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I said before that the cut we decided today is adequate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well there are many, many factors that affected the core inflation projections as we had it since January 2015.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The most important ones I've just mentioned: it's the oil prices, and the situation in the emerging market economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we've done since then is to create very favourable financial and credit market conditions so that firms and households, even though burdened by these external factors, could find credit easier to access and more abundant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen this through, especially, mainly through higher consumption and higher real disposable income.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the interesting thing to see is that now, for the first time this year, the recovery is becoming broader and is actually driven mostly by consumption rather than exports.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the other interesting thing to see is that consumption and real disposable income move together, namely the savings rate is flat, which is also a good sign.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we see that gradually our QE is translating into improving economic conditions in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The measures that the Governing Council decided today had been discussed in a quite detailed fashion by all the relevant committees, and basically our decisions do reflect their discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Responding to the question I was asked before, why have we chosen to widen the horizon, why have we chosen to introduce this reinvestment factor?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also this was analysed by the committees, and we basically followed their views in taking these decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I would say, first, it's too early to say the extent of our purchases of regional bonds that I've just stated in the Introductory Statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's too early to say, but it's also too early to say in which direction we're going to extend, if we ever need to extend.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the overall situation - it's been said several times that we wouldn't be able to buy the bonds, and in fact bonds are there to be bought in good supply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the second question, ANFA purchases are entirely a matter for national central banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Often it's very hard to understand the purposes as to why they buy certain bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Often, for example, very often it's for their pension funds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would exclude completely - you didn't say that, but you may have thought about this in your mind - I would exclude completely any possibility of monetary financing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are not buying from the primary market, and their investment policies are pretty broad-based.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a question that I think you should ask them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first point, we simply observed that cuts in the rate on the deposit facility vastly improve the transmission of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, some of you ask, or are about to ask, why we left the MRO rate [Main Refinancing Operation rate] unchanged: we left the MRO rate unchanged mainly because all the short-term interest rates now follow the rate on the deposit facility, which has become really the driver of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then this will have consequence, of course, positive consequences on the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: This is actually a very important question that we ask ourselves all the time, not only with respect to other countries here in Europe, but also with respect to the monetary policies and the central banks of emerging markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We really have to think and to reflect that we are bound by our mandates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandates are national mandates; our mandates are based on our own national jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This holds for the ECB, it holds for the Fed, it holds for the Bank of England: for all central banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But would this mean that we don't talk to our colleagues?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is a fairly extensive, I would say, habit of consultation, of discussion - of explanation more than consultation, of explanation of the reasons why we do certain things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have what we call the spill-overs and the effects of the spill-overs in mind, certainly, but as I said, we are bound by our mandates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first point, the balance sheet of a central bank is an instrument.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As such, it should be used to reach the objective, which is price stability, as we have defined here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there isn't a size that is better than another size.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The only gauge to this is to reach the objective of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I would say the other part of your question is, if need be, would we be able to sort of drain this liquidity in?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other question, now, it's not the Ombudsman of the European Parliament.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is the Ombudsman, and then there is the question by the European Parliament.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have updated our guiding principles for external communications to clarify and amplify what is already practised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: During the quiet period there will be no discussion of monetary policy with representatives from financial institutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the exact text, which was updated on 3 December, now reads: "The members of the Executive Board re-affirm their adherence to the quiet period principle, whereby speeches and public remarks, given in the seven days prior to each scheduled monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council, should not be such as to influence expectations about forthcoming monetary policy decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Similarly, the members of the Executive Board will not meet nor talk to the media, market participants or outside interests on monetary policy matters during that period."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we greatly appreciate the constructive dialogue we had with the Ombudsman on all aspects of transparency, which we value highly, and by the way we just received a letter from the Ombudsman, a highly congratulatory letter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a date, but there is also a condition, and the condition is - and it's part and parcel of our forward guidance - until we see a sustained convergence towards our objective of a rate of inflation which is below but close to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we give a date, and then we say if that is not enough, we can continue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And today we said that we are going to reinvest the principal of the bonds that we purchased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite important to understand that this reinvestment started before March 2017 but now will certainly continue after March 2017.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the bonds will stay on our balance sheet after March 2017.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We had a brief exchange on this issue, and our conclusion now is that, first of all, the first answer should be given by the Commission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is that we'll continue reflecting on this, and we will have a view on what is the degree of appropriateness of the fiscal stance; whether we have a view about the aggregate fiscal stance; what is the degree of compliance with existing rules; whether the flexibility which has been exercised before all the terrible happenings of this year - so before the recent terrorist attacks, but also before the refugees events - whether that flexibility would be justified.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: How do we assess the fiscal stance today given the presence of the previous flexibility, the refugees, the need for security of the euro area?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a very complicated question, so we are going to reflect on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can exclude completely any monetary financing, that's for sure, because they would be compelled to communicate this to the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is no monetary financing in these purchases; other than that, the national central banks decide their investment policies based on their needs, and it's their competence and their autonomy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of them communicate, by the way, and some others don't.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have central banks that don't tell anything about ANFA, so you wouldn't be able to know how many bonds they purchased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the question that you may have about ANFA should be asked to the national central banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I said it's very hard to understand, I'm sorry, I don't want to be misunderstood: it's very hard to understand what is the investment policy of the national central banks, because each one of them has an investment policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not that we have a say in their investment policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't have a say in their pension funds, for example.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, on the pension issues, really this is an issue for the institutions to discuss with the government as part of the review in January, and I have nothing else to add.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the recapitalisation of the banks, I'll give the floor to the Vice-President, but let me just say that all those decisions have been decisions by the banks themselves, and the government to some extent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: On this, there are of course investments, public investments, in the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They have been done, for instance, in the previous round of recapitalisations, with shares with limited voting rights but with full economic rights, meaning the same rights to dividends as any other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is in that respect not a problem of valuation of those public shares.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They participate, of course, in the economic results of the banks, but they are limited in terms of their voting powers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this time, as you have seen, in the case of two banks, they were able to fill all the shortfalls with private investors' money, and there are another two that were not able to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They were able to do so in what regards the shortfall for the baseline stress test and asset quality review, but not for the adverse scenario, and for that they will require some money, which will be public money, which may be invested into the banks in a proportion of 70% to 30%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: 70% in CoCos and 30% in shares, which of course will benefit from any profits or dividends that the banks will get in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the statement, that those public investments are worthless, is not correct.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Regarding the waiver and the participation in QE, you said everything you wanted to say?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: Because it's well known, by the way, the policy that we have regarding the two things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in what regards the waiver, the main condition is that the Governing Council will be satisfied that the country under a programme is complying with the programme, and that could even happen before the conclusion of the review, if we would be close enough to that end of the review and we would be convinced that the review would become successful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not a date; it's an assessment of compliance with the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Regarding the participation in QE, it's more complex and it does not depend only on the successful completion of the review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, this time I wouldn't say that we've discussed the side effects and risks, but it's a discussion that we have ongoing anyway.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are closely monitoring these risks; we are aware that these risks might be there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's why, first of all, try to know and learn as much as one can about these risks all the time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Especially the growth in credit accompanied by leverage, the phenomenon that we've seen pre-crisis, we don't see that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've just given to you figures about credit: credit's picking up, it's coming back, but it's very, very subdued yet, and we don't see especially systemic risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We may have localised risks in different parts of the financial system, and they should be addressed by macroprudential policy measures, certainly not by changes in monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: My frank answer to this is, "We don't know."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We certainly have in mind that the situation ahead is full of geopolitical risks, and that's why we have to be alert.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why we have to be certainly continuing our effort to pursue and achieve the price stability objective, well aware that the surrounding conditions may actually get worse because of these geopolitical risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I should say, in these present measures, the measures we've decided today, there is confidence but there is no complacency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I've said this: for us, the exchange rate is not a policy target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course it's important, for price stability and for growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So when we decide our monetary policy measures, we have in mind as objectives, inflation and the path to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, it's quite clear that whatever we do, and whatever everybody does in the world, every central bank does in the world, affects the exchange rate, and this in turn will have effects on price stability and growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's very difficult to respond to your question whether we have in mind a level of the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have in mind only our objectives of inflation, and to a secondary extent growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I will ask Mr Constâncio to answer the second question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Keep in mind, however, that we are not the resolution authority in this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's an important point to keep in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as your first question is concerned, let me just recall my speech in New York, which was actually quoted during our discussion today, saying that, first of all, we have the power, the willingness and the determination to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are no limits to how far we are willing to deploy our instruments within our mandate to achieve our objective of a rate of inflation which is below but close to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there shouldn't be any doubt about that, and we have plenty of instruments, as you know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We didn't want to discuss today the specifics of the instruments, but rather to determine and assess the stance that we may have to take in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here I'll read again these quite important words: "It will therefore be necessary to review and possibly reconsider our monetary policy stance at our next meeting in early March, when the new projections will become available."'

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: We have already communicated that the ECB had no interference in the decisions regarding Novo Banco, regarding in particular what you asked about the bail-in application.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From now on also there is a single resolution authority in Europe, the BRRD, and the rules about bail-in will be applied by that resolution authority, and also if we are talking about smaller banks by the national resolution authorities that exist in all countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not for the ECB/SSM to implement the rules about bail-in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First let me say that our monetary policy measures that we've undertaken since mid-2014 have been quite effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the pass-through of our measures to the lending rates - the borrowing and lending rates, the financing costs, the improvement in all financial conditions, and how these improvements are now being translated into real economic improvements, I think the pass-through has been quite significant if not spectacular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The measures we decided in December were entirely appropriate and have been effective, but they were entirely appropriate based on the circumstances that were prevailing at that time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The circumstances were basically - we look at several variables, but certainly we've looked, as I think I've said in the last press conference, at the exchange rate in effective terms; we looked at the price of oil; we looked at the growth prospects of emerging market economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just think about it: the price of oil has fallen by 40% since the cut-off date of the last projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The same thing we can say about the exchange rate in effective terms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you can observe the situation of the markets, both financial and commodity markets, and the geopolitical developments since then.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those measures, by the way, in December, were quite significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If one goes back, our extension of the APP and the decision to reinvest is going to add €680 billion to the liquidity, and it's an amount - I don't think people have reflected enough - it's an amount that's about two-thirds of the original size of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So now these conditions have worsened, and I think, to respond to your question, the credibility of the ECB would be harmed if we were not ready to review and possibly reconsider our monetary policy stance when we have full information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said before, the Governing Council reiterates that it has the power, the willingness, the determination to act, and the fact that there are no limits to our action, within our mandate, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also add one other thing that's maybe relevant in view of the impression: the Governing Council was unanimous in being committed to this line of communication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was another question, about the power of central banks to control inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's pretty clear that we are adapting our instruments to the changing conditions, and the conditions change because some global factors are at play, and we are doing whatever is necessary to comply with our mandate, and we are not surrendering in front of these global factors, actions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will confirm our determination to continue to comply with our mandate, which is to reach a level of inflation that is below but close to 2%, even - and actually even more so - in the face of adverse developments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I can only reiterate that there are no limits, and in some sense you should see the reference to the technical work: "In the meantime, work will be carried out to ensure that all the technical conditions are in place to make the full range of policy options available for implementation, if needed."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to make sure that if we are to decide about a specific policy instrument, we want to be absolutely confident that there are no technical limits to the size of its deployment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the refugees, I think I've commented on this in the past: the refugees are an extraordinary development which is changing, will be changing, the face of our society in Europe, as we know today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's entirely - well, it's not entirely in our hands; it's also in our hands, the opportunity, the capacity, the ability, the might to transform this development into an opportunity for future growth of Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer as far as our monetary policy is concerned, if these market developments and this heightened volatility in financial and commodity markets were to persist longer than in the short run, it may well become a factor in unwanted tightening of the financing conditions, and therefore that's one of the reasons why, as I read before, we will review and possibly reconsider our monetary policy stance in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are constantly monitoring markets and generally the financial sector, the banking sector, trying to see whether our monetary policies - I should say not only the ECB's monetary policy, but all the major central banks' monetary policies - could become a source of financial instability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so far we have not seen signs of potential financial instability of the like we've seen in the pre-crisis times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously our mandate is a mandate to reach price stability, and it's not exactly a mandate to protect banks' profitability, or for this matter insurance companies' profitability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course we are aware of the consequences of this, and the best answer to these concerns is to make sure that the overall economy returns to growth, to sustainable growth, with price stability, and that's the best answer for the stability of the financial and the banking sector as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The first question is really, we never addressed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've designed our programme according to certain parameters; so far our programme is proceeding smoothly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there were constraints of any kind, as I said, we'll have technical work making sure that we can use all the instruments up to their full availability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, the best answer to these recent developments in financial markets is to make sure that the banking sector is resilient, and I'm confident - actually it's more than confidence; it's a factual statement - that all the actions that have been undertaken, both in Europe and as well elsewhere in the world, have actually produced a much stronger banking sector than it was before the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense - but one should be very cautious here about not being too self-complimentary - but certainly the gyrations that we are observing in financial and commodity markets, on other occasions, in other times, would have severely tested the resilience of the banking and the financial sectors at that time, and so far we've seen actually that they stand pretty resilient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, first of all let me make clear that the reference to China in the accounts of our meetings last time ought to be read for what it is, namely the accounts reflect the opinions of some participants in the discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now coming to the substance of your question, there have been at least three main developments in recent weeks in China.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first was a PMI which was weaker than expected; the second was the overall situation in the forex market; and the third was the situation in the stock market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are carefully monitoring these developments, and so far all the economic indicators show that there is a gradual deceleration, by and large in line with our expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The outlook, however, for the euro area following these developments has been, as I was saying before, revised downward, and the effect of these developments on the commodity markets is quite visible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There has been a renewed decline since mid-October, with both oil price and commodity prices having reached lows by, especially, around the end of 2015 and now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So as far as oil prices are concerned, we have both supply and demand factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly what's happening in China is contributing to the demand side of this development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me, however, give you a line which has surfaced in the discussion: "What are we going to expect?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it was recalled that the Chinese authorities have a reputation for acting responsibly, and what they have done in, I would say, the last two weeks, shows that they are gaining control over their policy-making.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the refugees, the nature of your question is certainly important, but there is very little I can do about how the refugee issue is being viewed in one specific country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can only give general impressions of how we view the whole phenomenon, which, as I said, is an important structural, socio-political change, but also it could become an opportunity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me refer to what we are looking at when we have these dramatic movements in oil price, but also other commodity prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that if it were to be a short-term effect, as you seem to hint at, we would look through.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that's not been our experience over the last two years, at least.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at the materiality, namely the size, and when you look at that, as I said before, since the cut-off of the last projections in December, oil prices fell by 40%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we look - and that's also very important for us - we look at second-round effects, namely whether low oil prices and low commodity prices do feed into other prices, and then that could generate exactly what we want to avoid, namely a spiralling downward phenomenon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far we don't have that, but we have seen, we've got to be very vigilant about that, and even when we look at recent developments in the non-energy inflation, the so-called core inflation, we don't have many reasons to be optimistic about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the wage development, we don't have many reasons to be optimistic about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to take seriously the fact that low oil prices, low commodity prices for a long period of time may actually have second-round effects that we definitely want to take action against.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I mentioned those three; in fact, we look at many other factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by the way, let me state once again that the exchange rate is not a policy target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's pretty clear our actions have an effect on the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I was pretty clear also about specifying that the exchange rate I'm referring to is an effective exchange rate, so it reflects the actions taken by a variety of other countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that, the oil prices, and the growth process in the emerging market economies were three of several factors that we look at, and we have to look at, as changing the outlook for the euro area economy, and the medium-term outlook for inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's what we are looking at, what we are monitoring, and that's why I said we will review and possibly reconsider our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that we see major movements in the marketplace, and what could be the source of these movements, the causes of these movements?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether they're going to be transient, short-term movements, or whether they're going to be persisting; whether the markets will adjust to a different level or not: these are all questions that probably market analysts are better positioned to answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: That's a good question, because it allows me to clarify what is a significantly confused perception.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think there are very good reasons for returning to normality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the NPLs we talk about were fully identified and assessed by the comprehensive assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, the provisioning against these NPLs was fully determined by the comprehensive assessment, which means that no new unexpected provisioning, nor new unexpected requests for more capital will be made by the supervisor.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Specifically on Italy, the overall reading is that Italian banks have on average a level of provisions similar to what is prevailing in the euro area, and have also a fairly high level of guarantees and collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fourth, or fifth, point: the SSM, the European supervisor - I'm commenting on these things, but we should be aware we have a separation principle, so before preparing this answer I widely consulted with the chairman of the SSM, Madame Nouy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fourth, or fifth: the European supervisor, the SSM, is fully aware that to deal effectively with the NPLs, it takes years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not something which can be urged and resolved in a very short period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A good example is what's happening in Ireland, which is one of the most successful countries as far as recovery is concerned, and regaining market access, and they're dealing with the NPLs gradually.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we come to the questionnaire that was sent by the SSM: it was sent to several banks in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's an inquiry on how the banks are doing, are managing their NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, it is an inquiry on the governance of the NPL process management.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's to look at different national practices, with a view, finally, in due time, to get one best practice.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not an initiative that would push the banks to deal with the NPLs urgently, and as I said, we know very well that it takes a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The market behaviour with respect to banks depends on the confusion that was originated by the account of what this questionnaire was and what's going to happen, and of course all the discussions about the bad bank, and different valuations - you know about that as well, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we value NPLs, we have to be aware that a single number doesn't mean anything.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are NPLs vis-à-vis corporates; there are NPLs vis-à-vis SMEs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are NPLs of different kinds, and each of them might have a number.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So when we have a valuation of an NPL, this valuation will necessarily be affected by "What sort of NPL is this?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what sort of bank is actually managing this NPL?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the process of valuation has necessarily to be a granular process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, if one has in mind, say, a wholesale disposal of NPLs, then one will come out with a number, with a different number.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's what the difference is: between a wholesale valuation and a granular valuation of NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I don't think the markets are actually disagreeing with the assessment made by the SSM, but there has been a significant amount of confusion, and I hope that this exchange will help.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first point, I think Spain is one of the countries that has really achieved the most significant progress in its reform, and its structural reforms especially.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The figures that Spain has enjoyed in terms of output, recovery, growth, and by and large all sectors, are simply remarkable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so the country is now on its way to continue the recovery, to continue on its process of structural reforms, and it's quite clear, what you said, it's absolutely true: with very low inflation rates for a prolonged period of time, the internal revaluations become much more difficult.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's one of the reasons, by the way, why in a monetary union like ours, the objective of a rate of inflation close to but below 2% makes a lot of sense - makes even more sense in a monetary union like ours.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point, I don't think there is any disagreement between the Commission's view about fiscal policy and the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What the ECB has insisted - obviously in its own competence, because we are not the guardian of the fiscal policy in the monetary union; that role is the Commission's - what we always said is that fiscal consolidation should be growth-friendly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Namely, based on tax cuts, current government expenditure control, and possibly public investment with a high return, and accompanied by the structural reforms which will make potential output grow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Answering to your second question, first of all let me say that we use a variety of inflation expectation indicators, not only the five-year/five-year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly all inflation expectation measures, whether it's five-year, one-year, whatever, they have declined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They have declined, and I would say, more worryingly, their correlation with current inflation has increased, and therefore their correlation with the oil price has also increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why, as I was saying before, second-round effects are especially important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said before, the Governing Council has the power - and this answers your first question - the power, the willingness and the determination to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there are no limits to how far we are willing to deploy our instruments within our mandate to achieve this objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is what I said in the New York speech after the last press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'm sorry, but I'll have to abstain from making political comments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me say that our communication - well, you probably notice that as far as I myself am concerned, I abstain from making comments about markets, abstain from blaming markets, as such.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's very hard to put the blame of some disappointment on one side only.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In substance, I think the Governing Council is open to use all the necessary instruments to cope with a situation which is materially different from what it was in the beginning of December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First question, let me disagree with your reading of the minutes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me restate that this line of communication today was unanimous.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And finally to your more specific question , "How do you think you can put together a majority for taking monetary policy decisions?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, that's what we've done over the last four years, on and on and on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So one shouldn't have any doubt that the Governing Council in its collective wisdom not only has the power, the willingness and the determination, but also the cohesion that's necessary to take the actions that are needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point, about the objective of inflation: first of all, it's remarkable that at a time when you have people suggesting that we should revise the inflation objective to something lower than 2% - by the way, incidentally, you also have people who are saying that we should strive to have an inflation rate above 2% as well, so the camps are divided - Professor Issing confirmed the validity of the objective of an inflation rate below but close to 2% as the Governing Council definition of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: He also confirmed the validity of taking not the core inflation but the HICP inflation as its objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The horizon over which this objective is going to be reached is the argument of his interview.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here the view of the Governing Council is that we should absolutely reject any suggestion that we may do less than what's necessary to achieve the objective of the inflation rate of below but close to 2% without undue delay.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, the Governing Council is firm in assessing the necessity of reaching this objective without undue delay, namely to deploy all the instruments that are necessary to achieve this objective without hesitation; and mind, it's an objective in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, we have to understand each other what "medium term" means, how long it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the stance of the Governing Council and the ECB is the following: there are global developments; sometimes they're adverse - very often, recently, they're adverse - to us reaching this objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Either accepting a lower objective, which we don't do; or saying that this objective will be reached in a certain very large number of years, and we don't do that either.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the TLTRO I just can give you a brief overview of what this operation is, keeping in mind there's going to be a press briefing at four today for all the further technical details that you may be interested in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the TLTROs are refinancing operations that provide loans to banks with long maturity, and banks are given additional incentives to lend on the funds received.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The key features of our TLTRO programme are the following: we will offer four operations, one each quarter, starting June 2016, until March 2017.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The maturity of the operations will be four years each, so that the last TLTRO II will mature in March 2021.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Banks will pay the MRO rate at the time of bidding, so right now it's zero.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And they may even get a reduction on that rate which increases with the amount of loans they grant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the maximum reduction will bring the rate on the TLTRO II to the level of the deposit facility rate at the time of bidding.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The amount that banks can borrow is linked to the amount of loans that they have on their balance sheet, so a bank that's very active in granting loans to the real economy can borrow more than a bank that concentrates on other activities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The full list of features is in the press release that will be published after this press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Why did we decide to have another series of TLTROs?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, some of the main reasons are: loan growth in the euro area has been recovering now for quite a time, but it's still too low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, TLTRO II will - and we had actually a pretty successful experience with the first TLTRO - so we expect that TLTRO II will offer attractive long-term funding conditions to banks to further ease private-sector credit conditions and to stimulate credit creation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also it provides funding certainty - let's not forget it's a four-year operation - at an attractive price, in an environment of increasing volatility, and also an environment of large upcoming bond redemptions, bank bond redemptions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So banks face sizeable forthcoming funding needs, and so this occurs in an environment where the pricing of bank debt is volatile and uncertain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we think that in conjunction with all the other measures, standard and non-standard, in place, this TLTRO II will contribute to a return of inflation rates to an objective of close to but below 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me say that rates will stay low, very low, for a long period of time, and well past the horizon of our purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From today's perspective, and taking into account the support of our measures to growth and inflation, we don't anticipate that it will be necessary to reduce rates further.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, new facts can change the situation and the outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also add that the experience we've had with negative rates, in our case at least, has been very positive, in easing financing conditions, and in the transmission of these better financing conditions to the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are also aware that - by the way, here there are different views about whether negative rates have affected, or how they affect, the profitability of the banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me tell you: does it mean that any negative rate will be positive?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Does it mean that we can go as negative as we want without having any consequences on the banking system?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you probably know that we've discussed for some time the possibility of having a tiering system, so an exemption system for this operation, and in the end the Governing Council decided not to, exactly for the purpose of not signalling that we can go as low as we want on this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the Governing Council, although it gives a positive judgement about the past experience, is increasingly aware of the complexities that this measure entails.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said before, we think, and we have numbers that show - and the Vice-President is particularly well documented on this - that the aggregate profitability of the banking system has not been hindered by the experience we had of negative rates, and he can comment on that at great length.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course, this is an aggregate, and banks are not in the same position, and it doesn't mean that this is going to be true forever.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the bottom line of this is that basically more and more the emphasis will shift from rates instruments to other, non-conventional instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And one final word on this: you remember that negative rates were introduced for one specific reason: when interest rates reached the zero lower bound, the expectations for the future rates in the long term are only that the rates can go up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So with negative rates we were successful in taking these expectations down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the extent that we have other instruments to do this, we'll certainly shift the emphasis to other instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we've shown that through our APP purchases and other instruments; we've done that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: May I ask the Vice-President to comment on his views on the profitability of the banking system?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: The main point is, of course, that we have to consider a general equilibrium approach.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not just taking one particular thing and then drawing the conclusion that our policies would be creating problems for the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But even in what regards the pure net interest margin of the banks, what we see for last year - a year during which throughout the whole year there were already negative rates in the deposit facility, as you recall - there was an increase in the net income margin in relation to the total assets of the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Or if you wish, also, in relation to the assets that earn an interest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there was an increase, on average, of course, as the President referred to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is important because this is not just about the volumes - because there was some increase in credit - no, this is about the average rate in relation to total assets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This reflects the fact that one of the consequences of negative rates is to decrease the funding rates for banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because the whole set of rates in the money market, the short end of the interest rates, came down as a result of the negative rates, and the banks that used money markets to fund themselves had much lower funding costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fact that negative rates push down the whole yield curve, because by opening up the possibility in terms of expectations for future rates that the rates will be very low, the whole yield curve is lowered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this means as it is lowered that there are capital gains, because the reverse of this is that the price of all the securities go up, and so the banks indeed had capital gains last year, and that was a result of our policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the other thing is that, according to our counterfactual with our models, we can demonstrate that the growth of the economy was higher than it would have been if we had not taken those measures, which means that the reduction in impairment costs that the banks incurred last year is due to the continuing recovery of the economy which we helped with our monetary policy, and this reduction in impairment costs was an element, with all the others, that led the return on equity of euro area banks to go up from 3.8% in 2014 to 5.7% last year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And let me remind you that the 5.7% is also in real terms, because inflation was zero.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is the more general equilibrium analysis that has to be really considered when the question the impact of our policies on banks' profitability is discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We are confident that our decisions today in changing the parameters will provide the necessary boost for adequate operations of €80 billion a month until the horizon specified.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the answer, I think, and it's given €80 billion per month for the horizon specified.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is, we're going by investment grade of non-financial companies, and the committees will actually look into the specific definition of the companies you mention, that are not banks but are financial companies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, the final decision on not having a tiering system or an exemption system was not only the desire not to signal that we can go as low as we want, but also the complexity of the system is remarkable in an area like the eurozone, with many banks of different sizes, different conditions, in totally different market situations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it was both the desire of not signalling, but also the inherent complexity in that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think I've answered the other question as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: For me, there are different estimates as far as the potential volumes that can be mobilised in the corporate bonds markets, but I would defer to the press briefing later on to have an idea about that, rather than guessing numbers right now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just say that the number of €80 billion includes that, so we are confident - I was asked before whether we are confident that that number can be achieved without further changes: yes, we are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other thing is, well, the take-up of TLTRO is very difficult to - it's up to the banks, it's up to the demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We come from a successful experience with TLTRO I, as we know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do expect a very sizeable take-up given that the recovery is continuing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And given the very attractive conditions that are being put in place with these operations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think when we discuss these issues, really, one doesn't have in mind a specific country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you just have in mind the eurozone and what you want to do is to achieve price stability in the eurozone, not with a specific country in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you can see, the package is characterised by two different sets of actions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is a general easing, namely the cut in the deposit facility rate, the sizeable increase in the monthly purchases, and the forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then you have a second set of actions which is basically the TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I should also remember that in the asset purchase programme there's also other remarkable news, which is the broadening of the assets that we are purchasing to the corporate sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, all these actions actually complement each other, in both increasing the amount of financing, in making financing conditions easier for the whole economy, attacking different points of the real economy, and favouring the pass-through from the banking system to the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we do expect substantially easier financing conditions through the various channels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we do expect an increase in lending, but also increases, as I was saying before, in the bank bonds refinancing, so substantially easier financing conditions for the banks and for the final borrowers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense there are very strong synergies between all the parts of this package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Banks will pay the MRO rate at the time of bidding, so they pay zero now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the MRO rate were to change, they would pay the MRO rate at that point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So they pay the MRO at that point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then they may even get a reduction on that rate which increases with the amount of loans they grant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the maximum reduction would bring the rate on the TLTRO II to the level of the deposit facility rate at the time of bidding.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So a bank that borrows now would pay the MRO, zero.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then suppose that they actually go and satisfy the benchmark of lending: then they would get what the deposit facility rate is today, 40 [basis points].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: Just to add something - that's absolutely correct, of course; that's the way it works - but to a point of your question: the MRO rate is paid now, during the 12 months during which the four operations will be launched.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That does not have any impact on any possible increase in MRO rates down the road, in particular three years from now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That has already been paid by the banks when they borrow now, and then if the situation, hopefully, will improve so much in the euro area that interest rates can go up, there is no obstacle that is created by the TLTROs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a fixed rate now when they draw, when they go to the facility, which will be launched in quarterly operations, four quarters, four operations, as we announced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So 12 months from now, let's say, more or less, those four operations are launched, and they pay what they will use of those facilities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The rate which now is zero, it's the MRO rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First let me say that even though we've had this rotation system in place now for quite a while, it hasn't made any difference in terms of our discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Everybody, voter or non-voter, expresses his or her viewpoint and is duly listened to, and in fact things are changed in the course of the discussion, regardless of whether one is a voter or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the adoption of the decision, I would say that the majority in favour has been overwhelming.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just incidentally add one side remark: you're all aware that there is substantial pessimism towards the actions of central banks, and also with respect to the ECB, and there are many reasons, but one of the reasons that was quoted widely was the willingness of the ECB Governing Council to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the discussion today and the overwhelming majority with which the package was approved makes full justice of these doubts about the willingness to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it was all in all, I would say, a very reassuring discussion, very positive, very constructive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I can say, however, is that our mandate is defined as reaching an inflation rate which is close to 2% but below 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Which means that we'll have to define the medium term in a way that, if the inflation rate was for a long time below 2%, it will be above 2% for some time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The key point is that the Governing Council is symmetric in the definition of the objective of price stability over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
