text: Some banks have a business model which exposes them to the negative rates more than other banks, if they have a structure for funding themselves such that it's affected by negative rates more than other banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on the other hand, there are other banks where they can easily adjust to negative rates their funding structure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have situations where deposit rates are set at the minimum by law, for example.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To this extent, negative rates cannot be passed to depositors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I perfectly understand the viewpoints expressed by this sector of the industry that you refer to, and our point, the point made by the Vice-President and myself, was referring to the aggregate situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are also other banks completely different, for example, that suffer from negative rates for another reason.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They have a funding structure that adapts pretty well to the negative rates, but on the other hand, they have given their mortgages and loans, often, that are indexed to the Euribor.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As negative rates bring down into negative territory the Euribor, you see that their mortgages go to produce a loss unless the spreads are sufficiently high, which is not always the case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again, you have two different sets of banks: the banks where the spreads are sufficiently high can afford this effect on their asset side; but there are lots of banks the spreads of which are not sufficiently high.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's one more reason to consider the negative rates as somewhat complex in the multifaceted banking world that we have in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question is, if I can rephrase, "How can an expansionary monetary policy measure, or a set of measures like we've decided today, how could that change a situation where debt, both public and private, is excessive?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said last time at the press conference, "We don't give up in our fight to bring inflation back to our objective."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Suppose we were to give up, and rather than having inflation, you had deflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know that one of the most important negative effects of deflation is to increase the real value, the real weight of debt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to this extent, expansionary, accommodative monetary policy measures like the ones we've decided today are actually a very positive effect inducing people to reduce debt, not to increase it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to your first question is that it's not an overreaction to low oil prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a reaction to the fact that conditions have significantly changed since our last monetary policy measures were taken in early December, and this change was due first and foremost to a significant weakening of the global growth prospects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Incidentally, the IMF announced today that they are going to revise downward during the spring meetings their outlook for global growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second reason is that financial conditions have changed considerably in this period of time, and there has been a widespread volatility of high intensity for a reasonably long period of time at that intensity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that has caused, by itself, a tightening of financial conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, you have also the oil price, which first fell and then went up again, but still they are in a zone where they are consistently lower than a year ago, for example.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this package is not an overreaction to the oil price.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the adequate reaction to the weakening of the growth and price stability prospects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question is about the perceived lack of power of central banks, and it allows me to address the other two sources of pessimism as far as central banks are concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think the best answer to this is being given by our decisions today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a fairly long list of measures, and each one of them is very significant and devised to have the maximum impact in boosting the economy, and the return to price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have shown that we are not short of ammunition.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third source of pessimism is, "Yes, you are willing to act; yes, you have ammunition.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, that is quite interesting because, well, first of all we have plenty of data, from growth, to easing financing conditions, to what happened to the credit flows in the euro area since we started taking these measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So credit, I would say, volume-wise, spread-wise, between core countries and periphery, narrowed down - we can quite rightly say now today that fragmentation, which was the major problem of the eurozone until, say, two years ago, has now disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But even spreads between large corporates and SMEs have narrowed down considerably.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all this was transmitted into a growth recovery, which is not spectacular, but it's there, it's gradual, and it's been continuing now for several months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course the others would say, "You haven't reached your inflation target."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's going to take time because it would be foolish to think that we will go back to inflation of 2% or below 2% with an economy that hasn't recovered yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in order to get to our objective of price stability, we need first a stable, solid recovery for the euro area, and then you will see that the output gap will gradually close down and we'll start seeing movements on wages and prices, which are very important, of course, which we haven't seen so far in any significant way at a euro area average.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then we will see the return back to the inflation objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And also there is another observation to make here, when we talk about effectiveness.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Suppose we had embraced what two years ago I used to call the "nein zu Allem" policy strategy, so do nothing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And of course we deem that the counterfactual would have been a disastrous deflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what one can say is that the current fiscal stance is mildly expansionary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It used to be neutral last year; now this year it's mildly expansionary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would say from this viewpoint it's one of the drivers of the economy; admittedly not the major driver of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The major driver of the economy and the recovery basically remains our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we have the oil prices and then we have also, together with some progress on the structural reform side, we also have some mildly expansionary fiscal policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We haven't really thought or talked about helicopter money.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a very interesting concept that is now being discussed by academic economists and in various environments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Prima facie, it clearly involves complexities, both accounting-wise and legal-wise, for our view, but of course by this term "helicopter money" one may mean many different things, and so we have to see that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other point about negative rates, let me just say again what I said at the very beginning: From today's perspective, and taking into account the support of our measures to growth and the return to our price stability objective, we don't anticipate that it will be necessary to reduce further rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is what I said at the beginning and I will say it again now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, your question was about the worries about a general worldwide money expansion?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, our view on that is the following: first of all, the ECB has never started anything like that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even our measures today are entirely addressed to our economy, domestic economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of them are geared to lowering the yield curve; some others are geared to expand domestic credit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, let's not forget that in the G20 in Shanghai all countries took a solemn agreement that basically they would avoid such war.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it is true that some of the measures have obviously a spill-over on the foreign exchange market, but it's a very different thing between saying that we have increased the monthly size of our purchases from €60 billion to €80 billion, and saying that we are going to purchase foreign currency-denominated assets by €80 billion tomorrow, which is intervention.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, the answer to the first question is we really haven't discussed at all this and we think the measures we've taken today are adequate to address the change in underlying economic conditions since our last monetary policy measures were taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The macro-projections show that inflation will indeed be negative for several months this year, but by year end it will go up again, basically because of our monetary policy measures, which will anchor inflation expectations so as inflation will return to the objective of a rate of inflation which is close to but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Admittedly, the horizon, in other words the time that it's taking to get back to this objective, is now longer than it was, but this doesn't mean that we have deflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, the situation is substantially different from what it was in Japan in the '90s.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Before you close the press conference, there is one thing that I think is quite important that I should mention in the press conference, and it concerns the eurozone banking sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite important, and I want to point your attention to a communication by the Commission that was distributed this morning and that does clarify the nature of Pillar 2 requirements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this communication opens the way for a clarification by supervisors of the implementation of the measures that determine the so-called MDA, the maximum distributable amount.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: You'll get all the details of the corporate programme shortly after the press conference, but let me just say a few things here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can tell you that the universe is addressed to all non-banks; also to insurance companies that have a certain rating.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if a company owns a bank but its parent company is not a bank, it's suitable, it's eligible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if the parent is a bank then they are not eligible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And they will contribute to the overall size of €80 billion per month.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, let me first read to you what - because I was actually quite surprised by the interpretation my words had.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me read exactly what I said in the last press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The question was about what you asked, and I said, "We haven't really thought or talked about it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a very interesting concept that is now being discussed by academic economists and in various environments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It clearly involves complexities, both accounting-wise, legal-wise; and it may mean different things to different people."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then in answer to an MEP who asked me about the same question two days ago, I said, "The concept is fraught with operational, legal and institutional difficulties.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the bottom line is we have never discussed it."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Chair: Do you mind picking two out of your three questions?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: To your first question, let me say, the first thing is that we have a mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a mandate to pursue price stability for the whole of the eurozone, not only for Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This mandate is established by the Treaty, by European law.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We obey the law, not the politicians, because we are independent, as stated by the law.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by the way, all this applies to all countries, to all politicians in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This morning we had a brief discussion on this issue, and I can report to you that the Governing Council was unanimous in defending the independence of the European Central Bank and the appropriateness of the current monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, let me say that our policies are not very different from policies that are being implemented in a very large part of the world, in all the other important jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, if there were also structural reforms, the effect of these policies would be quicker.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the bottom line of this is that our policies are: the necessary policies for return of the inflation rate to our objective of a level below but close to 2%;, the necessary conditions for return of growth to a higher level;, and the necessary conditions for the return of interest rates to a higher level than today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other two questions, I can only say that the monetary policy measures that we have enacted in March had the effect of avoiding the second-round effects caused by the turbulence of the beginning of the year that would have had an impact on our medium-term outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are estimates by our staff of the counterfactual, of what would happen if our policies had not been put in place, but they do refer to policies that have been put in place since mid-2014, not exactly to the ones that we've decided to that point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the ones that I just mentioned, going back to 2014, they basically say that growth over this year, next, and 2018, would be 1.6% less than it would have been - than it will be, after the implementation of the monetary policy measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the inflation rate would have been negative this year, and if I'm not mistaken - it may well be I am - about half a percentage point less over the following two years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, these estimates do refer to the monetary policy measures that have been enacted since mid-2014.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: If I may respond to the second question, by saying that we haven't yet examined completely the details of this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can say it's a small step in the right direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would ask the Vice-President to respond to the first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: Regarding this issue, we have discussed it and we have participated very actively in the Working Group of the EFC that has addressed and prepared the report.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: And I have asked him to respond because he's the one who's going to discuss this issue tomorrow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: And also we have been very active in the Working Group of the Basel Committee.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So our position - which has also been discussed in the macroprudential forum where we have the Governing Council and the Supervisory Board at the same time - our position has been that first, there is reason to change the present system of zero risk weights; second, that the revision should not create undue turbulence in markets where sovereign debt is used, like for instance the repo market and in general short-term money markets; and third, that it should be a change in the international standard, meaning, coming out of the Basel Committee discussion - a principle, by the way, that is also mentioned in the Five Presidents' Report: that annual revision of the sovereign debt risk weight regime should be decided in an international context to ensure a level playing field.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are possible combinations of concerns with overconcentration of sovereign debt in the portfolio of some banks, by changing the risk weights accordingly and creating then a price disincentive for the accumulation of possible excessive holdings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the three principles are the guidance for our position in all these matters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And also, we think that this is a separate problem from any other problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's in itself a consideration, a reflection, that comes out of the crisis, and a consideration of proper treatment of credit risk in the accounts of banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me add, at least there are three sources of work, besides what's being done by the EFC and the ECOFIN.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is a report of the ESRB, another one will be a report of the ECB, and the third will be the report of the EFC, the Working Group on sovereign debt of which you are part.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'm sorry, the answer to the second question is the same: we never discussed it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the first question: now, we've taken these monetary policy measures in March, and it was a very comprehensive set of measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Since then, broad financing conditions indeed have improved, and we view these measures as being important in avoiding second-round effects in the wage and price settings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And, as I said in the introductory statement, growth is moderate but it's steady.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, as things are moderately improving, we've got to be very careful about not losing focus from our main objective, which is the return of inflation to our objective of a level close to but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And inflation remains very low, will possibly be negative in the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this combines with the global uncertainty that was, I would say, highlighted during the IMF meetings in Washington.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the result, the consequence for our monetary policy stance is that of course we keep the monetary policy stance as decided in March, and we now focus on its implementation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, our monetary policy course will continue to diverge from the monetary policy courses that prevail in other jurisdictions better placed in the recovery cycle.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, if there were an unwanted tightening in broad financing conditions that would alter our medium-term outlook, the Governing Council stands ready to act using all the available instruments within its mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'll answer the second question: as I've said many times, the exchange rate is not a policy target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's important for price, stability and for growth, and we've taken the measures in March, and these measures have been effective and will be effective in avoiding second-round effects in the price and wage setting behaviour.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me, however, respond to the first question, and I'll just, again, read what I said last time about the continuation of negative interest rates: "So the Governing Council, although it gives a positive judgement about the past experience, is increasingly aware of the complexities that this measure entails."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I've said before, and I've elaborated at quite some length last time about the complexities that this measure might entail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I should say that the experience has been broadly positive for the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have no evidence that it hampered the transmission of monetary policy, and when we look at bank profitability, we see that 2015,the first full year with negative interest rates has not affected, or has not caused negative interest income, net interest income going down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course we've got to be cautious here because we talk about the aggregate of the banking system in the euro area, and of course aggregates may actually conceal different realities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also saw no significant evidence that these negative rates had been passed through to the depositors or to the borrowers from the banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then one asks oneself, "Is this positive experience going to be true for any level of interest rates?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the issue of negative interest rates is not so much an issue of yes or no; it's an issue of extent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's why the Governing Council said that it was increasingly aware of the complexities that this measure entails.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said before, if there is going to be an unwarranted tightening of financing conditions that would alter the medium-term outlook, our medium-term outlook, the Governing Council stands ready to act with all the available instruments within its mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's mostly supported by consumption and now investment, and it's dampened by the external component.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our monetary policy measures have been supporting growth, and I should say with rare exceptions our monetary policy has been the only policy in the last four years to support growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so it will continue to do so, but clearly, as I've said many, many times, not only monetary policy is a necessary condition for returning to structural, long-term, sustainable growth, but then you have to have other conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First and foremost is structural reforms, and that's why the introductory statement today receives this renewed emphasis on structural reforms - which, by the way, was highlighted in the last IMF meetings as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the third - what the IMF called the three-pronged approach - the third condition to be in place is an appropriate fiscal policy, where we observed that for the euro area the current fiscal policy is lightly expansionary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But again, the issue here is not only a question of size, but for many countries, if not most countries, in the euro area, the issue is a question of composition.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A composition that is being called here "growth-friendly": namely a composition with lower taxes, lower current government expenditure, and more public investment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the second question really, I would say the bank lending survey shows that credit continues; it's pretty solid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It went up without interruption since the second quarter of 2014.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The number of rejections went down considerably and it has been going down steadily.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's also even more important, the continuation of this process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so together with the dramatic fall in rates and an increase in volumes, this shows that our measures are indeed quite effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was another question in the bank lending survey, where we asked, "What use are you going to make of the APP, the asset purchase programme, proceeds?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the banks answered that they were used mainly for granting loans, which is good evidence that the asset purchases, or the QE, as it is otherwise called, is being transmitted to the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But they also added that the consequence of the APP for them is more to adjust price and terms of the lending, more than volumes as such.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And also they answered about profitability, which is going up because of capital gains, and funding costs went down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these were the answers to the bank lending survey that portrayed a credit sector that is strengthening and is contributing to higher growth and to the return to price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's pretty evident that pension funds and insurance companies and other actors are significantly affected by the low level of interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, I would urge all the actors in this sector to resist the temptation to blame low interest rates as the cause of everything that went wrong and had been going wrong for years with this sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But having said that, I think they are being affected by low rates, although one should keep in mind that they also realised substantial capital gains on the bonds that we are buying, because some of them are amongst the main sellers, the main counterparties in our asset purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And also I would like to point out that low interest rates are not - in a sense, I did say before - are not a specificity of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The United States had zero interest rates for much longer than we've been having low interest rates, and clearly the pension fund industry and insurance industry have been affected, but in a different way, and certainly not in the same way as the eurozone and especially the German pension fund industry and insurance industry is being affected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, this has to do with a variety of reasons, some of which have to do with the current regulation, some of which have to do with the business model.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second point: low interest rates are a symptom of low growth and low inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said before, if we want to return to higher interest rates, beforehand we have to return to higher growth and higher inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, of course, we also need to look at real rates, not only monetary nominal rates, and if we look at real rates, one will see that the difference is much less dramatic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact, real rates today are higher than they were about 20, 30 years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I am aware that to explain real rates to savers may be difficult.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The discussions have been very positive, fruitful, and I would say quiet, and very friendly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Mr Schäuble himself returned upon his words - I don't have it here, what he said exactly, but you can check - saying that he didn't mean what he said, or he didn't say what he meant, anyway.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in view of my previous words - yes, he said, "I didn't say the monetary policy of the ECB is to blame for the emergence of the AfD," and he said, "I pointed out that the feeling of insecurity among people who have to be concerned that there will be no or negative interest rates for a long time contributes to the bewilderment that we have seen in many election results," which is what you were saying before, substantially, in your previous question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is the situation, which of course in light of what I said at the beginning in light of us having a mandate and being bound by the law, is certainly welcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, by the way - and I'm responding also to remarks made by other public figures - our policies are the same policies that are being enacted, by and large - of course, each country has its own specificity - the same policies have been enacted in other parts of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I think, of course, the answer I would give, "Yes, of course," but that would not be enough.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My predecessor, Mr Trichet, two days ago he gave an interview where he said, "I would have done the same things that Mario did."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So he confirmed what is the assessment of the Governing Council in its entirety, which, as I said, today defended the appropriateness of the monetary policy stance, and defended the independence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we had low inflation for a long time - and we are going to have low inflation for a long time - we should be patient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We should follow and monitor closely how the - well, first of all let me say one thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The future path of inflation is going to be supported by our monetary policy measures, first and foremost, by the recovery, and by the expected recovery and by base effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will see, as the first will more and more show its beneficial effects, as the second will more and more materialise, and the third, the base effects, will come true in the second part of this year, we will see that actual inflation will increase, and expectations will also follow that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is true is that in the course of 2014 there was an increasing correlation between medium-term inflation expectations and current inflation, and oil prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Which for us was the sign that it was important to act, and to act strongly, as we did.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The correlation with oil prices has decreased, but we have to wait.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: In answer to your first question, a polite, lively debate may even be welcome, because it helps us to explain better our monetary policies, and their shape and their success.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly criticisms of a certain type could be viewed or perceived as endangering the independence of the ECB, and therefore causing the sort of behaviour that you hinted at, namely delaying investment, delaying taking risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, we are independent, so we will continue in the course of the policy action that we consider appropriate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The result of all this is only that it will take longer for our monetary policy measures to produce the results that we want.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Any time the credibility of a central bank is perceived as being put into question, the result is a delay in the achievement of its objectives, and therefore the need of more policy expansion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point: first of all, let me state unequivocally that we view the participation of the UK in the European Union as mutually beneficial, and we will continue to say so in the coming weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly the discussion about this possibility has already produced some significant consequences on the markets, for example a depreciation of sterling, quite significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do expect a continuation of market volatility, certainly until the referendum; I don't want to speculate about the outcome of the referendum, but probably even after the referendum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is it enough to endanger the economic recovery in the euro area?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The assessment of our staff is that the risk of this happening is limited.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is no, we don't see a risk of scarcity, and we have not discussed other measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in answering this way, I will also in a sense anticipate my answer to your first question, and I'll read - I believe by and large it's the same words as the statement: "At our March meeting we decided on a comprehensive package of measures to ease financing conditions, stimulate new credit provision, and thereby reinforce the momentum of the euro area recovery and accelerate the return of inflation to levels below but close to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Since then, broad financing conditions have improved, also in the context of receding risk aversion at global level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our recent measures have been instrumental in avoiding that the financial turbulences that we observed earlier this year did not undermine the pass-through of our accommodative stance."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: To the first question I'll answer, basically, reading again what is in the introductory statement: additional stimulus beyond the impetus already taken into account is expected from the monetary policy measures still to be implemented, namely the TLTRO II and the CSPP, and will contribute to further rebalancing the risks to the outlook for growth and inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, what we are saying is that we have the June Eurosystem staff projections, and what's called the probability mass of risks over the years 2017 and 2018 has shifted slightly upward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, no, we haven't seen second-round effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But at the same time, in the midst of what one would qualify as good news as far as growth and employment are concerned, we still see no substantial pressures on the wage and price-setting mechanisms, with the possible exception of Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It goes without saying that the Governing Council remains watchful and alert to the presence of any second-round effect, and stands ready to act using all the instruments within its mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: To the first question, no, we think our measures make a lot of difference, and have made a lot of difference in the sense of being very effective, even with the present pace of structural reforms which could be faster.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's pretty clear that in the presence of a faster pace of structural reforms our measures would be showing their positive effects faster, but even in its absence they have been effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we see that basically the March package has been instrumental in avoiding a severe deterioration of financial conditions after the turbulences around the end of last year, and certainly has supported the recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I comment about the persistence of weak underlying price pressure, so we see growth which isn't really - I wouldn't use the word "sluggish" after the first-quarter data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, maybe the second quarter will produce a slightly lower figure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to see the full impact of the measures that we have decided in March and that will have to be implemented yet, in June - the two measures that I mentioned before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've commented about the rebalancing of risks, to that picture.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council acknowledged the significant progress made in the last two months which led to the agreement of the Eurogroup on 24 May.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it was based on the positive assessment by the institutions of the policy package adopted by the Greek authorities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the package sets now the basis for the completion of the first review under the ESM programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Eurogroup has asked the institutions to verify the implementation of the prior actions under the supplementary MoU, and this is an ongoing discussion with the Greek government.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Once the prior actions will be implemented, the Governing Council will take a decision leading to reinstatement of the waiver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, we've discussed this since, I would say, the beginning of the existence of the ECB, because our objectives are defined over the medium term, and there isn't a precise timeline for the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The length of the medium term depends on the nature of the shock and on the size of the shock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To give you an example, given the size of the shock that we had with the financial crisis, with the aftermath of the financial crisis, with the sovereign crisis in the eurozone and the repeated crises we had, we are seeing that the medium term for a return of inflation to our objective of an inflation rate of close to but below 2% is pretty long, and has been pretty long.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we continue insisting, saying that we want to reach this objective without undue delay, and when we say that we stand ready to act if needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the conditions under which we would act, that's another important question that's been asked, and in a sense it's a complementary response to the definition of "medium-term".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We would act if we were to see an unwarranted tightening in the financing conditions which would alter the medium-term outlook for inflation, and we would act if we were to see the persistence of second-round effects which would entrench the effects of lower oil prices into the wage and price-setting mechanisms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other question, the ECB is ready for any outcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, we've said, and I'll say it again, that the UK in Europe and the euro zone are mutually beneficial.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the ECB has a view whereby the UK should remain in the European Union, because the European Union would benefit from its permanence, and we believe that the UK too would benefit from staying in the European Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll also have to see what the ESM Board of Directors will decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But, as I said, there will be a decision leading to the reinstatement of the waiver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other question, indeed, we had a good first-quarter figure for GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We expect the recovery to continue, at perhaps a slower pace in the second quarter, but still a good figure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have headline inflation, which is what is in the forecast, because of oil prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time we had data on core inflation for the first few months of this year, probably the first three months of this year, which came out weaker.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is because of what I said before, namely that we don't see, with the possible exception of Germany, any substantial pressure in the wage and price mechanisms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We should also consider the producer prices also because of non-oil commodity price fall, and so that has to be taken into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to see the full impact of the measures that we've decided in March, both the ones that have been implemented and the ones that are going to be implemented in June, namely the CSPP and the TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the second question, I will ask the Vice-President to comment on the NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, I think right now - I've said - we have to focus on implementation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to focus on the effects of the measures that we've taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen that the probability mass of risks has shifted upward, although it's not a dramatic effect at all, and then we will be in a better position to answer your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: What is being prepared by the SSM is of course supervisory action as is appropriate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Which means that the SSM has been assessing - both in quantitative terms, which were basically known, but also in qualitative terms - what are the nature of the different types of NPLs that exist in the banks; and also examining the best practices in all member countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because as you know there is not a European regime dealing with the provisioning systems to prepare write-offs for the NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is now a homogeneous definition of NPLs, but that's the only thing that is harmonised at the European level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then as a micro-supervisor, the SSM will establish plans to have supervisory actions to individual banks to speed up the work-out of NPLs in order as quickly as possible to address that problem, working on the balance sheet of the banks, which of course implies that it will take some time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I'll answer immediately to part of the first question, because then I will ask Governor Nowotny to respond to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But just to give you an idea, the forecasts that we are discussing today are the product of a bottom-up process coming from the national central banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have our forecasts of two types: twice a year it's our own forecasts, and twice a year it's done by the national central banks based on their greater knowledge, or at least more detailed knowledge, of their economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is also something to be kept in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, there are many other ways in which your question can be answered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also say that our decision-making process is based on the collective wisdom of all the national central banks and the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there isn't one brain in Frankfurt that basically decides everything.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First, of course, we have the role of our participation in forming of monetary policy, which is just as we have it today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the Governing Council which means we have the ECB plus the governors of the national central banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in addition to this, of course, national central banks have a number of other activities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is that we are involved in payment services, so all the payments in Austria, to a large extent, go via, in this case, the Austrian Central Bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A very important role and increasing role is our role with regard to banking supervision: again this is something where we have the ECB, but the ECB does this for the 129 biggest banks directly, in joint supervisory teams, and part of these joint supervisory teams are of course experts from the national central banks; and for the less significant banks it's directly done by the national central banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are heavily involved in financial statistics, and of course the technical side of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That means the execution of monetary policy: how banks really can get to the loans given by the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think at whatever time span you think about, for the next 100 years I'm pretty sure there will be a national central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said in one interview, I'm sure the Austrian Central Bank will celebrate its 300th birthday, and I expect that at this time it will a lady governor who is at the head of the central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: This is a question that I am asked several times, very often, because clearly it is a concern for the savers of the euro zone, very much like it was a concern - it's been a concern for seven, eight years - for the savers in the United States, in the United Kingdom and in Japan.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It should be said that the low interest rates are a symptom of a weak economy, an economy where there is an excess of savings over investments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it should be said that the low interest rates, zero interest rates or even negative interest rates, are the right monetary policy measures in order to strengthen recovery and restore growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that point in time, interest rates will rise again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to say it briefly: for interest rates to be higher tomorrow, they have to be low today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also let me add that the ECB has a mandate to deliver price stability, defined as that rate of inflation which is close to but below 2%, and has to use all the instruments that are necessary to deliver that mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: You know we don't comment directly on exchange rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We say that the exchange rate is not a policy target, and it's not a policy target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, we say the exchange rate is also important for growth and price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the exchange rate is the outcome of several factors, one of which is the different position that the euro zone economy has in the recovery path with respect to other economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that will certainly elicit in the future, in the coming months, monetary policies that tend certainly not to converge; possibly diverge.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is something that we also want to keep in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, the exchange rate is the outcome of several other factors: what happens with other geopolitical risks that we have identified; what happens with the geopolitical risks that are near to us, concerning the United Kingdom decision; it's also the outcome of the behaviour of the price of oil and many other factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's hard to give one answer to your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question you ask me whether the Five Presidents' Report is still realistic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense, it's not a question you should address to me but to the leaders, because it's a political question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are the ones who are in the best position to assess the realism of their propositions, of their plans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what the Five Presidents' Report basically says is that if the monetary union remains incomplete it remains fragile, and it remains vulnerable to shocks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To shocks of an economic nature, to shocks of a political nature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in so being, it won't be a factor that will help the return of confidence in the euro zone and therefore a faster recovery and stronger growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I would abstain from commenting about the general proposition whether cash is necessary to freedom, but I can certainly say that our decision about the €500 banknote has nothing to do with the abolition of cash.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So much so that we are substituting the €500 with more creation of the €200s.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is simple, but it's very important to make it clear, because there has been confusion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Answering the first question, I'll in a sense restate what I said before: we will focus on the implementation of the substantial packages of measures that we decided in March; but also I think we decided a significant package at the beginning of December, the effects of which we are seeing, and will continue seeing in the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These June macroeconomic projections are just a snapshot of how we see things now, but we have to see what the full effect is of what's been decided before, and the effect of what's been decided but not implemented yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear, however, that we will not hesitate to act, and that is the meaning of the sentence in the introductory statement that contains the words "without undue delay".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this drives me to the second question, to answering the second question you asked.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are some conversations in the market about potential limits that this programme may meet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in case we were to face limits, the design of the programme contains enough flexibility so that we can adjust the programme in a way that would meet the desired size, and we have given in the previous months ample evidence that we are willing, able and ready to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the Convergence Report will show, as a matter of fact, that all the countries that haven't joined the euro don't yet satisfy the requirements for joining the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Although I should acknowledge very significant progress in stabilising, in consolidating budgets, in stabilising growth, and in pursuing the right economic policies, and often very significant structural reforms in many of these countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is we have to judge all these issues in perspective, really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if you look, for example, at the poll of the Eurobarometer, that shows that the majority of the citizens in these countries are still in favour of joining the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: To your first question, we have no evidence of withdrawing of deposits from the banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We actually have opposing evidence from central banks of other countries where interest rates became more negative than they are in the euro zone, and they don't experience any withdrawal of deposits from the banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, again, we shouldn't forget the experience of other countries like the United States, where they had zero interest rates for - I never remember whether it's seven or eight years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In our case, we started decreasing interest rates in November 2011, but still from a fairly high level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some people say we should revise it downward and simply accept the fact that we'll never reach 2%, and we should take 1% or 0%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And some say, "Oh, you should revise it upward and go to 3% or 4%, because in this way you will elicit expectations that you will go up with your policies."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the ECB position has been basically contrary to revising the inflation objective either way, and the reasons are different in different cases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The revision upward, frankly, would test seriously our credibility, because people would actually say, "How come you want to go to 3% when you're not even able to reach 1.5%?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by the way, each revision on both sides undermines the credibility of the central bank - for different reasons, but it undermines the credibility of the central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That effect by itself would raise the risk premium, and in so doing it would increase real interest rates and would go against the objective that we have of price stability but also against restoring growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the case of accepting a lower inflation target, this effect would be immediate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We would have an immediate increase in real interest rates, and therefore a further drag on the recovery and the return to inflation - and also there are many other reasons why, in the late '90s, all central banks of major monetary policy jurisdictions decided that 2% was the right objective and the right target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Where you lose flexibility in the exchange rate, you will have to have adjustments in wage and prices that are sticky downward, and so you need a certain cushion for carrying out these adjustments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the reasons for keeping this objective are overwhelming, and they work in both directions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First, as I said before, we should carry out the right monetary policy according to our mandate regardless of whether structural reforms are going to be put in place or not, because we have our mandate, and because ultimately - let's never forget the experience that Chairman Volcker had in the late '70s, early '80s - all in all, inflation is a monetary phenomenon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What makes a big difference, however, is that if structural reforms are in place, the time that it takes to reach this objective is shorter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And for us it would be out of our competence to actually decide which are the right structural reforms for each country, but it's quite clear that each country has an agenda of structural reforms, of those reforms that are more apt to that country's growth, to restoring competitiveness, to restoring competitiveness especially in the products and services markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You didn't say it but you may have implied it: whether accommodative monetary policy removes the incentive to carry out structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've discussed this on many occasions, and by and large we wouldn't agree with this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, we see the two things as complementary, and we think that the incentive to undertake structural reforms should come from other considerations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, a very high unemployment rate in one country should be an incentive sufficient to undertake the necessary structural reforms, much more than a high interest rate on the financial markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As I said, the countries themselves have the best knowledge, the best competence to decide which structural reforms should be implemented, and therefore I am giving the floor to Governor Nowotny to answer this question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nowotny: Well, but I would say, to follow your lead, I think that one has to be very careful to stick to the field of monetary policy that we have to take care of, so I do not think as a central bank as such we should develop specific ideas about priorities in structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think from what we see in general, we have structural reforms both in labour markets and the product markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are studies, especially by the IMF, where there is a certain sequencing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in certain circumstances labour market reforms might have priority; in other circumstances, product market reforms may have priority.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if I may say so, Mr President, we at the Governing Council are going to discuss this in more detail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As I said before, we discussed the general economic conditions and we concluded that we didn't have yet information to take decisions, and we decided, as I said, that over the coming months when we have more information, including new staff projections, we'll be in a better position to reassess the underlying macroeconomic conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No attention was really given to discuss specific instruments at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As I just said in the introductory statement, monetary policy is certainly supportive of economic activity and is focused on maintaining price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also other policy measures are needed in order to reap the full benefits of our monetary policy, and one of them is to address the non-performing loans and more generally non-performing exposures in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is a very important reform, and we certainly consider it important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't say we consider it a risk, as you said, but certainly it has to be addressed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other question, we have in place the rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have in place rules of state aid, we have the BRRD, and as I said several times, these rules contain all the flexibility to cope with exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The power and the responsibility in activating these rules and in complying with these rules lies with the Commission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first point, frankly, I can't remember whether the forecast was done before or after.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I know is that on inflation outlook, Brexit didn't seem to have any major impact at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Since we're speaking about inflation expectations, it's worthwhile pointing out that we have an increasing divergence between the SPF expectations and the market-based expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The SPF expectations basically remained the same: 0.3% this year, 1.2% next year, 1.5% in 2018, and 1.8% is the medium/long-term expectation of the SPF.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand we have the market-based inflation expectations, which in the days immediately after Brexit fell significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One immediate explanation was that there are technical factors that caused such a decline, namely that the impact on nominal bond yields was bigger than the impact on the linkers, and that reinforced this effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, even when the market sentiment recovered, we haven't really witnessed a similar recovery of the market-based inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So again, we can't say much about this at this stage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need a little more time to assess what is the state of the market-based inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, I just simply reiterate what I said before: I said that over the coming months, when we have more information, including new staff projections, we will be in a better position to reassess the underlying macroeconomic conditions and likely paths and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is one last sentence that I want to stress in response to your question: if warranted, to achieve its objective, the Governing Council will act by using all instruments available within its mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would stress readiness, willingness, ability to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Especially important for the eurozone, which is basically a bank-based economy, where the credit intermediation goes mostly through the bank lending channel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Bank equities in the aftermath of the Brexit were especially hit, and especially in the eurozone, and especially those banks with a high share of NPLs, of non-performing loans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Bank equity prices are of some significance for policymakers, because if they drop in the way they did, one would assume, if this is to stay, cost of capital would increase, and therefore the net return on lending would decrease and would suggest on the banking side a more conservative lending behaviour.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why we do care about bank equity prices for the transmission of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let's consider this in a little more, I would say the right perspective, but also the medium-term perspective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the solvency side our banks are better, if not much better, than they were before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me give you one number: the average CET1 - the CET1 for the 130 banks directly supervised by the SSM - was 9% in 2012, and it's around 13% today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from a solvency viewpoint one would conclude that a series of actions that have been undertaken in the last three, four years - like new regulation, supervision, a robust supervisory system and regulatory design; but also a new harmonised standard of classification of NPLs, and certainly substantial provisioning against these NPLs and other forms of weak parts of the balance sheet; and finally the role that our monetary policy played in this period of time - these are the reasons why banks are today better, if not much better, than they were in 2009.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The problem now that we will have to address is the weak profitability ahead, not a problem of solvency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, next week, on 29 July, the EBA will publish the outcome of the most recent stress tests for 51 banks in the European Union, including 37 significant institutions directly supervised by the SSM.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Moreover, the SSM has conducted the same stress test for an additional 56 banks under its direct supervision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And these stress tests will be one input to determine the Pillar 2 supervisory capital demands by the end of this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've said that the NPLs are certainly a significant problem for the future profitability, and for the capacity, the ability that the banks have of lending.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is a problem that needs to be addressed because it's an obstacle to the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One would say that the solution of the NPL problem is based on three pillars.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And third, government action, and first of all passing that legislation that would foster the development of an NPL market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this certainly involves a revision of existing personal and corporate bankruptcy legislation, but also other actions, and possibly also having a public backstop when at times of exceptional circumstances the NPL market is not well functioning, and certainly we want to avoid fire sales.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, the figure that circulated in the aftermath of Brexit was exactly what you said, an impact of 0.2% to 0.5% over three years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I believe the Commission has come out with a similar figure of 0.25% to 0.5%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we should take these estimates with some grain of caution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said it before: uncertainties, large uncertainties prevail, because first of all these figures will in the end depend on how long is going to be the stretch of time for these negotiations to be completed and therefore to give a certain outlook, which we don't have with us today; and second, these figures will also depend on what kind of outcome is going to come out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think they have to be taken with a certain grain of caution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is clear is that financial markets, and also the banking sector, in spite of the large changes in the stock prices, have reacted in a fairly resilient fashion to the event.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We haven't observed any disruption, neither in the financial markets sector nor in the banking sector, and this was certainly caused by the large liquidity being abundant; by also all the preparations that all central banks had undertaken before, ensuring that liquidity lines would be available; and certainly by the accommodative monetary policies undertaken by all central banks at the present time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also because of, in a sense, what I was saying before: by the more robust regulatory system all over the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think it's too early to say what is going to be the final impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The only thing we can say is that it's a risk that has materialised, and it's a downside risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as your other question is concerned, it's about, I would say, the possible execution difficulties that our QE programme may have to face.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First let me say that we view our QE programme and our TLTRO programme, all our monetary policy measures, as having been quite successful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are underpinning the return of inflation to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, as I had the opportunity to say before, we didn't give attention today to the discussion of specific instruments, but in the past we've given enough evidence, not only of our readiness to act and our willingness to act, but also of being able to adapt our programmes so as to reach the objective of a purchase of €80 billion a month until March 2017, and beyond if needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think in worrying about the coming months, whether we'll be able to actually fulfil this objective or not, I think proper attention should be given to the evidence that we've given in the past few months, and our ability to exploit the flexibility that the design of our programme gives us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we do take into account the various definitions of output gap when we design our monetary policy, including the one you mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: Just to add that I had quoted that work of our experts last year in my speech at Jackson Hole, among other, also internal, estimates of the output gap, which means there is a whole range of internal calculations with different models that go from -2% to -6%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we cannot really make a choice in a very concrete way and say, "This is better than the other one."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, this model that comes out with 6%, simplifying it, reaches that conclusion based on the assumption that the variables in the model would explain what has happened to inflation, and to achieve that reverse engineered, then it concludes that the output gap should have been -6% in order to explain the inflation that actually happened.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So everything has to be really analysed with all the uncertainties behind such a concept.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Your other question was about tapering: no, we have not discussed it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The decision about sanctioning Spain, or other countries for that matter, is entirely in the hands of the Commission, which has, as in other cases, the responsibility, the power and the knowledge to take a decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The message that will probably come out ­- well, the message that will come out, the message that I can foresee or expect to come out, will be a message of stability, and the message that will come out specifically from the eurozone will be a message of a recovery that continues, though at a slower pace, in the midst of great uncertainties.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Uncertainties that are not only - or not especially, actually - coming from the eurozone, but they come from various parts of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in this climate of general uncertainty, not necessarily economic uncertainty but probably mostly geopolitical uncertainty, it's very important that a message of stability comes out of the G20.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The financial system and the banking system are stronger than they were before, and so it's very important that a message like that comes out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, as you know, we are part of the troika because of legislation, the six-pack, the two-pack, that was passed years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that time there was a good reason for involving the ECB in the programme countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The eurozone didn't have any experience with how to manage these situations, and so it made sense to have all the players in: the IMF, the Commission and the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was also a good case for the ECB to be part of this, so that the ECB could actually have information about the solvency and about the financial stability of the states where the monetary policy counterparties would reside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, through the years actors have acquired experience, and the ECB, especially in the last two years, has carved a role which is both minor and more specific to its capacities, to its skills, namely the financial and the banking sector in these countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, to change the troika we need to change legislation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the European Parliament, it's the legislators, it's the Ecofin, it's the Eurogroup, and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so we are ready to give our contribution to that extent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, Turkey: it's very difficult to understand how these big geopolitical uncertainties would affect the recovery, because the channels are not obvious.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, in the case of Brexit there is an obvious channel, which is the trade channel, but is it the most relevant channel to express the impact of such an event on the eurozone?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One would rather think about the confidence channel or, for example, the financial service channels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now in the case of Turkey it's very likely that all these events might affect the confidence, but it's very difficult to foresee significant impact on the eurozone recovery, at least in the immediate future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: In terms of results, we see inflation moving forward according to our baseline scenario.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If anything there was a better-than-expected development in recent times, when headline inflation moved from -0.1% to +0.1%, and that's essentially due to changes in the price of energy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But even if we exclude food and energy we saw a positive development in the services inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We should also keep in mind, however, that core inflation is being set at values where no uptick has been shown now for several months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think we're moving forward at the pace which was expected according to our baseline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By year end there are certain base effects concerning the oil prices which will make inflation go up and stay for the next year at 1.2%, if I'm not mistaken, over next year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our monetary policy measures have been undertaken at the time when we had many other contrary factors or headwinds going against, so we should ask ourselves what would have happened in the absence of these monetary policy measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But when we look at the consequences, the impact that our monetary policy measures had on financial markets, I think there is no doubt that they've been highly effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to give you an idea of recent, just a few days: our measure of lending rates - it's a composite average of bank lending rates - is now at a historical minimum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The bank lending survey shows that now credit conditions and credit volumes are improving and they have been constantly improving now for several months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But even more importantly, when we ask banks - incidentally, the bank lending survey was taken before and after the Brexit, so banks had been given the opportunity to tell us, "Is what happened changing your views?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: and none of them seem to have given an answer to that, so perhaps it's just too early, but we didn't have any feedback from Brexit into their answers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But basically, when we are asking, "Why is credit going up?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When two or three years ago credit growth was still negative, the main answer to the question "What is the main motivation behind your lending decision?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They've been giving this answer about competition being the main driver now for several months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we consider this to be basically a product of our monetary policy measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all this is being passed through to the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're seeing this through the gradual economic recovery, which is moving forward at a steady and moderate pace.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not to mention, of course, all the figures that I mentioned in the past, namely stock prices, namely spreads, spreads between - we can say the fragmentation in the eurozone is by and large over - so spreads between core countries and periphery bank lending is over; spreads between corporates and SMEs have narrowed down a lot.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, public backstop is a measure that would be very useful but certainly should be agreed with the Commission according to the existing rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's important, and it's even more important given the existing rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All this should be agreed with the Commission, and DG Competition especially.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point about the NPLs in Italy: I think the very first measure - well, certainly, it's a big problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To address the NPLs when they reach this size has taken time more or less everywhere.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we should be aware that the longer we have this in place, the less functioning will be the banking system, or at least will be the banks with high NPLs, and so the less capable will be these banks to transmit our monetary policy impulses to the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, a high level of NPLs makes banks especially vulnerable to the markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As we've seen recently, bank equity stocks were hit especially for those banks with a high level of NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And one of the reasons why this is so is that the future level of profitability comes into question because a lot of capital is stuck against this level of NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So on one hand there is an interest in trying to resolve this serious problem as fast as one can.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, one is bound by the fact that it's by its nature a problem that is slow to be resolved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the question is what can be done to accelerate the solution of this problem?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of the measures is to have a well functioning market for NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Several things, but one is in my view dominant, namely to create a legislative framework where the NPLs can be traded and sold easily.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some steps have been undertaken in Italy in recent times; they're certainly steps in the right direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More should be done, and should be done especially to address the legacy NPLs, the past stock of NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, the legislative changes should be such that the legacy NPLs could be adequately addressed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The second question is easy to answer: I won't comment on specific banking institutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, the changes that are being suggested may be rational in their own sake, but it's very important that they take place in the proper framework.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, can we have a debt restructuring mechanism in absence of a common budget, or the somewhat more advanced idea of a common fiscal policy?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Are we sure that we have examined all the implications for financial markets, for financial stability, and more generally for stability at large, of big changes in the treatment of sovereign debt?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think these questions, or these proposals, which have their own rationale if taken by themselves, ought to be reframed in a more complete framework than the one we have today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I didn't know that, but I have no specific view on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decided that the €500 note is, I would say, a good instrument in hands that are not exactly proper hands.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, as someone said, we don't want to draw seigniorage from comfort to criminals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so we decided to stop production in some years - I think 2018, if I'm not mistaken, the beginning or end of 2018 - of the €500 note but it will stay in circulation and it can be converted at any time in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: This very same question was asked to me five years ago when I started this job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I answered that he's not a bank dealer; he's a trader in London, and that's it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our response lies in achieving our mandate, in achieving our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our response lies in ensuring what we call price stability, but in fact amounts to growth and job creation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our response lies in making sure the labour markets continue to improve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
