text: We consider this to be a very important contribution for also addressing the other sides of our continent that create so much worry in the rest of the world's eyes, and that's what we do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we are accountable for and that's what we believe we will succeed in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, I don't want to downplay the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To say that it's not a solvency problem but it's a future profitability problem doesn't mean that one downplays the problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's just, figure-wise, we see that from a solvency viewpoint our banks are better off than years ago, but certainly they do have profitability issues, and especially the banks with a high share of NPLs, but not only banks with a high share of NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of it has to do with the weak growth performance of the past few years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'm pretty confident that strong supervision and robust regulation, and better communication, indeed, by the supervisory authorities, the EBA and all this, will still improve the situation and the perception in the rest of the world's eyes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We tasked the relevant committees to work, as I think I said, on the smooth implementation, and the changes that are needed to ensure a smooth implementation of our programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we discussed the assessment of the economy and we discussed the broad macroeconomic projections, but we didn't discuss anything else.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: [Asked to address second question on extension of QE] That's what I'm saying: we didn't discuss it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I would answer both questions at the same time: our programme is effective and we should focus on its implementation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The current projections do reflect the full impact of our March decisions and we will continue with the implementation of the existing programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will use the words that were used by the chief economist, Mr Praet, in his presentation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: He says, "Over the coming months HICP inflation is expected to pick up, in large part owing to base effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yet underlying price pressures continue to lack a convincing upward trend, and remain an ongoing source of concern.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "Importantly," - importantly - "the projected path of inflation remains conditional on exceptionally supportive financing conditions which to a large extent reflect our accommodative monetary policy."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council tasked the relevant committees to evaluate the options that ensure smooth implementation of our purchase programme, and - let me remind you what I just said in the introductory statement - our purchase programme is intended to run until the end of March 2017, or beyond if necessary, and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as your second question, why we haven't acted now: the assessment was that for the time being the changes are not substantial, as to warrant a decision to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see that our monetary policy is effective - and we can discuss it later; it's fully effective, in fact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see that the full impact of the March decisions is now in the macroeconomic projections, but we also see that there have been considerable decreases in all interest rates, for example long-term interest rates are now below, I think, 43 basis points of what they were before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And these low rates do reflect to some extent expectations of a continuation, as I just said, of the extraordinary monetary policy support that's been extended.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Inflation is following the baseline scenario, so from that viewpoint, no more, no less.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will take a little longer than our previously forecast horizon to get to a level below 2%, but not much longer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So for the time being, the main thing was to make sure that the programme and the decisions that were taken in March can be implemented in the new constellation of interest rates, much lower interest rates, which clearly have restricted the eligibility universe, and that's why we task the committees.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So again, I can repeat, the existing projections are predicated, remain conditional, on exceptionally supportive financing conditions, which to a large extent do reflect our monetary policy, and therefore the Governing Council tasked the committees.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I remind you again that our programme is meant to run to the end of March 2017 or beyond if necessary, and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even today's discussion reiterated basically the unanimous commitment of the Governing Council to reach the inflation rate objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would say there is no question about - as I think I've said on other times - the will to act, the capacity to act, and the ability to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your first question about expectations: we're observing two types of behaviour here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the non-market based expectations, the SPF, which are by and large stable, and they tell us 0.3% for 2016, 1.2% for 2017, 1.5% for 2018, but the long-term inflation expectations remain stable at 1.8%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then we have the market-based expectations which have been trending down, I would say more markedly after Brexit, but even before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly one explanation for what happened after Brexit, or just around Brexit time, when these expectations declined considerably, one explanation is that these expectations are market-based and are based on bonds, bonds that are traded, and there have been significant market dislocations which altered the price of these bonds in a way that would not fully reflect the inflation expectation component.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But after that it's harder to explain, and it's more difficult.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also say, however, that these expectations are subject to considerable volatility, and that we have observed even in the past disconnect between the behaviour of these expectations and the behaviour of, for example, oil prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the conclusion of this reasoning is that we are monitoring these developments very closely, and we stand ready to act if we were to detect the signals that there could be second-round effects at play here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also add that all the evidence we have about probability of deflation measures, for example, they have not increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The first question relates to the effectiveness of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I don't want to go through the list of financial variables, namely interest rates, equity prices, et cetera, that have improved dramatically since the beginning of our non-conventional monetary policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me say one thing, which is probably the thing that matters most: while in the previous time we had observed fragmentation and we had observed very subdued credit developments, nowadays we can safely say that fragmentation is over; that credit is growing constantly and has been growing constantly since the beginning of 2014, month after month; that spreads that were dramatically fragmenting credit between different parts of the euro area, and different companies - between large corporates and SMEs - have vastly disappeared in the sense that they just reflect now what are risk differentials and nothing more than that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also say that from any bank lending survey, it appears that now credit is indeed reaching the non-financial sector of the economy, both for private companies and households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would conclude that our policy has been very effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And your question was, since your assumption is that it was weakly effective, then "would you consider doing more of that?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think my answer to that is, "certainly, if that's needed to reach our objective."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But suppose we had not done that, what would the situation be?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are interesting analogies here showing that, especially over the last six, seven months, the stimulus of our monetary policy basically counteracted the negative impact of shocks happening in other parts of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember at the beginning-of-the-year shocks; then we had Brexit, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we had not done that, the negative part of these shocks would have been affecting the euro area without any other factor offsetting it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question was on the negative side-effects of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, first let me reiterate that we have a mandate and the Governing Council is unanimous about complying with this mandate, which foresees the return of the rate of inflation to a level which is below but close to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, in a sense I've answered that in the first part of my answer: I would say that the transmission of our monetary policy has never worked better than it does today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see changes in interest rates in different parts of the markets that are immediately transmitted into changes in lending rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Volumes of lending, as I just said, are regularly increasing, and the surveys show both demand and supply going up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Surveys show that risk aversion is no longer a factor in lending, but it's actually competition between banks that's driving lending.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third consideration is that, some people are saying, negative interest rates would carry the risk of cash hoarding, hoarding cash.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mean, there are limited stories that obviously have a lot of coverage, but it's really not there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far - and I want to stress the so far - we have not seen that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen that, for example, bank profits went down between the first quarter of 2015 and the first quarter of 2016 by something like 20%, but they went down by 20% because in the first quarter of 2015 banks posted huge capital gains because of the beginning of our purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While, if you look at the net interest income, that stayed by and large stable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Does it mean that it's going to be this way forever?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are aware that the current situation of negative interest rates will certainly have consequences and challenges for the banks of which we have to be aware.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, a few concluding observations: first of all, I think low interest rates should not be used as the justification for everything that goes wrong with banks today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it would be a mistake to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And second, I think ultimately we've got to be patient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Interest rates have to stay low for the economic recovery to proceed, for the economic recovery to firm up, which in the end will have a positive effect on banks' balance sheets as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So as I think I said on another occasion, interest rates have to be low today to be high tomorrow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: To your first question, as I just said, right now the transmission mechanism is really working very well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the ability to make loans is not being affected by negative interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, consider that that's only one side of the story.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also have the TLTRO, and especially the TLTRO-II, which is helping the banks' balance sheet on another side.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the second question, just let me read to you the press communiqué of the G20 which just came out on September 5: "We are determined to use all policy tools - monetary, fiscal and structural - individually and collectively to achieve our goal of strong, sustainable, balanced and inclusive growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary policy will continue to support economic activity and ensure price stability, consistent with central banks' mandates, but monetary policy alone cannot lead to balanced growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Underscoring the essential role of structural reforms, we emphasise that our fiscal strategies are equally important to supporting our common growth objectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are using fiscal policy flexibly and making tax policy and public expenditure more growth-friendly, including by prioritising high-quality investment, while enhancing resilience and ensuring debt as a share of GDP is on a sustainable path."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But basically it's something I just said, I've been saying now for months: that to reap the full benefits - and I think I did say this even in the introductory statement today - to reap the full benefits of an extraordinarily accommodative monetary policy, one needs other policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They will look at all the options that might be used to redesign the programme under the new constellation of interest rates, and then we will have, of course, a discussion in the Governing Council about issues like the one you mention and others as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But for the time being they will examine - they will have a broad exam of all the options.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question: yes, indeed, we have numbers showing the impact of our monetary policy on growth and inflation over the forecast horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think - but I should check - because I don't remember them exactly - I think it's 0.5% over the forecast horizon as far as growth is concerned, and I think it's 0.3% as far as inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Or it's 0.3% and 0.5% - it's either - over the forecast horizon, from now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we should be able to give you full figures in a moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We haven't discussed either, so I can't answer the first question other than to say that we've not discussed them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The average consumer is actually the one who is now being the main actor in the recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This recovery is based - and that's why it's firmer, more robust than other recoveries we've seen in the past - it's based on consumption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Differently from past recoveries that were based more on exports, and then as soon as external conditions changed, they waned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's important, and of course the drivers of this recovery remain our very accommodative monetary policy - we in fact observe a continuation of growth in real disposable income, which of course feeds into consumption; the still relatively low oil prices; and what looks like a slightly more expansionary fiscal policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The ECB can't be in a sort of - let me say, what the ECB can do is to basically flag what is needed for monetary policy to be even more effective than it is at the present time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think what I just read from the G20 is quite a powerful statement of commitment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The G20, just to make sure you know - it's not central bankers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So they committed in their statement to use all policies - structural policies, fiscal policies, tax policy - and to make government expenditure more growth-friendly, which is something that all of you have heard me saying several times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To say, basically, that the composition of fiscal policy is as important if not more important than its size.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: After all, before the financial crisis, we have seen several countries in the eurozone increasing their government expenditure, and really drawing very little benefit in terms of output growth and employment, showing perhaps that size is not the first thing one should look at, but rather how this money is being spent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you heard me saying several times that a growth-friendly fiscal policy is one where taxes are lower, current government expenditure is lower, and investment is higher.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's encouraging to read this press communiqué because it really means a collective commitment by the governments of the G20, of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's an accumulated upward impact on GDP growth of 0.6% over the projection horizon[2], marginally above the impact entailed in the June 2016 projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In particular the September projection also entails a small impact on real GDP related to the corporate bond programme, which in the meantime has taken off the ground, and which led to a further stronger-than-expected narrowing of corporate bond spreads since June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For inflation, the cumulative impact is 0.4% over the projection horizon, in line with what was forecast in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you want to have the figures in 2015, then I'll provide you - I mean, I have the ones for June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, I can't answer positively to the first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's say we haven't discussed whether to discuss it yet or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, clearly to be in line with the recommendations of the Commission, lower surpluses, or a lower surplus for the euro area, would be welcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And certainly any action to this extent is to be welcomed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I've always been a little puzzled by the idea that is sometimes conveyed with these words.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not like we can lower the surplus if we push a button.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If an economy is naturally competitive, one can do economic policies that sort of get the benefit of this surplus and transform it into domestic aggregate demand, and I think that's the implicit recommendation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Countries that have fiscal space should use it, and countries that don't have fiscal space should instead focus - or should also focus, rather - on the composition as a primary fiscal tool.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's not - I always was kind of puzzled thinking that you can lower the surplus and then you move around these aggregate demand components: no, it doesn't work that way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: To your first question, I think Mr Schäuble was referring to world liquidity and not eurozone liquidity as such.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's very difficult to estimate what's the adequate amount of world liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It does depend on many other variables, one of which is the state of the economy, and of course for us what matters is price stability, because we have this in our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So liquidity is, if we look at that from our central bank perspective, like the size of our balance sheet, just a monetary policy instrument that we have to use for reaching our objectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is, as I said before, countries that have fiscal space should use it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer is no, I don't share it, and I'm not worried.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reason why TARGET2 balances go up following our QE has much to do with the settlement of the claims that arise with the implementation of QE.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the extent that these claims are settled by intermediaries that then redeposit this money in Germany or in the Netherlands, you will naturally see TARGET2 balances going up, and that has nothing to do with fragmentation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, it's a completely different phenomenon from what we observed in 2012 and 2011.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And frankly, the reasons why it was chosen, a 2% target, many years ago, are still there, but we didn't have this discussion yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Wage determination is a result, an outcome of the interplay of forces.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what one can make today - what central banks, what economists can make - is an indisputable case for the benefits of having higher wage growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact, because of oil prices, because of the big slack in labour market in the last few years, we had low inflation for a long time, and one of the questions we are asking ourselves is, "Is this protracted low inflation - has it filtered through wage negotiations somehow?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Either because you have indexation mechanisms, because they're formal or informal, or through the negotiation process?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If that were true, we would be extremely concerned, and we are monitoring these developments very closely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: [1]Please see below in the paragraph starting with "The Vice-President…" for the impact of monetary policy measures adopted in December 2015 and in March 2016 on growth and inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: [2]The estimates refer to the effects of monetary policy measures decided in December 2015 and March 2016 for the period 2016-2018.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is no, there was no discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In answer to the first question, it's really nothing new.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I myself and my colleagues, I think, said several times that when we speak of convergence to our objective, this convergence has to be sustainable and durable, and actually as a matter of fact should be self-sustained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, right now we're all aware that the monetary policy support that is in place is extraordinary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we know and I've said that the projections that are part of our outlook reflect financing conditions, which reflect expectations, that this support remains in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The financing conditions not only, of course, are the output of these expectations, but also of other factors - like monetary policies in other jurisdictions, but more generally of many other factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So they do reflect also the expectation that this extraordinary policy support will remain in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But does it mean that it can stay in place forever?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want a convergence which is self-sustained, in other words, without the extraordinary policy support that is in place now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, we've said several times that durable convergence means that this objective should be achieved in a sustainable and durable way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Namely, we'll look through blips that are caused by other factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me tell you that the second point was not discussed, but it's in a sense part of your first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We took stock of the ongoing technical work in the committees - work that is designed to ensure a smooth execution of the programme until March and beyond if necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We discussed various options, but options that really we consider in case we should be confronted with a shortage of purchasable bonds in some jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council reaffirmed the importance of very supportive financing conditions in fostering the recovery and a gradual return of inflation to levels close to 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Sometimes it's also important to say what we did not discuss, and we didn't discuss tapering or the intended horizon - and here comes the second question - of our asset purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by the way, the Governing Council reaffirmed that it certainly would take into account the input of the committees, but it just remains the ultimate decision-maker here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'm sorry to say, but we haven't discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We simply listened to the outcome of the committees' work and we mandated the committees to continue working.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said, the Governing Council will take as one of the inputs the committees' work but it remains the ultimate decision-maker.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: About the expectation, what's going to be in the agenda for the December meeting, we haven't really yet discussed that at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But more generally, it's quite clear that our decisions in December will tell you what we are going to do in the coming months, and so they will define the monetary policy environment for the coming weeks and the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: That was never discussed, as a matter of fact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, in a sense, why are we waiting for December?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because we want to see all the inputs that are useful to have this discussion, and that's important for having one view about which the Governing Council members can express their opinion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, to be more precise, we didn't go at all in the exercise of counting views or majorities - or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First, we briefly touched on negative rates, or low rates more generally, during the discussion we had about the current outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The conclusion was that they don't hinder the transmission of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have no evidence they actually hinder the transmission of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They have worked, like they've worked in other policy jurisdictions, and we are not the first to have low rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me give you again a few numbers, some of which you've heard before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, what would happen if rates had not been what they've been?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The numbers here are that our measures taken from 2014 to March 2016 have generated additional inflation, cumulative inflation over the 2016-2018 period of 1.4 percentage points, and 1.3 pp of additional growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is, just look at the behaviour of rates since then till now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I just spend a second on the recent BLS, the recent bank lending survey, we see that net loan demand continued to increase for all loan categories.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The credit standards continued to ease for households, and after nine months of continued easing they were unchanged for non-financial corporations, companies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And terms and conditions continued to ease, although banks expect a small tightening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The net issuance of corporate bonds in September has been very marked, and it's basically caused by our corporate bond purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lending rates are now at a historical low - that is another point that we want to remember - and the credit volumes have recovered since the beginning of 2014 from, by and large, -3% growth in 2014 to +2% growth now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as you can see the growth is still subdued.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are other important pieces of evidence that come when we look at M3, where we see that the largest contribution to the robust growth of M3 comes more and more from non-governmental sectors, namely households and firms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these are all pieces of evidence that our policy is being transmitted more and more effectively to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Bail-in rules are in place and they have enough flexibility that would allow to cope with a variety of possibilities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Commission has all the power to apply the rules and to interpret the rules according to existing legislation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, I don't see at the present time any such outcome or any such possibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other question: first of all I wouldn't make too much of that data point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's only the first data we see after a long sequence of positive data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, loan demand depends on many factors other than monetary policy, and we'll have to see what is the current economic situation concerning these two countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the aggregate of the eurozone the developments are what I outlined before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is no, we are not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All parties in doing what they do apply legislation, apply laws, apply rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: People may have different views about that, but the impression is not at all of a political war here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other point, we discussed scarcity, as I said: we had a seminar, they presented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Much of the discussion was about how to overcome scarcity if that were to become a problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The corporate bond purchase programme has been a success, so far, beyond, in fact, our expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not a current issue, but just in case, much of the discussion was around that theme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: In answer to the second question: we haven't discussed anything like that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, we simply took stock of the committees' work, and we discussed the current outlook, which hasn't changed much since the last time we met.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, I've seen the market reaction, and that's why I said that the Governing Council is the ultimate decision-maker that will use the input from the committees as one of the inputs in the discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's very difficult to answer about my expectation of a market reaction following kind of a random statement made by somebody who didn't have any clue or information about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Neither is the independence of monetary policy by the Governing Council threatened.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the inequality, we certainly have looked at that, and I think we've discussed that on other occasions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point is - and there is actually an interesting study by the Bundesbank on whether more generally non-conventional monetary policy measures increase inequality: the answer is, by and large, no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the reason is that the main source of inequality is unemployment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to the extent that monetary policy is effective, it will reduce inequality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Although as you buy assets from people who are wealthy in the short run, you certainly increase inequality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But when you look at things over the long run, no, the answer is no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On Portugal, the bonds are currently eligible as the first best rating is BBB- with a stable outlook by this rating agency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we know that if there is a downgrade, marketable debt instruments issued or guaranteed by the Republic of Portugal would become ineligible as collateral for monetary policy operations, and for purchases under the PSPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, we should acknowledge the remarkable progress that's been achieved in Portugal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, there are vulnerabilities that the government knows very well, and the government is aware that ambitious reforms are needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From our angle, there is one area that I want to highlight, which is the corporate debt restructuring and addressing the problem of the NPL, the non-performing loans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have expressed, like others, like everybody else, concerns about debt sustainability, therefore measures have to be undertaken to address this problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the Governing Council, when time will come, will assess in an independent way the debt sustainability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is that my perception is that the sudden stop, as it was outlined before, is not in anybody's mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there are many reasons, and fairly obvious reasons, why this is so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question: actually I never thought that we could profit out of sudden moves coming from unauthorised and probably uninformed sources.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have no idea whether the ECB profited out of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly I can only reiterate that profit is not the reason why we run monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As far as market expectations go, I can only, in a sense, respond by pointing to the fact that the current outlook and our baseline scenario of a rate of inflation which would gradually converge towards our objective, is predicated on the current financing conditions, which are accommodative because they are themselves based on the remaining in place, amongst other things, of the extraordinary monetary policy support offered by the ECB monetary policy, and that's it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Do I have a sense that they are complacent, or not?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think this is part of the more general category of financial stability risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We certainly continue to monitor financial markets, and so far we haven't seen evidence of bubbles.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I define a bubble as a marked rise in asset prices accompanied by a marked increase in leverage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we monitor financial stability risks; we have not seen any systemic bubble of any kind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have expressed several times the point that these bubbles ought to be coped with macroprudential instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On inflation expectations, we have two sets of inflation expectations: the survey-based inflation expectations and the market-based.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The survey-based have been by and large more stable than market-based ones, and in the long term point to 1.8%, if I'm not mistaken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The market-based inflation expectations have been more volatile as they are based on financial instruments, and therefore the market developments for these instruments do affect, in a sense, also the expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen that in the period immediately before and more markedly after the British referendum, inflation expectations by and large across all horizons have declined quite significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But then now, more recently, they are recovering their path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Though we have to be aware that certain stable pieces of evidence, like for example the correlation between inflation expectations and actual inflation, or inflation expectations and the oil price, have been themselves very volatile.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's very difficult to really draw any stable inference from these correlations at the present time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me read you the introductory statement: "Based on our regular economic and monetary analyses, we decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We continue to expect them to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time, and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I don't have to justify it; I just say that it's not true.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, both the corporate bond programme and the covered bond programme do benefit SMEs as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They have increased the issuance by large corporates, of course, but in so doing they free space in bank lending.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you can see actually that the spread between loans to SMEs and loans to large corporates has declined quite considerably.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Yes, the two options that have been presented were the ones that had been studied by the committees in the preceding months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One foresaw the option of continuing with €80 billion a month for six months, and the other one is the one that received a very, very broad consensus by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, let me say what I said during the introductory statement, but it does need some emphasis: the purchase of securities under the asset purchase programme with a yield to maturity below the interest rate on the ECB deposit facility will be permitted to the extent necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, the relevant committees will look in January and in the coming months when this could become a necessity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's more to give sort of an option for continuing the smooth implementation of the programme than for any other reason.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, about the general involvement of the ECB with the financing needs of the governments: frankly, there isn't any difference here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, first let me say that we have to go back to March 2016, when we up-sized our programme from €60 billion to €80 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that time the outlook for a sustained return to our inflation objective was much darker, and deflation risks were not immaterial at that time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So at this point in time, we basically judge that the outlook, for the sustained return to our inflation objective, is not very different from what it was at the beginning of the programme when it was scaled to €60 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And more specifically the risk of deflation has largely disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Uncertainty prevails everywhere, and we'll certainly see and assess the progress of the overall situation at the end of 2017.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But since uncertainty prevails everywhere, that's the reason for this sentence in the introductory statement that says, "If, in the meantime, the outlook becomes less favourable, or if financing conditions become inconsistent with further progress towards a sustained adjustment of the path of inflation, the Governing Council intends to increase the programme in terms of size and/or duration."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the Governing Council is acting in a pragmatic and flexible way to cope with risks that may materialise in this period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the second point, I have to refer to the committees' work on that point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, this is an option, not a necessity, and the committees will assess when and if it should become so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, the amounts of purchases and the maturities of purchases do depend on the current constellation of rates, and as this changes so it changes the necessity to buy certain maturities rather than others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, in a sense the intention, the underlying narrative of our monetary policy decisions was exactly to maintain the extraordinary degree of monetary accommodation that we have in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to this extent, without distorting prices, we'll certainly continue to exert pressure on market prices, to deliver exactly the degree of monetary accommodation that we want.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second purpose is to transmit a sense that the presence of the ECB on the markets will be there for a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So a sustained presence is also the message of today's decision, and that's why tapering was not discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that the vulnerabilities that both the banking system and Italy have have been there for a long time, and so they ought to be coped with.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm confident that the government knows what to do and they will be dealt with.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We seem to be fairly far away from any such high-class problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the word has several meanings depending on who is using it, but the natural way to look at a word like that is to have a policy whereby purchases would gradually go to zero.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, it's not even been on the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: You know that on the basis of the so-called separation principle, I have to answer your question by saying: ask the Supervisory Board for an answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is not really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to persist, and we know that there is gradual convergence to that objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the first question is that actually, as you know, the committees looked at that as well, and there was an increasing awareness of the legal and institutional constraints that would make such a change difficult, and that's why the removal of the so-called DFR [Deposit Facility Rate] floor was preferred.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, I don't have the estimates that embody today's decisions in measuring, in sizing the impact on GDP growth and inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the impact of the past decisions, which account for a cumulative 1.3 pp.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, certainly if inflation expectations continue their recovery, it will mean falling real rates, which, on one hand, will certainly have a powerful stimulative effect on the economy, and, on the other hand, will also have an impact on the real return on savings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will assess the situation in the coming months and we'll see what is the net balance of all these different effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is the situation; in a sense it's a situation that shows an improvement overall.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I should also say that in the meantime also yields on bonds are going up, and so it's not at all clear that in the end the real return on savings is actually going down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to see what happens on the nominal rate and the expectations of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is no, because the self-imposed boundaries to which Mr Mersch was referring are not the self-imposed boundary which we have removed today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the first question is that it's very difficult to assess what are the effects of these big changes, like the radically new administration - new in the way it looks at the world - in the United States, or for that matter even Brexit, or for that matter even the outcome of the Italian referendum a few days ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All three events were expected to have major effects in the world, and in all three cases, the markets, the financial intermediaries, proved much more resilient than people had expected them to be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So first of all, we know one thing: markets were more resilient, and this has probably many reasons, many causes, one of which is certainly the good work that regulators have done in the last seven, eight years to strengthen the intermediaries and the markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are also other good reasons: an overall better macroeconomic policy context.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the point is that all these events - especially Brexit and the new administration in the United States - have effects that are, by their very nature, going to develop their full dimensions in the medium to long term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we'll certainly see consequences of these changes in the medium to long term - not necessarily, as I was saying, in the short term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But these consequences are very, very difficult to assess now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's very difficult to assess what is the medium-/long-term consequence of a possible - possible - change in the US administration economic policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I should stress the possible, because we are still at a very early stage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: When I referred to dominant political uncertainty, I was not saying something extravagant or difficult or unforeseen: just look at the election calendar for the year to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Look at what's happening with the emerging market economies; look at what's happening also in some segments of the financial markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is a big uncertainty, much of which is political, and whether we can do something about that or not is an open question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think what the central banks can do is to keep a steady hand, namely to continue with the monetary accommodation that is necessary to achieve their objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, countries that need reforms have to undertake them regardless of what is the general political uncertainty, because the best way for countries to cope with this uncertainty is actually to restore growth and employment and job creation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, certainly, it can increase; it can even go back to €80 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, this number was quoted, so it's a range of options, and we will see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the key message underlying this sentence, "if, in the meantime, the outlook becomes less favourable,…" the key message is to show that there is no tapering in sight.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To show that the ECB is going to stay in the markets, to show that it will continue to exert pressure on market prices, though we don't want to distort them, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is yes, indeed, there is going to be a loss, but our mandate is to pursue price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Concerning this, the fiscal aspect, what we've said on and on, really, is that indeed other policies, one of which is fiscal policy, should also complement the action of the monetary policy in order to reap its full effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we also put emphasis all the time on the composition of the budget, in the sense of making it more growth-friendly, which basically means lower taxes, lower current government expenditures, higher investment expenditure targeted to productivity-enhancing investments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the size is concerned, it really depends on whether the countries have fiscal space or not, and we always stress the fact that fiscal policy should respect the Stability and Growth Pact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we always use the wording: it's the anchor of stability or credibility in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the reason for this is that, if you look, well designed rules, if they are complied with, are essential for two reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They give credibility to the governments that comply with these rules, and even perhaps more importantly, they increase trust between governments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And why is it so important that this trust is there?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's very important because when we talk about further steps towards deeper integration in our monetary union, these further steps are based on trust, and these further steps are necessary to complete our monetary union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can do so, and therefore make our union stronger, only if there is trust between governments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to the second question is no, of course, I'm not biased, and I think we've given plenty of evidence that the policy of the ECB - first of all, it's decided by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are there not as representatives of our countries - me less than everybody else, of course - but also we are there in our personal capacity, and our mandate is not to ensure some sort of national objective, but to ensure the price stability objective for the whole of the euro area, and that's what we have done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Incidentally, our policies are not very different from the policies that are being put in place by all the large central banks in the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, at this point in time frankly we don't see risk for the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I was saying before, the broader macroeconomic context is better than it was five years ago when we had contagion, but also financial markets and financial intermediaries are stronger.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these problems, though very important, though very urgent - and therefore they should be addressed with effectiveness and speed - remain contained within the individual countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, having said that, since I mentioned before that trust is one condition for our union to proceed, to progress towards a more complete, as one would say more perfect, monetary union, there's another condition that's also essential, and that's convergence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Countries need to converge, and in order to converge they have to undertake these structural reforms that would enhance convergence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And some of these reforms in some countries, each country has its own agenda for these reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fact that structural reforms and convergence are being pursued in various countries is important, not necessarily because it causes risks for the euro but because it strengthens our monetary union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We've been discussing this for, now, a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our view is actually that easing monetary conditions should help undertaking reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the structural reforms that have been undertaken in the euro area after the sovereign crisis were actually undertaken when interest rates were low, had already been low for a while.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, we should ask ourselves what sort of structural reforms are in a sense related to the level of interest rates prevailing in the markets?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reforms that have to do mostly with budgetary needs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Take the pension reform: it's quite clear that if market conditions are overstressed and countries have or are about to lose market access, unless they make their debt profile sustainable, in that case the level of interest rates certainly produces a pressure to change, to reform in the direction of making debt more sustainable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are many other structural reforms equally if not more important in the long run, like reform of the educational system, reform of the judiciary, the reform of the electoral system - take the case of Italy - the reform of the constitution, that have nothing to do with the level of interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So even logically there isn't such a tight link with the level of interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also we have internal research, as a matter of fact, that shows that there is no such link between the level of interest rates and therefore the degree of accommodation of our monetary policy and the willingness of governments to undertake the needed structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I must confess I know very, very little about this ESM loan to Italy for the banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just give you Article number 3 of the ESM.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It says, "The following criteria and hierarchy of prior actions shall be met in order for a request for financial assistance for the purpose of recapitalising financial institutions to be considered eligible: the beneficiary should demonstrate the existence of a lack of alternatives for recapitalising the financial institutions concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This should first reveal an inability to meet capital shortfalls via private-sector solutions, and secondly an inability of the beneficiary ESM member to recapitalise said institutions without incurring very adverse effects on its own financial stability and fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, the financial institutions concerned should have a systemic relevance or pose serious threat to the financial stability of the euro area as a whole, and the beneficiary ESM member shall demonstrate its ability to reimburse the loan granted," and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It basically shows that it's a rather complex thing, and it shows also that I know very little about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'll tell you what happened today: it was not discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: To some extent I've dwelt on these arguments before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We went back to when we increased the size in March, and we asked ourselves what were the conditions of the economy at that time, what were the prospects of a sustained return to our objective of inflation, what were the risks of potential deflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And at that time we thought that raising to €80 billion would have been an answer to the concerns that we shared, that the Governing Council had at that time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in deciding the new scale, the new size of €60 billion, we simply went back.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We just went through the same analysis, an account of which I've given, in a sense, during the introductory statement in various parts of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we also saw that the risks of deflation, the inflation distribution are much more skewed towards out of deflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second reason is the length of time, and that's where we wanted to assure a sustained presence in the economy, in the markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to assure that the ECB will continue to exert pressures on market prices, though as I said we don't want to distort them, and we want to assure that a reduction in size doesn't mean at all, as I said before, any tapering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's the logic behind the choice of €60 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I say, the programme remains flexible, and the flexibility is stated by the sentence that I read before, starting: If in the meantime, the outlook becomes less favourable, ….

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, it's an important change after many years that oil prices had gone down to, I believe, an unprecedented extent; now they're rising again, and the explanations are, in a sense, symmetric to what were the explanations for their downfall.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Namely, better demand conditions, better supply conditions, and to some extent, I think a significant extent, the reestablishment of some international agreements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no question that these higher prices will feed into higher headline inflation, though we have to see how this is going to be - and it's exactly the same considerations, I remember, as I was doing in the other direction two or three years ago - we have to see to what extent this is a one-off effect, to what extent it will have secondary effects, and to what extent this will affect inflation excluding energy which we are not seeing yet any effect of on it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said there is no sign of convincing upward trend in the underlying inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, as a matter of fact our programme says it goes until the end of December 2017 or beyond if necessary, and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the repo market, as you know, we've taken important decisions on the securities lending programme, and we decided that cash will be accepted as collateral for the PSPP securities lending programme, up to the limit of €50 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And details as far as this is concerned will be announced at 3:30 p.m. today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far the repo market is concerned, we are aware of the ongoing developments in the euro area repo market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue monitoring the developments, but the PSPP securities lending framework is sufficiently robust to ensure a continued smooth functioning of the repo markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are aware that our purchase programme has contributed, among other relevant factors, to increase the repo rates used to obtain collateral of the best credit quality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But despite these price increases, repo market volumes continue to signal functioning repo markets and price discovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So while we don't have any indication that higher prices for some specific types of collateral are hampering the transmission of our monetary policy, we have nevertheless discussed what the ECB could do, and I just announced one of the things that will be detailed in the 3:30 p.m. announcement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, you asked me whether it's still a high-class problem and the answer is yes, it still is a high-class problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point, really it's very early for us to comment on the to-be President Trump's statements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The only thing that I can recall as far as exchange rates are concerned is something that you heard me say many times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The exchange rates for us are not a target but they are important for price stability and growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a very strong international consensus in the G20 and the G7 to refrain from competitive devaluations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is a whole protocol in the various statements by the G20 and the G7 that basically states how countries should behave with respect to exchange rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, the answer to the first question lies in what we define as our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We define our objective first of all in the medium term, over a medium-term horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, it has to be a durable convergence, so it cannot be transient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, it has to stay there even when the extraordinary monetary policy support that we are providing today will not be there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fourth, it has to be defined for the whole of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think these are the four features that always characterised our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, I simply say again it's too early to say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The final outcome of the negotiations will be very important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also, whether it will have economic consequences will depend on the shape of the outcome and the length of time it will take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to the second question is actually given by our decision in buying below the DFR rate at shorter maturity, the details of which will be released in the press statement I mentioned before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That has greatly enlarged the eligible universe and we are confident about the smooth implementation of our programme, so we see actually no problems on that front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The whole strategy will be, as I said, delineated in the press statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we stand ready to upgrade the strategy or to revise the strategy as needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also these purchases below the DFR rate, don't forget, will happen if needed, if they are required.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now on the other point, it's too early to say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me say one thing about the Governing Council of today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The discussion was unanimous in looking back at the monetary policy decisions taken in December and stating that they were the right policy answer to the contingencies as viewed, as estimated in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More generally there was a sense of satisfaction towards the monetary policy stance that we have been pursuing now since 2014.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's increasingly clear that this policy stance had been successful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have seen that since 2015 we had each and every quarter GDP growth between 0.3 and 0.6% quarter-on-quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen that in December 2016, consumers' confidence is the highest since April 2015.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Economic Sentiment Index is the highest since March 2011.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The PMI composite output index is the highest since May 2011.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Unemployment in November last year was 9.8%, the lowest since July 2009.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So by and large, the euro area has created four and a half million new jobs over the last three years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More directly related to the question you asked, we've seen that the dispersion of the value-added growth across countries is at an all-time low since 1997.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that gives us a sense that if there are heterogeneities - and there are indeed - in the speed with which we are approaching our objective, they can be coped with.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, we see that inflation is mostly driven by energy prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see the underlying inflation pressures remaining subdued and especially nominal wage growth remains subdued.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On top of that we see, as I mentioned in the introductory statement, the risk coming from the global uncertainty situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the response to the first question is we haven't discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the second question, actually if you are referring to the very last statement by Minister Schäuble, he actually said that there are political problems in explaining the monetary policy stance of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I would say is basically the same thing I've been saying now for a few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Low rates are necessary now to get higher rates in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The recovery of all of the eurozone is in the interests of everybody, including Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The German savers have benefited, not only as savers but also as borrowers, as entrepreneurs, as workers - like all the other citizens of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to be patient; as recovery will firm up, real rates will go up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, since our last decisions in December, however, there is more room to diversify into the medium long-term spectrum of the yield curve gaining actually a better rate and a very short-term one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is in a sense, if anything, what you would call the rate of return conditions have improved in the last month and a half.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But really an honest answer would be, just be patient; as the recovery will firm up, real rates will go up as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This will happen for Germany and for other countries as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I just won't make any comment on that; it's just too early.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's see what are the real policies following these statements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'd rather comment on policies and policy actions than just statements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, as I said last time, it wasn't tapering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Or we didn't even discuss high-class problems of the kind that I was asked before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is true that when and if - well, I'm pretty sure that it will come, the time - and then we will have to have a very deep and very careful discussion and analysis of the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, we don't have - how do you say it - public admissions of guilt, Mao Chinese style, as a way of working; we simply had a discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was a general satisfaction that the policy is working.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I gave you a few signs that it's working, a few data, but there are other data; for instance the increase in the market-based [inflation] expectations, as you've seen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The survey-based expectation measures also increased, although they are stable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's interesting; they increased in the short term but they are stable in the long term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the risk of deflation according to any measure has largely disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The lending rates for households and companies have declined significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other thing, by the way, we pay a lot of attention to exactly because of the question I had before about heterogeneity - diversity in the progress towards our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We pay a lot of attention also to the cross-country heterogeneity of loan rates and that has gone down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even more interestingly, the balance sheet repair for non-financial companies has actually improved markedly over the last few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In general, more specifically the non-financial corporation, non-financial companies' leverage has gone down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also all this says basically that the conditions for the transmission of our monetary policy have improved, but all this doesn't mean that we can relax.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council is aware that it will have to keep this present extraordinary monetary policy support as necessary to achieve our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even though inflation has increased markedly, we know it's mostly driven by energy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point in time, the Governing Council decided to look through it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can ask the Vice-President, who is responsible for financial stability, if he has comments on that statement - or whether it's true, actually.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: No, I don't think so because the present legislation that is in place is being applied in all its details; that's the straight and true answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, in the BRRD there are in Article 32 number 4 item D conditions safeguarding questions of financial stability that can be used.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are in the law so they are in accordance with the rules that have been defined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Unfortunately on neither; I cannot comment on either of the two questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't ask my colleague, Danièle Nouy, to comment on our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me say about the inflation outlook: headline inflation in December increased markedly because of base effects and also because of higher oil prices, higher than expected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the outlook for headline inflation over the next quarter or two quarters maybe is higher than it was foreseen in the previous macroeconomic projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The key question now is what is the extent of second-round effects coming from this higher inflation?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, in so doing, we do exactly what we've done in the past when inflation was going down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll ask ourselves the questions whether the four features of our convergence process towards our objective are actually satisfied, the ones I mentioned before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to enter into the issue whether higher nominal wages certainly are positive from our viewpoint.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as you know, wages are being negotiated by the parts, by the social partners.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the central bank doesn't have a say in this, other than saying that a higher rate of growth of nominal wages certainly would move towards our objective of an inflation rate close but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However we should also look at productivity, how productivity performs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to the question is no because our objective is the inflation rate below, but close, to 2% for the whole of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: How likely - and that is in a sense the same answer I gave to the previous question - is it going to be that these divergences will be unmanageable?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We judge it not so likely; we think that these divergences will be managed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen if anything all these divergences narrowing down over the last two, three years and they will continue doing so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I think the important thing to explain is that the recovery of the whole of eurozone is in the interests of the German citizens as well as in the interests, of course, of all the agencies of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The present situation of very low or negative real rates will disappear as the recovery will come and will disappear faster as the recovery will come faster.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, it's also important to explain that benefits have accrued to all citizens of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Benefits coming from our monetary policy have accrued to all citizens of the eurozone, including the German citizens.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can see this no matter where you look; savers, borrowers, entrepreneurs, employees, workforce and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We don't see any country's debt as being unsustainable, so that's one answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course in the case of Greece there is a programme, there is a negotiation between member states, the IMF and the Greek government - and you know everything about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I will answer to the second question just pointing out to the experience you saw in the last five years and even before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've given plenty of evidence of being able to act in an independent fashion, bound only by our mandate, which is to have price stability, to pursue price stability as defined as an objective of inflation rate below, but close, to 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we've given plenty of evidence of being able to act independently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But basically, some of these questions have to impinge exactly on this point and I think the evidence is strongly in our favour.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, if you go back three, four years ago and you ask yourself which policies were in place that could actually create jobs and expand economic activity, then you see that the recovery gradually firmed up driven by consumption and investment thanks to the extraordinary financing conditions that the monetary policy of the ECB has created.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Probably not; probably there are other things if we look around.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But first of all understand we are biased, of course, in saying that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But even if we were unbiased, it's basically the most evident outcome of our policy that by itself pursues price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's exactly in achieving that objective that these jobs were created.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Answering firstly your second question, I spoke about recalibration because before I think it was March last year, the monthly flow of purchases was 60 billion euros because the conditions were such that would justify that amount.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then again we assessed the outlook in December and we downsized, so we recalibrated that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there was no tapering and what we're going to do in the future was not discussed today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, forward guidance has been one of the important parts of our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It gave a sign of a transparent reaction function by the central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's been very important in anchoring inflation expectations at the time especially when there was a danger they could become de-anchored.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have to judge in the oncoming inflation developments is essentially the underlying inflation pressures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words: whether the higher headline inflation, driven mostly by energy prices, translates its pass-through in an underlying inflation so that the overall inflation rate leads to a process that is durably and self-sustainingly converging to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's the assessment that the Governing Council will have to make in the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, let me give you the substance of the discussion we had at this Governing Council and in so doing, I will also answer your points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's actually been built, if one was to summarise, on three blocks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one is the acknowledgement of success; namely our monetary policy has been successful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me give you just a few numbers of why we say that and how we measure the success.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Since 2015 real GDP growth has been steady at between 0.3 and 0.6% quarter-on-quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Economic Sentiment Index in February this year is the highest since 2011.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The PMI composite output index, again this February 2017, is the highest since April 2011.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The unemployment rate in January was 9.6%; it's the lowest since May 2009.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Employment-wise, well, I said last time that in the last three years, four million jobs have been created.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, in fact it's more than four million jobs because there's been a recent revision in the number of employment figures in Germany, so it's even more than four million.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, incidentally, in just giving you these numbers about employment, let me add, those who had doubts about the equity of our asset purchase programme are being answered because the most equitable measure of all is to create employment and to decrease unemployment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The recovery broadened further in the last quarter last year across sectors and across countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The interesting thing which is continuing - I think I remarked about that last time - is that the dispersion of value-added growth across countries reached an all-time low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, countries seemed to grow more together; an all-time low since 1997.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
