text: If we move to inflation, I would say that risks of deflation have largely disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also those are longer-term horizons even though they are still below the level that is considered to be adequate for pronouncing victory on the inflation front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The financing conditions and credit demand have continued to improve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lending rates for households and companies have declined significantly by more than our key interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The cross-country heterogeneity - you remember the time when we had fragmentation - we had countries where our lower interest rates were not passed on to or through lower lending rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example loan rates in Italy and Spain have declined more than in Germany and France.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The borrowing conditions for SMEs have improved and the firms' demand for loans has increased considerably.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also very important, the NFCs' - the non-financial companies' - leverage has gone down quite significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, let me give you a final estimate of the impact of our monetary policy measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the three years between 2016 and 2019, the accumulated impact of our policy measures is 1.7percentage points on inflation and 1.7 percentage points on growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's basically the assessment that inspired the interventions of the Governing Council members; namely acknowledged the success of our policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second block was the one that you just heard me saying in the introductory statement; namely the appropriateness of the present monetary policy stance upon which these projections are based.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So based on current information, the monetary policy stance that I have just read in the introductory statement is considered appropriate by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third block was a discussion about risks, about the economic situation, how it has evolved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again there was a general recognition that the balance of risk has improved certainly as far as growth is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So following from this, it's quite clear that the assessment of certain scenarios that were considered very likely before is now telling us that these scenarios are going to become less likely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That had some consequences in our language; namely there was a sentence which has been removed from my introductory statement that used to say, "If warranted, to achieve its objective the Governing Council will act by using all the instruments available within its mandate".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's been removed, basically, to signal that there is no longer that sense of urgency in taking further actions while maintaining the accommodative monetary policy stance including the forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that urgency that was prompted by the risks of deflation isn't there; that was the judgement, the assessment of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second issue on which I would like to draw your attention is, as you know, the TLTROs are going to expire.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was no discussion about having another TLTRO, not at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we had - not an intense - but just a cursory discussion about whether to remove the word 'lower' from the forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, also before I get to that, let me tell you what I said in this press conference in March 2016.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said from today's perspective, and taking into account the support of our measures to growth and inflation, we don't anticipate that it will be necessary to reduce rates further.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course new facts can change the situation and the outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I'm saying this just to emphasise it's not a dramatic choice whether to keep or to remove it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the end, the Governing Council, given the fact that we can't yet say that we are there with a self-sustained inflation rate, preferred to keep this option in the language.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will continue to look through changes in HICP inflation to the extent that they are transient and without implication for medium-term outlook for price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, on the first question, I only remarked it was not discussed at all as a sign of the improved climate, so no member of the Governing Council felt the need to even mention this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, very much in the spirit of our forward guidance, it's there and it's potentially an instrument that could be used if the economic situation will warrant that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, there is no ideological or institutional or legal obstacle to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, well, frankly I don't see that; there are tensions but not anything that is that serious.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In any event, I've said it on and on; we are ready, the euro is irrevocable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And more than my words - we can discuss it further if you want - but the commitment first of all should be the experience we had by the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Incidentally, in the last full Eurobarometer more than 70% of the people in the euro area are in favour of maintaining the euro and this percentage is increasing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the midst of the crisis, three countries joined the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The euro is being perceived as being the prerequisite of the single market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there is no single market, there is no European Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Countries, no matter what their views are, have greatly benefited from the single market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all this speaks in favour - and especially also after the experience of 2012 - of looking at these developments with great attention, but no anxiety.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, I simply reported on the discussion; it's not a matter of being convinced or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One thing that one has to understand is that this is a gradual process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council members want to be convinced that they actually see a self-sustained adjustment in inflation rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said it in the introductory statement; there are no convincing signs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here, yes, "This reflected mainly this higher headline inflation, strong increase in annual energy and unprocessed food price inflation, with no signs yet of convincing upward trend in underlying inflation".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So at the same time, the projections are conditional on the full implementation of the monetary policy measures that I have just read out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I was saying we have acknowledged the progress on the growth front, on the recovery front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are pretty confident that, as this will proceed, this slack will close, the labour market conditions will improve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll start seeing that wage growth, which is the lynchpin of a self-sustained increase in inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the key variable that we should look at; it's not the only one but it's certainly key.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not that one is convinced or unconvinced all of a sudden.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are confident that we are progressing and we see we can actually assess the success of our decisions through the numbers that I have just given you on growth, on employment, on credit markets, on financing, on inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the other point, I don't want to speculate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The forward guidance now is this one and based on current information that's what it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It says that, "Until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in inflation, net asset purchases will continue at a monthly pace of €60 billion, until December 2017 or beyond if necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The interest rates" - where is it - yes, in the beginning it says, "Based on our regular economic and monetary analysis we've decided to keep the key ECB rates unchanged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We continue to expect them to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I remark here, it's an expectation; we expect them to remain at present or lower levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, as I said, the probability of an expectation that will actually materialise into lower level has gone down, given what I just said about the rest, about the progress we've made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the forward guidance, the Governing Council has decided to keep this forward guidance exactly as it stood before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think there is any merit in attacking Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First let me say that by the way, I have discussed this; I've answered the same question in European Parliament.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The currency of Germany is the euro and the euro area's monetary policy is conducted by the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB is independent as laid down in the European treaties and in the Statute.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The exchange rate of the euro is determined by market forces, which is consistent with the long-standing commitment of the international community to market-determined exchange rates as reiterated both at the G7 and at G20.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In its latest report to Congress released on October 14, 2016, the US Treasury itself stressed that Germany does not manipulate the currency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me give you the quotes, "The Treasury has found in his report that no economy satisfied the criteria, including Germany, for being called a currency manipulator".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second quote, "Germany has both a significant bilateral trade surplus with the United States and a current account surplus well above the material threshold".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the European Central Bank has not intervened in foreign currency since 2011.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we did it, we did it as part of a concerted intervention in order to stabilise the yen following Japan's earthquake and the tsunami.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is, I think, the answer to your point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, if we look at where the [real] effective exchange rate stands today with respect to historical average, we don't see especially that the euro is off the historical average.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the [real] effective exchange rate of the dollar is off the historical average.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it means that it's not the euro, which is the culprit for this situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, in your first question you're asking me how the consensus changes from time to time and meeting to meeting; I actually don't have a meter to measure that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, I think I gave you a fair account of what was discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nuances might have been different but I don't think - and in any event, I am not able to compare the degree of consensus today with the degree of consensus last time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But you asked me an even more difficult question; you're asking me to remember what the consensus was two years or three years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, on the first point I really don't have much to say; it's an entirely wholly political judgement here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is clearly the need to work more together because the nature of the problems that have presented to the European countries are - all of them, I would say - supranational problems.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, given that the political situations in different countries are different, it may well happen that countries are not equally ready to move together towards working together.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I guess that's where the reference to a multi-speed Europe comes from.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The acknowledgement that certain groups of countries, either because they perceive that their problems are closer to their own entity or because they are more willing to work together, are readier than others to do this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So my understanding of this is that whatever arrangement could be found, it is not clear yet which specific area would be addressed by this arrangement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But whatever arrangement could be found is going to be an open arrangement; namely ready to welcome any other country that would like to join.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I don't know enough about the specificities of this statement to elaborate more than that; perhaps I will know more tonight.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other point is about the distortions in the German market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, we've observed and we are monitoring them quite closely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We asked ourselves, what could be the reasons, the causes for these interest rate movements?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in a quite preliminary stage of our analysis so what I'm going to tell today is just very provisional.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are several causes; one is that certainly the German short-term bonds, more generally all the German bond market is viewed as a safe haven.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there have been flows towards this market and there has been what we call a flight-to-quality phenomenon as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if we limit our attention to the short-term segment, on top of that we see that the German short-term bonds are equivalent to putting money in the deposit facility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the share of those who don't have access to the deposit facility invest into German bonds, short-term bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why we have low yields in the cash bond market on the short term, but not in the repo market because investors are different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other cause, of course, is our purchase programme, but to assess the relative weight, it's still too early.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first two causes seem to be pretty relevant, pretty significant - perhaps more significant than our asset purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But perhaps we want to come back on this next time to have a definite view on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: In our introductory statement there is a reference to geopolitical risk or geo-global risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I am saying this because that's certainly a relevant risk source that we have taken into account in our discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If one wants to assess the balance of risk as it has been evolving over say the five, six months we would say that the domestic sources of risk have been more contained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The importance of domestic risk has decreased and the geopolitical global risk share of importance, if anything, has gone up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is a fair assessment - although we've got to be very, very careful about this assessment because our experience of the last year and a half has been that we were expecting some significant economic impact from the various risks that have been materialising.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember the Brexit, you remember the Italian referendum, you remember the new US administration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, these risks, some of them have materialised but we haven't seen yet a significant economic impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are all asking ourselves - there are certain risks that are unambiguously negative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that certain of these events - and I don't want to point out which one - will produce in the medium term a negative consequence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But so far, almost a year and a half has passed from the British referendum - perhaps I am not sure I'm right - but about eight months, nine months, yes and we haven't seen yet a consequence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't know yet how these risky events will reverberate on the economic situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, well, I think it's important to reiterate the commitments that were undertaken by our leaders and by our finance ministers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just read; the last one was on July 24, 2016 by the G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in Chengdu, "We reiterate that excessive volatility and disorderly movements in exchange rates can have adverse implications for economic and financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We reaffirm our previous exchange rate commitments including that we will refrain from competitive devaluations and we will not target our exchange rates for competitive purposes".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, a statement like this - or statements to this extent - have been the pillar of the stability that has accompanied world growth in the last 20 years and longer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's very important that these commitments or commitments of this type are being reaffirmed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But by and large, if I can repeat what I said before, the original formulation of the forward guidance maintained a certain amount of flexibility just in case certain very negative scenarios were to materialise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From today's perspective, based on the information we have today, these scenarios have become more unlikely to materialise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is relatively narrow if compared to the broadness of the issues that are going to be discussed by the finance ministers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We operate, we work and we craft our international position based on pursuing our mandate of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So even in international fora we look at what conditions internationally are supportive of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I don't have any message at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on your first point let me be clear; if we go back to when the euro was created there have always been people who said, oh, it's wrong, it's a mistake, cannot be done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They still were saying the same during the life of the euro and they are saying the same today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I find this position - and that will tell you in which way I am concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, not so much by the market developments, which I said before we look at and monitor with attention but without anxiety.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in a different way the euro, I was saying before, has been the cornerstone, the pillar upon which the single market could survive and could prosper and could increase prosperity of the member countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So without a single market, there is no European Union so that's why it's unrealistic to think anything different from the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Especially now that all European countries face geopolitical challenges - terrorism, migration, security challenges - the euro is a channel for solidarity across some of its members.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The leaders have expressed their clear intention to work together.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I recalled before even in the midst of a crisis three countries - Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania - joined the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was of course because of the direct benefits that such membership could bring, but also because of a sense of solidarity that such a membership would entail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to cut it short, the euro is here to stay.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the question is not so much if it's irrevocable - it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But then a more productive line of thinking would be, how do we make sure that we can increase prosperity, make it function better, this monetary union?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the course of its history you can see that many things have been done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, always in facing critical moments we tend to underplay our achievements in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in fact if you look at the Stability and Growth Pact, if you look at the SSM, if you look at the ESM, if you look at the extraordinary shows of solidarity that countries have shown towards members that were crossing - were being in a state of crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other side you can also recall the extraordinary efforts of the countries that were in a programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all this tells us that the commitment of the European and euro member countries' leaders to the euro is very, very strong.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we should ask ourselves, what can we do better to make the euro more resilient, stronger in facing a crisis?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course you know the way the ECB thinks about that, but there are many other routes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that today more than ever the situation is open to further progress.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear it has to be made more resilient; I think everybody would agree with that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Responding to the second question, we are - as you say, to use your words - more optimistic about the growth forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to see how these improved prospects as far as growth is concerned and the recovery and strengthening and broadening of the recovery, as I've said before, translate into higher headline inflation, into an inflation that satisfies the four features that were mentioned at the beginning: namely convergence to our objective of an inflation rate which is close but below 2%; that is a durable convergence, namely in the medium term so not transient; that is self-sustained, in other words a convergence that can stay there without this extraordinary monetary accommodation that's in place; and of course an inflation rate that meets the objective for all countries and not for one country only.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we haven't seen yet how these better prospects have translated and the reason why we haven't seen I've mentioned it before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's that we haven't seen yet any significant development on the wages front; that is the key point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think as I said, it's not the only point but it's one important element of our assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the other point, as you may imagine this question was asked at the time of the OMT, at the time of the London speech in 2012.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, the mandate of the ECB stays what it is; namely pursue price stability and make sure the conditions in which our work to pursue price stability is going to be successful, not more than that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, answering your second question, our bond purchase programme is on track both time-wise and quantity-wise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have no reason to be worried about this at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the other point, well, it's actually quite important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I was commenting before on the commitments that were concerning the exchange rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I can say the same about the commitments on keeping an open trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They have been the pillars of world prosperity for many, many years, many decades and so it's quite important that G20 reaffirms this commitment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know of the rumours but I don't know what to say about that, where they come from, whether it's true or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question first: we actually don't do monetary policy based on likely election outcomes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, we actually had a discussion exactly on the balance of risks, as far as growth is concerned, not inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And some of the members had, I would say, a more sanguine view of the economic situation, and others, while acknowledging that there have been improvements, on which I will say a few words later on, in the growth outlook, believed that such improvements would not warrant any change in communication as far as the balance of risks is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the end, the Governing Council agreed about this language that basically says - the one I've read before - that says the risks surrounding the euro area growth outlook, while moving towards a more balanced configuration, are still tilted to the downside and relate predominantly to global factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember that in a previous formulation we only said they remain tilted on the downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the Governing Council agreed about this, and I should say all members of the Governing Council agreed about this formulation, so we can actually speak of unanimity in this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also add that as far as inflation or risks to inflation outlook are concerned, there weren't really differing views.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The behaviour of inflation as it stands was basically shared by everybody.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As I said at the time, we don't comment on politicians' statements about our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Only to say that it's pretty ironic to hear these comments from people who've supported independence of monetary policy and the independence of the central bank all throughout.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Headline inflation declined stronger than expected in March, reflecting lower inflation rates for all main components, and underlying inflation remained subdued.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The short-term outlook was revised down due to lower oil prices and a weaker starting point for underlying inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Indicators of pipeline pressures show tentative signs of build-up of producers' prices and upward pressure at the early stages of the pricing chain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Wage growth has been picking up slightly from a very subdued level, yet the outlook for wage growth remains uncertain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So market-based expectations - well, we can talk about market-based expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in terms of my criteria, the assessment hasn't really changed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The criteria are basically that the inflation paths should converge towards our aim of an inflation rate of below but close to 2%; it should be a durable convergence, so not essentially produced by transient factors like we've seen in the headline inflation recently; very importantly, it should be self-sustained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The present inflation path is predicated on maintaining the strong monetary accommodation in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Self-sustained means that it will stay there even without such strong monetary accommodation on our side.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And of course the inflation we talk about has to relate to the whole of the eurozone and not one country only.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'm not sure I get the logic of the second question, but I'll try to answer that anyway.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, on the first question, the sequencing: I don't think there is any need to discuss this now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not seen any evidence, or any sufficient evidence, to alter our assessment about the inflation outlook, and we are not sufficiently confident that inflation will converge to levels consistent with our inflation aim in a durable, self-sustaining manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from today's standpoint there is no reason to deviate from the indications we have been consistently providing in the introductory statement to this press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me also just repeat what I said in thespeech at the ECB Watchers conference:

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "The Governing Council deems the current stance fully appropriate, it confirmed at its last meeting that net asset purchases will continue until the end of December 2017, or beyond… This implies that our various policy instruments are deliberately chained together in such a way that the forward guidance applied to our asset purchase programme - which is time- and state-dependent - extends also to our interest rate policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So our forward guidance is de facto on the entire package, not on any specific component of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this guidance relates not just to the conditions under which we would withdraw stimulus - i.e.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: the sustained adjustment in the path of inflation - but also to the sequence of measures we would use to do so."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, from today's perspective, the negative rates in conjunction with the other elements of our easing package, have turned out to be powerful in terms of easing financial conditions, and the potential negative side effects have so far been limited."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The current wording of our forward guidance reflects exactly this assessment of side effects, and from today's standpoint I don't see cause to deviate from the indications we've been consistently providing in the introductory statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second question, if I can rephrase it: is the experience we had in 2011 going to be repeated today?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In 2011, we forget, but we actually had a high rate of inflation for several months, above 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are now not having a high rate of inflation above 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We actually have a very subdued underlying inflation rate and volatile headline inflation led by developing oil prices and unprocessed food prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, you're right in a sense that there is one sentence less, but this one is there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On page 2 you have: "Moreover, the ongoing volatility in headline inflation underlines the need…"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you read the end of page 1, beginning of page 2…

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, the one that is not equal exactly like in the last statement is the balance of risks sentence, which repeated twice that the risks remained tilted on the downside in the last statement, and you can find it only once on the second page.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We don't have an estimate of the NAIRU at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We base our estimates on a variety of indicators, so in this sense we avoid the trap of being linked to a precise number which depends on a variety of factors, and we use a fairly wide range of indicators to inspire and inform our policy-making.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you remember in 2013 we were speaking of a recovery which was fragile and uneven, and now it's solid and broad.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the important point is also that this recovery has broadened, which wasn't the case before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know - I think I've hinted at that or explained that on other occasions - we have a dispersion index of value-added growth, showing value-added growth in different countries and now it's at a historical minimum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The unemployment rate is at the lowest since May 2009, though it's still at 9.5%, and this may tell something about the need to do structural reforms, because there's no doubt that some of this unemployment is structural and not cyclical.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the employment figure is even more impressive: euro area employment increased by almost 5 million jobs over the last three and a half years, offsetting virtually all of the employment losses seen over the crisis period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, incidentally, here, the employment creation should benefit the poorer households, so this is a response to those who were criticising our asset purchase programme as increasing inequality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no better measure to improve equality than increasing employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in fact consumption, which is the primary driver of this recovery, is led by an increase in real disposable income, which is led not so much by wage increases, but by employment gains.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Market-based inflation expectations, however, have shown a behaviour - they had been increasing until February; then they declined; now they kind of seem to be there, and they do reflect an underlying behaviour of the inflation risk premium, which in turn reflects mostly developments outside the eurozone, in the United States, and perhaps some political uncertainty everywhere.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, the survey-based measures suggest the long-term inflation expectations have remained anchored.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also the financing conditions and credit demand are going well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you think the growth rate of credit has increased by five percentage points - going from negative to positive, by the way - in the last three or four years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also one of the symptoms of fragmentation, which was the difference in loan rates, both funding rates for banks and lending rates, now has somewhat disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically the spreads do by and large reflect different risk situations, risk premia.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even leverage to some extent has decreased, especially in the private sector, in the NFC part.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all in all the improvements are there, have been continuing, have been broadening, but we still have many fragilities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of which, speaking of leverage, is given by the fragility in the banking sector and the NPL stocks in many countries that could have a much higher credit growth had it not been for the NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is no, it doesn't affect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are young enough in our mental processes that we can make a difference between facts, assessments and history.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we judge and take our decisions based on the facts and on the analysis of the outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The discussion focused really on the balance of risk concerning growth, not inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your question is related to what we call easing biases, both the lower and the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, the easing biases are meant to cope with tail risks concerning the inflation rate, not growth directly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that as growth perspectives improve, certainly the probability of these tail risks may go down, but we are not there yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have to accept the fact that the security lending is a decentralised activity that's carried out by the different national central banks, according to common guidelines of course, but it's carried out by different national central banks, not [only] at the ECB level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the main conclusion is that it would be premature to react or make policy decisions based on future policies pursued by the US administration at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We could say that one thing, perhaps - but one has to be very tentative in this - one thing that may have come out of the meetings is that perhaps the risk of protectionism, trade protectionism, may have somewhat receded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is that certainly markets are in the course - not us, but markets - are in the course of reassessment of the US fiscal policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, you answered it yourself: we look at averages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is not expressed in any individual country's inflation - by the way, growth is not part of our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is price stability, and that is expressed in terms of the rate of inflation for the whole of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the support for the euro, at least according to the latest Eurobarometer estimates, remains pretty high.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's 70% across the euro area and it's more than 50% in all countries, each and every one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So according to this measure, the support for the euro is still very strong.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To ignore the social uneasiness would also be a mistake, and I think both the IMF and especially the European Commission are quite right about being aware and alert to this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear now, everybody would acknowledge, that globalisation had extraordinary benefits but also created losers that were not taken into account for several years and were not considered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the Commission especially, I think rightly so, doesn't at all backtrack from the benefits of globalisation; that would not be the right way to go.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly it should have a much greater social consideration for the ones who don't gain or actually get harmed by globalisation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I will answer the second question: the answer is no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Going to the first question, first, some structural reforms have been undertaken in the past few years in several countries in the eurozone, so the picture is not uniformly bleak.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's also true that of recent, the pace has slowed down, and I'll say a word why this is so, but just to give you an example of why they're so necessary: one of the problems that the eurozone - Europe in general - has is low productivity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's now quite established that the largest part of the gains in productivity is obtained by transfer of technology from the more efficient companies, firms, to the less efficient ones.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So not so much by innovation, at least in Europe - also by innovation, but mostly by transfer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In order to allow this transfer to happen, there must be a business environment, an economic environment which is conducive to produce such a transfer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's where the structural reforms come very useful, to create this environment where this transfer could happen, and therefore productivity could increase, with corresponding increase in wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, it's quite clear that once countries enter into a very important political and election cycle, the push for legislating structural reforms becomes less vigorous.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, this by itself doesn't justify any absence of action, because even without legislation you have implementation of previously legislated reforms, and frankly it's common assessment that in some countries there is a lot to do in terms of implementation, even without thinking about new legislation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why, although aware that the political conditions aren't there for legislating, the ECB continues to renew the appeal, the plea, to undertake structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We don't do monetary policy on the likely outcomes of elections, but of course we ask ourselves how political uncertainty can affect our monetary policy decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the answer is, to the extent and only to the extent that - we don't react to political uncertainty by itself, but we certainly internalise the information that comes from the fact that political uncertainty may affect our medium-term outlook for price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to the extent that political uncertainty has this effect, we internalise this information - together with lots of other information - in taking our monetary policy decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is linked to global factors; the other one is more domestic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One interesting fact is that over the past few months the balance between these two risks has slightly changed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense, the domestic sources of risk have diminished, and global, geo-global sources of risk have increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of them are exactly the ones you exemplified a moment ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But others, for example, have to do with how the UK economy will be doing post-Brexit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We always assume that in fact - we shouldn't think that it's over.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course the consequences, especially the trade linkages, are there, and are going to be a source, a channel of economic consequences coming from this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course the final outcome will depend on the shape that the final negotiation will have, how long it will take; but it's quite clear that even now this uncertainty about the length and the shape is producing economic consequences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the other factors are really very much what you exemplified before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And add to this also possible negative surprises in some emerging market economies: that's also a source.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We shouldn't forget in early 2016, at the beginning of the year, we had big worries, if you remember, about what was happening in China.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the first question, in a sense I've answered it before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me summarise by saying that in the Governing Council meeting we discuss policies, not politics.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the second point, let's read it together: "Since our meeting in early March confirmed that the cyclical recovery of the euro area economy is becoming increasingly solid" - so it's a process in evolution - "and that downside risks have further diminished" - so it takes stock about downside risks: so far they have diminished, and the cyclical recovery is becoming increasingly solid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's an evolution that we see from survey data could continue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The headline really is this: "The risks surrounding the euro area growth outlook, while moving towards a more balanced configuration, are still tilted to the downside and relate predominantly to global factors."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, I just wanted to reread the speech at the ECB Watchers conference so as to make absolutely clear there is no difference on the sequence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, that's what it says and that's what the introductory statement says.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, we didn't have a vote, so I can't really say unanimity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But basically I didn't hear any dissenting voice by any Governing Council member with respect to the proposals that have been just stated in the introductory statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other thing - basically, we've defined our objective: our objective is a self-sustained, durable convergence towards an inflation rate which is below, but close to, 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This convergence is predicated on the very substantial amount of monetary accommodation that I've just mentioned in the introductory statement, and it's predicated on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what it is in the projections and that's what it is in our programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As you know, we have a separation principle, and we never comment on individual institutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I can say, as far as we are concerned, we can only express appreciation for the timely action of the SSM.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the Vice-President wants to have any comment on that I will give him the floor, but otherwise we don't comment on individual institutions, and as you know, we have the separation principle.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: Yes, of course because it was a decision of the ECB that was at stake.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That decision was based on the BRRD, and the reasons that triggered that decision were related to the liquidity problems.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it was not a matter of assessing the developments of the solvency as such, but the liquidity issue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is stated in Article 32, number 4, item C, that the fact that an institution is unable, or there are sufficient objective facts that show that it is about to become unable, to satisfy its debts and liabilities, that's a reason for the declaration of an institution being failing or likely to fail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then after that declaration, the process was given to the Single Resolution Mechanism that then is in charge of resolution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So our role as ECB was just the declaration that the bank, for liquidity reasons, was failing or likely to fail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, you're actually asking me many questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the downward revisions in inflation: as a matter of fact, very little has changed as far as inflation is concerned, because it was 1.9% in April, if I remember, and we all remember the serious concerns, if not the outcries, that inflation was going up too much, and now it's 1.4%, and it's mostly - actually, almost entirely - driven by the price of oil and price of foods.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from that viewpoint nothing has changed in substantial terms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What needs to be explained, however, is the flat and low profile of the underlying inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That has to do mostly with the subdued nominal wage growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are many reasons, and some of them may be more important than others - it's hard to say which is which - but basically the reasons that are behind this are certain structural changes that have taken place, one of which is certainly the backward-looking negotiation of nominal wages, looking as a sort of reference of inflation, looking at low inflation rates as a basis for current negotiations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All this recovery is happening with very strong creation of new jobs, so there is definitely a very significant increase in labour force, labour participation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, we have evidence that many - it's hard to say what is the percentage, but many of these new jobs are so-called "low-quality" jobs, where we're talking about temporary employment, we're talking about part-time employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are many; so much so that the ECB in a recent paper has developed some measures of a broader concept of unemployment which is broader than the official rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It may well be that this is actually slowing the growth of nominal wages as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More generally, structural reforms that have taken place are good for growth, certainly, and are good ultimately in the medium/long term for employment, but also, in making the markets more flexible - especially the labour market more flexible - do tend to produce a lower growth in nominal wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all this makes us think that some changes in the structure of wage negotiations have taken place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the first thing is, basically, we need to be patient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need to be patient because we know that the labour market slack is actually tightening, the output gap is closing, and we know all these factors in the end, their effects will fade away.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The job quality will improve, productivity will increase when the cyclical recovery goes up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we look at the uncertainty dimension of inflation, we see two phenomena.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So deflation risks are not there any longer, and that's why we have removed one of our easing biases, which was exactly addressing the tail risks of the inflation path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we also see that the uncertainty about the path of inflation has also decreased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So as the output gap will close and the unemployment rate will go down, we are becoming also more confident that the inflation path will converge towards our objective in a durable way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that - and here I come to the other part of your question - we need to be persistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need to continue to accompany the recovery with our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue with our purchases, and the introductory statement again is quite clear: it says we confirm our net asset purchases at the current monthly pace of €60 billion, and these purchases are intended to run until the end of December 2017, or beyond, if necessary, and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, I want to emphasise that basically the ECB will be in the market for a long time, when we say that "the net purchases will be made alongside reinvestments of the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the asset purchase programme", and just a little later on we say that "a very substantial degree of monetary accommodation is still needed."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "If the outlook becomes less favourable, or if financial conditions become inconsistent with further progress towards a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation, we stand ready to increase our asset purchase programme in terms of size and/or duration."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the bottom line basically is that the Governing Council trusts the strength and the power of our purchase programme, and that's it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nothing substantial has happened to inflation other than the oil price and the price of food.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Everything stayed - as I think it was well said by Governor Hansson this morning: if we compare inflation now with inflation in December, we see that underlying inflation is basically the same for year after year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, since we have stronger confidence in the path of inflation convergence and we've seen that the tail risks of deflation have definitely disappeared, we felt confident in removing the easing bias as far as the interest rate was concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: You asked me about normalisation: was it being discussed?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, there are people who - one or two Council members observed that we have to think in perspective to the link between the asset purchase programme and the inflation convergence, so there were some few - two, actually, if I remember, two, I guess - observations of this nature, but there wasn't any discussion like that on normalisation, as you mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other point was about why we left the other bias, the APP bias, easing bias.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first is an expectation that interest rates will remain at present or lower levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, if you ask me now, "What do you expect?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would say that based on a current assessment, current information, I don't expect lower interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you ask me, "But in case things were to worsen, are you ready to lower interest rates?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's part of a reaction function and it does say that if things were to turn less favourable - and here, just stop a moment: if things were to turn less favourable, it's a set of contingencies which is more benign than the tail-risk contingency embodied in the expectation on rates, and as such it's still there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If things turn out to be less favourable we are ready to expand our APP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: As I said before, after the declaration that the bank was failing or likely to fail, because there was a bank run and a liquidity issue, which is sufficient justification for that declaration, then the matter went to the Single Resolution Mechanism.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: Well, the Board is the deciding body of the SRM.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The SRM is the mechanism, as the SSM is the mechanism for supervision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the matter, after the declaration, went to the resolution mechanism, to their board, to take decisions about resolution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So after the declaration of failing or likely to fail we had no interference with the subsequent decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm talking about legal competences, and we have to be very formal in this matter, as you will, I'm sure, fully understand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Legally our competence was just to declare that the bank was failing or likely to fail for liquidity reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As far as the first question is concerned I would defer to Governor Hansson, and then I would just add something at the end, please.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Hansson: I think this is an issue of capital mobility, and we get this question all the time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We use the principle of connected vessels: that this is a common financial market and therefore changes that take place in one particular jurisdiction spill over to the whole eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So while it's true that we don't have a lot of direct purchases here, in the end let's say most of our credits are all linked to Euribor, and Euribor is not set in this country but is set more broadly in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think one of the signs might be that right now we have the highest inflation rate in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in some sense it's probably working, but through different channels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I will only add to this that Estonia being such an open economy, it benefits especially from the positive effects that QE has on the rest of the eurozone as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, the experience of the last few years shows that the economic and monetary union, with the many benefits that it's brought to the eurozone, is also fragile.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's fragile for various reasons, one of which is that it's incomplete.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's the sort of consideration that is at the basis for the Commission's recent work.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Commission has published a paper with different scenarios, and before the Commission's paper we had the Five Presidents' Report, where there was a blueprint - we would say a forward guidance - with two horizons, really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is shorter-term, where there are certain measures, certain decisions that can be taken, especially as far as completing the banking union is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then we have medium- or long-term horizons where new changes in the economic and monetary union could be introduced, but they do require a more extensive change in our treaties, in our treaty foundations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I guess it's to be welcomed, this new work on strengthening the monetary union, especially having in mind that we need to repair the fragilities that have appeared in the last few years in the union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we can discuss what we talk about, but this is a broader discussion, and it's not finished yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, we removed the interest rate easing bias because the tail risks on the future path of inflation have disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is to say, deflation risks have definitely gone away.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The lower - the possibility that the DFR, deposit facility rate, could go lower - was predicated on the strengthening or the materialisation of this tail risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, does it imply anything as far as the reaction function is concerned?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If things were to turn out in a way that these risks were to reappear, we'd certainly be ready to lower rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, the programme is running smoothly and as far as the future is concerned the programme has enough flexibility, and we'll certainly look at that when the time comes if need be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the meantime the Governing Council Members reiterated their confidence in the strength of the programme, in the power of the programme, and as you've seen from the introductory statement they confirmed both the programme and the forward guidance that's associated with that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: With respect to the second question, I kind of answered an almost similar question a moment ago, namely, the programme is running now smoothly and when and if we face problems we'll use the flexibility that the programme itself embodies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said, the Governing Council members reiterated their confidence in the strength and the power of the programme as it stands today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other question, which was the first question: the first thing to remember is we have a mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not specified in government budget support or other considerations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's been said that savers are being affected by our programme, banks are being affected by our programme, banks' profitability is being affected; now it's governments' budgets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, there are always countries that anticipate, countries that lag behind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our programme has in mind price stability and that's what we have to remember.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly, those countries which have a weak budget position and low growth and lack of structural reforms will be, certainly, more affected than others by a possible increase in interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We didn't have a discussion of when and if to reactivate, but certainly it's a topic which from time to time resurfaces in our discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so it was raised this morning; it was raised in other meetings in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no specific reason to have it introduced again, but we are certainly reflecting on it, also for the sake of symmetry with growth and with the growth of output path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be confident that the inflation rate is durably converging towards our objective of an inflation rate which is close to but below 2%, and it's a self-sustained convergence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, it's durable but it's also going to stay there once we withdraw the monetary policy support.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The four conditions are in the definition of our objective, which is a durable, self-sustained convergence of the rate of inflation towards an inflation rate of close to but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly the stronger is the economy, the stronger is the decline in unemployment rate, the more confident we become - as we did today - that the convergence is on its way to actually satisfy the conditions that I mentioned in its definition.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second point about inflation - I said it at the beginning: nothing has substantially changed as far as inflation is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is going to be also in the coming months, by the way, a significant amount of volatility due to oil prices and food prices, but the underlying inflation is basically staying what it is today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what we see now, based on the current information, is a path of low inflation, underlying inflation, and flat across time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just give you a few numbers to answer your question more fully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've just said, by the way, that growth has been just revised from 0.5% to 0.6% in the first quarter, and so the annual growth for this year is projected to be 2% rather than 1.9%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also, if you look at various indices, the PMI, which is an index we use to assess the state of the economy, is now at the highest level since April 2011.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Economic Sentiment Index is close to the level it had in 2007, which is an all-time high.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The unemployment rate was 9.3% in April: it's the lowest since March 2009 - with all the qualifications that I've made before about having a broader concept of unemployment as one of the reasons why we don't see much growth in nominal wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And almost 5 million jobs have been created in the eurozone in the last three and a half years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The recovery is proceeding based on consumption and investment, and consumption and investment are growing because of QE also - not only, but also QE.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because interest rates are low, labour income has increased; wealth, households' wealth has also increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Financing conditions remain extremely favourable, and this is essentially because of QE.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the pass-through of our monetary policy decisions has probably never been as effective as it is today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is passed into lower lending rates, much closer spreads across the eurozone, closer spreads across sectors and between different companies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I've said in the introductory statement that the SMEs are also benefiting greatly from the QE policy and from our monetary policy measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me respond first to your first question and give you a sense of the discussion we had today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We reviewed the economic and financial developments in the euro area, where we took stock of the continuing improvement in growth momentum, but also of the fact that the inflation rate is still subdued - and really there isn't any convincing sign of pickup for underlying inflation - while noting that the headline inflation will still be fairly volatile in the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was a general reiteration of the point that convergence of the inflation to our objectives remains conditional upon the very substantial monetary accommodation that is now in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, all in all, one could try to summarise the exchange of views we had saying that it was around the concepts that we've expanded on on other occasions, like the concept of confidence that is basically generated by the growth momentum; but also the fact that we need to be persistent and patient, because we aren't there yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also were unanimous in communicating no change to the forward guidance; and also we were unanimous in setting no precise date for when to discuss changes in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, we simply said that our discussions should take place in the fall - or in the autumn, since we are in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, concerning your second question, it's true there have been movements in bond prices, asset prices, exchange rates and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the conclusion is that the financing conditions remain broadly supportive to secure a sustained return of inflation rates towards our inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Long-term yields have risen, but they still are low by historical standards.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Sovereign spreads have tightened, and some issuers have seen even falling rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ten-year GDP weighted average of euro area sovereign yields stands close to its level at the beginning of the year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Bank lending rates continue to be at very supportive levels, and the Bank Lending Survey suggests that banks expect a further net easing of their credit standards across all loan categories in the third quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The repricing of the exchange rate has received some attention during the various exchanges of views, and in various ways.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's been something that, just as I said, has received some attention.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I won't comment on market reactions, but let me give you the bottom line of our exchanges: basically, inflation is not where we want it to be, and where it should be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are still confident that it will gradually get there, but it isn't there yet, and that's why the Governing Council reiterated the forward guidance, the asset purchase programme, the interest rates and all this package of monetary accommodation; and reiterated that the present very substantial monetary accommodation is still necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me read the introductory statement: "Therefore a very substantial degree of monetary accommodation is still needed for underlying inflation pressures to gradually build up and support headline inflation developments in the medium term."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me just make clear one thing: after a long time, we are finally experiencing a robust recovery, where we only have to wait for wages and prices to move towards our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the last thing that the Governing Council may want is actually an unwanted tightening of the financing conditions that either slows down this process or may even jeopardise it; and that's why we retain the second bias, or let's call it, reaction function.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "If the outlook becomes less favourable or if financial conditions become inconsistent with further progress towards a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation, we stand ready to increase our asset purchase programme in terms of size and/or duration."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think the Governing Council has given enough evidence that when flexibility is needed to achieve its objectives, it has been very able to find all that was needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I reviewed the financial markets developments a moment ago, and I think I put them in the proper context, but nothing like BoJ was discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me just comment on your parallel with the Sintra speech: our assessment is that what I've just said, at Sintra and Tallinn - because we have to go back to that, the Q&A and the introductory statement - aren't very different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On all occasions what we did was to basically take stock of the unquestionable improvement in the growth outlook in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we asked ourselves the question, "Why isn't this showing up into a higher inflation rate, headline and underlying inflation?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we went through a series of reasons that have to do with the labour market, have to do with backward-looking wage negotiations,with productivity, and in Sintra this analysis was quite broad, quite detailed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then we said, "Are these factors going to be permanent or temporary?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We said, "Well, they're going to last some time, that's for sure, but probably they're not permanent because as the economic recovery improves and the growth outlook improves, all these reasons will lose some of their effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, the labour market slack may be bigger than previously estimated, but as the economic situation and growth improves, so will the labour market, and this will be absorbed," and so on for all these various reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We think - nobody can be 100% sure, and we think that it's going to take time but in the end - although, as I said, nobody can be absolutely sure about that - in the end these reasons will lose some of their effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's why in Sintra I used repeatedly the concept - together with confidence, that in the end we'll get there - the concept of persistence or patience.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Stimulus upon which all the path of inflation is projected, is conditional.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we said that our monetary policy will accompany the recovery, and that is, I believe, not only in Sintra, but also in Tallinn, and certainly today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all this says basically that the ECB, the Governing Council - first of all - trusts the strength and the power of its monetary package in all its elements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, it says that the Governing Council is ready to use the flexibility that is needed to make true its monetary policy package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And third, it says that the ECB will stay in the market for a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in conclusion, I'm not sure I see big differences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, reflation means - you have reflation when the price level has fallen below the trend line and it recovers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It recovers from below the trend line: that's the technical definition of reflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the speech in Sintra and before, we said that reflation has replaced deflation - or risks of deflation, really, better.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We are confident that this process can be managed in a smooth way, and so we see our programme proceeding in a smooth fashion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, the Governing Council has given enough evidence in the past that it can actually use all the flexibility that is needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point, we've gone through this several times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Greek Government has decided, as you said, to tap the market, and of course it's up to the government to decide about this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sound implementation of the programme and credibility are essential, however, for restoring market confidence, and we have to take note that the national central bank has expressed some concern about that; although there has been serious progress in place in Greece throughout the last several months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But issuance - the way we see this is the issuance activity should be part of an overall strategy where you have the completion of the third programme and also a return to the market, but it should be in a lasting way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's premature to talk about other things, and what you suggested, or also other programmes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, I never, ever comment on market developments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, this is exactly what is going to be the substance of our discussion in the fall.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the answer is yes, the ECB considers it useful, important, essential, and that's the sort of discussions we'll be having in the fall.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The first answer is no, it's not been discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second answer is, really, in a sense, we are thankful to the Staff Committee and IPSO when they address mistakes that we, like everybody else, make.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I sincerely wish to work - not only I, but also the Executive Board Members and senior management - wish to work with the Staff Committee and IPSO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The problem is that it's very difficult to have trust - you know, trust is a two-way route, where it's very difficult to trust someone who discusses things on the press and the news wires and so on, each and every time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And frankly, also for the staff, which is a staff of world-class quality, to be seen in the press as being continuously discussed must be - it's a little sad.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that what should be improved, perhaps on both sides, is the way to work together, not necessarily our hiring practices, which, as I said, when they need correction, we correct them without hesitation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: That's exactly why we are having this discussion in autumn, and why we didn't want to set a precise date; because we have to have all the available information at that point in time, which we'll certainly have by then.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's going to be a discussion which is made up of different parts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't look only at the growth recovery, of course, in assessing whether the monetary policy stance is appropriate or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also have to look at - actually, first and foremost we have to look at the path of inflation, whether it converges in a sustainable and self-sustained manner to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's why I said before: in the presence of this growth recovery, if we are to experience an unwanted tightening of financing conditions that may jeopardise the convergence in the medium term of inflation to our objectives, then we'll have to act and we'll have to use the APP bias and other measure as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why this discussion we're going to have in the fall is multi-faceted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the first question is we haven't discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question really asks whether something has changed following the financial crisis so that the response of wages to an improvement in the labour market is different from what it was in the past, before the crisis; and the answer is yes, certainly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has changed, and there is a variety of factors why this has changed that I went through explicitly during my speech in Sintra, but as well on other occasions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The key issue for us is: are they going to be permanent, or structural; or in the end will we go back to a sort of relationship between the labour market, between unemployment and wage growth, like we used to have in the past?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The conclusion we draw - as I said, with great caution, however, because it's not something where one can be 100% sure - the conclusion we drew is that in the end, yes, we will go back to a relationship like we had before the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I focused on the labour market, but in fact there are other reasons why this response may be delayed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, the de-leveraging process is another reason why this is slower than you would have in normal times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In general, after a protracted financial crisis and a long recession like we had, you would expect phenomena like hysteresis, phenomena like, as I said, backward-looking wage negotiations, like the de-leveraging - so it's a variety of phenomena and some of them have to do with the labour market; others don't.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All throughout, we are confident we are moving through, but it's a combination of confidence and prudence and patience.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'm sorry, but the answer to the second question is, we haven't discussed that, and to the first as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We haven't discussed what we are going to do in view of September, or even less so what we are going to do after September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, it was a unanimous conclusion, exactly: Don't set dates.
