speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need to have lots of information we don't have today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the Governing Council didn't want to be forced to take decisions in absence of full information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is that we haven't discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We haven't discussed that but, as I said, we gave you enough evidence that it was the case all the time that when the Governing Council needed flexibility to carry through its monetary policy it was successful in finding it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first point, we didn't actually discuss this, not this time, but on other occasions we briefly touched upon it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, the answer is, first, the reasons that led, to my understanding, all the major central banks in the world to adopt a 2% objective, or around that concept, in the early 2000s, are still valid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And specifically in the euro area, for the ECB, are still valid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, it's true, our monetary policy measures have been in place now for quite a long time, but they've produced very significant effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can say that today there were created in the last three years, if I'm not mistaken, around 6 million jobs: much more than any time before the crisis in the same amount of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All the economic sentiment indicators, the survey indicators, are either at all-time high or close to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the policies have been unquestionably successful on the real side of the economy; it's the response in terms of inflation that we are still waiting for, and looking and monitoring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the answer to that is, we've got to be patient rather than changing the objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, if you ask yourself how credible is anybody, really - an individual or an institution - that when it doesn't attain the objective, changes it, and makes it attainable, changing the definition?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, the whole reasoning could be done the other way around, if we had inflation 4% and we wanted to bring it down, and we decided that 4% is the new objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, I think to even discuss changing objectives at this point in time would be destabilising for the expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, if the Governing Council had decided to define autumn as 7 September, we probably would have said that 7 September is going to be when we'll decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your other question, what information - it isn't that we are looking for a specific data point which triggers one behaviour or another.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In September we'll be having the macroeconomic projections, we'll be having staff macroeconomic projections, so there is more information that we can look at between now and then.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's basically the sense of the Governing Council that we will have more confidence in taking a decision with more information than we have today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Your question actually reminds all of us that what we say about growth momentum, strong recovery, is an average.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That in fact, as you said, there are spots which haven't seen such great recovery, and they, in a sense, don't appear when we give this average, aggregate description.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is something that should always be kept in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we say we've created jobs and the labour market is improving, no question that is true in the aggregate, but still that doesn't deny the presence of areas where slack remains significant, and unemployment - and youth unemployment especially - remains significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, we should always remember that our mandate is neither growth nor employment, but it's price stability, and that's where our monetary policy is geared for, and that's what we have to look at in terms of deciding whether we're actually moving successfully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, again, in a sense, it goes beyond our remit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to take this into account in our minds: our remit is the one of price stability, and that's what we have to look at, and we have to aim our policy action to that objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, your questions lead me to give you a pretty short account of the discussion that has taken place today in the Governing Council, so duly will respond to both of your questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly all members of the Governing Council intervene, speaking as far as the economic situation is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They spoke on three topics; growth, inflation and the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On growth there was a general recognition of the progress made by the eurozone recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's robust, it's broad-based and it was recalled six million jobs were created since 2013.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This recovery is really the base for our confidence that inflation will eventually converge but also, as I'll say in a moment, that patience is needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why the introductory statement I just read to you says therefore a very substantial degree of monetary accommodation is still needed for underlying inflation pressures to gradually build up and support headline inflation developments in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On inflation, as I just read in the introductory statement, there was a downward revision mostly due to the - or mainly due to the - exchange rate appreciation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there was a certain, I would say, broad dissatisfaction with the inflation, though noting as I said in the introductory statement that core inflation actually is doing slightly better.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there was a broad dissatisfaction I would say tempered by the confidence that inflation will eventually converge to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This confidence, as I said a moment ago, is based on the good conditions and the good and improving and broadening conditions of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But even looking at growth, how this recovery remains dependent on our monetary policy... Basically, if you look at the drivers of the economy, you see that consumption is doing well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Consumption is doing well because of personal disposable income is increasing because of employment gains and because households' wealth is increasing as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Investment is doing very well because corporate profits are good, because interest rates are low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Exports are also doing well, although clearly we should expect consequences from the appreciation of the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So now this leads me to report to you what the conversation was about the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You wouldn't be surprised hearing me saying that the exchange rate is not a policy target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's so important that the medium-term outlook for inflation was revised downward in the staff projections mainly due to the appreciation of the exchange rate, which means that we will have to take into account this element in our information set in our future policy decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the last monetary policy meeting there were concerns expressed by a few.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These concerns were now reiterated by most members at this meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course one issue that was discussed was how much of this appreciation is due to completely exogenous factors, how much is simply the natural outcome of the improved economic conditions in the euro area?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there was by and large broad consensus on the fact, as I just read in the introductory statement, that the recent volatility in the exchange rate represents a source of uncertainty which requires monitoring with regard to its possible implications for the medium-term outlook for price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the other topic we discussed was basically the calibration of our policy instruments starting with next year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, let me say offhand what was not discussed; what was not discussed was the sequence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So interest rates, as it's written here, will remain at their present levels for an extended period of time and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What was not discussed was changes in issue or issuer limits to the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I should say just before you ask me other questions, the discussion was very, very preliminary and was meant to ask questions about the different scenarios and what the transmission channels or different scenarios was rather than expressing policy options or policy preferences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Otherwise I would have reported to you about the policy decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the discussions about different scenarios concerned the length of the programme, the size of the monthly flows and so it was, as I said, a very preliminary discussion mostly geared to ask questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The pros and the cons of different scenarios were discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But by and large, on this point what the Governing Council will ask for is, will want to see, is the work by the committees; they were tasked to continue working on that so they will have full information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But one thing is clear; the bottom line is that interest rates will stay, as it's written here, at the present levels for an extended period of time and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Following the recent appreciation of the euro, financial conditions unquestionably tightened in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But they remain broadly supportive of the non-financial companies and enterprises.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question is about the date; we had a brief exchange on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council has reiterated it's this fall as the period when these decisions will be taken because the decisions are many, complex and always one naturally sort of thinks about risks that may materialise in the coming weeks or months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is the caution about not specifying a date.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Probably the bulk of these decisions will be taken in October.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, we haven't discussed really the scarcity issue because so far we've given plenty of evidence that whenever there were … by the way these problems, these doubts were present at the very beginning of our programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've consistently shown that we've been able to cope with this issue quite successfully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you may remember, the change allowing purchases below the DFR - the Deposit Facility Rate - and below two-year maturities considerably expanded the eligible universe of our programme, giving it more flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm pretty confident that when the policy decisions time comes we'll certainly be able to exploit all the flexibility that the programme has in its construction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, expectations are not destabilised at all, in my view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In any event I think policy decisions that have many dimensions and are complex need time to be taken, need the reasonable consensus to be undertaken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, the fall is the date that's been announced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said before, unless a risk that is not seen today materialises, we should be ready to give the bulk or to take the bulk of these decisions in October.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Our programme is a programme that has been designed in order to pursue, in order to implement our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is the pursuing of price stability for the whole of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense, that's what determines the size, the design, the composition of our programme, not specific national interest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One can naturally explain very clearly that whenever one has sort of appeared, when people seem to say, "Oh, you bought more bonds of one country and less of another" it's happened because of temporary technical factors that have been corrected in the subsequent months and weeks, weeks, and months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's due mostly to liquidity considerations, the rhythm of the reinvestment programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One can easily explain that, so no; the answer to your point is no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, certainly we've said that we foresee a reinvestment programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This reinvestment programme, by the way, will become more and more sizeable of course as our QE programme has been continuing now for years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the reinvestment programme will become sizeable and will continue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, the use of repayments is for that purpose; to reinvest in bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, as I said before, there are temporary deviations from the capital key.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There have always been temporary deviations from the capital key for the simple reason that some countries do not participate in the QE programme; Greece and Cyprus.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So no wonder of that, there is no mystery or no surprise there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There have been deviations, there will always be deviations from the capital key due to the liquidity conditions due to the fact that we're going to be as market neutral as possible in our purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if you have very tight liquidity conditions in one market, you just slow down with purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also there are natural times of the year, like it happened in August, it's going to happen in December again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these deviations from the capital key don't indicate anything else from what I said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now on the potential financial stability risks stemming from monetary policies that are very accommodating for a long time, it certainly is a danger, but do we see that now?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the various markets - the stock market, the bond market - the prime commercial real estate is the only area where you actually see stretched valuations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But even in the residential real estate you see situations where prices have been going up pretty fast in some large cities, in some countries, but not on average and not in other cities in the same countries or in other countries at the same speed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other important consideration to make is, even though we see stretched valuations in some markets - as I mentioned before, the prime commercial real estate market is one - we don't see the other component of a bubble which accompanied in the pre-crisis time; namely an increase in leverage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see that credit remains pretty subdued all across the board.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also one has to consider that were we to see such situations at the local level, the answer to that should be macroprudential instruments by the national governments and not changes in monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's as far as these issues have been raised in this conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, it was not discussed so I am not in a position to comment on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, if Mr Constâncio wants to answer there?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we are prepared; the single supervisory mechanism is prepared to deal with those types of institutions, some of them similar to institutions that already exist in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So no problems, specific difficulties will come from that development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first, you see, there are two sentences in the introductory statement, "At the same time, the recent volatility in the exchange rate represents a source of uncertainty which requires monitoring with regard to its possible implications for the medium-term outlook for price stability."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then you have another sentence that says, "This autumn we will decide on the calibration of our policy instruments beyond the end of the year, taking into account the expected path of inflation and the financial conditions needed for a sustained return of inflation rates towards levels that are below but close to 2%."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the second point, I don't think we are in a period of high uncertainty; I think we are starting what to do next year when the present programme expires.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also let me add that these changes published in the forecast are not new.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They've been made several years ago, as a matter of fact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't know if they have been very successful in helping the central bank to get out of the uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the uncertainty is the element and the metrics, sometimes they've been successful, sometimes they've been judged not to be as so successful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The way staff projections are produced, the way they are communicated, even all our communication is the result of many, many years and the work of many, many people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we learn from our history, from our experience, from other central banks' examples as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's not something we can go lightly trying to experiment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This issue, by the way, had been discussed by my predecessor - the one you mentioned about the Bank of Sweden, Bank of Norway at that time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: My answer is that I don't comment on levels of the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I left university many years ago, more than I want to remember.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to the second question is really, we will announce when we are ready.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We think we are going to be ready for much of what we have to decide by October.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, the Governing Council is kind of reluctant to commit to a precise date.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sense is that in October we should be ready but if we are not, then we will postpone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second thing is that we don't know exactly if any serious risk materialises which warrants such postponement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Right now, judging from the way the work is going, we should be ready when I said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The rate that was used in the projections is around $1.18 vis-à-vis the US dollar.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: Yes, as you know, the exchange rate is fixed, is treated in the projections all the time as a constant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The value in the market of the cut-off date of the projections is the one that is inserted and considered in the projections, so it was mid-August.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I'm not in a position to say that because as I said, we haven't discussed the first part; namely the actual numbers for what the APP programme is going to be in next year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I said one thing here; I said that we expect the interest rates to remain at their present levels for an extended period of time and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: About the exchange rate, I don't know how much it's trading but we're talking about the $1.18.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's roughly around $1.18 and was August 14thso we will have to see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now I'm told it's $1.20, okay, but I don't comment about levels of exchange rates anyway so…

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, the important aspect of the current discussion, that's your first question, about the European monetary union, its reforms is that the member states have realised how incomplete is our monetary union at the present time and how such incompleteness has made the crisis that we are just coming out of more serious than it would have otherwise been.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's to be welcomed, the fact the member states - because you see, the task to discuss and design the reform of the monetary union is not the ECB's task; it's the member states' task.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's going to be a certainly complex discussion that will take place in the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB of course stands ready to help in this discussion but we are not party of this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your second question is, should we be resigned to low inflation?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said many times that inflation will eventually converge to our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Essentially two factors; first, the fact that we keep in place the extraordinary degree of monetary accommodation, and the second is the broad, robust, solid recovery that we see across countries and across sectors now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This recovery is having a profound effect on the labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mentioned before about number of jobs being created since 2013; six million.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are many other indicators that are given to you on other occasions showing the strength of this recovery that also now touches upon investment and the strength of consumption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This recovery gradually will close and it's actually closing the output gap and will gradually close the labour market's slack.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this labour markets slack is turning out to be bigger than was previously estimated and we went through this on another occasion, why this is so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nominal wages, which are a primary driver of inflation, are also lagging behind what one would've expected from such strong recovery across the board.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've discussed this on another occasion and some of you were there when I gave a speech on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But basically, it had to do with backward-looking wage negotiations, trade union strategy geared mostly about stabilising the job rather than going for wage increases, about low productivity, about other factors like the global value chain in a supply of factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, some of these factors will disappear - none of them disappears quickly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of them will disappear first as the labour market's slacks close.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some others will stay for a longer time, but there's no question that with the ongoing recovery in the end the inflation rate will converge to our aim in the way we want; namely in a doable fashion and based on a self-sustained path where there is no need for our monetary policy any longer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So confidence, patience - because we have to be patient for that - and persistence, however; that's very important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We shouldn't sort of either change the definition because we don't reach the target, or change or lose trust in our monetary policy, lose confidence in our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I won't comment on the Italian intention, but I will comment on the Estonian decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No member state can introduce its own currency; the currency of the eurozone is the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, we have a growth-based recovery where growth is solid and robust and I said before across countries and sectors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is still a big labour market slack that needs to be filled.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the key point is that we don't have a dual mandate like the Fed, where we can sort of look also at conditions of unemployment in the labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Price stability for us is defined as a level of inflation that is close but below 2% which should be reached in a self-sustained and durable fashion - and we are not there yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council wants to get there and there is nothing that will derail its will to get there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, this anxiety should be also based on facts because so far, everybody benefited greatly from this monetary policy, all countries benefited greatly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this angst so far has no evidence that could justify it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the first question, we didn't have a discussion about the relative importance of stocks versus flows.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, we have full confidence that the French government knows exactly what to do to undertake the needed structural reforms and amongst the targets that all structural reforms of the labour market had - now, whether they achieve that or not is another issue - but certainly one of the main targets was the elimination of dualism in the labour market because one lesson we learned from the crisis was: All the jobs that have been created in some countries which had very rich labour markets, - these jobs disappeared with the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the early 2000s some countries facing very rich labour markets created or passed legislation which allowed the new entrants in the labour markets only if they were based on labour contracts which were very, very flexible with respect to the ones that were already in the market, the already employed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This way, between 2000, 2006 millions of jobs were created in some of these countries and by 2008 most of these jobs had gone; it's simply the crisis destroyed all of them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, the flexibility that was introduced with these contracts fell disproportionately on the young sectors of the working population.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think this has been well understood by everybody and I think all reforms or labour markets should aim at decreasing or eliminating this dualism.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: With respect to the second question, our mandate is defined on the basis of our jurisdiction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what other jurisdictions, especially large jurisdictions, do is certainly part of our information set, but in a sense doesn't affect our monetary policy strategies other as a source of information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also we have to see what this will imply for interest rates, what this will imply for financing conditions in general.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They, if anything, may be part of our information set that defines our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would be sort of cautious about imagining that we coordinate our actions, that we place strategic games in between us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My expectation of course in 2020, our inflation rate will converge to our objective, but we didn't discuss it today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: In answering your question, based on the conversation we had, I said that what was discussed was a set of different scenarios.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We discussed the size of the programme or better, we discussed the trade-offs between different possibilities about length and size and the pros and cons of different scenarios and the transmission channels of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had a staff projection here that basically revised downward the inflation rate by some amount based on the appreciation of the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, when the exchange rate changes and the change is purely exogenous, you have a pass-through on inflation, which is - I think it was 0.5%, something like - I gave this number a time ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When the change in the exchange rate is not entirely due to exogenous factors, the pass-through is lower.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the sense of the discussion we had is that there were differing views about what is the intensity, how much is exogenous, how much is endogenous?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there was a general, as I read in the introductory statement, concern that the recent volatility in the exchange rate represents a source of uncertainty which requires monitoring with regard to its possible implications for the medium-term outlook of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also consider another factor to this; that in judging the medium-term impact of a certain change in one of the financing conditions variables - and the exchange rate is indeed one important one - one also takes into account the credibility of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is also a factor that plays a role and as I said before, the Governing Council is firmly committed to this monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The negative side effects of the quantitative easing programme I don't have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not that I don't have any information; we don't see negative effects of this programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But they are vastly overwhelmed, offset by the positive effects so the answer is no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course the negative interest rate is a different thing; it's not the QE.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There, there are obviously side effects to the negative interest rates; we've discussed them many times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But again they are vastly offset by the continuing increasing evidence of the effectiveness that negative interest rates are having on - and the positive effects that negative interest rates are having on growth and therefore on the recovery and therefore on price stability in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be a press release, a press communique at 15:30 CET detailing more about - well, developing transparency and detailing more about the - how the asset purchase programme will evolve in 2017.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The only thing that I can say about that is that we will continue buying sizeable quantities of corporate bonds in the programme and then you get the rest, yes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I can anticipate some of the things you're going to see shortly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So as of January 2018, the Eurosystem will publish ex ante the monthly redemption amounts for each component of the APP for the Eurosystem as a whole for the following rolling 12-month period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the Eurosystem, as you know, conducts the reinvestments in a flexible and timely manner in the month they fall due or in the subsequent two months if needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore net purchases per jurisdiction may fluctuate owing to the timing of these reinvestments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Reinvestments will take place in the same jurisdiction as principal redemptions with the aim to minimise deviations from the capital key.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you'll get the press release shortly after the press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But clearly, the press release would also devote some space to communicate in a transparent way how this reinvestment - which is becoming more and more important, of course - is going to be carried out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The discussion was there were - let me say this; the atmosphere was pretty positive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All the Governing Council members in their interventions emphasised the better conditions, the growth momentum, as I just said unabated growth momentum and improving labour market conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They stressed how this number, seven million, almost seven million jobs in the last four years, it actually continues to increase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Both private consumption and private investment, which is also remarkable, because for a long time we haven't seen any significant upward trend in investment, is actually picking up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They emphasised how the earning capacity of households is increasing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the real disposable income is actually increasing because - mostly because of gains coming from greater employment and how household wealth is increasing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This also being supported of course by our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So on inflation, of course this positive picture on the growth side is - on inflation is different because we - inflation is still not at our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said I think last time, too, we foresee a V-shaped profile of inflation mostly due to a base price effect of the oil, of energy, and then 1.5% the year after.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all this in the end converged on this scenario that I've just presented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course there was some difference of views on some aspects of this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the scenario that was discussed this morning was the one I've just mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, the guidance on reinvestment is not related to rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sequence stays what it is, namely this - the interest rates will stay and they remain at their present - are expected to remain at their present levels for an extended period of time and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However as we moved forward not only this year but also in a previous years, the amounts that we've purchased, the stock has become more and more important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This year as we continue asset purchases, it will keep on increasing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the commitment that the Eurosystem has taken today is that it will reinvest the principal payments for maturing securities purchased under the APP for an extended period of time after the end of its net asset purchases and in any case, as long as necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course as I said I want to stress the importance of reinvestment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll never forget that in December 2015 in one of my press - usual periodic press conference like this, we announced a series of measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also said, 'Look, we are going to reinvest this.'

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not only that but it was actually considered to be totally marginal and in fact there were many sort of wrong estimates of what these potential reinvestments might be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this stock now is sizeable and has become an important component of our - as we say here, this continued monetary support is provided by the additional net asset purchases by three elements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sizeable stock of acquired assets and the forthcoming reinvestments, so the stock and the reinvestments, and by our forward guidance on interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the flexibility, I think on the credibility, on the potential constraints, I think you've been asking - not you [personally]- been asking this question - "Will you make it?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: - since the very beginning of the QE programme, or at least at regular intervals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Each time we gave plenty of evidence that both our design is flexible enough to cope with the potential limits, and we gave plenty of evidence that the Governing Council is committed to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I don't have a number of that today, but you will get much information in the press release.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Unless the Vice-President has a number on that, the investments will be carried out in a flexible way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The modalities of the reinvestment are going to be described in this first press release.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll continue buying these, by the way, according to the present conditions until December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So as far as any clarification is concerned about the future, we have time until I would say December or even earlier.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the same question as before, so one thing is our reinvestment and that is going to be massive, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Vice-President wants to, sorry, to say something on that?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: No, you will have the numbers because we announce precisely at 15:30 CET that we will start disclosing the pattern and amounts of reinvestment per month for the following 12 months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you will have all those numbers - which are quite sizeable per month.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think on average we are talking about many billions per month, on average.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are big differences from month to month because it depends on the dates of when the bonds reach maturity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course reinvestment is then sizable, say like €10 billion per month.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's just to restore the amount of the stock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The amount of the stock in itself produces an effect, of course, on markets because we are talking about asset markets where the stock is always potentially in play.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the stock is also important for the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me just make one point; the press communique will not contain a number at 15:30 CET.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Yes, so it's going to be carried out in the way I kind of described before, in a flexible way and you will get more information in the press communique.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the other question it's the same as before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see, so far you've been - you, as I said; all of you have been asking this question on and on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, our programme is flexible enough that we can adjust its size.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can carry through smoothly and that's been the evidence we've given until now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, this time of course we are also going to have the reinvestments of the existing - of the maturing securities and we still have our forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in terms of our capacity to achieve or to have a monetary policy stance which will support the sustained inflation objective - self-sustained inflation objective - we are well placed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The 'well past' is a concept that is such that it should anchor interest rate - short-term interest rate expectations in a way that is supporting the achievement of our inflation aim, namely a self-sustained durable convergence of inflation to our objective of an inflation rate which is below but close to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the second question is concerned, I think I wouldn't rule that out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't rule out the fact that there are international global factors underlying the inflation development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We all know that delocalisation of certain production centres and more generally the globalisation and the different retail networks that are operating today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But our view is and our policy is designed and based on the - on a view that looks at the output gap and looks at the unemployment rate, defined in various ways of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are now looking at the broad definition of unemployment, and looks at the factors that will cause an increase in inflation as the unemployment rate will decrease and as the output gap will shrink.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So our attention today is really more on the factors that are close to us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, there may be global factors but we can't do anything about that, but we can do a lot about domestic factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First and foremost is the speed of response of nominal wages to the closing output gap.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's where our monetary policy becomes essential and that's what our monetary policy has in a sense contributed to create more than seven million jobs in four years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As far as the first question is concerned, my understanding - of course I am with you now - but my understanding is the market reaction was pretty muted to our announcement, to our policy announcement in spite of the fact that it's a policy announcement of a certain importance, which seems to say that our communication to the market has been pretty effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also we are going to have a communication conference in two weeks' time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you're cordially invited to participate there and it's jointly organised with the Federal Reserve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's going to be here in Frankfurt and I'm pretty sure there will be many interesting insights about communication there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the second point, no, it was not unanimous.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would characterise the discussion as ranging between consensus, broad consensus on several issues and large majority on other issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More precisely - well, first of all let me step back.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have said several times that the present situation is a situation that does call for confidence that we will be able to reach our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: After all, the overall economy, the growth rate, unemployment, the labour market, what I have listed before are all positive indications - and the survey data as well show an increase in momentum - are all positive indications that we are moving towards a shrinking output gap and an improving labour market, which eventually will produce higher nominal wage growth and therefore higher inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this confidence is also tempered by the fact that we know that all this process, it still relies very much on our monetary policy support.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not self-sustained yet and therefore we must be patient and we must be persistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, the discussion today was reflecting different degrees of confidence or patience, persistence and prudence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, there wasn't much of a disagreement about the flows or other parts of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were different views about whether, should an end date have been announced or not?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But again the large - and here that's the area where it's large majority and not consensus - the large majority of the Governing Council members preferred to keep it open-ended.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I would give the floor to the Vice-President for the first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: No, regarding the first question, let me recall what was the decision that was announced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a decision about new loans, new flows of loans and potentially new NPLs that would be formed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is then a target for the formation of provisions when new NPLs would be - would emerge so that the formation of provisions would have to go up to 100% of the exposures during two years in the case of the exposures are not secured by any collateral, and seven years if they are secured by collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's this decision that was taken and so it means of course that with a stronger economy and better management of credit risk, the levels of NPLs for new loans should be way below what they were during the crisis, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second thing is, at the same time next year enters into force the International Financial Reporting Standard 9, which changes completely the calculation of impairment costs and provisions, meaning that from January next year, mandatory in accounting terms any new financial asset - say the loan - that goes into the books of the bank already has to calculate the expected loss during the next 12 months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there will be some provision charge for any new loan as a result.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If after that recognition moment there is some aggravation of the prospect of that asset not performing well, then the accounting rules - the new accounting rules - impose that the expected loss for the whole life of the asset has to be front-loaded and immediately recognised as a cost.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these accounting rules reinforce very much the treatment of new NPLs, so go in the same direction and can be meaningful, because indeed as I said, may lead to a full recognition of losses for the whole life of the asset so - which means that the new rule also or the new target for the treatment of NPLs can be more or less already accommodated by what will be the imposition of the new accounting rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the thing is not adding perhaps too much to what the IFRS 9 would impose so - which means that the targets as they were defined are important, but are at the same time reasonable and in complement with the change in the accounting rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's important to ensure that from now on, the banks are careful enough in managing credit risk so that there is no further undue accumulation of NPLs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then there was also the announcement that we are now looking about the stocks, but nothing has been decided about that yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking of course very carefully because it's different to deal with presumably the new NPLs and deal with targets for the whole stock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Final comment: the targets that were then defined will - the implementation and the compliance with these targets will be subject also to a supervisory dialogue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The banks will have to comply or explain and they can explain that they have done the utmost to comply and could not do it for understandable reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's in the context of a supervisory dialogue that these new targets will be applied in order to contain for the future this problem of NPLs so that we don't have again an accumulation that creates, as we now are seeing, problems to the profitability of banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The monetary policies of different jurisdictions reflect the different positions they are in achieving their objectives and the different positions the economies have in the business cycle.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As such, the US recovery is way more advanced than ours.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the inflation developments, because we are concerned about price stability, are way behind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our decisions today are consistent with our - with the feedback rule we've been having all throughout.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When the general conditions improve and we see that our inflation objective is closer, we have downsized asset purchases in the past or we have upsized them in the past as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On one hand it does reflect an increasing degree of confidence in our capacity to reach a self-sustained inflation objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other, it takes stock of the fact that we are not there yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, headline inflation if anything will decline in the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our annual projections that I mentioned a moment ago are for 1.5% this year, 1.2% next year and 1.5% again the year after.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not there yet and that explains the difference in our stances, basically.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: You know, it's very, very difficult to comment about developments that change every day.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To conclude now that there will be financial stability risks will be premature; we have to see what's going to happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But rest assured we look at that with attention, great attention.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to the second question is, we really - no, we haven't discussed it at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the first question, I said before that the decision today is for an open-ended programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I may add certainly it's not going to stop suddenly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not going to stop suddenly, it's never been our view that things should stop suddenly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's open-ended and the large majority of the Governing Council expressed its preference for keeping it open-ended.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of course is to reaffirm a steadfast commitment of the Governing Council to pursue the price stability objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also it's due to the fact that there is still a large amount of uncertainty and therefore prudence has inspired many governors to opt for this possibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: No, I am saying that the second question; we do have a sequence which is defined and reaffirmed today so…

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, but the question here was the sequence about net asset purchases is defined today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The new sequence you are pointing out was actually the same question I have received before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There isn't any sequence between the balance sheet - the stock and the interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, as far as the second question is concerned, we're really talking about nuances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The general picture is a picture of a part of the world which is doing pretty well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Growth is growing and momentum is also growing and labour market and everything is doing - well, I think it's, I can't remember how many quarters of consecutive growth, 17 I believe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now it's a 0.7% growth as I just mentioned, which was higher than the 0.6% that was expected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So at the same time we don't see yet an encouraging sign neither in the nominal wage growth nor in underlying inflation, although one has to say underlying inflation is slightly - is higher than it was in historical trough at the year-end last year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it was basically most - as I said the large majority if not consensus was in the end for a solution for a decision which was prudent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The bottom line is prudent, which was both confident but also patient and persistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the time frame - I think I said it before - we don't have a fixed time frame.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we define a medium-term concept it's not a fixed time frame; it really depends on how we are approaching to the achievement of our objective of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think comparisons with other jurisdictions are not really appropriate because of, in a sense, what I said before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our, first of all, institutional differences but also different positions in the business cycle, different formations, price formation mechanisms, different labour markets, different speeds of response.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in a sense, our experience with monetary policy has been quite different from what the Fed has done until now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, this is today's decision and as up to - this is taken on the basis of information we have today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a commitment to undertake these purchases and to have the reinvestment of the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the APP for an extended period of time after the end of its net asset purchases, in any case or as long as necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we have the full allotment, the longer-term refinancing operations, the fixed-rate tender procedures with full allotment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we have the forward guidance of interest rates and this is based on the present information set.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, the answer to the second question is no; it's simply the - a part of the monetary policy decisions taken today, the decision to ensure adequate liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we don't have any relationship between that and the forward guidance of interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first just let me answer, saying that there were two issues that were not discussed today - well, probably many others - but as far as relevant to our today's decisions, two.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One was parameters change and the other one was the sequence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not concerned about that because we - as I said before we'll continue - and the press communique will have words to this extent - we'll continue purchasing ample quantities of corporate bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we certainly monitor that development like we do on other developments in various markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there isn't anything special that one would flag about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: So the answer to the first question is no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, there was also another thing that's not discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We discussed whether it was proper having open-ended or closed end.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said a few members would rather have a closed end date or an announcement or some signal that we would go towards that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But then the large majority of the Council preferred to have it open-ended.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think this word had been pronounced, if I am not mistaken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In any event it was not discussed and so this is not tapering; it's just a downsize.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said before, it's consistent with our feedback rule which had been - we've been using all throughout.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second question, the answer is no because our mandate is price stability and not what's happening in different countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is: I can't elaborate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the terms of language will remain the same as last time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, by and large the overall discussion today reflected the increasing confidence that we have in the convergence of inflation towards a self-sustained inflation path in the medium term and towards our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Generally speaking, the growth news is very positive; I can elaborate on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all in all, the revision in the macroeconomic projections goes in the right direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The second question, I cannot answer that: we haven't discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually in a sense it seems even more a remote possibility than it would have been a year ago or even six months ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But on the other point, if we go through the statement I just made, just let me go step by step.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all the forward guidance on interest rate is unchanged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We say we continue to expect interest rates to remain at the present level for an extended period of time and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, we confirm that from January 2018 we intend to continue to make the net asset purchases under the asset purchase programme at a monthly pace of 30 billion until the end of September 2018, or beyond if necessary and in any case, until the Governing Council sees - et cetera - so there isn't any change in the language or intentions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, quite important, the Eurosystem will reinvest the principal payments from maturing securities purchased for an extended period of time after the end of the net asset purchases and in any case as long as necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we add the considerations on inflation where, even though the situation on growth has improved - and by the way: will continue to improve - has improved more than expected and will continue to improve, that's what all sentiment indicators say and also our staff projections say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We say price pressures remain muted and have yet to show convincing signs on a sustained upward trend.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the conclusion is: an ample degree of monetary stimulus therefore remains necessary for underlying inflation pressures to continue to build up and support headline inflation developments over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, we didn't discuss cutting the link.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you noticed, we haven't used the word recovery; we use the word expansion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As the economic expansion gains further strength and keeps on broadening, naturally the stimulus will come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We said that in the introductory statement; it will come from all the elements of the package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore, as a consequence, also the component coming from the forward guidance of interest rates will gain further and further importance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is a natural process led by the recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense our monetary policy accompanies the recovery, as I had chance to say in a speech some time ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, see, we defined it; the answer is, it's close but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The issue here is more how strong is the convergence path towards a self-sustained and sustainable inflation rate which is close to but below 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The developments that we are witnessing in the real economy certainly increase our confidence for an output gap that will get closed in the course of the next year and improving conditions in the labour markets, which in due time should increase pressure on nominal wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, that has been one of the variables we've been looking more at as one of the drivers of the underlying inflation and therefore one of the drivers for a sustained progress in headline inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The programme has been discussed, designed and decided upon a month-and-a-half ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is what stands in place both as far as the size, the volumes, the timing and the open-endedness of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, the difference in the monetary policy decisions and therefore in the interest rates decisions that were taken on the other side of the ocean reflects the different positions of the two areas in the economic recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Economic recovery in the United States is - at the present time, by the way, it's stronger in Europe than in the United States - but the stage at which the economic recovery is in the United States is more advanced and especially so when we look at the wages behaviour, the nominal wages behaviour.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the monetary policy does reflect differences in the stage at which the two jurisdictions are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the other question you asked is whether this affects negatively the European economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We haven't seen any effect from this, meaning that the present constellation of rates by and large reflects the differences in the stage at which the two economies are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: About whether we are confident whether we'll reach our objective, the answer is: today certainly more than we were two months ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's pretty clear that the strengthening of the economy is the basis upon which the output gap will close, the labour market conditions will improve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We discussed exactly this in Sintra and in other places; how in the end wages will react to these improving conditions in the labour market, in spite of the many factors that I've discussed in Sintra.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But by and large they tend to be factors that will disappear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The negative effect of these factors will disappear with the continuing improvement in the labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We didn't discuss this today, by the way, but the last discussion we had a month-and-a-half ago showed that the Governing Council, its vast majority, wants to keep, to retain the open-endedness feature of the asset purchase programme as it's been designed in the last monetary policy council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's the answer to the first point and it's motivated by, basically, the fact that in spite of the significant improvement in the real economy, in GDP growth, in the labour market and frankly in all sentiment indicators, in all business confidence, consumer confidence indicators, in production indicators, PMIs, we see this momentum continuing unabated and broadening its scope.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In spite of this, the decision is justified by developments on the inflation side - and, as you know, our mandate is defined in terms of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So ultimately that is our yardstick and because of that, the Governing Council wants to maintain a steadfast commitment to price stability in keeping, in retaining the open-endedness of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second point about the bonds, well, first of all let me say that this programme is one of our policy tools that we consider important - very important - for the attainment of our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The scope of the programme is not to maximise profits or to avoid losses, so let's keep this in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, running such big corporate programmes, it's not unusual that losses may be happening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, as regards all other central banks that ran similar programmes, do we know whether they had losses or not?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, because they are not disclosing the issuers, the issues, the volumes, the holdings; they're disclosing very, very little.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if anything, we are different because we are much, much more transparent about our programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also say that we are consulting with the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I cannot elaborate a lot about what we are going to do next.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly we have a risk framework which has served us very, very well since the beginning of the existence of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly if we need to draw lessons we'll do - we'll certainly draw lessons from this experience.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are always open to improve, but as I said it's been very, very good.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also as soon as we got news, we stopped buying.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we did what was required from us to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also let me add that the losses that had been reported are by and large exaggerated by a factor of 10 with respect to the actual measure of the losses.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But having said that, having said all this, the losses are there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are not realised and so the issue is, who's going to pay for these losses?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is that these losses really represent a small digit factor number of our €1.6 billion net interest income we produced last year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our objective is an inflation rate close but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, it doesn't mean that it has to be - it can go over 2% and come back.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're talking about in the medium term, let's never forget that and it has to be self-sustainable and self-sustained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Namely, it has to be there without our monetary policy support.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's quite early before we talk about changing our monetary policy support.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Though in the presence of an expansion which is gaining momentum our confidence towards this objective is actually increasing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said before, it's certainly greater than it was in the last monetary policy meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first point, that's what I meant when I said that I cannot elaborate more when I answered before because we are consulting with the rest of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As far as your second question is concerned, I can't really answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At some point we'll certainly look into the overall tax package and we'll come out with assessments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Don't forget that taxation is not in the realm of our competences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly in order to assess whether this is going to have an impact on the European economy, we will certainly look into this, but we haven't done it yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first point, it does echo a previous question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point in time, this is something the likelihood of which is very, very small.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the issue is important; the issue is more generally one of policy space.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Do we have policy space in case something unforeseen, unlikely happens?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the issue of policy space doesn't concern only the monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It concerns first and foremost the need to make our economies more resilient to unforeseen events which cannot be dealt with by anticyclical policies or by monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So first and foremost, we say this now, we said it so many times at the end of the introductory statement; this appeal to structural reforms, that's what we should aim at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, the fiscal policy space is also very limited to cope with sudden downturns and that's why we are pleading for rebuilding fiscal buffers using the benefits of this economic expansion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to the second question is, I cannot say how I see myself.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly if we are to raise interest rates, it would be good news all in all because it would mean that we are back on a path to an inflation rate which is self-sustained and sustainable through the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our monetary policy has accompanied first the recovery and now is accompanying the expansion of the eurozone economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As the recovery was gaining strength and breadth, the nominal amount of monetary accommodation has gone down so much that we halved the asset purchase programme monthly flows.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we took decisions to accommodate the monetary size of our monetary accommodation to the growing economy, to the economy which was previously recovering and now expanding.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the first question is no, we haven't discussed changes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the second question is more general: we always discuss financial stability issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We certainly closely monitor the financial stability risks that may emerge from a situation where we had very, very low interest rates for a long period of time, abundant liquidity for a long period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, we are not seeing systemically important financial stability risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see the local spots where valuations tend to be overstretched.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also as soon as you ask this question, one should also ask the question, how is leverage?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because a bubble is also the outcome of two components.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There, differently from other parts of the world, we don't see leverage for the private sector going up for the whole of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, debt - debt to GDP or debt to value added or debt to assets depending on the measure - actually continues to decrease with different intensity depending on the measure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we don't see the other component even in those local situations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We assess whether the markets are closer or not to develop a financial stability situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there are markets where valuations have been more stretched than others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we ask ourselves, what is the right answer to this problem?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The right answer is to have in place macroprudential instruments that are effective, strong and well-targeted to cope with these risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly it's not to change monetary policy because of a financial stability risk in a certain part or in a certain market of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I think your question identifies a real problem we have in a part of the world where democracy exists.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So with democracy you have elections; with elections you have governments that need to be formed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The citizens of this part of the world take the time that's necessary to form a government that is stable and effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have our views about what should be done about the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course we are entirely in the hands of the citizens of Europe to decide how to pursue these views in a democratically accepted fashion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not in our hands to decide the timing and, to some extent, even the shape.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have our views; we think technically what should be done in order to make our economic and monetary union stronger than it is today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But how and how fast this would be achieved is not in our hands.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, it's entirely in the hands of the government to decide about a fourth programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the Greek economy has fragilities that need to have a programme to be addressed, it will be up to them to decide that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As regards what you asked about liquidity of the banks: what we've seen in the past few years is that liquidity is a consequence of the economic policies that are being pursued by the governments, by the authorities and the reception the markets give to these policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I should speak for the ECB only, but we made this point on and on throughout the Eurogroup, in all institutional setups: The independence of the statistical institutions and their people is of the essence for the credibility of the data which form the basis upon which economic policies are designed, accepted, presented and financed in the specific case of Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all actions that tend to undermine this credibility are certainly not to be shared or agreed by the ECB and the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, all this has been said in full respect of the independence of judiciary of every country, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As regards the risk to the inflation, we can safely say that deflation risks have disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can also safely say that the likelihood of having low inflation in the 0.5%, 0.6% that we've seen until, what, a year ago has certainly decreased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see that the muted response of wages to the improving conditions in the market, in the labour markets and more generally to the closing of the output gap is, if compared with other recoveries and economic expansions, is way slower than we had in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this cautions us - - while we're confident that things are going definitely better also on the inflation front- that cautions us from making bold statements about the fact that inflation cannot turn down and become again low for long.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As regards the sudden stop: sudden stop means that we go from 30 to zero?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether sudden stop becomes an extension of the programme or becomes tapering, that's what you want to know; we haven't discussed that either.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: As regards your first point, that is not the view of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point: our mandate is not growth, it's not employment, it's price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in a condition where we have to infer from the strength of the growth momentum and the improvement in the labour markets what's going to be the ultimate effect on the objective that defines our mandate, which is the inflation rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've qualified this objective in saying that the process towards converging, the process of convergence of this inflation rate to our objective, has to be - before we can remove the ample monetary support - it has to be self-sustained, i.e.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: not in need to be supported by our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's the yardstick and that's where we are today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why we always talk about response of the nominal wages to improving conditions, because that's what we have to understand well; namely the response of nominal wages growth and the reasons why such response is lagging.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: It's not so, it doesn't affect the neutrality of the purchases - and I'll tell you the reasons why you observe these deviations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB doesn't favour certain countries over others in its PSPP purchase programme implementation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, purchases are guided by the ECB's capital key, which takes into account GDP and population.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, focusing excessively on any particular purchase period, for example on 2017 only, could result and yield wrong interpretations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The overall stock of Eurosystem PSPP holdings is the relevant metric for any assessment of the programme and not the recent purchase flows.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to give you an example: currently the Eurosystem holdings of German securities are above the German share of the ECB capital key.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This equates to the Eurosystem holdings€18 billion more in German securities than what is implied by the [German] ECB capital key share.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course the largest deviation from the ECB's capital key is Greece due to their ineligibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In addition Eurosystem holdings of Portuguese securities are 1.8%, which is 27% below, compared to [the Portuguese] share of ECB capital key, which is 2.48%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These flows can differ as the design of the programme is flexible and the distribution of actual purchases often deviates from the ECB capital key.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
