text: For example if we fall short of purchase targets in one jurisdiction for market liquidity reasons, then the shortfall is made up in others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This has happened since the beginning of the programme so it's nothing new.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Moreover, this is particularly relevant for the process of reinvestments, where the amounts to be reinvested are sometimes distributed over three months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This can lead to temporary changes in the relative net purchase shares.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In certain countries, implied purchase shares are above the capital key percentages as we don't buy the required bonds in other jurisdictions due to various programme constraints, for example eligibility criteria, issue and issuer limits, market liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, all these adjustments reflect the programme's inbuilt flexibility and the commitment to a continued smooth implementation of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our purchase shares are guided by ECB capital key as opposed to market cap[italisation], which is our reference for all other purchase programmes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Moreover comparing and finally individual jurisdictions net issuance and the actual purchases in the respective countries suggests, all other things being equal, that the downward impact of the programme on yields for countries such as Germany should be higher than on other countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me get the record straight because several members of the Governing Council were surprised by the reading of the accounts - by the effects that the reading of the accounts had on the markets and they asked me to clarify this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, there is no difference between the accounts and what I said in the press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I was asked was, did you discuss cutting the link in your guidance between the APP - the asset purchase programme - and inflation and what is your view on that question?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually in a sense, I went beyond what was in the accounts in my press conference because I said as a consequence of this continued expansion, also the component coming from the forward guidance of interest rates will gain further and further importance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense our monetary policy accompanies the recovery, as I had chance to say in a speech some time ago - but we haven't discussed the link.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the excerpt of the accounts says: looking ahead the view was widely shared among members.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the Governing Council's communication will need to evolve gradually without a change in sequencing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The only discussion that took place was about the need to have a discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see, my press conference went in - started going to the substance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the actual discussion in the Governing Council was only scheduling the discussion which was to take place in the early part of this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We really went through the events since October to now and trying to basically assess whether something has changed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There hasn't been much of a change other than a continuing strengthening of the economy more - to some extent even more - than expected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we have as I said downside risks relating primarily to geopolitical and especially foreign exchange markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Price pressures are muted, underlying inflation still doesn't show signs of any convincing upward movements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Price pressures along the pricing chain remain broadly stable and subdued.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Recent data on wage growth confirms some lift-off] from its lows of 2016 second quarter, but it's a lift-off so far mostly due to wage drift, not negotiated wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to look better and see whether this picks up and is confirmed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The survey measures of long-term inflation expectations remain broadly unchanged, while market-based measures have increased to 1.76%/78%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large there isn't much of a change, which led us to simply restate the policy, as I've just said in the introductory statement, where basically we continue the monthly pace of €30 billion extended to run until the end of September 2018 and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no need for me to read it again, I guess.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also we went through how we judge whether progress in achieving our inflation objective has happened, has taken place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The inflation rate has to be on a path that reaches levels below but close to 2% in the medium term, so it's not touch and go; in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's one important thing that several speakers have remarked today; is that our commitment to this objective remains firmer than ever.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So most members reiterated the steadfast commitment to reach our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is that when we look at inflation paths over the coming weeks, months, years, we have to see - we'll see a range of paths but this range has to be pretty narrow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, we have to be convinced, we have to have confidence in the degree of convergence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the other thing that we will certainly look at that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then the third criteria is that this convergence should be self-supported.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, will have to do without our monetary policy support.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, even when we judge that adjustment has progressed towards - has progressed enough, our monetary policy will remain very accommodative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because we will continue reinvest and for - as I said in the introductory statement, for an extended period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Especially the interest rates will remain at the present level well past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's of fundamental importance in our forward guidance; well past the end of our net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have observed, however, since December that the expected path of short-term rates, interest rates has moved upward and that the exchange rate volatility has increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We discussed some of the causes of these developments and there are basically three sets of causes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Naturally, as I think have said many times, as the economy improves this will accompany quite nicely our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary policy will accompany the improvement in the economy in a way that the relative influence of the four pillars of our monetary policy will change and will move more and more towards reinvestments for a long period of time towards the importance of the stock of bonds as being accumulated and towards especially, as I said, the forward guidance on interest rates and the well past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is one cause is the improvement in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second cause of these movements that was found is the heightened market sensitivity to perceived changes in our communication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, however, there is a third reason which is - this relates essentially to the exchange rate- that the use of language being discussed in exchange rate developments, that doesn't reflect the terms of reference that have been agreed lastly on October 14th2017 in the IMFC in Washington.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Anyway, someone else will ask this question I was meant to answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, on your first question, first of all let me always reiterate what I always say when we talk about exchange rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't target exchange rates and we say exchange rates are important for growth and for price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, certain movements in the exchange rates to the extent that are justified by the strengthening of the economy are part of nature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a fact of nature, so the issue is whether these other movements in the exchange rate which may be caused by the use of language that I said is not part of the terms of reference that been agreed recently, whether that has an effect on our inflation path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's too early to assess whether the pass through has already taken place and what's going to be the extent of this pass through.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's pretty clear, however, that some people are questioning the extent by which pass through actually happens nowadays.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's pretty clear that very large movements in the exchange rate are bound to have a pass through.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In any event, the language that we agreed in Washington said this: we recognise that this is the communique of the 36thmeeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee in the IMF.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all the ministers and the governors there we recognised that excess volatility or disorderly movements in the exchange rates can have adverse implications for economic and financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will refrain from competitive devaluations and will not target our exchange rates for competitive purposes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the answer to the second question, yes, I said that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said that as far as I was concerned, I said we didn't have a proper discussion and we didn't have a proper - we didn't have any discussion today at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I said as far as I was concerned, we'd never stop the programme abruptly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, here we have to distinguish between sudden stop, an extension of the programme and gradual tapering - and that's exactly the discussion that we will have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's one part actually of the discussion that we will have and the discussion to which the accounts that you read were referring to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First, the answer to the second question; we've received the letter of the Ombudsman - the work of which, by the way, we appreciate greatly - and we will respond in due time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a procedure in place: we'll assess the letter, we'll assess the comments and then we'll respond.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, these are volumes and they follow also principles of market neutrality and so it's difficult for me to answer your question now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One should not look at monthly purchases because they may reflect temporary market conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a certain size that will develop across the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, when I said that, some people actually understood differently; they understood that it would be an extension.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Others, as you probably did, there would be a gradual tapering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But others, later on, there was a comment as far as I'm concerned this programme could actually stop immediately and markets reacted as if that were a serious contingency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just want you to distinguish between the three choices, the three options.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then you can go back to exactly what I said when you asked and give some probability to which one of the three is probably the surer to happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the other question is, wage negotiations belong entirely to social partners.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We observe what's happening from a monetary policy angle, where we consider a wage growth - nominal wage growth - as a very convincing sign of future inflation convergence to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, we don't want to encourage any sense - just we look at that with the detached eyes of the policymakers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me whether it's limited to Germany or will spread to other countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This will depend very much on the conditions of the labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly in Germany, labour market is experiencing the pretty tight conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other countries the labour market's slack is still pretty wide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also it depends on what sort of bargaining strategies the social partners have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example in some countries, even though the labour market is tight, the unions are not negotiating for higher wages immediately but rather for job security.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is plenty of evidence that even though employment's gone up a lot, a lot - much of it is of a temporary, part-time quality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to assess what are the different negotiating strategies before we can conclude that one single nominal wage negotiation in one country will actually spread its effects to the rest of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I will answer the second question, but first let me give the floor to the Vice President on the financial stability risk caused by the negative rates for a long time on lots of assets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: Yes, as the President said, negative rates have been in place for quite some time and we see a situation where no one can talk about, say, asset price bubbles in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have overstretched valuations in some places in what regards commercial real estate or high-yield bonds but nothing else.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In what regards the normal corporate bond market, using different models to calculate the fair value, we see that the prices in the market are indeed close to the fair value.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In spite of prices of housing being increasing recently, nevertheless the analysis of fundamental values showed that this is in line with the fundamentals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To quote some numbers, prices are increasing around 4%, prices of housing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Credit to mortgages, credit to house purchases is increasing at 3.3% - in the period of 2003- 2006, was increasing at 10%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is indeed no general situation of overvaluations on average in the residential properties.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course in some countries, in some regions of some countries, yes, there are price increases that can be seen as excessive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as you know, several countries have taken macroprudential policies of a regulatory nature to face those excesses.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the proper way to go and as you know, now we have also as ECB responsibility in what regards macroprudential policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's being applied, it's being used and there is indeed no general situation of overvaluations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The effect on banks of negative rates, also we have shown several times that taking into account all the effects of our policies, that on average they have been favourable to profitability - which by the way has been increasing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The banks have been increasing profitability; still low, yes, but increasing, which again shows that the policy of negative rates has been absorbed by the banking sector and has not created a problematic overall situation to financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On your first question, the need to rebuild fiscal buffers - part of this expansion is cyclical and at some point will stop.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Interest rates some time in the future will stop being so low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that point, all governments will want to have policy space - especially in case the stopping of the cyclical expansion is not going to be benign.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They will want to have policy space; they have to recreate policy space.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why budget consolidation now, when the time is good, is actually favourable and it's a good thing to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are saying that not only with respect to Italy, but actually it's all over , with few - very few exceptions, what's happening now is that in fact one sees that there is no budget retrenchment or even there is budget expansion at the time of a solid expansion in the economy and with very low interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Answering your second question first; yes, there was concern, several members expressed concern and this concern was also - in a sense was broader than simply the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was about the overall status of international relations right now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the answer to your question is yes; we are concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is also an additional concern that the Governing Council and introductory statement itself in a sense hints at, if all this were to lead to an unwanted tightening of our monetary policy which is not warranted, then we will have to just think about our monetary policy strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was something that has actually been said in the introductory statement, it's also been expressed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me about the various communications; well, I think you see the same thing in the other jurisdictions as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All the communications that you've seen since December have in common three characteristics that were reiterated today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, all of them are based on a steadfast commitment to the objective of the 2%, close but below 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, no communication whatsoever questioned the sequence whereby interest rates would stay at the present level well past the end of the net asset purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then of course you have nuances which were picked up by the market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are in the range of normal differences of views.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the first question is that based on data, on today's data and today's projection, I think I see very few chances at all that interest rates could be raised this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is whether this squares with fundamentals or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Rather than asking this question, which is really very difficult, we should ask; is this movement being produced?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words is it endogenously produced by the strengthening of the economy, by an uptick in inflation or in wages?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is the difference between the monetary policy cycles and the recovery cycles in the various economies, the difference, does this difference grant such movements in the exchange rates or not?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These are the questions that we should ask at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have received the letter which was published and we are assessing it and we will respond according to the existing procedure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, incidentally the Ombudsman also acknowledges that there is no evidence that these meetings could have directly influenced or have had an adverse impact on the ECB's supervisory tasks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: She also acknowledges that the ECB must have dialogues with market participants and also acknowledges that the ECB has a robust system of safeguards in place to manage its contacts with the financial sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, I don't want to discuss further because we are in the course of assessing this letter and preparing our response.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, about the first point, I can only express a wish here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think that the differences between the various members of the Governing Council are as substantive as they were on other occasions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, they are much less substantive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember the three elements: confidence in the convergence of our inflation path to its objective, but also since we don't see now in the data much of inflation, it's patience and persistence in our monetary policy accommodation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The three elements combine themselves in the various members of the Governing Council's view of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we are talking about; some of them are a little more confident perhaps because they live in jurisdictions where inflation and developments are a little more encouraging, or the labour market conditions are tighter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Going back also to one question: where however we have to be careful is that when - there may be differences about when to say certain things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example we can all agree about certain things, but we may disagree about when to move forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's where the market wants to be informed clearly because markets of course have expectations not only about the path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The path is the policy path, but also about the announcement dates, the timelines and that's where discipline is needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I was saying, this in a sense is a second degree of importance difference with respect to the first.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, the overall situation doesn't justify profound existential differences at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your second point was, in March we'll have projections and then we'll assess really how things stand at that point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, I said that the exchange rate has moved in part because of endogenous reasons; namely the improvement in the economy, mostly improvement in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In part for exogenous reasons that have to do with communication, but not by the ECB, but by someone else.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This communication, not the ECB communication, but someone else's communication doesn't comply with the agreed terms of references; that's what I said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a difference between designing monetary policy with a view to pursuing price stability and your objective, that you have to because of your mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That design of monetary policy may well have consequences on the exchange rate, but these will be indirect consequences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Different is when I go and sit - well, not me; someone else - goes and says that basically, a good exchange rate is good for exporters and it's good for the economy and it's good.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That agreement, subtle as you want, has been in place for decades now whereby policymakers, of course if you do take monetary policy decisions, they may have consequence on the exchange rate on both sides- on all sides of our monetary policy jurisdictions, and it's both sides of the ocean but also other countries as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the explicit targeting of the exchange rate is something that really goes back many, many years ago before these terms of reference were agreed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to your first question is basically, when we recalibrated our net asset purchase programme last October, we had to weigh, very much as we are doing today, confidence versus patience and persistence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had the discussion about that, whether it should be six months or nine months, whether it should be 30 or 40 or 20 per month.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: After all analysis and models and discussions we came out with these figures of 30 per month until September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a matter of educated judgement based on data, on projections of inflation, on what is the - in a sense the best design that would produce the convergence in the safest way to our path and also in the most reliable way to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the second question: we are trying - that's why what you say is absolutely right; you have that as a possibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that's why in defining our objective of inflation we use several measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We use headline inflation, which includes these effects but we also use underlying inflation which excludes food and energy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All this, mind, our objective is defined in terms of headline inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But to gain sufficient confidence that the convergence towards our objective is in the medium term, is stable and is self-sustained we need to have evidence also from the other definitions of inflations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, data that don't change because say the market for a certain commodity all of a sudden changes, supply or demand change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We always think and have our discussions and deliberations based on the data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To this extent, we are data dependent and basically, that's what the data tell us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On oil price, yes, indeed; increase in oil prices may be compensated by appreciation in the euro, although it's not easy to understand exactly the timing of these compensations because oil prices have gone up, gone down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The time that it takes to pass through is variable but if you take just the oil price and you translate it in the exchange rate, of course it does compensate that - which doesn't mean by the way that this doesn't imply that we sort of accept a certain level of exchange rate as a good thing or a bad thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just I'm answering to your questioning in sort of abstract terms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, the first question: let me just read to you the sentence we have removed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, it was a sentence introduced in 2016, when we cut our monthly purchases from €80 to €60 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thinking about that, you can just figure out, how different the situation was at that time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sentence says: if the outlook becomes less favourable or if financial conditions become inconsistent with further progress towards a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation, we stand ready to increase the asset purchase programme in terms of size and/or duration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, what we did was to remove the explicit reference to the likelihood of an increase in the pace of purchases in the near future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We shouldn't forget that we have kept the other reference to such a possibility when it says: the Eurosystem will continue to reinvest the principal payments for an extended period of time after the end of net asset purchases and in any case for as long as necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All in all, if you read this decision - by the way the decision was unanimous - that's what it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's substantially a backward-looking decision without signals or implications for either our expectations or our reaction function.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still expect the key ECB interest rates to remain at their present levels for an extended period of time and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We confirm that our net asset purchases at the current monthly pace of €30 billion are intended to run until the end of September 2018, or beyond if necessary - and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what the decision is and that's what it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, if I may elaborate on the second question about Latvia.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why today we are sending a letter to the European Court of Justice.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council has decided, again unanimously, to ask for clarification by the Court of Justice of the European Union whether individual security measures imposed on the Governor of Latvijas Banka by the Latvian Anti-Corruption Authority on 19 February 2018, have had the effect of relieving him from office and they comply with Union law, in particular with Article 14.2 of the Statute.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are asking the ECJ for a clarification on the present situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, on the first question, as I said, it was a unanimous decision and there wasn't much discussion about other possible changes in monetary policy for the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just so that I can give you a sketchy summary of the discussion, it was a kind of a fairly, in a sense, usual blend of confidence, persistence and patience.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of confidence - because the latest incoming data on growth reduced the variance of the path of inflation converging to our inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also persistence and patience - and here of course you have different views, some people are more confident, some people are less confident and therefore they stress the persistence and patience.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was a somewhat repeated reference to the uncertainty surrounding potential output growth path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reason for that is that first of all, we discussed several times about how complex the measurements of unemployment are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But also there is a fact that strong growth may produce stronger potential output growth as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the past structural reforms, the increases in labour supply, the increase in participation rates, the increase in productivity, basically all this increases the uncertainty about the potential output growth path and therefore about the size of the slack in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Another part was devoted to assessing the progress of - well, the possible progress we've made - about inflation, where we said that basically, inflation, headline inflation, will hover around 1.5% for the remaining part of the year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even though we have strong growth, we still have subdued inflation and our mandate is in terms of price stability, so victory cannot be declared yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The exchange was about emphasising all the pillars of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the reinvestment policy for an extended period of time, as I've just read.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Especially we have the forward guidance on interest rate path, and they were all important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am sorry, you also asked the question about trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The immediate spill-over impact of the trade measures, just if you have a static estimate, it's not going to be big.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what strikes me is that whatever convictions one has about trade, we - and certainly the Governing Council is on this line - we are convinced that disputes should be discussed and resolved in a multilateral framework, that unilateral decisions are dangerous.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also there is a certain, I would say, worry or concern about the state of international relations, because if you put tariffs against your allies, one wonders who the enemies are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think these are two general considerations that are quite relevant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on assessing the final impact of these measures many factors come into play.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, is there going to be retaliation or not?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, what's going to be the response of the exchange rate?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far we've seen that whenever there was a threat of putting tariffs towards another country, it was the dollar that would appreciate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third and most important is an aspect of all - I wouldn't call them yet trade wars, but certainly of all the trade exchanges that we've seen - and that's the effect on confidence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The effect on confidence is very difficult to assess, estimate, forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If it is a negative effect on confidence, that's going to be negative on both inflation and output.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We were so focused on our decision on monetary policy that we didn't discuss this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the point is generally speaking that fiscal sustainability is of utmost concern in countries which have high debt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the second question is easy to answer: I let others judge, it's not up to me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first and we were always - and it goes back in tradition - not to discuss risks about inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point here is basically that we see headline inflation driven often by energy prices, food prices and other components that are more volatile.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we look at underlying inflation to judge the robustness of the convergence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These measures of underlying inflation are still - some of them actually ticked up a little.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense, I said before that the decision we took today is obviously using incoming information like, as I said, the reduced variance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Otherwise it's really backward-looking; it doesn't send any new signal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, this experience we had certainly is giving some lessons we ought to really reflect on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, what has been the role of the ECB in this so far?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB has cooperated, has informed and has requested and this is what the ECB does everywhere in these situations with the anti-money laundering, with the national competent authorities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you said, as you heard many times, the ECB is not competent in money laundering and it doesn't have investigative powers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, the current situation as far as anti-money laundering is concerned is not satisfactory.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What you would like to see are two things: more cooperation between national competent authorities on money laundering; more exchange of information; more coordination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a spectrum here: it can go from having a regular and frequent formalised exchange forum or even go up to a centralised authority.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second aspect is the cooperation between national competent authorities and supervisors, both national supervisors and the SSM.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's key because the money laundering activities as far as banks are concerned have produced, unavoidably, reputational and legal consequences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore they create reputational and legal liabilities and therefore the supervisor is going to be called in to react to these risks or prevent them from happening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what's so important; the cooperation between the competent authorities and the supervisor.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, a partly different thing is about the Emergency Liquidity Assistance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have expressed in the European Parliament a view that I share with many Governing Council members and many board members, but it's not something that can be implemented immediately.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My view - which by the way we had this experience, we had other experiences - where the conclusion can't be other than - ELA should be centralised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, it should be given through a process where the Governing Council participates and discusses and, in the end, decides.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is not possible legally now so it's an evolution of the system that at present time I judge unsatisfactory and needs to be changed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, going back to your first question, first of all I don't think Mr Coeuré said flows don't matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Okay, but you see how it makes a big difference whether they matter or they matter slightly less than stocks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first time that a reference to stock was made was at the end of 2015 in a press conference I had where there was, I remember, a vast disappointment about the measures that the Governing Council had just decided and I pointed out that even though the measures were probably not fulfilling your expectations, we still had the stocks that were going to go up over the oncoming period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that time, markets paid no attention whatsoever to stocks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the reason is not that there is actually more than a trade-off; I would say that the two are complementary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When the flows were huge and the stocks were small, the flows mattered more.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, gradually this has changed but this doesn't [mean] - that flows don't matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact, flows at the present time matter a lot also because of the sequence that we have in our monetary policy decision that it's cast in stone whereby the interest rate path depends on the dates of the net asset purchases programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the discussion today showed that all four elements, including the reinvestment policy but especially the forward guidance on interest rates, are important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Listen, you keep on asking questions as if tomorrow I'm going to leave.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I still have quite some time before my mandate expires.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I may be willing to answer questions about myself at the date which is closer to the end of my mandate than it is today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other question, as I said, it's fundamentally a backward-looking measure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, we had several revisions of the growth outlook and at the same time, we have a narrowing of the convergence path, of the variance around the path, which basically explains why in a sense we are confident.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also if you read the words, these are really unlikely contingencies now, the ones that would suggest that we would activate this easing bias.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was the reason why we did it and why we did it today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The second answer is that the market in the United States reacted to a number about inflation - which was falling by the way - and a number about nominal wage growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense they reacted with a sharp market correction, which was in a sense amplified by the conditions of financial markets, especially the stocks, especially the equity market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was mostly limited to the equity market and it was pretty short in terms of reaction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In Europe we don't see wage growth of that amount, we don't see inflation rates of that amount.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: If we make exception for what's happening in the United States between market correction, statements, various statements on trade and other issues, you would agree you don't see much volatility in our financial markets in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If anything, the volatility is mostly caused by our own statements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This angst that everything should be clear in advance isn't reflected in the markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me add that the reason why we have these discussions is that there are different states of mind regarding the new information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is uncertainty about the size of slack and this uncertainty is more present in some members than in others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In some members there is a little less confidence and more desire to wait for more data and to see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in others, there is more confidence in the fact that they would like to say things sooner rather than later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But so far whatever the difference is on when to say things, the basic point is that the policy continues to remain reactive and not proactive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: What we have seen in the past few cases of elections outcomes doesn't suggest that markets reacted in a way that would undermine confidence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reaction to the Italian elections has been more or less the same as it has been to other elections, to other major political events, where most observers were foreseeing sharp corrections or high volatility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's not to underestimate the fact that protracted instability may undermine confidence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said before, anything that undermines confidence is negative, has a negative effect on both inflation and output.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was when I was discussing trade measures, but it applies to all kinds of contingencies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: It's a very broad question and therefore it's very difficult to answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More generally what one can say is that all the reforms that have increased productivity and growth ought to be left in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If these reforms had negative distributional consequences, producing a more inequitable income or wealth distribution, these distributional effects ought to be taken care of.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think if there is one aspect in which, generally speaking, policies not only in Europe I would say, but all over the world, have been insufficient, was to take care of the distributional consequences of reforms that basically were positive for growth, but not necessarily for equity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, I really don't want to comment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can only say that the euro is irreversible and progress on deepening - and I just read it in the introductory statement, where the Governing Council's view about this can be found - the Governing Council says that deepening Economic and Monetary Union remains a priority.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council urges specific and decisive steps to complete the Banking Union and the Capital Markets Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on what you said, certainly I think the gender balance ought to be improved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, let me congratulate Mr de Guindos because the Governing Council approved him.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am absolutely confident that he is going to be a very, very good colleague for all of us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the ECB is concerned, there will be a press release because we are also working on improving our gender balance situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be a press release stating what sort of initiatives we've undertaken and the board has approved recently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These initiatives are undertaken because we've made significant progress since we set explicitly our targets - explicit targets which had not been set before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Still, this progress is less than what we wished for.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We introduced the gender targets in 2013 and the interim now, right now - actually at the end of last year - 27% of management positions were held by women compared with an interim target of 29%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the most senior management roles however, the share was 17% against an interim target of 24% so we've got to do some work here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is basically to ask the head hunters to focus on gender in the recruitment process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Another one is to sort of motivate the business managers to keep vacancies open and possibly until the objective is reached.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are various issues that we've done some work on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was also another important point in that the recruiting panels will now have a considerable presence of women.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense there are often unconscious biases that play a role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why it's necessary to assure a, I would say, much more significant presence of women in the recruitment panels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why we said that the risks to growth are balanced in the sense that we have some upward risks domestically, but some downward risks globally.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that if we have retaliation, we may have effects on confidence that I mentioned before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This would certainly at the very least introduce higher uncertainty in the future growth path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More generally, I think there are two main risks that one can see today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is this one that I mentioned related to trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is also another risk that is less mentioned these days.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the risk of financial deregulation in other major jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We should not forget what the situation was before the crisis - in the years leading to the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Like today, we had an expansionary monetary policy which was justified by the conditions at that time, as ours is justified by the conditions today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the 10-12 years before the crisis there had been a systematic disruption of financial regulation in the major jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This combination, we may disagree whether the source was predominantly one or the other, but certainly nobody would disagree about the combination of the two.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would flag this as one major risk for the years ahead: that we repeat the same mistake.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I should say also that the 'we' is not right in this context because in the eurozone both national legislators and European legislators and the European Commission are certainly not on that path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are talking about a global market and so massive deregulation in one part of the market is going to affect the whole world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, the information will follow our gradual assessment of the convergence of our inflation path to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As we see more information coming that says that this convergence is progressing, is becoming more robust and is becoming more and more self-sustained, so will be the information - it will be clearer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll be in a position to provide you with more clarity about the oncoming developments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, responding to the first question, that's what I read here, and I repeat it: regarding non-standard monetary policy measures we confirm that our net asset purchases at the current monthly pace of €30 billion are intended to run until the end of September 2018, or beyond if necessary, and in any case until the Governing Council sees a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Before I reiterate this, we continue to expect the ECB interest rates to remain at their present levels for an extended period of time and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We deal with price stability for the eurozone; that's what matters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't look at individual countries - or we do look at the individual countries only as far as the developments in individual countries are useful to assess the convergence to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is price stability for the whole of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, on the first point, as a matter of fact the BIS, the Basel Committee was not able to agree on a treatment of the sovereign exposures in the banks' balance sheets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, most countries don't have any specific risk weight with respect to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, our experience from the crisis in the eurozone has shown that sovereign bonds are not riskless: they're risky and they are in the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These are risky assets in banks' portfolios, so we have to take this into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, we want to keep a level playing field across the world with a treatment of similar risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a complex issue that people are working on in the European Commission, in the European Parliament.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the other point was about inflation; shall we throw away the books?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I think this was suggested, or it was more frequent, about until a year ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then you had two views: one was that we should lower it to 1% or 0%, some people said and others said we should raise it to 4%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ones that were suggesting 4%, the idea was that then expectations for inflation will adjust and therefore the policy would have to become even more accommodative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point is, basically, that the ECB is following best practice like all the other central banks - or most of them, certainly all the large central banks in the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on the other hand, there are serious costs about changing course on credibility and the anchoring of expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can go on on this for a while about changing objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's always wrong to fix attention to one specific week or one specific month.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know this - there is a certain amount of flexibility around purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, what's happened here is that we had a higher seasonal amount of purchases at some point and therefore we kind of averaged down with lower purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This coincided also with a downsize of the programme that took place after December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no specific strategy behind the lower amount of purchases of the private corporate bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the first question perhaps suggests that I report on the exchanges we had today because this would explain the answer to your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the interesting thing is that we didn't discuss monetary policy per se.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All Governing Council members reported on the situation of their own countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that since our last meeting, broadly all countries experienced, to different extents of course, some moderation in growth or some loss of momentum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the indicators that showed significant, sharp declines, we see that, first of all, the fact that all countries reported means that this loss of momentum is pretty broad across countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also broad across sectors because when we look at the indicators, it's both hard and soft survey-based indicators.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Sharp declines were experienced by PMI, almost all sectors, in retail, sales, manufacturing, services, in construction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we had declines in industrial production, in capital goods production.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also we had declines in national business and confidence indicators.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And these declines were sharp and in some cases, the extent of these declines was unexpected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The issue is how the Governing Council has read these new developments and I think this was your question, really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, we have to look at - the present figures now - first of all, the decline stabilised and the levels at which they are today are still above historical averages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, these declines happened, as I've just said in the Introductory Statement, after a period of very strong growth for the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had four quarters, if I'm not mistaken, at 0.7%[1].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we discussed the possible causes of this or how to read through - to read this normalisation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly there is some unexpected component, as I was saying, which is mostly due to temporary factors like the - especially in one country it's cold weather, it's the strikes, it's the timing of Easter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are several temporary factors which may have produced this unexpected size.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then the discussion was how much of this is supply, is the effect of supply constraints that are limited to labour shortages in some sectors like construction?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are also other phenomena like for example the drop in backlogs, in manufacturing and capital goods sectors that would - could suggest a softening in demand and therefore warrant monitoring by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if I had to just give you an idea what the bottom line of this discussion is in my view, it's basically caution in reading these developments, caution tempered by an unchanged confidence in the convergence of inflation to our inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The overall growth remains, as I've just said, solid and broad based.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The risks are broadly balanced but, as I said, with more prominence to global risks and I mentioned protectionism.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, having said that, measures of underlying inflation since our last meeting moved sideways.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There hasn't been any convincing upward trend or signs that this upward trend is about to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are certain encouraging signs on nominal wage growth where we start seeing some movements which may support price pressures in the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is about it - I think I've answered your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said caution tempered by an unchanged confidence that inflation will converge towards our aim over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But such convergence remains conditional on an ample degree of monetary accommodation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the end, steady hand were words used in the discussion in the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our policy has, as you've just reminded us, served us well and will continue to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore the other words we used were patience, prudence first of all in assessing, patience and persistence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, it goes without saying that the Governing Council shares its steadfast commitment to price stability, defined as a rate of inflation which is close but below 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on your first question you're right; the exchange rate stabilised and recent volatility is less.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to your second question is in the very carefully prepared opinion of the ECB that was submitted about two weeks ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the first question: we have to see what the exchange of, so far, rhetoric - almost rhetoric - about protectionism will produce.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we have an increase in tariffs, increase in protectionism, there may be direct effects, trade related effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They don't seem to be so far from what we can appreciate now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However we don't know the extent of the retaliation yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously we can't know now what are going to be the direct effects of potential retaliation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is certainly known is that these events have a profound and rapid effect on confidence, on business confidence, on exporters' confidence generally speaking.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is why we say there are risks and these risks have acquired more prominence recently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll have to see, basically, how the growth outlook and therefore how the change in the growth outlook could alter what is the convergence of our inflation rate to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the first question is we haven't discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It would be premature for me to make any comment about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the second question is concerned, to some extent this increase in yields in the United States ought to be expected for at least two reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is the different position in the business cycle of the US economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They have, I think, an unemployment rate which is below 4% amongst other things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a natural development of the economic situation in the United States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: No, don't get me wrong, we are concerned about these developments and we have to assess their impact on the medium-term outlook for growth and prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mentioned before caution and I mentioned some developments that the changes in these indicators - that may suggest a more durable softening in demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore they warrant monitoring so we will have to assess this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I described however how all this is happening in a context of an economy which is still very - which still grows strongly, which is just past the period of a year or even more than a year, with very strong growth given the history of the eurozone and more generally of Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question is about whether the increased demand has actually caused an increase in potential output growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From this viewpoint it isn't necessarily linked to an overshooting of the inflation rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It simply would suggest that there is more room for keeping the ample monetary accommodation in place, be it based on assets or be it based on keeping low rates for a longer period of time while at the same time if it were the case of a durable increase in potential output growth, well, at the same time the neutral rate would be higher.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It actually doesn't necessarily suggest any overshooting of inflation; it's in a sense two different things, really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is actually a very, I would say, legitimate question and a proper one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the reason why we didn't discuss monetary policy per se is that the reading of the current developments since the beginning of the year is actually very important in deciding the next steps.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Careful assessment, monitoring, the use of more information, are all important components in the next decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The very first thing we have to do is understand exactly - and place what's happened in the proper context - whether it's temporary or permanent, whether it's more supply or more demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether it's something that is just the beginning of a more significant decline or it's simply normalisation after a prolonged period of very strong growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, this is combined with my answer to the previous question; what has happened to potential output growth?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was estimated a few years ago to be - I can't remember what the figure is; has it gone up permanently or not?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a complex reading which is essential I think for informing our next decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You are right to ask why not discussing monetary policy; that's the answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, thank you for the question and for the terms of the question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will certainly miss you, miss the ECB - miss everything that I have been doing, for many years now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have been a member of the Governing Council for 18 years, eight as Vice President of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I have worked in central banks for 33 years of my life.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's really a change which I am contemplating with equanimity, no big deal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Regarding your question - which is an important one of course - as other central banks, after the big crises and all the unconventional measures that we had to take, started to normalise and thinking about the future monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the first thing to retain is nevertheless that the set of unconventional instruments that were used are now part of the toolkit of monetary policy to be used if necessary in situations that may justify again that those instruments would be used.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thinking more about the future, as was implicit in your question, I have doubts that on the other hand, one can go back to the simple life of monetary policy as it used to be, with very small central bank balance sheets and just policy targeting the overnight money market rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Perhaps things will have to change a bit for two main reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one is that the structure of the financial system has changed enormously.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even in Europe we are now a much less bank-based system than we used to be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In my presentation of the Annual Report in the European Parliament I had the occasion of quoting the numbers, which are impressive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to sum up, if you take the financing of non-financial firms and you take only the debt instruments of financing non-financial firms, in 2007 61% of debt instruments were bank loans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you take total external financing of non-financial firms including then equity instruments, bank loans represent only 15% of total external financing of non-financial firms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, the structure has evolved dramatically, which means that the system that monetary policy has to think about, to decide on proper transmission of monetary policy, is different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second element which makes it different is that the complexity of the financial sector and the growing importance of the non-bank part of the financial system mean that the spectrum of interest rates that are more and more relevant is different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary policy trying to influence only the overnight rate perhaps will not be enough.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not fully sure of that but I think reading, by the way, several academic papers that have been thinking about this, that other instruments may become necessary and a broader targeting of other interest rates to ensure an effective transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All central banks are now thinking about this medium-to-long-term future of monetary policy in an ever-more-complex environment of finance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Yes, the present situation is one where Latvia can't vote until there will be a governor in place and so that's a fact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is, I think the reputation of the ECB is pretty good.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It may happen that - we are people - so members might have problems.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, what we care about however - different judiciaries in different countries will do their jobs - what's really very important for us is that the independence of the central bank governors, even personal independence beyond the institutional independence, be preserved and be protected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On this point, the Governing Council is absolutely compact and in full agreement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Constâncio: Well, on the particular point of financial stability and NPLs, let me first start by signalling that the situation has continued to improve enormously for various reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly one of the reasons has been the pressure exerted by the SSM, by ECB Banking Supervision on the banks that have higher NPL ratios.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Indeed those banks over-complied with the targets that they defined and were part of the supervisory dialogue with the SSM, which is a good sign.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the end of last year, the average ratio of NPLs over total credit was 4.8% coming below 5%, which is big progress - although more progress is necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's an average; the situation as you know is quite heterogeneous particularly in six countries where the numbers are well above the average.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Progress is still necessary and the progress has to be gradual, as everyone acknowledges.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It cannot be done from one moment to the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, the banks are much better capitalised than before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's very important because it means that in the short term, the question of NPLs is not a question of immediate solvency issues because the banks have the capital.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The problem is that having an important part of their total assets in assets that are not generating normal income affects the profitability of the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course if the bank is not profitable for many years then the solvency issue may arise later down the road.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Indeed in terms of the common equity capital ratio, the average now is 14.3%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No bank, however small, has less than 11% in common equity - and that's not total capital; it's just common equity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All these considerations are important, as it is also important to look to the SSM Regulation that brought supervision to the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There you see that there are micro-supervision competencies and macro-supervision competencies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB inherited then also a macroprudential capacity via the SSM Regulation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB's banking supervision, or SSM, has in its mandate, in its basic legislation, both dimensions of supervision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to your first question is that we did say on a variety of other occasions that we will be reacting to any unwanted or unwarranted tightening of financial conditions that might affect our medium-term outlook for price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we say that the ample degree of monetary accommodation remains essential to guarantee the self-sustained convergence of inflation to our inflation aim, that's what we mean.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We mean that we are ready to adapt this ample accommodation to any unwanted tightening of financing conditions that may alter our medium-term outlook for price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, you are right; there haven't been many steps recently in completing the banking union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There has been a prolonged discussion so you should understand that this is mostly for member states to discuss.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not really, in a sense, party to any negotiation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These are important decisions and are, to some extent, political decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, it's unquestionable that the decision that leaders took in June 2012 to proceed with the banking union, to create the SSM, to create the Single Resolution Board, to establish the Single Resolution Fund and ESM were all decisions that were addressing evident fragilities - apparent fragilities - of the monetary union, and which were made evident by the crisis but were actually pre-existing the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are several reasons why a banking union and a capital market union are essential for risk sharing in the future, without even thinking to fiscal capacity or other forms of risk sharing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's overdue; progress should be made, that's what we say each and every time in our Introductory Statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, we cannot do much more on that and we certainly contribute as an advisor to the ongoing discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, the first question, clearly the ECB welcomes any work on deepening the monetary union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's apparent that the political decisions that underpin such progress are easier in certain countries than others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be patient; simply there is no alternative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our leaders have to discuss the pros and the cons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All of them are aware that the monetary union remains fragile if this progress is not achieved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's something on which all of us can count; their awareness.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course all of us would have liked that the repair after the crisis would have been shorter in time, as it had been the case in previous episodes of recession.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this was very special and much more severe than normal, and so affected the financial system and the banking sector in a big way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that these types of crisis take more time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can look back, and perhaps with a little bit more optimism than was implicit in your question, in the sense that we can say that most of the work has been done and that we are on the path to - as this press conference also indicated in the initial statement in the answers of the President, that everyone feels confident that we are on the way to the normalisation of our objective regarding price stability, and meaning that most of the way has been achieved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course when we leave with a sense of the work almost done in that respect and that monetary policy, perhaps hopefully in the next few years, will not be as exciting as it has been during the years I spent in the Board.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I came on the 1stJune 2010, at the peak of the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, that's a sense of fulfilment but at the same time, yes, we would like to see the work done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, it's never done because we know that some time down the road there will be another recessionary episode - very unlikely of the same scale of the one we had - but it will come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The conditions now of inertia, of self-sustainability, of growth at this moment in the euro area allow us to contemplate a few years of growth if there are no external shocks that can derail this smooth development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We all know that these external shocks may indeed happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, before we leave, just let me share with all of you just two words on Vítor Constâncio.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You've been next to me on this podium now for almost seven years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Plus six years as central bank governors we've been sitting next to each other at the Governing Council, fiercely disagreeing on a variety of things, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But basically, with an enormous - actually agree more often than not - and an enormous respect for you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just one thing; I think you know it, but I just want to let you know this and tell you in front of all our friends here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have been a fundamental presence in the Governing Council and in the board.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have been fundamental in taking key decisions over the last six years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's with the memory of your advice and the passion that you put in carrying forward your arguments and your convictions that I will always remember you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, one word however before we leave in which I want to welcome Vítor's successor, Luis de Guindos, who will join us as of 1stJune and attend our press conference in Riga.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: [1]According to Eurostat, euro area GDP quarter-on-quarter growth was 0.7% in 2017Q4, 0.7% in 2017Q3, 0.7% in 2017Q2, and 0.6% in 2017Q1.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, frankly, we didn't discuss if we want to raise rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We said at least through the summer - let me re-read this because it's quite important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We keep them unchanged and we expect them to remain at their present levels at least, at least through the summer of 2019 and in any case for as long as necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see, in a sense this and the other question you asked about "subject to incoming data," it really tells something about the environment in which we took this decision when news are still good, but they're not as good as they were a quarter ago, but are still solid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The quarterly real GDP growth moderated to 0.4%, so 0.4% is less than 0.7% but it's still high growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we go through the various causes of this moderation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, it's a pullback from the very high levels of growth in 2017, mostly justified by an extraordinary pickup in exports, which is unlikely to repeat itself now, compounded by an increase - an undeniable increase in uncertainty - and for a variety of reasons really, mostly geopolitical reasons, and some temporary and supply-side factors at both the domestic and the global level as well as weaker impetus from external trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The assessment that the Governing Council gave of the current economic environment, of the underlying strength of the economy, while being overall appropriate for achieving the decisions that were taken today, doesn't want to underplay the existing risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, we may well have this soft patch being somewhat longer than it is in the staff projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In some countries, for example, it is foreseen that it may extend into the second quarter, but this at the same time doesn't tell that the underlying strength isn't changed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The underlying strength of the economy in the medium term is what we assess to be adequate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as whether a specific risk may have an impact, we've seen some volatility, then it has receded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point in time, we have a variety of reasons - this is just one of them - which we felt is less than it was two weeks ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, to say that we anticipate - because that's what we say - a series of actions, means that based on the current assessment, we are taking these actions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have this forward guidance on interest rates which is both state and date dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This in a sense shows the environment, as I said responding to the first question, in which these decisions were taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
