text: We've taken these decisions knowing that the economy is in a better situation with an increase in uncertainty and at the same time, probably because of information that came after the cut-off date, probably in some countries this soft patch, as I said before, will continue in Q2 while the projections have revised Q1, but have kept unchanged the Q2, Q3 and Q4 for this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, basically the Governing Council judged the progress towards a sustained adjustment of the inflation rate towards our aim to be consistent with our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, the situation is overall similar and in fact you will notice that they still remain broadly balanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At some point, we say that so far, because we have an unquestionable increase in the geopolitical global uncertainty, we may also have some increase in the - but less so - in the domestic uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On growth we are going to have positive surprises from the fiscal expansion in the United States and very likely fiscal expansions, but this is more medium term, in the eurozone, in several countries in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, we didn't discuss the reinvestment policies you have noted; we will discuss it in the future meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point in time, we believe there was enough to communicate for just one meeting and we will cope with this later on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just respond to your second question, so we went through a pretty extensive discussion on the existing environment, on the economic scenario now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we went through the assessment of SAPI [sustained adjustment in the path of inflation].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We went through whether it's convergent, so we went through what's convergence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There we looked at projections and we compared projections across time and projections with other sources of what is inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, these projections over time and compared with other sources showed a remarkable improvement with respect to not long ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we went through the examination of confidence, whether we can call ourselves confident about this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again we looked at expectations, both market based and the SPF, the ECB Survey of Professional Forecasters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, we went through the assessment of resilience; in other words, is it a durable convergence, self-sustained convergence?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to that was positive as well and I think the market reaction to our announcement shows that it is a self-sustained convergence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For two reasons, given the present economic situation, but also we always have to remember that the continuing convergence is conditional on interest rates remaining; on reinvestment for an extended period of time; on all the other decisions we have taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The general character of the decisions was - basically remains - to be patient, to be prudent and to be persistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was unanimously confirmed, so the decision was a unanimous one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, let me draw more carefully your attention of what unanimity means in this decision, in this context of the decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, on forward guidance: the decision was unanimous about its date and state dependency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will see that all throughout there is a desire to maintain optionality in each and every part of this decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the state, in the case of interest rates, we say at least through the summer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will point out the various parts where optionality comes in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second point about reinvestment; there is unanimity about the extended period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The intent there, as you see in the IS [Introductory Statement] is to avoid any sort of tightening of the excess liquidity conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then let's look at the various parts where optionality comes in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, you have, as I said before, at least in other words, "We decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We expect them to remain at their present levels at least through the summer of 2019 and in any case, for as long as necessary."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point where optionality comes in is at the end of the paragraph that says, "In any event, the Governing Council stands ready to adjust all of its instruments as appropriate to ensure that inflation continues to move towards the Governing Council's inflation aim."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here it comes, the other part of the option, "in a sustained manner."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third part where it comes in is when we say that we anticipate that after September 2018, it's subject to incoming data, confirming our medium-term inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will reduce the monthly pace of et cetera, net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other point is where unanimity is also quite an important thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It basically was an agreement that APP is not disappearing; it remains part of the toolbox.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a new instrument of monetary policy that will be used for contingencies that we don't see now, and that's what we anticipate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it remains now as a normal instrument to monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fourth part that you will see coming several times in the introductory statement is when we say, "Today's monetary policy decisions maintain the current ample degree of monetary accommodation that will accompany the continuing recovery."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you correctly pointed out, the fact that it's been a unanimous conclusion gives special strength to this - to today's monetary policy meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, of course the second question I will not answer given what's been said at the beginning; that I am not taking questions on a court case that's pending.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just tell you about the second question; the ECB isn't taking any side in this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB wants just to be assured by the European Court of Justice about the measures that are needed for the ECB Governing Council to function properly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, tapering: we haven't really discussed policy options because this meeting has been in a sense thoroughly prepared through very good and intense work by the committees of the national central banks and the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we reached this decision time, we were all quite well prepared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We could easily converge on a set of decisions that, as I said, had unanimity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, on your first point, yes, we've seen a significant rise in sovereign yields on the back of political uncertainty around the end of May.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those yields are currently at more elevated levels compared to our last meeting in April, but not as elevated as they were in the immediate aftermath of these events.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Contagion was not significant, if any, if at all, so it was a pretty local episode and so we haven't seen the redenomination risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was a discussion, if we go back in 2011 and '12, about redenomination risk but the situation was entirely different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's quite important to remember; it was a situation that was actually attacking, was a lack of confidence attacking several countries at once.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Financial market tensions at that time were much more extreme in scale and in scope.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also at that time, the institutional framework of the euro was not as developed as it is today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we have several new safeguards against redenomination risk, so I don't think this discussion was meaningful today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We certainly monitor financial market developments carefully, but so far we haven't seen contagion, really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now on reinvestment: we haven't decided yet but it says something that we said there is unanimity about the definition of extended period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly there is the collective intention of the Governing Council members to avoid any tightening of excess liquidity conditions or any unwanted tightening of monetary and financing conditions that may spur from the reinvestment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we will discuss this in time; markets have their own expectations as well, they have expectations about interest rates and so, we look at that as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far, I wouldn't want to say anything more than that because we, frankly, didn't discuss that other than in the terms that I mentioned to you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, let me just say one thing about the sovereign re-pricing, the sharp re-pricing in sovereign bonds we had some time ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just let me say first of all we shouldn't dramatize changes of policies too much.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have 19 countries; we are bound to have 19 elections every now and then.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It may well be that different views from before are being expressed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is important, however, is that these differences are going to be discussed within the existing treaties.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These discussions ought to be carried out within the existing treaties even if these discussions were to contemplate changes because after all, we are talking all the time about deepening our monetary union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This discussion is happening within the existing treaties, within the existing framework.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third point: it's important that these discussions do not destroy the progress that's been achieved after a lot of sacrifice.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some countries have been doing well for many years, but others are just starting doing well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's important that these discussions are carried out in, with a language that doesn't destroy the progress that these countries have achieved after so much sacrifices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Four: the euro is supported, is the currency of 340 million people and has - enjoys now - a 74% support across the citizens of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can take your conclusions, but one conclusion is that it's irreversible because it's strong, because people want it and because it is of no benefit to anybody, to discuss the [euro's] existence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, as I said, the answer to the second question is given by the statement that says, "The Governing Council decided to keep the key ECB interest rates unchanged and we, the Governing Council, expect them to remain at their present level at least through the summer of 2019, and in any case as long as necessary to ensure that the evolution of inflation remains aligned with our current expectations of a sustained adjustment path."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, as you've seen however these policy rates being what they are, as low as they are, don't imply that what's being claimed very often: that the savers are being deprived of their income, of their interest, because savers can well invest in other assets as well and they have done so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They don't imply that bank profitability is being affected, as people claimed two years ago, because we see that bank profitability, even insurance companies and even pension funds are actually doing better because the level of these rates was important for the recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All these people have actually benefited more from the recovery than they were harmed by the low level of interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Overall the balance is vastly positive, as we see this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your first question relates really to the criteria for declaring that a self-sustained adjustment has been achieved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here the Governing Council discussed whether there is enough convergence of inflation towards our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we compare the measures of inflation, both headline and core inflation or underlying inflation, now, today, with the same measures, say, in 2015 or even '16, we see that the progress since then has been truly remarkable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second criteria, yes, it's converging, but how confident are we that this convergence will continue?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here the Governing Council went through a first of all discussion of comparing different expectation measures from different sources.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second comparing projections of inflation across time, in other words, how were we projecting the path of inflation, say, two years ago and then a year-and-a-half and then a year ago and then six months ago and then three months ago and then now?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third: we look at what we define confidence intervals around these projections and we see that this confidence interval is narrowing, it's shrinking.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, while we were talking quite frequently about three years ago about surrounding uncertainty of our projections, now it's disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fourth - and it's very important - the tail risks, risks of deflation, have disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's very important, because again if we go back two, three years ago we would see that there was a serious risk of, what we call de-anchoring of inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why the well-anchored inflation expectations together with an economy which is, continues to be strong, make us think that we can be confident about the convergence of inflation because of the improving labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we look at nominal wages for example, we can say now that it's just the data that's come out yesterday, if I'm not mistaken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It shows a 1.9% nominal wage growth compensation per employee for the whole of the eurozone on average, which means that some countries are above that and some countries are less than that, but it's pretty encouraging.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's actually always said; that that was the key variable we would look at for convergence of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It appears that it's self-sustained, as you can see from today's decision and the reactions to the decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I can answer both questions because distribution of tasks is the President's responsibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I see that this is a passionate question for many of you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, they have not been distributed yet and so far they have been reassigned to the same board members as they were before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first question actually was: does it mean "through the summer," does it mean September?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, if it had meant September, we would've said September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said at the very beginning, it tells that this decision has been taken in the presence of a strong economy with increasing uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the bank was declared failing or likely to fail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Secondly, in the test of public interest it was negative, so it wasn't subject to the traditional resolution procedure according to the resolution directive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The bank was put under the insolvency proceedings and this is local regulation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that I have to say that with respect to insolvencies and insolvency regulations that there are gaps and differences among different countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that this is something that we have to make progress.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the information that we have is that one of the alternatives of the Latvian law on insolvency is the possibility of self-liquidation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that now the authorities have given the go-ahead to this possibility and it's going on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here perhaps the lesson that we can draw is that in order to have a level playing field, we have to make progress in terms of consistency and coherence among different countries with respect to insolvency regulation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I think actually you asked two questions to get one answer; that it really doesn't pay at all to discuss the existence of something that's irreversible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It can only create damage and this holds true both ways, really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the first question is really, I can only respond reading again what this means, "We expect them [key ECB interest rates] to remain at their present level at least through the summer of 2019, and in any case for as long as necessary."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here the intention is to give a time dimension but not a precise one, for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of which is that it's both state contingent; in other words, we have to look at the general situation of the convergence process and its state.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It would be very difficult to say that at the precise, at 3:00 pm of that day, of that month we've actually reached exactly the convergence that we have been aiming at in the last six years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said at the beginning, it also shows the general uncertainty that has increased over the previous weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other point, the other question was whether we discussed reinvestments in July; we haven't decided yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We haven't decided, so we are going to discuss it in one of the future meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, we have to be very mindful of the excess liquidity conditions in the markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the remaining net asset purchases of this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the forward guidance on interest rates and we have the reinvestments of the stock of bonds that we purchased so far.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is another important decision that we'll take in the months ahead.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can agree with you that the certainty about this last dimension is important, so we'll have to cope with this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your last question is too difficult for me or in other words, it does require a political judgement which in a sense goes out of the task of a central banker now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the first question relates to what's happening on the trade front between US and, well, not only European Union, actually; it's the US and the rest of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense, it's important to know that the projections do not contain the effects of trade measures that have not been implemented yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They only contain the effects of the measures that have been implemented already and the direct effects of these measures are pretty limited.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course to the extent that there is going to be a general retaliation or a further implementation of further measures, the effects can be more significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think in another press conference I stressed an effect which is in a sense harder to quantify, but it's probably the most important one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the effect of general confidence, that a round of measures and retaliations may produce on the world economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's more urgent than ever that these discussions, again in a sense like other discussions I pointed out to before, are being run within the existing multilateral framework.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense that is as important as the nature of the measures that are being discussed because if we undermine the multilateral framework that has accompanied our existence since the war, since the Second World War onward, and has accompanied the very long prosperity that the world enjoyed since then, then we are going to create a very serious damage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've gone through this - not we - but our ancestors have gone through this already, so no need to repeat the experience and we've seen where this has driven all of us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the estimate of the ECB as far as the effects of the various policy measures, - but mostly it's QE, of course - over the last three, if I'm not mistaken, cumulative effect over the last three years: it's 1.9% additional GDP growth, if I'm not mistaken, and 1.9% additional inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, on the first question, the rates will be changed depending on what is the state of the convergence process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you can see again from this sentence, it says, "at least through the summer of 2019", but then it says, "in any case for as long as necessary these rates will not be changed to ensure that the evolution of inflation remains aligned with our current expectations of a sustained adjustment path."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is what the sentence says and I hope that in the next year we will be giving an assessment of convergence that is positive and confident.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, the ECB communicated already last week on this topic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, one shouldn't get obsessed about weekly figures of flows because one is bound to get confused, the first remark.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second remark is that in that month, in May, it was not only Italy but also France, Austria, Belgium, so their share in net purchases went down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, this is nothing new; it's the result of rules that have been communicated a long time ago and agreed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the reasons why one shouldn't be obsessed with the weekly or monthly figures is that there are redemptions and redemptions are very hard to foresee on a monthly basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to have a little flexibility, a month, between two months at least, to compensate - which is exactly what happened in this case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In May the ECB purchased €3.6 billion of Italian bonds, but this was higher than what it purchased in March; it was €3.4 billion and what purchased in January, €3.4 billion, so no conspiracy here!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question really, we basically took note of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I understand that this afternoon the Commission is having a meeting exactly for this reason.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We took note of this meeting and if one can say something that's general, it's a good sign because it shows that there is a willingness to discuss trade issues in a multilateral framework again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It would be difficult for us to go beyond that because we really don't know the substance of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, no, we didn't discuss the reinvestment policy today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, let me stress that our enhanced forward guidance, which is both date-based and state-contingent, conveys the Governing Council's expectations that key ECB interest rates, as I said in the Introductory Statement, will remain, we expect them to remain at their present levels at least through the summer of 2019 and, in any case, for as long as necessary to ensure the continued sustained convergence of inflation to levels that are below but close to 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, this enhanced forward guidance has been very effective, as broadly reflected in surveys, market commentary and market prices, in aligning expectations of the future rate path with the anticipations of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this stage we don't see the need to modify or to add new language to our forward guidance on rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the second question, different monetary policies do reflect the response of monetary authorities to different positions in the business cycle.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We said several times that the exchange rate is not a policy target; that it's important for growth and price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is an international consensus that has been going on now for years - for decades, perhaps - about abstaining from competitive devaluations, so that's the answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Incidentally, if one looks at the nominal effective exchange rate of the euro vis-à-vis all the partners, all the trading partners, as a matter of fact the euro has appreciated considerably over the last year, year-and-a-half.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On protectionism, no, we haven't done any further analysis than I have outlined last time and the reason is that we basically have to see exactly what's going to be implemented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen and we have analysed that the implemented, the direct effects of implemented tariffs, as I said last time, are limited.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But clearly, a trade war where you have rounds of retaliation and rounds of responses would create an entirely different climate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We would have to assess both the direct effects, which may be significant as the numbers significantly go up, and the indirect effects of confidence on - especially on business investment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We haven't done anything different from last time yet, so we'll have to assess in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly, just to make it clear, the capital key remains our anchor in what we do on reinvestments, just to clear the slate from any doubt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I think the best way to answer both questions is to give you a short account of what's been our discussion today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, first of all, the Governing Council took note that there hasn't been much of a change since last time; has not been a change in the assessment of the outlook - of the medium-term outlook - for growth or inflation, nor in the monetary policy message.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first point is that it's now clearer than it was before that the moderation in growth - and here I am addressing your first question - depends essentially on the pullback from the unusually strong growth rates that we've seen in the first - the last three-quarters last year, which were caused by - predominantly by an unusually strong export performance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now there is a pullback and the export performance is much less strong than it was before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some sluggishness in the first quarter is continuing in the second quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I would say almost all indicators have now stabilised at levels that are above historical averages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Overall the risks to growth have been assessed as still broadly balanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Financing conditions remain stable and the labour market continues to improve, thereby supporting private consumption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also the accommodative monetary policy and the resulting financing conditions do support private investment, as we can see from the figures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on inflation - and here I am coming to the other point of your question - it's true that headline inflation is now 2% from 1.9%, but if you look at the inflation, so the next question that one should ask is - is this going to be sustained?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is that if we look at inflation excluding oil and food it's now 0.9% from 1.1% last time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The underlying inflation remains muted so we see encouraging signs here and there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, one positive development is the nominal wage performance where, you remember, we've seen a pickup in nominal wage growth across the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Until recently this pickup was mostly produced by wage drift, while now we are seeing that there is a component, which is the negotiated wage component, which is now - right now the main driver of the growth in nominal wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The conclusion was that the assessment of confidence that we expressed in Riga about convergence of inflation to our objective, is still warranted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore prudence, patience and persistence are still going to be the keywords that inform, inspire our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, I'll address first the second question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me clear: the only version that conveys the policy message is the English version.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We conduct our Governing Council in English and agree on an English text, so that's what we have to look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, as you've seen, the term structure of money market rates reflects the - it reflects two things; reflects the pure expectations of the future path of the policy rates, but reflects also the uncertainty that surrounds the evolution of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I think I said last time, as far as pure expectations are concerned, they are very well aligned with the anticipation of the Governing Council that policy rates will remain at their current levels through the summer of next year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then you have the uncertainty component in the term structure; this of course tends to be more variable and shifts with risk perceptions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we see is that this component now may have increased since our June announcement due to various factors, including the state of the debate on trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me now address the first part of the question about whether we can see an impact coming from higher nominal wage growth that could compensate trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Frankly, we haven't done this analysis yet but we do see growth rates stabilising at this level, which is actually pretty good for the eurozone after this unusual performance in exports.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do expect the second part of this year to continue being on solid growth, broad based across sectors and across countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, first of all let me make a general point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the way in which a monetary union settles its payments and it's devised to make sure that money flows unencumbered across countries, individual sectors, companies - all economic agents.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the first thing that we should always keep in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second thing is; how do we interpret recent numbers, which show an increased number of TARGET liabilities of certain countries?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, this again is a question that was asked several times in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Most of the movement in TARGET2 liabilities depends on our own asset purchase programme and depends on how and where - especially where - the balances of the purchases of bonds are settled.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: About 50% of the institutions - at least this was the number until a few months ago but I think it's still valid - 50% of the institutions that sell bonds to the national central banks are not in the euro area and settle their account with one or two core countries where the financial centres reside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense you see that the accounting and settlement of the balances do depend on where the settlement is made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has nothing to do with capital flows [flight] from one country or another.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just keep in mind: 80% of the institutions that sell - banks, namely - that sell bonds to the national central banks do not reside in the country where the purchasing national central bank resides.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You'll have a lot of inter-country payments and flows that do not say anything very specific about the overall situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Going back to the recent movements in the liabilities of certain countries, you see that first of all they are not unprecedented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not the first time; we've seen movements as large or even larger in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, as a consequence of what I just said, they are of a second order with respect to the massive movements produced by our own purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The people who want to cap it, collateralise, limit - the truth is that they don't like the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They don't like the monetary union because the only way a monetary union can work is if it has an efficient payment system, which is what TARGET2 is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's just too early to understand exactly what part of the liabilities do reflect political uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'm sorry, we haven't discussed that at all so I can't answer this question now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We actually haven't discussed anything about reinvestment policy, but you can have another question if you want.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Frankly, I had not realised all these anniversaries myself!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I read about some market commentaries recalling that this is the anniversary of this and now you telling me about this other anniversary, I was surprised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At least then I ask myself; what does it show?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it shows that these are very distant times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Especially the anniversary from the 2012 speech tells that basically, today the euro is - they look so distant because the euro is now on much stronger foundations than it was then at that time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's very much due to the fact, to the important reforms that have been undertaken by our governments in terms of completing, though there is still a road to do - to go, in completing and strengthening our monetary union and by structural reforms undertaken by national governments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the Introductory Statement I said that they have to be decisively stepped up; that's true.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this has the danger of making us forget how much has been done already in this field.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's true, the ECB now is a different central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's true what you said; it has a very different and much, much richer set of monetary policy tools and so that is certainly important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The real reason for the Governing Council to be proud is that it has delivered price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has delivered price stability in the most difficult circumstances through all these years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll stop here because I speak too much about these anniversaries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer about Greece is, we take note and actually we welcome the successful actions undertaken by the Greek Government so far.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking forward to a successful completion of the programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I take your words of reintroduction of Greece into the programme as whether Greece can be part of QE.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Right now, Greek paper, Greek Government bonds are not eligible for QE.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The waiver was there while the programme was in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: After the programme expires, the waiver expires and that's what it is right now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other point is kind of strange; why should rate hikes be influenced?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Maybe in the perverse minds of some market players might - this may be true, but certainly not in the Governing Council members' minds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I think both questions are answered saying that we live through an extraordinary time in the aftermath of a great financial crisis, which in many countries actually took the shape of a Great Depression, as severe as - for certain aspects, even more severe than the Great Depression itself.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore the proper monetary policy response was the one that was decided by the Governing Council throughout these years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think both questions can be answered in this way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The extraordinary historical circumstances produced a pretty exceptional monetary policy response.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I'll answer the second question, because the first question has a quick answer; we haven't discussed it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question is: as you've seen, as I've stressed in the last Riga monetary policy council, all the statements, the Introductory Statement and all the formulation of all the monetary policy tools, contain a repeated optionality and flexibility, putting the Governing Council in an ideal position to react to events.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of these events are part of a foreseeable future based on the current set of information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some other events may well not be foreseeable at the present time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't want to exclude the possibility that they may happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me say something that I should've said at the very beginning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are actually witnessing a drama - a tragic drama of spectacular proportions in Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just want to express the solidarity and the closeness of the Governing Council members to the Greek people on this occasion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to your second question is that we have seen growth rates now for some time above growth potential.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My reading is here: we will reduce the monthly pace until the end of December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We anticipate that, subject to incoming data confirming our medium-term inflation outlook, we will then end net purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's the text, that's what we've discussed; we haven't elaborated on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me make clear that it's - when we stop, this doesn't mean that our monetary policy stops being accommodating.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The amount of accommodation will remain very significant, through our reinvestment policy and through our forward guidance and interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the first question is, yes, it's consistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have seen convergence and that's what the discussion today confirms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are seeing convergence of the inflation rate to our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have confidence that this is happening, confidence based first and foremost on our monetary policy, which remains accommodative and second, on the underlying strength of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ever-improving conditions of the labour market - we'll maybe elaborate on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The latest number about employment, it says that 9.2 million jobs have been created in the euro area since 2013 and rising wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are confident that our present monetary policy stance is consistent with our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second point: our objective is an inflation rate which is below, but close to 2% over the medium term; we stay with that, that's our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, frankly we haven't discussed and we haven't - as I said last time, we haven't even discussed when we are going to discuss it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, having said that we have two meetings before year-end.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's just a matter of - we'll take this decision in the coming days, really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was going to be at the level of committees first and foremost because it'll have to be prepared - properly prepared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Other than that, as you've seen from my reading, the reinvestment statement is exactly the same as before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we haven't discussed either the "Operation Twist" or whether to reinvest in different maturities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think what I said last time - and I can confirm that even though we haven't discussed, I believe the Governing Council would be pretty unanimous on that - is that the capital key will remain the guiding principle.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's actually a comment made on other occasions in different contexts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The mandate of the ECB is price stability in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: QE has been one of the tools we used to pursue this task.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the past the ECB was asked: why are we keeping, for example, interest rates negative and we are depriving the savers from their income?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Or why are we hurting insurance companies, banks, through low interest rates?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As always answered, the mandate of the ECB is not to protect bankers' profits or insurance companies' profits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this case, responding to your question, it's not to ensure that government deficits would be financed under all conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, considering the first questions, the increased uncertainties in some emerging markets is certainly one factor that adds to the general uncertainty in world markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But having said that, so far the spillovers from Turkey and Argentina to other countries have not been substantial.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Once again as we've seen two or three years ago with similar crises in emerging markets, once again it is shown that the countries that are most vulnerable to contagion are the countries which have the weakest fundamentals; namely high current account deficit, high inflation, high budget deficit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Other emerging market countries that have better fundamentals have not been affected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's one key consideration which is also, in a sense, seen from the perspective of the eurozone reassuring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far we've seen quite limited contagion at least in the aggregate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course we can have individual situations of significant exposure to local crises.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's different because that would affect individual entities, but not in the aggregate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is the general change in the situation of emerging markets, which by the way doesn't include only Argentina and Turkey because big changes are also happening in China of a different kind, however, not financial stability-related.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second source of uncertainty is indeed the potential - we haven't seen much of it yet but it's one of the risks we're looking at, we are certainly monitoring - the potential financial market volatility generated by changes - gradual, at measured pace as you know - changes in monetary policy in the main jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is one potential risk of enhanced financial volatility and we're also monitoring that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly the major source of uncertainty that we see in global output comes from the rising protectionism.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the major source of uncertainty which, by the way, is reflected in the current macroeconomic projections only to the extent of the measures that have been implemented already.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The current projections do not reflect measures that have been announced, measures that have been threatened.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, there we have to look at basically three factors that may make this uncertainty more severe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is clearly, we have to see, we have to assess the extent of an escalation; that is one factor that certainly we have to look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The so-called confidence effects; besides the effects on prices and tariffs and quotas and volumes, trade and so on, what is going to be the effect on general confidence of an extended trade war?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third factor which makes any assessment quite difficult is to assess; what are the implications on the international value chain of changes in tariffs of a broad and significant proportion?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the answer to the first question is we are really interested to see; what are the proposals of the Commission?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We stand ready to cooperate with the Commission on defining or enhancing the international role of the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, it's not part of our mandate but we certainly stand ready to work with the Commission and with the other member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, well, this answer could be very long.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll tell you what I would like to remember of that period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, for us the crisis actually started before Lehman.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first serious signs of an impending crisis actually date back to September 2007, so much so that by the end of 2007 the G7 and, right after that, the G20 decide to task what was called the FSF; the Financial Stability Forum, which is the precursor of the Financial Stability Board, with a response to the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The FSF created at that time a working group across countries and produced an answer by April 2008 with 77 recommendations, most of which have been implemented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I remember of that instance is the extraordinary effort of international cooperation at world level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, even before Lehman it was quite clear that the financial crisis was coming and it would have unprecedented proportions and was worldwide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is what was at the basis of this really unprecedented and international effort.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can say that since then there hasn't been one aspect of the banking business that has not been touched by the regulators and the supervisors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All this effort was in a sense crowned by the agreement that was found by the Basel Committee and by the GHOS; the governors' enhanced supervision in Basel at the end of last year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it took ten years to actually crystallise the effort, by the way many parts of this had already been introduced in the supervisory practices and in the regulation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other jurisdictions we could sort of fear a backtracking to a world where there is less regulation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just look at this; the common equity tier 1 ratios were something like around 8%, 8.5% in 2008.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The leverage ratio was 3.7% way back then and now it's over 5%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also liquidity management, morale, risk management, governance have all been overhauled by the legislators, by the regulators and by the supervisors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer of course is no because in the meantime a lot of this business has migrated from the banking world to the non-banking world, the so-called shadow banking.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the next step will be to ensure that equally strong regulation and supervision, of course one has to take into account the differences in institutions, would also be applied to the non-banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the answer to the first question is no, we haven't changed the balance of risk about growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, risks relating to rising protectionism, vulnerabilities in emerging markets and financial market volatility have gained more prominence recently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are also upside risks, one of which is the fiscal policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fiscal policies in several euro area countries are going to be probably less neutral than we had expected some time ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's one, but the other much more important consideration is that we are observing an underlying strength of the economy that makes us think that the downside risks are going to be mitigated by this fact, by the - as I mentioned before - improvement in the labour market and the rise in wages, which are the main drivers that support consumption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Private consumption is supported exactly by these two drivers primarily, and only secondarily by the increase in wealth, in household wealth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Investment is also being supported by the quite accommodative financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even though they have tightened somewhat since the last meeting, the lending conditions to firms and households remain very favourable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me say something I was about to say before when I was asked about Italy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, words in the last few months have changed many times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are now waiting for is facts, and the main fact is the draft budget law - and not only that - and the subsequent parliamentary discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to see how that is and then savers, capital markets, investors will formulate their view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Unfortunately we've seen, as you said before, that words have created some damage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Interest rates have gone up and they've gone up for households and they've gone up for firms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, this is another interesting point: all this hasn't created much of a spillover to other euro area countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's remained, at least so far, pretty much an Italian episode.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, having said that we have to basically be aware that the Italian Prime Minister, the Italian Minister of the Economy, the Italian Foreign Affairs Ministers have all said that Italy is going to respect the rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Look, the first answer is we haven't seen any contagion yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second thing is, I repeat what I said before: the ECB will stay with what the Italian Prime Minister, the Italian Minister of the Economy and the Italian Foreign Affairs Ministers have said; namely that Italy will respect the rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Today just not long ago the private sector working group has recommended to use the euro short-term rate - that's why it's called ESTER - the euro short-term rate as an alternative free rate as a replacement for EONIA that no longer meets the criteria of the EU benchmarks regulation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will see its use restricted as of the January 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we welcome this decision, because also it brings the euro area closer to other jurisdictions where this issue's been addressed already.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we want to state clearly that the private sector plays the dominant role in ensuring a smooth transition, but this transition's just started.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a subgroup of the working group led, by the way, by a former colleague of mine in the Executive Board and a countryman of Mr de Guindos, Mr González-Páramo, that actually will oversee exactly the point that you raised; namely what should be done to ensure the robustness of the contractual arrangements that are based on other benchmark rates on Euribor and EONIA?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we can't say much about the future of Euribor because that depends very much on the administrator of Euribor and on the regulators; namely ESMA and FSMA.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, I do agree with this assessment, which is also the assessment the IMF now has been saying for several months; the debt levels worldwide remain high, or in some parts of the world have gone up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the euro area is concerned however, things are slightly different - not in the sense that debt is not high; debt is high in the euro area as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It went down and a significant de-leveraging has taken place both in financial and non-financial parts of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The balance sheet of both financial companies and industrial manufacturing companies is now much stronger than it was before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Public debt stays high and that's why we always say that countries where public debt is high should be the first to rebuild fiscal buffers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Otherwise if we have a new crisis they don't have any policy space.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm sorry, both questions might be in principle very interesting questions but we haven't discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm pretty sure there will be a time when we will have to discuss these questions but it's now premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Answering the second question first, we actually didn't discuss that to any extent other than saying two things that I can remember of our very short discussion is that this fiscal expansion is pro-cyclical.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are dangers that its effects could wane in 2020, so the risk there is of an increase in interest rates accompanied by a weakening of economic activity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's I think the only point that was briefly discussed in the various presentations that were made about the state of the world economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, yes, we had this drop in industrial productions but again - this was looked at as one of the signs of convergence of the economy to its steady state path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Namely we had quite unusual strong growth last year based also on a pretty strong unusual export performance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the external part of this growth now is getting weaker and therefore we do expect some weakness in the domestic part as a reflection of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, the domestic part remains resilient because of the consumption and investment performances I have hinted at before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the unanimous view of the Governing Council was that the present monetary policy stance is robust; namely even if there are limited changes in policy parameters due to the various effects we've just discussed, the policy stance doesn't change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the first question, the question is; was the assessment that risks are broadly balanced shared by all Governing Council members?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course there were different nuances because countries are growing at - still by the way the dispersion, I often mention this number, the dispersion in growth rates in gross value added across the euro area is at its lowest historically.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to go back to the early '90s to find the same low rates of dispersion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Still when you look forward, you certainly have countries where growth is more buoyant, countries where growth may be less buoyant and downward revisions may be more significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That may well be not because of external factors but because of endogenous facts that we haven't seen yet really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: About the emerging market countries, exchange rate effects on the euro area, we briefly touched on that in one specific context, when we say that the foreign demand is weaker for the euro area, and this may be due to the stronger exchange rate of the euro, we have to keep in mind that the depreciation of the Turkish lira actually accounts for much of that effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was the context in which we briefly discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have to say that really in the aggregate, what's happening in Argentina and Turkey so far doesn't show any significant spillover, although at a level of individual institutions one may well see significant exposures to local realities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, yes, it's been used well in the sense that the intended effects of the QE - mind, I speak for the aggregate of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This holds also for the other question you asked me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can speak for the aggregate of the euro area and we project what I just said about growth rates for 2019/2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of going back to whether countries have used it well or not, yes, they used it well in a sense because we see a pickup in growth everywhere.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: An employment situation which is by and large improving almost everywhere, some countries more than others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If your question is meant to say; shouldn't governments have taken advantage of the situation of such low rates to decrease budget deficits, to restore?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, they should do it certainly, they should definitely do it: rebuild fiscal buffers, take the opportunity of low interest rates to carry out a sound economic policy with a budget which is growth friendly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Keep in mind that this is a good situation for doing that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: About inflation: I said inflation is going to hover around the present level for the rest of the year and then I gave numbers for next year and 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, these numbers are the result of two different components.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We project slightly lower oil prices but significantly stronger core inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's because of the underlying strength of the economy and the rising wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course nominal wage growth is higher in countries like Germany and lower in other countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, even though underlying inflation remains muted, by and large we see pickup in nominal wage growth everywhere.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This leads us to say that the projection of inflation we've given, which is the result of these two components, will reach our objective over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't carry the same risk analysis for inflation as we do with growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To some extent - but not completely - to some extent the two things are interrelated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this assumes that lower growth translates immediately into lower inflation in the long term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are times when this isn't true so we have to judge there, basically.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the projections that we have on inflation reflect oil prices and all the other components of the inflation rate definition.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On reinvestment: I said the committees because certainly it's not a simple question so it has to be worked out technically well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we can actually discuss in the Governing Council, but there will have to be preparation to that extent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me answer the first question; it will require a little time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, the Governing Council discussions you've seen from the introductory statement confirmed the balance of risks and of course didn't take any decision on monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was acknowledgement of a somewhat weaker momentum, but in the midst of most eurozone countries - which still have positive output gaps, and slightly expansionary and sometimes in some cases pro-cyclical fiscal policies in some countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is clearly certified by most survey indicators that have come out since the last time we met.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But these indicators remain above - and in some cases well above - historical averages and certainly is certified by slower growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then the issue is: what are the reasons behind this weaker momentum and these weaker survey indicators?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here we go into a variety of explanations, one of which certainly is country-specific factors; so-called idiosyncratic phenomena.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is having quite a powerful effect for this quarter but not next quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Last time we discussed the export performance saying that last year, 2017, had an extraordinary export performance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we're coming back to normal and so we had a decline in exports that seems now is reflected in the current weaker momentum, but seems now to have come to a halt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the stalemate between US and China, with Brexit, with Italy, with financial market volatility, so a bunch of uncertainties.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we have perhaps the one important part of the explanation; it's simply that we're having growth returning to potential after 2017, where it was clearly above potential.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not simple here to distinguish what is transitory from what is going to be permanent, what is country specific from what is extended to the whole of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is actually having an impact on consumption and investment and what is not having an impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For one thing, we still observe consumption; pretty strong, buoyed by an expanding employment, an expanding labour market, rising wages and so business investment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also the emerging market economy situation seems to have stabilised somehow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All in all, the assessment of the Governing Council was, yes, there is a weaker momentum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, there are weaker survey data coming out and maybe some more expected in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But is this enough of a change to make us change the baseline scenario?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These risks are not being considered at this point in time enough to change the balance of risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course we'll have to see the projections in December and that was also one other consideration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On Italy, you have to remember that Italy is a fiscal discussion, so there wasn't much discussion about Italy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, the Vice-President, Dombrovskis, was there and basically, I asked him permission to quote him, to quote what he said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: He said, "Of course we have to observe and apply fiscal rules but we're also seeking a dialogue".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's what it is, but then I could answer other questions about the facts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, I didn't say there wasn't any risk of contagion; I said at that point in time there was no sign of contagion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Okay, let me also respond to the other part of the question I was asked before about; what are the facts?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The context of our discussion today was, as I said before, the statement by the Vice-President of the Commission, who said of course he has to apply fiscal rules but he's also seeking a dialogue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point of context is what I said in the previous press conference in the IMF, during the course of the IMF meetings, is that I'm personally - and that's a personal perception so take it for what it's worth - I am confident that an agreement will be found.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That means the lending rates are going up still moderately, I should say, for households and for firms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It means that households will have to pay more for borrowing from banks and so do companies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course in the case of companies that finance, fund themselves issuing bonds, the pass-through from the capital markets to the bond market - to the corporate bond market - is obviously faster.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For them, the increase in borrowing rates has been more marked and quicker.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, all this likely means that it will have effects on credit and ultimately on growth and, by the way, on the very same space that is needed for fiscal expansion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense, if the interest rates keep on going up, the room that is available to expand the budget gets smaller.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, the increases in interest rates have been there now for a while.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've analysed it both from surveys and through direct evidence; these increasing rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But these increasing rates are not so far - at least banking rates - are not significant, or not material.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However we have now the bank lending survey of this quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It does say that basically, terms and conditions applied by Italian banks on new loans to enterprises and households for house purchases, tightened.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Terms and conditions - so not standards - terms and conditions tightened in the third quarter of 2018, driven by a higher cost of funds and balance sheet constraints.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Since the last time I spoke about this, we have observed some increase in interest rates in some other countries, or non-core countries, let's call them this way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so again the issue is: what's the cause of them; because these countries themselves had specific idiosyncratic phenomena, facts, events that may justify, and have been estimated to justify, some increase in rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far we reached I think the conclusion that it's kind of hard to distinguish.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There may be some spillovers but they are limited; that's the current assessment and I will keep you posted as the situation will evolve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The discussion in the Governing Council showed that there isn't much of a change in inflation, really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at surrounding developments, we see that negotiated wages keep on going up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a very comforting sign because it means that wage increases - which by the way in some core countries have been quite significant - wage increases are going to stay.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are not temporary, they are not drift determined but they are negotiated wages so they're going to stay.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They've been quite, in some countries, significant but in general nominal wage growth is picking up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other thing is that the labour market keeps on expanding but it's progressively, gradually tighter and tighter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third thing is that capacity utilisation rates in most countries are pretty high.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Frankly, after all this assessment we have no sense that we should doubt our confidence that inflation is gradually converging to our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But having said that, we reaffirm the fact that our monetary policy needs to remain accommodative and a considerable degree of monetary accommodation is still needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I see that there are lots of concerns - well, not lots; some concerns about APP maybe ending at the end of this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me tell you one thing that I've said on and on and on: even if it were to end, monetary policy will remain very accommodative by the reinvestment, especially the reinvestment of the considerable stock of assets that we have in our balance sheet and our forward guidance about interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me read this about the introductory statement to the sentence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It says, "This support will continue to be provided by the net asset purchases until the end of the year, by the sizeable stock of acquired assets and the associated reinvestments, and by our enhanced forward guidance on the key ECB interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In any event the Governing Council stands ready to adjust all of its instruments as appropriate to ensure that inflation continues to move towards the Governing Council's inflation aim in a sustained manner".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On Italy, I don't have a crystal ball; I don't have any idea whether it's 300 or 400 or whatever.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If they lose value, they are denting into the capital position of the banks; that's obvious, so that's what it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, I'm still - I shouldn't say optimistic - but I'm still confident an agreement will be found.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But basically, yes, you have a dent in capital position.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then of course you have weakening funding conditions as well and all this is going to translate into different lending terms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you've seen, the language is exactly the same as before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said a moment ago, you have to consider: the monetary policy will remain very accommodative even in case we were to decide to end QE at the end of the year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, will the end of QE put pressure on spreads?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, but let me say first one thing, let me repeat one thing: over the past few months we have not bought Greek bonds, but we have bought Italian bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Still in spite of that, we saw that the spreads between Greece and Italy narrowed down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the case of a suspension of QE, you would expect that spreads are going to be affected depending only on the net issuance of different countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if countries were having the same degree of issuance, the same net issuance, you wouldn't see any change in spreads.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The end of QE is not a selective measure addressed to any specific country; it's a monetary policy measure that is justified by our confidence in the convergence of inflation to our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the first question is whether I have sympathy for this or that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the Commission; the Commission is the ultimate guardian of the Stability and Growth Pact, not the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will completely defer the answer to the Vice-President of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Luis de Guindos: Well, we do not comment on any sort of ruling from the courts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We respect the rulings from the Supreme Court of Spain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the first question is that we haven't discussed what we're going to do next.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I told you last time, we had two meetings before the end of the year and we didn't discuss anything in this meeting so we're going to discuss in the next meeting, where we'll also have the projections, which will also cast some more light on what's going to happen next.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do think that we still have tools in our toolbox that we can use, different contingencies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The TLTRO was raised by two speakers only but not in any detail, but this is just an example of how the toolbox is still quite rich in terms of monetary policy instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question you had, what I would answer, I would answer that central bank independence is a precious thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's precious because it's essential for the credibility of the central banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Credibility is essential for effectiveness, so central bank independence in terms of how to comply and deliver their mandates - which in our case is price stability - and central bank independence in choosing the instruments that are more appropriate or most appropriate to pursue this objective, is crucial for the effectiveness of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If one thinks about that, one would conclude that actually the legislators themselves, often the very same people who are arguing for the central banks to do this and that, should be the first ones to care about monetary policy effectiveness and central banks reaching their goals, pursuing their mandates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, answering the second question first, we don't see such a risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This links with the previous question about central bank independence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Central bank independence is predicated on monetary dominance, not on fiscal dominance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To finance government deficits is not part of our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, as you will remember from the previous crisis, we have OMT as a specific instrument.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Other than that, we are in a regime of monetary dominance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We haven't discussed that in the meeting, but just keep in mind - and you are right -there's a capital key readjustment at the beginning of the year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's also another capital key adjustment with Brexit, so that's also to be kept in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Forward guidance on interest rates, you remember it started in 2013, if I'm not mistaken, and then it evolved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It became guidance on asset purchases and reinvestments, so it has served us very well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has kept anchored the short-term part of the yield curve while the QE was actually addressing the long-term part of the yield curve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Contrary to - or let me put it this way - better than the experience in other jurisdictions, it has served us very, very, very well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You look at the amount of volatility and there are all kinds of indicators showing that it's been very successful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then of course we always discuss whether this should be state contingent, or data based - or both - as it is in our case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, our experience has been quite positive with guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second question is how frustrated - well, it's not a matter of being frustrated but the fact is that our monetary union remains fragile if it's not completed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I say completed, I mean the Banking Union, I mean the Capital Market Union, I mean the fiscal capacity, the design of fiscal capacity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All these things by the way are intertwined because the better it is the Capital Market Union, probably the less need we have for a big fiscal capacity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To make progress on this we need, I would say, by and large the right political contingency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not something that central bankers or Eurocrats can push forward by themselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
