text: These are big changes very often in the way powers are being distributed between national parliaments and national executives and European authorities, or even without an authority, European rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point, my sense is we've got to be patient because we are not driving the political developments; we are part of them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the second question is concerned, namely what can one do as far as banks are concerned given the widening of the spreads that has taken place in the last five/six months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There may be other answers, but the first answer that comes to mind is: first of all reduce the tone and don't question the constitutional, existential framework of the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second is reduce the spreads, so do policies that lead to a reduction in the spreads.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the first point about the capital key, no, we haven't discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'd be surprised if we were to use a different concept other than the capital key.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We used that for a long time now with the asset purchases and so I'd be surprised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, we haven't discussed that, but you correctly say that there is a strange pro-cyclicality here between the revision of the capital key and the economic situation of a country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: True, but these adjustments to the capital key happen every five years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense, it's just a country happens to have a lower GDP because of a variety of reasons that may have nothing to do with cyclical stimulus.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, I think I've said a few times, we are not party to the negotiations and so everything will depend on what is the final outcome of the negotiations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We certainly are monitoring and working together with the Bank of England to identify potential risks of a sudden hard Brexit event.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me repeat what I think I said in the European Council: it would really take an extraordinary amount of lack of preparation to materialise the financial stability risks that might come from a hard Brexit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By and large, I'm still confident that a good common-sense solution will be found where financial stability risks will be minimised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If this lack of outcome of solution will continue and will approach the end date, the private sector itself will have to prepare on the assumption that there will be a hard Brexit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't call it necessarily big financial stability risk, but certainly financial uneasiness in markets and intermediaries and CCPs and their member banks and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think you're asking very good and very serious questions, but I am not the one who should answer these questions; I think you should ask them to the commissioners.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is available for the ECB towards a specific country is OMT.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The OMT, as you remember, is subject to having a programme with ESM and is also subject to the assessment by the Governing Council of the ECB that the undertaking of the OMT doesn't prejudge the monetary policy for the whole of the euro area, but that's what's there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate, as I said before, is a mandate towards price stability, not towards financing governments' deficits or adhering to a fiscal dominance situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said before, we don't have a crystal ball here to say what's fair or what's not fair.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, that's also one of the reasons why usually central banks don't target specific rates because it's very, very difficult to assess what is a fair or equilibrium rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, how could I not share what this colleague of mine has said?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've got to be prepared of course and whether there are bubbles or not is a different thing, it's a difference assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to look at specifically the situation of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are certain segments of financial markets, like prime commercial real estate and high-yield or leverage corporate, where the valuations are actually stretched according to any standard.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Most importantly, we don't see that buildup of leverage that we'd seen before the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, the private financial sector is not overleveraged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact this is one of the reasons why - even in the face of one-off events, that on other occasions would have led us to say that there would be trouble in the financial markets, enhanced volatility, interest rates going up, take the case of Brexit, take the case of elections in Europe here and there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: People were expecting serious consequences on financial markets - it didn't happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, because monetary policies remained accommodative throughout and second, because the private financial system not being over-leveraged was able to continue giving credit to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why we should not be - as I think almost all my colleagues always say - complacent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to your last question is absolutely no, it's not our job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I started all this discussion saying this is a fiscal discussion and it's not the central bankers' job to play the mediating role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is nothing I know more than what you do know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think in the end it's just good common sense, perception of what is the goodness for the country and the interests of the public, of the households, of the people that will lead parties to converge to some sort of agreement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What you said is absolutely correct: if there were a situation where there would be a sequence of downgrades of the four rating agencies and so on, there are rules in place that would actually do what you just said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I wouldn't speculate more than that about saying what if.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question I think you have to wait for the press release at the end of this press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what I can do is to read you one of the decision-making points which is the one you are probably asking for.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council decides that under the PSPP, the public sector purchase programme, as a rule redemptions will be reinvested in the jurisdiction in which principal repayments are made, but the portfolio allocation across jurisdictions will continue to be adjusted with a view to bringing the share of the PSPP portfolio into closer alignment with the respective national central bank subscription to the ECB capital key.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what I can read to you now; the rest you will learn from the press release.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, in a sense that was the focal point of the Governing Council discussion; what sort of assessment would the Governing Council give about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if I had to draw a conclusion about the sense that transpired from the discussion, I would summarise it with just a few words; namely, continuing confidence with increasing caution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just happened to read it before coming here; I will quote to you the results of a survey with small- and medium-sized enterprises in a moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So first of all when we look at what it is today, first of all we see that monetary policy remains very accommodative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, I think there is some sort of confusion here about termination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It does continue because we are committed to maintaining the stock for an extended period of time as it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On top of that we have announced our forward guidance, we can come back on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you look at the economy, well, you still see the drivers of this recovery are still in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Consumption continues to grow, basically supported by the increase in real disposable income, which, if I am not mistaken, is at the historical high since six years or something, and households' wealth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Business investments continue to grow, residential investment, as I said in the IS [introductory statement] is robust.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Everything, all this when we look at all these drivers of the recovery, yes, it's true, it's just weaker.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not just one-off; it's been weaker for a while now and that's in a sense the discussion - the sense of the discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, we ask ourselves first of all how quick this is, how weak this is and what causes this weakness?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are certain one-off factors in some countries, in some sectors which probably are transient, but there is also a permanent component to this, which is the landing of the eurozone economy on a path, closer to potential.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we had in 2017 a pretty unusual year and so now there is some landing on a closer path to potential.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the introductory statement quoted uncertainty: geopolitical uncertainty, emerging market economies' vulnerabilities, financial markets' volatility and perhaps another cause.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point of this is that - yes, the threat of protectionism is the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other point that was discussed; all these are specific factors of uncertainty but generally speaking, these factors may change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, the trade situation based on the latest statements is probably better than it was two months ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some emerging market vulnerabilities now seem to be less urgent or less dangerous than they were two months ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the meantime, others are looming up so the overall environment, the overall atmosphere has become one characterised by increased general uncertainty, which takes the shape now and then of different phenomena.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think this is at least considered by the Governing Council one of the reasons, if not the main reason, for this weaker data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can see this because if you look back when we took this decision that we would expect to terminate the APP, the net APP purchase now, back in June, well, since then what you see is basically financing conditions that have been by and large the same, if not even more accommodative, with interest rates which went down, in fact, but risk premium has increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what is at the root of some of the declines in asset prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the sort of discussion and it's a discussion, as I said, continued confidence with increasing caution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's interesting in our usual periodic survey that we do with small- and medium-sized enterprises, now this survey terminates in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They say that basically, the results are consistent with economic expansion, which continues to be supported by accommodative financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nevertheless SMEs signalled some rising concerns on their business environment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A large share of SMEs reported higher turnover, so positive news.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see, all this is news of lower growth but not low growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other results are basically consistent with this two-phased assessment of the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, the answer to the first question is, we didn't discuss it this time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we had wanted to specify a length of time, we would have done so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you reflect on the specific formulation, you will see the benefits of keeping it this way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I won't speculate on the people, what you call general understanding, of what an extended period of time means.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the other point is about, no, it doesn't - As a matter of fact, the LTROs had been mentioned by some of the participants to the discussion, although we really had not discussed in substance but we are reflecting, this is another instrument of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue reflecting on that, like on the other measure you mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that this will address that but will generally address monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will be a major contributor to maintaining the monetary policy very accommodative as it has been and the financing conditions accommodative as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to the second question is actually no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're always concerned, of course, but we think we have - and if you read the formulation of the monetary policy guidance today - we think we have instruments to address such a contingency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, one feature of this formulation is that we want to… Let me step back.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this climate that I characterise as being of great uncertainty, the monetary policy formulation that we have wants deliberately to keep optionality as a dominant feature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense, the answer to your second question is yes; we have instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your first question; no, we haven't discussed that but you see, when you reflect on our guidance, you see that it's both date contingent and it's also state contingent, namely depending on the situation of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you see market expectations of interest rates moving ahead in time, it's the market's reading of the general situation of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Yes, the decision was unanimous, which is quite important, and it was unanimous.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On wages, you see, this is one part in describing why we consider the baseline scenario still valid, I have not mentioned the wages, which have been steadily increasing since 2016.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Compensation per employee in the third quarter of this year went up for the eurozone to 2.5% from the second quarter, it was 2.2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Negotiated wages again for the eurozone, at 2.1% in the third quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see this quite broad based so it's not limited to one country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll say a word about Germany in a moment, but it's actually broad-based.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see this in industry, in construction, in various sectors so not all sectors, but almost all sectors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Agriculture is not part of the sectors where you see this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, however in certain countries this higher growth rate in nominal wages is even more significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Negotiated wages in some sectors like construction are between 4% and 6%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As one would expect actually, in various degrees you would expect that these higher nominal wages will be passed through into higher prices at some point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, how fast depends on many factors that we have discussed on other occasions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But one certainly is the extent to which profits are being squeezed by these increasing wages and, by the way, other production costs and before they can be passed into higher prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The evidence we have is that quite clearly, those parts of the eurozone that are closer to full employment, if not at full employment, project higher nominal growth, higher growth of nominal wages, project a greater squeeze in profit margins.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Other parts of the euro area which are lagging behind in terms of growth, in terms of employment, and also in terms of wage pressure, are also lagging behind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we would expect is that this pass-through will happen, will take place but it will be not uniform across the region but it will reflect basically different economic conditions in different parts of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, your first question is actually quite broad and in a sense I'm kind of biased to answer this question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll be briefer than I would like to be, but certainly especially in some parts of this period of time, QE has been the only driver of this recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are lots of numbers that we can give about how it did change financing conditions in a way that - in many ways.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let's not forget that interest rates had dramatically declined even before QE but they continued to do so after QE.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then there were the other components; namely the term premium component and the fact that QE actually was crucial in decreasing the risk, the asset risk, of the banking system in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We view this as - but I don't think I'm the only one to be the crucial driver of the recovery in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the time, by the way, when also other drivers were not really - especially in the first part, there was no other source of growth in the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, demand and exports actually went up in, if I am not mistaken, later on in 2015 even when domestic demand was not a driver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll have plenty of time to comment on - I'm making a general assessment of its effectiveness.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other thing, you see, you asked me whether the fact that markets are foreseeing the first - are expecting the first rate hike by that time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, first of all you have two sets of expectations; you have the market expectations, you have the survey expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Survey expectations are in their great majority, still, date based.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also true that they show a lesser conviction about when the first rate rise will happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Still the majority of the expectations is focused on through the summer guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They project a rate increase at that time because they think that the economy will worsen in that fashion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words this shows that they well understood our reaction function, because in so doing they make financing conditions easier.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, there is a process here; we have to start the process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, on the second question, we don't have an explicit risk assessment for inflation but as you've seen from the projections, it's by and large what it was before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other question was, if we are ready to use asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, we didn't have to discuss this because we decided that our baseline is still valid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense there are two conditions: The first one is to see how strong is the convergence, the second how sustained is the convergence?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We concluded that we are confident and we remain patient and persistent with our accommodative monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far there was no need to ask ourselves this question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is something we are monitoring carefully, whether low interest rates do affect banks' profitability and to what extent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far - and it's now quite a time that we had these interest rates, by the way on the short-term part of the curve, The net interest margin of the banking system reflects certainly what happens on the short part, but also what happens all along the curve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The conclusion that we've drawn until now is that if there are - and there are now - some negative effects on profitability, they are more than offset by the benefits in other parts of the bank's balance sheets because of the asset purchase programme, of the recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I'm not mistaken here, the Vice President may correct me, but one of the main factors that increases banks' profitability in the eurozone so much so that now the return on equity is by and large the same as of other international banks - is the increased provisioning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The increased provisioning, it has become possible because of the improvement in the economy substantially because of the recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it also tells us something; that the increase in provision is not something that happens every year on a continuous basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But at some point its profits have to come from all other sources.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your first question is about the completeness of the monetary union construction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be both alert here in all this and humble.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be alert and admit that our monetary union construction is not completed, remains fragile and needs developments in the area of the banking union, the capital markets union and also in the creation of some sort of fiscal concept, which is still quite unclear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From this viewpoint we certainly welcome the steps that have been taken now by first the Eurogroup and hopefully by the European Council tomorrow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are steps in the right direction and they are steps towards this completion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's clear that more needs to be done before we can declare victory and say that we have a banking union like, say, the United States or the capital markets union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On other occasions I've also discussed how both of them are very important in sharing risks from recessions and helping stabilise the economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense if they were completed, less urgent would become the construction of what we call fiscal capacity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly we also have to be humble and acknowledge that all these decisions are political decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In all this, the ECB is in a sense an adviser - hopefully a trusted adviser - but cannot be a decision-maker.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On the first question, the answer; no, we haven't discussed other options or other tools of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly the general intention of the Governing Council is to keep liquidity as available as it needs to be for a monetary policy to be geared for objectives to be attained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The TLTROs, as I mentioned before, were mentioned but not discussed in any substance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course the Governing Council is aware of the different factors that will affect liquidity and excess liquidity over the coming two, three years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At some point in time, our committees will start to work on that and we will have a discussion of this and a decision on this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point, well, we have a risk management framework which is quite impressive, that starts with eligibility criteria of different bonds, that goes to provisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can't now remember how many provisions we have, but one is risk, the second is exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third is, well, we have both credit risk and we have interest rate risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also you have to take into account the way - and frankly, on this point I cannot give you an answer - but the way the value of bonds is being posted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I do believe for public bonds it's amortized nominal value, amortized cost, so it's not marked to market, but you're asking about private bonds here so it's different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then I cannot answer to that question, but basically we have such a layer of risk provisions that I think we are pretty safe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But mind, the purpose of a corporate bond programme is not to maximise profits or minimise losses; it's monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some accidents may happen and they have happened in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, the answer to the second question is relatively straightforward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Trading policies are not negotiated at country level, but are negotiated by the Commission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly different countries have different interests, but these interests are being brought together in the Commission's negotiation with their partners.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I said is that news about trade seemed to be slightly better.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Don't make me go through the list of things that are now slightly better, because next time I'll have to go through a list of things that are definitely worse because the situation changes depending on many things, including moods.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not that we model mood change, but what is true is that all this - not only in the trade area - but consider Brexit, consider other geopolitical events.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All this and the very same changing of this has increased general uncertainty and if we - and certainly it is bound to have effects, or it had effects, on confidence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Confidence, or decreasing confidence, certainly has effects on investments and other business decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer is yes; QE is part now of the toolbox, it's permanent and it is something that may be conceived as potentially usable in contingencies that the Governing Council will have to decide on and will assess in its full independence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think this in a sense, it's always been like this, we believe, but now it's been sanctioned by the European Court of Justice ruling.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a very important ruling in the existence of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a sense, now one can say of course we all were convinced of that before, but now the ruling of the Court has sanctioned our conviction that the ECB now is by and large like other central banks of major jurisdictions, as far as the array of tools that it can use.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: You asked me about the 20thbirthday of the euro?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you take these 20 years, you see two different periods.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first period was the culmination of a prolonged cycle of great moderation and the second one has been an ongoing crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again it's like when you asked me about the QE, whether I thought it was a good thing or a bad thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, whether everybody participated to this success or not, that's what we should ask.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because it's clear that not everybody participated to the benefits of the common currency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of it has to do with national responsibilities, but some of it doesn't.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I would wish the euro now is a candid close introspection that could inspire future action on how to complete the Monetary Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, since you mentioned France, first of all let me say: The people of Strasbourg and the families of those hit in the terrorist attack, have my personal and the Governing Council's and the ECB's condolences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wish to express first our feeling towards what happened.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not really going to comment on what's happened.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We certainly blame and condemn violence and we'll also say that just the right to protest is part of our democracies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm confident that the French government will address this problem in the best way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is the slowdown going to worsen or stay as a shallow lower path?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, several speakers actually raised this issue but no decision was taken because we didn't discuss policies this time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Quite clearly, the assessment will have implications about policy but we didn't discuss them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see, underlying inflation has been muted, has been moving sideways, it's higher than the low levels reached about a year ago and … On what our confidence is based, it is based on the continuation of the economic expansion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is based on the strong labour market performance, though it's slowing down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's based on the encouraging pick-up in wages, nominal wage growth has gone up especially of course in the core countries and especially in Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Both compensation per employee and negotiated wages show a pick-up, consistent significant pick-up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the issue is we see all these components moving in the right direction and so the question is why haven't they passed through?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are observing is that there is a profit squeeze so it's a matter of time that of course this pass-through will happen first in the parts of the eurozone where the labour market is stronger, unemployment is lower, especially in some countries where basically there is full employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then of course the financing conditions and our monetary policy that remains fully accommodative, strengthens our confidence in this process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Since you're all asking, let me give you a summary of the meeting now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, what you care most, were we unanimous?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Okay, we were unanimous about acknowledging the weaker momentum and changing the balance of risk for growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're all in agreement on that and we were unanimous in assessing the factors that have caused the slowdown, namely first and foremost there is an increase in general uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This increase in general uncertainty has been produced by the threats of protectionism, doubts - actually extensive doubts - about the multilateral rules that have underpinned our growth since the Second World War.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The protracted and unclear outcome, the protracted negotiations and their unclear outcome yet about Brexit and of course the implications that this might have, I have said many times that if you compare the potential disruption coming from Brexit for the aggregate of the euro area, well, just looking at aggregate numbers it doesn't seem to be an extensive disruption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have to take into account things like value chains and we have also to take into account that some countries are more exposed, of course, to events in the Brexit case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that just is a sign of a contribution to the increase in general uncertainty and then of course we have the political developments in some countries in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is another set of factors that is specific; factors that are specific to certain countries and this has to do with the slowdown in China and the waning effects of fiscal package in the United States and the car industry in Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All this, it's a pretty long list of factors so the issue is now, and that's again there was unanimity, in saying that the key aspect to assess is the persistence of the general uncertainty as being produced by these factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly if all this were to persist, we should expect a longer weak momentum beyond the near term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then finally there was also quite, I would say, unanimity about assessing the likelihood of a recession as being low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, again I don't want to give numbers here but some of them are very low, others are on the average since the last 60 years or 50 years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in any event pretty low - of course again in an area like the eurozone, these estimates ought to be taken with some caution because if you have a serious recession in one part of the eurozone, that can spread to other parts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, it was unanimity about assessing this likelihood as low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nominal wage growth continues to be significant and of course the lower energy prices support real disposable income for households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also there is another factor to keep in mind that makes the present situation different from the situation we had at the beginning of the great financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This time banks' balance sheets are much stronger than they were before the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course we have local episodes of weakness but by and large, the banking sector is much stronger than it was at the beginning of the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the conditions for a continuation of credit to the economy are in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then the discussion focused on persistence and there were two viewpoints.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For some, China, the slowdown in China won't last long because we have confidence - and we do have confidence - in the government's measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Everything we know says that the government is actually taking strong measures to address the slowdown.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the end, the Brexit thing will not affect the EU economy that much, but especially there was one aspect of the discussion is that all these uncertainties, all these risks are being addressed by the policy response of the authorities in these countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The specific episode of the car industry in Germany will soon wash out because there is going to be a rebound in the sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One thing that basically of course we all agree is that if there is going to be clarity on the exports and the trade sector, much of what we are seeing today in terms of weakness will very likely wash out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For others however, the downside movement in all industries, in all indicators, both hard and soft, has lasted now several quarters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All these risk factors are not going to disappear and they are affecting confidence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you see, these are the two perspectives in the assessment of persistence, having agreed about everything else.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The conclusion of all this is that the Governing Council will give itself more time to assess whether all these risk factors have affected confidence and we are going to have another discussion in March when we'll also have the new projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, about inflation, of course going back to the first - the other question I had, focused first of all on headline inflation where clearly it's being driven by oil prices mostly, but also by food and services prices, to a much lesser extent, and on underlying inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Here I've answered, too; I basically gave you the sense of the discussion in answering your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course if this momentum were to last long and if the convergence were to happen around growth potential or even below growth potential of course the time that it will take for the inflation to converge to our aim and objective will be longer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But all throughout this and again there was agreement about the monetary policy that has been accommodative, very accommodative, even though we stopped the net asset purchases, it wasn't a tightening, as some people have said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually it's been very accommodative for a variety of reasons, the term structure curve flattened, the term premium is negative and so even the discount component to stock prices has contributed to stock prices - to keep them higher.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Most importantly, liquidity conditions are abundant and will remain abundant so as I said, several speakers mentioned the TLTRO and that's it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Yes, you see, I was asked the same question last time; not sure it was you, but the fact that the market… Let's go back to our forward guidance and it says we intend to continue reinvesting in full the principle payments from maturity - no, the other part of the forward guidance is we continue to expect the key ECB interest rates to remain at their present levels, at least through the summer of 2019 and in any case for as long as necessary to ensure the continued sustained convergence of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When markets place the first rate hike in 2020, they are using the state contingent part of our forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They assess the economic prospects that way and it shows that they have understood our reaction function.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In so doing, in the flattening of the yield curve that has taken place continuously by the way since we announced the end of the net asset purchases starting in June last year, they are providing accommodation through that channel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we have to assess then the developments and if this persistence will continue, we'll have to validate this indication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point in time, we just assess the situation.]

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to see first how protracted this slowdown is going to be, how persistent the factors that have originated the slowdown are going to be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This applies to fiscal policy as well, by the way fiscal policy in the euro area now is slightly expansionary, certainly more expansionary than last year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is true in Germany but also true in many other countries, if not all countries I think of the euro area in their draft budgetary plans are presenting expansions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first point, just go back about what I think I said last time: negative interest rates affect negatively the net interest margin and that's almost a tautology but especially because interest on deposit is set to zero.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But when we look at their effect, the effect of negative interest rates, which by the way have been a very effective monetary policy measure and it is an effective monetary policy measure now, it remains so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the effect of negative rates on profitability of the aggregate of the banking sector, we see that by and large the positive effects of the recovery generated by the more accommodative, more expansionary monetary policy produced by the negative rates compensate, offset each other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll have to see now how the continuation of negative rates will affect this balance, but let me also add another factor; that profitability in the eurozone, banks' profitability, is affected I would say in many cases much more significantly by factors like cost-coverage ratios that in some countries are way, way above any average.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the presence of stocks of non-performing loans, that by all accounts are way above any average; by overcrowding, so there are structural and business model-specific factors that affect the overall profitability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's in this sense that I said we will continue to monitor the profitability of the banking sector very, very closely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I just said shows how important this is because that's one of the main differences between now and the situation we had before the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The main difference is that banks are strong now, or at least stronger, certainly stronger than they were before the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a key for making sure that any downturn in growth doesn't transform itself into a recession.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You're right, it does point to a very slight tightening of credit standards, but the result of that figure is mostly centred in Italy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a tightening that has not spread to the rest of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other question we are still in the assessment mode and today's meeting was about that, not so much the policy mode.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me say at the very beginning that the nature of our forward guidance, which is both - it is date but it's also state contingent - has already produced a reaction in terms of increasing the degree of accommodation of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's been producing this reaction over the last several months, flattening the curve and producing all the effects I mentioned before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Next will depend on whether we will end up assessing this slower growth, or the factors that have produced this slower growth as persistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course I don't want to speculate about what contingency would call for a specific instrument but if you look at the number of instruments we have in place now, we can conclude that it's not true that the ECB has run out of fuel or has run out of instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, LTROs and TLTROs, both of them, have been very useful and very effective in restoring transmission of monetary policy across the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember when they were implemented, the LTROs was 2011-2012, the TLTROs came later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They were more targeted to lending but they have been unquestionably effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In a somewhat more I would say polite way, what these economists are saying is, if we are to do TLTROs, there should be a good case for monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, we want to have TLTROs or LTROS to address cases of existing or likely fragmentation in the monetary policy space.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, we don't want to be again in the situation where we were in 2012, '13 and '14 where we lowered interest, policy interest rates, and this was not translated into lower lending rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if that's necessary we'll do whatever is necessary to address this point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually what they are saying is that there must be a case of monetary policy for doing it, so it shouldn't be something that we do it as - and they are right - as a sectoral measure, as a country-based measure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of our instruments have already been playing their accommodative role in the past few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Others may been enacted depending on the evolution of growth and of the factors that have originally produced this slower momentum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, I would ask the Vice President to respond.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: De Guindos: With respect to the second question, as you perfectly know, BBVA has launched an internal investigation, that is underway.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Today it has announced that it has started also a sort of forensic probe that is going to be conducted by a third party.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that we have to wait for the conclusions of these probes and these investigations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We expect that the conclusions will be available as soon as possible because in these kind of circumstances, time is of the essence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, you see, when I said we still have instruments in our toolbox, first of all let's go back to when we announced the end of the net asset purchases, which was June last year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that point in time, actually we decided to - well, there are several things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The stock of bonds we own is not indifferent, it's pretty big.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More specifically, it's 25% of total government debt in eligible universe now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To stabilise the stock by itself does require purchases of bonds every month, which this year is about of the order of €15 billion, which was by and large the same amount we were purchasing on a net basis until December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The important thing for judging and the result of… The important thing for judging whether this is contractionary or is accommodative, is the stock relative to the volume of bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't expect the stock of government bonds to increase in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, the stock of government bonds relative to GDP has been declining since 2014 in the aggregate of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we have exceptions but what matters from our viewpoint is the aggregate of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the volume of long-term bonds is not growing and we expect it falling until 2021 by and large by 6%, so the pressure on rates will be less and less by itself, which also says that liquidity will remain very abundant well into the next decade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you go and measure this, you see what I think as I said before where you look at the risk-free rates across maturities, you see both the level and the shape of the term structure, they've gone down, they've flattened and the term structure and the level has been going down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, ten-year Bunds are now lower by 20 basis points since June and rates kept on going down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course the spreads is a different issue; the spreads in different countries or for certain segments of the bond market have evolved depending on specific sectoral or country conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course let me finish, so we have a long list of instruments now, we have the reinvestment, we have the forward guidance, date based, we have the APP, we have TLTRO, we have lots of instruments and we stand ready to adjust them or use them according to the contingency that is produced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the first question is definitely too difficult for me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can't answer that question because I just wouldn't know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second question is in a sense, the account I gave you of the debate of the discussion we had in the Governing Council answers this question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One part of the participants, let me put it this way, doesn't exclude because we are not yet at the level of having certainties but doesn't exclude all in all a more benign outcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Another part is closer to exclude this and just work fora downside, so it's… Therefore the consequence of this discussion will reverberate in the market rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Actually it's not that different because in the US, you've seen inflation hovering around 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It means that it's taken several number of years - and mind, the US is more advanced than we are in the business cycle really - so it's taken several number of years in US to have this pass-through from wages into prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would expect that if it takes the same number of years we may be there as well, but it's been… Inflation is not far from the target in US.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The timing of monetary policy actions in all jurisdictions is dictated by the respective positions, by the positions of the economies in the respective business cycles.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Structural differences may play - may make a difference but you know, structural differences were there before and are going to stay there later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's hard to understand how they can influence but certainly they may have an effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's hard to say, it's hard to project these difference in dates to different businesses but we have to keep in mind that once we are at the same stage with the labour market, the same degree of tightness everywhere in the eurozone, because one feature of the eurozone is its heterogeneity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In some parts of the eurozone, we have no doubt these parts are at full employment and have been at full employment for a while, so much so that if anything, the obstacles to higher growth are now to be found in the scarcity of labour or in the scarcity of skilled labour or in the capacity of the plant and equipment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in other parts of the eurozone, unemployment is still high, significantly high, and so you have slack there so you have slower wage momentum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have lower demand which hampers the pricing capacity of firms and therefore the pass-through into higher prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's heterogeneous and that's one thing to keep in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you know on various occasions, various governments have attacked both supervision but also monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All of you certainly remember other instances where the ECB monetary policy was being publically criticised by prominent politicians.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, it's understandable that when things don't go their way, the politicians would protest and say what they want.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course people know that the mandate is about to end, but we have no say about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, these processes have always been decided by other people in other fora and central bankers have no say about that, so we wait for the decisions taken by the European Council, by the Eurogroup.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I said banks are stronger in comparison with what they were, how they were at the beginning of the great financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, banks can be stronger but if you look at the capital ratios today they are much higher than they were in 2006.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also risk management, controls, the overall banking sector has, partly in response to the regulation, partly in response to their own - a change in their own business practices, is stronger than it was before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Given that, we certainly know that we have as I mentioned before in a different context, we have cost coverage ratios which are above any - in some parts of the eurozone - are above any comparator.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have NPL stocks which are high and that, what you said, actually shows the case for a speedy elimination of NPL stocks because it does strengthen the economies against a recession.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It does ensure the people of these countries that a recession doesn't become again a credit crunch which worsens the recession again, which was the experience in the great financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't know much, frankly, about the Danièle Nouy package and so these questions, you will have to ask to Enriaand maybe he has an Enria package to propose .But I don't know much about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the possibility of recessions in Germany and Italy, I think I have discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Right now the Governing Council doesn't assess this as a likely possibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, likelihood of recession changes from different parts of the eurozone, but overall in the aggregate, there was no sense that the recession was a likely event.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is no, we are not considering experiments in this field.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the first question, there is a vast amount of work that's taking place across different central banks and centred in the BIS, the Bank for International Settlements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To say that this would lead to a change of this importance any time soon would be wrong, would be an exaggeration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually rather the opposite is true; it's rather the risks of movements like that which by the way I know that in some countries have been asked by the public, in some countries, not many, very few as a matter of fact, are close to doing something like that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the studies, the work that has been done highlights more the risk of an approach like that for monetary policy, for the banking system, for financial stability than the benefits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's a snapshot of how things stand at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: I am sorry, I am not in a position to comment on this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Actually if I am correct, the word stepped up was used for structural reforms but the conclusion is the same.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether you talk about structural reforms, or progressing economic and monetary union building, deepening, the pace has slowed down considerably.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reason, basically, is that these are big important changes and therefore they need the support of the people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I said it on another occasion, in both these areas, you've got to be humble.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can design what's the optimal set of measures to take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In all cases we made the examples of structural reform or economic monetary union deepening but then the timing of implementation of these measures is an entirely political decision and so I have no doubt about the political commitment by our leaders, by our governments, by most of our citizens, you have seen the euro now has an approval rate at its highest since its beginning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I have no doubt about the political commitment on the deepening economic and monetary union, but I have no say on its timing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, you know that we've been working with the Bank of England now for several months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We cooperate actively, we had a working group identifying what the main risks could be, could materialise in the financial system, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We identified several areas for action: one, potentially the most important one, is the area of centrally-cleared derivatives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But then the Commission intervened with a pronouncement basically allowing the UK central clearing -CCPs to continue serving EU clients and members for a period, if I am not mistaken, of 12 months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other areas of non-centrally-cleared derivatives, insurance contracts, they do present risk but they can be addressed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are being addressed by the private sector so work has been done in the financial sector to be prepared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we have to see because it's such a - it's an important event.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Its length, also its protracted length of time also is not benefiting the overall economic climate in UK but also in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The design of the TLTRO responds to a variety of objectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The key objective derives from how the situation of bank funding looks like over the next few years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the coming years we will have a congestion for bank funding caused by the coming to maturity of the existing TLTROs, the coming to maturity of sizable amounts of bank bonds, various regulatory compliances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The TLTROs, as has been said in the introductory statement, maintain [and] preserve favourable bank lending conditions and a smooth transition of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the precise design, whether it's two instead of four, do reflect the changed conditions we have today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, further details especially on the pricing and other details, will get to be known in due time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second question really addresses the substance of today's meeting so let me give you a broad account of how this meeting unfolded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In so doing, I think I'm pretty sure I'll respond to some of the questions you intend to ask.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the decisions: It's four sets of decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We moved the calendar-based part of our forward guidance from September to December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second, we confirm the reinvestment in full of the principle payments from maturing securities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you understand the importance of the chained element in our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having moved the calendar-based, so does the expected - well, whatever the horizon is going to be during which the purchases will take place to keep the stock unchanged, so you see this is adding accommodation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To answer your question, as a matter of fact you asked me is this adding accommodation?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The financing conditions have been - well, monetary policy has been very accommodative, but also financing conditions as a matter of fact have even eased since our last meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is also partly due to the structure of our forward guidance so that expected interest rates have gone down since the last meeting and especially at the end of last year as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then the third element is the targeted longer-term refinancing operations that we've just discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we have the fixed-rate tender procedures with full allotment for as long as necessary, at least until the end of the reserve maintenance period starting in March 2021.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These are decisions that have been taken following a significant downward revision of the forecasts by our staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, you've seen and you've just heard me say that optionality is reiterated in all instances, which means that the Governing Council is both willing and committed to act when if needed, amplifying the use of these instruments based on the data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third is what I just said; all this takes place in an environment where monetary policy accommodation is already very substantial.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second point is, how did we get to take these decisions?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was unanimity and I think given the complexity of the package, I think it's a very, very positive sign for the cohesiveness of the Governing Council and of our deliberations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, what is the general context in which these decisions have taken place?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, we're coming - and maybe we still are - in a period of continued weakness and pervasive uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why the forecast has been revised downwards quite significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I will come and comment in a moment about the pervasive uncertainty but the factors that have originally caused this weakness, which are mostly of external source, are still there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The uncertainty is partly related to how long these factors will continue affecting the world economy, the eurozone economy and confidence more generally.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are two observations to make about the assessment of the outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First, the Governing Council expressed confidence, all members expressed confidence in the baseline, which means that we assess the probabilities of a recession as being very low, as well as the probabilities of a de-anchoring of inflation expectations are indeed very low in our assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the reasons are the same that underpinned the strength of our economy in our previous meetings; namely nominal wage growth continues, labour market, though at a kind of slower rate but continues to improve, consumption remains by and large in good shape.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary policy remains accommodative and now is even more accommodative, and financing conditions, as I said, have eased up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They were already very easy and they eased up further.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a second factor that we've taken into account in maintaining this confidence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's that it's true that these external factors continued to be hanging on, continue to be weighing on the eurozone economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's also true that governments are responding in their respective jurisdictions with policies that are addressing these problems in the US, in China.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point to be kept in mind is that you've seen that the revision of the inflation path basically says one thing; we have confidence that [inflation] will converge but we also, at this point in time, think that it's going to take longer to get there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the weaker growth probably will further slow down the pass-through from higher nominal wages to higher prices, higher inflation and possibly also slow down the closure of the output gap.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These two reasons are important to be kept in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the other important part of today's decision is that we maintained the risk assessment as tilted to the downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is infrequent because we usually say when we take some policy actions, the risks get back into balance, but it's happened on other occasions in the past, but not frequently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, because we are aware that our decisions certainly increase the resilience of the eurozone economy but actually can they address these factors that are weighing on the eurozone economy in the rest of the world?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They cannot, so the threat of protection is one factor.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Geopolitical considerations also related to whatever happens about the United Kingdom Brexit or United Kingdom exiting, or not exiting, or in the forms in which they will exit from the European Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The emerging market vulnerabilities, what's happening in China, we know that the Chinese government has reacted, the US government has - the US monetary policy has changed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example in the US, we have to take into account that there is going to be a waning effect of the fiscal package so a slowdown is projected there all over.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, our actions increase the resilience of the eurozone economy and so make us confident, keep us confident that convergence to a sustainable rate of inflation - our objective - will happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is that our projections take into account the protectionist measures that have already been implemented, but they don't project an assessment of future measures or of how the current negotiation will actually end.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, well, you see optionality is everywhere.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the issue is whether we see contingencies that would justify the use of certain instruments instead of others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to speculate at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point in time, we've just taken all these decisions and we think they are the right decisions and the adequate decisions to be taken at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me add one thing: we didn't tighten when we stopped the net asset purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We didn't tighten monetary policy contrary to what some of you say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not even sure it's one of you, but just it's been said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to give you an idea, the balance sheet of the ECB is about 42 - 43% of the eurozone GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In order to keep this stock unchanged, we continue purchasing something in the order of €20 billion a month of bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This happens in a context where the debt to GDP ratio in the eurozone is actually falling.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The simple action of maintaining the stock unchanged in this context actually is a continuous easing because interest rates are pushed downward by this action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can see this because since we decided in June last year, interest rates have gone down, they keep on going down, the term premium is negative, so conditions are very, very accommodative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you add to this what I've just said, it's the chained element of this, of the horizon over which we'll carry out purchases to keep the stock unchanged moves together with the forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To finish the answer, what today's decisions also say is that we've changed the calendar-based part of our forward guidance based on the information we have today and it's data driven.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense we are very open to act and determined to act when it's needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Several members of the Governing Council presented the option of changing the calendar date of the forward guidance to March next year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And other members discussed what the consequence of a protracted period of time with negative rates, so lower or low for longer, could imply for banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there was no trade-off between the two, there was no trade-off and in the end we converged on a package that basically reflected the views of all the members of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second part of your question is whether… Well, markets have pretty well understood our reaction function.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in placing the expected date of the lift, [of] the DFR, some time in 2019 - before it was later, now it's moved back - and so the changing calendar in the calendar part in the date of our forward guidance becomes necessary when you kind of want to give credibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because clearly, if you have market expectations which are far away from the foreseen date of the guidance, then of course credibility becomes an issue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this sense, I think we've if anything enhanced the credibility of the forward guidance with today's decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The first question is really, I can't say more than I said in the introductory statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The pricing, the shape and other details on the TLTRO will be made known in due time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I just said about whatever incentives, the language you've just quoted, it's the intention of designing in a way that gives built-in incentives for credit conditions to remain favourable, but doesn't get further into being more specific at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the Supervisory Board, yes, well, it is a process which will be carried out in a completely transparent way in the coming weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's with a change in the chair and so on, so everything's been delayed; it will take place soon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, two things were present; pervasive uncertainty but also a definite worsening in the projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fact that the climate has become more uncertain doesn't mean that one has to stay put.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You just do what you think is right and you temper, however, what you are doing with a consideration there is uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, in a dark room you move with tiny steps.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Or in other words, you try to be proactive rather than reactive to contingencies because, for a variety of reasons, the situation can then unfold in an unforeseen and unwanted way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question, our forward guidance has been designed with two legs; the state and the time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Both of them reinforce each other and both of them give credibility to each other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To have a state only is kind of, as you said, perhaps gives more flexibility but at the same time, being vaguer is less effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, it's not me, it's the Governing Council, but I have no comments to make.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first LTROs were quite effective for the time when they had been designed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But they were used - not 100% of course - but they were used also to kind of buy sovereign bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that time, the yields on bonds were high and banks especially in parts of the eurozone, where to lend to the economy was very risky because these parts were in huge recession, they bought sovereign bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What then we wanted to achieve with the "T" was to make sure to minimise this possibility to make sure the banks borrow at a very good rate, but in order to lend to the economy and to firms and households in the private sector, not to buy sovereign bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's easy for us to plead for more action at European level in all directions; institutional, policies and so on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we should do it, but we should be aware that these are political decisions that governments can take or have to take, but they have to explain to their citizens.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's relatively easy to advise about the right policy, much more difficult is to implement it in a democratic society, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think certainly, I've said many times, the European construction is still fragile.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The completion of the banking union is essential, capital markets union are all essential things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, some of these things are very, very close to being implemented because much of this has been agreed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The remaining differences don't seem to be of an order of magnitude that could stop the whole process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would say when the political contingencies, when the political stars will align, I am absolutely confident we'll see fast progress on all these fronts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, Philip Lane is an excellent acquisition for the ECB but we are not going to ask him about this Eurobond thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Eurobond is again not something that the ECB can force or just decide about; again it's an inherently political decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And of course this doesn't detract at all from the argument that it's absolutely rational to have a safe asset at European level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's fundamental, but one thing is to say it's fundamental, another thing is to decide and defend this decision in front of your citizens, which may have different views about that from the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, on your first question, a TLTRO is an operation which allows banks to borrow money from the ECB at somewhat more favourable terms than the banks could do going to the market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the issue is not whether there is a subsidy or not; there is a subsidy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, it depends very much on how it's designed of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there were no subsidies then nobody would take up the TLTROs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The issue is whether the TLTRO fulfils monetary policy objectives and helps the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe it has always done that, it's been very effective, as a matter of fact, in reactivating the banking sector in the eurozone and in transmitting - especially the TLTRO - transmitting the better lending conditions to firms and households, to the private sector in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's the yardstick of successful TLTRO and certainly I have all reasons to think this will be designed exactly with the same effectiveness.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we've been… Well, in any event, today we are not behind the curve for sure, but even before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because the way the monetary policy has been designed after June, would produce automatic accommodation that would make financing conditions easier as far as the monetary policy component is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then of course since I said and it was like that before, too, just since we are in our deliberations data driven, when it's become necessary to add to this automatic process, we did it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer is no to both questions, actually.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was no discussion about QE, not at all, and there is no lack of recovery in the eurozone economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have dwelled long enough on the worsening of the economic outlook, but we're all still talking about weaker growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The economy continues to expand, the labour market continues to add jobs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nominal wages continue to grow - as a matter of fact, at a higher rate than they used to a year go or two years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even, interesting, the dispersion amongst growth rates of nominal wages across sectors and countries is now at a historical minimum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point is that we've got to be patient in terms of pass-through.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see nominal wages going up and we don't see prices going up at the same time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be patient, because first of all, now we are having a slowdown but also because the mechanism whereby increasing the cost, wages and also other parts of the cost components are transferred into prices, has changed structurally in the last few years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You've seen this in the United States and you're seeing this in Europe now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question, you find a hint in the introductory statement about how a proper fiscal policy could actually help not only the recovery, not only the convergence of inflation to our objective path, but also on the issue of external surplus when you read the last section of our introductory statement, which says: "The implementation of the country-specific recommendations as recently communicated by European Commission, has been scant or not much at best."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then it says - it's a change with respect to previous IS: "regarding fiscal policies, the mildly expansionary euro area fiscal stance and the operational automatic stabilisers are providing support to economic activity."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then it goes into the same usual statement for countries with high debt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see that there is a clear recognition of what you said, but again to this I would apply the same degree of humility that I would apply to the - in answering to the question about Europe and whether Europe is responding or not, are political decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
