text: Even though we may be convinced that it's right, we also have to be aware that we are not the ones who implement these decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Yes, well, there was a concession to my past academic experience, but no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is no to both questions and the effect that negative rates might have on banks' balance sheets is complex and was not… The specific mitigating measures were not discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was a discussion about the need to examine this issue in depth because negative rates have been quite successful in our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They were a powerful instrument in enhancing, fostering the recovery and converging to price stability and achieving our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are several analyses trying to assess what's the effect of negative rates for some time on banks' profitability but they're very, very complicated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the way in which a negative rate affects the banks' profitability depends very much on what business model the bank has.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have situations where this influence is very, very important - it's significant - and situations where it's not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you combine in the aggregate you don't see much in spite of the many years that have passed by.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second point, one may argue that certainly at the beginning combined with QE, there were benefits coming from the recovery, coming from the selling of the bonds with QE and there were costs coming from the negative rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, how all this has evolved through time is quite complicated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also again talking about the aggregates, but that's why I'm not satisfied with looking at aggregates so much, but that's what we have to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see that when you talk about profitability of European banks, well, it's certainly lower than profitability of American banks, but not much lower than UK or Japan, whether they have mitigating measures or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are many elements that affect the profitability, so we have to look at this issue in somewhat greater detail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not necessarily related to the negative rates but more generally, what are the components of banks' profitability that are being affected by our monetary policy and one of which is the negative rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Thank you because I didn't comment exactly on the factors for the slowdown of 2019.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are two sets of factors; external and internal to the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The external factors are - I hinted at them before - it's mostly a slowdown in world trade due to a slowdown in China, various emerging market vulnerabilities, a potential slowdown in the United States and I think a general sort of lower confidence produced by the trade discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly this diminished confidence filters through countries and sectors and it's one major factor for the slowdown in the eurozone economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of them are sector specific and country specific; namely car industry in Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are also other sectors in other countries, one of which is certainly Italy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Where the uncertainty comes into play is, how long these factors will be weighing on the eurozone economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I'm not sure that equity markets are more bearish because they actually regained everything they lost in the last part of the year last year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They gained it back and plus, but we have to see what are the sources of this increase in stock prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In some parts of the world, this is caused mostly by earnings expectations that are good.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other parts of the world, this is caused by a decrease in risk premium and earning expectations actually appear to have less of an influence in explaining price increases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that says something about the expectations about the economy, the future evolution of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Mind, there is another factor which actually has played quite an important role especially at the beginning of this year and that's the discount factor; namely if people have a lower discount factor they tend to have higher valuations for the stocks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore that's the element that's mostly affected by monetary policy - or expectations about the discount factor.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Updated on 12 March 2019 to correct an error in the transcript of the questions and answers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, I would say to the second question, I would answer it's too early.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you read the statement I just gave, there is the - we, in a sense, - the Governing Council gives the criteria upon which this assessment for both the TLTRO III and the mitigation of possible side-effects would take place, the conditions under which the analysis would be carried out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll take into account a thorough assessment of the bank-based transmission channel for our monetary policy, as well as further developments in the economic outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are looking at that, both things, and right now it's too early to decide about both.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would say the Governing Council was, I would say - we didn't vote, so it's not unanimous or anything - but it just had a consensus on the need for further analysis on both issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That, in a sense, includes the first question, because this language echoes what I did say in the ECB Watchers' speech, and that's it; we've got to look at that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at the functioning of the financial intermediation channel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, the assessment of the bank-based transmission channel of monetary policy, as well as further developments in the economic outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to see how the economic outlook will turn out between now and the next monetary policy meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Where, by the way, we also will be having the new projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Now, your first question points out the continued deterioration of inflation expectations over the last several months, and we had quite a substantial analysis of why this is so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that the sliding of the five-year-to-five-year inflation expectations corresponds to a deterioration of the economic outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also quite clear that as the economic outlook, especially the economic activity slows down, also markets expect less pressure in the labour market, but we haven't seen that yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have underlying strength in the economy, and so we analyse why this is so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is that inflation expectations have deteriorated predominantly because of the risk premium, or the negative risk premium, which is a big difference to 2016.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You may remember that in the early part of 2016 we had a similar deterioration of inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that time it was not so much because of the risk premium, but it was a real danger of de-anchoring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is good news in the sense that it says that expectations are responding to the economic outlook, but not de-anchoring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, this increase in the negative risk premium might reflect either the market perception, that we don't have instruments, and I think we've shown that we have plenty of instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If anything, the market reaction to my ECB Watchers' speech last time shows that we have plenty of instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, that market reaction demonstrated that markets have fully understood our reaction function.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second possibility is that we may well - I mean, the markets may think - the Governing Council would tolerate low inflation, too low inflation, without being de-anchored, but low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, we remain fully committed to return inflation to 2% without undue delay.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, let me also point out another aspect of this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our inflation aim doesn't imply a ceiling at 2%; inflation can deviate from our objective in both directions, so long as the path of inflation converges to our medium-term objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second question is about this threat of tariffs from President Trump toward the Europeans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, we listed the threat of protection as one of the potential factors dampening growth in the euro area - and elsewhere in the world, as a matter of fact - so this is not different from this viewpoint.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, we have to see, first of all, what happens, because as you've seen in the past between words and deeds there is often a big gulf.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly, even the fact that these threats are being vented with some frequency, they certainly undermine general confidence, and there is no question about the fact that that's one of the reasons for the general weakness in the euro zone, I believe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Elsewhere in the world the confidence weakening has come from various threats, various vulnerabilities - it's a combination of effects - but certainly also from these threats of further protectionist measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: He's a great addition to our team, but it's not that we actually put our decision making in our calendar depending on who's going to be on board or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, we didn't, and I've said this in the beginning, the details of the precise terms of new targeted long-term refinancing operations will be communicated at one of our forthcoming meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the pricing of new TLTROs will take into account two criteria - and I gave the two criteria before - but we haven't discussed that today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, we haven't discussed the merits or the cons of mitigation measures either.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to identify that with a specific word, and I never did.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we started a process where we will analyse all measures, and specifically the two that I mentioned in the introductory statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This analysis is based on these two criteria, and that's it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need further information that will come to us between now and June, and in a sense the projections that we'll have in June by the staff of the ECB will be an important part of this information set.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, Philip Lane is a fantastic addition to our team.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a fact, and, by the way, so we ask ourselves how much has overall profitability of banks been affected by the negative deposit rate?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are actually in the process of carrying out this analysis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you compare profitability of banks, I mean, euro zone banks - by the way, we're talking about large aggregates, to the point of being meaningless, because the way this negative deposit rate affects different banking institutions is very different, banks' business models are profoundly different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the aggregate we see that profitability of euro zone banks is by and large like the ones in Japan, higher than in the UK, where there is no negative rate, and of course, lower than in the United States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then, of course, but I did say in my ECB Watchers' speech that we look at this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, look, as it says here "We will also consider whether the preservation of the favourable implications of the negative rates" - because we want these implications and the market reaction to my ECB Watchers' speech, basically, made clear that markets understood our reaction function - and it says, [whether] "favourable implications of negative interest rates for the economy require the mitigation of the possible side-effects, if any, on bank intermediation".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, really, for the second question, we haven't discussed that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What the Governing Council did today was to assess the outlook, which is a picture of weakening growth, to reiterate confidence in the convergence of the inflation path, based on a series of factors, and then reassert, reiterate the readiness to use all the instruments that are necessary to cope with the contingencies that come ahead.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was, I would say, unanimous, this deliberation to use all the instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I did say something at the beginning, this time it's not the right time to say, "I don't like this instrument", or, "I'd rather prefer another one".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Once we will be approaching that point with the information coming about the economy and inflation, we will be better positioned to see whether first, whether further action is needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, let's not forget the forward guidance has indeed, in the past few months, automatically responded to the weakening economic conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's not forget, also, that this forward guidance is chained with the horizon over which we'll carry out the repurchases of the bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you see, it says "we intend to continue reinvesting in full the principal payments for maturing securities purchased under the asset purchase programme for an extended period of time, past the date when we start raising the key ECB interest rates".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So whenever the date when we raise ECB interest rates moves forwards, so does the horizon over which we'll actually undertake the purchases, and in any case for as long as necessary to maintain favourable liquidity conditions, and an ample degree of monetary accommodation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you see that in the existing toolbox, and enacted toolbox, we already have optionality to extend the existing instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But with the statement today, the Governing Council also said that it's plainly open to use all instruments that would be required by the needed contingency as we gather further and further information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you've probably seen - you must have seen from the accounts - there were other members that actually wished a much more extended forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is part of natural discussions we had, and again, like for the other instruments that we briefly mentioned before, we didn't discuss this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was not - if I have to characterise this meeting - it was not an operational meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was more of a meeting that would characterise the stance of the Governing Council towards further action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, people are acknowledging, Governing Council members are acknowledging the weakening of the cycle, the weakening of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fact that this weakening will extend into the rest of the year, the weakening of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact, I just said that inflation would probably bottom out in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, they acknowledged also the underlying strength of the economy, the fact that some of these temporary factors are unwinding, and so it was a meeting where the main goal was to reassert the readiness to act if the contingencies would warrant so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again, as we move towards June when the new projections will be available, we'll be gathering more and more information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again, there is a difference with 2016, and so that's what we see now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You may remember - no, I don't think you would - but just in my ECB Watchers' speech I gave a number of - I think there had been - 50 soft patches in the last 50 years of the euro zone, and only four recessions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So for what it's worth, really, that's historical evidence looking at the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But overall probabilities of a recession, also implied financial probabilities of a recession, remain on the low side, and certainly less than the same probabilities would look like in past recessions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, in the previous episodes of a recession we would have seen a much higher probability of an oncoming recession than what we see today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, the Governing Council stands ready to adjust all of its instruments as appropriate, if that contingency were to materialise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, we would wish to have much more cross-border lending than we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this is also a part of the ongoing discussion on creating - on finishing - the banking union and creating a capital markets union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, what we are observing is that in some countries where credit growth is especially significant, part of this growth can be explained by the participation of banks, especially large banks, in syndicated loans that actually get used in other parts, other than their countries, where these banks are established.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In relation to the TLTRO, no, I don't think the liquidity gets necessarily trapped in the countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the other question was whether one would associate the presence of mitigating measures with a lengthening of the period during which interest rates remain negative or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have the sense that you are right; the markets perceive it this way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't know what to say, really, because it's a fact that we had negative rates now for many years, and there were no mitigating measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also a fact that the impact of negative rates changes: it's very different when they start, and then when they've been in place for a long period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, on your second question I will answer saying exactly the same thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't tolerate too low inflation; we remain fully committed to using all necessary instruments to return inflation to 2% without undue delay.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Likewise, our inflation aim doesn't imply a ceiling of 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Inflation can deviate from our objective in both directions, so long as the path of inflation converges towards our medium-term objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I believe I must have said something close to this, or something to this extent a few other times in the past few years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mean, many of your questions could be captured by the following question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you are to introduce mitigating measures for banks, for the side effects of negative interest rates on banks' profitability, would this imply low rates for longer, or lower negative rates?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We said that we want to analyse the side effects, and possibly the mitigating measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are not even discussing the first stage of this reasoning, not even to mention what this would imply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just restate one thing, that the market reaction to the ECB Watchers' speech, whether it was linked to this part or to another part, showed that markets understand our reaction function.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Central banks can on occasion, and especially the ECB, can certainly defend the European framework and point out to ways to improve on it, to complete it, or to remedy the weaknesses that the recent, and not so recent, experiences have shown.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I don't think central bankers would be right to intervene in that political debate, either in the European context or in a national context.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I gave two speeches of recent; one in Bologna, and the other one in Pisa, both focusing - the one in Bologna especially - on the fact that in this globalised world where challenges are global, we've got to be together to be truly sovereign, to be true masters of our destinies, because on our own we would have no way to cope with these global challenges.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The evidence is in front of our eyes every day.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In Pisa the speech was more oriented to explain why the euro has been a very positive experience, and at the same time to identify the weaknesses of the present situation and what we should do to make sure that the benefits of the euro and Europe in general are distributed to everybody.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On Brexit, I think the consequences of Brexit are different, whether it's a hard, disorderly Brexit, or whether it's properly managed and with an adequate transition period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So for me, again, two days, whatever, before the vote - I mean, they're having votes every day - it would not be right to anticipate one thing or another.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is clear, however, is that the whole discussion on Brexit, which has lasted now many years, really, is part and parcel of the overall uncertainty that is hanging over our continent, and I think it's hanging over the UK as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's probably unavoidable in very important political discussions, but that's a fact for our economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, we need to look with attention at the real implications of Brexit on the real economy, which, as I've said many times, in the aggregate, if you take the aggregate numbers, you don't see - you wouldn't expect much of an impact given the relative size of the two entities, but there are two important caveats to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is that certain countries are especially exposed to the UK economy, and of course they will have consequences, and these consequences may be serious, and these serious consequences are bound to reverberate in the rest of the continent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second caution is that the value chains are very extensive, and the ramifications of value chains are also quite broad.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if we are to reach a point where these value chains, which is not at all to be taken for granted, by the way, but if we are to reach a point where these value chains were to be broken, then we can have lots of local and possibly serious effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The data on the Italian economy didn't come as a surprise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There had been already downgrades in the forecast, in the growth forecast for Italy and for the rest of the euro zone, as a matter of fact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite clear that the priority there is to restore growth and employment, and Italy knows how to do it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's very important that these priorities are being pursued without causing an increase in interest rates, because increases in interest rates are contractionary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think, in simple words, that should be the aim of economic policy now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: You're asking me a very difficult question, which has not been addressed by the Council, and we'll have to see exactly what it means, what it's driving, whether it's justified or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But having said that, the Fed is embarking on a revisitation of the monetary policy framework, and again, we have to see what's going to come out of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These are not processes that can be discussed in one or two meetings, so it may take several months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The role of a supervisor when witnessing mergers is one where you want to make sure that the transaction is successful, and to be successful means that it not only pleases shareholders, but actually creates an entity which is strong, and capable of coping with the various challenges.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that the role of the supervisor is not necessarily one where it wants to address the agents towards a certain direction, unless the direction they've chosen is leading to a suboptimal outcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think there is a clear preference toward that - I don't think so - that's my own view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There isn't a clear preference towards having one or the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is pretty clear, however, is that the banking system in Europe is overcrowded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Part of the structural weakness of the banking system in Europe is caused by the overcapacity in banking, which is not overcapacity in the sense that there is little production of credit; it's overcapacity in terms of number of people, number of branches, costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're talking about countries where their banks have a cost income ratio of over 80%, 90%, and they even quarrel about negative deposit rates as being one of the causes of their lack of profitability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think there are a series of actions that improve the business model and rationalise the business model.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is an issue about, there is a relationship between scale and the capacity to undertake the investments that are needed to improve technology and be competitive, especially in certain business models.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't argue that all business models are like that, but certainly in some of them there's this situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, let me just say, first, it's not ten years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's several years we've been having this in place, and we've changed instruments, and frankly, the outcome, the results of our monetary policy action is in front of our eyes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You may remember how the situation was in 2015, 2014, 2012.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we had to cope with a series of crises really produced by the great financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The improved conditions all across the board are a testimony that our action has been quite effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The issue that you are mentioning is that we don't see inflation going toward our objective as fast as we had expected, and there are reasons for that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We mentioned what the reasons are, and we mentioned that the risks are tilted on the downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Does it mean that we ought to raise interest rates in the meantime, since our rates so far have not produced any outcome?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact it is one of the reasons why we are confident that the inflation rate will converge to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we didn't have that monetary policy we would still be less confident.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we are to raise interest rates, we would become less confident of such an outcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The environment proved much more challenging than was expected, say, three years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The external component is what's weighing on growth now, and that is not going to last.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is the way I would answer your point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The outcome of our discussions, basically, determines how cheap or how expensive it is to borrow money.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nowadays, interest rates are very low, which means that borrowing is cheap, which means that you can borrow money to buy a house, or a car, or other consumption goods more easily.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This means that they will create jobs, and in due time this means - and we are seeing it - that wages will go up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Wages are actually going up, going up finally and well-deservedly in all countries, but of course, especially in Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This, in due time, will produce also price increases, and prices will go up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Before we say goodbye to each other, I wish to acknowledge one thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was the last monetary policy meeting for Peter Praet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Usually what happens is that Peter comes in on the day before and he presents a vast, ample, and quite detailed explanation of the economic outlook, going from the rest of the world, and then zeroing in on Europe, gradually.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then the day after he presents his views on what sort of monetary policy action we should consider, undertake, analyse, or anything like that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Much of what I say in the press conferences and what I read in the introductory statement has been based on his work, on work that he and his staff and the team and the rest of the ECB does with him.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would like to take this opportunity to express my deepest thanks to him.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: You have to distinguish between market-based expectations of interest rates and survey expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The extension of the six months of this forward guidance basically takes into account the prolongation of uncertainty with respect to what we saw and believed and deemed in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen the threat of rising protectionism and, in fact, the point made by someone about what markets see in this protectionism threat and they seem to see much more than simply the damage to the economies coming from trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They might see a much broader phenomenon questioning all the multilateral order that we have lived in since the Second World War.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then of course the uncertainty about the Brexit negotiation and the uncertainty about the vulnerabilities of certain emerging market countries, which are important, more generally the uncertainty about global trade growth has extended beyond what we believed in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, data about the economy are not bad.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There isn't, as you've seen, any substantial worsening in the outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other part, the other question is about the slide in inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are, based on various analysis, no threats of de-anchoring inflation expectations, but certainly there is a considerable mass of distribution between zero and 1.5% now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, this fall, this slide in inflation expectations is not happening only in Europe; it's also happening elsewhere although admittedly from higher starting levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there must be some sort of global factor, but it's certainly something that we take into account in our policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, if I have to give a broad summary of the discussion, I would say it was centred on three key concepts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, there is still confidence in the baseline, but in the midst of increased and prolonged uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Prolonged means that this uncertainty is not going to go out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In March we might've hoped for a trade deal, we might've hoped for a decrease in uncertainties more generally.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We might've hoped for a different evolution in the Brexit, but now it's different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's one, but there is some acknowledgement of the economy at the same time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These risks have gained importance and gained projection and we can go through these risks one by one - more analytically.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a third element that has characterised our discussion today and you can find some words to this extent in the introductory statement; namely the readiness to act in case of adverse contingencies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This time the discussion has become, I would say, more granular in the sense that - and you'll see this in the accounts of the meeting - in the sense that several members raised the possibility of further rate cuts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Other members raised the possibility of restarting the asset purchase programme, or further extensions in the forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the conviction that we should pursue our objective in a symmetric fashion was also expressed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, let me add that in case these adverse contingencies were to happen, certainly fiscal policy will have to also come into consideration and play a fundamental role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Two wrinkles to this, but why don't I leave this to other questions?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Commission has concluded that Italy must reduce its debt-to-GDP ratio and this opinion will go to the Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By then the Italian Government will produce - and that's what's been asked - a medium-term plan for reducing debt-to-GDP ratios.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, keep in mind that we are not the interlocutor; it's the European Commission and Council at this point, but I don't think it's going to be asked anything that would ask for a rapid decline in debt-to-GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We all know that to make the debt-to-GDP decline fast is impossible, so it was going to be a medium-term plan which, however, has to be credible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Credibility is measured by how it is designed, how it is planned and the actions that will follow from the plan itself.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now about the mini-BOT, I think I've answered this question in the past when the possibility was raised; they are either money and then they are illegal, or they are debt and then that stock goes up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly the reading that people have and markets have of this mini-BOT doesn't seem to be very positive, but I'm only just stopping at what I said; it's either money or debt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me say it's a reflection that has just started today in this meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not discussed which contingency would call for which instrument.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the possibility of restarting the asset purchase programme, let me say that we have now, having abstained from purchasing bonds, considerable headroom anyway.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also have the comfort of the law after the European Court of Justice gave explicitly broad discretion to pursue in a proportionate manner our objectives and comply with our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other instrument that was supported was a possible decrease in interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, about the point I said in the introductory statement, it's quite important; there was a quite long discussion about whether the period of negative interest rates and whether especially the extension in the forward guidance is affecting banks' profitability in a way that could hamper lending.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These are answers in the aggregate; within the aggregate there are many different situations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the aggregate the answer was that so far we see no effect for a variety of reasons, which, however, it's not at all granted as a result, if we were to further extend the forward guidance or if we were to decrease interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why the introductory statement makes reference to mitigating measures in that case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other question was whether the possible rate cut in some other jurisdictions might affect the European economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I think it's a question we've asked ourselves several times in the last few years and I didn't speak about the financing conditions now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I should say that financing conditions with respect to the last monetary policy meeting have become slightly, slightly tighter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is on the account of the fact that stock prices are now lower and the euro has appreciated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The effective exchange rate of the euro has appreciated and so I think that's the answer to your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Let me say I just can't comment about national developments of this sort, but I can tell you that Governor Vasiliauskas is a very trusted member of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, you asked me about unanimity; yes, sorry I didn't answer before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second thing is about FinTech: yes, I did say this by the way in the brief courtesy speech that I had last night.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think Lithuania is second only to the UK as far as licenses for FinTech companies are concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a major source of future growth for Lithuania and of course also future concern for future attention in terms of supervision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example what I learned in preparing for this visit is that Central Bank of Lithuania has created a sandbox where FinTech companies can actually test their innovation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Vasiliauskas: Yes, so as probably you know, FinTech is of course on our agenda and the reason for the various developments in FinTech area is related to the concentration of our banking markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we have to keep in mind all possible risks which can come with the new technologies, especially cybersecurity, etc., etc.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The question is a very complex question, but as I said this is one of our strategic goals; to develop this area of the business.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we see it as possibility for the future of Lithuania.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly the manufacturing sector and in general the European manufacturing countries are more exposed to external demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Weakening trade growth affects the manufacturing sector more than other sectors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had temporary factors before relating to specific industries, you remember.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had a falling car production, we had other specifics, but then there was a rebound.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Both the original factor and the reaction to them, it's either waned or is gradually waning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, as I said, the service sector is still holding on, and investment is still moving forward, and construction especially is also helped by the mild weather, progressing with good numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The key issue is: how long can the rest of the economy be insulated from a manufacturing sector that keeps on being weak?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's what the Governing Council had in mind when they said they stand ready to use again instruments like lower interest rate or restarting APP that have not been used for a while now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the TLTRO: in deciding the shape and the price of TLTRO, two sets of considerations came into play.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Banks over the coming three years will have a series of funding pressures coming from the necessity to issue bonds for complying with regulatory requirements - some banks at least - coming from the need to pay back the previous TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all in all, the TLTRO has the nature of being a backstop as far as banking liquidity is concerned and so there is an intent here of making sure that in the future we mitigate potential cliff effects as we maybe see today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a slight disincentive with respect to the previous TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also there is another intent there that is to minimise the possibility of carry trade because the goal of TLTROs is to increase lending to the private sector, to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, the pricing is very generous altogether if compared with alternative sources of funding.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, the answer to the first question is no and the answer to the second question is that I think if there was someone who had doubts about our policy space, today's discussion really makes justice of any doubt about it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The policy space is there and the exchanges we had today is that if adverse contingencies were to materialise, the Governing Council stands ready to act and use - as I've said many times - all the instruments that are in the toolbox.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The answer to the second question is … first of all I was pleased and second, the answer is no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was in acknowledgement of the work I've done for Europe and for the Eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the first question is concerned, what we have to do as monetary policymakers is to ensure that monetary policy remains accommodative and can support economic activity and convergence of inflation towards our objectives even when the world or external or internal contingencies worsen and make more difficult for the economy to continue growing at a sustainable pace, and for inflation to grow and converge at a sustainable pace, in a sustained manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Otherwise whenever the source of a shock is external, there would be no point in having a monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've said many times that we are not at all accepting what the current market-based expectations are telling us because of course the survey-based expectations continue being well anchored in the long term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: The second question, you see, is the world more normal today than it was a year ago or three years ago?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Monetary policy uses the instruments that are adequate to cope with the contingencies and the challenges that come out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we say the monetary policy is non-conventional, that we are far away from normalisation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are far away from normalisation because the rest of the world, the rest of the challenges are far away from being normal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's been like that now for many, many, many years following first the great financial crisis, then the sovereign debt crisis, then the Greek crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we have the threat of rising protectionism, the geopolitical threats that we see every day.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have developments in the Eurozone itself that warrant this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will answer your second question later on; I have to check one detail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In any event, there will be a press release coming out at the end of the press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, it's absolutely essential to coordinate anti-money laundering at international level across different countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are serious problems of communication - within each country - between different agents: the supervisors, the judiciary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then there are communication problems between different countries' supervisors, between different countries' authorities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What's been done so far is trying to give some soft power to the EBA.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that we should go well beyond this and ideally create a European authority for anti-money laundering, with powers, with jurisdiction that would empower the authority to overcome the obstacles that today hamper communication and an effective policy against money laundering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: It seems that the presence of rising threat of protectionism, the geopolitical factors that are weighing on the Eurozone economic outlook would rule out any increase in interest rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's exactly I think what I said before; that we ought to protect the financing conditions in the Eurozone and maintain a very accommodative monetary policy even in the face of challenges that may materialise in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: First of all, the current conditions are not even comparable with the conditions we had way back seven years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's about seven years ago, it's slightly less than seven years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the lowest unemployment rate in many, many, many years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've seen growth in employment, so we have both a decline in unemployment and a growth in employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have basically by and large tight labour markets everywhere in the Eurozone and rising wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The overall economic situation is different, but certainly we have to be prepared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even though, as I said, the Governing Council today confirmed the present baseline, also acknowledged the risks to this baseline and how these risks have prolonged themselves and have in a sense also increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore the discussion really clearly stated the readiness to act in a less general way that I have reported to you on other occasions, but more specifically, in a more granular fashion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The use of forward guidance, I agree with you; it's been quite effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we've been using it for several years and it's been quite successful in steering market expectations and basically, it's become the major monetary policy tool we have now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we've decided really in a sense protects the baseline from these risks in this contingency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if we are to see different challenges, then the Governing Council - as I said before - stands ready to use all its tools.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think it's related to me, by the way, the forward guidance being effective because the way it's been designed and the fact that the reaction function has been very well explained and in a sense going back to market expectations - what they are telling us - is that, yes, the reaction function of the ECB has been well understood.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: Well, it's very difficult to foresee hypothetical events where you assume that the President of the ECB doesn't behave in a way to preserve the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's just a hypothesis that I do not want even consider.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In any event, it's the Governing Council that decides; don't forget.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: We are talking about different jurisdictions, different economic environments, so central banks react to their economic situations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example I think today's statement by the Bank of England saying that maybe rate hikes could be necessary in the near future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Each jurisdiction is different and I believe that today's discussion shows exactly this point; that there is confidence in the present baseline, but also clear acknowledgement of the risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The beginning of a granular discussion about what to do, one of which is exactly cutting interest rates further, if adverse contingencies were to be realised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other question relates to our mandate; it's not our task to decide our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However, I can say that some time ago there was a research showing that, regardless of what the mandate says, in other words, whether it has only price stability or employment as well, central banks - by and large - have produced the same outcome in terms of price stability and employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether in practice this is going to make a big difference, I don't know, because this research, by the way, is not recent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly if I look at our own experience, all given the circumstances in which the last few years have evolved, all our monetary policy was constantly utilised for obviously price stability as our mandate requires, but also it was in the direction of creating more employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the employment numbers, over the space of five years, ten million new jobs have been created.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Or it just happens because you do monetary policy that's oriented to price stability?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think ever so many jobs have been created in such a short time in this part of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Draghi: On inflation expectations I think I've covered it before: of course we are concerned but we don't see signs of de-anchoring, frankly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why on other occasions I made the point of stressing that the Governing Council is not resigned to having a lower rate of inflation forever - even for now, in fact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All policies are oriented towards having a set of expectations, market-based expectations, because as I said survey-based expectations continue to be anchored at a level of 1.6%/1.7% in the long term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also market-based expectations which would be more consistent with the policies we have and with the convergence of inflation to our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This drives me straight into answering your second question: clearly, there is some disconnect here between what markets are seeing in the future and what people expect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see, you compare surveys with market-based expectations, both for growth as well as stock prices, earnings, inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fall in inflation expectations, I was saying before, happened also in other parts of the world, probably not by the same amount and certainly starting from higher levels, but it did happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Markets seem to appear to see something bigger than simply trade disputes and whether this is correct or not, certainly this is what they price in their future transactions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The broader issue is: do they see a disruption of the order which goes beyond trade?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But, from our side, what we have to do is to take this reading seriously and be prepared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First let me give a sort of summary account of our discussion as it's taken place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the first discussion where there was broad agreement, broad convergence of views, was the assessment of the current outlook; namely an outlook where you still see signs of strength in the economy as I just read.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Generally speaking, you have resilience in the service sector and the construction sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, this outlook is getting worse and worse and it's getting worse and worse in manufacturing especially.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's getting worse and worse in those countries where manufacturing is very important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But because of value chains, this propagates all over the Eurozone and so this must be taken into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reasons were basically found to be in the general uncertainty that's now been with us for several months, actually more than a year, and which relates as I said many times to trade wars, to geopolitical tensions, too.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, also the possibility of a hard Brexit certainly is another factor to take into account and the slow rotation of the Chinese economy, all these factors and probably others are affecting the present outlook and weakening it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our last projections were in a sense suggesting that we might have had a rebound in the second part of the year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now incoming signs show weakness of growth in the third quarter as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All in all, the balance of risk was assessed to be on the downside, for the reasons that I've just mentioned, and also for the very fact that the simple - and this point I've made at other times - the simple prolonged lingering of this uncertainty is by itself a materialisation of one of these risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the inflation side, we basically saw inflation which is below our aim and we see projected inflation that says that convergence is further out in time, though as I've said on another occasion, the informational content of market-based inflation expectations has to be assessed, taking into account certain technical conditions of these markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However also in the SPF, the Survey of Professional Forecasters, inflation expectations have gone down so that's what led the Governing Council to these proposals, to the various proposals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, if I can go through them again: First of all the introduction of the easing bias through the introduction of the word "lower", and at least through the first half of 2020 and in any case, for as long as necessary to ensure the continued sustained convergence of inflation to our aim over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will see in the set of proposals all over a consistent degree of optionality, very much in the same way we've done on other occasions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We intend to continue reinvesting in full the principle payments for maturing securities purchased under the asset purchase programme for an extended period of time past the date when we start raising the key ECB interest rates, and in any case, for as long as necessary to maintain favourable liquidity conditions and an ample degree of monetary accommodation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we move to this point where we underline the need for a highly accommodative stance on monetary policy for a prolonged period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The acknowledgement that inflation rates, both realised and projected, have been persistently below levels that are in line with our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then it says accordingly if the medium term - and this is the trigger for our action, which basically reflects very much what I'd said in Sintra - outlook continues to fall short of our aim, the Governing Council is determined to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then there is another new language here: in line with its commitment to symmetry in its inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's another part of the language that is new.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That says again what I said in Sintra but it moves a step forward; namely that we stand ready to adjust all of our instruments as appropriate to ensure that inflation moves towards its aim in a sustained manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then there is another new part where we say that we've tasked the relevant Eurosystem Committees, so we not only affirm our determination but we move a step forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We task the committees with examining options, including ways to reinforce our forward guidance on policy rates, mitigating measures such as the design of a tiered system for reserve remuneration and options for the size and composition of potential new net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On other things most people converged with this, otherwise we wouldn't have this in the introductory statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But again whenever we have a package so complex as this, you would expect that people have different nuances about different parts of the package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point is that it was approved as a package after a fairly broad discussion, by converging to what I have just read to you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's what it is at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me more specifically about the mandate to the committees.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're here, we have a list, that's what we know, that's where we stand, ready to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we have had in the past and that's what the language says, basically.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question I'll be in a better position to answer you in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the time being however, you can refer to my Sintra language, the language in my speech at Sintra, where I talked about the headroom and the limits and how to view these limits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other point: no, there isn't any change really.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact, it's true it's not there in the first page; it's in the fourth page, it's just what it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we had a discussion about symmetry and there is a sense in the Governing Council that there should be a reflection on the objective: namely is it is close to but below 2%, or, should we move to another objective?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were different Governing Council members suggesting that we should carry out a reflection on this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, it's an important change so we just want to think about it seriously.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the meantime, however, the main thing in this introductory statement is that the Governing Council - I think I have said this many times, but now it's in the introductory statement - reaffirmed its commitment to symmetry around the inflation aim, which in a sense is 1.9 - it's close to, but below, 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, we say we don't like the current inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, there is no question about accepting lower inflation as we are seeing today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The bottom line of the discussion that I reported to you before is that we don't like what we see on the inflation front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The symmetry means basically that there is no cap, or 2% cap, and that inflation can deviate on both sides.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Symmetry means that the Governing Council will act with the same determination whether inflation is above or below the inflation aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's important to read in the full context.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nuances were mostly, if not only, about what to do, whether we should have a package, what to do first among this list of instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, you know that some Council members have doubts about the two-tier system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we had that discussion as well and now the statement says that if we are to lower interest rates, that will come with mitigating measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's reflected well in the breadth of the mandate that's been given to the committees.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second point where you asked whether there was any discussion today: no, there wasn't.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There wasn't because the sense is that we see an outlook… Well, first of all, on the inflation front we don't like what we see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, we see an outlook which is in a sense… Let me just step back and recall: in the last G7 meeting when I was asked to make the assessment for the euro area economy, I said, "Look, it's difficult to be gloomy today because the present situation is one where you see signs of strength."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, you see especially in certain sectors, in certain countries, a quickly deteriorating economic outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Given that we had the last June projections we decided that we want to see the next projections before taking action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And also the sense is that all this is pretty complex, and needs preparation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On both questions, we placed ourselves in the hands of the committees, so first question is: what shape will the tiering system have?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to have the committees' work and decide how to design the system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly the experience of other countries' central banks will be an important element in this design.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We wanted to have a broad mandate but not that broad, after all, but basically leaving us some leeway for the committees to reflect, because of the complexity of the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So they have to assess many aspects of the current outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I just said, it was a meeting where we… It was based on two… If I just try to summarise the main lines of the meeting, one was an assessment of the current growth outlook and especially of inflation, current and projected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, inflation expectations now have been at historical lows for some time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: With the admission - and that's again very important - with the admission that we don't like this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second part was based on how to design this preparation, but not really discussing the various aspects of this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still see the risk of a recession as being pretty low, all in all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still see signs of resilience in the labour market, which continues to improve, admittedly with a lower and lower momentum.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are going from a peak to peak here in terms of jobs created, in terms of unemployment rates, in terms of employment rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, in some countries manufacturing is a very important part of their economic activity and a slowdown in that part is affecting other countries as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What's hitting the manufacturing sector in Germany and also I think in Italy and to a lesser extent, in other countries, is what you would call an idiosyncratic shock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We said that the mildly expansionary fiscal policy is supporting activity in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if there were to be a significant worsening in the Eurozone economy, it's unquestionable that fiscal policy - a significant fiscal policy, mostly in some countries but also at the euro area level - becomes of the essence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was a point I made in Sintra but I started making this point way back in 2014 in a Jackson Hole speech: monetary policy has done a lot to support the euro area and continues, as you can see today, to do a lot but if we continue with this deteriorating outlook, fiscal policy will become of the essence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question: I can restate what I said in Sintra: we don't target exchange rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is price stability and we have an international consensus about avoiding competitive devaluations and we stick with that international consensus, which has been, by the way, a pillar of our multilateral construction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There have been these various observations and we simply restate our mandate on this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the second one: no, it isn't any order - and it's deliberately so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even whenever I said all instruments are on the table, I myself have been very careful about not saying what we'd like more, what should come first, whether they should come together or whatever.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's just that we are not yet at that stage.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other question is about whether we reached the reversal rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point to be made is that on the last occasion when we extended our forward guidance last June, the analysis would show that at that level of interest rates or this level of interest rates, and for that period of time of the forward guidance, the consequences on the profitability of the banking system were not significantly negative or negative at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, there was no evidence that this would have any significant impact on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So now we have to see if further negative rates or even possibly - but we are not talking about it now - a different calendar [date], would affect banks' profitability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly there is a danger to protract the negative rates for a long period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It did the trick because it raised inflation from where it was in 2014.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time we had the materialisation of a variety of risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What monetary policy has done is really counteracted the influence, the effect that this materialisation of various risks might have had on economic activity and inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On economic activity you can say it really did the trick in the sense that we moved from massive unemployment to a condition that most people would define, certainly in certain countries, as one of full employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Each time we meet, we have the number of jobs created and that keeps on going up now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are now at 11 million over a five-, six-year period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Never have so many jobs been created in this part of the world over such a stretch of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We lay out the conditions for the price, for the cost pressures to be passed into price pressures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, this pass-through is taking longer than expected and so that's why we've got to keep being persistent and patient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, this slowing in the pass-through is not something that we're experiencing only in the euro area, as you know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's pretty spread, but that doesn't really exempt monetary policy from undertaking its task and doing what is necessary to achieve its objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And let me repeat here: it's fiscal policy, which will be called into action soon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, I haven't come to a determination of what I will be doing in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think she'll be an outstanding President of the ECB and I'm saying this with the knowledge that comes from having known her for longer than she and I may like to remember.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if you think about the way decision-making has been actually done in the IMF, it's collegial; it uses the vast input of the staff, of economists.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It involves discussions with colleagues, with the staff, with the various parts of the IMF.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It isn't that different from what we do at the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Looking back at all our experience and comparing it with what happened in the United States - and by the way, I think I went through this comparison in my speech in Sintra - you see that a supportive fiscal policy allows monetary policy to perform the same task as we did with less side effects and faster.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When the outlook deteriorates, this becomes more and more important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For me going beyond this, at this stage, would be premature but I think we should have this in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think fiscal policy was important, is important, will be even more important if the economic situation deteriorates everywhere.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think fiscal policy should be pursued, maintaining credibility on the markets because if you expand and interest rates go up, then of course you frustrate the main aim of fiscal policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's really important and each country has its own agenda on what is the best fiscal policy to be activated against idiosyncratic shocks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is: we discussed not the substance but when to have a discussion about this, which is in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you see, the introductory statement says: in this context we have tasked the relevant Eurosystem Committees with examining options, including ways to reinforce our forward guidance on policy rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you can see that the mandate is broad there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the committees that will think and they will discuss and they will make proposals to the Governing Council on the occasion of the next projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On inflation expectations, it's true, it's market-based inflation expectations that are being questioned for a variety of reasons; are they a completely reliable indicator?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then some say different expectations, more relevant to the real life of people, of individuals ought to be considered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point is that we still have that as a yardstick and it would be a mistake to be complacent about that - which doesn't rule out an examination of all these other expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But keep in mind that the Survey of Professional Forecasters' expectations have declined as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is something I would point your attention to, because SPF expectations have been pretty sturdy for a long period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the fact that they, too, have gone down is something that we should look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, that's not what we are seeing in construction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Houses get built and then as you can see from house valuations, they are going up in several parts of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'm not sure that this negative conclusion about the effectiveness of lower rates on the economy is warranted by facts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly we have to ask ourselves: are all these instruments going to be effective forever?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Maybe there are as well, but would that exempt monetary policy from doing what is necessary or what we believe necessary based on the current information?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On Libra, we didn't discuss that in this meeting of the Governing Council, but we did discuss this quite extensively in the G7.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The bottom line of this discussion is that there is interest of course by the G7 governments, and I believe by all the governments in the world, for this development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there was a pretty unanimous view that there are concerns as well as interest and we and they better first address the concerns.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These concerns are concerns about cybersecurity, AML/money laundering, terrorism financing, use of these currencies for criminal purposes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All this is linked also to the anonymity, how would this work?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Tax evasion, monetary policy transmission, financial stability and the global payment system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They need to be addressed before the regulators can have a look at this with genuine interest and positive interest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why we have had this meeting today, starting the possibility of actions in the future, if there is no improvement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to the first question is the usual one; the transmission channel of lower rates hasn't changed, it's the same.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Policy rates affect the short anchor, the short-term part of the yield curve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Asset purchases basically affect the longer-term part of the yield curve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Both are relevant for investment and, so that is one answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the other I really should refer to the language because just hinting that they may look at other instruments would go beyond the discussion we had.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's broad but it doesn't say that they should look at other instruments at all costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is the starting point, that's what we have, that's what we know and that's what's been tested over the last few years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then it mentions the part about "including", and okay, there we are looking forward to seeing new things, if there are any.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course I am very honoured by that, but I am not available so it's not an issue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first point, no, it didn't come up during our discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of the response to that, I gave it in Sintra, I said very, very simply, "We have a mandate which is price stability."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, our credibility is not tested vis-à-vis the 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's been tested so far to an objective of close to but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the main answer to you is this: we don't see a de-anchoring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see a considerable mass of expected inflation moving to lower levels of inflation and that's exactly what we are seeing: 1.6% is the inflation rate that we see in 2021 in our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's something about which the Governing Council said today in the introductory statement: we don't like it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why the introduction of the word symmetry has to assert in the clearest way such a determination to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question: as I said before, the transmission channel is the same as before and we do expect all this will affect both directly inflation expectations and indirectly through the support of economic activity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see, at this point it's not clear yet whether it's going to be what's been called a sag, namely a very protracted period of time at lower growth, but how much lower is this growth going to be?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to do everything that's possible to avoid that monetary policy might be a hindrance, in other words, highly accommodative monetary policy is there to stay for a long period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I can, before giving you the sort of the chemistry of the meeting let me just spend a word trying to explain what we have actually done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think as I kind of sketched in the Introductory Statement there were three elements that prompted action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Along the lines, by the way, that you would find in my Sintra speech.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all after, and again if anything after Sintra the case became even stronger because the protracted slowdown in the eurozone economy is actually more marked than expected, this is the first element.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second element is the persistent and the persistence of downside risks of trade nature but also geo-political nature in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by the way our baseline scenario that actually contains the third reason for acting, namely the downward revision in projected inflation with the inflation expectations at this low level and the current underlying inflation being muted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This baseline scenario is also relatively favourable because it doesn't contain the case of a hard Brexit for example, the probability of which has gone up over recent time, and it doesn't contain some of the trade measures, trade escalation at least, some of the trade escalation that's taken place since August.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So with this relatively favourable baseline scenario there was a downgrade in inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
