text: And that's what prompted the measures we've taken and let me just spend a word explaining them and then I will answer your points more specifically.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the lowering of the DFR, the Deposit Facility Rate, together with the reinforced forward guidance operates all throughout the yield curve, especially in the short- and the medium-term segments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then you see that there is a different forward guidance today, it's a strengthened state-dependence, there is no more calendar-dependence and this should give a pretty good guidepost, pretty clear guidepost for rate expectations by linking our policy to more stringent conditions for the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Over our projection horizon, projected inflation will not only need now to converge but also as I think I read in the Introductory Statement, also stabilise around a level sufficiently close to but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reference to levels sufficiently close to but below 2% signals that we want to see projected inflation to significantly increase from the current realised and projected inflation figures which are well below the levels that we consider to be in line with our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our guidance would remain forward-looking but at the same time it contains elements that protect us against the risk of over-reacting to transitory shocks to inflation as well as against forecast and measurement errors, as we would emphasise that convergence should be robust, that's important, and also important is the reference to underlying inflation that will have to increase to ensure that the pick-up in inflation is backed by a sustained build-up of domestic price pressures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's the explanation of the first few elements of today's decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now I can also give you an explanation of why the restarting of the APP is appropriate but we can defer this to the next question perhaps.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And let me now move to the other point, your first question was about the chemistry of the meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all let me start from one thing about which there was unanimous consensus, unanimity, namely that fiscal policy should become the main instrument it's quite clear that in order to raise demand in an effective… you've seen the language of the Introductory Statement after many years I think of being more or less the same about fiscal policy that has changed and I think there was complete agreement about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if you see also if you compare what's happening now that jurisdictions where inflation rates are higher and you look at monetary policies that are broadly comparable in terms of easing capacity, you see that fiscal policy did play in these jurisdictions a much more active role than it played here and I'm talking now not only about this year, last year, I'm talking about the last six, seven years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Almost all the things that you see in Europe, the creation of more than 11 million jobs over a short period of time, the recovery, the sustained growth for several quarters were by and large produced by our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was very little else, of course there were structural reforms in some countries, in some countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So now it's high time I think for the fiscal policy to take charge.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, there was a broad agreement on the parts concerning forward guidance and the rate cut and the reinvestments and the TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you can see that that part was by and large agreed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then there was of course more diversity of views as it was vastly pre-announced by statements on all newspapers, wires, television and so on, there was more diversity of views on APP, but then in the end the consensus was so broad, there was no need to take a vote.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the decision was in the end assured by a very broad consensus, as I said there was no need to take a vote, there was such a clear majority there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I will say one word about where the main differences actually lay in the discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think there was again full agreement about the need to act, but the difference of views were about the severity of the outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words the majority of the Governing Council believed that the outlook was deteriorating as I said in a way greater than expected and the revision in the growth and inflation projections granted full action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point was about the need to act now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As usual you have always views that say let's wait and see and the Governing Council decided to act now this time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the third is about the appropriateness of the APP, by the way one reason to also act now concerns inflation expectations that we've seen not only the ones that are now at low levels but we see that inflation expectations are not de-anchoring but are re-anchoring at levels between zero and 1.5% which is not our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's why the Governing Council, in full consistency with its mandate, did decide to act now and the package is quite powerful both in the short run but also in the long run in designing action over the coming months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the appropriateness of these instruments because some think that the APP is appropriate only for risks of deflation, others thought that the level of interest rates is already so low that it doesn't need action on the APP, but the majority of the Governing Council believed that action was warranted and so that was the chemistry basically.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now the limits, there was no appetite frankly to discuss the limits for one good reason, because we have relevant headroom to go on for quite a long time at this rhythm without the need to raise the discussion about limits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the first question is concerned we really think this package is adequate to re-anchor inflation expectations and by the way again if I may repeat myself, if fiscal policy had been in place, or would be put in place, the side effects of our monetary policy would be much less, the action of our decisions today would be much faster and therefore the need to keep in place some of these measures would be less.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we believe this package to be adequate and your other question was about whether we discussed, no we didn't, we didn't discuss changing the marginal lending rate, no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: I'm sorry the answer is that I can't tell you the numbers, we never did it, we're not going to do it, just to let you know that there was no need to take a vote as I said because there was such a significant majority.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: OK there was no discussion about the type of assets meaning that by and large it's going to be the same we purchased in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now with helicopter money I've got to be very cautious because last time I was asked this it was about a year, year and a half ago, I said well it may be an interesting thing but we haven't discussed it and immediately everybody said: "oh they are talking about this," it has not been discussed, it is not an option that we considered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Thank you, now the first question I in a sense answered to the first question on the occasion of the first tweeter and the answer is very simple.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a mandate, we pursue price stability and we don't target exchange rates, period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On negative rates I think today, I have said several times negative rates have been actually a very positive experience in terms of stimulating growth, sustaining inflation but it's quite clear, and I did say this several times, that they have side effects and they have negative side effects and it's not so much that we want to protect bank profits, that's not, certainly not our mandate but it's that we want to protect the smooth transmission of the lending channel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We should never forget that the European economy is a bank-based economy, that lending goes through banks and we want to protect the transmission of monetary policy through the lending channels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's the, shall we say the philosophy behind the tiering measures, the mitigating measures that we have discussed and approved today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: I think we don't discuss, by the way when we have our discussions we discuss the presentation of the Chief Economist, the proposal of the Chief Economist and this proposal did not contain options, it was what I just read in the Introductory Statement and I commented about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, we made the case for fiscal policy to sustain demand and we make this case on and on, even more frequently in the coming future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We actually didn't discuss, if you read, we didn't discuss the stability pact and as a matter of fact we have a sentence here that says exactly that the transparent and consistent implementation of the European Union's fiscal and economic governance framework over time and across countries remains essential to bolster the resistance of the euro area economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, countries that have fiscal space then we say they should act in an effective and timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Governments with fiscal space should act in an effective and timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Exactly, in view of the weakening economic outlook and the continued prominence of downside risks in countries where public debt is high governments need to pursue prudent policies that will create the conditions for automatic stabilisers to operate freely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the stability and growth pact discussion is essentially a discussion between member states and the Commission and these are the statements that we can make today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yeah the other question is whether we can, this again it was a question that has been asked many times you can imagine over these years, and by the way you have two different camps here, the ones who say: "listen, given that you are still kind of far from say 1.9 whatever is our aim, why don't you cheerfully and happily accept 1% as an objective so you can claim victory."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's another camp that says: "if you raise your objective to 4% people will believe you and their expectations will go up."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to pre-judge, by the way all this will be the topic of the strategic review that the next President will carry out together with the Governing Council, the reasons why we, during my tenure, we always objected to changing the target, by the way the reasons are different whether you go up or you go down, but there's one common reason that when you change a target that you can't reach the action is not very credible, if you can't reach two why are you going to go to four, and on the other hand to change the other side would have other drawbacks and so for a variety of reasons we've always refrained from changing this, but this as I said is going to be one of the topics of the strategic review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: The answer to the first question is that we take our decisions really not with the idea of creating the kind of a ground for my successor but we've taken our decisions as I said at the beginning on the basis of objective elements that have to do with a weakening of the economic outlook, weakening that is more serious than expected, and with a revision in the inflation projections and with the persistence of uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these are the elements at the basis of our decisions today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now on the second question you know we stick with the G20 consensus, namely that we will never pursue competitive devaluation, so we expect that all the G20 members would underwrite the same consensus.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: I think that this concern is very well placed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we should be aware of the side effects of our policies, be they interest rates or asset purchases and we are monitoring, we are closely monitoring the side effects; the Vice President through his financial stability action is closely monitoring all these effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now to many of these side effects the answer is not to change monetary policy but rather implement specific macroprudential policies but as I said this has been a constant point of action, a constant point of concern.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Thank you, well when we approved … the first question is about TLTROs, when we approved the TLTROs basically if I remember correctly there were two criteria, the first was to ensure that our monetary policy would be transmitted through the bank lending channel and the second would be that these conditions would be dependent on the macroeconomic outlook which has worsened since we approved the TLTRO and therefore there has been an adjustment in the TLTRO's conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is about recession, we still think the probability of a recession for the euro area is small but it's gone up, but still we believe it's still a small probability, while with respect to Germany as such, well we've seen today two business cycle institutes saying that it's either a recession already or they foresee a clear recession or it's about to get into a recession, I'm not … and so that's the case, but that's the case for timely and effective action on the fiscal policy side.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way let me say something I've said many times, it's in a sense easy to make recommendations to governments to do this and to do that, so in doing so and you know this, I've said this many times, we've got to be extremely humble.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's something that we should say because the instruments ought to be activated, as I said everybody was unanimous about that today, but we should also be aware that there are objective and specific difficulties about doing this in different countries by the way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Thank you, the answer to the last point is no, we haven't seen that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we still are very concerned about the pension and the related services industry and certainly this is one of the side effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, it's quite clear that to the extent that negative rates prompt or speed up the recovery they will also benefit pension funds and insurance companies, so the main point here is really negative rates are necessary instruments of monetary policy and this is what the Governing Council has stated now for quite a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has created a lot of positive effects, how do we speed up these effects so that interest rates can go up again?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the answer is once again fiscal policy at this point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way as a matter of fact I understand the Dutch Government has a 50 billion investment programme and that's a good time to activate it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Thank you, the answer to the second question is actually it was not discussed, so we really start with that definition and with the aim as it has been expressed and the symmetry means that we react to inflation rates that are below our aim with the same strength we would react to inflation rates which are above our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It seems obvious but evidently it needed to be re-stated and so now concerning the Asset Purchase Programme let me just say a few things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all it has a larger impact on longer-term rates and provides further support to the funding costs that matter for business and households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also with this formulation the horizon of net purchases dynamically adjusts to changes in our interest rate forward guidance and therefore works in the background to keep a lid on medium to longer-term interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By adding to the stock of assets and re-investing for longer we can postpone an undue tightening in term premia which mechanically occurs as the APP's portfolio loses average duration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In addition, APP net purchases have strong signalling effects and wealth effects on the balance sheets of banks and other entities and the APP tends to have a more powerful effect on the formation of inflation expectations by demonstrating our commitment to use all instruments in pursuit of our aim.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember me saying this that all instruments were on the table, they were all ready to be used, well today we did it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: There was certainly discussion about the proportionality but it did not concern so much the negative rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words the consensus was I would say very, very, very broad on cutting the rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the proportionality discussion was mostly focussed on the restarting of the APP, where frankly the side effects are less visible, they may be there but they are less visible than cutting the rates for the reasons that we have discussed before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Oh well I think I expressed that before, we should not, I mean we should be very aware of these side effects, in fact one of the answers we have is with the tiering measures that we approved today, we're trying to protect the transmission of our monetary policy through the bank lending channel from some side effects that the negative rates might have, that's one example.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course there are many other side effects we should be aware of that go beyond banks as it was asked to me a moment ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First the first question, we certainly are aware of the side effects, the negative side effects on the people especially in those parts of the eurozone where the negative rates are being passed to corporate, so far as far as I understand its [only] corporate depositors, but it's an increasing percentage of them, so we are concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And part of the reasoning about this is again which has to do with the transmission of monetary policy, part of the reasons why we approved the tiering measures today, the mitigating measures is also to try to soften, to reduce this transfer of cost to the borrowers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we should be ultimately confident that with the recovery and the re-starting of the anchoring of the inflation to our aim, the interest rates will go up at that point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: People should be explained that negative interest rates are a necessity and that's very important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think the trust in the ECB ultimately will be based on whether it has delivered on its mandate of price stability or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has delivered on a variety of fronts, as I said before, more than 11 million jobs being created in a few years and I'm pretty sure, and the German citizens certainly benefited from the ECB's monetary policy for a long time and quite significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now the second point is about the comments made that negative rates, negative rates are clearly … I mean it's something the banks would like to have positive rates, unquestionably, so whenever they have negative rates they don't like it, but I wouldn't go as far as saying that negative rates would cause the collapse of the financial system because before getting there one has to look at other things of our banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example the cost income ratio, many of our banks have cost income ratios which are completely way off any average indicator, both in Europe and even more so in the world, if compared with other banks in the other parts of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are certain structural weaknesses in the banking sector, more pronounced in certain parts of the eurozone than in others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think these sort of considerations affect much more than negative rates, banks' profitability, banks' capacity to lend.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The necessity to adjust the business model to the digitalisation, to the changes in technology is something much more compelling than being angry about negative rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Well I must confess we haven't discussed this side of the usefulness of our package for one good reason, they are packages not meant to finance Government deficits, our package would be in full respect of the Treaty which forbids monetary financing, so our objective is price stability and we want to deliver on our mandate, so whether which country would benefit, which country would be more comfortable with the present package was not an issue of discussion today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Thanks, the first question is definitely yes and the second question you know all these innovations in monetary policy need to be looked at and studied and thought over.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These are big, big changes in the way monetary policy works and we have not discussed this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They may be part of this strategic review in the future but at this present point the Governing Council never discussed, well you've seen how cautious we've been in not … and by the way in the end we decided not to change the inflation target for many years and so now these are momentous changes in the way not only monetary policy but the whole economy is supposed to work.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also let's keep in mind all the times that giving money to people in whatever form, it's a fiscal policy task, it's not a monetary policy task.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Well, the IMF didn't say that the negative rates are ineffective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, the overall assessment of negative rates is generally positive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For us, it's very positive; it's been a very positive experience.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Negative rates have stimulated the economy and affected positively employment, and so all in all we're exactly in the direction we wanted them to be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the IMF also raised concerns about potential side effects of very negative rates for a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The discussion really didn't go into too much detail, but we are also aware of that and we are monitoring these risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I should say that first of all we should distinguish different categories: banks, insurance companies, pension funds and other intermediaries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, the improvements in the economy have more than offset negative side effects from low rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fact that we are monitoring this constantly is shown by our decision in early September of introducing a tiering system, which basically partly compensates the banks from the negative rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have discussions, everybody has discussions, all jurisdictions have disagreements when monetary policy decisions come to be discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These disagreements are often made public, often they are not, so I think it's not been the first time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've taken this as part and parcel of the ongoing debate and discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Since you're going back to the issue of voting and committees, let me just give you a few highlights.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, I will read sentences from the public account; the account you've seen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First, all members agreed that the further easing of monetary policy stance was warranted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we had an open discussion about the choice of instruments best suited to address current challenges.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we start going bit by bit, saying what sort of majority was for each part of the discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We say a clear majority of Governing Council members supported the broad package of measures that was ultimately decided upon in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A large majority of members agreed to change the modalities of the new series of TLTROs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Members generally agreed with the proposal to enhance the state-based component of the Governing Council forward guidance on interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A clear majority of members agreed with the proposal to restart net purchases under the asset purchase programme, with the modalities that I've just explained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A very large majority of members agreed with the proposal to lower the rate on the deposit facility by ten basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, a majority of members went along with the proposed introduction of the two-tier system for reserve remuneration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This comes straight from the public account that you've seen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No surprise that today, basically, the proposal of the chief economist - namely, to maintain the monetary policy stance - went, basically, through and was approved with unanimity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, coming to your point about the committees, let me again go back to the Introductory Statement in July, where we tasked the committees with examining options, including ways to reinforce our forward guidance on policy rates, mitigating measures such as the design of a tiered system for reserve remuneration, and options for the size and composition of potential new asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then, we have already gone through this on other occasions, but the function of the committees is to provide technical advice to the Governing Council and that's what they did.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then the Governing Council of course decides as it deems appropriate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not the first time that the Governing Council has a different mind; it's happened many other times, so no surprises there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's all in a sense confirmed by maintaining the monetary policy stance today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the main risk from all viewpoints, but especially also from a financial stability viewpoint, is a downturn in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether it's global or it's the eurozone, that I think would be the main risk from all viewpoints: from the side of convergence of inflation to our objective obviously, from the angle of maintaining a high level of employment and of economic activity and of nominal wage growth as we have seen today, and from the angle of financial stability itself.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because clearly one of the great benefits that the banking sector - actually all players in the financial system - had from this accommodative monetary policy was the extraordinary improvement in the quality of their credit, of their assets more generally, which comes with a recovery, which basically affected positively the profitability of the banking system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: No, Christine Lagarde didn't take part in the discussions, but she was there without taking part in the discussions or the deliberations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Basically, let's ask ourselves: what was the main goal of the September monetary policy decisions?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was to cement the accommodative monetary policy stance that was embedded in the expectations as they had been affected by the regularly, continuously weakening medium-term outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the Governing Council today, the discussion felt that this has been very largely achieved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, we saw the flattening of the yield curve, we saw the now complete transmission of a lower deposit facility rate into lower short-term rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have observed there is partly due to the fact that there may be a part of these expectations which was not warranted by the weakening economic outlook, which went in a sense beyond the economic developments which might have been disappointing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second and probably more important reason for the developments we've seen is the overall uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In one way, one has the sense that somehow the lower likelihood of a hard Brexit over a cliff edge has improved the overall situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by the way, on this specific point, it's true that it's improved in the short term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The likelihood of having a cliff edge has gone down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, the medium-term uncertainty is considered with concern, and the rest of the geopolitical uncertainty has continued to affect markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually, I don't think the market misread; actually, the market showed that they understood perfectly well our reaction function.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Now, on your first question let me say this: unfortunately everything that's happened in September since our monetary policy decisions has shown abundantly that the Governing Council's determination to act in a substantive manner was justified.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had all kinds of survey indicators and now also some - few, but some - data showing further weakening of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just one number that I remember is the PMI in manufacturing is now at the lowest level since 2012.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Another point of observation that I would say not only we - but everybody - use to assess the resilience of the economy, is to look at what extent the weakness in the manufacturing sector is actually spreading to the services sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Until a month-and-a-half, two months ago, we could say the service sector was fully resilient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we're seeing the PMI in services also declining sharply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we have many other indices pointing in that direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, regardless of the developments in the German economy, I think that the decisions taken in September fully justify the continuation of an accommodative monetary policy stance and the maintaining of favourable financing conditions for the non-financial corporations, companies, and the small and medium-sized enterprises.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now the second point, it's quite clear that central banks ought to continue to cooperate, no matter what happens in other parts of our institutional system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Cooperation of central banks within their mandate is essential and a forum like G20 or other multilateral fora are more important, more essential than ever.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, first of all let me just refer to Peter Praet's words.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is true that during 2017 we gradually changed our monetary policy stance and we were preparing to exit that stance of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But then conditions changed and what prevails over everything else is the determination to pursue the mandate for which this institution was created and for which we work.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore we had to change course and get back into the present stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also add one thing: that if there is one take from the recent IMF meetings, it's that the paradigm of reference has changed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Until not long ago, the IMF and all the observers would say that, yes, interest rates are low and they may stay low for some time, but then they will go up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the sense of many discussions at the IMF is actually that they will stay low for a long time because the real rate of interest has also declined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This implies that the exit from unconventional monetary policies has shifted forward in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I feel like someone who tried to comply with his mandate in the best possible way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Well, I'm sorry I can't answer either question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Saying that, I always focus on things that can be done, not things that you can't change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can't change the past unless you're a historian, so I focus on what's being done and assessed by facts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the second question I'll answer immediately: no advice is needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, she has a long period of time ahead during which she will have to form her own view, together with the Governing Council, about what to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'll stop here, really, because this question is going to pop up again and again; how do you judge the past?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If nobody is asking this question, I'll come back to you later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: First, let me respond to the first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, that was raised because it's open-ended and so naturally people ask: when are you going to bump into these limits and then what happens?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's going to take quite a bit of time before this issue will realistically present itself as a problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But all estimates, by the way, have to assume something about the issuance of bonds and clearly, there you make certain assumptions about what fiscal policy is going to be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Under reasonable assumptions, not extreme either way, there is enough time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Frankly, what I think I said in the last press conference; I don't see this problem coming up again any time soon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Different calculations may reflect different assumptions about issuance, so that's one part of the answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other part of the answer is that clearly, these limits - and I've said this again many times - these limits first of all are self-imposed and, second, are specific to the contingency in which they were originally stated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the ECJ has granted ample discretionary power to the ECB within its mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have capital key rules in the way we purchase bonds and the relevant key is the stock of capital.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even though we may observe deviations in terms of flows, it's the stock that we have to look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There, frankly, we don't foresee substantial material deviations in the aggregate, in the months and years to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your second question, I'm afraid I can't answer; I would never dare to judge fiscal policies in one specific country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Well, I think about the first question I have the same answer; there isn't anything specific… Actually if there is one general thing I'm proud of, it's the way in which the Governing Council and myself have constantly pursued our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is something we collectively should be very, very proud.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we can talk about legacy and all this later, but in a sense this is part of our legacy: never give up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I should say, I can't really answer this question because there was someone of great authority who said immediately that this was dubious biology.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would not really develop this concept any further.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Now, there was no reaction on my side, so there was no reaction at all, and today as I said before, the discussion was basically supportive of the chief economist's, of Philip Lane's proposal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a matter of fact, some of the dissenters, one of the dissenters called for unity and the full implementation of the policy package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One thing you can get out of this meeting, besides the various substantive issues being discussed, was a sense of a general call to unity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the next question, as you know generally speaking, I don't have any set idea about that, but if you want more information, just ask my wife.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Well, on the gift I received way back in 2012 in March, I think there is an old German saying that says: "Geschenkt ist geschenkt", so I plan to keep it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other issue, I think ultimately it's the reality that speaks more strongly than any other voice.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the reality together with the conviction that we did what we did always in pursuing our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Very often, criticism addresses issues that really are not pertinent with our mandate, and we stayed firmly on this course, on pursuing our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Sorry, the first question is about the political pressure?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: No, that's why I don't remember the question; because I have no answer to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, I have no advice for Christine; as I said, she knows better than anybody else what to do and what to say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the second point, is there political pressure on central banks?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can actually see more political pressure in the last year than in many years before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I had occasional exchanges with this or that finance minister, but it never became anything comparable that you see in other countries today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, especially at this time, in this instance, this question is quite important because I said last time, I repeat it today: monetary policy will continue to do its job; so don't think that monetary policy just relaxes and stops working.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's quite clear that with fiscal policy, the objectives of monetary policy will be reached sooner and with fewer side effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reason lies mostly in what I said before: with the real rate, the natural rate of interest declining, that's where the space for fiscal policy comes in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if one was to see higher rates sooner, fiscal policy should be active; although probably monetary policy will continue to be accommodative even if fiscal policy will become more expansionary in the early stages of this expansion at least.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Given that's the situation, that's probably going to stay like this for some time in the future, what is the relationship?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In some of the speeches I gave, I said that central banks are independent but they are independent in an interdependent world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to the extent that their inactive fiscal policy doesn't prejudge the objective of price stability, there is no contradiction, there is no threat to the monetary dominance of the central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Well, the answer to the second question was part of the design when the PSPP was introduced years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that time, it was deemed that to follow the other channel, the reverse auction system, would not be proper, would not be suitable in the situation present in Europe, in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, there isn't any special policy reason, but it was very much a matter of technical convenience.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first question, I don't want to make anticipations on whether fiscal policies will react sooner, also because the issue is far from being simple.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know, we say in the introductory statement that the countries with fiscal space should act and countries without fiscal space should create the conditions for their automatic stabilisers to operate freely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Would there be stimulus which spills over outside the countries that actually undertake fiscal policy if they do so?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: How much of this would go into the countries that need it?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is very much intertwined with the progress that the EMU - the Economic and Monetary Union - will make on designing a central fiscal capacity with genuine capacity to stabilise the economy over the cycle, which doesn't exist yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's far from being a discussion like you might have in one country or jurisdiction, where the issue is whether to expand the deficit today or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, the previous question I had about the debt brake makes sense.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In this part of the world, to have an active fiscal policy of the size that might be required… By the way, the present fiscal stances might be expansionary, but if a broader fiscal action were to be required, it's the governance issues which are the most important ones.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's one of the most important things; that one should attempt to be not boring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, the other question is really very deep and not easy to answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly this experience has been very intense, profound and fascinating; I take this with me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then how much of this will get into personal reflections is too early to say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said this many times and for much part of what I'm going to do next, as I said before just ask my wife.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, Isabel is an excellent economist and she will do very well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: She has all the capacities to do very very well: enhance the discussions, outside, inside the ECB, actively participate in the work of the ECB, so we would welcome her appointment very warmly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: I'm sorry, you asked whether the expansionary monetary policies of central banks is the second-largest risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can answer for the eurozone; in the eurozone, and it's a question we ask ourselves every day, many times a day, and I'm saying this because we monitor the market developments very closely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see some segments of financial markets where valuations are overstretched.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One case is real estate, for example, and especially prime commercial real estate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the causes of these overstretched valuations often don't lead directly to our monetary policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For prime commercial real estate, it's the action of international investors who are investing heavily in that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For real estate, certainly the low interest rates are important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: However when we go and look at how the mortgage market is behaving, in other words if there has been a spike in mortgage lending, we don't see that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see some increase in mortgage lending in the new mortgages, but overall if you take the aggregate figures, still they really show a solid expansion but nothing… We may have other segments to watch, but frankly, all in all we don't see bubbles.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we see some bubbles, they are local bubbles that should be, for example, some segments of the bond market, the high yield leveraged bond market - which by the way is not a big issue in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's more of a big issue in another jurisdiction, but we have to make sure that our banks don't invest into this market, as they used to do before the financial crisis, when they bought lots of stuff that then didn't perform well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For that, the remedies, the answers for many of these potential local bubbles are macro-prudential policies, supervisory policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly the other important issue is that much of this danger, much of this risk, much of this search for yields happens in the non-banking sector and more specifically in the so-called shadow banking sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Unfortunately there, the perimeter of macro-prudential policies does not include that sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have some visibility, pretty good visibility, into what happens in the banking sector, which by the way still is about 80% of credit intermediation in this part of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we don't have much visibility for the rest of the financial sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm talking for the non-banks, so for the shadow banking sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: I will say something about that in a moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Well, on the first question, it is clearly a success, and it's a success of first and foremost Greece, of the policies that the Greek governments have undertaken together with the solidarity and under the advice of the IMF, the ESM and, to a limited extent, the ECB as far as the banking and financial sector is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the main effort is being done by the governments and by the Greek citizens that certainly had to pay a very high price - a terrible price as a matter of fact, especially in the early stages - of a debt deficit financed bubble.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also in a sense a risk if these policies are not continued, but we see all the developments there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a good time for Greece now and frankly, if you compare with three, four years ago it's a good time for Europe, for the eurozone countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We often tend to be rightly anxious about our objectives when we consider them now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In fact some historical perspective, especially when we judge countries and governments, is very important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You had a second question about what to fix in the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is one thing that all the successful monetary unions have, and that's a central fiscal capacity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, whether this should be a budget or should be a system of insurance… So it's very important to have something of that nature of an adequate size, something that can be used counter-cyclically, something that basically would take care of the fact that the national fiscal policies have, in my view, limited spill-overs on the rest of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So one needs to have a central fiscal capacity and of course this should be designed in a way that doesn't create moral hazard.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's one of the main reasons for the slow progress on that front: it is the risk that the mechanisms would be used for increasing moral hazard.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: Believe me, it's been important for me a lot, so even though I've been a central bank governor before - for six years I had the privilege of sitting in the Governing Council under the presidency of Mr Trichet - the quality of our deliberations owes so much to the quality of the work of the staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's important and I think in my view, that's the main ingredient of everything we've done and it's the main ingredient in the success of the ECB in its being a credible central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the main ingredient in the big changes that the ECB had in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we ought to be very, very grateful to our outstanding staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Things have changed completely and frankly, everybody now in Italy said and stated that the euro is irreversible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So while there may have been hypothetical doubts in one part of the governance of the country, there aren't any more, so it's been accepted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Also, you see, it's part of the normal eurozone developments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The popularity of the euro, you said - the first question - the criticisms are across the region.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, in a sense they are across a region, but the point is that at the same time, the popularity of the euro has never been so high.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what's happened in Italy is actually where the euro popularity had gone up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course I've tried to do as much as one can do in here, but I think that more can be done, should be done, and one should never be tired of doing it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We here, in a multi-country monetary union, have a difficult… Many things are better here than they are in other jurisdictions, in one-country monetary jurisdiction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there's one thing that's clearly more difficult; namely to reach to the public of 19 different countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, here national central banks are key for communication and they can do, and they do, much more in a sense than a single president or board member can do, because it's a constant communication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in this sense, it's very important what you said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is one other aspect I would just dwell a moment: the natural counterpart of central bankers are the ones who have to implement the monetary policy decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are naturally the banks and the financial markets and other financial intermediaries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, the independence of a central bank is also based on the support that it enjoys.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore, what happened in communication by central banks over the last ten, 15 years is a complete transformation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nowadays, nobody would pride himself or herself saying: if you have understood me, you are stupid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We all strive for transparency and as you see, as you just - thank you for having said that - for candour.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that has changed, but would we be naturally speaking to the large public?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One has to be cautious about that because as soon as you change your audience, you change your language and you naturally step into a different realm: the realm of politics.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So yes to an open, broader communication, certainly, but it should be done with caution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Draghi: So, I should thank you and the thanks are actually substantive; they are not formal only, because of what I just said about communication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Communication has become a tool of monetary policy, so your interaction has been essential in our monetary policy decisions all throughout these eight years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other thing, frankly, is that with your inquisitive questions, you have stimulated our striving towards greater transparency and greater candour.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again compare to the last 20 years - communication in central banks, and how it changed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it did change for a great part because of your role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think that by themselves, central bankers would have changed communication if left free to be opaque.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you very much and all the best to all of you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: Before the questions I'm going to take just a couple of minutes of your time to tell you a few things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is, each and every President has his or her own style of communicating.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know some of you are keen to compare and rate or rank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I've said before, don't over-interpret, don't second-guess, don't cross-reference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Point number 2, this introductory statement probably rings a few bells for those of you who follow those documents very carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But some of you will be disappointed that it does not include anything having to do with the strategic review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is intended to be that way, so the introductory statement does not include, does not refer and should not be associated with the strategic review that we are considering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll be happy to give you - I can do that now actually if you want - a little bit of my thinking and our collective thinking on the strategic review because I know that it is of interest to some of you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, there is nothing unusual or extraordinary about having a strategic review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I actually consider for myself that it's a little bit overdue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Legitimately so, because there were many other things to do but the last strategic review was in 2003.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's been 16 years since there has been a strategic review, so it's quite legitimate to have a strategic review at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, that strategic review needs to be comprehensive, needs to look at all and every issue, will turn each and every stone and will take its time but will not take too much time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By that I mean my plan is to actually get the review started in the course of January.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Don't ask me which week or which day or which second, but it will be in the course of January.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our goal is to complete it before the end of 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, about the strategic review, it will be reaching out to not just the usual suspects, but it will also include consulting with Members of Parliament and I've committed to that with the European Parliament.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will reach out to the academic community, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will reach out to civil society representatives and it will aim at not just preaching the gospel that we think we master, but also listening to the views of those to whom we reach out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is the point of every strategic review by all central banks that are conducting this exercise to actually look at their objective, how they define their medium-term objective in particular, how they give content to the price stability that is in their mandate, and it is the only objective that we have in our mandate ourselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that topic indeed will be core and centre to our strategic review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no preconceived landing zone at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Indeed it will also address the major changes that have taken place over the course of the last 16 years, and by that I include the massive technological change that our societies are facing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will include the immense challenge that climate change is addressing to each and every one of us, wherever located, and whatever our mission and duties.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will include aspects of inequality that are certainly rising in our economies, and all of those will be addressed with a view to exploring each and every corner of the business that we conduct as a central bank to see how those businesses are affected and how we can take them into account to better respond to the mission that we have, and to deliver on our mandate: serving the euro area citizens, and delivering on the mandate of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's on the strategic review, and if you have additional points that I can answer, I will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I will not go into much further details when it comes to the substance, because the framework has not yet been completely agreed and discussed with members of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have certainly made a point of my tenure to include members of the Governing Council and to seek their views and their consideration before any decision is made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me add I have huge respect for the work that you do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But you are not the only audience, and I would also encourage you not to try to draw too many conclusions or decisive findings from communication that I would address to a different audience with a slightly different language in order to be maybe better understood by those who do not have your level of skills and in-depth knowledge of the matters that we deal with.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I don't know, I will tell you that I don't know!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: One thing that the introductory statement does not specify, but you will find it I'm sure in the findings of the Eurosystem macroeconomic forecast, is that in our 2022 forecast for inflation, while the entire year is forecast at 1.6%, the fourth quarter is at 1.7%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Directionally, it is slightly increasing over the course of the 2022 forecast that we have for inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On TLTRO: my recollection of what was taken this morning was something like €97.3 billion, which is a little less than what was coming for maturity Do I regard that as half success, half failure?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would tell you two things; one is, I think we have seven auctions in the course of this TLTRO III - so I would not draw a conclusion from this one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would wait a little bit, particularly given the fact that this one is taking place at year end.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At year end, you close your book, there are many considerations that come into play, so I would not draw too many conclusions from this one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would have preferred it to be a little bit higher, closer to €120 billion than to €100 billion, but we'll look carefully at the next one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On the timing of the strategic review, there is never a good timing because you could argue equally that if and when you have delivered on the way in which you've defined your mandate, then why bother about a strategy?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My purpose is really, after 16 years of the same strategy, which is the rule today and that we will respect and will continue to respect until such time when our strategic review is completed, by the way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it is timely, coming to this job new.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's just the most appropriate moment to rally support of members around the table to re-examine the effectiveness, appropriateness of each and every single instrument that we've used in the past to take assessment of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then to redefine for ourselves what exactly will be this medium-term objective that will deliver on the mandate that we have, which is not changing by the way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You said that we change our mandate -- no, the mandate is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The way in which we deliver on the mandate is the one that will be under the strategic review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Side effects: well, first of all we are very aware of the side effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's been a constant in the policy of the Eurosystem to actually measure, monitor the side effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is part and parcel of the work that is done, and we will certainly continue doing that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, what we have done was always intended to deliver on the mandate as defined under the current strategy, to create the conditions for growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On that point I think that the use of interest rates in particular has been quite efficient in order to lower the financing costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That clearly seems to have worked and seems to work properly when I look at the increase in the volume of financing both for the non-financial corporates and for the households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I look at the decrease in the cost itself, I think that this is a policy that works.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the side effects are a preoccupation, there is no question about that, and we would not be doing our job if we were not monitoring and being extremely attentive to that balance of cost benefit of such measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On the first point, the reversal rate: my understanding of the reversal rate is that you are facing a reversal rate when credit begins contracting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's how in economic theory the reversal rate is defined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Given the progression rate that we are seeing at 3.8%, the most recent one, in the non-financial corporate sector, 3.5% and growing in the household sector that certainly does not meet the definition of credit contraction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Are we attentive to that credit expansion and those credit numbers?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we are, because it's clearly one of the clear objectives that we have to facilitate the financing of growth, to facilitate the investment, facilitate the creation of employment and so on, and so forth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not seeing it and of course we are looking very carefully at the indicators of credit growth in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, it is weak growth and it's not at potential.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The 1.4% for 2022, we're getting close to the growth potential of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It would be very welcome to have other policies join the monetary policy in order to support the reduction of slack and to arrive at that growth potential and why not exceed it?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that would be very welcome, both in fiscal terms and in structural reform terms as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Japanification, I don't think that we are there at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that, certainly from the enterprise credit, there is a major difference between the situation that Japanese enterprises are, or Japanese households are, relative to the situation of the euro area equivalent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think that Japanification is in the cards at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: All right, on the toolbox, I'm not going to revisit the past, number 1.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Policy decisions that were made, stand, and were re-endorsed yet again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My view of it is that they form a package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were several components to that package and I think that the intention was for some of the measures, such as the interest rate, to actually have an impact on the short-term end of the yield curve, the forward guidance that was also part of the package that gives a clear calendar and induces an automatic adjustment, depending on the state of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It also gives and is intended to have an impact on the medium-term end of the curve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The asset purchase programme that was re-initiated is intended to have an impact on the long end of the yield curve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Based on what we are seeing, all three seem to have had the impact and certainly it has been perceived as such.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not going to dissect between each and every item of the package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The two-tier system was clearly an additional attribute in order to deal with some of the negative effects that you've referred to, and is also part and parcel of the package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't take a view on one element or the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other point that you made, to me it is critically important that a central bank be independent and that in all its operations, behaviours, its independence be respected and be valued.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what you describe to me is a policy mix of first order, except that I would put a) monetary, because this is our shop b) fiscal because that's the next possible tool that can be used and c) structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it takes many to actually dance the economic ballet that would deliver on price stability but also employment and growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't see anything wrong with policymakers actually agreeing that they're going to make the efforts that they can in order to reach their respective goals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: I see exactly where you're trying to get me!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But once and for all, I'm neither dove nor hawk and my ambition is to be this owl that is often associated with a little bit of wisdom.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not full of vanity but I will certainly try to bring the best out of the members of my Governing Council in order to arrive at monetary policy decisions and use of instruments that will be as consensual as possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not suggesting that we will arrive at complete agreement on everything, and I'm sure that the strategic review, particularly in our definition of the medium-term objectives and how we go about it, will be a source of great debate amongst ourselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'm also of the view that once something has been debated at length and in depth and in honesty and with good faith, then some decisions eventually stand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is also something that we will be assessing as part of the strategic review because I think that we need to look in retrospect and assess what has been most helpful, what has worked best, what combination of them has worked best.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think that I would reduce it as you have to interest rates or unconventional measures, because I think within those unconventional measures, you have a variety of things that allow to target better, to also give a better indication of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think in that respect forward guidance is also a very interesting set of components that anchors into time, that gives a sequence, that gives enough clarification to something that by nature is going to be a little bit ambiguous nonetheless.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it introduces this element of mechanicalness or automaticity in how things are re-stated in the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On your technical discussion of the measure of inflation depending on whether you measure HICP inflation as it is, with or without food and oil prices, or whether we use market-based instruments or survey-based instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we need to look at all of them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I very strongly believe in the trends and in the direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that we are all concerned, and I'm concerned as well, with the 0.1 more or less in that direction, but directionally I think that we are seeing some consistent move.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As part of the strategic review, I also think that we will have to look into that because inflation perceptions can differ as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of the national central banks in the Eurosystem are actually paying close attention to that and are trying to measure those components as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The whole debate of whether or not we take housing into the measurements and what portion of housing and how do we dissect between the asset value of the land and the actual use of the premises.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those are tricky technical questions that we will have to look at, and on which we should also take a view because there is - you're right - quite a difference between the various perceptions, anticipation, expected inflation depending on how we measure it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So outside this point in time, we take all of it into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I personally and I don't know if Philip [Lane] would agree with that or if Luis, you would agree with me, but we look at directionally whether we are consistent between the various measurement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think increasingly we will have to look at how it is disaggregated as well as part of our deliberations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the outlook, as I said, relatively weak growth, let's face it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I think gives us some hope, and you alluded to that, is the fact that those downside risks that we had on the horizon are less pronounced and we are not going to bet on how phase 1 of the trade discussions between the United States and China are heading, and when they will be completed, and what it will deliver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But certainly if we compare with a few months back, it's heading in a better direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will know by the end of today what is the outcome of Brexit - sorry, not of Brexit; I shouldn't say that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is the outcome of the UK election, which will have a bearing on what happens to Brexit and the transition period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's also an element of uncertainty that is probably loosening and that will give us a bit more clarity as to the environment in which we operate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: For the instruments, I think it is completely legitimate to take stock and to assess the effectiveness and the efficiency of the various instruments one by one, taken together and what leverage they have exercised and what result they have delivered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As to the future, I think it's going to be for the Governing Council to actually define how as part of the framework we will be considering those.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I see very much the strategy as a house that we build stone by stone, one after the other, and I think that's one element that will have to be decided by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the digital currency, first of all I would like to pay tribute to somebody who is leaving at the end of the year, who has been instrumental at the ECB and way beyond, to help us understand a bit better and with more clarity the difference between the bitcoins of this world, the stablecoins and the digital currency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By that I mean Benoît Cœuré, who has been a member of the Governing Council, a member of the Executive Board of the ECB, and who is finishing at the end of this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: He produced a paper which was commissioned, if I recall, by the G7.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But he also very ably participated in a paper that was prepared by the ECB, that was distributed by Vice President de Guindos at the last ECOFIN, if I recall, which has the benefit in three pages - I think that's a huge challenge - to draw the line between what we are talking about; between the bitcoins, the stablecoins and the digital currency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the latter point, the digital currency, we have set up a taskforce and we will accelerate the effort of this taskforce, drawing on the resources of the entire Eurosystem; meaning the national central banks that already participate in that research, that have already committed to the project in terms of experimentation, pilots here and there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So harnessing on all those experiments that have taken place and all the research that has already been put into this effort, together with the work that has been done here also, we will… I think we're trying to do that by mid-2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will identify the purpose that we have with that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Are we trying to have inclusive finance at all costs - at no cost?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's a whole range of objectives that can be pursued, so I think we will start by doing that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we will identify the technicalities of it all, which is not a given, particularly when you talk about the Eurosystem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that there is also great interest outside our regional area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know for instance that Canada, the UK, certainly other countries are also looking very deeply into that, to see if it makes sense, what purpose it serves and how we can best deliver on it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My personal conviction is that given the developments we are seeing, not so much in the bitcoin segment but in the stablecoins projects, and we only know of one at the moment, but there are others being explored and underway at the moment, we'd better be ahead of the curve if that happens because there is clearly a demand out there that we have to respond to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would like to add a footnote to that: I think the benefit of the paper is that it also draws a line between this sort of glamorous central bank digital currency, much talked about and worth exploring, and the digital payment systems that we have and that exist.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have several items that are completely digitalised that are not at the front end and that the banks' clients do not perceive as being in operation, but where settlement and clearing are actually taking place instantly thanks to the digital payment system that has been put in place; notably within the Eurosystem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So on those digital systems that exist, some of which need a better take-up by some of the members of the system, I will continue to push because I think we have something which is really worth developing and encouraging.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm talking here about TIPS and PEPS and all those acronyms that I should not be using, but I don't know what they stand for.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All I know is that they deliver in digital terms the operations of clearing and settling, sometimes in one single operation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On your first point, and concerning the use of our various instruments in order to deliver on our mandate, we have one objective and that's price stability as defined under the strategy as it stands today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the goal, that's the aim and that's what we are pursuing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't venture too much into this theory of the output gap, how much slack there is, how much slack there is not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Informed by good discussions that I've had with colleagues on the other side of the Atlantic, including at the Fed, they had… They now say actually that they had strongly underestimated the slack of the employment market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My hunch is that we do, but I would not guesstimate on that particular front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we tend to get it more often wrong than right.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's not passing out judgement on the forecasting ability of the ECB, because I think that we do actually have more trust in our forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On Greece: well, first of all I would like to compliment Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Greece has been the long story for me in other capacities and I'm really delighted to see the progress and to see the recovery and to see the results.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's very impressive both on growth and on the primary surplus.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have my views on that, don't need to repeat them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The various public purchase programmes of the ECB are subject to eligibility criteria and they're also for the benefit of the entire Eurosystem and all people in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
