text: So my guess is that as soon as Greece reaches those eligibility criteria, it will become eligible instantly to those programmes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Until such time we have to respect the eligibility criteria and we have to play by the rules.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: Well, thank you very much for asking about the Green Deal that was presented yesterday by the President of the European Commission, my friend Ursula von der Leyen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am very pleased to see the ambition of what she has announced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I very much hope that this ambition can actually be endorsed by all European institutions in their respective territory, with their respective mandate, and in compliance with the treaties.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What it means is that in our strategic review, we will take up climate change, we will take up the fight that is taken up by the European Commission and I hope other European institutions, and see where and how we can participate in that particular endeavour.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'm only sorry about one thing: I was hoping yesterday morning that the taxonomy was a done deal and unfortunately, theCoreperas I understand has not found an agreement yet on taxonomy, which would be extremely helpful for us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not commenting on any particular country; you will appreciate that, but when we say that we want to deliver on our mandate, we also know that monetary policy is going to be supported and boosted by other policies amongst which the structural reforms that will improve productivity, that will improve growth, creation of employment, certainty of the economic players.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in that respect, clearly reforms are a necessary component of addressing the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On the European Stability Mechanism, and I am saying it on purpose rather than ESM, because I think each and every word actually matters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's about stability, it's a mechanism that would be in place if completed and if embedded in the treaty, and it's European.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's nothing that is intended to disrupt, to damage or to hurt any particular member of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we had had the ESM in full place, including the collective action clause and the debt restructuring mechanism, if we had had that in place at the very early days in the Greek crisis, I think collectively we would've been much more capable of resolving the issue in a more expedited manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The debt restructuring process that it took as far as Greece was concerned was difficult, took much longer than I think it would have with the ESM.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can't rewrite history and it's a counterfactual that I am using here, but clearly having rules established, having CACs - the collective action clause - that are intended to avoid the behaviour of some very toxic creditors, as I have seen them acting in other countries, I think it's beneficial to any country that finds itself in a difficult position, and to assume that it's intended to target a particular country I think is completely misguided.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the banking union, I was really encouraged to see the paper produced by a colleague, Olaf Scholz, and clearly there are areas that are in debate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The weighing of sovereign bonds is clearly one; it's one where Italy is showing some openness, as I understand, and I think it's great progress.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whatever progress will happen in that area will actually be good, because banking union is one of the necessary attributes together with capital markets union, in order to make sure that we have a monetary union that works and that where the different elements actually support each other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My answer is very quick; no, we have not discussed it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you very much and I'll see you next year, so happy holidays, Merry Christmas and whatever you celebrate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I hope you are happy and making other people around you happy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Okay, on the trade front, I think you're quite right in signalling that trade is actually an important element in our considerations and particularly in assessing the downside risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think one critical development since our last meeting in late December has been the conclusion of phase one of the negotiations between US and China.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That in and of itself has a variety of consequences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It certainly has slightly reduced, if not vanished, but it also has consequences in terms of international trade at large, and indirect consequences for those regions or countries around the world from which trade will be diverted in order to deliver on that phase one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is something that our teams are looking at very carefully to assess exactly what will be the impact on the net basis for the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of the trade relationship between the US and the EU, I took some comfort from the meeting that was concluded a couple of days ago between the President of the European Union Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, with the President of the United States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While we all know that the results of those meetings are preliminary, the tone and the determination on both sides to draw positive conclusions from that meeting and to indicate determination to pursue the negotiations and the approach to the trade relationships between the EU and the US, I think, is to be taken as a positive signal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that the President of the Commission will be visiting the United States in February.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would expect continued work to be ongoing between the parties by then, and hopefully some positive developments out of that February visit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, we're going to monitor that very carefully and see what the signals are with due consideration for the limitation of signals relative to what the outcome of final negotiations can be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In relation to the setting of rates, particularly by Sweden, I think I'll leave it to the Swedish central bank and to Stefan Ingves to actually indicate on what ground, for what reason there was a determination to actually return, for the moment at least, to a zero interest rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My understanding of this conclusion is that there had been a positive outcome of that period of negative interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And drawing from that, given the economic circumstances and the inflation expectations, it was legitimate and their decision to actually return to the zero rate, where they are at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Every region and every country has its idiosyncrasies and rationale.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think comparisons in that respect are odious, as we all know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, everybody is going to look at what conclusions are drawn from that monetary policy reversal, if you will, in Sweden but I wouldn't draw any conclusion as far as our policies are concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said very clearly I think in the introductory statement, the Governing Council is going to be very attentive to any and all developments in all directions, both in terms of growth but obviously in terms of inflation, which is our measurement of price stability, and will take whatever measures are necessary, as appropriate, in order to respond to our imperative to deliver on our mandate of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was a bit of a long-winded one but you had three questions in one, so it had to be long.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On the inflation target, we have a policy by which we operate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a strategy that was defined and that has inspired the policy decisions that were made and that have been made up until this day.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That will continue to inspire the policy decisions that are made until a strategy has been adopted - which is a while from now but I'm sure you'll have questions about the strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In that respect, I would just adhere to what that strategy was, what its developments were over the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the point of symmetry is very clearly referred to in the introductory statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One press conference after the other, so I would refer you to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You very gently nudged me into having a view as to whether there should be a band, as to whether there should be this, that or the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that some commentators would love me to disclose my principles, my views and my philosophy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it would be largely unfair to the strategy review exercise that we are embarking upon as of today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My mission as President of the Governing Council is to harness all the views around and to make sure that we come to as close as possible a view that is shared by all, in order to have as consistent and as effective a monetary policy in order to deliver on our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said last time around, we are going to look at many issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A lot of hard work is going to be put into the exercise, but I would not exclude, preclude or anticipate how we are going to deliver, because that's the point of our strategy review exercise; it's how we deliver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you asked me about the risk tilted to the downside, and how much tilted to the downside but less so than last time around.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think one of the key considerations we had on our mind was indeed the change in the level of uncertainties about trade and trade relationships, and the expectations we have that those uncertainties will be dealt with, hopefully in the future with the same type of approach… negotiations rather than adversarial positioning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Was there a discussion as to whether it was closer to balance than it was tilted to the downside, but less skewed than it was?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, we always have those discussions and that's, I think, completely justified because of the very mixed picture that we have of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you focus on certain signals, or if you focus on certain indicators or certain surveys, then you could have less downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you focus on others, you could be a little bit more downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we tried to arrive at exactly what we thought collectively, unanimously actually, was the right level; which was still to the downside but less pronounced than it was at our last press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: You know, I wish I was a financial adviser but in my position, I am not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that Germany has plenty of terrific financial advisers, excellent bankers and they will not be short of good advice to their customers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would simply say that the role of the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem at large - which includes all national central banks - is to deliver on price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of the avenues for delivery of that price stability is to make sure that there is growth of our economies and that that growth is sustainable and solid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The study and the work that has been done internally at the ECB demonstrates that because of the monetary policy, including very low rates and possibly negative rates, because of that monetary policy, millions of jobs were created throughout the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Growth was higher because of that so that's a very, very strong argument to explain why monetary policy had to be what it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you have noted, in my introductory statement - and I don't differ from my predecessor on that front - I think having amplifiers of our monetary policy by having the right fiscal policy, be it by way of additional spending or reduced taxation, for those countries that have the space to do that would certainly help in that regard.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: Well, first of all, I regard our Governing Council, our deliberations, our scrutiny of the economy and our determination to deliver on price stability as our mission and my mission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, there are very interesting phenomena going on in the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But when something as important as our Governing Council meeting is scheduled, I don't see any reason why we would change it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will see whether next year or the year after and so on and so forth, whether we need to reorganise a timetable, but at this point in time, frankly I think it would've been unwarranted, to say the least, to change anything.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Point number two, on the scope of the strategy: we are going to review a whole host of issues so yes, it will have to do about how we deliver, how we measure, what tools we have, and how we communicate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will really encompass the entire communication approach when it comes to decision-making, to publication, to the use of language that we have, to the outreach, to the engagement with all stakeholders.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All of that is going to be part and parcel of the strategy, so it's a broad exercise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it touches on your first point: my commitment was really to be able to listen to the expectations of the people, to better understand their economic concerns and their imperatives, and how we can deliver on them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue to benefit from the work of the researchers, of the top-notch economists, of the academics and, yes, their views will be harnessed at various events that will take place in the course of 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is also going to be our task and our goal to listen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That resonates with those of you who know how the Fed has organised its "Fed Listens".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be different because 19 member states do not all speak the same language.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we want to reach out to people, we are going to have to use people's language, literally.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will involve all the national central banks, which will be also active participants in the process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what I mean by including, reaching out and addressing the concerns.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that I have addressed that point earlier on by indicating that we have to use all the instruments that are available and that are proven to be effective - we will measure effectiveness, by the way - in order to deliver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: You know, I have a very simple-minded approach to your first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, we will have a new strategy when we have concluded the exercise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our expectation at this point is that it will take a year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our hope is that we can agree on that new strategy of the European Central Bank around November/December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: December, in my view, would be the probable date for the conclusion and the communication of our strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I say it will be over when it is over, what it means is that in the meantime, irrespective of our deliberations, our consideration, or engagement with academics, with economists, with civil society, with European parliament and so on and so forth, irrespective of all that - which will progress in parallel and will keep a lot of people busy both here in Frankfurt and in the 19 national central banks - we will conduct the same usual exercise of monitoring, analysing, drawing conclusion about the macroeconomic situation, about the monetary situation, about the markets, because we look at that as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we will draw our conclusions, which will be independent from the strategy review that we're conducting separately.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think I'm disclosing any secret, because at the time, some of you commented about it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were some Governing Council members that were a little bit sceptical about the effectiveness, the benefit, the justification of the tiering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the overall view - I think it was unanimous, actually; I didn't hear anything to the contrary - the unanimous view is that the tiering system is operating extremely well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no discussion at this point in time to change the limit of six times, as you know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But since September or since it was decided and as of the effective date, as you know there was instant movement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has proven to be effective, no question about it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On climate change, what I said, I say and I will continue to say is that it is everybody's responsibility, wherever he or she is, to see what he or she can actually do to fight climate change and protect biodiversity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me tell you what we already do, because it's not as if it's a newborn baby because I arrive; quite a lot had already been undertaken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would refer you to an excellent speech that Benoît Cœuré had given back about six or eight months ago about these topics.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just want to summarise what we do, because there are always questions and testing of her views versus the rest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, we have as you know an ECB staff pension fund and I'm looking at my paper because I don't want to give you anything that is wrong.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We replaced the previous benchmarks for the equity funds by their low carbon equivalents.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That came on the top of the selective exclusion and proxy voting guidelines that have already been in place for much longer than me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It does not apply to a very, very sizeable amount; it's roughly €1 billion, but small rivers make very large oceans eventually when they are protected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second deals with the ECB's own funds portfolio and that applies to the ECB paid-up capital and the general reserve funds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Altogether that's roughly - that's a little over €20 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On that, we're investigating how climate change-related considerations can be better integrated than they are at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a first step, we have decided to increase the share of green investment held in the portfolio, subject to availability and liquidity of such funds, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the third step has to do with our monetary policy portfolio, which is much larger.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, there is only a portion of that which is in corporate asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's roughly, take it or leave it, €200 billion relative to over €2 trillion for the entire asset purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think on that, the strategy is going to have to review what it can - what the Bank can do, should do, how much it collides with the mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If so, I think we should very expressly say so, but if it doesn't, I am giving you a for instance; it's not something that has been opined upon, that has been considered at all, but you can look at what ESG, for instance, criteria are respected by the issuers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can assess the value of collateral in order to determine what is the risk associated with collaterals and so on and so forth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In addition to that, there is work also that is ongoing in various departments at the ECB to make sure that the climate risk is actually embedded in the work that they do in terms of risk assessment, in terms of models, in terms of their forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is work in progress; it's not something that is completed and that is finished.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will, myself, finish with the area of financial stability because there is also work going on in order to define better stress testing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That framework normally should be completed at the end of 2020 at the latest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is work that is internal to the ECB, and that is separate from what the SSM is doing as well separately.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also have, together with the European Systemic Risk Board, a pilot framework that is under review as well and which should be completed as well in the fall of 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a lot going on and as you will see in the press release that you receive later on - in a very short while actually - you will see that environmental sustainability is captured very well in the description of our strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, we will not leave any stone unturned, and how we measure inflation is clearly something that we need to look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, the issue of housing and the distinction between the owner occupancy versus the non-owner occupancy, the reality and the perception, the difference between large urban centres and rural areas; all of that is infinitely difficult to apprehend and to calculate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we need to look at it and we need to understand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we believe that there is a clear miscalculation between what is there - which is roughly 6% of budget, if I recall - and what is the perception, we need to understand why.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there is a real difference, which there might well be, then we need to pass that on to Eurostat and have Eurostat do further and additional work.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not suggesting that it's going to be resolved in one year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I was Finance Minister in France, we had our issues with the value of real estate and it took a lot of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm concerned about low rate, because low rate is predicated on low growth, and I would much rather have much higher growth, higher rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This would be a really nice problem to have to deal with, but this is not the situation we have at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will see that as part of our strategy review, we are going to look at the potential side effects of the current circumstances, which are low rate - let alone negative - but we have had low rates for a period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That hampers our ability to respond in case of exogenous shock, as you know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Slow growth: I think we'll cross that bridge when we have to cross that bridge, but as you also know, different tools apply to different portions of the yield curve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's hope we don't have to do that, because growth doesn't slow and growth continues to not only stabilise but accelerate in the going future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That would be a nice problem to have to deal with, but if it did not, then we really have to ask ourselves at which end of the yield curve we want to operate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That will determine which kind of instrument we want to use.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: It's difficult to disagree with that finding of the BIS, that climate change is actually a threat to financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What's more, it's that it's a threat and a risk that is hardly measured and taken into account by many actors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I believe that the action taken by the - suggested by the BIS, the action recommended by other central banks; I can think of Mark Carney from the Bank of England, for instance, are completely justified.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I was personally very pleased to see that the private sector is actually also taking action in that respect, and certainly would welcome the involvement of other operators including their accounting firms and those that are setting the international accounting standards as well as the large asset managers, as we've seen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we badly lack harmonised measurement systems that can be generally accepted and that are actually implemented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is more of a personal view, if I may say, because it has not been debated in the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not suggesting that I would sort of give you the ECB doxa on this matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would be surprised if they were very much against that position.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I tried to do when describing for you what we were already doing was to show that, while we might not be ahead of the curve yet, we are not sitting on our bottom doing nothing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are taking climate change into account in order to improve the way in which we operate at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Wherever we have the option to include climate change as one of our tools, we are doing so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is going to be an important matter that will be debated during the strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Where does it impact the way in which we operate?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: You're completely right in that the situation has completely changed from 2003.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We published a study just before December that takes stock of the last 20 years of euro use and implementation and monetary policy delivery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For ten years, the goal was to fight inflation, because inflation was way too high.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then the financial crisis was the pivotal point at which eventually inflation was too low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's been a reversal of the situation and requires in my view that we actually look at the strategy very carefully to see how effective we can be in view of the change of circumstances, some of which are structural factors that are here with us to stay.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you look at the ageing population, when you look at the low productivity, these are probably going to be with us for a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We cannot operate as we did back in 2003 - which doesn't mean to say that we have to necessarily change this, that or the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have to look comprehensively at the effectiveness of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One thing that I know is central and anchored in our considerations will be the mandate that we are given under the Treaty, which is that of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On fiscal expansion, I would first of all observe that at the euro area level, there is a very mild fiscal expansion as we speak.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would also observe that two of the countries that have fiscal space, and I can think… You know who I am talking about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Two of those countries are now seriously looking...One has certainly gone pretty way out in order to explore how to expand more fiscally with their respective domestic budget.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We just need to all keep at it, not because I want to influence fiscal policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's for the authorities that have competence in that respect to decide, but simply because a good fiscal support would give much more effect to our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: You know, on climate change: I know that we will have a debate and I know that there will be discussions and it's already out there, that debate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If they do so, then yet again the legitimate authorities to implement climate change policies will feel that job is done, they don't have to worry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm aware of all that, but I'm also aware of the danger of doing nothing and I think that failing to try is already failing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We should at least try to explore every area where we can actually participate in a determination that is now the determination of the European Commission, of many of the euro area leaders, and which is now also creeping into the private sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's my personal take on that and I was very pleased to see that the environmental sustainability has found its right space in the monetary policy review that we are embarking upon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I draw a line between consensus building and repressing alternative views, and I can assure you that we are not short of alternative views, right?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are multiple views around the table on multiple aspects of monetary policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not a despotic President of the Governing Council; all views are welcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All governors have their space and time in order to share their perspective and submit their views.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the end of the day, and at the end of the process, we still have to complete the introductory statement and release the monetary policy decision if and when it is expected and required.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's intended to arrive at the best possible common understanding and a final decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It means that we are converging altogether towards a decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It may well be that we do not have unanimous decisions and that at some stage it will have to be a majority decision, but we need a decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: You know, it's one of the questions that I have asked the teams; what happens when Brexit happens?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Have we taken all the steps that we had to take?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Have we alerted sufficiently the private sector operators to themselves take the right measures?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to remind you, back in March of 2019, we activated swap lines with the Bank of England to make sure that on both sides of the Channel, there would be enough euros and sterling so that operations could continue in a smooth manner despite the implementation of Brexit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have alerted and reminded the banks of all the necessary measures that they have to take in order to be in a good position to continue to operate irrespective of Brexit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have good reason to believe that this is so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Don't forget that there was this high-level working group between the Bank of England and the ECB at the level of both President and Governor in order to make sure that they had checked all the boxes and covered the potential risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There can always be a risk somewhere, but I think that in good conscience, we have looked at everything that we thought was necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: I very strongly support the President of the Commission in that respect, and in many respects, for that matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are taking steps and we have taken steps already in order to play the role that we should play, concerning the fight against climate change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will look as part of the strategy review at what options we have to be even more intrusive, more active in relation to the corporate purchase plan that we have in place, and which continues to operate, as you know, because we are purchasers on a monthly basis of €20 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will look at that and see how we can play a role in accordance with our mandate, indeed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On that word, I think in accordance with our mandate indeed we have to stop the exercise, it's perfect timing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: I would, first of all, like to indicate to you that we very much operated in the same setting at the Governing Council of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, some members were in the room, other members were online and participated fully to the discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had a good outcome, so much so that we actually had a unanimous decision on the various elements of the package that I have announced to you earlier on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, this unanimous decision that was reached today was clearly determined by the fact that we believe that we have the most efficient, best targeted and most focused set of tools to address the kind of risks that we are facing under the current circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, if we are to compare one instrument versus the other we certainly considered all together that the use of this additional €120 billion asset purchase programme on the top of pre-existing programmes was the most efficient response to the market excess sensitivities that we see at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question had to do with how we are going to organise this asset purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can assure you on that page that first of all we will make use of all the flexibilities that are embedded in the framework of the asset purchase programme, and that, second, at the end of the asset purchase programme we will converge towards the capital keys.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: I think it is clear to all of us that the economies of the world, and certainly the economies of the euro area are facing a major shock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the response to your question will clearly depend on the speed, the strength and the collective approach that will be taken by all players, and as I have said at the very beginning of this introductory statement, first and foremost, and on the frontline in our analysis of the situation are the fiscal authorities and the European institutions that harness fiscal authorities and advise in that relation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is the reason why we are strongly encouraging and hoping for that ambitious and coordinated fiscal response that I have mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, the strategy review is clearly deferred for the moment and we have in particular decided to postpone by a matter of six weeks the first next big meeting that we had in our deliberations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So instead of focusing on 1 April, we are now looking at the end of May.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will determine based on the development of circumstances and the success in containing and delaying the spreading of this virus how and when and at what speed, and under what circumstances, and using what tools, we will be able to have our deliberations within the Governing Council; but more importantly our reach-out effort, in order to include academics, non-governmental organisations, members of parliament, and representatives of civil society at large.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because, clearly, the facilities that we had and our determination to reach out is impaired by the circumstances under which many of our euro area governments are now handing the risk situation that they're facing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: Our mandate is price stability, and, clearly, in the face of the current circumstances we have to use all the tools that we have available in order to almost surgically support and contribute our part to this collective approach that is badly needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not going to comment on decisions that are made by a government outside the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our job in that respect is to analyse the economic consequences that will result from those decisions, and to assess which segment of the economy will need support and will benefit from the tools that we are deploying at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of issuer limits I've already discussed that matter during the previous question, and it is clear that we will use in the work that we do in the coming weeks and months all the flexibility that is embedded in the framework of the asset purchase programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look carefully at the introductory statement, we do put some emphasis on the private sector bonds, because we believe that that is where there is currently acute sensitivity, and clearly, in due course and depending on developments on all the markets where we operate, we will have to target and use the flexibility that is needed in order to respond to the excess sensitivities that we see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: We do not determine our monetary policy stance on the basis of currency variations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are attentive to it, but this is not a determining factor, and the euro depreciates, appreciates, re-depreciates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the key issue is currently to face the fundamentals of the economy and to make sure that the liquidity risk doesn't materialise, that the credit continues to flow to the economy, and that we address the market excess sensitivities in order to restore some stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I remember saying when my predecessor and friend, President Draghi, left, and when I had interviews before the European Parliament, that I would hope that I would never have to do whatever it takes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is good about our today's deliberations is that there was rallying support around the table to use all the tools available and to consider adjusting our instruments going forward in order to target those risks that we see as threats to stability in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't have a claim to history for being whatever-it-takes number two.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I really would like all of us to join forces, and I very much hope that the fiscal authorities will appreciate that we will only deal with the shock if we come together.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On the latter one it's very simple: we are certainly not at the reversal rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mean, if we were at the reversal rate we would not see the growth of credit as I have described for you, both to the households sector and to the enterprises sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, no, we are not at the reversal rate and we are certainly not at the lower bound rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If, in the future, it is necessary for the purpose of dealing with the risks at the time to address that through the DFR, we will do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other point, I think I have dealt extensively with these issuer limits, and all I have to say at this moment, again, is that we will use all flexibilities embedded in the framework of our asset purchase programme, and bear in mind that we are likely to see increased debt issuance on the part of a few countries if only to deal with the fiscal resources that they will have to mobilise in order to put in place the healthcare systems that will be needed to respond to the spreading of the disease.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On the eurozone level - and at the European level at large, but I'm more concerned about the euro area, of course, in my position - I think all governments have to be on-deck and ready to act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I also think that all the European institutions have to join forces and rally around this collective package that needs to be put in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in very frequent dialogue with the European Investment Bank, for instance, and with the European Commission, clearly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: With the European Stability Mechanism I have not had very recent discussions, but it's clearly one of the players on the European scene, and I think that all players have to play their part in due course and to join hands.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's a collective effort that needs to be developed here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: As I've said, the decision was unanimous and that unanimity I think carries a long way in demonstrating our resolve to deal with the issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, as to markets, first of all, it takes a little bit of time, generally, for decisions to be analysed, digested and appreciated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fact that we are dealing with this full allotment liquidity facility at reduced rate compared with the current situation, the fact that we are putting in place a massive targeted long-term refinancing system that is available to all with a particular focus on SMEs, and with multipliers that are significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the volume of lending that can be accessed, we're talking about 50% relative to the previous loan book, if you will; we're talking about an entry rate of -25 basis points, and we're talking about an ultimate interest rate based on the track record of the lending institution of -75 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not sure that you can actually so much rival with that at the moment, and by the way, comparisons are odious.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: On the guarantee scheme, I think I was very explicit in the introductory statement on that, but I'm happy to restate it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are making available to all enterprises, with a focus on SMEs, massive refinancing means at very preferential rates, and in significant amounts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To encourage banks to actually use that facility we believe, and we have put in the introductory statement, that guarantee schemes would very much be in order.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in other words, it's a guarantee that is put together by the state, or an agency of the state, or a European agency in order to support all a part of the risk that is actually taken by the bank in extending lending facility to an enterprise, notably, in a sector which is particularly exposed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mean, that is how we believe that the financing we're putting in place will be most efficient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, whether that is conducted at the national level or at the European level is for the policymakers to decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What matters to us is that it is in place as rapidly as is possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some countries have already taken steps or are exploring steps in that direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would certainly, for the efforts that we are undertaking, I would certainly hope that they do that promptly in order to make sure that credit continues to flow to the economy, particularly the SMEs that are vulnerable in the present circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My point number two has to do with more debt issuance coming down the road depending on the fiscal expansion that will be determined by policymakers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, we will be there, as I said earlier on, using full flexibility, but we are not here to close spreads[1].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is not the function or the mission of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are other tools for that, and there are other actors to actually deal with those issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: As I said, we really deliberated long and hard all together to really assess what was the most efficient tool that we could use in order to target the risks that we have analysed in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We strongly believe that the asset purchase programme temporary large envelope with no monthly pre-determined allocation, which helps us actually focus on how the risks develop, is the most efficient tool that we can use under the present circumstances, and we shall use it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reason we are referring to the private sector contribution, is that it is currently a sector that is under massive stress and causing significant and excessive sensitivities on markets, and pose a risk to stability, but flexibility will be used.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we assess the risk and we measure where it is, we will apply this flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the CSPP, we have the PSPP, we also have the asset-based securities purchase programmes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will deploy all the purchase programmes that we have in order to focus on the risks as they are, and trust me, we will do that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: Let me come back a little bit to the risk channels as we see them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are facing something that is different from the great financial crisis, by the way, at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We analyse it as a crisis that is fuelled by a supply shock, followed by a demand shock, and with great financial uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the face of that, our analysis is that the response should be fiscal first and foremost.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I don't think that anybody should expect any central bank to be the line of first response.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if you look at the fiscal measures that have been announced for the moment in the euro area, which we have done yesterday, if you recap all that has been announced - not including the European Commission - you arrive at a total of about €27 billion, which is more or less a quarter of 1% of the GDP of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Hence the reason why we are calling in our introductory statement for an ambitious and collective fiscal response.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I believe that from the European Central Bank's viewpoint we are expecting and anticipating that this response will be ambitious and collective, and we are doing our part using the tools that we have, which we believe will be best targeted to the risks that we see likely to develop in the near future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is liquidity risk, that is an interruption or significant slowdown of the credit flow to the economy, and the financial excessive sensitivities that we see at the moment which create instability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are trying to address these three risks with the three tools that I have just mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Unlimited and generous access to liquidity, number one; considerably more attractive targeted long-term refinancing operation, particularly for the small and medium-sized enterprises; and a specific envelope of €120 billion for a special asset purchase programme that will deploy and use all the flexibility embedded in the framework of the APP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: Let me just backtrack a little bit and share with you the macroeconomic analysis that we have of the current situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We regard the current shock as severe, but still temporary, if the right set of policy measures are decided by all players.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What happens after a severe and temporary shock, provided that the right measures have been taken by all the players, is that the economy will then bounce back.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, for all of us that try to do a bit of forecasting, we initially thought that the shock would be during the first quarter and the rebound would progressively start in the second.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, everybody knows it's moving to the line and it's going to be a shock for the first two quarters, and the rebound will be in the second half.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, that schedule in and of itself and that timetable is shifting gradually.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the best thing to say is that there will be a rebound.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To time it precisely is uncertain, but we still very much hope that given that the right measures are taken by all the players, there will be a temporary nature associated with that very severe shock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If that is the case, our forecast for '21, very slightly reduced already, will reflect the bounce back of the economy, probably in the second half.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: 2022 will also have a much better forecast, and the numbers will be published this afternoon in our macroeconomic projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So with that, clearly, there is a shift that we are seeing in the economic cycle, but we still see inflation in 2022 at or about 1.6%, as will be published later on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We shall see, because, clearly, all this forecast will have to be revisited on the basis of the policies that are taken by all the players in the next few weeks, I hope, and not months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I hope that addresses your issue of the inflation movement as we forecast it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will be lower than expected this year, it's obvious.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even if you take out the oil shock, which will have an impact, clearly, the trade-off between the positive and the negative impact on inflation of the current development, whether it's a demand or a supply shock, and the contribution of the demand versus supply to the current shock is going to be determined probably in a while, but we cannot tell exactly how that trade-off will take place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's very likely that inflation will be lower than whatever we had forecasted this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would be dishonest if I was telling you something different, but what I'm trying to tell you is that we hope very much for a temporary nature of all these developments, followed by a bounce back that will take us back to a medium term that will be more in line with our forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All we know for sure is that risks are definitely tilted to the downside; that's for sure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: I don't mean to be re-reading something that maybe you've read, but there was a press release that was just issued by ECB Banking Supervision, and clearly, as of now, because that was decided earlier in the day by the ECB, which had to approve those new measures, banks can fully avail of capital and liquidity buffers, including Pillar 2 guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Banks will benefit from relief in the composition of capital for Pillar 2 requirements and ECB will consider operational flexibility in the implementation of supervisory measures, depending on bank-specific circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think in relation to buffers, that's a clear use of all available buffers as they were designed for the current circumstances that we are facing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: Well, Italy will be - Italian banks, Italy, Italian households, Italian enterprises - will be fully beneficiaries and eligible to all the tools that I have just mentioned, whether it's the massive liquidity access at very reasonable and preferential rates compared with what we have now, or whether it is the targeted long-term refinancing at very attractive rates as well, or whether it's the use of the special envelope of the asset purchase programmes, all of that can also help Italy, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President Lagarde: I'll tell you what I'm particularly worried about: it would be the complacency and slow motion process that would be demonstrated by fiscal authorities of the euro area in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, I very much hope that at the euro group meeting that is taking place on Monday and based on recommendations and guidelines by the European Commission on Friday, there will be a decisive and determined move in the direction of this ambitious and collective fiscal response that we have been calling for.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, unless the situation develops very rapidly for the better, it's unlikely that you will see both of us at the next press conference, because we're moving into split teams, including at the executive board level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our next Governing Council meeting on 1 April, if I recall, will actually be entirely online.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will very shortly take your questions but before that, on behalf of the entire Eurosystem and all members of the ECB, I would like to acknowledge once more that this is a global health crisis and that the highest priority has to go to trying to save lives and prevent the spread of the disease.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Since our last press conference, on March 12th, it's about three additional million people who have been infected by coronavirus and a third of them in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And while it is heartening to see the curve of death flattening, we must remember that each death is a tragedy for those who stay and we would like to express our sympathy and our condolences to all those who are suffering those deaths.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we would like to also express our gratitude, deep gratitude, to all those, from doctors to nurses, to ambulance drivers and all those who actually are on the front line of this fight against the virus and who risk their life.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I told you those are very strange and uncertain times and it is in a way demonstrated by the absence of Vice-President de Guindos next to me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Vice-President de Guindos is with us online, we have been operating in split teams and therefore we do not see each other, we do not contact each other, and he is with us on the phone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there are questions directed to him he will be able to take them whenever it's convenient, but he is with us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: With that, we are going to operate also in a strange way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The room is not like any room that we have had in press conferences before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you are all online and I know that you are submitting questions or you will be submitting questions in relation to the Governing Council that has just concluded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am going to take the opportunity of this first question to take you back a little bit to the last two days that we've had with Governing Council members.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I also want to take this opportunity to walk you through the masses of changes that the Eurosystem and the ECB together have decided and, for most of them actually now, implemented in the last few weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of the current situation, we are facing an economic contraction of a magnitude and speed that is unprecedented in recent history.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The spread of the coronavirus and the associated containment measures have literally halted economic activity to a large extent across the globe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are seeing a rapid evolution of the economic effects of the necessary containment measures in our area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Initially there were only some sectors that were badly affected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We were talking about transportation, we were talking about tourism, we were talking about entertainment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Gradually as the containment measures took hold, entire sectors of the economy to a large extent were simply shut down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's reflected and it will continue to be reflected, the hard numbers are just beginning to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We just had a few numbers from the first quarter and frankly, our forecast for the second quarter in our severe scenario points to minus 15% on a quarterly basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Consumer business sentiment indicators are in freefall, while labour market conditions have deteriorated massively.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the PMI composite, for instance, in April 13.5 and it comes from 29.7 in March and before that, 51.6 in February.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That decline, which is also quite remarkable and explains quite a lot of things, was driven by the manufacturing sector but very much so by the service sector as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The European Commission Flash Consumer Confidence also dropped to minus 27.7.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at labour forces, 718,000 companies in Germany have applied for the short-term special work programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In France the number of companies that have applied for the chômage partiel - the unemployment special schemes - went from 24,000 to 425,000, covering over 10 million employees.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do not still have clarity about the course of the pandemic and the duration and the degree of remaining containment measures that will be taken, which of course is critical for us to actually take an assessment of what the economic situation will be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It makes our job of forecasting, and all those who are trying to forecast around the world, extremely difficult.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, our growth scenarios on an annual basis, from the mild to the more severe, vary from 5 to 12% negative depending on the containment measures that are taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course as and when the containment measures are lifted, we expect a recovery of economic activity, but we cannot tell at what speed and what will be the scale of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, let me turn to the number of measures that we have taken since March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All those measures are aimed at 1) ensuring ample liquidity conditions 2) protecting the smooth flow of credit to business and households and 3) preserving highly-accommodative financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is the pandemic emergency purchase programme, €750 billion, combined with our increased APP decided on the 12thMarch - €120 billion combined with our monthly purchases of €20 billion monthly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have over €1 trillion that we can deploy and use until the end of the year to purchase assets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our new targeted lending facility provides for around €3 trillion in liquidity to banks at a negative rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, we have also significantly eased our collateral rules to ensure that banks can continue to make use of the refinancing facilities, ensuring that our monetary policy tools remain effective even in times of severe financial market stress, and against the backdrop of looming rating downgrades.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These measures altogether form a really powerful package and are providing crucial support to the euro area economy, notably to those sectors most exposed to the crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will tell you, as the economic situation is evolving rapidly, we are constantly monitoring the situation and evaluating each of those measures as standalones and as part of the package to test whether they are still properly calibrated and sized appropriately.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In light of this, and with the view to further ease the conditions for banks to provide credit to the real economy, we decided to take further action today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We reduced the interest rates for the period from June '20 to June '21 by a further 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The rate in TLTRO III can now be as low as minus one percent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also decided to create a new instrument that we call PELTRO; the Pandemic Emergency Longer-Term Refinancing Operation, which is intended to support liquidity conditions to the entire euro area, to the entire financial system, to contribute to preserving the smooth functioning of money markets by providing effectively a liquidity backstop.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These operations will be carried out as fixed-rate tender procedures, with full allotment, at an interest rate that will be 25 basis points below the average main refinancing operation rate or MRO rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council - and we discussed that over the last two days - is more determined than ever to strengthen its commitment, to ensure supportive financial conditions across all sectors and countries so that they can absorb this unprecedented shock that we are experiencing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: With this in mind, we will make full use of the flexibility that is embedded in PEPP and in other components of our policy toolkit to ensure that our monetary policy stance reaches all sectors and countries in the same manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm saying all that to you to address your questions because as one of the decisions that we made and that I just commented, we decided to enlarge the pool of collateral by effectively freezing ratings where they were on April 7th.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We provided for a floor which is at CQS5, but that gives a large pool from which banks can actually draw in order to get financing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me remind you that again we are fully flexible, we will look at all options, we will determine and monitor and we will make sure that our monetary stance and our monetary policy transmission are both effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, let me remind you that OMT was conceived back in 2012 and there was full publication about the terms and conditions and characteristics of OMT.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: OMT was intended for particular country cases and particular circumstances where, because of fiscal policy or structural policy misguidance, there was a potential risk out there that the euro area be at risk and that it would be self-fulfilling.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are facing a situation where it's not a single country, but it's all countries, where it's a global shock that applies in a very symmetric way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The best tool that we have in our toolbox is indeed the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme, PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course OMT remains part of the toolbox and we are not suggesting that we would eliminate OMT, but for the crisis we're going through at the moment, PEPP is clearly designed to that effect, added to which the triggering of OMT of course is a matter for the Governing Council to decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On your first question relating to the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme: let me just remind you that it's a programme that is a standalone, very exceptional programme that is intended to address the issue of the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is unlike any other programme, which is why it was targeted, it was temporary and it was flexible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll remind you that the life of that PEPP is going to be determined by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will not end earlier than the end of calendar year but depending on the length of the crisis - and this will be the determination of the Governing Council - it might be extended further than the end of 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is also not the only programme that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have purchase programmes, including the €120 billion that were decided on March 12th.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have our recurring monthly €20 billion programme that is also in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's not just focus on PEPP, which is very specifically designed, but let's make sure that we understand the whole firepower that the ECB has available, which is north of €1 trillion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on PEPP I just want to take you to exactly the wording that we have, which relates to the flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From memory, what was decided and it was the fruit of significant discussions all in the light of the exceptional circumstances that we were going through, we have very specifically the fact that to the extent - and I quote - "That some self-imposed limits might hamper action that the ECB is required to take in order to fulfil its mandate, the Governing Council will consider revising them to the extent necessary to make its action proportionate to the risks that we face."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's a very clear indication that if it is so necessary because our action is impaired by those self-imposed limits, we will revisit them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know that the legal act was published shortly after that, which distinguishes very clearly the APP holdings from the PEPP holdings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that we have to make full use, and continue to make full use, of that flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Indeed, we stand ready to revisit, to examine and as is mentioned very clearly in the introductory statement, to calibrate and to adjust the size and the composition of PEPP in size, in length, in order to make sure that our monetary stance and our monetary policy is properly transmitted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the interest rate: you know, we look at the bulk of what we've done since early March and we believe that between the massive liquidity facility, between the revised and much improved TLTROs, with the enlarged pool of collateral from which banks can draw, combined with an interest rate that itself was already at low level, we have the combination as a package to actually address the current circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the Bank Lending Survey that was published a couple of days ago is absolutely explicit in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The way by which yields on many of the government bonds have evolved over the last few weeks is also indicative of the action that we take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: All right, the yield curve control policy: as I just said, I think the combination of tools that we are using at the moment enables us to operate across the entire curve and to actually deal with all maturities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether it's the short end, the long end of the curve, we are in a capacity to deal with the two key objectives that we have, which are; to make sure the monetary stance reaches its goal, and that monetary policy is properly transmitted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All of that within our mandate and all of that with the ultimate objective of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, clearly we are operating under very specific circumstances and the combination of those tools enables us to satisfy those objectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said earlier, we will use any and all flexibility that we have in accordance with our mandate in order to make sure that our monetary policy is properly transmitted to all jurisdictions, from east to west, from north to south, to all sectors of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the flexibility to do so, so we will use it full fledge.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On OMT, I think I've already responded, but I'll be happy to expand on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: OMT was created in 2012 - different times, different issues - and it was designed for countries but taken in isolation, that were facing particular serious circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, countries had to be subject to an ESM programme, which had conditionalities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those September 12thconditions also provided that the Governing Council would consider OMT warranted from a monetary policy perspective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council needs to assess that there is a clear monetary policy justification and objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said earlier, OMT is not necessarily best suited for the present contingencies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: OMT is in the toolbox, it is there but given the symmetry of the shock, clearly the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme is designed specifically to that end; to make sure that the monetary stance reaches its goals, monetary policy is transmitted throughout the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: PEPP provides that; it is exceptional, it is temporary, it is targeted and it's intended to be used with great flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do use flexibility in how we use PEPP and on that particular page, I am pleased to report to you that the Governing Council has decided the publication principles that will apply to our PEPP programmes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That had not been clarified yet and you'll be pleased to know also that we will apply the same granularity principles that apply to APP, but we will publish on a bi-monthly basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it will be accumulated over two months, but it will be as granular as the APP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But given the specificity of PEPP, we considered that it was most appropriate to do so on a bi-monthly basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I told you, our aims are twofold and we will not tolerate any risk of fragmentation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will want to make sure that there is plenty of liquidity, we will want to make sure that credit flows to the economy, that our monetary policy stance and transmission are effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will do so in whichever country needs to benefit from our determinations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are determined to use all those tools and we are determined to deploy full flexibility, as I've just indicated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: To your question, is the ECB going to buy junk bonds; we have not discussed any change to the APP eligibility framework at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the PEPP I would like to remind you that we have already given a waiver of eligibility requirements for securities issued by the Greek government.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was also part of the multiple decisions that we made in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said already, we have been very, very clear - and if I need to repeat it again, I will repeat it again - we will not accept fragmentation of monetary transmission in the euro area or any pro-cyclical tightening of financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So within our mandate and with these two principles in mind, we will adjust as and when needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think you had a second question and that had to do with the PELTROs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I don't know exactly what you wanted to know about PELTROs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: PELTRO is an additional tool in many ways because we had initially thought that the LTRO decided on March 12thwas only a bridge until the next entry into effect of TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decided to actually put in place PELTROs to provide additional support to liquidity conditions in financial markets, contributing to preserve the smooth functioning of money markets by providing an effective liquidity backstop.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Extending it beyond the normal counterparties that we have, the Governing Council has not discussed that, but once again we are in such uncertain times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is such a threat to the economic fabrics of our societies that we have to be open-minded and look at all possibilities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not closing off anything in that respect, but we have not discussed it in the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: You know, our PEPP is as I said one huge component of our purchase programme capacity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Don't forget that you also have these other components that bring it all together to over €1 trillion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, as I said, we will use full flexibility to deploy this particular powder in the right direction where we feel that there is a risk of tightening and where we feel that we need to intervene to protect and preserve our monetary policy stance and our monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, flexibility means across classes of assets, across jurisdictions, across time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of timing I also remind you that the length, the duration of that PEPP will be determined by the Governing Council, taking into account the pandemic crisis time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We take into account all indicators that we can and our purposes are very simple; monetary stance, monetary policy transmission, appropriate level of liquidity, making sure that credit flows.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That takes me to the second part of your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: TLTROs and this particular one in its latest iteration that can go all the way down to minus one percent at which banks can finance themselves, is intended for the real economy, is intended for credit to flow to the real economy from the large corporate to the sole entrepreneur, and everything in between.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is associated with a threshold that banks have to demonstrate they are reaching.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, if they make sure that they don't leverage, if they continue to have a full exposure and that they continue to give credit to the economy, then they become eligible to this particularly favourable rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not without consideration that we have reframed this TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not intended for banks; it's intended for the financing of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We regard that as an absolute imperative if we want the economies of the euro area to actually be in a position to resist the extraordinary shock that it is suffering, and to be in a position to pick up strength and to continue to exist and invest and create those jobs that are being - that are vanishing at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I'll start with the last one because that's one that is also taking a lot of our time and a lot of our concern.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are operating under pretty much lockdown status at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I take the opportunity of this press conference to actually thank all staff of the Eurosystem and those here at the ECB who are making huge sacrifices every day to actually deliver, be able to be on the markets as actively as they normally are, and all that despite teleworking, despite children at home and all the rest of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are also taking the hit in the same way and having to face the same hardship on a day-to-day basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We try to guard against the difficulties that could arise from that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking at how, as the German regulations, prescriptions and recommendations evolve over the course of the next few weeks, how we can also ourselves make sure that we exit without jeopardising our operations, without making the system at risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would like to actually tell you that those people who work in teams between various countries are also experiencing some tough times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I can tell you is that because of the social distancing, because of the way we have to work, this return to normal, so to speak - which will be a new normal - is certainly not in the next few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking at way down and probably out in 2021 in terms of return to a new normal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment it's going to be gradual and with two imperatives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one is to make sure that staff are safe, stay healthy, are protected and 2) that we honour our mandate and we do our duty to the citizens of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Permanent character of the crisis: we certainly hope that this is not the case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As our macroeconomic team has forecast, while the next quarters will be difficult, we are also looking at a pick-up and at our recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
