text: The forecast that you will see in June, I hope, and the scenario results that you will see tomorrow - because we publish tomorrow the scenario - indicate actually a recovery and an uptick in the situation in 2021.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We very much hope that it will not be permanent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I hope that the European agencies and institutions under the leadership of the European Council and the Eurogroup, will do everything they can in order to have a joint approach and in order to show solidarity to those that have been most affected by the current crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Financial stability: I would simply like to say that since the last great financial crisis in 2008, the banks are in a much stronger position.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, many of them have made a very significant effort to reduce their non-performing loans and have done so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, at the moment, the point is to focus on defeating the economic consequences of the pandemic, but obviously financial stability will remain of concern.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The SSM, under the leadership of Andrea Enria, obviously is looking at that from a microprudential point of view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: First of all, I highly recommend that you look at the scenario publication tomorrow, because they go into great details on those numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, I'm going to refrain from making any kind of guesstimate of what we see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are certain to see is significantly reduced inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: How much is going to be very difficult to determine, and why is that?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because of the lockdown, essentially; because the price formation mechanisms are not in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Added to that, simply the collection of data about prices is sometimes very significantly impaired.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think clearly, in the short and medium term, we are seeing inflation expectations and forecasts that are significantly lower than what we had seen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The longer-term expectations have not been significantly affected, but we are in a completely exceptional situation which, by many accounts, prevents forecasters and estimates from having any of accuracy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On your first question, which has to do with whether or not we include junk bonds, as you call them, in our purchase policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to insulate the way we conduct policy from the effect of the pandemic and avoid self-fulfilling pro-cyclicality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue to observe the situation and take appropriate and proportionate action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Aside from that, the Governing Council has not discussed this matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point, which has to do with the Karlsruhe Court decision, I just want to remind you that the ECB is subject to the jurisdiction of the Court of Justice of the European Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The PSPP has been judged by the Court of Justice of the European Union as in line with our policy mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have indeed taken note of the judgement, which is directed at the German government and at the German parliament, and we are confident that a good solution will be found.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A good solution that will not compromise the ECB's independence, will not compromise the primacy of the European Union law or the ruling of the European Court of Justice.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB Governing Council regularly assesses the effectiveness, the efficiency and the cost-benefit of its monetary policy measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It does so on a regular basis and as you can imagine, given the package that we have debated and eventually discussed and agreed upon, this has been the case in great depth during the course of our morning session.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is typically reflected in our accounts and it will indeed be reflected in our accounts as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, your question helps me, reframing a little bit for you, the cost-benefit - and I was tempted to say the benefit-cost because there are a lot more benefits than costs - of our PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, I would observe that the PEPP has already demonstrated that it is a very successful programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we used it, actually very shortly after we announced it on the 18thMarch, it has prevented the downward spirals in financial markets and reduced any tail risks at the time without which we would have been in a seriously different situation in terms of both growth and inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are two main factors that have led us to reconsider PEPP and certainly expand the size of PEPP as well as its duration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first factor is that the outlook for price stability has been significantly affected by the fallout from the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I mentioned earlier on, we had to revise our inflation outlook and if you look at the medium-term horizon of our projections, which is 2022, we are now talking about 1.3 as opposed to 1.6, which was the horizon that we had back in March prior to the COVID-19.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second factor that has also led us to reconsider PEPP and to increase its size and extend its timing, is that financial conditions for the euro area as a whole are significantly tighter today, as measured by average sovereign yields and broader metrics of financial tightness, in a situation where the economy needs easier conditions to achieve price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In that context, we judged that it was necessary to increase the size.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can assure you that there was a unanimous view in the Governing Council that action had to be taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the face of that inflation outlook, and given our mandate of price stability, action had to be taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we decided to increase the size of PEPP in order to 1) ease aggregate financial conditions 2) safeguard the transmission of our monetary policy to all asset classes and jurisdictions thanks to one particular aspect of PEPP, which is its flexibility in conducting our purchases and 3) help us back to what I would call the pre-COVID inflation path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That justified fully the expansion of PEPP by the amount that I have mentioned, which is €600 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Why did we extend the horizon to June of 2021?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's because we have a sense that by then, inflation hopefully will start kicking in again and we will have a better visibility of the situation at that point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also coherent with a lot of our other monetary policy tools, those that we have either determined in March, or fine-tuned and improved at our last April monetary policy Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of reinvestments that we have agreed to push at least until the end of 2022, we have determined that because it helps ensure that financial conditions remain sufficiently supportive over a possibly very protracted recovery phase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It also reflects the nature of PEPP, which is different from the PSPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If only for these two reasons we believe that giving a bit more visibility and certainty over that horizon was certainly a good decision to make.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: First of all, on the choice of €600 billion, obviously there was a debate within the Governing Council as to what would be the appropriate size.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We collectively determined, and there was broad consensus around that proposal, that the €600 billion should over time bring us significantly closer to what I have called the pre-COVID inflation path, while allowing us to monitor how some key developments unfold in the coming months, that will indeed impact our policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we will understand a little better how the economy rebounds in the third quarter and then later on in the course of the coming months, to have a bit more clarity because of course we have better data, better numbers and we can come up with some more reliable scenarios and even a projection.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is still surrounded by a lot of uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that that will bring us, as I said, significantly closer to that path of the pre-COVID inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, I just want to remind you that we have decided to use PEPP but it's not as if it was PEPP and nothing else.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a whole package of tools that we are using to a great extent addressing all sectors of the economy, all axes of our action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll just remind you that for instance, we start with a very low interest rate, which is associated with forward guidance, which as you will have noticed has not changed, as indicated in the introductory statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are also using and we will be seeing very interesting developments in June, the TLTRO - Targeted Longer-Term Refinancing Operations - which are really offered to the banking sector at extremely attractive terms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again to remind you: if banks keep their exposure to the economy and keep lending particularly to the corporates but also to the SMEs and to all the family of borrowers around, in that case they can obtain an interest rate which is -1%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's also a major tool to make sure that the economy really is flooded with the credit capacity that banks can intermediate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I also would like to remind you that we have a liquidity facility, which is the LTRO, which has operated as a bridge, which will now be supplemented by a PELTRO, which is pandemic-specific and which will also operate as a liquidity facility that is available for those of the banks that do not want to necessarily use the TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have plenty of tools and of course we have the whole category of asset purchase programmes, the PEPP being one of them, and very specific to the pandemic circumstances, and as a result being temporary, being targeted, being proportionate in response to the pandemic crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Final point, because it's also an important one associated with TLTROs, is the enlargement of collaterals that we have decided, and which is certainly helping banks to come up with more papers in order to obtain refinancing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of PEPP as the best possible instrument at the moment, one item in the package of tools that we use and the size of which we believe as a Governing Council in broad agreement is perfectly appropriate and adequate in order to respond to the needs, I think has determined us to act in that direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think you had an additional question on DFR [deposit facility rate].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, we also as a Governing Council decided that under current circumstances, clearly the PEPP was the best instrument to use both in terms of monetary stance but also in terms of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: In relation to the Karlsruhe constitutional court decision, the ECB as you know is subject to the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice, the Court of Justice of the European Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our PSPP, which was the subject of the Karlsruhe constitutional court ruling, has been judged by the Court of Justice of the European Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has been judged as in line with our policy mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have, all of us, taken note of the judgement passed by the Karlsruhe constitutional court, which is directed at two parties; the German government and the German parliament.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are confident that a good solution will be found which, as I said already, will in no way compromise the independence of the ECB, the primacy of European Union law and the decision by the European Court of Justice.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have done at the Governing Council meeting, and what we do regularly whenever important decisions are made in terms of monetary policy, is to debate and to assess the effectiveness, the efficiency and the cost-benefit of one measure or the other, and the package of measures together.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have done that indeed this morning, as we regularly do, and that is and will be reflected in the accounts and indeed in the minutes of the meeting that we had.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we are focused on the mandate that we have to deliver on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is price stability, as defined since 2003, as you know, by reference to inflation close to but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our inflation outlook is a very important determinant of the decisions that we make.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a single mandate, we have a yardstick that measures it and until such time when we resume and complete our strategy review, this will remain so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Hence when we see an inflation outlook at the end of our projection period, in 2022 at 1.3%, we make the determination that measures are needed, action is necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do so by using the entire package and selecting in the toolbox that we have the instrument that will be most flexible and most potent in order to help us return to the pre-COVID inflation path that we had known back in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Let me just remind you what I would call the dual key of PEPP is: on the one hand, it has a monetary policy stance about it but on the other hand - as you know because that was the one that certainly predominated in the early phase of the crisis - it is critically important because of its flexibility in order to transmit monetary policy, in order to reduce market stress in order to avoid fragmentation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it clearly has those two missions, so the PEPP as I said also earlier on is temporary, is targeted and it's really intended to deal with the pandemic shock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's in response to that shock that it was put together and in order to make full use of that instrument, we have to be mindful of the two functions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In response to the pandemic shock and the resulting downward pressure on inflation and the medium-term inflation outlook for the whole euro area, that's the response.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Financial conditions for the whole euro area are significantly tighter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not country specific so we are now talking about the monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All of that is happening in a situation where the recovery is going to need easier conditions to achieve price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: PEPP purchases in all euro area jurisdictions are needed to further ease the general monetary policy stance, supporting funding conditions in the real economy, especially for all businesses and households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the monetary policy stance, we need to use it across all jurisdictions, no question about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, when it comes to banks, as I reminded you, the TLTRO III in its latest iteration, which was decided in April, will begin in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are very confident that given the attractiveness of the TLTROs and the rate that will be available to banks that at least maintain their exposure relative to the benchmark that has been decided, they will benefit from an interest rate which is -1%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, that should certainly help with reviving the economy, with maintaining the credit flow to both corporates and households, and within corporates to SMEs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That transmission of monetary policy mechanism has to work and has to continue to be efficient in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are confident that combining all the tools that we have in our toolbox, leveraging PEPP as we do under the decision that we have made today, we will actually serve both aims that we are pursuing, which is to make sure that credit flows through the economy and that we return to the inflation path that we had pre-crisis so that we can deliver on our price stability mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: In relation to the risk of disinflation, this is clearly a matter that we have discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is, as I said earlier, an issue that is very central to our macroeconomic radar screen, if you will, because this is the yardstick against which we measure price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we see an inflation outlook which is at the end of our projection period, at the end of 2022, at 1.3%, we are certainly not close to the 2% and below 2% objective that has been set.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, that is the reason why we decide to use in the current circumstances the most efficient, the most effective and the most flexible of the instruments that we have at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is clearly with the purpose of getting back to the pre-COVID inflation path that we use this tool as well as all the other tools of the package.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Concerning the German constitutional court ruling that was issued on May 5th, again: the European Central Bank is subject to the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice and the European Court of Justice back in December 2018 has judged that the PSPP - which was also the object of the German constitutional court - was in line with our policy mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we have taken note of the judgement by the constitutional court of Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That judgement is directed at the German government, at the German parliament.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are fully confident that a good solution will be found that will respect the independence of the central bank, that will recognise the primacy of European Union law and that will also respect the European Court of Justice decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, one of the matters that was under review was the issue of proportionality and as the Governing Council regularly does, and we did it this morning, we reviewed the effectiveness, the efficiency and we measured the cost-benefit of the measures that we were proposing in our policy recommendation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had a very clear and good debate about this matter and this is always reflected in the accounts and in the minutes, and it will be reflected in the accounts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, first of all, I want to come back to that because it was clearly in the birth certificate of PEPP and it is clearly alive as we speak and as we use PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, it has a backstop function, if you will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's intended and it has demonstrated its capacity to deal with short-term market stress.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has the capacity to address the risk of market fragmentation and it is of course an instrument intended to improve the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look carefully at documents - as I'm sure you do - you will note that there is a reference to the determination to address the outlook related to or resulting from - I can't remember the exact words - from the pandemic situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we mean by addressing the outlook, from a central bank point of view, it's clearly the inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The two keys are active, were embedded in the first place as I said, in the birth certificate of the PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is both about stance and it is about transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly in this particular moment, the stance is probably a bit more relevant than the monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is certainly one of the key attributes of PEPP, to be able to use these functions with flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just want to come back to this issue of flexibility because we have said very clearly that flexibility came in a three-pronged approach: 1) across time 2) across market segments and 3) across jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The flexibility that we've used across time is pretty obvious because we have massively front-loaded our purchases to respond to the volatility, to the lack of liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you go back to March 26th, which is when PEPP began purchasing - which by the way is a remarkably short period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was decided on the 18thin the evening and it was first to market on the 26thMarch.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We front-loaded purchases because at the time, if you remember, end of March/beginning of April, there was significant volatility, lack of liquidity in many market segments, and we had to step in very massively.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That had an impact; it's measurable and it's strong, so that's the first aspect of flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look carefully at what we did with PEPP, the crisis highlighted an unprecedented need of short-term liquidity by firms as the lockdown measures were beginning to dry income streams.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the time, if you remember, issuance by corporates was virtually nil.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we have record issuance to date, and what have we done from the total purchases that we've made?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't have the exact number with me, but it's north of €30 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: [1]I could double-check for you if you want, but I am sure you'll be able to do that as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We did that and we also decided to shift a large share of our purchases to commercial paper.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are seeing evidence of the success of the measures because commercial paper rates have started to stabilise and issuance of longer tenors is rising as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, the ECB's capital key guides the benchmark for our purchases of public sector securities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We assessed that there was a strong and urgent need to purchase with deviation from the benchmark guidance, as we faced, and still continue to face, risks of fragmentation that threaten the smooth transmission of our monetary policy across the entire euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we have used, and we will continue to use, the PEPP to counter such risks of fragmentation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would like to reassure you that the guiding principle of flexibility will be maintained throughout the lifetime of the PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: As I understand it, we missed a little bit the beginning of your question, but I think you raised the issue of the international role of the euro as a currency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, first of all, as you know we will publish next week our report on the international role of the euro, so it's with a little bit of pride that I would take the view that the euro has an international role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I look at the number of swap lines or repo lines that have been asked or requests that have been submitted to us, it is clearly a currency that is in demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fact that it is one of the currencies in the basket of currencies that are used to determine the value of the Special Drawing Rights is also an indication that it enjoys the status of international currency and is recognised as such.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, clearly the issuance by regional agencies, whether it is the ESM, the EIB and indeed the Commission as it did previously in the EFSM, is contributing to reinforcing that role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think the role of the euro as an international currency will be primarily supported by a deeper and more complete economic and monetary union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have - and I hope that we will - go deeper and further in terms of capital markets union, in terms of completion of the banking union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we need these two to really reinforce the economic and monetary union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have very much hope that as part of the agenda in the coming months, the Commission will be able to push those agenda items and that the European Council under the leadership of Charles Michel will also push these agenda items.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You also asked me a question about the issuance of debt in a particular country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would probably give you a broader response because it is not specific to Greece.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you look around the world, all countries at the moment are resorting to fiscal tools in order to respond to the extraordinary and terrible consequences of this pandemic which is affecting us all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So using the fiscal tool is generally leading to many countries having to issue more debt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point in time, there was no alternative than to actually issue debt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would observe that the service of debt, which matters as well a lot to determine the debt sustainability, is currently very low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Final point: the combination of fiscal policy and monetary policy, which clearly at the moment are supplementing each other, are working hand in hand, are aligned with similar objectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That hopefully will be critically important to restore economic conditions that are better for people's income, better for people's jobs and will be more conducive to a growth that in the European Union under the leadership of Ursula von der Leyen, President of the Commission, has identified as hopefully more green and more digital.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, first of all on the recovery fund: I would observe two things; one is, it is a proposal and it should not be seen in isolation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a proposal that will have to go through the process of the agreement through the Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I don't doubt for a second the determination of the European leaders at large to really respond to the challenge of the pandemic, and to respond to the needs of the recovery plans that have to really pan out throughout the whole European Union, and that have to reach by sector and by regions those that have been most affected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are certain segments of my communication where I want to be very, very specific.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I describe for you, for instance, the flexibility as we apply it, I want to cover all items of flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Or if I am quoting specific references from a particular decision that has been made, or from a Governing Council statement, I don't want to betray them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So now and again, I hope you don't mind not seeing my eyes too clearly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In any case, you don't miss much, I can assure you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will occasionally take the liberty to read things, yes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Your first question on the PEPP as to whether it will be used in full or not, let me first of all remind you that the PEPP has a dual function and has had that function ever since inception.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was really in the birth certificate of PEPP on day one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first function is to address the risk of market fragmentation and impairment to monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second function is to ease the monetary policy stance in light of the contraction that resulted from COVID-19.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In addition to the dual function, the PEPP is also marked by flexibility, which is one of its key elements, and we have made full use of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to remind you, we have purchased over €360 billion in the first couple of months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was at the end of June, effectively, and we will make use of that flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As some of you have noted, we have slowed down a little bit the pace of purchases because financial markets have been more stable, because the fragmentation risk has really significantly been reduced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But having said that, the overall envelope and the horizon of PEPP were calibrated in order to meet both functions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore - and we don't see it for the moment, frankly - but unless there were significant upside surprises, our baseline remains that we will use the entire envelope of the PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there were those very significant upsides then we shall see, but this is not what is in the cards at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, the second function of the PEPP that I have mentioned, - which is the monetary stance in order to respond to the shock of coronavirus - is still around.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still need to address that, so we will continue to use the envelope of the PEPP and make sure that it helps us to get back to the trajectory of inflation pace pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question has to do with this risk of a two-speed recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Before COVID-19 hit all of us, there was already a divergence and a degree of divergence among the euro area member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, facing the COVID-19, there is a risk that that divergence persists.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it should by all means be avoided, which is why we together with all members of the Governing Council strongly welcome the RRF - the Recovery and Resilience Facility - which is precisely intended to address those countries and help those countries that have been most hit and most severely hit by COVID-19.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not only that, but also which is intended to invest in those sectors of the economies and in those developments that will actually be transformational and hopefully will be so on a pan-European basis, thereby reducing hopefully the degree of divergence that we had observed in the first place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: During this meeting of the Governing Council, we really spent a good deal of time looking at the economic circumstances, looking at the macroeconomic numbers, looking at the developments as we saw them in order to evaluate our monetary policy tools and how effective and adequate they were.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Really, seeing the developments in the economy, we really felt that we were in a good place at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: May I remind you that since last June, we have significantly expanded the PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have had a major, major take-up of the TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, those two components, added to the whole rest of the monetary policies that we have in place, tell us that it's effective, it's adequate and it is working.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our experience with the two-tier system has been very positive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is working as intended; namely to preserve the accommodative impact of our negative interest rate policy while alleviating its direct side effect for banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has also encouraged additional borrowing and lending activity in the inter-bank money market, including cross border, which is a sign of defragmentation that we welcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, both the multiplier and the remuneration rate on exempt allowances can be changed over time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we don't see at the moment any particular reason for doing so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually we have not discussed that because we don't see, in the monitoring that we do very carefully, a need to revisit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the growth outlook and whether the developments that we are seeing are a concern; of course it is a concern.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a concern for the livelihood of people, it's a concern for the life of people and it's a concern for policies that should all be geared at helping people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of impact on our own forecasts and our own scenarios, clearly we have taken into account the environment in which the euro area operates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have taken into account the potential risk of a second wave and the measures that would be taken as a result of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in that context you can rest assured that the scenarios that we had and the baseline that we have retained back in June actually do take those elements into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We very much hope that there will be more improvement than worsening of what we had anticipated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On your first question, ever since we've begun implementing the PEPP back in March - and even more so since June -euro area financial market sentiment has improved, although financial conditions remain still tighter than before the outbreak of the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Since the announcement itself, the sovereign and corporate bond yield spreads have narrowed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Corporate bond issuance has picked up and equity prices have increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Compared with the time of the PEPP announcement, euro investment grade corporate spreads declined by more than 80 basis points, while high-yield spreads declined by more than 250 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see significant improvement, but having said that, we are not exactly back to where we were before the pandemic started.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For example, government bond yields are still higher in most jurisdictions than before the outbreak of the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is highly relevant from a monetary policy stance perspective because sovereign yields are the basis of the pricing of other financial products and loans to businesses and to households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are very attentive to those numbers as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, I would like to observe that TLTRO has been a great, great success.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have had, as you know, an intake north of €1.3 trillion, which is way above market expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, it has to do with the attractive terms under which TLTRO was offered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, it was also successful because there was clearly a demand, and third, it was successful because there was no stigma associated with using the TLTRO.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Overall you had three good reasons for that programme to be extremely successful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second question that we asked ourselves during the Governing Council is: what did we want to do with TLTRO?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, clearly what we wanted was to encourage banks to continue supporting the economy, to continue extending financing to both firms and households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are seeing in terms of increase of lending to firms and stabilisation and slight increase of lending to households, is comforting because there is a significant increase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to give you an example: in the last three months, lending to firms has been in the range of €250 billion, which is the largest take-up ever in a period of three months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: TLTRO was vastly successful because of the conditions under which it was granted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It seems to have met the purpose that we assigned to it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will determine at the end, in September '21, when we actually account for the lending and we compare that with the benchmark that had been agreed, whether there was in fact a significant and at least maintained lending to the economy, and the favourable terms and conditions of 50 basis points lower than the DFR, whether that rate will be available to banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the attractiveness of it, but it was with conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is something which is mentioned in the Bank Lending Survey that was just recently published.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's fair to say that the banks are anticipating a net tightening on the back of what has been a clear loosening of credit terms before that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we have to take that factor into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, we also believe that this anticipation by the banks is clearly related to maybe the fear of a cliff effect in case the guarantee schemes that have been extended by governments to banks were to expire.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In that vein and on that page, I would like to mention that the Commission, as you know, has recently published some best practices and guidelines to implement those guarantee schemes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From our perspective we encourage, certainly, fiscal authorities to look at it and to make sure that they can avoid that cliff effect and they can manage sufficient of a phasing out so that we can avoid the cliff effect that would lead to potential tightening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Our assumption, given what we read, what we know, what we discuss with colleagues in the Commission and other players, our assumption is that the RRF - the Recovery and Resilience Facility - will come about and will be a strong mixture of grants on the one hand and in larger proportion than loans on the other hand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly there are strong expectations for the purposes that I have indicated before, which have to do with addressing the damage caused to those countries and those sectors that have been massively hurt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, moving forward, common schemes and European goods that would be the greening and the digitising of our economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's hardly surprising that in any of these European important projects, game-changers in many ways, that the concerns of each and every member are taken into account, are identified and that the negotiation process that no doubt will take place will try to address that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly from our perspective, we very much hope that the RRF in the amount of €750 billion that comes on the top of the €540 billion associated with the three programmes already decided and approved by the European Council, will come to support the recovery and to look into the future with a view to greening and digitalising the European economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Concerning the PEPP, as I mentioned earlier on, one of the key elements of the PEPP which differentiates it from other purchase programmes is flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's flexibility across time: you can frontload, you can slow down, you can re-accelerate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's flexibility across asset classes: as you know, we've extended the assets that we purchase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's flexibility across jurisdictions, and that touches on the capital key that you've just mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Capital keys are the benchmark, but clearly in the name of flexibility and in order to be effective, efficient, proportional, we can deviate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There has been deviation, as you have observed from the published numbers that we released recently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Countries like Italy, Germany to a lesser extent, Portugal a little bit, are north of their capital keys.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: France is below, so deviation is part of the flexibility principle that we apply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Flexibility is the key principle that distinguishes the PEPP from the others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will never let capital key convergence that will take place at some stage impair the efficiency of the monetary policy that we have to deploy, with the dual function that I have mentioned earlier on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, concerning the strategy review, we had a discussion on that on the occasion of our Governing Council, and it is clear that the strategy review has to resume shortly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will be in September that we have our first meetings and review and discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would probably say second half of 2021, because there's an awful lot of work that needs to be done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you have hinted, the pandemic crisis that we've gone through and the impact that it will have on our economy, on inflation dynamics, and on lots of other matters that will be discussed during the course of the strategy review, will have to be taken into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is something that we have resolved around the Governing Council table: to take into account the learnings from the pandemic in our strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Another item that we decided as well was to have a whole session that will be dedicated to climate change and a whole session that will be dedicated to financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had bundled these two in the first place, and both the Vice President and myself are very happy that they form two separate items that will give rise to two sets of publications and measurements of impact and relationship between monetary policy and those two items.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I'll start with the second part of your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It gives me a chance to actually wish the very, very best of luck, determination and high spirit of cooperation to our colleagues and friends that will meet at the time of the European Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the President of the European Council, President of the European Commission, and obviously the German presidency, I say: you are carrying a lot of hopes and expectations and we hope that you succeed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Vice President and I have been long veterans of endless European meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's often the case that in Brussels, things take time and negotiations consume a lot of that time and a lot of energy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My sense is that a very large number of leaders are perfectly aware of the importance of not wasting time and of being able to signal to the Europeans, signal to the investors, signal to the world, that there is a level of consensus and a determination to invest together, to recover together and to support each other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That will be demonstrated by a good agreement, an ambitious agreement that would come about relatively soon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said to colleagues at the Eurogroup that it had to be fast, flexible but large as well - and I would certainly stand by those three adjectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sound is not ideal so I did not understand the first part of your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You were worried about the cliff effect of some of the various employment and unemployment schemes that exist around Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is the same concern that I have expressed in relation to the guarantee schemes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Hopefully fiscal authorities, governments will take it to heart to phase out gradually as the recovery takes root because clearly, we are in a timing dilemma where you really want to sustain the economy, support it, and at the same time encourage its pick-up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Hopefully the furlough schemes, the unemployment schemes, the part-time schemes that have been put in place will not stop short of the recovery having already taken hold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Yes, we are measuring the effectiveness, the efficiency of our measures on a very regular basis and we have on the occasion of this Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have to bear in mind that monetary policy measures take always a bit of time to work their way into the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It doesn't work overnight so it takes a bit of time to transmit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, we are already seeing signs of the effectiveness because clearly, one of our determinations is to help support the flow of credit to the economy, to households, to families, to businesses, and to help funding those conditions in all parts of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are seeing is that overall financial conditions have eased from the tightest levels that we had seen after the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is thanks in a large part to the comprehensive monetary policy measures that we have taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, clearly we are not back exactly to where we were before COVID-19 started to hit our radar screen and then affected all of us very severely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the bank lending to firms - which is a good indicator - it has increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From March to June, as I said, the corporate take-up of lending was unprecedented: €250 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've never seen such a high amount, and this brought the annual growth rate of loans to firms to 7.3% in May, which is up from the cruising level that we observed in February, which was 3%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, with regard to lending to families the monthly change in May returned to the pre-COVID levels after having been much lower for a couple of months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other characteristics which tell us that our monetary policy is working is that, contrary to what happened in 2008-2009, banks have taken comfort from the monetary policies that we decided, and from the governments' guarantee schemes that were put in place, not to reflect the shock to the economy in the terms and conditions of their lending.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was not the kind of tightening that was observed back in 2008-2009 at the time of the great financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Final point, and that's really based on more modelling than empirical data, our measures are providing critical support to growth and inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Based on our measurements, we estimate that the measures that we have announced between March and June are estimated to add around 1.3 percentage points to euro area real GDP growth until the end of 2022 and 0.8 percentage points to annual inflation over the same period of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So our conclusion is that based on observations of stabilisation, of reduced tightening, of improvement in the lending terms and conditions and the increase of it all, and based on our modelling of the impact of our measures, we believe that what we are doing is effective and efficient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I would say that first of all, what we have done has actually worked - and a lot was actually done, if you look at the entire panoply of tools that we have used.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is clear that, had there been more pan-euro area fiscal measures, it might have been even more efficient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me observe that both at the national level and at the regional level, meaning at the euro area level, there were fiscal measures that were taken quite rapidly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fiscal measures amounted to roughly 4% of European GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's not including the guarantee schemes that had another roughly 20%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The €540 billion are the three schemes that were put in place at the European level for employees in terms of unemployment, for companies in terms of additional guarantees, and for sovereigns at the ESM.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those are also good fiscal measures that are available and some of which are already taken up, but that will clearly add to the monetary arm that we have deployed full-fledged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On your first question, it is clear that we have to be very attentive and we have to monitor very carefully this cliff risk that I mentioned earlier on, and that the link between weak corporates and banks has to be attentively monitored, too.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me observe that banks are much better capitalised now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the end of 2019, euro area's biggest banks reached capital ratios of 14.8% versus 10.4% in 2010, so they are stronger.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The capital position results in a total excess capital of three percentage points; that is also called the management buffer, when considering all capital requirements including Pillar 2 guidance, demonstrating an overall strong ability to cope with unfavourable adverse circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, combined with our monetary policy measures announced since March, there have also been a number of measures that were decided by the Supervisory Board of the SSM that have actually encouraged banks to use some of those buffers and to respond to the current crisis in order to adjust and in order to continue to support the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, it's going to be a question of phasing out and making sure that that support lasts long enough so that the recovery takes hold and root, and can then pick up speed and help companies restore their activity and continue to develop the creation of value.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As to the mandate, it is in the articles of the ECB, it is in the Treaty, that the ECB has a primary mandate - and it's different from the Fed in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB is an institution that needs to conform to its primary mandate of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was decided by a strategy review that took place back in 2003, which decided that the best measurement was close to but below 2% inflation measurement in order to determine whether or not that mandate of price stability was satisfied.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's certainly one of the issues that we will be reviewing and discussing on the occasion of our strategy review, which is yet to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But, I agree with you that it's a difficult thing to communicate to our colleagues, our compatriots and to the Europeans at large.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, it matters so much because if there is no price stability, then clearly the economies cannot function in a sustainable, in a solid way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether you look at the corporates, whether you look at families, whether you look at governments, price stability is a key element in order to actually decide to invest, decide to employ, decide to enter into such-or-such fiscal policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Price stability, which itself includes multiple factors, is our compass and has to be our compass.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me give you an example which maybe will speak better to European friends, colleagues and compatriots.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I said recently that climate change was a matter that concerned and was particularly relevant to central banks, I had in mind our primary mandate of price stability because climate change has an impact on inflation dynamics, has an impact on productivity, has an impact on monetary transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The more uncertainty you have, the more externality is not factored in, the less certain you are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it requires that the price stability mandate measured with reference to inflation decimals, as you just said, is also understood as embedding multiple other factors that probably speak more to European compatriots and friends.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On the question of the impact of the pandemic on trade, I think there will be an almost mechanical impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are seeing it in a way with some of the results that are trickling in from Asia.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of those countries that were relying significantly on trade are having to reconsider and are having to rely more heavily on their domestic market rather than on their exports.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is simply caused by the fact that, as the pandemic is moving in sequences and some countries are recovering faster than others, they have to - not retreat back behind their borders - but simply deal more internally because economies that used to be their clients and that addressed demand to them simply are not functioning at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I also think that there will be a cultural and sociological and maybe philosophical change that will result from the pandemic, which is very well described by some of your excellent journalists, in that proximity will matter, in that consumers will be more attentive to the origin of goods, to the place of manufacturing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Corporates themselves which had been largely dependent on faraway supply chains, or very complicated and fragmented supply chains, suddenly rediscover the benefit of proximity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think the combination of the mechanical impact and the sociological - let's call it that way - impact of the pandemic will indeed have an impact on trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point, we have not at the Governing Council yet concluded as to how exactly we are going to communicate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a sort of cut-off date by which we will communicate the overall strategy review results.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it may well be that in the course of the strategy review, we decide to publish on a sequential basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Yes, indeed the Governing Council discussed the appreciation of the euro but as you know, we do not target the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is price stability and clearly to the extent that the appreciation of the euro exercises a negative pressure on prices, we have to monitor carefully such a matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question concerning changes to our programmes, we as always look at how effective and efficient our policies are and our purchase programmes have been.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So when we look at the impact that a programme like the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme has been, we can only acknowledge the fact that it has been efficient and it has been effective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether you look at the sovereign yields across the euro area, whether you look at all indicators of fragmentation, you can - and we can - and we certainly did take stock of the fact that it has worked in relation to both stabilisation of financing conditions and in respect of the risk of fragmentation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In addition to that, clearly in terms of monetary stance we also acknowledge the fact that PEPP has also served its purpose, although initially it was not intended for that particular aspect of our monetary policy, but it did.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we decided to maintain our accommodative monetary policy, and certainly under current circumstances it is very likely that the full envelope of PEPP will be used for the purpose of developing those policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me take the opportunity of your first question to first of all acknowledge and celebrate the fiscal measures that were taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had repeatedly over the course of time asked for fiscal measures to be taken, and for fiscal policies to work hand in hand with monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is clearly something that we have seen since mid-March both at the national and at the European level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you combine all the fiscal measures that were taken at national levels, you arrive at roughly a number of 4.5% of GDP consisting of measures that really have an impact on the outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is not to mention the measures that were taken under the headline of guarantees, which roughly account for about 20% of GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said in the introductory statement, the Governing Council strongly welcomed not only the three safety net measures that were decided earlier in the summer to help both employees, companies and sovereigns in total amount of €540 billion, but it did really welcome strongly the breakthrough of the Next Generation EU fund of €750 billion which clearly will have an impact most of which, by the way, is not included in our projection as they are being published today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these fiscal measures were necessary and I'm only pleased that they could be taken in due course and sometimes with the necessary waivers and exemptions that were required at the European level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just add a few words about the programme that we put in place; the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me remind you that it had two functions and it was initially calibrated for €750 billion that was back on the 18thMarch.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The dual function was the following: the first function was to stabilise market, to ensure a smooth transmission of our policy measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second function was to ease our monetary policy stance, to help counter the substantial downgrade of our inflation outlook caused by the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The PEPP announcement already in March, and its recalibration later on in June have successfully stalled the tightening in financial conditions and contributed to easing the overall monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, with markets stabilising and risks of fragmentation subsidising, I'll remind you that we are pretty much back to the pre-COVID levels in terms of both spreads and dispersion of yields.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The flexibility property of PEPP, which is distinct from the attributes of the APP for instance, has become less prominent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The role of the PEPP in easing our monetary policy stance has taken a central stage instead.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The PEPP as an emergency programme was clearly responding to the needs of the time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would add that the TLTRO that you have referred to has also served the purpose that we intended, which was to make sure that the economy was receiving abundant liquidity in order not to accumulate liquidity, not to build buffers, but in order to make sure that lending to the economy was taking place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: TLTRO III was calibrated with that in mind, so if banks can actually access a borrowing interest rate which can go down to -1%, it is only under the condition that the lending to the economy, corporate and households, is actually tantamount to what it was or more than what it was, prior to COVID-19.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: TLTRO III is very different from TLTRO I and TLTRO II in terms of take-up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've observed at the time of this massive take-up for the first operation, roughly €1.3 trillion, that it was very well spread throughout the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it wasn't country specific, it wasn't a category of banks in a country; it was across the board.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other thing that we have observed, which tells us that it is effectively working, is, first, the low interest rates which continue to apply both for corporates and for households and, second, the increased credit that is lent to the economy: 7% for the corporates, 3% for the households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The banks themselves in the July bank lending survey that we have published actually say that TLTROs have helped them to lend to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those banks that have taken up TLTROs have actually a larger proportion of loans to the economy than those that did not take up TLTROs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in this stock-taking exercise, both in relation to PEPP, in relation to continued Asset Purchase Programmes otherwise and in relation to TLTROs, we believe that our monetary policy tools as calibrated have worked well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I think I have just actually addressed the point that you are raising, which is the dual function of the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was a programme in and of its own and it had in its DNA, as I think I have mentioned at one of our last press conferences, flexibility which was clearly intended to address the issue of dispersion, the risk of fragmentation and intended to make sure that our monetary policy was transmitted across all member states of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, that function has worked, is working and is critically important in order for our monetary policy to actually transmit throughout the whole region.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has a dual function in that the other function has to do with the monetary stance, and clearly it will continue to address and deliver on that dual function.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We very much hope that it continues to work on both accounts, both the stabilisation of financing conditions, the risk of fragmentation, but also the monetary stance in order to make sure that inflation is going towards the medium-term objective that we are pursuing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, we increased the size of PEPP back in June and that was clearly intended to respond to the circumstances and to make sure that all the consequences resulting from the pandemic could be addressed through that Pandemic Emergency Programme, whether it related to fragmentation, to financial instability, or to the monetary stance that was a direct consequence of the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that continues and we've extended, as you know, the duration of our purchases as well as indicated the time frame during which we would continue to reinvest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also indicated that all of that should not in any way predicate any obstacle to our delivery of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your second question, which is a broad one, has to do with the strategy that has been developed with a bit of a lag time attributable to the pandemic by the Federal Reserve board.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, we have noted - as you have - that the dual mandate price stability and employment that the Fed pursues have been revisited.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have commented upon it and we have taken good note of those changes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as we, at the ECB, are concerned we had started our strategy review just like the Fed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We pressed the pause button during the time of the highest level of the pandemic crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually our next seminar which will focus on inflation measurements is due to be held on September 23rd.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This whole period of COVID-19 has not stopped the work streams, the ten work streams that have been assigned with specific research and analytical themes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we feel that we are up and about and ready to, as I said earlier on, turn every stone that will help us define our strategy in order to make sure that the ECB is fit for purpose and our monetary policy can deliver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it would be totally unwise and not loyal at all for me to already prejudge what the strategy review deliberations will be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's an enormous amount of work that is being done, but there will clearly be a focus on our definition of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a cornerstone of any strategy of any central bank around the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, according to Eurostat's flash estimates, inflation decreased to -0.2% in August from 0.4% in July.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That decrease, which hit the front page in some corners and was argued about, reflected a drop in inflation excluding energy and food as well as lower food inflation, which were partially offset by less negative energy inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Overall energy inflation remained a drag on headline inflation, but with less negative rates since June, still reflecting the old price drop in the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Food inflation in contrast increased sharply in April, but this surge has since unwound and movements have normalised again to usual seasonal patterns.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Inflation excluding food and energy declined as expected to 0.4% in August - and why is that?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, it is due to the temporary VAT German decrease and to the postponement… I'm sorry that I'm going into details but that's what it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the postponement of garment sales in two of the major countries of the European Union, from July to August, and also to weak consumption demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, the September 2020 projection that will be published shortly does not foresee deflationary risk, and it would not be a good economic analysis or inflation analysis to conclude that because of one measure or one month of negative results, we are heading towards deflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the contrary actually; deflationary risks which were slightly higher back in June in our latest projections have receded in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know it's a bit of a convoluted way to address your question but I wanted to do that because the -0.2% in August was a bit of a wake-up call for some.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't think that it is actually descriptive of a situation that we are interested in, which is the medium-term evolution of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I have to say that I agree with your analysis of the changes that we are seeing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a crisis like no other and it is a recovery that is very specific and very unusual as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me also say that the mandate of the European Central Bank is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the extent that we can contribute to economic development by securing price stability, this is our way to share the mission and the duties that we have in order to restructure and reorganise the economy in order for it to grow to the benefit of all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, let me also mention that the way in which the Next Generation EU fund has been decided and the special focus that has been given to the green and digitalisation dimension of the investments seems to us to be exactly the right determination in order to respond to the challenge of restructuring the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If that in terms of investment is coupled with the right economic structural reforms in order to make sure that there is good leverage of those investments, then certainly the response to the challenge will be strong.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would like to mention another way in which - well, two other ways - in which we contribute our share under our mandate to the restructuring and the recovery of our economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one is using an instrument like TLTRO in the volume that it has, this is clearly intended to fuel credit to the economy, to make sure that operators, whether they are families or enterprises, can actually have access to credit and can participate in the recovery of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, under our various purchase programmes as you know, we have an allocation that is dedicated to public institutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to the extent that the European Commission, either directly or through other entities of its choice, issues bonds and raises financing, then certainly it would qualify as a public institution, the bonds of which we could buy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not that I'm looking forward to it, but it is also our way to participate in the effort that will be a much more collective effort and that is these new instruments that were decided over the course of the summer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I think I've been quite clear and quite explicit in the introductory statement concerning the role that the appreciation of the euro plays.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will refer you back to page 3, at the top of the page, where we say: at the same time, in the current environment of elevated uncertainty, the Governing Council will carefully assess incoming information, including developments in the exchange rate, with regard to its implications for the medium-term inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a good observer of our introductory statements, exchange rate and the appreciation of our currency was not mentioned in previous documents.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is clearly an indication of the fact that we do not target, but we monitor and we monitor carefully because obviously the appreciation of our currency has an impact on our inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, it's not a policy target for us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not going to comment on the level of our currency, but it is clear that the external value of the euro is an important determinant of price setting in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will continue to monitor the development and be very attentive to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think you had a second question which had to do with Brexit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Brexit, I think, for quite a while has been included as one of the downside risks attributable to geopolitical development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The negotiations are handled very ably by Michel Barnier under the mandate that was assigned to him by the European Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We very much hope that after the Brexit that was decided and became effective as of January 2020, the outcome of the negotiations, notwithstanding the negotiation posturing, and what has been observed in the last few days, will lead to a positive outcome so that the projected downside risk that we have included in our projection will not be made worse.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: As I said, the European Central Bank does not target the exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is price stability and to that end, we have a medium-term inflation aim which we try to pursue using all the monetary policy tools that are available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is clear that we are currently observing through the analysis that we do, we are observing negative pressure on the price level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is partly attributable - largely attributable actually - to the appreciation of the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While we don't target at any level, and I have not, do not and will not comment on any level, we are also monitoring carefully the appreciation of our currency in relation to its impact on our inflation medium-term level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other question, let me take this opportunity to remind you that if and when necessary, and warranted by circumstances, and in accordance with our mandate, the Governing Council is determined to use all the policy tools that it has available, and to deploy them and calibrate them as necessary and as appropriate in order to deliver on our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That applies to all our policy tools, so I did mention the particular impact of PEPP because that is the most recent development that we've had and recalibrated back in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I did refer to the APP and to the targeted long-term refinancing operations because they were also the latest one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it doesn't mean to say that I am excluding all the other tools that we have available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Indeed if and when it was needed, we will not hesitate to use the tools as appropriately and as adequately as is needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are circumstances under which Asset Purchase Programmes are more efficient in order to reach our goals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have considered for the last few months that the Asset Purchase Programmes were the right tool in order to reach our goal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Let me tell you that we have not discussed any expansion of the envelope of PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You're giving me a very nice opportunity to hand the floor over to my colleague, Vice President de Guindos, because your question clearly relates to a topic that he is even more familiar than I am about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: De Guindos: As you are fully aware, we do not enter into any kind of assessment of evaluation of concrete operations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have made this generic recommendation based on financial stability considerations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of the main vulnerabilities that we have indicated in the past and most prominently after the pandemic, is the low profitability of the European banks and the low valuations that this low profitability is giving rise to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a generic call, a generic recommendation as I have said before in order to improve the profitability of the European banks to get rid of excess capacity and to reduce the cost structure of the European banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we do not have any sort of concrete comment with respect to very specific or particular operations as the one that you have mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I think we have said for a long time that for the currency union to be more complete and its architecture designed to the full possible extent, we would like to see a fully-developed banking union with all its attributes so that there is a euro area banking system with easy cross-border mechanisms, with resolution mechanisms, with backstop facility in place and with much more solid principles of a union than we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, I think we've also consistently indicated that we would like to see a capital markets union which would apply throughout the euro area at least, and that would facilitate access to capital by enterprises and large corporates, without the discrepancies and the different regulatory regimes and filing requirements that currently apply in order to make sure that money actually flows to where it is needed in order to finance investment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we clearly also are pleased to see that there is at least embryonic joint fiscal capacity that was decided pre-COVID-19 in order to facilitate convergence and competitiveness and hopefully investment on a cross-member state basis throughout the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would mention those three key components in order to strengthen the currency union that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm delighted to see that under the presidency of Paschal Donohoe we have a convergence of view on some of those items in order to support the euro area and make it a stronger player on the European scene.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On our strategy review, as you know we had to pause for a little while because of COVID and because of the necessity to actually concentrate all the brain power and all the forces of the ECB on devising those new tools and making sure that we could actually respond to the objectives that we had.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are now resuming our strategy review with the appropriate sequence of seminars with reactivated work in the various work streams that have been identified.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
