text: But on the fiscal front, I think that nationally and regionally there is that joint effort, which is significant, which is there, for which there is a political will of 27 countries, which is always a bit of a challenge as opposed to when you have one fiscal authority and one single country as is the case in the US.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on that page, I would really want to take this opportunity to wish my colleague and friend, Janet Yellen, the very best in her endeavour to lead the US economy in the way that only she can do it, inclusively and very smartly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question had to do with, I forgot now, because I got carried away with this fiscal aspect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You wanted to know whether I would deliver a speech in Amsterdam to describe precisely with a great level of detail, what we mean by favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have no plan scheduled for the moment, but it is pretty obvious that we understand what the general principles of the determination of the favourability of financing conditions are, and I have indicated the reference to holistic, multiple indicators, all sectors, and the key anchoring of my favourable financing conditions compass onto inflation, and how it can be used in order to counter the negative impact the pandemic has had on our inflation path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it's pretty clear what we want to achieve and how we will define those favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we will be assessing that on a regular basis, and clearly there will be yet another assessment that will take place in March, and obviously at the time when new projections will be available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, the anchor of inflation and how it impacts on the compass of the financing conditions will be even more explicit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm going to go back to that same sentence, which, you know, as you can imagine, it has been very carefully drafted and elaborated, and there's one word that I would call your attention to, and it is the word "equally".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, that sentence which is following the one that I read earlier, so I will not impose yet another reading, although I love to read, but this one says, "If favourable financing conditions can be maintained with asset purchase flows that do not exhaust the envelope over the net purchase horizon of the PEPP, the envelope need not be used in full."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "Equally", so what we signal with "equally" is, it's a balancing act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If, and I'll read the sentence, "Equally, the envelope can be recalibrated if required to maintain favourable financing conditions to help counter the negative pandemic shock to the path of inflation."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, I think it goes, I don't need to re-explain yet again, as I said, our compass, driving force, is the favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The anchor is the countering, the downward impact on inflation, on our inflation path, the downward impact of the pandemic on the inflation path, and if we determine that the financing conditions are favourable, then we adjust.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If, on the other hand favourable financing conditions cannot be preserved, as the pace of purchase has been decided, we will adjust upward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if the envelope is not sufficient, then we will recalibrate the entire envelope.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's really identified with a very high degree of flexibility and the capacity to adjust, because we are prepared to adjust all our instruments, not just the pace of purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, our mandate is price stability in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, when you, when I hear the word "fragmentation", I think about monetary transmission, throughout the whole of the euro area, throughout the member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is a driving, that is also a key function.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's one of the two functions of PEPP in particular under the extraordinary circumstances that we are going through.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Non-performing loans, this is a matter that clearly belongs to the supervisory arm of the ECB, and as you know, Andrea Enria has been very explicit about non-performing loans, he's been very explicit about what the banks should do, in order to recognise non-performing loans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: He's been very explicit as well about the asset management companies, or company, whether it's a combination of national levels and a holding at the European level, or a European entity and I will not venture in that particular field, because it belongs to the supervisory side and, as you know, we have a division of labour here at the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I'm really sorry that you see it as confusing, because it's not intended to be confusing, so let me restate again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have an envelope of €1,850 billion that is available, that can be used flexibly, depending on whether or not we reach our objective of preserving favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we don't need to use the whole envelope, because the financing conditions will have remained favourable, nonetheless, we will not use the entire envelope.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If on the other hand we need more than the envelope, because the favourable financing conditions have not been favourable and preserved as such, then the envelope will be reconsidered and recalibrated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other point that I made earlier on is that we have not only expanded PEPP, back in December, we have extended PEPP over the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, until March 2022, you can expect the ECB to be present in the market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And, you know, it is not going to be linear, it is not going to be a fixed amount, so yes, we will have to look carefully at the financing conditions, and those people in the market understand as well when and how financing conditions can evolve and change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it's not as simplistic as a linear, fixed amount, but it's also driven by the fact that we want to be able to maintain favourable financing conditions, because this, we believe that this will actually induce consumers to spend, investors to invest, and ultimately economy to fare better and inflation to go up towards our aim, therefore helping us deliver on our mandate of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, I hope to have clarified a little bit for you what you felt was confusing, and to have, I hope to have removed a bit of that confusion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the strength of the euro, let me just tell you that we are monitoring very carefully exchange rates, very carefully, because we know that exchange rates have an impact on prices, and clearly play a part in our inflation forecast, and what we can deliver with our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we are very attentive, and as I said earlier on, all instruments can be adjusted and nothing is off the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I'm now getting old enough to be realistic and to observe the development of the situation, which is really hard to predict, and really hard to forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think what we are observing on a preliminary basis, because this will really be the subject of our March monetary policy Governing Council meeting, but what we are observing is a decline in growth in Q4, and as we all know, when you have a decline in Q4, when you have negative numbers, negative numbers, we'll see that decline in Q4 will travel into Q1 and will also impact the economic outcome for Q1, added to which, as you've said, there are more containment measures, there are intensifications of lockdowns.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, lucky or not, but we had anticipated the continuation and the lockdown measures that are currently in place, not to the curfew hour, if you will, but certainly it was included in our forecast, and that leads us to conclude that our forecast for 2021, around 4 per cent, 3.9 if I recall, is still broadly valid at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the short-term risk is tilted to the downside, as well, no question about it, uncertainty is in the air.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we shall see, but we don't have enough clear, hard numbers yet to revise in any way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All I can tell you is that our forecast for 2021 is still holding as we speak.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, I hate to read yet again, so I won't do it, I fear of being accused of reading so much.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But, as we have discussed in December, we have expanded the volume of PEPP, from €1,3[50] to €1,850 billion, we have extended the duration, because we believe that, because of the contagion, current developments, because of the containment measures, we believe that an extended period of time is warranted, and we have associated those two measures, expansion and extension, with a variable, which is favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is what we strongly believe in, and we have hope that favourable financing conditions will continue and will be sustainable going forward, but we have to be prepared for all options, as a result of which we have identified that envelope, which is either not going to have to be used, if we meet the requirement of the favourable financing conditions, or which will have to be increased, recalibrated, if more is needed in order to respond to this expectation of the favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can't tell you more than that, it's a package, it came together, with TLTRO, which was also increased in volumes and extended over time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It comes on the back of very low interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it's a whole package, which, if coupled with our forward guidance, which is also very explicit, forms our monetary policy at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your first question is really why did we not start a bit earlier?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the answer to that is that of course we have flexibility but we made a commitment back in December that we would preserve favourable financing conditions that would entail tightening that would prevent us from actually following the inflation path that serves for us as the anchor of our policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have on the one hand flexibility, you have on the other hand a commitment to preserving favourable financing conditions and a clear link to the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is clearly a monetary stance decision and therefore one that requires the Governing Council to be involved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Given that we were a few days away from Governing Council meeting on monetary policy, number 1, and that we were a few days away from having the projections provided by ECB staff, we thought it would certainly be a better idea to do the analysis or the joint assessment that we want to conduct in order to determine what kind of significant increase, as you rightly said, would be needed in order to respond to the commitment that we made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Do I have a number in mind to explain significant?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to that is no, and no for a very specific reason: it's that we want to deliver on our commitment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That commitment made in December, as I said, was to preserve favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But to actually assess jointly favourable financing conditions, determine their favourability in relation to the inflation outlook, we are not bound by any particular, specific number.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what the Governing Council has decided is to - and I'll read exactly the sentence because I don't want to stray away from what was decided, by total consensus by the way - "The Governing Council expects purchases under the PEPP over the next quarter to be conducted at a significantly higher pace than during the first months of the year."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is what has been decided by consensus of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking at a time horizon of a quarter, which conveniently coincides with the staff projections that we receive on a quarterly basis and which will enable us to actually identify whether the financing conditions have evolved, remained favourable and actually help us to counter any downward pandemic effect on our inflation path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I'm also happy to explain exactly what we mean by financing conditions and favourable financing conditions, because I know that this was a question that many of you had.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, and I am sorry if I'm stealing the thunder of some of those who wanted to ask that question, but I know that it's a question that is on your mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we measure financing conditions, I use two words that some of you found either questionable or a bit strange.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I use the word "holistic" and I use the word "multifaceted".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It wasn't a fancy or a tantrum on my part; it was very targeted at particular indicators.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we mean by holistic is that we cover the whole chain of transmission from the upstream stage where you find the risk-free interest rate, where you find the sovereign yields, to the downstream aspect of the credit terms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That clearly includes a multiplicity of rates that we all look at as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has to do with a stage where monetary policy acts with a lag.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Upstream, essentially down to risk-free interest rate, sovereign yields, it's a segment that actually responds quite rapidly which is measured on an ongoing basis, and where our monetary policy can be most efficient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What's important is that actually financial institutions, those that provide financing to the economy, actually use those rates to determine the credit terms that they are then going to offer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That upstream is clearly an important component but it is not the component of our assessment of the financing conditions, which is why I use the word holistic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We go from upstream to downstream and the second word that I used, which is "multifaceted", was also apparently a bit of a puzzle for some.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, multifaceted, we organise information in a multidimensional form that might be more convenient for some of you, where each indicator can be studied in its own right, and assessment is not based on an aggregated synthetic measure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't operate mechanically; we look at all the indicators, we focus indeed on what is upstream because that's where we can act and that's where banks and providers of financing actually take their cue about the credit terms that they're going to offer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also important to be multifaceted because there are some downstream components that are not necessarily going to be influenced by upstream movement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Take for instance some fiscal measures that have rightly been decided, such as providing moratorium or guarantees.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If that was withdrawn, well, clearly it will have an impact on the downstream aspect of the indicators.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the same way, our TLTRO is also helping the downstream aspect of what we are looking at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the reason why we look at financing conditions, looking at the upstream, the downstream but looking at them in their own right in a holistic way, all of it, the whole transmission chain, and each and every one of them because they might respond differently depending on what is addressed to them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the second question of course is: how do we assess favourability?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, if you look carefully at the introductory statement, we refer to a joint assessment of how financing conditions and our inflation outlook have evolved since the last time we identified favourability and concluded with our assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at the main drivers of course, so concerning the anchor that I have used as well the last time we had the press conference, it's the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The assessment of the financing conditions, determination of how favourable they are is going to be done in conjunction with the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The compass that we have, another word that I used as well, is the financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we use all that and with a bit of good work, good analysis based on projections and this joint assessment, our monetary policy will contribute to taking the economies across the bridge of the pandemic that we are suffering from and have been suffering from for the last year or so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your last point, as I said: quarterly basis is very convenient because it helps with having the right data, the right assessment, the projections of our staff sometimes checked by the national central banks as well twice a year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have fresh data, fresh information that is extremely useful in order to look at these two components that I have discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The anchor inflation outlook, how does it evolve, how does it look like in the medium term?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the compass that we use, which is the financing conditions, which we committed to preserve as favourable in order to resist the downward impact of pandemic on our inflation path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that some of you listening are looking at weekly numbers, fair enough.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the Governing Council is not micromanaging the operations and, in that vein, actually, I would like to tell you that when you look at this coming Monday, don't expect a huge big rise, okay?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have still a good volume of redemptions this coming Monday.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can also tell you that we are beginning to implement the decision that was taken today to significantly increase our purchases as of today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The real pace on a weekly basis, which some of you are interested in, is not going to be visible or strongly visible this Monday.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But again we are looking at a time horizon which is longer than the next week, and the Governing Council meets any time when it's needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're getting very close to the first anniversary of days when we were meeting almost on a daily basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's when we started PEPP, so if it is necessary in order to respond with flexibility and to deliver on our commitment to preserve favourable financing conditions, the Governing Council can always meet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But clearly, the Executive Board can also use the flexibility that is embedded in the programme in order to actually deliver on the decision that was taken today, which is to use flexibility in order to significantly increase our purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me remind you once again that when we assess favourable financing conditions, we do it with a series of indicators that go from upstream to downstream.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that Philip actually in his recent speech very clearly indicated what was the composition of those upstream and downstream elements and what was the interconnection between the two and why the upstream actually mattered, without prejudice to us also looking very carefully at the downstream.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do that on the one hand, and to assess favourability we look on a quarterly basis at the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the basis of the commitment we made to preserve favourable financing conditions, that determines the decision that is made by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the occasion of this particular monetary policy decision, the Governing Council by consensus at the table decided that it was warranted to significantly increase purchases for the next quarter with a monthly reference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no reference to any kind of yield curve control if it is the question that you are angling at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are preserving favourable financing conditions with a look at the inflation outlook that we have and how one contributes to reducing the downward impact of the pandemic on our inflation path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, look, what we did with the envelope was quite spectacular I would suggest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was then again increased by €500 billion in December, and in December, we clearly focused on preserving favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I have not repeated it ten times, I don't think I will have said it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment, we probably have about €1 trillion left in the envelope.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's very clear also in the introductory statement, to preserve favourable financing conditions, if we need less than the whole envelope, we will not use the whole envelope.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If, equally, to preserve favourable financing conditions we need to recalibrate the whole envelope, we will do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, again, it's flexibility within the monthly purchases under the quarterly decision that is made by the Governing Council and it's flexibility as to how we use the overall envelop during the life of PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first one, let me make a few comments about inflation, because if you look at the staff projections which will be released later on this afternoon, you will see that our inflation forecast is of 1.5 for this year and then moves down to 1.2 and finishes in 2023, which is our medium-term horizon, at 1.4.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is possible that this year, particularly at the end of 2021, inflation actually hits 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I will tell you something: we will see through that for a very clear reason and that is that inflation will most likely go up possibly to 2% because of some technical and temporary reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just mention a few and we can go through the list, but it is the German VAT return, which has had an upward pressure on prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is the significant modification of the weighing in the HICP basket to adjust to the change of consumer behaviour and consequences that it has in '21.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has to do with some idiosyncratic factors having to do with Italy and France that have extended into '21 some of the sales, particularly in the clothing industry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has to do of course with the increase in prices in the oil segment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, for all these reasons that are, we believe, temporary, technical, as I have just tried to explain, we will see through that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is important for us to actually look at what happens next and to look at the medium-term inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, because of subdued demand, and second, because of the slack in the economy that will gradually over the course of the recovery reduce, but which is large and has a significant impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, for all these reasons, we believe that, while it has increased a little bit in the first two years, in the third year, we are still at 1.4, which is far away from our inflation path pre-pandemic, and of course, far away from our aim which is close to, but below, 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's what I really wanted to explain in relation to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's how we see it and clearly our inflation aim, and our inflation path pre-pandemic, remain two very important anchors of the monetary policy decisions that we will make.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The question about climate, so I think that it is almost unanimous within the Governing Council that climate imperatives are nothing less than imperatives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have said repeatedly that it is the biggest challenge that is addressed to us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Hence, in my view, any institution, whatever its mandate, whatever its remit has to question itself and wonder what can be done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, obviously, an independent central bank has to deliver on its mandate and we need to do that and we need to look at what we can do in compliance and in respect of our mandate, without over-interpreting the mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Using this primary objective, which in my view justifies fully that climate change matters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Appropriate supervision that falls under the responsibility of Andrea Enria, but on all those accounts we have to explore what we can do, how efficient we can be in doing so and to your very clear question, it will apply of course to how we value collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will apply to how we value corporate bonds, with proper risks being taken into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, at this point in time, the main responsibility in my view, in the view of the Governing Council, lies first and foremost with governments, governments at the European level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Europe is delivering in that respect, but with governments in the various member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be a staged approach where clearly information, disclosure, investment will all be required in order to address the climate change issue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, while we are on the same page in many ways with some of the civil society organisations, we cannot help but regret enormously the approach, the conduct that was adopted which clearly by paragliding on to the roof of the ECB is exposing people's health, life possibly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't think that this is the necessary way to conduct a dialogue, but we will definitely continue this dialogue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all I'm delighted that my colleague Fabio Panetta decided to quote a French group.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I go back again to the introductory statement and will be happy to read it again, although you have it in front of you I'm sure: "The Governing Council expects purchases under the PEPP over the next quarter to be conducted at a significantly higher pace than during the first months of this year".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I tell you that we are moving into action as early as tomorrow, I think that that fits the bill.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you will find some that will want a little more, a little less, a little this, a little that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Suffice to say that there was consensus at the table of the Governing Council today to do exactly that, conduct a significantly higher pace of purchases during the next quarter as compared with the first three months of this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, on the issue of the massive fiscal stimulus that is likely to be signed into law probably today and will give, knowing the Treasury head Yellen, the efficiency that she has I'm sure that there will be immediate implementation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because of rules that many of you are familiar with, until a piece of legislation is voted, we cannot take that into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Hence, it is not embedded in our projections, but we do - and the introductory statement makes reference to the external demand, to the impact that a massive fiscal stimulus will have on our pace of growth that it will have on trade of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we believe that the Biden plan is actually going to have an impact, not to be overestimated though, because clearly there will be a lot of domestic measures that will impact predominantly the US domestic markets, but it will have an impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: An external demand that is addressed to the euro area and to other countries of course will generate probably and will have an impact on our growth projections, and that will indeed be reflected in three months' time when we produce our June projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One thing that I will say is that the big difference if you will between the Biden stimulus, which as I said, debated, voted by the two houses, signed into law, cheques in the mail and our massive fiscal stimulus here in Europe is that there is a bit of a lag time between the two.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Next Generation EU, as we say in the introductory statement, is critically important in order to help stimulate the European economies from a fiscal point of view and is also terribly important for two other reasons: because it needs to address the issue of heterogeneity between countries and between sectors, and it needs to focus on what will be productivity enhancing and moving our economies and our Europe into the future with the focus on digital and green.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is a time lag between the two, let's face it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, while we import a bit of yield increase, the trade movements are going to come, but our own fiscal measures are not kicking in yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the risk of boring all of you, I think that when the Governing Council by full consensus decides that purchases under the PEPP over the next quarter will be conducted at a significantly higher pace than during the first months of this year, it is not an insignificant commitment that they're making.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I remind you that it comes on the top of the monthly €20 billion that are purchased under the APP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think there is a serious taking into consideration of the undesirable yield increase that we are seeing, that we have seen in the last few weeks, a portion of which certainly is attributable to the inflation expectations and the GDP growth expectations in the United States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I hope we can move fast on the fiscal front here in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, obviously staff here at the ECB have been very diligently looking at the Biden plan and trying to assess on a very preliminary basis what the impact will be on both growth through the trade channel in particular, and also on the inflation expectations and particularly on the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That will be reflected in future projections because this has not been taken on board this time around.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think they also want to have a look very carefully at what is eventually delivered after the signing into law of what has been voted yesterday by the House of Representatives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, we are not focusing on any particular segment of the yield curve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to look at the entire yield curve and when it comes to mind that the ten years sovereign yield is one that is often referred to, it is not the only one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will look at the entire yield curve which has evolved in a slightly different way depending on whether you are in the two to five years or way beyond including up until 30 years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not going to take you through that again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I hope what we mean by holistic is clear enough.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we mean by multifaceted is clear enough as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know those are not usual words for this particular type of press conference, but never mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can always expand our vocabulary as long as we know what's behind it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the European asset management company, the ECB is continuously monitoring the impact of the COVID-19 crisis on banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A large-scale system-wide increase in NPLs would require a comprehensive approach at the national and EU levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, based on the development and the monitoring, different policy options are being considered and could be further explored.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly at the ECB we have taken note of the Commission proposal to asset management companies that would operate at the national level and we agreed that this is a useful way to manage a systemic NPL problem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you also know, my colleague Andrea Enria has had in mind a more pan-European approach.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This might come along later, but I think the key urgency is to make sure that there are mechanisms in place that can deal with the risk that bears on banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question concerning the appreciation or the level of the euro at the moment, I have said it before, I repeat it again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not targeting any particular exchange rate for the euro, but equally we monitor very carefully the development of the rate because clearly it has an impact on economic activity and the outlook for price stability in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has been quite volatile lately and we do monitor carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think in the current environment the ECB will continue to monitor developments in the exchange rate, but we don't focus on the exchange rate as such.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We focus on the impact that it has on prices and the implication that it has for the medium-term inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, I would like to observe that, although it's in the remit of the Commission and the Council, the decision to extend or to activate the general escape clause, to keep it alive if you will - I never know whether it's activate or deactivate - but to keep it in place, in other words, escape is allowed and some of the current constraints under the current SGPs are waived.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Their decision to extend it until such time when the European economies are back to pre-COVID-19 is, in our view, the right approach.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are consulted and this is certainly the position that we would take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the extent that under the winter projections, the Commission foresees the return to pre-COVID-19 in mid-2022, this is actually appropriate in our view to keep that waiver until such time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our hope is that by the time the general escape clause is deactivated and constraints return, SGPs will have been revisited and will have been improved in order for it to be more simple, more focused on productivity, investment, and also indeed with the fiscal discipline embedded, but probably with a renewed look at what criteria, what measurements are used.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was decided back in the 1990s and the situation has changed significantly since those days.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's only fair to look at it again and to see what is mostly needed in order to give both stability and solid sustainable and stable growth going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, thank you very much for your question, really it gives me a chance to go back to the key part of our deliberations, which has to do with really taking a good look at the economic situation both from a growth perspective, from an inflation perspective, from the financing terms that are available in the context of forming our joint assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of outlook, it's very much a "on the one hand, on the other hand" situation because there are clearly signs of improvement that are coming from essentially an improvement in the rollout of the vaccination plans in most euro area countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, we are clearly seeing continued contagion, continued pressure put upon some of the economic sectors as well as the health sectors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Equally, also on the more negative side, we are seeing the risk of the potential evolution of the virus, variants that can constitute a threat.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still have this overall environment of uncertainty about the economic situations that really surrounds the near-term outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it is very much reflected in the consumers' behaviour because when you look at the retail sales for instance, they rose in February but they remain certainly well below the pre-pandemic level and well below the fourth quarter of 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, you have now a service sector that seems to be bottoming out, which is still in contractionary territory.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The PMI on services is, if I recall, at 49.6, so short of the 50, but heading in the right direction and let's not forget that this was the sector that was most affected by the economic recession.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's very much as I said, on the one hand, on the other hand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we look now at the risk assessment that we always conduct as well, we still have the same risk assessment as we had back in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still see near-term risks tilted to the downside and we still see medium-term risks much more balanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Overall everything that we have looked at in terms of high-frequency indicators, latest information, data, surveys, really confirm the projection that we had back in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's on all accounts and in terms of inflation numbers we are also on the same page as we were with our projections back in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you asked me a second question, which had to do with the appreciation of the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do not target any kind of exchange rate, but we monitor very carefully exchange rates and variations because, clearly, that can have a downside impact on prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I'll take your second question first because really it's a case of everybody having to do their job and everybody having to comply with their respective mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is price stability and we are riveted to the aim that we have under the circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So NextGenerationEU is clearly in the fiscal domain, as are some national decisions that have been made, that are being made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fiscal authorities have to do what they have to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We certainly complete each other, complement each other, but we are not substitutes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there was delay or any hurdles that would not be overcome, it's not a question of substituting because we are complementing each other, each of us in our respective area and with our respective mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the PEPP purchases, you did pick up that in the Introductory Statement we decided to keep the pace of purchase at a significantly higher pace.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just want to remind you that when we do that, it's with a view to preserving favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decided that we had to take action and we significantly increased our pace of purchase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That decision was made on the [11] March and was readily implemented not for the entire month - which is really the relevant period of time when you want to assess the pace of purchase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We implemented right away as of the 16 March [on settlement basis], and we have continued doing so without any wavering, and in a very determined and decisive way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There has been a clear and significant increase in that pace of purchase and it will continue to be that way because as I said earlier on, our assessment of the economic situation is broadly the same.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The joint assessment that we do on - I was going to say, on an intermediate basis as opposed to the comprehensive assessment that we conduct at the time of the projections - also lead us to believe that we need to continue those purchases at this significantly higher pace than during the first two months of 2021.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On the first one: let me just assure you that on the occasion of this Governing Council we did not discuss any phasing out of PEPP because it is simply premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would also observe that any determination concerning the pace of purchase under the PEPP is done not on a date or a calendar basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We conduct a joint assessment of those financing conditions throughout the whole spectrum, and the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the combination of the two - the financing conditions and the inflation outlook, it's on the basis of these two elements, which are quite complicated in their own respect, each of them - that we determine the pace of purchase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we have done this time around on an intermediate basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will do it again in June, when we have the projections, but any phasing out was not discussed and it is just premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the bank lending survey, I would just remind you that - and I think it's mentioned very clearly in the Introductory Statement - that loan volumes have actually slightly increased over the last quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The BLS is also forward-looking and translates really the sentiment and the views of banks as to their future activity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This BLS, as far as the sentiment about their future activity, indicates two things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is, there is moderate tightening as opposed to much stronger tightening in the two previous surveys, so while it is still tightening, that tightening is moderate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, there is the view by banks for their future activity that there will be less demand originating from the non-financial corporate sector on the grounds of less need for investment and capex in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third point that we take away as well, and that's what banks are actually saying, is that TLTROs, TLTRO III in particular of course - PELTROs to a certain extent for some banks - are playing a critically important role in helping with their lending operations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The recent take-up that we have seen back in March of the latest TLTRO operations is evidence of the fact that banks are drawing benefits from those TLTROs, under the condition, I'll remind you, that they continue to extend lending to the economy at least on par with what they were doing pre-pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: One thing that you got absolutely right - and it's probably because I have repeated it extensively - is that our pledge is to preserve favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a result of that, back in March we significantly increased the pace of purchase and we have decided today to continue to proceed at this significantly higher pace of purchase relative to the first two months of 2021.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the financing conditions throughout the chain, from upstream to downstream, we are seeing broadly stable financing terms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's pretty much reflected in all the measurements that we are looking at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't only look at bond yields whether they are real or nominal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course we do the difference and we draw the line between what's real and what's nominal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we try to understand what is the originating factor of any movement up or down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are seeing broadly stable conditions overall, whether it's bond yields or whether it is corporate or household interest rates and terms and conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your question about the weekly numbers: I would like to once again draw your attention to the fact that weekly numbers are not the most relevant numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that some of you will continue commenting on weekly numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fine, but what matters much more are the monthly numbers, and that's how you can really understand the trend and the pace that we are adopting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to encourage any of you to do the maths, but we do them as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we compare what has been purchased on average, taking into account January and February, compared with what we did in March - which was only half a month, remember, because we only started [with settlement] on 16 March - we have significantly increased the pace of purchase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are back pretty much to the numbers that we had back in July.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, we have decided this time around to continue at this significantly increased pace of purchase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also look at net purchases; those are the numbers that we publish and that are most relevant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, obviously there is the composition within those numbers and you have to appreciate obviously redemptions and arrive at the right comparisons, but trust me, those comparisons indicate a good significant increase in our pace of purchase - and will continue to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On the phasing out and the transition question that you had: as I said, this matter was not discussed because it is premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still have a long way to go until we have crossed the bridge of the pandemic and the recovery is sustainable, solid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've referred to an economy on crutches; one fiscal crutch, one monetary crutch.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The economies of the euro area have to go across the bridge of the pandemic and have to be on solid and sustainable ground in order to walk on a self-sustained basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, obviously we look at what other central banks around the world do on a regular basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All banks, including Canada, Japan, the Fed, the Bank of England, all of them because we are close-knit and we appreciate what is being done and why.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Each and every country has its own specificity and its own accompanying measures that complement their monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm referring here to fiscal plans that can be significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question: the first conclusion I draw is that competitive sports in all categories, whether it is synchronised swimming to trampoline, can actually equip you with a little spirit of competition, hard skin and the desire to excel in your sports - but also in politics, if one desires to go into politics.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This clearly seems to be the case with Ms Baerbock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second lesson I would draw is that you don't need to be a seasoned grey-haired or white-haired person to enter into politics and be recognised for your own talent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I very much welcome an athlete, a young woman and certainly one who has a very high concern for climate issues and protection of the environment, which as you know on a personal basis I care for.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It also shows that Chancellor Merkel has not discouraged younger women to enter into politics.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's a very high tribute to a woman who has led this country where we are currently - Germany - for 16 years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: You rightly pointed out that our intermediate assessment and our review of existing data, information, high-frequency numbers and all the rest actually confirms our projection of March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously I'm not going to give you any specific number concerning a particular quarter because that will be done when we publish our projection next June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Overall, what staff of the ECB are saying is that their projections are very much confirming - or rather the current economic situation and the outlook as we see it at the moment are confirming - the direction of the projections, as published in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They also confirm that while the first quarter might - we are very attentive - but might very well be negative, on the other hand the second quarter is pointing to a positive outcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your second question puzzles me a little bit because I don't know what is the normal pace of purchase of PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decided in December to no longer be operating on the basis of a linear volume, but we decided to commit to preserving favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is a determination that we made in December, that we demonstrated in March, that we observe now, and that will guide our assessment - a joint assessment, comprehensive this time - next June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a joint assessment that we are bound to make either at an intermediate level when we don't have the projections, or on a comprehensive basis when we have the projections, to actually jointly assess favourable financing conditions throughout the supply chain of financing, and the inflation outlook, and the impact that one has over the other with a view to returning to the pre-pandemic inflation path, which is clearly going way, or some way, into the inflation aim that we have, which as you know is close to but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Don't take me literally, but it would be nice to move in tandem with the Fed because that would mean that our inflation numbers are aligned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, clearly Fed has a dual mandate, 2%, with employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are close to but below 2%, but if you look at where the Fed is, where we are, when you look at expectations in the United States and expectations in the euro area, we are not on the same page.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It would clearly predicate that we will not operate in tandem with the Fed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's very much a given and it's not me looking into a crystal ball; it's where we are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Slack in the economy, our assessment at this point in time is that we will - the euro area economies will return on average to the pre-pandemic economic level in the second half of 2022.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm taking precautions here because when I say on average, there will be divergences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be countries that will be lagging behind because of multiple factors, but on average we are seeing the euro area economy back to pre-pandemic level, second half of 2022.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It doesn't mean that all slack will have been absorbed because my take is that entering into the pandemic, there was some slack.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My hope as well is that there will be as many jobs, newly created, and that the ECB will contribute to such developments by delivering price stability as our mandate so requires.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, as you know, interest rates are the traditional tool of monetary policy and based on our experience, the negative interest rates are continuing to be an effective tool for providing monetary policy accommodation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we have clear evidence that cutting rates below zero provides additional stimulus to the euro area economy, as rate cuts are passed through the bank lending rates, and overall financing conditions of firms and households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, in the whole of the euro area negative rates are passed on to corporates, to a large extent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not all banks do that, but many banks do that in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as households are concerned, it's 5% of deposit accounts of households that are imposed negative rate consequences by banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's double that amount, so based on our numbers, based on the data provided by banks, it's 10% of those deposit accounts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I completely appreciate that people who are saving are not satisfied with being charged the consequences of negative rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have to look at the situation from a global point of view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We cannot look at a particular depositor or a particular category.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to look at the whole economy, and we know that by putting in place those negative interest rates we are effectively supporting the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are encouraging enterprises, families, households, young couples to actually borrow at very low rates in order to invest, in order to buy their first apartment, in order to buy some equipment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The contribution that that is, in order to support the economy, in order to make sure that jobs are kept, in order to make sure that corporates can continue to operate and produce, is clearly a trade-off against some aspects that are resented by those that are only savers, and are not borrowers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In every household you have savers and you have borrowers, so there is always a trade-off.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to look at the aggregate euro area economy ourselves and deliver on our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Thank you for asking your question on a project that keeps many, many of our very talented staff busy at the ECB, but also in the National Central Banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's really a project where everyone is involved and everybody is contributing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are well into the second half of our strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still have more work to do and more seminars that are planned in the weeks ahead.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My commitment is that we will deliver on our strategy in the fall of '21.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we manage to conclude our set of seminars and to conclude our deliberation to arrive at this new strategy before that, then of course we will come to you and to Europeans and to the European Parliament and to all those that we are accountable to earlier than that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fall of '21 is clearly the deadline that we have set for ourselves in order to deliver on the strategy and its outcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking at multiple options, proposals, views, recommendations and we are not yet landing in any particular zone that will be the ultimate conclusion because we need to keep all options open.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a commitment that I have made to the Governing Council members as I am leading this exercise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I promise that we will not deliver until everything has been examined and conclusions have been reached.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some more attractive, others more alternative, but we'll get there when we get there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: As I just indicated in the previous response, we are looking at multiple options, multiple proposals as far as our strategy review is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we also have our business-as-usual track of business, which consists of deciding monetary policy every six weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On that particular track, we are guided by the decision that was made in December, which is not yield curve control, but the commitment to preserving favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know it's a little bit more subtle, it's a bit more complicated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It requires that we analyse the financing terms that are available from risk-free rates all the way down to terms and rates available for corporates and households, and the inflation outlook and the impact that one has over the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's more complicated than having just a yield definition that we would just abide by, but this is not the choice that was made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are loyal to the decision that was made in December, applied in March, reiterated in April and that we will also take into account to calibrate our monetary policy decision in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On tourism, I think we are both well placed to address the question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Do you want to take it, the one on tourism?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Spain is clearly one of the countries that has fantastic tourism.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: de Guindos: Well, I think that is going to depend on the evolution of the vaccination process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the vaccination rollout gains momentum - and we expect that this is going to gain momentum - well, we hope that a high percentage of the population will be vaccinated and that this is a positive sign, a positive indication that perhaps the summer season will not be totally lost, as it was in 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Vaccination is going to be the driver, in my view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Yes, and I think in quite a few of those countries we are seeing a gradual acceleration of the vaccination base and that's really much in demand for those economies that are particularly sensitive to the social distancing rules, as tourism can be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the debt question: all countries around the world, and the euro area countries are no exception, but all countries around the world had to increase their debt because they had to respond to the worst possible crisis that the economies had had in post-World War times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was just no question as to whether or not the 60% threshold should or should not be exceeded and whether you were below the 60 or way above the 60, debt had to be increased, full stop.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The real question is: what use is made of debt now going forward?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly the use of debt in the first few months of the pandemic had to do with keeping the economy afloat, making sure that businesses were not going down the tube, making sure that people were not left without income.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The real question now is: what use is made of debt?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is the public spending targeted and temporary in order to cross the bridge of the pandemic, as I have indicated earlier in the first instance?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, is this public financing going to be spent on productivity-enhancing reforms that will actually improve the growth potential of those economies?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If that is the case and financing terms remain attractive relative to the growth that can be developed as a result of those targeted temporary measures and productivity-enhancing measures, then this is debt put to good use.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that has been described much more so by fiscal authorities and governments than by me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, this is a matter that will be reviewed by the European Commission, by the European Council members in order to redefine the terms of the Stability and Growth Pact .

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this is a matter which is not for the European Central Bank to decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, thank you for that open question because it gives me a chance to tell you a little bit about how this meeting went.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me start with what would be my take-away of the overall analysis that we conducted, the joint assessment that we had and the conclusion that we reached.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And let me drill down a little bit on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We spent a lot of time looking at the quarterly staff projections and went deep into each and every item of those projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In conclusion of this work, I could say that we were somewhat more optimistic about the economic outlook than we were three months ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The latest signal that we are getting signals a strong rebound which is starting with the second quarter and hopefully will be amplified in the third quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We took that moderate optimism from the fact that, number 1, we are seeing that the vaccination roll-out has accelerated significantly and is increasingly out-pacing other advanced economies' vaccination roll-out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, we are seeing that containment measures are gradually lifted which should lead to a vigorous bounce back in that sector which was most affected, which is the service sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the service PMI, for instance, it is clearly now in expansionary territory.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It went up from just marginal 50 in April to now 55.2 in May.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Equally, when we look at the sentiment that is regularly published by the Commission we are also seeing a sharp increase in May.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually [April was] the largest increase that they had ever recorded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We expect private consumption to rise sharply as the containment measures are gradually lifted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's good news from the services point of view, which was most affected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the manufacturing sector, which earlier on has been robust, it continues to be robust.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the Europe PMI manufacturing, it has stabilised at very elevated levels to be at 63.1 in May.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also looked into those supply-side bottlenecks that clearly have an impact in the short term on our inflation, particularly now, but for the short-term outlook as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's all on the positive front, but we also acknowledged and looked into those uncertainties that we have on the horizon, which have to do with the evolution of the pandemic and how we see little nests of revival based on another kind of variant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are also dependent on how fast the containment measures will be lifted, particularly for those countries that are most sensitive to the service industry, the activities that are most a factor of social non-distancing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, if those containment measures are lifted early on - the tourism season, for instance - a lot of the transportation activities will pick up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a result of that, our staff increased their projection for '21/'22 and kept it at the same level in '23.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then the big job of the Governing Council after that, after it has looked deeply into our projections and what we see in terms of macroeconomic situation, our job is then to look at the financing conditions on the one hand and the inflation outlook on the other hand because we do conduct that joint assessment which we decided back in December, that we confirmed again in March, and which determines our monetary policy reaction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the financing front, we clearly see broadly stable financing conditions taking together the corporate and the household sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a little bit of an increase in the corporate sector which is clearly attributable to two particular countries; one is the Netherlands, the other one is Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is probably attributable to some tactical approach taken by the banks in those particular countries to take full advantage of the TLTROs' conditions and to make sure that they catch up with the commitments that they have to take under TLTROs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Overall, absent those particular factors, we see a little bit of tightening - very, very moderate though - but there is a potential that what we observed on the market interest rates actually could pass through or is at risk of passing through to the financing conditions that are applicable to the corporate sector in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the household sector it is not the case because the financing of the household sector is at rock bottom at about a 1.31% interest rate, which has never been so low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, this is the first part of the joint assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do the joint assessment, and we look on the other side at inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said in the Introductory Statement, we are seeing some short-term improvement of the inflation number and our assessment for '21 is 1.9%, which is clearly north of what we had in our last assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we need - and we did that throughout our discussions - we tried to really dissect what is underneath and what is the lasting impact of some of those factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that it's worth reminding ourselves where we were a year ago compared with where we are today, because that's how inflation is calculated; year-on-year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A year ago a lot of activities went down, prices were under downward pressure, clearly, and the down movement that we saw at the time has now - and is being - compensated by an upward movement that we see in many of those prices that went down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A clear example of that is the energy prices, where if you remember, the price of oil and all derivative products went way down and has now recovered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see what we call a base effect between '20 and '21.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will see more of it because there is another base effect that will be attributable to the German VAT.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A year ago, 1 July, there was a decrease of VAT in Germany, deliberately, in order to support the economy and sustain demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be seeing the base effect in the months to come, which is probably a reason why inflation in some countries, Germany being one, will go north of our forecast for the whole of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mentioned earlier on the bottleneck issues which will push certainly production prices up, but what we need to really focus on - and that's what we did - we need to focus on services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Services is predominantly labour and we need to really dig down into the labour cost, into the wage increases, into the collective bargaining agreements that are reached currently and will be reached hopefully in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In that respect, we don't see much by way of service prices going up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at many of the service industries, prices are not moving much.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see a little bit of movement, possibly, and we hope that we will see more of it and that more of the price pressures are actually channelled into higher wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are not seeing much of that at the moment, probably because of the slack that we have in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's not forget that if you compare with a little more than a year ago, we have 3.2 million more people unemployed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you take the combination of the unemployed and those that are under furlough schemes, we're talking about 15% of people who are not on the job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These particular aspects were really examined in great detail to understand what is behind inflation, why it will impact significantly 2021, to a lesser extent 2022 because some of the base effects that I have described for you will begin to fade and will not actually have much of an impact in 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But - and that's a but and it's important and we discussed it at length - there is something that is moving a bit and that is core inflation, when you take out energy and food.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On that front, there is a slight movement upward, which has now been repeated for a couple of months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the reason why our forecast for core inflation has gone up a bit to 1.1 in '21, 1.2 in '22 and 1.4 in '23.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are far away from our ultimate aim; close to but below 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we certainly are not where we would like to be once the pandemic is over.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are seeing some movement there and we will continue to monitor that carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment, certainly in headline inflation, due to temporary, specific factors that I have just described and I have no reason to believe that it is going to last through and will be included in a rise in inflation that we would see in our medium-term projection.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Sorry if I was a bit long, but I have taken you through our deliberations throughout.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: That takes me to the decision that we actually made, which is, as I said, a steady hand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Based on the joint assessment that I have just described, what the Governing Council has decided - as I read in my Introductory Statement - is to expect net purchases over the quarter to continue to be, and I would like to quote the Introductory Statement for you, "to continue to be conducted at a significantly higher pace than during the first months of 2021."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we are going to do that in the next three months according to market conditions, which clearly include seasonality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will do that with the core attribute of PEPP, which is flexibility across asset classes, flexibility across time, flexibility across geography, as you know well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is done on the basis of, as I said, the quarterly joint assessment that is decided by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then it's for the Executive Board to actually implement and deliver on the basis of this joint assessment, and according to market conditions including seasonality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question: I'm afraid you'll be disappointed because I might just very well refer to my Lisbon line.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's too early, it's premature, it's unnecessary to discuss those longer-term issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those matters have not been discussed by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: You're going to be bored with me, but I am going to repeat myself.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Any discussion about exit from the PEPP, as you just mentioned, would be premature, it's too early and it will come in due course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Certainly for the moment it's too early and premature, as simple as that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has been suspended unfortunately because of COVID-19 and the enormous amount of work that just landed on the shoulders of the very same staff that was working on the strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some would consider it undue long and we are certainly working really hard to complete this process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I hope that we'll be able to give the outcome of the strategy review in the second half of '21.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I still stick to that, but anything having to do with PEPP and any kind of transition, exit, whatever you call it, has not been discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The commitment that we made, the monetary policy decision that we made in December and then in March, which were both critically important, is to make sure that we preserve favourable financing conditions while also being very attentive to the inflation outlook, with a view to resisting any downward pressure that would not help in returning to the inflation path of the pre-pandemic period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we do and that's how we conduct our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Financing conditions comprise a whole range of indicators from, as I said, financing conditions for corporates, for households, for sovereigns, market interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We assess that and then we identify the inflation outlook, the various components, the likelihood of our projections, and we come to a monetary policy decision which, as I said, is in a way a steady-hand translation of what we decided in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: The proposal that is made to the Governing Council included the words that I have repeated, which you find in the Introductory Statement, which is the proposal to conduct purchases at a significantly higher pace than during the first months of 2021.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was no alternative wording and there was unanimous support for the Introductory Statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there was broad agreement over what was being proposed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the baseline and whether or not we take into account alternative variants and evolution of the virus: we will publish later this afternoon our scenarios.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do have the baseline and we also have a scenario that is the mild scenario and a scenario that is an aggravated scenario.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's in those scenarios that you will find some of the hypotheticals that you refer to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: You're quite right that the inflation forecast, the inflation projection, has been revised upward for '21 and '22 and not for '23, and that's for the reasons that I have explained earlier on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is also - and I have discussed that quite a bit - the movement on core inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are clearly seeing improvement and that dates back to December because our forecast for the core inflation outlook has been revised gradually, slowly, by 0.1% over the course of the last projection exercises.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that's certainly one of the reasons why we believe that the steady hand is actually the right response in the face of these improvements in core inflation, which we will continue to monitor very carefully, added to which you will have noticed as well: the balance of risk which was tilted to the downside in our last projection, is now considered as balanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point: we forecast inflation at 1.9% this year and 1.5% in 2022, and we assume in that respect that some of the bottlenecks that we know of at the moment - which theFinancial Timeshas referred to in various articles actually - that some of those bottlenecks will gradually fade out because it is a matter of the supply response.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If chips are not being produced in sufficient quantity in a particular part of the world, there will be in the course of time additional factories, additional work processes, put in place and possibly the offer of products is revisited as we know is the case for instance in the automotive industry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, the assumption is from our perspective that many of those bottlenecks will actually be overridden by the ingenuity of those who produce and those who revisit their supply chain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On your first point, I said that there was unanimous support for the Introductory Statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was debate on the pace of purchases, on some of the analytical aspects of the use of our instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the reason I use the words 'broadly agreed' by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were, here and there, a couple of diverging views and not unanimous consent across the board.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
