text: So, I am very transparent and very clear; Introductory Statement: unanimously supported.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On scarring of the economy: we are still concerned about the scarring that will be left by the pandemic, whether it's in relation to labour in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Economists will use the hysteresis reference, where clearly as a result of a change of consumption pattern, a change of supply chains, there will be more and different jobs coming.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be more people than were already anticipated that will have to get additional training, that will have to adjust to new tools and possibly acquire completely new skillsets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's one of the reasons why we believe that the Next Generation EU plan is a critical financing element to actually transition into the post-pandemic period and help those that will be most affected by the scarring impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On the inflation having a more persistent impact as a result of the pandemic, I am assuming that you're referring to economists such as Larry Summers, maybe Olivier Blanchard and a few others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that their point has more to do with the massive stimulus that has been given by the various plans, including in particular the last Biden plan to be voted, a plan of over $1.8 trillion, and the fact that there might be overheating as a result of that, and therefore inflation that would be higher than what is currently expected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that the US economic situation and the euro area economic situation, is a very different story.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The two economies are at a different point in the recovery cycle.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fiscal stimuli that have been put in place at least at end of 2020 and beginning of 2021 are of a different magnitude.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a result, whatever is ultimately the characterisation, the longevity of the price upward pressure that would occur in the United States I think is completely different from anything that we will see in the euro area, although of course there will be some spill-over, as I think I have indicated at our last March conference, as a result of the Biden plan, but certainly of too small a magnitude to actually make a huge difference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The pandemic is also a factor of what happens domestically but also what the spill-overs from the global economies will have on a domestic economy, and we will be very attentive and we will look into that as we look carefully at the exchange rates as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point: I'm no longer familiar with the situation in El Salvador.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that it's a country that is under an IMF programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the issue of having a dual tender in a particular economy is a difficult one and that certainly does not change our approach to crypto-assets and to the regulation, supervision and proper classification that they should be under in order to avoid misinformation and misleading representations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: As I have said, all the key points that are in the Introductory Statement that I have read to you have been agreed and have been seen as acceptable by all members.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We did debate whether it was right to actually move from this slight downside risk that we had back in March to this more balanced assessment - to this assessment of more balanced risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, you will definitely hear about the decision that will be made by the Governing Council concerning the digital euro, but I just would like to warn you in advance that this is not the final goal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My colleague and board member Fabio Panetta has explained that very, very clearly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Mid-July, the Governing Council will approve to go ahead into an exploration phase that will include multiple aspects from technology to privacy to inclusion, and everything in between.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not as if the decision was final and made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Exploring all these matters will actually take a lot of effort, a lot of digging and will bring together the whole Eurosystem because it obviously involves all the NCBs around the ECB on this matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will obviously hear about it, but all I am trying to say is; let's not assume that we are jumping to conclusions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This decision will be; do we explore further or do we not spend much more resources on this project?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: As I said, the Governing Council conducted this joint assessment of the financing conditions against the background of the inflation outlook, and then the decision was made to continue to purchase at a significantly higher level than during the first few months of [the year].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, there was some debate about that because obviously we had to analyse both the financing conditions and the inflation to lead us to the decision that was made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The decision is very clear and straightforward and everything that is actually embedded in that Introductory Statement was supported.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Concerning your first question: what we always do when we make a monetary policy decision is to assess the effectiveness, the efficiency and the proportionality of our measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a result of that, we have to look into the potential side-effects or the real side-effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as we're concerned, for the moment, the benefits that we have from the monetary policy decisions that we have taken going back to the beginning of the pandemic, back in March 2020, up until now, is that it largely outweighs the indirect effects that you are referring to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In relation to some of those risks, there are alternative measures that can be decided either from a macro or from a microprudential point of view or from a fiscal point of view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But all in all, when I look at the counterfactuals, what would it have been?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Where would we be had the European Central Bank not taken the decisions that it took, to make sure that we were not going to move from a pandemic situation to a cataclysmic recession situation that we would have had?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By doing what we did, we made sure that financing was flowing into the economy and that any risks of poor monetary policy transmission would be avoided.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the same token, we also enabled fiscal policies to be supportive and accommodative as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the joint fiscal and monetary approach that was so critical in order to actually resist what could've been a very dramatic spin into a disastrous economic situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that comparisons are odious, but comparing the US economy as it stands and the euro area economy as it stands, I think it is not in the cards.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As we said, we are starting from a different base in terms of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of fiscal stimulus in '21, different story as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of point in the recovery cycle, not the same place yet, although clearly our vaccination roll-out is accelerating and now clearly outpacing the vaccination cycle that the United States and other advanced economies are going through.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you look at inflation there are domestic factors, and we have to be attentive to the global situation and how other economies - whether they are advanced, including the largest one, or whether they're emerging economies - how they are faring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That has spill-over effects or that has impacts - but are we at exactly the same point in the cycle?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me get back to the basics, as I call them, which are: symmetric 2%, medium-term orientation and the acknowledgement that the effective lower bound operates as a constraint.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The essential feature of our strategy is our commitment to reach the target; to reach that 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we say that it's a symmetric 2%, the Governing Council regards as equally undesirable deviations that are either positive or negative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third point: we know that 2% is not going to be constantly on target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There might be some moderate temporary deviation in either direction of that 2% - and that is okay.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are very concerned about is any sustainable, durable, significant deviation from the target - and that will require forceful reaction in both directions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fourth item, which is going directly to your point, is that we recognise that the effective lower bound constitutes a constraint.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore we have to take specific action in order to simply maintain the symmetry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In that situation, it requires an especially forceful or persistent reaction in order to avoid that negative deviation from the target risks entrenching inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In case of an adverse shock in that situation, more forceful and especially forceful reaction will be needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Closer to the effective lower bound, those actions might be more persistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This may imply that for a transitory period, inflation is moderately above our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The key commitment we have is our commitment to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We respond to the effective lower bound constraint by deciding to take especially forceful or persistent action in the face of adverse shocks in order to avoid that inflation expectations be entrenched.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Turning to your second question - and I'm sure that you have read already carefully the two-page policy strategy statement, and we have a whole section in that statement about our instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not randomly that they are mentioned, interest rates, first, and the other tools that we have used with good success over the last ten years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is very clear to all of us members of the Governing Council, that the key and first and foremost instrument that we will use, and that we use, is the ECB interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The whole category of them was mentioned in my introductory remarks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also acknowledge that in circumstances such as the one we are operating under, the other tools that we have used successfully over the last ten years are necessary tools in order to respond to the possible adverse shock that we are facing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a result of that, those tools - by that we mean the forward guidance, the asset purchase programmes, the targeted longer-term refinancing operations - TLTRO - and the negative rates eventually - are necessary tools that will remain in the toolbox and that we will be able to continue to use if needed, in accordance with a good proportionality analysis that we would always conduct.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first point: what was decided by the Governing Council was to account for the consumer cost of the owner-occupied house.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it has nothing to do with the investment cost that an owner incurs; it has to do with the consumer cost that the owner of a house actually incurs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is that particular portion that we want to take into account in order to respond to the frustration of many of the Europeans that we have consulted, and that reached out to us, that the cost of housing was not properly accounted for in the inflation measurements, as they saw it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look historically over the course of time, it is not a very significant variation from the inflation as measured by the HICP; it is quite minimal and it varies over time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are periods of time when those consumer costs are a bit higher and there are periods when it is a bit lower.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On average it's a minimal uptake from the HICP number, so that's the impact that it would have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point: let me again repeat what we have agreed and what we have committed to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are committed to target 2%, and we are defining very clearly what symmetry is to us; equally undesirable deviation on both sides of the target, positive or negative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also acknowledge that, given the effective lower bound, that constitutes a constraint on us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to take some special action to restore the symmetry, if you will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To that end, we recognise that in case of adverse shock it will require especially forceful or persistent action on the part of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also acknowledge that, given that especially forceful or persistent action, this may imply transitory periods in which inflation is moderately above target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are multiple ways to deal with the effective lower bound.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is something that many central banks around the world are facing at the moment in these circumstances of low interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our response to that effective lower bound - which we account for, which we acknowledge - is this especially forceful or persistent reaction in order to avoid that low inflation actually entrenches inflation expectations at a lower level than our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's our response, so let's try not to compare it with what others are doing elsewhere.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are multiple ways to deal with it; this is our way of dealing with the effective lower bound in order to restore symmetry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the press release on climate change - if you look at the back of that press release you have a timetable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm very keen on that timetable, as are all members of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was carefully drafted and prepared to give not only the purpose that we have, the action that we take, but also the timeline by which we deliver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not words, words, words; we are facing an issue - climate change - which is the major challenge that the world is facing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not the primary actors; we are not driving the bus, if you will, but we are on that bus.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to look at whether or not under our mandate it has an impact on price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, it's not just words, it's not a speech; it's a commitment of the entire Governing Council with delivery time, deliverables and pursuit of objectives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a pretty strong step forward that the Eurosystem is committed to at large.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have now set up a climate change centre here at the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All the committees that are working on the framework, on the operations of our monetary policy, are mobilised to do the work that is needed in order to deliver what needs to be delivered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't mean to go through the entire list that you have on those two pages of our timeline, but we take that very seriously - and action has already started.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other question, "this strategy is really not much".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me mention the key changes that I see myself.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We went from below, but close to, 2% to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is simple to communicate, it is solid, it is well accepted in the international economic community.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a good balancing act between having enough room to manoeuvre in order to resist and fight disinflation and avoiding the welfare cost of having too-high inflation, 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second: instead of having this, I would say, rather unnoticed-at-the-time symmetry - because that was, you are correct, mentioned in the July 2019 introductory statement of the monetary policy - we put it right in the centre of our statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We define symmetry; there is no ambiguity which was associated with the symmetry that might have been alleged to be under the two rather than on both sides of two.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's this two, simple and solid, it is symmetric and we reaffirm that the whole Governing Council regards as undesirable deviations on both sides of symmetry, which is the perfect explanation of what we mean by symmetry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, we recognise very specifically that the proximity to the effective lower bound requires, as I have said twice - but I am happy to repeat it ad nauseum, that's okay - forceful or persistent monetary policy action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're just not saying symmetry in abstracto; we say we know that at the effective lower bound it is more complicated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is that trap element about it and it needs to be resisted because otherwise we run the risk of having inflation expectations entrenched.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is very detrimental to price stability and the room we have to manoeuvre.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fourth: we just discussed it with the previous journalist; we want the owner-occupied housing cost to be better factored into the HICP new format, if you will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the meantime, we will take into account existing indices that actually reflect those owner-occupied housing costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fifth: climate action is squarely in the middle of our strategy as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's associated with the timeline that I have just mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's very important that it be, as such, squarely in the middle of our strategy and central to what we will do in terms of our monetary framework and in terms of our monetary operations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The models that some of our teams are working on at the moment will also be very innovative in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, but that in a way has more to do with our internal operations, but it's also critically important: that instead of having those two flow of analyses - the economic analysis and the monetary analysis - we are now clearly saying economic analysis on the one hand, monetary and financial analysis on the other hand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We recognise that those two flows of analysis will need to be integrated because there is so much interference and interconnection between the two, as we have clearly seen since the great financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've only mentioned the key changes that are embedded in the strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can assure you that it has been a lot of hard work amongst all of us in the last few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question: I want to repeat and reaffirm as strongly as I can that our commitment is to deliver on our target; our target is 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are committed to delivering on that price stability target that we have newly defined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We recognise that there will be a constraint to that effect because of the lower bound environment in which monetary policy action is taken; as a result of which we know that to resist in the face of adverse negative shock, we will have to deploy an especially forceful or persistent reaction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we want to do, as you very well picked up, is to avoid that the negative deviations actually entrench inflation expectations, which would indeed be detrimental to the price stability objective that we pursue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the process of defining our commitment, this especially forceful or persistent reaction, this may well imply for a temporary period inflation that is moderately above target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is no, very squarely, because there are multiple ways to respond to this effective lower bound constraint.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Ours is the one that I have described; which is to accept this especially forceful reaction, or persistent reaction, depending on how close we are to the lower bound.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is perfect recognition that this may imply temporary deviation, a temporary period in which inflation is moderately above our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll tell you something that will be different on 22 July, which I think is the day of our press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Based on what we have agreed in our strategy review, the introductory statement that I will read to you and that you will receive, will be shorter, crisper and probably more to the point and with less jargon than what you were used to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'm just cautioning many of you, because you might be disappointed not to see the usual series of paragraphs and be able to do the compare-line-by-line, because we are determined to improve on our communication and to make it probably more plain English, shorter and easier to understand, including by the experts that you are around this call.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that's one of the changes that we will see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of toolkits, as I said, all the tools that we have been using which are listed, in paragraph eight of the statement, they're all there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They're listed in pecking order, if you will, and all those tools are in the toolkit, are in the box, and will be used as appropriate and taking into account a proportionality analysis that we conduct before we select the instruments that we want to use in order to reach our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To give you an example of a forceful monetary policy reaction, I would say, in my relatively limited history as President of the ECB, I would submit that the PEPP that we built and further developed in the course of 2020 was definitely a forceful reaction with a twofold approach, of course, but certainly a forceful reaction in order to maintain price stability as much as was possible under the incredible circumstances that we faced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would also submit that we didn't do badly in that respect, and that certainly we were not at the aim of below, but close to, 2%, but certainly we did not observe a massive destabilisation of prices, but we are not where we want to be, clearly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that there are some proponents of the view that, because of the additional regulations, because of the requirements, because of the transition cost, it will have an inflationary impact, but I think that there are others who view that, with cost of energy possibly declining, and other secondary effects of those changes, it will actually have a deflationary effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think the jury is out, and certainly for the moment at least, we at the ECB have not concluded on either side of this proposition, and I think it remains to be seen what the exact impact on inflation the greening of our economy will be, but for the moment we are probably in the latter camp than the first camp.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In relation to the clarity and the solidity of our objective, I think if you were to ask those who, back in 2003 - which was 18 years ago - have indicated below, but close to, I think remembering some of the comments made by one of my predecessors, Jean-Claude Trichet, at many ECOFIN that I attended as then Finance Minister, it was pretty clear in his mind that the ideal level was much, much closer to 2%, and was probably a 1.95%, rather than these inflation expectations that we have at the moment, either market-based or survey-based, as a moment when we would begin to tighten, which I think are ill-founded, given our strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I don't think that by having this simple and solid 2% we are actually pushing out the potential tightening that would take place, no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I fast-forward into the future and I think to myself what will our portfolios look like, I would say two things: whether it is the Asset Purchase Programme, or whether it is the collaterals, I think that the disclosure will be required for any bonds, any collateral, to be eligible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So disclosure will be an absolute requirement, otherwise no eligibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm in my science-fiction moment, because you're asking me to fast-forward into '24, which is even beyond our projections horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would say no bonds will be eligible unless it includes all the required disclosure, and by that I mean not just those that will be prescribed by the European Union, but possibly more, because our internal rating might be even more stringent than what will be established under the CSRD and other requirements that would be imposed by the European Union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I say disclosure, it might also imply elements of the transition plans that many corporates are putting together, will be putting together, and updating on a regular basis so that they are actually feasible, practical and convincing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, I'm sure that by then, 2024, our excellent teams will have devised ways of making sure that we conform with the terms of the Treaty that require proper allocation of resources, and by that I mean that risks will be better taken into account in order to determine the actual value of some of those assets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from a risk management point of view there will certainly be breakthrough changes that will have an impact on the value at which some of those bonds are in our current portfolio and would be there in four years' time, or those that would eventually be purchased then.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, whether that is by way of tilting, whether this is by way of haircuts - I don't know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are multiple facets to those particular solutions, but I'm sure that they will have found what is needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I would hope that we manage our risks in a more solid way in order to conform to the Treaty, and to good management principles, and I would also assume that we play a bit of a catalyst role so that other purchasers, other investors also follow suit, as many actually have announced they will, and I hope that that will be an encouragement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would like to mention, by the way, that we are one of the large purchasers of green bonds and have relaxed some of our requirements in terms of structure of those products in order to accept those bonds that are climate change-related in terms of structure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I would say, first of all, because we've learned from history, and we've observed what has worked, what hasn't worked.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of our work streams - we had 13 work streams studying all aspects of monetary policy and what impacts monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of those work streams focused on the interaction between fiscal and monetary policy, and studied not only Europe but other countries, including, for instance, Japan or the United States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It appears quite clearly from those studies that were conducted that the combination and the coordination, without much consultation actually, between fiscal policy and monetary policy can play an amplifying role or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, counter-cyclical good fiscal policies, when they take place at the same time as monetary policy can actually amplify the effects of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not sure that this is something that we have observed very much until the beginning of the pandemic when we saw, effectively, a strong, robust fiscal policy also support our monetary policy and vice versa, and I think that the combination of the two showed that it was actually quite potent, as opposed to what was observed after the 2011 European sovereign debt crisis, when monetary policy was very much on its own and fiscal policy was tightening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that that's one example of learning from the past that we can endorse and work with.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, I think the fact that the Governing Council was unanimously in support of this strategy review, unanimously concerned with delivering on the target of 2%, and totally on board with what it would imply in order to deal with the constraints of the effective lower bound, I think gives added credibility to the commitment that we have, and I was particularly pleased that after the effort that was conducted for 18 months there was this unanimous support.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, I would say that - and that's, again, looking into the future -the severity of the financial crisis and the incredible and tragic situation of the pandemic have been exceptional moments which have been resisted, but have not enabled us with the monetary policy that was deployed, sometime often too much in isolation from fiscal policy, to deliver on the target, on the aim that the ECB had.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So let's learn from the past, stay together in this commitment to deliver on our target, and demonstrate that we mean what we say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would observe that we are in the second half of this year, and when something is ready, you don't want to procrastinate, sit around and continue a process that has successfully been completed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think it is thanks to the enormous amount of work that was produced by staff of the entire Eurosystem, with the staff of the ECB having clearly a driving seat in the exercise, but drawing on all the resources from all the national central banks, that we had this good process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My hope would have been to deliver much earlier, let's face it, but we had to suspend the process for six months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had 13 work streams working on 13 key themes, for which you will be receiving, by the way, before the Sintra conference, a very significant amount of extremely valuable working papers that have helped us in elaborating our views in confronting our positions and in reaching agreement, but it is because of that work that we managed to advance fast enough.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Otherwise, you have the risk that you know quite well, a leak here, a leak there, and before you know it, you don't control the process any more.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think it was actually beneficial that we could early on - everybody complains that Europe is always late.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first point, I've partly responded earlier by telling you that the below, but close to, 2% was, effectively, very close to 2%, at least in the mind of those who invented the formula of below, but close to, 2%, at the time when the worry was excessive inflation, and not too low inflation as we have it at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Are we trying to move the goalposts because there are factors that increase prices at the moment?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I really don't think so, and this is certainly not the intention.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just want to remind you that the seminars and the discussions that we had about the 2% took place about 12 months ago, at a time when inflation was certainly not rising, or at a time when prices were not rising, as they are at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Added to which - and that would be the second part of my response to you - is that we will see through inflation as we see it at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have good reasons to monitor carefully, to analyse very cautiously, to be vigilant about underlying inflation in particular, and to try to disentangle what is volatile, oil-related, food-related, to make sure that our assessment is valid, but at this point in time we certainly believe that this is a transitory movement that is attributable to some supply shortages, some bottlenecks, some oil-related factors, and some very specific issues relating to VAT increase, and all the rest of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is clearly not a little device - no, not at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that this 2% is clearer, simpler to communicate, solid, and a good balance, added to which it gives us parity with a lot of other central banks around the world which are also operating at 2%, which is the generally-accepted definition of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point, I think the reason we included the owner-occupied housing cost, and only the consumer part of that, not the investment cost - I want to be very specific on that - is really caused by the very strong feedback that we heard from the Europeans with whom we had those many outreach events, and who were vocal and loud on the fact that housing costs should be properly accounted for because they constituted a major component of their budget.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's what has really caused our determination to include them on a temporary basis as additional component, and hopefully, if Eurostat is also in agreement with us, on a more solid and permanent basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, I will need at least an hour to go through all your questions!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You cover huge ground, so let me tackle your first question, which had to do with how we reached our decision in relation to forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me take you back just a little bit to our strategy review and the strategy - the monetary policy strategy that we adopted unanimously.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have to think in terms of the strategy that we adopted as the framework within which we weave monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is really the basis against which we develop monetary policy as we go, and depending on circumstances, so unanimity there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was unanimous agreement around the table that we had to revise our forward guidance, and that forward guidance had to implement our strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We did not have unanimity, but we had an overwhelming majority about the calibration of the forward guidance on ECB interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what I had anticipated and what matters most is the fact that directionally, we were all on the same page and determined to revise the forward guidance as we did, but also to make sure that it is geared to implement our strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's very bluntly how it happens and what matters really is this chain of events, if you will, amongst us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you asked me to dissect the forward guidance that we adopted, and if you don't mind, I am going to take you through a little exercise of going through that long sentence, which is probably the one that is a little bit more lengthy in the whole presentation that I gave you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a bit more lengthy because the forward guidance rests on three key criteria, if you will, or three legs of forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, in support of our symmetric 2% inflation target and in line with our monetary policy strategy, so we are well anchored in our strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We remind ourselves that we are targeting 2% inflation and our commitment is symmetric.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council, so it is not relying on any kind of projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is the Governing Council in its judgement that expects the key ECB interest rates to remain at their present or lower levels until - and that's when it begins to be important - we see inflation reaching 2% well ahead of the end of our projection horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Leg number 2: durably for the rest of the projection horizon and, third leg, we judge that realised progress in underlying inflation is sufficiently advanced to be consistent with inflation stabilising at 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We add to that a sentence that you might remember from the strategy review, which is: this may also imply a transitory period in which inflation is moderately above target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, by these three legs we are essentially saying, first of all, that we want to see inflation reach 2[1]% well ahead of the end of our projection horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well ahead first of all is determined by judgement of the Governing Council but it is essentially the midpoint in our overall horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to remind those of you who do not necessarily know what our projection horizon is, at the moment we project '21, '22, '23.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we want to see at least 2% on the horizon, but well ahead of the end of this horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second aspect is that we want that 2% to be durable, so we want it - and that's the second part of the statement - it says: durably for the rest of the projection horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it can oscillate a little bit but it cannot go below 2%, essentially.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third one, which is important as well, is that we want to look at the current circumstances and in particular the current underlying inflation, to see whether directionally these underlying inflation components actually lead us into that upward trend that will help us reach the 2% target that we are committed to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you've got three legs: one that is in the present, you could argue that there is an element of outcome based in that one, where we look at the underlying inflation factor and we see whether directionally we're aiming towards our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we want to see it on the horizon but we want to see that to have been sufficiently lasting so that essentially at midpoint it is already there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third question that you asked me had to do with the Delta variant, and on that particular point: our projections from June actually included some assumption that certain containment and lockdown measures would be continued into the third quarter and some of it still remaining during the fourth quarter of 2021.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is factored into our projection, and all the elements that we are observing at the moment, whether it's by PMI or whether it's hard data, are really confirming our projections for the second quarter, which is coming strongly, and for the third quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we are in the hands of those who are going to take all the necessary precautions to make sure that that contagion is not producing the negative economic effects that we have seen in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Vaccination is clearly one of the components that we'll look at carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second consideration that we debated around the table, because it varies from one country to the other, is the fact that over the course of those waves - first, second, third waves and now fourth waves - the citizens, governments, health services are getting a bit more used to the responses that must be given in order to address the health of people, but also not to damage too much the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I have tried to describe as well as I could the forward guidance on ECB interest rates and the fact that it is really taking into consideration three key criteria over the space of time in order to make sure that we have solid lasting elements that will actually be useful to guide our action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would say that it's an indication that none of us would want to tighten prematurely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we're informed by past experience and by most recent history.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think this element of patience that you have between the midpoint and the end of the horizon and the fact that it has to not only be sufficiently early and way ahead as is indicated in the forward guidance, but also lasting, is precisely intended to avoid premature tightening that would be detrimental for the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the combination of patience in order to gain confidence is what we discussed and what we tried to embed in that sentence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the rest: essentially I would summarise it by steady hands.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The use of our instruments such as PEPP, APP, has been steady hands because we conducted the joint assessment that you are all now familiar with, which is to assess the financing conditions and determine whether they are favourable all the way through from market interest rates all the way to household loans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we take a good look at inflation and its various components, so based on that joint assessment, which essentially is broadly in line with what we saw in June, we decided steady hands to keep this significantly higher pace of purchases compared with what we did earlier But PEPP, that was not discussed as a programme, and anything like that would be totally premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, I think it means exactly what is written in that statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that it's going to take a little time to unpack it and really understand all the subtlety and the details of it, but it's pretty straightforward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want at least 2% at the end of our projection horizon, which by the way varies over time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do forecast '21, '22, '23 but as you know it slips into yet another year when we get closer to the end of the first year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in December '21 we will add an extra year, so it's a little bit misleading to say your first or your second year - which is why I prefer to adopt the midpoint reference in terms of indication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It doesn't mean to say that it's cast in stone, because, by and large, the Governing Council will use its judgement to apply those criteria which I have mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On inflation: let me remind you what we are doing at the moment, and that is really the second part of the discussions that we had today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not changed in that respect, and we are still looking at making sure that we can preserve favourable financing conditions to all sectors of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We would counter any tightening that would counter what we want to realise in terms of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to alleviate the downside impact of the pandemic on our inflation target, and that's what we are aiming for with our PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are still in that period of crisis, which is why PEPP is still ongoing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that any particular exit would be absolutely premature in that respect, but our goal is to come back to that pre-pandemic moment and the inflation target as we had it at the time in our forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I'm again going back to the sentence that encompasses our forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We say in particular that interest rates will remain at their level or lower levels until such time when the Governing Council sees inflation reaching 2% well ahead of the end of our projection horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's obvious that the 2% that we see at the end of our projection horizon and therefore which is based on a forecast, so it will be determined by staff forecast plus the judgement of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are saying here that it's not going to be mechanic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is going to also leave some space for Governing Council judgement, but it will be based on a forecast of what inflation is expected to be, the outlook for inflation at the end of the horizon - which as I said is either three years from now or a little over three years if we are at the end of the current calendar period.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I hope that clarifies your concern: clearly to have inflation at the end of the two years' projection horizon requires that it be the outlook for inflation that we are talking about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you're right that the decision that was made on 18 March in relation and that actually constituted PEPP indicates that the PEPP, the pandemic emergency purchase programme, will continue until at least March '22, and such time when the Governing Council determines that the pandemic crisis is over.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Many of us are economists, not all actually; some are even lawyers by background but we are clearly informed - as you are - by scientists, by experts, and by the observation of facts when it comes to employment, manufacturing, services, trade in the economic translation of what the crisis is about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's how we will proceed and our hope collectively is that thanks to vaccination, thanks to determined action on the part of all citizens, that pandemic crisis will be over sooner rather than later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, let me clarify that latter point: we revisited and revised our forward guidance on ECB interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we did, and our exercise of revisiting it was limited to interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Under the condition that we currently face, forward guidance can reinforce our commitment to attaining the inflation target that our policy rate will be lifted only if the evidence is sufficiently clear, sufficiently persistent, sufficiently lasting and we have the degree of confidence that our inflation rate will reach 2% on a durable basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we don't only use forward guidance, as you know very well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other instruments that we have in the toolbox and that we are currently using will continue being used.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The forward guidance is a way for us to operationalise our strategy review and to give sufficient guidance about that patience and that determination, but also about the exact criteria that we will need to see set, reached in order for us to take any action on the interest rate front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is not a matter that we have discussed on the occasion of this monetary policy meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: TLTRO has been one of the two key tools that we've used.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: TLTRO III and the various operations that we conducted were critically important to make sure that liquidity was abundant, to make sure that banks could finance the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We saw a very large uptake of the first few operations, particularly that in June[2]last year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The most recent one has been reasonable but not as large; probably because there was already a lot of liquidity available for the firms and because some precautionary lending had been put in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I would underline, by the way, in terms of financing and funding is: what we are finally observing for the first time, which is that the business that is coming back for loans is coming back for capex.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's coming back for investment, and that to us is a very important sign that there is confidence in what is yet to come and in what the business will hopefully - those investments will generate in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On the latter, it's fairly straightforward: we have not discussed that particular issue and there is nothing to report on that matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the pace of purchases of PEPP: we will continue to be guided by the joint assessment that we have committed to, which is favourable financing conditions throughout the economy, all sectors included, and the outlook for inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On that front, we are very, very attentive to all the components of inflation, and while we are seeing some - we have seen some rise in inflation, 1.9% in June after 2% in May - we also want to go underneath that inflation to understand exactly what is going to move.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have some pretty positive signs in the short term, although the medium term doesn't look as promising.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think all of that is premature, if I may say, because we will be delivering our projections in September, which will be more indicative of what we see on the outlook front in terms of possible revision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't know to what extent it will be revised up or down, but it will certainly have an impact on what we do going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, thank you for your questions because it gives me a chance to actually reiterate what is the purpose of our strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our monetary policy strategy is intended to deliver on our mandate, which is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have done - in addition to multiple other points, but you seem to be particularly interested in that one - is that we have revised our measurement of the price stability objective by clarifying the numerical target that we have, which is 2%, number 1.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second: we have very explicitly indicated that it is symmetric, and that deviation up or down are both undesirable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third: we have very specifically identified the need when we are at the lower bound to take some specific measures and to react especially forcefully or persistently as we get closer to the lower bound.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the aspect of the monetary policy strategy that I think is pertinent for your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not intended to push into time the hiking of interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not intended to keep interest rates low for longer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Frankly, the quicker we can do that, the quicker we can use those other tools that we have not used a lot in the last few quarters, which is the interest rate, but we are not there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we need to take the action that is identified in our strategy review as now developed and operationalised by the forward guidance on ECB interest rates in order to deliver on the objective that we have offered 2% inflation target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are at the effective lower bound, we need to respond especially forcefully, persistently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need to observe our forward guidance that has now been approved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we do that properly, if we are determined then we will reach 2%, and once we reach 2% then other decisions will be made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not to keep low interest for longer; it's to reach the objective that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other one: I just want to confront you to the counterfactual; if central banks had not done what they have done, if governments had not used the fiscal arm that they had to use during the pandemic, what would have been the situation?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: How would all that have stood the course of this economic crisis?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think that the question was: is it monetary financing, is there fiscal dominance?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Governments have safeguards and will hopefully work soon on the new framework that they have to safeguard their respective action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we had to do what we had to do; there was no question in my mind that we should not have done what we did.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: You know, on your first question I think you will be better off asking them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to put words in their mouth, and everybody is free to say what they want to say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What really mattered to me is that first of all we had a very friendly, open, substantive discussion around these issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, our strategy, which is the foundational document which is our constitution, our framework if you will, has been adopted unanimously by all members of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All members of the Governing Council agreed that we had to revisit our forward guidance and that we had to frame it in such a way that we could deliver on our monetary policy strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the calibration, the timing, all of that is a matter - it's not minimal, but it's the practicalities of a general principle that was agreed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's best that you ask them the question and it's a very, very small number of Governing Council members.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I am sure that you will find their door, as you will no doubt be very interested.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are playing with two different times, if you will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A lot of what is anchoring our forward guidance is actually the projection horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are talking about, depending on when you start the clock, three or a little over three years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the projection horizon and that's where we have set our three legs, the three conditions, the three criteria to trigger our decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The medium-term horizon is probably a little beyond that and is also helping us take into account other matters that have nothing to do with inflation calculation, but which have to do with employment, with climate change, with factors that we have to take into account, but that are not specifically driven to inflation, and our inflation forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: First of all, I would not anticipate what our inflation forecast will be next year, and the year after; we know well that forecasting is a tricky game - not a game actually - but it's a tricky exercise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment what we have is a forecast at the end of '23 of a sizeable 1.4%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We'll see what that is in September and I think that we have to take each quarter of projections as they come and then adjust what we need to adjust using all our instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes indeed, we believe that forward guidance is going to play a role in the set of tools that we have available, some of which we are using extensively at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said also, we will continue to determine by this joint assessment whether financing conditions remain favourable in order to support the recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will look jointly at inflation and see what movement there is to be seen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second point was about the owner-occupier housing costs, and on that page I just want to signal that I have written to President von der Leyen to ask her to please commission Eurostat in order to accelerate the work that they do in order to capture owner-occupied housing costs for the future so that we have an index that includes the owner-occupier housing costs together with other costs, and certainly to take that into account better in the index.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the meantime, we are also taking into account those costs using alternative indexes when available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a matter that we discussed a little bit as well in the course of our meeting today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: We did not discuss any relation between APP and interest rates, and we really focussed our exercise on the work on our revisiting and revising the forward guidance on ECB interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is the transitory period and inflation moderately above target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is often referred to as overshooting, so what we are saying here is that we accept the fact - this is what is meant by this may also imply - that there will be moderate overshooting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not going to venture in any particular numerical assessment of what is moderate overshooting as opposed to excessive overshooting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not deliberately overshooting but we recognise that the especially forceful or persistent policy decisions that we make may imply moderate overshooting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: You know, on our meeting today: I'd like to just come back yet again to the fact that the framework and the key agreement that we have amongst ourselves is a unanimous agreement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As there was unanimous agreement around the fact that we had to develop forward guidance, adjust it to the new circumstances of the new strategy that we have and make sure that it is operational.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, where there was some divergence, as I said minor divergence, but they are to be respected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I have been on record several times to say that it's perfectly fine that some might disagree.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the disagreement is at the margin - as it was today - it reinforces the collective direction that we have discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then you go into the choice of words, and you can write all the articles in the world about this!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is really important to me is total agreement and unanimity on the strategy review, and the agreement to disagree on the margin on the calibration of some aspects of the forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am sure you are going to do your job and try to figure out who said what to whom and all the rest of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We did revisit our forward guidance on interest rates of the ECB, and that's all that we discussed for the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, I would be very keen to hear from you whether this monetary policy statement is more palatable and not overly disturbing for those of you who are used to identifying and red-lining what word has changed here or there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a significant change, but I am very grateful that all members of staff have made the effort to make it clearer for all those who care to read it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would preface my response to your first question by a quote, actually, in a way, which is, the lady isn't tapering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because what we are doing is recalibrating PEPP, which I'll remind you is the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme, and we are recalibrating just as we did back in December and back in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are doing that on the basis of the framework, which is a joint assessment, so we look at the financing conditions, and we concluded that they remain favourable, and we do that on the basis on the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as you rightly pointed out, our inflation outlook has been upgraded, and it has been the case for '21, significantly, '22, quite significantly, and to a lesser extent, '23.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But across the board, you have an improvement on the inflation numbers for the whole horizon that we look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also look at other indicators, and on those accounts as well, there has been a significant improvement of the inflation numbers, both for '22 and '23.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, on the basis of that joint assessment, and because we know that we need to keep favourable financing conditions, this is the commitment that we have and this is what we agreed in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that we can maintain those favourable financing conditions with a moderately lower pace of purchase, and, of course, the choice of words is relevant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is moderately lower than what we have done in Q2 and Q3.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, you know, the September meeting is conducted in the light of our projections, and what we are seeing is clearly an improvement on many fronts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The inflation numbers have been upgraded as I've just indicated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The employment numbers have also improved and the unemployment situation is serious, of course, but more benign than was anticipated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, on the basis of all that, and the success of the vaccination campaign, which we have all along said was critically important to determine the economic recovery, we believe that the euro area economy is rebounding.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that gives us the confidence to take the measure that we have taken, which, as I said, is a recalibration of our Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme for the next three months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, thank you very much, and it's very nice to see you as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a significant improvement from previous press conferences, so we're probably heading in the right direction here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The next step will be to actually see each other with appropriate distance between us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the commitment for favourable financing conditions, I'll remind you that that was decided at our Governing Council meeting in December, under the auspices of the PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So PEPP is an emergency programme, very specifically designed for the circumstances that we have been facing, that we still face today, but that are currently clearly improving.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this commitment to the favourable financing conditions is one of the two parts of the joint assessment that we conduct to determine our pace of purchase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we have a framework that is very clearly designed and that operates in relation to PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The day when PEPP is over will presumably indicate that financing conditions are favourable, and that the economy will have recovered in such a way that the downward impact of the pandemic on our inflation outlook has been resorbed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At that point in time the job is not finished, because we are still targeting our 2 per cent, which is now clear and straightforward, as a result of our strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Symmetric 2 per cent, in the medium term, with a special focus resulting from the lower bound.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, that will continue, and the driver of our work going forward after PEPP will indeed be the mandate that we have to maintain price stability, as measured by our target of 2 per cent inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, which has to do with PEPP in general: What we have done today, with the Governing Council members, unanimously, is to calibrate our pace of purchases in order to continue to deliver on our goal of favourable financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not discussed what comes next, and this is something for which we will prepare in the months to come, and I think there will be more interesting matters that will be debated in December, and of which, clearly, you will be informed in due course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, thank you for the first question, because I'm going to take advantage of that one to say a few words about inflation and how we conducted our discussion on inflation, because it is a case that in many countries in the euro area, people are seeing prices increase and they can feel it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to really go under the skin of inflation before we actually assess whether it is temporary, whether it is going to last.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that leads us to the conclusion of our inflation outlook, which, as you know, is 1.5 at the end of the projection horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have essentially three factors that are driving prices up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first set of factors has to do with the reopening of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It went down massively, and prices by the way at the time also went down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The economy reopened and, from a supply point of view, from a demand point of view, of course, there is pressure on prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can see that in what we call the base effects, a lot has to do with energy prices, which constitute a large component of these base effects on inflation, And you can see that in the German value-added tax (VAT) impact, which obviously will continue to play out until the end of the year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You see that in the carbon tax that was decided also in Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, those are the base effects, reopening of the economy related factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As part of those reopening-of-the-economy factors, I would emphasize the supply bottlenecks effect, and this is something that the corporates and the companies are telling us, or telling you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are bottleneck effects and not just in the semiconductor business, but in all sorts of sectors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These sectors are more or less affected, depending on how much they rely on either raw materials, or equipment, and where they get their supply from.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is impacting the durable and the non-durable goods.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, how strong will that effect be, how long will it last, is something that obviously remains to be seen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have put that particular item - if you remember the monetary policy statement that I read for you - we have put that in the inflation analysis, where we say that if those supply bottlenecks last longer than expected, then it will increase prices and will have an upside pressure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we're not certain, because typically what we have seen in previous situations of that nature is that when you have a bottleneck in your supply, you try to find alternatives to that supply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as a result of that the supply bottleneck impact on inflation is reduced and eventually goes away.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the same vein, if it's bottleneck inflation that applies without too much effect on the demand front, it's not necessarily conducive to second-round effects on wages in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, that's the second one [set of inflationary factors], which is a subset of the reopening-of-the-economy consequences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third one, which is quite interesting as well, especially when you disaggregate it, is the inflation that is related to services, because we have seen a reopening of the economy on the service front, in the most recent months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And when you analyse where the inflation is in that segment of services, you see that most of it is actually coming from what was subject to social distancing and what obviously has been reactivated most recently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, those are the three key drivers of inflation at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But, as you can see, many of them are of a temporary nature, and will last for a period of time, and will then either fall out of the period of reference, or will fade out over the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One component that we are addressing, monitoring, and checking very attentively is the second-round effect, is the impact that price increases will have on wage negotiations, and that is what could actually fuel a more persistent and durable price increase and inflation going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On that wages front we are not seeing much by way of significant increase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be very attentive to the autumn negotiations that are typically taking place in some countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But at this point in time, we don't expect these wage increases and these wage negotiations to be very strong and we see probably a gradual and moderate [wage] increase as a result of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, that's what I really wanted to try to explain to you in response to your question about inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, concerning PEPP, you know, that's a discussion that we will address comprehensively at our December meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As the term of PEPP approaches, we need to obviously discuss the terms and conditions of how that term occurs, and you will hear me again on this matter, certainly at our December meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, on your first question about how confident we are, I observed that, since the beginning of the year, we have regularly upgraded our forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If anything, we might have been on the too pessimistic side to begin with.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what I look at more - more so than analysts' notes, which I'm attentive to, of course - is the projections that are produced by staff, how they compare with projections that are produced by other international institutions, such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and other similar institutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that the economy is going to continue to benefit from further unwinding of containment measures during the second half of '21, into '22 as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also make the assumption that bottlenecks will be circumvented by the economic operators in the first half of '22.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that we will be back to the pre-pandemic, 2019 level at the end of this year, which is two quarters earlier than we had initially anticipated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And while we still have a lot of slack, both in production and in unemployment, we are also seeing that slack being resolved and reduced more rapidly than we had anticipated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, that gives us good reasons to believe that '22 is going to be another good, solid year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not upgraded our forecast for '22., We still are at plus 4.6 per cent[1], in our forecast, and our risk assessment, as I mentioned earlier, is broadly balanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, if the pandemic is resolved faster because of even further vaccination coverage and if the booster is adopted by many, that is going to be an add-on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If more savings are being used by consumers, that will also support consumption, which has been one of the big drivers of the recovery so far.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's still that, you know, chunk of saving that was accumulated over the pandemic period, which has not been tapped into, which might be tapped into, so that's for the upside side of our broadly balanced risk assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the downside, clearly, we could have a massive fourth wave, or other variants coming to the fore, for which vaccinations don't work.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mean, you have all these possibilities as well, and the supply bottlenecks, which, as I said, we anticipate, will be circumvented in the first half of '22, but which could last longer, and which would have a side effect on inflation, putting pressure up, and which would weigh on the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on the other hand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think you had a second question which had to do with stagflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, our primary mandate is price stability, but we are also keen to see an economy that recovers fully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And for that to happen, of course, jobs have to be created, and the furlough schemes that are in place and that retain employees in their positions but not in actual employment, need to be pursued.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And those two million people - still more than in 2019 - that are unemployed, have to also return to employment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, if that is the ultimate result of this recovery, then I don't think that we will be heading towards stagflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: Well, thank you very much, for this question, it gives me a chance to actually repeat yet again, because I think it's an important consequence of our last July meeting, the three criteria that are applicable for our forward guidance on interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that forward guidance, as you know, has been modified and/or clarified to a great extent by including three criteria.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is, we need to see inflation outlook at target, that is at 2 per cent, well ahead of the end of our horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, we need to see it through, also to the end of the projection horizon, and, third, we need to have sufficient elements and indication of progress in the underlying inflation criteria, at the time when we make the decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, you have these three criteria, and you have the other element of our forward guidance, that remain intact, and which actually play a role in signalling to markets what will be the sequence of events from asset purchases to interest rate hiking.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it also gives me a chance to remind all of us that PEPP is a very specific programme, intended for the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has an emergency character to it, and when that PEPP comes to its term, then clearly, we have all the other instruments available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in terms of purchases, we clearly have the Asset Purchase Programme, the APP, which we have on a standing basis ever since October 2019, and that clearly is intended to be continued, and will be debated, as I said, at our December meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's entirely premature to evoke it, and it has not been discussed on the occasion of this meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, when we determine our pace of purchases, we are attentive to the entire universe of bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not paying special attention to the fiscal commitment of one country or the other, or the bond issuance of one country or the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we look at the entire universe of bonds that is available, will be available, and is being announced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's how we determine where our purchase pace is going to be applied.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we do so, as I said, based on two things, under our joint assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is the favourable financing conditions, the second is the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On your question about the decision that we made today, as I said, it was a unanimous decision, in all respects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, the pace of calibration was agreed, the moderately lower determination was agreed unanimously, it was all unanimous.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, I'm sorry for those who like to set the doves against the hawks, sorry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For this time, there's not much that you can actually draw from dissenting votes, because we all agreed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: TLTROs, you're right, there will be one more operation in December, and we will clearly have to discuss what comes next on the basis of the situation at the time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that that will be part of the overall re-examination that we conduct at the time of our December meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
