text: When it comes to interest rate hikes, we have a forward guidance which has been approved by the Governing Council which identifies three pillars or three criteria, if you will, that need to be satisfied in order for rates to be hiked.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to insult you by repeating those three criteria, but I will actually!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the inflation at target, which is 2%, well ahead of the projection horizon; we have, second, the durability so that we see it staying at target until the end of the horizon; and third, we need to see underlying inflation that is sufficiently strong to determine progress towards target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will apply these three criteria at each and every step of the way, and we will determine if and when they are satisfied in order to possibly hike rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But don't forget that we also have a sequence, and the sequence is that we will not hike rates until we have completed net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think what comes first comes first; we have to look at net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are conducting a step-by-step guide of those net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will determine in March what is the assessment, on the basis of the data that is then available and we will see what pace, what speed, what amounts we will apply to this net asset purchase programme for the rest of '22.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me a more political question on which I am not going to take a political stance, but I will simply say that the geopolitical clouds that we have over Europe, if they were to materialise, would certainly have an impact on energy prices and, through energy prices, an increased cost throughout the whole structure of prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It would also impact growth as a result of reduced income and possibly as a result of reduced consumption and deferred investment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The pure economic impact would certainly be more significant than what we are seeing at the moment in terms of prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are very attentive to that and by the way, we include that in our scenario when we prepare the projection and the work that is submitted to Governing Council members at the time of the next Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will say separately that peace is a lot better than any kind of war from an economic point of view, and I have seen that in other parts of the world in previous lives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the latter one: it's obvious that monetary policy has to continue to support the economy and you mentioned it yourself: the whole panoply of instruments that we use, that are currently working, is also explaining some of the good results that the economies are showing at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the upside surprise: we did not only use the word upside in relation to surprises; we used it in relation to risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We hardly ever - I'd have to double-check in the last 20 years, we may have in the past - but in the recent past we have not actually mentioned, we have not included in our monetary policy statement the characterisation of risks in relation to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that is a very explicit indication that it might very well be significantly higher than what we had expected over the course of the year, and possibly higher than we had anticipated at the end of the year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Risk is to the upside, in particular in the near term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for your pointed question, but I am not going to speculate on what the Governing Council will decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think you have the answer, but I am not going to speculate here on what the decision will be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually we have not discussed TLTROs at all in this particular Governing Council meeting, and it's one of the items that I'm sure we will debate at our March meeting, or later actually.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think they end in June '23[2]if I recall, yes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I said that there was general concern around the table about inflation and the impact it has on our fellow Europeans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Equally, there was general consensus about the outcome of our decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't call it a monetary policy decision, so to speak, because what we are doing is we are continuing the normalisation of monetary policy and we are considering what will possibly happen and what options we offer ourselves, what optionalities will be around in response to the uncertainty at future monetary policy meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we did in depth and very thoroughly today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was general consensus on these issues around the table, I can assure you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you asked me a question about the spreads: I would like to just observe that we are not seeing any such development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While yields have moved up, spreads have not widened in any significant manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we very much look into these matters very carefully and we have no reason to believe that it is going to be different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If it was, we are obviously going to respond and we have all the tools, all the instruments and the adequate flexibility if it is justified.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is the case that the very high inflation numbers that we observe are at least 50% caused by energy prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Oil, gas, electricity and they all interrelate, gas having a stronger bearing than in previous years because of the price mechanisms depending on the length of contract and all the rest of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will spare you the details, but 50% of the current inflation is caused by energy prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the ECB was to first of all reduce and finish its asset purchases, and then raise interest rates in short order, do you think it would have any impact on energy prices?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, it is not in the ambit of monetary policy to decide the price of the barrel that is organised predominantly outside of Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, true that most of those contracts are in the US dollar currency but if I look at the significant appreciation/depreciation, it varies a little bit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to be in the wrong numbers, but it's no more than 3% over the course of the last 12 months[3].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think that we can attribute to the European Central Bank the high cost of energy which impacts 50% of the inflation and the price paid by the consumers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, the European Central Bank and its Governing Council at large are focussed on its mandate, which is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are going to stick to the objectives that are set by the Treaty; that is price stability at 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Believe me, as soon as it is required and the conditions are satisfied, we will act because it is our duty and we shall do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And clearly, we will have a very sophisticated determined approach and analysis to doing that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will only do that in the sequence that we have fixed for ourselves, and which has been agreed, which is that we will look at net asset purchases first, gradually, on a data-dependent basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you asked the question about net asset purchases, and I'm not sure exactly what your concern was about the net asset purchases and what is the… What was the question?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Shortly before is probably a little shorter than just before, and that again is going to be in the estimation of the Governing Council, data dependent, and based on the assessment that is conducted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would say this: we are not there yet for the reasons that I have just mentioned, which are that we will be very faithful to our sequence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will stop the Pandemic Emergency Programme net asset purchases in March and then we will look at the net asset purchases under the APP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Don't assume too much in terms of the immediacy of hikes; we will not be complacent, but we are not going to be rushed into a process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will follow the sequence that we have set for ourselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will verify the forward guidance criteria and we will be gradual in whatever we do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, on the latter question: I have not seen what Carmen has written so I'm not going to comment on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: She is an expert on sovereign debt and she has held that view for a long, long time that excessive sovereign debt is a great burden and should be addressed by sovereigns.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not going to challenge or second-guess her analysis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know this is her field and I am not surprised that she's addressing that in her capacity as chief economist of the World Bank and clearly, I am sure, focussed on emerging markets and low-income countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second-round effect, don't get me wrong: what we are saying is that we are not seeing wage increases that would be likely in the conditions of the markets as they are, where we are seeing unemployment as low as it has ever been, where we are seeing participation back to the level where it was pre-COVID, and where gradually the output gap is closing and there is less and less slack in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are waiting for that movement on wages and our duty of course is to make sure that through a second-round effect, that would not be addressed by monetary policy, inflation would run out of control and would spiral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is not what we are seeing, and we certainly don't want to see it, but I am not here saying that there should be wage moderation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is clearly an adjustment to be had which I am hoping we will see in the course of '22.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That would be the economic logic of what we are seeing at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, as I am finishing on that question, I think we should be a little bit cautious about what I am hearing a lot, which is constant comparisons between the US and the euro area, the Fed and the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are really operating in different environments, with different economic data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to give you an example: our demand here in the euro area is pretty much back to where it was pre-COVID.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Ask yourself why; this is because of this massive fiscal stimulus that the US economy has had, unlike the euro area, where it has been more moderate, not excessive and which is producing the sort of measured pace at which some factors are significantly improving.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, in terms of Governing Council: we had very intense discussions about the current economic situation, about the outlook, about the uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as with most institutions, communities, families - and probably you all - the war of Russia against Ukraine has tainted and overshadowed a lot of those discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were different views around the table - in all directions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But after those good discussions there was a determination by all Governing Council members to rally the proposal that was put together by the Executive Board and presented by our Chief Economist.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It delivers on the mandate that we have, which as you know is price stability in the face of what we are seeing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The decision that was made was to progress step by step, to acknowledge the added uncertainty that we are facing and to therefore have added optionalities so that we can in all circumstances respond in an agile way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will have noted that our decision in relation to asset purchases under the APP is conditional and clearly states that we have a declining pace of purchase for Q2 and that for Q3, if the outlook for medium-term inflation is confirmed by the data, we will indeed end asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if on the other hand the data - which are critically important because we are data dependent in our decisions - do not support this medium-term outlook as we see it now, then we indicate very clearly in the monetary policy statement that I have just read that the Governing Council stands ready to revise, both in terms of timeline and in terms of volume, its purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is a conditional provision that you see in our decision and we are not in any way accelerating.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was in line with our December meeting, with our February meeting and press conference, and what we are doing is confirming our step-by-step approach, our maximum optionalities in the face of maximum uncertainty, but also delivering on our mandate which is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The medium-term inflation outlook both in the baseline delivered by staff and in the scenarios that you will see tomorrow in detail, which are all of course a worsening of the situation, there is not a positive and a negative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in all those baseline and two scenarios the medium-term inflation outlook arrives roughly at target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think in terms of optionalities, I'll be happy to expand a little bit because this is clearly what has guided us, added uncertainty, added optionalities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are clearly identifying the pace, we are procuring a situation where we can decide some time after net asset purchases what decision we should make in relation to rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of timeline, we're also saying that we will end net asset purchases under those data that I have just described in the course of Q3.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Q3 is three months, so we tried to have as much optionality in order to deal with the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have underlined in my response to you "some time after", which is a substitute to "shortly before".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously "some time after" is an open time horizon which will be data dependent; the occurrence of which will be data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will have difficulty addressing your second question because I don't know what is my dominant scenario.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a baseline and we have two scenarios; one is adverse, one is severe, and you will have all the details of those scenarios tomorrow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Suffice to say that watchers are not those who make Governing Council decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is the Governing Council, 25 sensible people around the table, who look at what the mandate is, what the projections deliver, what the medium-term outlook for inflation looks like, what the risks are, what the uncertainty is, and on the basis of all that, who are trying to deliver a predictable course while being very cautious.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's really what we did and doing what you have to do should be the predictable thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Adding uncertainty to an uncertain situation would not have been the right answer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We came from a "shortly before", because it addressed actually one end of the spectrum relative to the others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other words, the time it takes to purchase assets relative to the time when interest rates could be hiked, and it did say "shortly before".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there was an assumption that there would not be such a long period of time between when net asset purchases would stop and when there would be a rate hike.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was decided, and we debated that indeed, to replace it with "some time after".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That respects the sequencing that we had, which is net asset purchases and subsequently, the Governing Council looks at all the data to determine whether it is time to hike rates or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It can be the week after, but it can be months later, and by that I think we want to indicate that the time horizon is not what is going to matter most.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the data that will support the decision that is made by the Governing Council to assess the medium-term inflation outlook and whether a rate hike is warranted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will have noted, by the way, that we have removed the bias that we had by eliminating "lower" in relation to our interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: De Guindos: I will try to answer your question on financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, it's quite clear that we have seen since the beginning of the invasion volatility, tensions, stress in financial markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think that perhaps the main point that I would like to stress is that this situation is not comparable to the one that we had two years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Liquidity has not disappeared from the markets and despite the situation and tensions that we have seen in certain financial and capital markets, well, liquidity, as I have said before, has not disappeared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have seen a lot of volatility for instance in equity markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As well, we are also looking at what's happening with corporate bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of corporate bonds, spreads have widened, but as I said before, liquidity has not faded out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, there is a very specific market that we are looking very carefully at and that is the derivative market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Mainly, one part of this derivative market is the commodity derivative market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far, in the clearing houses we have not seen any sort of a special volatility there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All the margin calls derive from the increase in commodity prices, having honoured, but we are closely monitoring the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, in the government bond market as well, we have seen ups and downs in terms of nominal yields, but the spreads have been quite contained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the conclusion is: Russia is important in terms of energy markets, in terms of commodity prices, but in terms of the exposure of the European financial sector to Russia, it's not very, very relevant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Simultaneously, the size of the Russian economy is quite limited; it's only 2% roughly of the world economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the situation, perhaps the main conclusion, is that the strains and the tensions that we have seen are not comparable at all to what happened at the beginning of the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: On your question concerning CBDC, you know my views on CBDC and you know that I have pushed that project.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fabio Panetta is working hard on that together with members in the entire Eurosystem with the high-level taskforce that is working really hard on moving forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in a way, I am really pleased that attention is now focussed on the role that cryptos can play and the role that Central Bank Digital Currency can have when they are implemented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council decided back in October '21 to launch a two-year investigation phase, and it is at the end of that investigation phase that the decision will definitely be made to launch the CBDCs and to make it a reality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am confident that we will move ahead, but that's going to be a decision of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's an imperative to respond to what the Europeans expect, and I think we have to be a little bit ahead of the curve if we can on that front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we can accelerate the work, I hope we can accelerate the work.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will certainly support that and I was delighted to see that in the United States there was an executive order by President Biden to actually expect similar effort and focus and progress on CBDC, cryptos.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that it will take all the goodwill of those who want to support sovereignty, who want to make sure that monetary policy can be transmitted properly using our currency, will endeavour.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the issue of financial stability, I totally concur with my Vice-President de Guindos, but I will also point you to the last sentence in the first paragraph of our monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that there has been an abuse of that, but we mean it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will take whatever action is needed to fulfil the ECB's mandate to pursue price stability and to safeguard financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are actually exploring together with other European authorities and in particular with the Commission how we can deploy tools in order to support the Ukrainian people and the Ukrainian authorities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So clearly looking at how support can be structured, whether under an existing product - you mentioned swap line, repo line, or other products - because clearly, we have conditions under which we can extend swap lines and repo lines.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If those conditions are not satisfied, we need to find alternative ways of providing support.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is what we are doing both in relation to the authorities, but also in relation to the people of Ukraine who, when they become refugees, unfortunately past the border need to access alternative currencies to theirs, which as a result of the decision that was made is not convertible as it used to be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I hope that in the next few days we'll be able to provide tools and means to extend support to both the people and to the authorities together with the Commission and sometimes in some cases national authorities within the Eurosystem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other point: let me just make that clear once again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The decisions that we are making today are the logical continuation of our December decisions, of our February communication and we are on this path which is data-determined and which is also delivering on our mandate which is that of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are not talking about accelerating, we are not talking about tightening; we are talking about normalising simply because we acknowledge the fact that in the present environment, which is that of high inflation and not low inflation as it was in the past, the support that net asset purchases can give to policy rates is getting close to conclusion, and .

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: therefore requires that we decelerate the pace of purchases, consider the fact in Q3 - or at the end of Q2 rather - to decide whether depending on the data that we get, we effectively conclude net asset purchases, the principle of which was agreed today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question I'm sure that some of you will really enjoy picking up the phone and trying to question who said what, when, and on what topic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were some members who thought that given the uncertainty that we have, we should be uncertain as well and do nothing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were other members who thought that despite the uncertainty we should move ahead and not have any conditionalities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that the proposal that was debated and supported by the Executive Board and presented by Philip Lane, the Chief Economist, was this balanced approach of taking into account the baseline produced by staff, acknowledging the inflation numbers that we are seeing now and the inflation outlook that we have for the medium term, to propose a path that reduces net asset purchases, brings us to concluding the net asset purchases under the conditions that data actually confirm the outlook that we are seeing now and that we are seeing in the scenarios produced by staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's what the package was - and it is a package; it's a package of determination, conditionalities, the removal of the "shortly before" which has not been replaced by "shortly after" but by "some time after", so as to delink, and maximum agility and flexibility as you will have seen in the description of the various instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that was published in the press release and I'm here referring clearly to flexibility that we give ourselves under the PEPP reinvestment policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Speaking of reinvestment, let's not forget that we have five… Maybe I'll have the right exact number that I can give you in terms of reinvestment policy under the APP [and the PEPP].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Anyhow, we'll have more than €5 trillion worth of assets that we will be reinvesting over the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not as if we were ending, tightening monetary policy going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are normalising monetary policy with the caveats that I have just outlined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, obviously when we look at the medium-term inflation outlook we also do a risk analysis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While we are clearly of the view that given the drivers behind inflation, energy predominantly for the moment, supply bottlenecks, food price increases and a broader increase of prices in general which is coming from energy predominantly and translates throughout all the items, clearly risks to inflation are to the upside particularly in the short term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But possibly also in the medium term, but not exclusively, because risk to inflation could also be to the downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you mentioned some of the investment projects, some of the fiscal spending that will probably take place over the course of the next few years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If anything, it's a good reason that we should stick to our mandate of price stability and of bringing medium-term inflation outlook to our target of 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first one, which relates to the fiscal effort: we clearly point out in the monetary policy statement that fiscal support will continue to be critically important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What form it takes, whether it is a national fiscal effort, with a good focus, with a target on those that are most affected by the current crisis - particularly the energy crisis - or whether it takes a European-wide format is something that obviously the leaders will have to decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm sure that they are, as we speak, or as they meet, addressing those questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we have a long-standing record of arguing for some fiscal facility at the European-wide level in order to respond to shocks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are clearly facing a major shock, whether it is just the pure war or whether it is the energy prices, but this fiscal facility that we've advocated, we stand by it and do believe that it can be extremely helpful particularly in order to move Europe to a more integrated basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On when energy prices will stabilise: in our assumption and in the scenarios that have been developed there is the assumption that oil and gas and energy prices in general will throughout the projection exercise stabilise, certainly not in the short term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are not seeing - and that takes me a little bit away from energy prices but it's clearly related to how long it takes to stabilise - but what we are not seeing so far and we are very, very much scrutinising the numbers, is wage pressure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the numbers for the fourth quarter of '21, the [negotiated] wage increases have actually been lower than the average of 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are trying to get as much intelligence and as much understanding of how and where wage pressures are going to come from because it will have an impact on the underlying inflation that is integrated in our medium-term outlook and in our forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would have to double-check on your first question because I am not aware that the plan to reduce dependency on Russian gas was incorporated as a geopolitical decision or as an energy decision made by the European authorities and with the national leaders of the Member States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I know for sure is that we factored in a significant increase of prices, wherever that product comes from.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the "some time after": I know this seems like great elaboration - and in a way, it was.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We could have substituted the "shortly before" by "shortly after", but that would've made it too time dependent in terms of decision-making.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to be data dependent, so whenever the data confirm that the medium-term inflation outlook is at target, then the decision should be made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are guided by our strategy review, we are guided by our forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not guided by a time element that would predicate that within X weeks, or within X months, a decision will be made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the deliberate use of "some time after" opens sufficiently wide an interval of time so that we can review the data, determine the robustness of the data, make sure that some uncertainty has cleared a bit so that we can make a decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't know how I can more explain this "some time after", but that's what our debate was about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again if I can just insist on that: we want to have as much optionality as possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We recognise that there is huge uncertainty and that things can go in all sorts of directions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to be able to respond to those circumstances, and to do that we need to have all options on the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We keep all the options open and we will proceed, and we are proceeding, step by step.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: De Guindos: Well, what I have to say is that Sareb was part of the package to rescue the Spanish financial system, and it was agreed with the European Commission, with the ECB, with the IMF.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While Sareb was perhaps the most powerful instrument in order to clean up the balance sheets of the Spanish banks, I think that is right; it has a debt of €35 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as well now, it has assets worth clearly beyond €31 billion/€32 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So Sareb has been quite a useful instrument, of course used as well, and this instrument was used in other countries like Ireland, for instance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that what we have to do is to try to gain time in order to get advantage of the evolution of real estate in Spain that now is much more positive, and to reduce as much as possible the level of debt of Sareb.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question I would call your attention to a particular sentence in the monetary policy statement (MPS), which reflects the evolution of the Governing Council assessment of the current situation five weeks after the last monetary policy Governing Council meeting that we had, which is a very short interval as opposed to other periods.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is the sentence that begins the second paragraph of the MPS, where we say: "At today's meeting we judged that the incoming data since our last meeting reinforce our expectation that net asset purchases under our Asset Purchase Programme (APP) should be concluded in the third quarter".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is a much stronger affirmation of our assessment of the data, which, as you rightly pointed out, had indeed changed since five weeks ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was an interim Governing Council monetary policy meeting, and we affirmed the net asset purchases' very likely conclusion in the third quarter, without being more specific, but being open-minded as to when in the quarter that is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third quarter has three months, and I think the determination around the Governing Council table was to take stock of the projection exercise at the next monetary policy meeting to determine exactly the timing of such conclusion of the net asset purchases under the APP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question about how many interest rate hikes are projected by markets, let me tell you that we are sticking to our sequence, and this is very much what we did on the occasion of this Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sequence that we have adhered to, that we have agreed, is to complete net asset purchases first, and some time after that decide interest rate hike and subsequent hikes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I remember last time around on the occasion of the last monetary policy press conference, I was asked specifically what was meant by the "some time after".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "Some time after" is intended to serve our determination to have both optionality, gradualism and flexibility, which means that this "some time after" can be anywhere between a week to several months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will deal with interest rates when we get there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question concerning the potential boycott of oil and gas - and I'm assuming that you are referring to oil and gas out of Russia, and the initiative of the boycott being either one party or the other, the supplier or the purchaser.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just, first of all, state that this Russian war against Ukraine is not just causing economic problems; it is causing a huge humanitarian crisis, massive economic damages, and cost and risks way beyond Europe.I've noted the joint statement by the presidents of international institutions [President Biden and President von der Leyen] to support that we all focus also on the food crisis that is going to be hitting low-income countries and other people than the Europeans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, on the oil and gas front, an abrupt boycott would have significant impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Any such risk, obviously, reinforces the determination of the Europeans to move towards cleaner energy, to move to non-fossil fuel in general, and to reduce dependency vis-à-vis Russia.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But have we actually factored in exactly the net amount, the trade-off resulting from any such boycott?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We simply know that, obviously, some countries within the euro area will be more affected than others, and we also note that the Europeans together under the leadership of the Commission are looking at ways to adopt joint approaches, joint policies, joint purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This certainly is, together with moving to a different energy mix, the right approach to take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second part of your question dealt with the tightening of rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have commented on the bank lending survey, which indicates that there is and there was during the first quarter a certain tightening by a larger number of banks answering the surveys.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All that being said, the volume of loans to households in particular still stands quite strongly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So even if there is tightening, particularly concerning the terms and conditions of those lending arrangements, in terms of both rate and volume we are not seeing yet the outcome of this tightening that you referred to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Equally true that in the bank lending survey respondents are indicating that they expect further tightening in the coming months, and clearly that is associated with the war in Ukraine, with the additional supply bottleneck issues that will affect corporates in particular, and the general confidence impact that the war has on both corporates and consumers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me, first of all - again, this seems like a re-reading exercise, but I think it matters, because those are parts of the sections of our monetary policy statement that were clear changes from the past and indicate the direction that we are taking.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is actually something that you will find in the conclusion of the monetary policy statement, which is in the penultimate line, and it says: "We stand ready to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate, incorporating flexibility if warranted, to ensure that inflation stabilises at our two per cent target over the medium term".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is language that you know quite well, but the overall sentence is something that is worth taking notice of.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Optionality, gradualism, flexibility are concepts that we have outlined before, so we are really very much in a normalisation process, and we are continuing along the path of that normalisation process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has been the case in the last couple of years, and particularly two years ago, if you remember, that flexibility served us well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's on the basis of that recognition of the value of flexibility, in particular in order to make sure that the monetary policy stance is properly transmitted and that unwarranted fragmentation is avoided, that we are recognising this and we are mentioning flexibility as one of the principles that we want to apply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Two years ago you would remember it was necessary, and we moved promptly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If necessary, we move promptly, and as I have said in my ECB Watchers speech a few weeks back, we will design whatever additional instrument is appropriate in order to deliver the flexibility that we believe is useful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would add as a footnote to that, that the reinvestment policy that we have decided for PEPP back in December, is actually coined with this flexibility possibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have not only indicated that reinvestment would be extended until 2024, but we also said that, if necessary, we would apply flexibility in the reinvestment policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that really captures the philosophy that we have in relation to flexibility and the need to properly transmit the monetary policy stance throughout the whole of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You had a second question, on wages and the possible second-round effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I have told you at the last press conference we had that we were particularly attentive to wages, and we continue being so, because that is a critically important component to assess inflation outlook in the medium term, and to help us determine our monetary policy stance and the need to move at a certain pace.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the wages, we are looking at it very carefully, and what we are seeing are relatively muted, generally, wage increases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the latest numbers that are available it is January, and it points to a 1.6% increase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, this is looking backward, obviously, and we have to be particularly attentive to movements as they develop, and we know that the longer inflation numbers are at the high level where they are, the more likely it is that wages negotiations, salary entry levels, renegotiations of existing agreements will actually take place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we had a good discussion on those issues at the Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In some countries it seems that unions or employees and employers are managing to reach agreement which take into account the risk of redundancy and threat to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In other countries there are much higher demands for wage increases and wage renegotiations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will continue to look at that extremely carefully and be attentive to potential second-round effects as a result of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Do we have trust in the work that we do?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Do we get our forecasts and our projections perfectly right all the time?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, I spent a few years of my life operating with other forecasters and top-notch projectionists who didn't always get it right either.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But do we trust that we monitor all the data that we need to monitor, that we apply all the economic wisdom that we can, that we use as many possible models as are available, that we try to improve on the economic results that we produce?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Did we make a mistake, did we get it wrong in the past?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to be a little bit humble in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be cognisant of the fact that when there is a war, when there are major developments that are not predicted, that are not part of past patterns, it is incredibly difficult to actually integrate that into the models that help us offer projections to European colleagues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The same is true for national central banks, by the way, and the same is true for many, many projectionists and for many forecasters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have that humility, and we recognise that we have to not only look at forecasting models, but also look outside the window and try to figure out what is happening and what is the likely impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Looking at past history is not in and of itself sufficient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, who knows what impact and development the war is going to have on our economies?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On this issue of flexibility and the fragmentation issue, and the need to make sure that monetary policy is transmitted in an unimpaired fashion, we constantly try to improve on the toolbox.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We constantly look at what works, what will help us provide the flexible, efficient and proportionate response to the situation, and this is what is going to continue to happen in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am happy to repeat again the value that we give to flexibility, and the need to embed flexibility in order to make sure that we transmit monetary policy throughout the euro area, but this is what our work is cut out for.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me deal with the real and the good question that you asked.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is not me withdrawing the need to be humble in the face of what our projections can offer, but obviously, in deciding in particular next June - because that is going to be our next projection monetary policy meeting - in June we are going to look at our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you will remember, back in March we had projections that included a baseline and a couple of scenario analyses as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't know exactly whether we are going to come up with a similar exercise with one baseline and two scenarios, or whether we are going to have one baseline, one scenario, or some sensitivity analysis in particular areas where we believe that we need to pay special attention.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will use that, of course, because it is there, it has to be used, it is informative, but I think when I refer to humility I meant we cannot be exclusively and only rivetted to the projections produced by our models.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to look at historical developments of similar situations, and have an element of judgement in our assessment of the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what we see at the moment is certainly reinforcing our determination that in the medium-term our outlook for inflation is at around 2% and there is one other section that I would like to refer you to in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's one that is just before the risk assessment which deals with inflation, where we say: "While various measures of longer-term inflation expectations derived from financial markets and from expert surveys largely stand at around two per cent, initial signs of above-target revisions in those measures warrant close monitoring".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will be looking, of course, at our projection.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we will also be looking very carefully at market and expert surveys, in particular in relation to inflation expectations, because the last thing that we want is to see inflation expectations at the risk of de-anchoring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I did refer very specifically to the last sentence of our conclusion, which says "incorporating flexibility if warranted".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Flexibility is a principle that we believe has served us well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That we need to continue to integrate in our monetary policy determination, if warranted, if required, and as I said, if necessary we can move very promptly, but I did not say that we were building a new instrument.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can certainly do that, and we can do it in short order, and are capable of being operational, as we have demonstrated between 12 and 18 March 2020, for instance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me about the - essentially, what you said is, given the numbers that we are facing, given the situation, why did you not accelerate more?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It gives me a chance to remind all of us that we are in a process, and that process started back in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In December we announced that we were putting an end to PEPP, that we had a policy of reinvestment of PEPP that would extend to 2024, that we would apply flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In February I communicated that we were going to accelerate a bit, and March certainly was a strong signal of what we were considering in terms of terminating our net asset purchases under the APP, and I think that we are being a little bit more specific now in terms of what we see and the likelihood of this happening in Q3 at any point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have numbers that have been flagged for purchases in those next few months, and we have now an ending point which is a quarter at possibly a point in time during the quarter when we put an end to net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As to your question on spread, clearly, we need to make sure that our monetary policy stance is transmitted throughout the entire euro area, and this was the tool that we built with PEPP back in March 2020.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first part of the birth certificate of PEPP was antifragmentation; the second part was monetary policy stance, and we were delivering that product in short order.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has proven very efficient, and I think it is learning from this and recognising that flexibility is important that we will continue to deliver our monetary policy going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are on a journey, and clearly, as I said, we started the monetary policy normalisation journey back in December, reconfirmed in February, clearly indicated in March, and we are restating this determination on the occasion of this monetary policy meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have, as I said, added a few particular attributes to the decision that will be made in June when we have the next projection round, which is when we can take stock and actually assess exactly the timing of the conclusion of our net asset purchases, which will then trigger, some time after the end of the net asset purchases, interest rate hikes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to have both flexibility and move gradually and keep all the options open.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be mindful of the fact that not only do we see very high inflation rates, clearly, in some countries much higher than in others, but on average 7.5% is a very high number.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are also seeing a medium-term outlook for inflation gradually moving back to closer to our target, to 2%, and possibly from above, rather than from under.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These will be better advanced and better documented at our June monetary policy meeting, but we are on that journey.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, you give me a chance to actually, yet again, clarify that what is happening in the economy of the euro area is very different from what is happening in the economy of the United States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether you look at employment, whether you look at wages, whether you look at actually the general attributes and instruments of the monetary policy at the moment in the United States, our economies do not compare, and if anything, I believe that this is likely to be accentuated by the fact that the euro area is probably going to be more exposed and will suffer more consequences as a result of the war by Russia against Ukraine.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The United States will not bear as much the brunt of the consequences from an economic point of view, I would suspect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Comparing our respective monetary policies is comparing apples and oranges.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not applying policies to the same economic situations at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I talk about normalisation of monetary policy I think of the kind of instruments that we are using, I think about the rates that we have in place, I think about the use of our balance sheet, and I think it is very much in that order that we will be looking at normalisation of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a bit premature, because as we did during the Governing Council today, we looked at the short-term, what limited updates and numbers we have, and what qualification of our stance there should be as a result in terms of signalling what we will do next during the third quarter of 2022.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Quantitative tightening is something that comes clearly at a later stage in that journey, and we are not there yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The sequence that we have adopted, which is embedded in our strategy, which is very familiar to you, is net asset purchases have to conclude first, before we decide on whether we hike interest rates and by how much, and then we will look at balance sheets, but for the moment we are more thinking about the reinvestment policies that we have agreed, both in relation to the APP and the PEPP portfolios.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In relation to flexibility, I think I have been very clear to indicate that we believe that flexibility is helpful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have seen it being very operative back two years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is now specifically mentioned as something that will be incorporated if warranted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is totally premature at this point in time to indicate when any such flexibility will be deployed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The purpose of the flexibility is to make sure that monetary policy is properly transmitted throughout the whole of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if and when it becomes necessary we will know what to do, as I said, if necessary, and promptly, and it will be operational.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other question, do we believe that ending net asset purchases will reduce the price of oil?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is also, obviously, the case that we have to be attentive to the inflation shock, to the impact that it has on wages, to the consequences that it could have on inflation expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And for all these reasons we believe that in sequence it is necessary, given the financing conditions by the way as well, that we put an end to net asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a very high probability, let's put it that way, because we have not decided it as specifically as that, but the wording of our second paragraph in our monetary policy statement is sufficiently clear to indicate that at this point in time we believe that there is a very high probability that it will happen and that it could happen any time during the third quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is for those reasons that we believe that it is our duty, in order to ensure that inflation stabilises at 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Based on the scenarios of last March, you are right that in 2024, which is not necessarily the medium-term but the end of our projection, it moves between around 2% and a little below 2%, but I think that our forward guidance will be determining and helping us determine at the June projection meeting, if we decide to terminate net asset purchases, what exactly will be the policy going forward in terms of rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the risk of repeating myself, the specific role of flexibility will depend on the concrete circumstances that we face.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decided in December that in the event of renewed market fragmentation related to the pandemic, reinvestment under PEPP can be adjusted flexibly over time, over asset classes, over jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think those same principles would apply to the flexibility that we would want to develop and deploy as applied to other sets of circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can design and we can deploy new instruments to secure monetary policy transmission as we move along the path of policy normalisation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have shown that on many occasions in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Staff is extremely good at, not only thinking on their feet, but also providing proposals in short order, and I know that they will be able to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is in situations that demonstrate unwarranted and exogenous causes, that impair monetary policy transmission, that will lead us to use those flexibility aspects of instruments or programmes that staff will be working on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second issue concerning FX and exchange rate, this is not a matter that we have discussed, but as you know, we are always attentive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not on the occasion of this Governing Council, but this is obviously a matter that we are attentive to, because it does have an impact on inflation, and inflation is, obviously, the key of all our concerns, given its magnitude and its potential impact on second-round effects and inflation expectations, and in view of our mandate, which is to maintain price stability and to deliver inflation at target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council, on the occasion of this meeting organised outside of Frankfurt, in beautiful Amsterdam - thanks to the National Central Bank of the Netherlands - focussed primarily on the challenge of high inflation facing the euro area, and on taking further steps in our normalisation path that we started back in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not a question of catching up; it's a question of using all the tools that we have in order to deliver on our mandate of price stability and in order to bring inflation down to target over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our analysis was obviously that inflation was undesirably high and that we had to take the steps that I have identified in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would like to add that it's not just a step; it's a journey.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We gradually over the course of time put ourselves in a position to move away from unconventional monetary policy, which will actually be taking place as of 1 July, in order to use more conventional tools which are the interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the issue of the interest rates: we also identified a path, which is not only limited to a particular move, but a series of moves over the course of the next few months depending on the medium-term outlook of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second issue: we have to have the right monetary policy stance; that is critically important and that is what we are doing with that identification of the journey that I just mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we also have to make sure that our monetary policy is transmitted throughout the entire euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To that end, obviously, we need to make sure that there is no fragmentation that would prevent the adequate monetary policy transmission throughout the entire region.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that we have described them in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is obviously the reinvestment capacity that we have under the PEPP, which is a complete reinvestment package that totals €1.7 trillion, that will be reinvested with total flexibility if warranted across time, across jurisdictions, across products.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If it is necessary, as we have amply demonstrated in the past, we will deploy either existing adjusted instruments or new instruments that will be made available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are committed to proper transmission of our monetary policy, and as a result fragmentation will indeed be avoided to the extent that it would impair that transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had very productive discussions in Amsterdam and these discussions concluded with an unanimously approved decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are on a journey, but this is clearly an important step in that journey given that we are actually deciding to end net asset purchases under the APP as of 1 July, which effectively means that we stop before - for all sorts of market operation conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are also setting a path in which July and then September are the next first steps along the way of hiking interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While we intend to raise interest rates by 25 basis points in July on the basis of the assessment that we conducted today, we also indicate that - and I will read very carefully for you because it was obviously a sentence that we drafted carefully in order to capture our commitment - I'll read you the whole paragraph, actually, because it's a really important one: "We undertook a careful review of the conditions which, according to our forward guidance" - you all remember the forward guidance with the three conditions - "should be satisfied before we start raising the key ECB interest rates."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Accordingly, in line with our policy sequencing, for those of you who wonder why we didn't do it today, well, we have a sequencing in place that dictates - and we want to be predictable on that front - that we first of all stop net asset purchases and then we look at interest rate hikes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, in accordance with our policy sequencing, "we intend to raise the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points at our July monetary policy meeting."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And - that's the September that you were asking me about - "looking further ahead, we expect to raise the key ECB interest rates again in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The calibration of this rate increase will depend on the updated medium-term inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the medium-term inflation outlook persists or deteriorates, a larger increment will be appropriate at our September meeting."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is pretty precise as a commitment, but it is also a factor of how the situation evolves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, if the medium-term outlook persists as we see it now, or even deteriorates - which of course we don't wish, but it could happen - then obviously the increment will be higher than 25 [basis points].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then we go further because we take a third step along that journey to indicate what we will do beyond September, which is also the anticipation that further rate hikes will be necessary on the basis of the data that we collect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to give a reading exercise because some of you occasionally comment on the fact that I read too much, but this one, I really want to read it a bit because it matters - and every word matters, including plural versus singular - to your point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we say is: "looking further ahead" - so today we say that - "we expect to raise the key ECB interest rates" - the three of them - "again in September" most likely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "The calibration of this rate increase will depend on the updated medium-term inflation outlook."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And here is the important one: "if the medium-term inflation outlook persists or deteriorates, a larger increment will be appropriate at our September meeting."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that you took the example of, if you are at 2.1% in 2024 or beyond, then the increment adjustment will be higher.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Do we expect that our July interest rate hikes will have an immediate effect on inflation?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to that is no and I would like to develop that a little bit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, because of the anticipation of our monetary policy, because of the inflation and growth outlook, financing costs have already moderately but significantly increased, whether you look at corporate bonds, whether you look at sovereign bonds, whether you look at bank costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those financing costs have increased and with the signal that we are giving here, particularly concerning the short-term rates, this signal will continue to have an impact on financing costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, typically monetary policy decisions have a longer-term impact in relation to inflation itself, so we have to stay the course, be determined, committed to delivering the 2%, but we cannot expect that to happen on the 22 July for a decision that we would have made in July.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, because you mentioned inflation expectations, we observed that inflation expectations are well anchored and we certainly want to indicate to those who form expectations - whether they are markets, whether they are experts, whether they are consumers - that we are determined to delivering on our target of 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore expectations should absolutely remain anchored because we will deliver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The neutral rate: this is a topic that we have deliberately decided not to have on the occasion of this Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am sure that we will ad nauseum argue as to whether it is 0.96 or 1.97 or beyond, or below or whatever.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Suffice to say that the neutral rate over the course of time for multiple reasons, having to do with productivity, with demographics and all the rest of it, has gone down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But where it stands exactly, we have decided not to discuss it on this Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Believe me, we had plenty to discuss so we saved a little bit for later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To be fair as well, it's not something that we can observe and determine with precision today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's as you get closer, we will understand better where exactly it stands - and we will debate it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, on the issue of forward guidance: I'm assuming that you're referring to the forward guidance relating to asset purchases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if you look at that forward guidance, we have actually changed it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you recall, the forward guidance that we had referred to favourable financing conditions and to the accommodative aspect of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have changed that and if you look at the third paragraph on the second page, we do refer to the fact that we will do so for as long as necessary to maintain ample - not favourable - liquidity conditions and an appropriate monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we take account of the change that has indeed taken place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A lot of the tools, the forward guidance, the considerations over the last 11 years had to do with exactly the opposite movement; trying to bring inflation up because it was too low, and often at risk of deflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we are in the opposite situation, where inflation is too high and we need to bring it back to our target of 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, I'd like to say that our staff do the best work they can do and apply their whole consciousness and professionalism to producing those projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, those projections are not just the ECB; the projections that you have in front of you are the projections of the entire Eurosystem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's the ECB and 19 national central banks including the great Bank of the Netherlands, which has actively and always actively participated in this exercise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it's a cohesive work that is done, that is tedious, that is iterative and that really checks everything.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, it is clear that the massive energy prices hike and the war in Ukraine and the fast pace of the recovery have taken all forecasters by surprise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I actually thought you would ask me a question like that: so what did I do?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I looked at other - I hope I can find it now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Anyway, it doesn't really matter if I don't find it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The point being that all international institutions, all forecasters of repute have actually made the same mistake of underestimating or not anticipating some of the developments such as the war, such as the energy crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fourth point: I think we, the Eurosystem and the ECB in particular, are the only central bank which has gone back to the work that was done, which has looked under every stone to understand where the errors came from.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I use the word errors with some trepidation because it's mis-forecasting caused by very unpredictable events.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Three quarters of the forecasting errors are actually attributable to energy prices and the rest is largely attributable to bottlenecks that have lasted longer than had been anticipated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So again they do everything they can, as well as they can.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They make the same kind of forecasts as other international institutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Events that have developed are not captured in either models or sometimes just the sheer imagination of us all, when we talk about the war at the doorstep of Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fourth, we do the introspective exercise of trying to find out where it went wrong and we will continue doing so in the future because we have to improve, no question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the reinvestment policy that we decided for PEPP and for the APP, both of them, will now be operative as of 1 July for APP and has already begun for PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a matter that we will be discussing within the Governing Council, which we have decided not to debate today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had, as I said, plenty to do already in the last couple of days.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we will be looking at it and I have to tell you something: there are some of us on the Governing Council who will be interested not only to deploy flexibility, if warranted, on clusters of assets, by jurisdictions, over temporality, but some of us are also interested in looking at how we can support the financing of the measures needed against climate change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've said already before that a green LTRO was interesting to consider.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the reinvestment decisions that we will make in the coming months and years might also be inspired by this concern that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your point number two is: why not 50 [basis points] in July?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, we are coming out of 11 years of no interest rate move.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are on our path to exit negative interest rates soon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is good practice, and it is actually often done by most central banks around the world, to start with an incremental increase that is sizeable, not excessive and that indicates a path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, the decisions that we have made today are not just one intention of one single month of July.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a whole journey that will take us back to the 2% target in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also want to observe how markets are going to operate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I have mentioned, we couple our July determination with our September indication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I want to take you back to the monetary policy statement because I think that the key principles that we will be inspired by in order to be predictable by you, but also to set the rules according to which we will proceed, are captured on the top of page 2, and say the following: "throughout this process the Governing Council will maintain optionality, data-dependence, gradualism and flexibility in the conduct of monetary policy".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all four will matter and there will be circumstances when one might be more important than another.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There might be other circumstances where the pecking order will change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think by doing that we are trying to have as much optionality as we can, be able to use flexibility if and when warranted and necessary, be as data-dependent as we have demonstrated and we will continue to demonstrate, and also deploy the gradualism that will be appropriate given the circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think in times of great uncertainty, gradualism is probably appropriate, more so than if the path is clear, well identified and we all understand where we are heading.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second issue I just want to yet again come back to this issue of fragmentation, because I know that this is dear to some.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just want to reiterate that within our mandate, we are committed to preventing fragmentation risks in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fragmented financial markets would obstruct the monetary policy transmission and undermine the possibility for the ECB to achieve its price stability mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the reason we monitor constantly, and that is the reason we have available at hand all the dimensions of flexibility that can be applied to our reinvestment policies under the PEPP, because flexibility conditions are clearly associated with PEPP to the extent that it relates to consequences of the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we know how to design and we know how to deploy new instruments if and when necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've demonstrated that in the past; we will do so again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a case that a large portion of the inflation that we have analysed is attributable either directly or indirectly to terms of trade; what you call imported inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether it is energy, exogenous bottlenecks, that is clearly a so-called imported inflation; but it's not it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are clearly seeing an unprecedented 75% of the items considered to measure inflation being above 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That applies to non-energy industrial goods, it applies to services and it is partly a factor of the energy passthrough - but not only.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Number two, we are also very attentive to wages, wage negotiations and to the risk of second-round effects and potential spiralling.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not seeing the risk of spiralling at all, but we are seeing wage increases that have picked up particularly since March and that, as we indicated in the monetary policy statement, would not be entirely surprising whether it is by way of catch-up effects or by way of general wage increase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are also aware that Germany, for instance, will implement the [higher] minimum wage as of 1 October.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is largely and certainly much more so than in the US for instance - to come back to your questions about the difference between the EU and the US - it is more so imported inflation than it would be attributed to overheating demand, as is probably more so the case in the US.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's spreading more broadly than strictly speaking in energy-related sectors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then you had another question: it's a bit of a story of on the one hand, on the other hand, the current situation of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is probably more of the negative hand than the positive hand, but we have both.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the negative front we clearly have the continued impact of the war in particular, the reactivation of lockdown measures in China which went away, then are maybe slightly coming back.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The bottlenecks impact that it induces and the dampening effect it has on growth, not to mention the reduced disposable income that some of the households are suffering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But on the other hand, you have entire sectors of the economy that are recovering, and when you look at the tourism industry, the accommodation industry, hospitality: those sectors are really recovering at a fast pace.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We looked on a per-country basis at the prices of hotels, of restaurants; it is clearly on its way up with a strong demand in those sectors in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We cannot exclude also - we hope, that remains to be seen - that some of the factors that have a dampening effect on growth will gradually fade a bit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In relation to the July rate hikes that we discussed, we certainly considered that the three rates would be impacted by the hike, not just the deposit facility rate (DFR).

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For future references: as of September, we might also apply the principle of hikes to the three, but we have not discussed that yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the intention will probably be to have a close look at that and to determine whether or not we want to just keep those spreads or return to a better symmetry between those three.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's clearly to be debated at either our next meeting or the September meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the conditions that would trigger the anti-fragmentation: let's be clear, the critical point is monetary policy transmission and we are very attentive to make sure that it transmits throughout the entire euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is no specific level of yields increase or lending rates or bond spreads that can unconditionally trigger this or that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The principle is that we will not tolerate fragmentation that would impair monetary policy transmission, and we will determine on the basis of circumstances, of countries, how and when that risk is likely to materialise, and we will prevent it.
