speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can only repeat what I have said, which is that we will not tolerate fragmentation that would impair the proper transmission of monetary policy throughout the entire euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do have existing flexibility that is embedded in the reinvestment of PEPP, in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have demonstrated in the past - we will demonstrate if necessary in the future - that we can design, we can deploy the appropriate instrument to prevent that risk from materialising.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: De Guindos: You know that in our statutory review we included a reference that twice per year, we would include financial stability considerations in our monetary policy making.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We did it in December and we have done it now in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, here the message is quite clear: the vulnerabilities of the financial system in Europe have been defined in our financial stability review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Refer to problems in terms of valuations of financial assets, in terms of margins of the banks and in terms as well of high valuations in some spots of residential real estate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the conclusion that we have reached, that is included in the monetary policy statement, is that in the short term, the normalisation of monetary policy conditions can give rise to additional stress in the short term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the medium term the tightening of financial conditions could be positive in order to try to address some of the vulnerabilities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, this is the main conclusion, and we try to make an assessment that covers not only the short term, but as well the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I would just like to add something because we are here, standing in Amsterdam, and my colleague Klaas Knot is with us and for those of you interested: we had just a fantastic meeting that was organised under the auspices of De Nederlandsche Bankunder the leadership of Klaas.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's been just a really good, fruitful and productive experience.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Geography matters, and hospitality can help a great deal, so thank you to the Netherlands and thank you to the National Central Bank of the Netherlands.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually, your question helps me give you a bit of an insight of what happened during this really important Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Governing Council members around the table made two important decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one had to do with interest rate hikes by 50 basis points - and I will come back to forward guidance in a minute - and also decided to approve at unanimity, unanimity of the Governing Council, the Transmission Protection Instrument.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So let me come back to the interest rate hikes that we decided, and I will come back, as a result, to your forward guidance question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We debated internally within the Governing Council about the pros and cons of sticking to the signalled 25 basis points of July, which entailed the other forward guidance that we gave in respect of September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And having weighed the pros and cons we decided, on balance, that it was appropriate to take a larger step towards exiting from negative interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We did that on the basis of several indicators, several elements which we believe constituted a change relative to our June Amsterdam meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I can come back to those four elements, because I think they're important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They all relate to a materialisation of inflation risks that we had flagged in Amsterdam, but which we have seen materialising in the meantime.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the second important component that played a role in our decision was that the situation has changed in relation to transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had not implemented yet the flexible reinvestment under PEPP, and certainly we did not have at the time a transmission protection instrument.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So these two elements combined - realisation of upside risk to inflation plus the presence and the operationality of the flexible reinvestment under PEPP, and, more importantly, the unanimous support of the Governing Council for the transmission protection instrument - led us to decide a larger-than-what-had-been-signalled rate hike on the occasion of this meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is really what, if you want to go behind the curtain of the Governing Council debates, this is what took place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would add that in relation to the rate hikes we had the debate, weighted the pros and cons, and at the end of the discussion all members of the Governing Council rallied to the consensus of 50 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a strong indication on both accounts in relation to the higher step that we are taking to exit from negative interest rates, and on the other front, which is making sure that our monetary policy stance is transmitted smoothly throughout the entire euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the TPI is, obviously, an instrument that will help us deliver on our mandate of price stability, bringing inflation in the medium term back to 2%, and under that TPI all members of the euro area can be eligible; all of them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will find in the press release later, after this press conference, the detail of the eligibility conditions, but all members of the euro area are eligible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council, in its discretion, in its assessment will determine on the basis of the eligibility criteria, on the basis of the indicators that will signal or not unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics, whether or not a country is eligible and whether it activates the TPI.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, as I have just described TPI - and I'm happy to come back to that in terms of eligibility conditions and decision-making of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: TPI is a programme that is designed to address a specific risk that all euro area countries can face, so all euro area countries are, in principle, eligible to the TPI.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Subject to being considered by the Governing Council as eligible to the TPI, on the basis, notably - notably, not exclusively, it will be the discretion of the Governing Council to make the decision - notably on the basis of criteria that are very specifically spelt out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If and when the TPI needs to be activated, obviously, the Governing Council is going to conduct a thorough assessment of the situation in the affected countries, and the decision to begin TPI purchases, as I said, will be in the entire discretion of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, clearly, to assess whether you have unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics, the Governing Council will take into account multiple indicators to determine the warranted versus unwarranted, and to determine the orderly versus disorderly, and multiple indicators have been discussed and will be taken into account by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think what I tried to explain in my first answer is that in June we have signalled - it's not exactly what I said, by the way, neither in my blog nor in my Sintra speech, just in case you are interested, and very scrupulous and scrutinise those documents.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But at our Amsterdam June meeting we signalled our intention to increase by 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that was a signal - some degree of forward guidance to that signal - that was coupled with the signal that was given in relation to September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Given the decision that we are taking today, which is to increase - and remember Amsterdam, for those of you who have forgotten - was we intend to increase by 25 basis points, and at our September meeting the incremental increase will be possibly larger than 25. ,And some of you have assumed that it might be 50.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we decided to go for 50 basis points hike in July, and therefore, the combined forward guidance that existed for September is no longer applicable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think if you go back to the monetary policy statement you see very clearly that from now on we will make our monetary policy decisions on a data-dependent basis, will operate month by month and step by step.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what happens in September is going to depend on what data we have for September, but we are definitely on a normalisation path, in order to reach our medium-term objective of 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will determine in September on the basis of the data that we receive - and this is an [ECB staff macroeconomic] projection exercise in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So on the basis of the data that we receive at the time of those projections, we will determine what step we take on the normalisation path that we are taking in order to deliver on our medium-term 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, that doesn't mean to say that we are changing the ultimate point of arrival.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are accelerating the exit, and we are following the path of normalisation that we have flagged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, we are moving all three interest rates by 50 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, obviously, the cost of funding for banks and the cost of credit for those who borrow from banks is, assuming good transmission, which I do, given that we have a Transmission Protection Instrument and that we are very attentive to that, will go up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Why is that actually beneficial, at the end of the day, for those in the retail sector, for those consumers, for all economic agents?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The most precious good that we can deliver, and that we have to deliver, is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to bring inflation down to 2% in the medium-term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the imperative under the treaty, that is the strategy review objective that we have set for ourselves, and it's time to deliver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as publication is concerned, publication will take place in due course according to publishing principles and rules that we apply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the other question is concerned, I would just like to clarify that, if TPI is activated, it will avoid interference with the appropriate monetary policy stance, and we will address the implications of TPI purchases for the scale of the aggregate Eurosystem monetary policy debt security portfolio, and the amount of excess liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not going to go through the details of exactly which mechanism, sterilisation or otherwise, we would be using.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: These are practical matters that certainly have been discussed, have been agreed, but, if you don't mind, the Transmission Protection Instrument is intended to facilitate, enhance, transmission of our monetary policy stance in particular circumstances that we will address, and the ECB will be capable of doing that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the ECB is capable of going big for that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You give me another opportunity to clarify exactly what TPI is about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: TPI is going to be an addition to our toolkit, and it can be activated to counter unwarranted disorderly market dynamics that pose a serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy across the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because we want to make sure that we deliver on our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to make sure that our monetary policy stance is transmitted throughout the entire euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not the only tool that we have in our toolkit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have two existing tools already: We have, number one, PEPP, and in particular the flexible reinvestment of redemptions, as we announced back in June, which is now operational.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the flexible reinvestment of PEPP is operational, and it allows us to deal with unwarranted fragmentation risks that are created as a result of pandemic risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have OMT, which gives us a tool to deal with unwarranted impairment to transmission that are caused by redenomination risks and that are country-specific.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And now we have TPI, that I have just described, in order to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have the three instruments in the toolbox, and they all can be operated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I have said, and I will repeat, TPI is a programme designed for specific circumstances to address specific risks, but that is available to all countries of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because our concern is that monetary policy is transmitted throughout the entire area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So when the Governing Council will determine that a country is eligible under the four criteria that I am happy to come back to, if you want, and on the basis of the indicators that there is disorderly market dynamics, then it will decide that that country is eligible to TPI, it will activate TPI, and, as I said earlier on, there is no ex-ante limit to that programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I'm happy to go through the four specific criteria if any of you are interested.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there are four of them, and I think it's important that we understand that on this occasion, like on any occasion having to do with either monetary policy stance or monetary policy transmission, the ECB determines in its own discretion, not being hostage to anyone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the four criteria that it will use will be indicative, will be elements of information that it will take into account in order to make its decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the first one is compliance with EU fiscal framework, and that can take one of two forms, either not be in excessive deficit procedure, or having failed to take the effective action in response to [European] Council recommendations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's on the fiscal framework, and obviously borrows from another European institutions, which is both the Commission and the Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second is the absence of severe macroeconomic imbalances, and again, it borrows from other European institutions in relation to the excessive imbalance procedure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third is fiscal sustainability, so this is making sure that the trajectory of public debt is sustainable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to do that the Governing Council will take into account analysis by the European Commission, by the ESM, by the IMF, by other institutions, but it will certainly be together with the ECB internal analysis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Fourth: sound and sustainable macroeconomic policies, complying with the commitments submitted in the countries' recovery and resilience plans for the RRF [Recovery and Resilience Facility], and the European-Commission specific recommendations in the fiscal sphere under the European Semester.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you have a combination of criteria ranging from fiscal to macroeconomic, to compliance with the RRPs [Recovery and Resilience Plans] in particular, and obviously the DSA [Debt Sustainability Analysis].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all these four categories will be taken into account by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: , But once again, the Governing Council decides in sovereignty in respect to eligibility to the TPI.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, the primary mandate of the ECB is price stability, which we have defined as the 2% inflation medium-term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: ,And what we observe is on the outlook front and on the inflation front, and we try to assess what are the risks to both.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've explained that in detail in the Monetary Policy Statement, and made specific reference to the unjustifiable, unacceptable invasion of Russia against Ukraine, and consequences as a result of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are seeing upside risk to inflation, particularly in the short-term, but spreading.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So as ECB what we have to do is act in relation to inflation given the circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To your question about the impact of gas, it is clear that energy prices play a critical role in the high inflation numbers that we are seeing, that are undesirable, and that we will, unfortunately, continue to see for some time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are very attentive to what happens on the energy front, and in particular on the gas front, because it has an impact on electricity prices, as we all know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, most recent evolution concerning the gas supply through Nord Stream 1 in particular, is obviously a factor that we take into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: , And the decisions that have been announced by the European Commission in relation to savings, in relation to solidarity, in relation to inventory, are also taken into account in relation to the role that energy plays in relation to inflation, but also, obviously, in relation to growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at our projection dating back to June, we look at the most recent forecast published by the Commission last week.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Under the baseline scenario there is no recession, neither this year nor next year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just remind you that the ECB does not take a stance on political matters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Political matters are for the democratic process of each and every member state, and that is certainly the case for the country that you are referring to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Among other [reasons], due to the country-specific macroeconomic landscape, and that has happened in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the Governing Council will make the assessment of whether a country meets the eligibility criteria or not at the time when it has to make those determinations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it will do so having a threefold assessment, if you will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, it will determine a comprehensive assessment of market and transmission indicators.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, it will at that time evaluate the eligibility criteria.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third - that's very important - it will have to make a judgement call that activation of purchases under the TPI is proportionate to the achievement of the ECB primary objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, those of you who are familiar with the legal requirements and with the concept of proportionality will have understood what I mean by that, but this is, obviously, operational in relation to any activation decision that is being made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: I think your second question will be addressed my colleague, the Vice-President de Guindos.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, it's very difficult to give an opinion when you do not know the concrete details of the tax.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do not know whether it will be a tax on profits, it will be a tax on assets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's the first thing that we have to say; we do not know the details, and so our opinion cannot be complete in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I can tell you is what has been our policy line in the past with respect to taxation of banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at our opinions in the past, they are quite clear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What they tried to make quite explicit is that the tax should not impair credit extension, credit growth, because this is important for economic activity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, that we should try to avoid any sort of tightening of financing conditions for households and corporates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Finally, that the tax should not damage the solvency of the banking industry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This has been always in the opinions that we have produced in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has been always this kind of message to the governments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I repeat again, we do not know the concrete characteristics and features of the Spanish tax that has been announced, as you have said, by the Spanish Government.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so in order to have a much more concrete and specific answer and response and opinion, we will have to wait a little bit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: To your first point, that helps me to yet again come back to TPI, because in a monetary union there is an inherent risk, particularly the monetary union that we have here in the euro area, there's an inherent risk that a large shock can create fragmentation risks, and that can lead to self-fulfilling market dynamics that are not warranted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It matters for the singleness of our monetary policy in our monetary union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: , But those impediments can have different sources, and that is the reason why we have several tools.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said earlier on, we have the flexible reinvestment of PEPP, which has been deployed, and is currently operational.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have OMT, which was decided back then for another unwarranted, disorderly market dynamic, but having to do with more country-specific matters, and closely associated with the redenomination risk, because that's really what it was designed for at the time, if you remember.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we were short of this particular tool, which is the one that we have in front of us, the Transmission Protection Instrument, that is not related to redenomination risks, but to the unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that can impair the proper transmission of monetary policy throughout the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Which is, as I said again, it's with no limitation ex ante, which has been designed carefully with adequate attention paid to the safeguards that are necessary for that instrument to be valid, and with a creditor seniority that is pari passu with any other creditor in order for it to be efficient and not to crowd out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's what we have done, and I can assure you that we would rather not use TPI.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Governing Council would rather not use it, but if we have to use it, we will not hesitate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reason we decided, by total consensus around the table, to depart from the signal that we had given back in Amsterdam, was twofold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Number one, we had clear realisation of upside risk to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: , And I can give you a list of those examples: inflation going from 8.1% in May to 8.6% in June, way above our forecast; seasonally-adjusted month-on-month inflation rates that show strong inflation momentum for nearly all components; number three, a broad range of indicators of underlying inflation that have continued to increase; and pipeline pressures that are rising to record high levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And, added to that, which relates, essentially, to inflation, the euro/dollar rate that has fallen substantially in the last few weeks, which obviously has a bearing on inflation going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's on the basis of that set of monetary-policy-stance related elements that we have taken the decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, two-fold, inflation-related, and second, the fact that the concern that we had about monetary policy transmission is addressed by, number one, the deployment of the PEPP flexible reinvestment policy, and second, the unanimous support of the entire Governing Council to a strong and powerful transmission protection instrument that I have just described earlier on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So on the stance front we had good reasons to revisit, and on the transmission we are confident that the existence of that instrument, its ability to be deployed, is actually reinforcing our capacity to deliver on our price stability mandate and to walk that journey of monetary policy normalisation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, as I said earlier on, going from the signal [of] 25 to the 50 [basis points] that you are seeing now, is a higher step out of negative interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are now moving in one go to zero.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Does that mean that we are changing the terminal rate at which we want to arrive?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Does that mean that we are going to move extremely fast?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, we will be operating month-by-month, meeting-by-meeting on the basis of data, and we will adjust and calibrate accordingly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are much more flexible; in that we are not offering forward guidance of any kind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are data-dependent, but the ultimate destination of our policy path remains the same, which is to progressively raise interest rates to [a] broadly neutral setting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you are asking me next 'What is the neutral setting?'

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I can observe is that it has changed over the course of the last few years for a reason of factors having to do with demographics, with productivity and all the rest of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As seen by markets, it has also significantly adjusted in the last few weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will cross that bridge when we cross that bridge.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's a rather historical moment for me, at least, for two reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is it's very good when a whole team - the whole Governing Council - 25 members around the table, actually are in complete alignment and support for a transmission protection instrument which we regard as critical in order to properly transmit our monetary policy going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in that respect, at least from the President of the ECB point of view, yes, I think it's quite a gratifying moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It means that staff has done an enormous amount of work, that all members of the committees that are bringing together the expertise of the national central banks - Bundesbank included, of course - have worked really hard, and that we have come to the same view without any reservation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's the first time in over a decade that we raise interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And moving out of negative interest rates, by all accounts, certainly to me, is going to facilitate a number of things that we can explain to European citizens in order to help them understand what we are trying to do in order to reduce inflation and in order to procure price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in those two respects, yes, but, you know, I have a short history as a central banker.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's one that is intended for transmission of monetary policy throughout the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we intend to use it as a tool to make sure that monetary policy is transmitted throughout the region, our region, and is smoothly transmitted, without being impaired by unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will see, because the press release will be out in two minutes, and it will not give you, by the way, all details.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will give you some of the eligibility conditions, some key terms and conditions, but you should not expect all details to be there, because there is an element of discretion and judgement on the part of the Governing Council members to decide or not on activation and to assess eligibility or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are certain components that are best kept unpublished, undisclosed, uncommented upon, and I am sure that you understand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This instrument has been developed in record time by our teams.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We work fast, and we can do so at any point in time, in relation to eligibility, in relation to activation, in relation to drafting, which has been the case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On TLTRO, as you will have noted in the monetary policy statement, there is a particular sentence which says, 'In the context of our policy normalisation we will evaluate options for remunerating excess liquidity holdings.'

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What has worked in one direction has to be identified, analysed and properly addressed in the other direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Other principles apply, and that's what we will do in the near future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question: the Governing Council unanimously decided to raise the three key ECB rates by 75 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had different views around the table, a thorough discussion but the outcome of our discussion was a unanimous decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I have said before, and as I have repeated in that monetary policy statement, since our last July meeting we are data dependent and operate meeting by meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had the inflation numbers and the growth outlook, of course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in the face of these extremely high numbers - the last [inflation] reading was 9.1% [year-on-year] for a monthly reading, but if you look at the last ten readings, they were the last ten highest readings in turn - we had a good analysis of the decomposition of the sources of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A good analysis of where the inflation actually lies and what products are particularly affected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course energy is still the major source of inflation - [energy price inflation is] 38.3% compared with a year ago - slightly moving down in these August numbers, but it is still a dominant factor, as is in the increase in food.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we also have an inflation that spreads across the whole range of products in particular in the service sector, where supply factors are less prevalent and where demand plays a role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have a range of products and services that are actually north of 4% [inflation rate].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the face of an inflation that is extremely high, that is of a magnitude and persistence across sectors of that nature, obviously determined action had to be taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is very much in line with our determination to actually normalise monetary policy as we started back in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So for those who consistently repeat that the European Central Bank is lagging behind, I contend that we are on a journey that started back in December where we decided to put an end to the asset purchases, the PEPP and then the APP, to move out of negative interest rates as we did back in July and now to continue on our normalisation path, with a frontloading exercise that we conducted today, because we believe that the deviation from target is such that it warrants this frontloading.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also decided that this was not an isolated decision, but that we would raise interest rates further.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We didn't say that we would raise interest rates by 75 [basis points], as if 75 was the norm; it is not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will determine meeting by meeting on the basis of data how we reach that level of interest rates which will actually return us to the 2% target in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our forecast at the end of December [2024] - which is not the medium term but it's the end of our projection exercise - is at 2.3%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not there, so we have more journey to cover going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You were interested in the flavour of the Governing Council meeting; we had a very cordial, effective, deep discussion on all these matters and that certainly helped us on the basis of the proposals by staff and the recommendation by our chief economist Philip Lane, to actually go collectively in the direction of this 75 basis points hike.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you asked me about how close we are to "the rate".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether you call it a neutral, a terminal is obviously different but I would like to say this: what I know today is that zero is not the neutral rate and that where we are is not the neutral rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It takes frontloading, it will take further hikes in the next several meetings of a magnitude and at a pace that will be determined meeting by meeting and on the basis of the data that we receive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are certainly heading there because that is where we believe that we will actually deliver on our 2% medium-term target as indicated in our strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The baseline [GDP growth] outlook is 3.1% for 2022, 0.9% for 2023 and 1.9% for 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the baseline that we have in the projections by staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also have - and I think you will be receiving those documents as well - we also have a downside scenario that has been produced by staff on the basis of assumptions of risks in particular, some of which have already materialised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In those numbers you will see thatgrowth outlook is at [2.8]% for 2022, at -0.9% for 2023, and at 1.9% again for 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So while even in our baseline, we foresee some stagnation for the last quarter of 2022 and the first quarter of 2023, in the baseline we don't forecast negative growth in 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the downside scenario we do; that downside scenario differs from the current situation in that it includes in particular total shutdown of all Russian gas supply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, we are almost there, there is still a bit of flow going through the Ukrainian ones, but we also foresee rationing across the whole euro area and no measure of compensation between the shortage of gas supply and other alternative sources of supply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So nothing coming from either Asia or other producers of gas and in particular I don't think we take into account the liquefied natural gas (LNG) that we could be sourcing more of it from Norway or from the United States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a really dark downside scenario but it's one that concludes to a 2023 recession.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is the downside scenario; it is not the baseline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the issue of quantitative tightening: what we are focussed on at present is the most effective and most proportionate and most appropriate monetary policy instrument that we can use.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe at the moment that it is the policy rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are using the policy rate, we will continue using that policy rate in the next several meetings, as I have said, and of course we will look at other monetary policy instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a matter that we will of course debate amongst members of the Governing Council in due course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To your first question: I think it's a process of normalisation that we have started.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, beginning in December, out of negative territory in July and moving with this frontloading step in our journey of normalisation towards such rates that will be compatible for us to deliver and ensure a return to our 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Once we have reached that level of normalisation that will enable us to have the confidence that we will return to the target of 2% in the medium term, then we will examine what is the situation on the basis of data, on the basis of what monetary policy can contribute to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will cross that bridge when we cross that bridge.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment, we are actively busy and engaged in normalising our monetary policy and in making sure that we actually return to our 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other matter that you raised: you will be getting a technical press release that will describe precisely what decision we made in relation to the remuneration of government deposit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My recollection is that we're moving from zero to DFR (deposit facility rate) but I don't want to jump-start and I will let you just consult with great interest the technical decision that is embedded in the press release!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will not surprise you if I say that of course we do not target any kind of exchange rate for the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course we monitor very carefully and just like all of you, we have noted the depreciation of the euro relative to a basket of currencies but more importantly, relative to the dollar.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to give you an order of magnitude: it's since the start of the year 12% relative to the dollar, and 4% in nominal effective terms relative to other currencies in general.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that it does have an impact on inflation with a lagging time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has direct and indirect effects as well, and we are very attentive to those, but we do not target an exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not done so and we will not do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other question on TPI: you know, I don't have much more to say on TPI than I did last time around in July.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know that some would like to have masses of information on TPI.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If and when the criteria are met and the eligibility conditions were satisfied, we stand ready to use TPI, no question about it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question: I'll remind you that the TLTRO changes of conditions that were introduced during the pandemic were engineered, designed and intended to encourage banks to lend to the economy - which is what we all wanted, which is what was predominantly done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The TLTRO pricing that was then designed was intended to that effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, it's obvious that as we are shifting to positive territory in terms of interest rates, there are multiple dimensions of our operational frameworks, our remuneration mechanisms, that need to be revisited.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a matter that we will take up, that will see some resolution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has not been debated on the occasion of this particular monetary policy meeting, but it's an overall review that we will obviously conduct in due course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question: look, we are in a situation where at zero interest rate - and even with this frontloading - we are stimulating the economy, with an expansionary monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, doing that when we have 9.1% inflation and projected inflation at the end of our projection period north of our target at 2.3%, simply does not warrant that accommodative monetary policy continues to stimulate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mission is to restore price stability, it's to return inflation back to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a result of that, we are determined to do this job and we will continue to make the decisions on the basis of data, meeting by meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously if we are faced with a major supply shock, if for instance gas prices were to continue to skyrocket, we will take that into account both in terms of the consequences on growth, which will be recessionary, but also consequences on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That work will be done in due course, as I said, meeting by meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I can tell you for sure is that as we are so far away from the rate that will help us return inflation to 2%, our hikes have to be not only timely but of a magnitude that brings us closer and more quickly towards those rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, a contrario, am I saying here that as we get closer to those rates the incremental interest rate increases will be smaller?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No I am not saying that because we will proceed meeting by meeting and on the basis of data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I can tell you is that the further away we are, the larger the step we are taking.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a matter that is going to probably agitate debate and everybody will have their view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's obviously one that we have to decide again as we get closer and as our forecast tells us whether or not we are reaching our goal; the 2% medium-term target inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is what on every occasion will help us define whether we are at that particular rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You remember that last July we decided to no longer rely on forward guidance on many aspects, and to work meeting-by-meeting on the basis of data, with the exception of the reinvestment programme on APP and PEPP, for which we still have some forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the forward guidance that we have on APP is that maturing securities which were purchased under APP will continue to be reinvested, as long as is appropriate, in order to maintain ample liquidity conditions and an appropriate monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For PEPP it's not exactly the same forward guidance, but we also have forward guidance, and we refer to at least the end of 2024 without interfering with our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, what we are doing now is focusing and giving priority to the policy rate, because we believe that it is the most appropriate and most proportionate, most efficient instrument that we can use in order to return inflation to the 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We, of course, examine all instruments, and the reinvestment policies that we deploy are part of the instrument, but now is not the time, and we would regard it as premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will happen, but on the basis of data, on the basis of our analysis meeting-by-meeting, and once we have determined that these policies of reinvestment, or discontinuing reinvestment, are going to be necessary and appropriate to help us return to the 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: About underestimation of inflation: this is a matter which has been raised by many.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Can we work on the basis of numbers that are produced by our economists?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We were as blunt as to actually examine why and where the errors came from, because, yes, we made forecasting errors, as did all the international institutions, as did most of the economists, because it's virtually impossible to actually anticipate and include in new models COVID, the war in Ukraine, the energy blackmail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So yes, we made those errors, and when you go under the surface and try to find what is the origin of those errors, it's predominantly related to energy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So while I take the blame, because I'm the head of the institution, and yes, we made forecasting errors, but those errors were made by all forecasters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We came forward with the causes for the errors, and I can assure you that the staff constantly improves, tries to embed in the models what should be embedded which was not up until now, and that we also apply as much judgement as possible to be as accurate as we can.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is a fact that because these matters could not be anticipated, we have had to revise our projections, absolutely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you very much for your questions, but we actually took the decision today that we would continue to raise interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not just frontloading and then we are done with it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are frontloading and we will continue to increase rates meeting-by-meeting on the basis of data, because we believe that we are far away from the rate at which we hope and we'll see inflation return to the 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not scratching my head around the neutral rate versus the terminal rate versus the r* and so on and so forth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we know is that we want to get to that 2% medium-term target, and we will take the necessary steps along the way in order to get there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, it's probably more than two, including this one, but it's probably also going to be less than five.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I leave it to you to decide whether it's going to be two, three or four.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have at least a ballpark idea of how long it will take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the length of the journey, and this is the reference that we make to "timely": we want to return timely to that goal that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you've asked me if the tightening in the bond market is going too far or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not a bad anticipation that they've done, I would say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not sure it's perfectly accurate, but it's not a bad market assumption, in current conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Netherlands is in the region of the high-inflation countries, but it's not the highest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are further and higher rates, particularly up north and in the Baltic countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are very aware of the heterogeneity that we have between, say, Malta and France and the Netherlands and Latvia, for instance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to care about all citizens of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think for many years what my predecessors have tried to do is to make sure that we didn't go into deflation territory, and that is the reason why there was a negative rate since 2014, and why there was quantitative easing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The situation has significantly changed in the last 12 months, and I'm not trying to make a fine point or be cute about it, but we haven't tried for years to reduce inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Inflation is a phenomenon that we are facing and have been facing for the last 12 months or so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are now on that path of normalisation of monetary policy, so we are exiting that period of quantitative easing and negative rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are now moving into positive territory at a frontloaded pace, and we are determined to return to the 2% medium-term target that we have under our strategy review, and as a common denominator within the Governing Council, and we will take the steps that are needed to that effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The future will tell, but what I can assure you is that we are determined to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Inflation is a terrible phenomenon, and particularly for the less privileged people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our job is to return inflation to 2%, and we will deliver on that job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We should not expect, and nobody should expect that inflation is going to return to 2% in the next three months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because there is a lag time between the time when we make the decisions and when it actually translates through the transmission channels to the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And also because it is still predominantly a supply-driven phenomenon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I cannot convince the big players of this world to reduce gas prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I cannot reform the electricity market, and I'm very pleased to see that the European Commission is considering steps to that effect, because monetary policy is not going to reduce the price of energy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will give a strong signal to people that we are serious and that we will contribute to reducing inflation, but if the cause is predominantly supply-driven and based on energy prices that keep rocketing, this is for somebody else to do the job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we will do ours; we will do our job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're taking a major step by frontloading, and we know that we have more steps to go towards that rate at which we believe that we will return inflation to 2% in the medium-term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If it means that we have to go further than whatever rate you refer to, we will do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because we have a goal, we have a mission, we have incredibly high inflation numbers, we are not on-target in our forecast, and we have to take action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't want to see second-round effects; we want all economic actors to understand that the ECB is serious about returning inflation back to 2%, in whatever decisions they make.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I meant is that - and I think I was quoting another famous - not that I'm famous - but a famous central banker, who said that it was not just about science, but there was also an element of art about it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think what I understand that to be is that we cannot be purely mathematical.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We cannot be exclusively driven by the outcome of models, however sophisticated they are, however judgement we put into the selection of assumptions that we make.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also have to include in those decisions that element of collective judgement that we try to bring to the table in the course of those discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, what I'm saying is that we are not on a set course, other than being driven by our goal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So our decisions will be made meeting-by-meeting, will be data dependent, be state dependent, and what I'm trying to explain is that we are not trying to mimic any other central bank, we are not transforming a frontloading exercise into a permanent exercise, but if the data on our meeting-by-meeting review suggests that we should take a high hike of our interest rates, we will do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is not pre-set, it is not predetermined, and it will be decided meeting-by-meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the certainty is that we are far away from the goal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are taking a major step today by frontloading, and we will decide more interest rate hikes in the future over the next several meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question, I think you know the answer to the question, but I'm happy to repeat it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you compare the situation of the US and that of Europe, and in particular in relation to inflation, inflation in the United States is largely driven by demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the euro area it is largely driven by supply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not exclusively - there is also a portion of demand in the sources of inflation - but it's predominantly supply.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you look at the labour market, which is an important phenomenon to appreciate, whether we have a risk of further escalation of inflation and second-round effect in particular, we see a US market which is - some of you say it, actually - "red hot", where the rate of vacancy to unemployed person is 2 to 1, whereas, here in the euro area at large it's 0.3 to 1.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A third difference is that, clearly, in their normalisation path and possibly tightening path, the Fed is starting from a different base from that of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We were starting from negative territory, moving out of it, and going further on that normalisation path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think there are multiple other differences that I could give you, but I think those are the ones that will matter most for your analysis of the difference in inflation situation that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the need to accelerate, what I can tell you is that at this point in time, with the numbers that we have, with the dynamics that we see, with the sources of inflation, with the forecast that we have, we are determined to move.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to move at this timely pace that is referred to in the monetary policy statement, which means that as we are deviating from target, and with the high numbers that we have currently, we need to frontload, as we have this time around, and we need to continue hiking.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, we had to accelerate, because when you are faced with new data, with new analysis, with new forecasts, you of course have to adjust.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that our credibility will be judged by whether or not we return inflation to the 2% medium-term target as we are committed to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the impact of the depreciation of the euro in effective terms and relative to the dollar, I don't have a decomposition right now of how much exactly it contributed to the inflation as it stands, but it will be available in the documentation that will be published later on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Suffice to say that, indeed, it has a direct impact on our imports in particular, to the extent that most of the energy products are issued and denominated in US Dollars.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is a bag of questions that you put into one question!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have done with the decision taken today is making yet more progress in withdrawing the accommodative [policy] and [the] support to demand that was made available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Have we finished the normalisation of our monetary policy as we have called it?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have reiterated now is that we are going to decide the future path and pace of our rate increases on the basis of the data that we have, and we will do so meeting-by-meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are very much and deliberately turning our back to forward guidance, which is not helpful in the current circumstances given the level of uncertainty that we have pretty much all around.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what we are saying here is: Number one, we continue and make substantial progress in withdrawing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have further rate increases in the future so the normalisation process continues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At some point in time, we will have of course to identify the rate which will deliver the 2% medium-term target that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To do that, as I said, it will be data dependent and it will be meeting-by-meeting but we will look precisely at three key factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to give you a bit of flavour of how we are going to work in the next meetings that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First, we will look of course at the inflation outlook, which takes into account the evolution of the economy, including the higher likelihood of a recession.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So number one is the inflation outlook, this is what we are fighting, it's inflation, that's the first one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second is, we will also take into account the measures that we have taken so far because in the last three meetings including this one, we have hiked by 200 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, we will also be attentive to the transmission lag of monetary policy and we know, as we do that, that any decision that we make is not going to have an immediate impact on inflation, but will be subject to the time lag that always affects monetary policy decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That gives you - I hope - a bit of the flavour of the thinking and the rationale behind those decisions that will be made and those hikes that we will decide in the near future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think you had a second question which had to do with our balance sheet, so you covered it all in one question - not all because there are lots of other interesting and decisive matters that we discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, let us call it the reduction of our APP monetary portfolio.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a matter that we have discussed at our last retreat amongst ourselves, the governors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We did not discuss the substantive issues today - deliberately - because we decided on a lot of issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what we decided is that we would pursue that discussion and we would decide the key principles of the reduction of our APP monetary portfolio in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that gives you a bit of an indication of when those key principles will be discussed and decided, and I will be very pleased to inform you about those principles at our next monetary policy meeting in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that has to be of course in advance of the decision to implement and to roll out this reduction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think what we decided is clear and straightforward: it's a significant rate increase, 75 basis points, twice in a row.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decided to do that in order to pursue the substantial progress that we have to make in order to withdraw monetary policy accommodation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our sense is that we have already made significant progress, as I said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is more ground to cover, and the question of what that pace will be - what will be the magnitude of future rates - will be determined meeting-by-meeting and will be data dependent, adopting the review of the three factors that I have referred to earlier, which are roughly and quickly: inflation outlook, the measures we've taken so far, and the time lag of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I cannot tell you much more than that at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I stand by my comment: significant progress, withdrawing accommodation, more ground to cover.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have acknowledged that more rate [hikes] are in the pipeline, but at which pace, to which level I cannot tell you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we had a slight discussion about how not necessarily helpful this evasive neutral rate is and we decided to stick to withdrawal, completing that job and then taking a step to decide whether we need and how much we need to go further.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not by simply normalising monetary policy that we will identify and reach the interest rates that are necessary in order to deliver the 2% inflation target, over the medium term, that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question about TPI: we did not discuss TPI at all and we have said - and I have said -very clearly that in order to trigger TPI we will look at a series of indicators, amongst which are the spreads, the yields, but a few other indicators as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then we will determine if one country or several countries are or not eligible to TPI on the basis of criteria that I have also described for you in the past, which have to do with debt sustainability, the macro framework as well as fiscal policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think in the present state of uncertainty, with the likelihood of recession looming much more on the horizon and the probability of it having increased, everyone has to do their job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is our primary mandate and we are riveted on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are determined, all of us on the Governing Council, to deliver that price stability, which we have defined as the 2% inflation target in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We of course have a dialogue with fiscal authorities and when I sit at the table of the Eurogroup in particular, with colleagues who are finance ministers, I explain the point of our monetary policy, which is to fight inflation and to bring it down back to the 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously they take into account their imperatives but also the purpose of our mandate, to reduce inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that I must have repeated many, many times the famous triple T, which is "temporary, targeted and tailored", which from our perspective will help them address the needs of the most affected by income erosion and also by inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But without fuelling inflation on a broad basis, because that would be utterly counterproductive in that it would require that we take harder monetary policy measures in order to deliver on our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is the nature of the debate that we have, and we are all attentive to what happens in neighbouring countries in the euro area as well, and I think that the messages speak for themselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me about systemic risk: maybe I would turn it over to you, my dear Vice-President, but I just want to remind you that the ESRB - of which I am the President - has actually called the attention of all supervisors and regulators to the need to really focus on buffers and protection against potential risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Vice-President de Guindos: In two weeks, we will be releasing ourFinancial Stability Reviewand perhaps the main messages that we are going to include there are first, that there is a deterioration of the financial stability landscape in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This has to do with the outlook: lower growth, higher inflation, financial conditions have been tightening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will refer to, for instance, the situation of households, corporates, governments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, banks are much more resilient than they were for instance ten years ago, at the beginning of the financial crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have some concerns with respect to the non-banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the non-banks, taking into consideration the outlook, taking into consideration the situation of inflation, taking into consideration what is happening now in terms of financial conditions, then we have to be very vigilant because we know perfectly that perhaps in a remote corner of the financial system, we can have a situation that could become difficult or complicated, and amplify the financial tightening that we have seen over the last months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Joke apart, you asked me about the number of rate [hikes]and in the past, I did communicate our intention to move towards the neutral rate as a first step in the normalisation process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I am telling you now is that we have made progress on that normalisation path, but that we still have ground to cover, okay?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As we have made that progress, I am also telling you that the ultimate destination that we want to reach is the rate that will deliver the 2% inflation target in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That rate, by the way, is not necessarily the rate at which we will have considered that normalisation is completed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It may well have to go beyond that, but what I am also telling you is that we are going to decide meeting-by-meeting on the basis of data and using the three categories of considerations that I have mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know the path, we know the journey, we know the destination - which is not as clear as a figure that you would like to pin down because we cannot do that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not even, in October, at a meeting when we have a set of data that helps us have projections: outlook for growth, outlook for inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have that in December and we will take all these elements into account to determine what rate, by how much the rate will be increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will see there on the basis of data, on the basis of a possible recession, if it unfolds that way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the basis of the inflation outlook, which will be influenced by that eventual recession.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the basis of what we have done, on the basis of the lag time, time lag.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we will decide if at the following meeting we also have to proceed along those lines.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I have said, the rate will be the one that delivers the 2% medium-term target that we have in order to deliver price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, on the second point: I am very sorry that you could not read much into the TLTRO description that is included in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will have, by the way, plenty of technical details as to how it works but let me take a few minutes to explain to you why we made that decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because in the first place, when we modified the terms of TLTRO III back in the days of the pandemic, we made that decision for monetary policy reasons in order to incentivise banks to go contrary to what they would normally have done, which would've been to restrict lending.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We wanted to support lending and therefore encourage them by offering terms that were very attractive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was the monetary policy background against which we decided to revise the TLTRO III terms and conditions at the time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, in between we have been utterly surprised by the unprecedented rise in inflation in a very short period of time that called for a change of our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You've seen that we've moved from negative territory before July to now the 150 basis points for the DFR.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need to have the best possible transmission, and that is the main reason why we are changing the interest rate - and I'll come to that in a second so that you fully understand - that will apply as of November.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're doing that to make sure that there is no obstacle, that there is no deterrent to the transmission of our monetary policy, and that banks will actually transmit the lending rates, which by necessity of our monetary policy stance are higher and have to be higher.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Reason number two: it is also going to reduce the size of the overall Eurosystem balance sheet, which also goes in the same direction as our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third: it is also going to increase the pool of collateral that will be available going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that this is a sensitive issue give the scarcity of such collateral.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The key point is proper transmission of our monetary policy and elimination of obstacles that stand in the way of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I am going to tell you in very simple terms because you will find a technical annex which is fairly complicated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in very simple terms what we are doing is looking out to November 23rd, so it gives time for everyone to adjust and to be prepared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are raising the special interest rate, which will no longer be the rate that applies up until November 22ndunchanged, but from November 23rdonwards it will be the DFR.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is what we are doing, in addition to which we are opening three additional windows during which banks will have the opportunity to pay back if they so wish.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you're referring to the September projections that we produced at our last monetary policy Governing Council, and we had the baseline scenario, which for 2023 gave us plus 0.9%, and the downside scenario which gave us minus 0.9%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your question, really, is are we already in that downside scenario, and are we not facing the likelihood of a recession in '23.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Number one, we will know a lot better at our next projection exercise in December, when all the data are collected and we can offer you some new projections which will take into account all the developments that take place before the cut-off date that will be shortly before the Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Point number two, if you look at the downside scenario, many of the assumptions that we have made at the time have not materialised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in the assumptions we had a complete shortage of Russian gas.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had assumed no substitution whatsoever, and we have seen in the last few weeks that, thanks to the effort of the Commission, of various member states, there is a phenomenon of substitutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had assumed that commodity prices would continue to rise, and what we have seen is commodity prices declining, and for some of those commodities actually declining significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are not in the assumptions of the downside scenario.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is that to say that we are in our baseline?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, because there have been developments that are hallowed with uncertainty, but that are clearly - and we say so in the risk assessment in the monetary policy statement - which are clearly to the downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will incorporate those risks, if they materialise, in our baseline in December, which will give us a chance to have a more accurate picture for '22, '23 and '24.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But when you look at all the intermediate indicators that we observe in between two projection exercise, there is a slowdown at play.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still see very strong labour, and all the numbers, except the intention to hire, but other than that they are positive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We see fiscal support in discussion at the moment - and I'll come to the end of your question on that front - but pretty much all other indicators are pointing downward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you referred to some of the measures that were decided by member states, in order to curb energy prices, which are, you will remember, contributing massively to inflation - plus 40.7% from September '22 versus September '21 - it's a massive increase, and a significant contribution to the inflation that we are facing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I was going to give you a Normandy response, but that's not the appropriate way to address it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is all going to depend on how it is designed, what kind of transfers are operated, and how transfers, if such transfers take place, are financed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously, as we say in the monetary policy statement, we welcome structural reforms that will target the energy markets in particular, and we hope that these reforms can be led and developed by the European Commission for all European members, if at all possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first one, we have to do what we have to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is price stability, and we have to deliver on that using all the tools we have, and selecting those that will be most appropriate and most efficient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we're doing today by deciding a rate hike and by changing the interest rate of TLTROs going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is that to say that we are oblivious to the risk of recession?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously not, and obviously we are concerned, particularly about those who have low income and who are more vulnerable to not only the risk of recession, but to the reality of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we fight inflation we think of our mandate, but we think about those people who are suffering most from inflation, and we will continue doing so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that in the present set of circumstances, given the instruments and the analysis that we can do, the decision that we made today is the most appropriate in order to restore price stability, which, as you know well, is critically important for not just the stability of prices, but also for the economy to actually prosper and recover.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously, recession likelihood numbers resulting therefrom will be taken into account in the analysis that we conduct at our next December meeting, when we have far more in-depth data and information.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question that you ask, just as we cannot and will not be fiscal-dependent, we will not and cannot be financial market-dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We take into account financial market expectations; we look at them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is one of the elements that enter into our considerations, but this is not it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, we've got to do what we've got to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said to you and to your colleagues from Croatia, welcome.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're very pleased to have you with us today, and I'm personally delighted that Croatia is joining the club.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's no longer 19 member states; it's 20 member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As of now, as you probably know, there are already 20 governors at the Governing Council table, because your governor is already participating as an observer, not participating in the votes actually, but he's there with us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know, because there is a lot of work that has been going on for the last 12 months at least, that a lot of precautions and a lot of measures have been decided by the Croatian authorities, both the Ministry of Finance and the Croatian National Bank, in order to alleviate the risk of price increases that happen inadvertently as a result of conversion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So whether it is by way of required comparator of prices in the previous currency versus euro, or whether it is the special accountability of all the price setters, I think that Croatia has actually learnt from what we all have gone through more than 20 years ago, when the euro was introduced in a much smaller group of countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I really hope that all Croatian economic actors will feel compelled to actually respect those requirements, which I know are embedded currently now in the draft laws that will be implemented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is it going to be multiplied as a result of the fact that there is high inflation, and way-too-high inflation?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I certainly hope not, but we will have to see, and I think that it will be the vigilance of the competition and price authorities in Croatia, as well as all of you, to actually make sure that this is not the case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, first of all, I think it's always nice when you have a new member and an additional member in the family, and we are certainly thrilled about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a country that has made tremendous effort to align with the rules and regulations, to comply with the expectations and the requirements, that has passed all the tests, both under the review of the Commission and with our own legal assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a great development that is taking place in very early '23, and it's a vote of confidence for the euro area, and we hope to help each other, and certainly to offer the shield of the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, first of all, I don't want to comment on political discourses and I would certainly refrain from that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
