text: And as is always the case at the Governing Council meeting, there were a variety of views expressed and I think that it's fair to say that everybody agreed that increasing rates was necessary; that second, we are not pausing, that's very clear, and, third, we know that we have more ground to cover on the basis of the baseline that we had, which is still guiding us until we have our next projection exercise, and on the basis of the data that we have received in the course of the last few days and that we brought together during the meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the ultimate balancing act, which received almost unanimous support and that is reflected in the monetary policy statement in front of you, was really predicated on the methods, the data we received, and the understanding that where we are is totally consistent with the baseline that we had for the outlook last time around.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Remember, at the last March meeting that's what I said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And second, that underlying inflation is still high and third, informed by the bank lending survey and the data that we have concerning interest rates, which is a little bit outdated because it goes back to February, the transmission of our monetary policy is working at least [with regards] to the financing leg and we are not yet certain about the next leg, which is transmission from banks to the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's on the basis of all that, that we made our decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now that we have increased rates significantly and sometimes by very large increments, establishing absolute credibility on our determination, it was sensible, in view of what I have told you, to return to a more standard increment, with the understanding that, based on the information we have today, we have more ground to cover and we are not pausing - that's extremely clear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: De Guindos: Turning to your second question, I think that we should start with a consideration: if you look at the characteristics of the US banks that are running into difficulties, I think that there are some common features.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one is that they are medium-sized, regional, they share very concrete and very idiosyncratic business models, and they are quite open to interest rate risks - they are vulnerable to an increase in yields.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think that this model, this situation is not extrapolatable to the European banking industry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will not repeat what we have said many times - that European banks are resilient [because of] their levels of capital, levels of liquidity and quality of the liquid assets - but I think that simultaneously, we have to remember that an increase in interest rates, in yields, is positive for the European banks because the increase in margins outweighs the potential losses that this increase in yields could cause in fixed-income portfolios.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think that it is quite clear that there is no space for complacency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of the things that we - all of us - have been surprised about is how rapidly a bank run can take place and how rapidly a bank can be emptied.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think that this is the combination of new factors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one is digital banking and the second one is social networks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The combination of both have even led to a new situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that as supervisors and regulators we have to bear in mind this new framework because we believe that this is going to be key in the near future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm tempted to remind you of the Emerson quote, "it's not so much the destination that matters but the journey", and we are on a journey and we are not pausing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Under the present circumstances and based on what we have, which is the baseline of March, we know that we have more ground to cover.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a clear reference in the second paragraph of the Monetary Policy Statement [in which] we explicitly refer to that by saying that our future decisions will ensure that the policy rates will be brought to levels sufficiently restrictive to achieve a timely return of inflation to our 2% medium term target and will be kept at those levels for as long as necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We covered a lot of ground in the last nine months [prior to today's meeting], moving from minus 50 basis points to plus 300 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As to the exact amount, by how much we increase rates, as I said in my introduction in the response to the first questions, there were a variety of views.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some governors suggested that maybe 50 [basis points] was appropriate, others believed that 25 was appropriate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I didn't hear anybody suggest that zero would be appropriate, which confirms to you that this is a hiking journey that we are on and it will continue to be so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But at the end of the deliberations and having had a chance to confront our views and answer the questions and really put everything in perspective, there was a general and very strong consensus behind the decision that you have in front of you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't have a magic number of what constitutes "sufficiently restrictive".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that the honest answer is that we will know what that is when we get there and we are in the process of moving into that direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think what's important is to understand what it means to have restrictive rates and to be in restrictive territory.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the best example is to see whether the rate decisions that we make, the rate increases that we decide, are actually having an impact on the economic actors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And when we look at the Bank Lending Survey or when we look at the interest rates and the pace at which they have increased over the last few months, it is obviously the fact that interest rate decisions that we made and the interest rates level we are on are having an effect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't know because we are not seeing the transmission at this point in time into what I call the second leg of the economy, which is the real activity, which then has an impact on prices and then reduces inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are seeing inflation coming down, don't get me wrong, because headline is coming down as a result of energy prices having come down significantly, as a result of the easing of bottlenecks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are not yet seeing the complete impact that we desire in order to arrive at the 2% medium term that constitutes our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are very attentive, we look at that, as you know it's one of the three components that we look at, the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Number one, we made the decision but the decision specifically says "we expect".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we expect to let the APP run down as time goes by.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In answer to your question about whether we go to zero: if we do, then it's going to take [at least] the next 15 years, so I don't think I'll be around for that, I know I won't, and I'm not sure that you will be around either.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the ultimate perspective is that one, as we consider things today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've decided to expect the effectiveness of the decision as of July, saving a little bit of optionality just in case, simply because we have seen that the partial reinvestment that has been effective since March has actually run very smoothly and has been well-absorbed by markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't see any point in not accelerating the move because there are valid reasons for [doing] that: it lowers the amount of excess liquidity, complements our policy rate, reduces the side effect of a large balance sheet - all of that completely justifies the fact that the APP is let to run down gradually over the course of time, which will be an average of 25 billion per month that will not be reinvested, roughly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, running the whole APP programme to zero will take [longer than] 12-15 years, given the maturities we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would just reserve one thing, because we discussed it during the Governing Council and it's not reflected in the Monetary Policy Statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, we have adopted a tilting approach to our reinvestment policy of the APP and in particular for the corporate bonds, which are the prime targets of that tilting, in order to privilege those corporates that have a good environmental footprint, that have a transition plan and that disclose all the appropriate information about their plans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course if we go to full run-down, that tilting process is not going to be applicable because there will be nothing to tilt it off, there will be no basis for that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The jury is out as to how we can continue to deliver on our Paris agreement compliant investment and reinvestment programme without the reinvestment phase and how we address that, which is something that we agreed we would take into account and consider to see how we respond to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was a general view that that was the right move, completely sensible, legitimate at this point in time given the market absorption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some might have preferred to wait until the June meeting to announce it, given that it's effective as of 1 of July.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But with the principle of predictability that we had agreed in the first place, we thought it was just better off to just announce it with reserving a little optionality on the side.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know of one and only one target and this is our medium-term target of 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course the Bank Lending Survey that we receive on a quarterly basis informs us about the tightening of credit to the economy, and it also informs us about what the banks assess will be or will not be the tightening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite a sophisticated survey which is really for information, intelligence, anticipation of the credit tightening now and the credit tightening going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also illustrative of the demand and that's an interesting point because in the Bank Lending Survey, the demand from corporates is really, really down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's a learning we take, which indicates that our interest rate policy is beginning to have an impact, because, when asked, the corporates - and we had a corporate survey conducted - say "it's the interest rates, it's not that we don't want to invest but the interest rates are pretty high".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that [brings us back to the question of] restrictive territory or not: yes, we are in restrictive territory because if that is the response of corporates, then it shows that [our policy] has worked.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On Credit Suisse, number one, it was addressed very swiftly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Swiss authorities maybe did not have many choices and it was very specific and probably a long-lasting issue that was lingering and had been lingering for a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I certainly would not draw the conclusion that the merger between UBS and Credit Suisse to be decided is an indication that there is a financial crisis, far from it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that we also learnt the value of having rules and the ability we had to come out very quickly on the pecking order of creditors actually mattered a lot and I think we can also take a bit of learning from that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When creditors and investors know exactly who is going to bear the brunt of outstanding liabilities in a situation of insolvency, it just helps.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: De Guindos: On the question about the indicators that we consider, that we look at: we have a range of indicators, for instance equity prices, bank bond spreads, the evolution of deposits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not seen the kind of situations that happened in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had an increase in tensions after the events in the US with Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are continuously looking at those indicators but, clearly, now the conclusion is that the European banking industry has been clearly outperforming the American one in terms of the tension [reflected] in these kinds of indicators and potential stress in financial markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Data dependency is not forward guidance, and I'll try to explain that to you for a second.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not giving you the forward guidance that "come what may" or "subject to" or "until such time we will do this or that."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had it in the past and it was very appropriate to have forward guidance as we were at the lower bound, and that was a tool that was very useful.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I'm telling you now is given our baseline, the findings that we have, the data that we can analyse today, our judgement in the room is that we are not pausing, that applies to today, based on what we see we determine that we have more ground to cover.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not saying that in the abstract, I'm saying that with reference to the baseline of March, to what we are seeing in development and I'm here saying we believe that we have more ground to cover.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not state-dependent, it is not time-dependent, it is a judgement that we make today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I hope I have been clear to try to explain to you how we can actually say that very firmly without giving forward guidance and being data-dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Come the June meeting, come the July meeting, come the September meeting and so on and so forth, we will look at the data and we will use the three criteria of our reaction function for monetary policy purposes and we will make our decision on a meeting-by-meeting basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had long discussions about core [inflation], and we actually had many more discussions on underlying inflation, because core is interesting, core is easy to communicate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You take headline, the whole basket of everything that's in the index, you take out food, you take out anything having to do with energy and you have core.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we want to go a little bit deeper into the index and the evolution that we see and we have multiple measurements that you are familiar with, you know the trimmed mean, the PCCI [Persistent and Common Component of Inflation], the PCCI excluding energy and so on and so forth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at all of those and we try to understand from the evolution that we see what is the likelihood of inflation evolution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, I'm not maybe addressing your core versus headline question but I'm simply saying that headline is the objective that we have, it's the target that we have, that we've agreed in our strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: People see all prices increasing and we are working for the people of Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Core, easy to communicate but maybe not as informative as we want it to be, so that leads us to dissect, in far more details, inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for that question because it is food prices that are hurting most, particularly the most vulnerable people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that because in the basket of consumption the most vulnerable spend a lot more on food than those who are well-off.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we pay special attention of course to food and the increase in prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have seen it go down, if you compare March and April numbers it is going down, but we have to be extremely attentive because there are multiple factors that apply to food prices, that apply to processed food prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we have also flagged the fact that profits last year and particularly in 2022 have contributed to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This year, 2023, what we have seen of 2023, we see more wage increases contributing to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We would hope that through a good social contract, these drivers of inflation do not activate each other in what I have called in other places a tit-for-tat - I want more wages, I'm not going to give up on profits - and you are then at risk of something that is much more difficult and would lead us to have to take more active measures in monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, I wish I could tell you "of course it will continue to go down" but I'm observing that it has gone down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are other factors that will come into play, you know, clearly climate change is something that will have an impact probably on a sectoral basis, probably in relation to certain food items.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What happens in Ukraine is also going to bring another uncertainty in the background of cereal price in particular, but commodity prices have gone down, that is a fact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know I've heard the fiscal dependency, I've heard the finance dependency, I had not heard the Fed dependency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB is an independent central bank, looks at what others do around the world, from New Zealand, which has been an interesting innovator in the field of monetary policy, all the way to the Fed and others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's obvious that the US economy, in whichever way it evolves, has spillover effects around the world given its size, the depth of its financial markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But you know we have a target, we have a journey, we know as of today that we have more ground to cover and whatever the decision of the Fed is in the next few weeks, months, we are going to be riveted to our objective and will of course take into account variables.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know the currency for instance has an impact, any spillovers will be taken into account, but we are not Fed-dependent in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As to the actual tightening impact that the APP run-off has, I don't want to commit a number, but it does not have a massive impact suffice to say, but we can give you separately the exact amount that has been calculated, but it's not material.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, of course we are aware of these households that have contracted loans with floating rates, variable rates, whatever you call it, and from Finland to Portugal, from some of the Baltic countries to Spain, it is the case that some families are hurting because the reimbursements that they have to honour have gone up as a result of the interest rate increases that we had to decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is unfortunately not something that we can alleviate or attenuate because our task is price stability, our task is to reduce inflation and the tools of choice that work in that respect is the interest rates and we have to use that interest rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some countries are taking particular steps and measures and some financial institutions are also looking at offering moratoria or delays.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that the best we can do is to really tame inflation in a timely manner, meaning as fast as we can, in order to then facilitate a return to different interest rates that would not be as high in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm not here making any commitment to cut at any point in time, thank you very much.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for giving us that angle from the East.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know I would hope that, together with my European colleagues, we can, one, learn from colleagues, particularly Japan, which is moving into a new direction with a new governor.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So anything that will be the Japanese monetary policy going forward and any understanding that we have of their strategy review, which he has announced, will be of interest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would be very happy to share with him the learnings from our strategy review which I had started when I took the job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would also hope that we can explain to colleagues from Canada, Japan and the United States that the Europeans together are going to continue to demonstrate resilience, capacity to operate together.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I would hope that in that respect something that we say in the statement here will resonate, which is to agree on the fiscal governance in short order, so that in addition to having a monetary policy that is common to 20 countries, we also have a fiscal framework which gives governance to the 27 member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that fiscal policies that are determined by member states are also focused on value for money, for lack of a better word, in other words putting in place the right reforms, focusing the spending where it is going to increase the competitiveness and the efficiency of the economy which is something that is absolutely indispensable in order to have this social contract which is often associated with Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On QT let me be very clear, QT is the decision that we expect to implement as of 1 July concerns APP reinvestments only and nothing else.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have forward guidance on PEPP reinvestment, nothing until 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will find, I think in the annex to my statement, a reference to the PEPP and to the principle of flexibility, which we believe is an important key aspect of PEPP going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So those tools are intact, we are not planning on not reinvesting anything that comes for redemption under the PEPP agreement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If anything, we have managed to offer the possibility for banks to accelerate and anticipate the reimbursement, which I think has avoided a cliff effect, that we would have had, over a trillion euros would have become outstanding in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thanks to the accelerated reimbursement we are now down to 477 billion, I'm checking the numbers because I want to be clear on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not a surprise, it's a come due date and reimbursements are due and I know that banks have prepared for it and that there is a lot of liquidity out there to continue to prepare.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, you know it wouldn't surprise me if some of the facilities that we have that are standing facilities - liquidity windows that are available, full allotment and rates that are well-known to all - would be used again, because that's a perfectly normal job of a central bank to actually provide liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know we have weekly, we have the LTRO, three months, full allotment on all those liquidity facilities and if anything was to happen we have demonstrated in the past that we can be inventive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, this meeting was the meeting of a Eurosystem projection exercise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We essentially did what we said we would do: data dependent and using the three elements of our reaction function to determine what was the right decision today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the reason why we increased all three rates by 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can even go further than that: I can tell you that, barring a material change to our baseline, it is very likely the case that we will continue to increase rates in July, which probably doesn't come as a big surprise to you, but that's what I'm telling you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is so because we are determined to reach our target in a timely manner, and to continue to apply the principles that we have applied today: data dependency, the three elements of the reaction function, and moving meeting by meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously, we are better informed at each projection meeting which happens, as you know, in June, in September and later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To your second question: I don't know what difference to make between a pause and a skip.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have not studied enough the press conference of my friend and colleague, Mr Powell.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as far as the ECB is concerned, I said what I said: we have hiked interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Unless there was a material change to our baseline, we will continue to hike at our next meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we are not thinking about pausing, as you can tell.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wish I could give you the very simple answer where I say when we are there and when financing conditions are such, and the tightening has reached that level for corporates, for mortgages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But unfortunately, it doesn't work like that because what we know is the target that we have - which is price stability as defined by the 2% medium term - added to which we want to be confident that it stays at that target of 2%, which is why duration matters as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is going to be a factor of those three elements that we will be looking at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it's the inflation outlook, which is every month, and every three months in particular, informed by all the new financial and economic data that we receive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can assure you that we look at multiple cuts and subsets of inflation to arrive at what is thecorestof the core.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't limit our review at core; we go further than that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's a whole variety of the prices and the inflation that we look at, and we need to see that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need to be confident that it is heading down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment, we have some of those measurements declining a bit, some of those sort of stable and others still going strongly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The third component is the strength of transmission, which we measure at each and every step of the way from the market rates, bond prices, credit by banks, bank funding.And then to the economy, where we refer to the 4.4% and 3.4% [April bank lending rates to] corporate and households, because that's how it is transmitted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, that's the path that we want to see delivering so that we head towards our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we have done, that's what we will do and we will stick to that methodology.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, your first question referred to the core inflation revision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We revised 2023 and 2024 and ultimately to 2.3% [in 2025] which moved by 0.1 from the previous projections [of 2.2%].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think on the basis of that you can easily conclude that we are not satisfied with the results of that inflation outlook - which is only one of the three components that we look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the reason why we are making the monetary policy decision that we make today, and why we are thinking that, unless there was a material change to the baseline, we would again hike interest rates in July.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The terminal rate is something that we will know when we get there because it is not what is driving our analysis and our deliberations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is driving it is the ultimate destination, which is the 2% inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we want and there are lots of components that come in to help us arrive at the 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We spent a lot of time on the labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We spent a lot of time because it is becoming one of the major components of the drivers of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To oversimplify: energy played a significant role, then food kicked in, and energy is now fading, has moved now in May and is in slightly negative territory.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But labour, and wages in particular, is playing a significant role as a driver of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's quite extraordinary because there have been more people employed, the average hours have been up, wages are increasing - we had 5.2% growth for the first quarter in the compensation per employee -, and the output is where it is: stagnant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, there is an issue of unit labour cost -in other words, productivity - which clearly has an impact on inflation as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue to really monitor and dissect as well as we can this entire enigma of the labour market - which is, as I said, playing a critical role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's especially important because many services which are playing a large part in our economy are labour-intensive, and wages in that respect play a key role.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is partly, by the way, the reason why we have - I was going to say upgraded, but it's not upgraded-, but why we have increased our projection for core inflation in both 2023 and 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first one, our revision to core inflation - I've started answering already in the previous question-, a lot of it is attributable to the unit labour cost.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The rest is what you have in the monetary policy statement, which is past upward surprises.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it's a different starting point, which is informed by data that came in after the last projection that we made in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The latest data that we had in terms of inflation was from January.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, things obviously changed between those January data and the May data that we have incorporated because we cut off on the 23 May[1].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The large part of it is the unit labour cost.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have to tell you that it was quite a harmonious discussion and a very good and thorough economic discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, we went really deep into the analysis of the labour market and tried to really understand the forces behind inflation to better fight it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, I just want to remind that it was a twofold decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was, number one, the 25 basis points but it was also the decision, or the confirmation, that we would stop any reinvestment under the APP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in the middle of that fight against inflation and this is what we know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're going to get to that 2% and we're going to reduce it to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What happens next is another story, but we want to be at target and we want to be confident that it remains at target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, the two elements are going to really drive our monetary policy going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the lag time: we know that there is lag time, that the decisions that we have made in the last soon-to-be-a-year - which are monumental, by all accounts, both in terms of speed, in terms of height, volume of hikes, if you will, and we are seeing some effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are seeing it in credit, both in volumes and in rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is some lag time - not that much by textbook standards, which will typically say that it's anywhere between 18 and 24 months, maybe a bit more.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But because it is so unprecedented and such an exceptional situation, we really have to monitor that very carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether it is going to be faster, whether it is going to be a bit more slow because there has been variation in the terms of loans, for instance, to both corporates and mortgages and therefore the transmission is not operating as smoothly as it would if everything was at floating rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All of that we are looking at extremely carefully to measure the transmission and see how fast it moves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to see it all the way down to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's difficult to say whether we're in the same position as the Bank of Canada because we did not pause.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, in a way we don't have to ask ourselves whether we are at neutral rate or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we are not where we want to be if we want to reach our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of having to pause or having to skip: as I said, number one, we have not discussed it at all and we have not begun thinking about it because we have work to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I thought you were going to say that it's an important month because we are celebrating our 25thanniversary - which was also the date when the ECB was opened first on the ground here in Frankfurt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, the objective that we have is very clear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The journey to get there is not over and we have ground to cover.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we will be as restrictive as long as needed in order to make sure that we reach that destination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Under the current parameters, 2.2% in 2025 is not satisfactory and it's not timely - which is why we are making the decisions that we are making today, and later on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the end of June banks will reimburse €477 billion that they had borrowed under TLTRO, which was this very special facility that we had put in place to help the financing of the economy at the time of the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those loans were granted for periods of three years and there were various operations in the course of the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The repayment which is coming due now, is known and has been known for a long time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually it was so well-known that it should have been a lot higher than that but we took measures in order to avoid that we had this sort of cliff effect of a massive reimbursement which would have exceeded €1 trillion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But banks know about it, they have known about it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They have done their funding plans in order to respond to the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In any event, we have the normal facilities available, whether it's MRO or LTRO if that was ever needed, just in case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The APP reinvestment will be completed at the end of June, and we will let run-off take place as of July.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have experienced that partial reinvestment now for a few months because it was decided back in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Given the amounts that we are talking about, we have reasons to believe that it should be absorbed also in a smooth manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will, as I said, always have the means to take action and to use all the tools that we have available if it was needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The labour market situation and the employment situation is the good news in Europe, and we have never seen the unemployment rate be so low.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Actually in our forecast we see the unemployment rate go from this 6.5% that we have now, to 6.3%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also see wages continuing to increase in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you really asked me specifically the question of whether corporations and labour - and I'm using that term in a generic, comprehensive way - will find the terms under which they don't contribute to fuelling even more inflation that would call on us to take harder monetary policy measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think economically it is justifiable, it is rational, but of course humans are humans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's going to be for the parties around the table to actually determine what they do going forward in terms of allocating profits and organising these social relationships.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What they can be certain of in their discussion is that the European Central Bank will take all necessary measures to return inflation to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That, they can count on, and we are confident that we will get there so I hope it helps in their deliberation going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The persistency of inflation, as I said, has a lot to do with this unit labour cost that I have mentioned earlier on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is really the strong - I don't want to use sticky component, because it is going to be persistent, and we know it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Numbers will continue to be high in the months to come, by the way, because we believe that services are going to continue to grow strongly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're heading into the summer: all the summer activities, whether it's transportation, whether it's hospitality, whether it's vacation, all of that is going to go well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, that persistence is to be expected in the short run.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It declines in 2025 and we have not revised upwards significantly for 2025 because we believe that other elements will kick in, which will reduce inflation numbers - unless risks were to materialise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But under the baseline, the indirect effect of energy costs will continue to fade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can still find them in prices, but it is going to gradually fade out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We expect the persistence of inflation to gradually fade away.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, first of all on wages: we are not seeing second round effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The only thing that I'm trying to say here is that we have to avoid what I have called the tit-for-tat where, in response to inflation, both corporates and labour want to receive full compensation - which obviously would possibly lead to that second-round effect that I was alluding to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously, the sooner the better in terms of when do we bring inflation back to 2%?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be also realistic, and we have to be measured in the response that we give, but very determined in the delivery of those measures, and persistent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We just all wish that everything was clear and simple, wouldn't we?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I said - and thank you very much for your question - is that unit labour cost, which is slightly different from wages, negotiated wages, however you want to measure it- is having an impact, or it is rather causing the revision of core inflation projection.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can certainly have that projection and at the same time acknowledge that today we are not seeing any spiralling of wages and prices that would cause this second-round effect that we would be very concerned about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The TLTRO reimbursement that is falling due at the end of June, which was anticipated, known by all parties involved, is taking place at the end of June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will, as a result, reduce the balance sheet of the ECB by €477 billion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second part of the decision that we made today was to stop reinvesting redemptions under APP, and let APP move into a run-off mode.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That means that, for instance, the PEPP continues as it was indicated in the only part of forward guidance that we still have in our monetary policy, which is until 2024 we continue the reinvestment and we apply flexibility if, and where, it is needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The cut-off date for technical assumptions, such as those for oil prices and exchange rates, was 23 May 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The projections for the global economy were finalised on 23 May and the macroeconomic projections for the euro area were finalised on 31 May 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just remind you what we have been doing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I will come to your interest, which is what happens next.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me just remind you what we are doing, and what we have been doing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are raising interest rates, all three rates by 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is the ninth decision to hike that has been taken in a matter of one year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So invariably, on meeting after the other, we have raised rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this decision that was unanimously agreed amongst all members of the Governing Council is driven by one key determination, which is to bring inflation to target, our target, which is medium-term inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have decided as well, and I will come to your minimum reserves remuneration as well, because that was your second question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have also decided, and I'm going to quote, because it is a sentence that you might hear over and over, not only this time, but also next time and future times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We say "our future decisions will ensure that the key ECB interest rates will be set at sufficiently restrictive levels for as long as necessary to achieve a timely return of inflation to our 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, some of you may have noticed a slight change of a verb.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think it is predicated on our determination to be data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, I have said on many occasions that we had ground to cover or that we have more ground to cover.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I am saying here is that data and our assessment of data will actually tell us whether and how much ground we have to cover.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are deliberately data-dependent and we have an open mind as to what the decisions will be in September and in subsequent meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because this determination based on data might vary from one month to the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we might hike and we might hold, and what is decided in September is not definitive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I hope it is very clear that we are not in the domain of forward guidance but we are very strongly rooted in our determination to break the back of inflation and to take inflation back to 2% in the medium term on a sustainable basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to do that, we will be informed by data, we will analyse the data and we will then decide at that point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have the inflation outlook, we will have two readings of inflation with all the underlying dissection and understanding of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will have even more understanding of our monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that will be repeated every Governing Council after every Governing Council, so that we can make sure as I said that we break the back of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our primary job is to set monetary policy so that inflation stabilises at 2% over the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we also have a public duty to make the implementation of our monetary policy as efficient as possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So by cutting the remuneration on minimum reserves only, that's the basis that we will use.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Cutting it to zero, we will reduce the amount of interest that we pay, which means the implementation of our policy is going to be more efficient.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the same time, it is going to have no impact on our policy stance, which is currently determined by the remuneration not on minimum reserves, but on excess reserves, which as you know are far more plentiful than the minimum reserves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More efficiency and that's also of course predicated on the principle of proportionality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not discussed the reduction of our balance sheet and we have obviously acknowledged that the balance sheet has been reduced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it has been reduced as a result of, number one, the reimbursement of more than what was expected to be reimbursed under the TLTRO reimbursement in June, and also by the fact that we have not only stopped net asset purchases but we have stopped any reinvestments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, the balance sheet of the ECB is reducing as a result of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have not discussed any further reduction at this point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other question, as you know, transmission of monetary policy is one of the three metrics that we use in order to determine our monetary policy stance, the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is the impact on lending, lending for banks, lending by banks to both corporates and households?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we try to measure that as accurately as possible by looking at volumes of loans, by looking at rates, by looking at obviously the bank lending survey that many of you have commented on yesterday, which informs us about what banks anticipate and in which areas, in which directions they expect to either increase or reduce the volumes of loans and reassess their risks in relation to borrowers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's the first leg and there are clear indications that our monetary policy is transmitted though that channel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The next one, which is the second leg, is transmission to the economy and from financing to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are really now beginning to see transmission materialising, whether you look at investment in housing, whether you look at investment altogether, there is obviously a decline on those two accounts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Still too early and there is certainly more in the pipeline, but we are definitely seeing monetary policy being transmitted and being transmitted strongly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's obviously the case for the first leg and it is now also beginning to be the case in the second one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will have to understand something, which is that I am not repeating things if prompted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what I just said in response to the first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I just want to repeat it for you just to make sure that I am as clear as you would expect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are moving to a stage where we are going to be data-dependent, and we will take the new projection by staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are going to take more information about how transmission has taken place and on the basis of that, we will determine whether we hike or whether we pause.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what I can assure you of is that we are not going to cut, that is a definite no!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But on the other side, it could be hike, it could be a pause.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if it is a pause, it would not necessarily be for an extended period of time, because as I said, it will vary from meeting to meeting, because we continue to decide on a meeting by meeting basis every time informed by the data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I hope it is as clear as I can be, because we are, and that was absolutely endorsed by the Governing Council, which has validated this decision unanimously, determined to operate on that basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You always ask something that I should repeat or that I should endorse but I am not doing that, sorry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, if my colleagues take this view or another, that's fine.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And they can certainly be free to expand in one way or another.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can assure you that on the occasion of today, it was a unanimous determination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The determination is rooted in one very simply direction: 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: 2% is the goal and we will get there, come what may.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: With respect to commercial real estate, it is quite clear if you look at our financial stability review that we have paid a lot of attention to commercial property and to the decline in prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This decline in prices started even before the tightening of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you know, the different agents and players that are exposed to commercial property market are mainly non-banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is something that we pay attention to, that we have analysed in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there is a clear divide between commercial and residential property.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the case of residential property, we have not seen any decline in prices but what we have seen is a slowdown in the evolution of prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But commercial property is something that we have paid attention to and will continue to pay attention to in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lagarde: And on your second question, I think you raised the question of the potential risk of second round effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just take you back for a second, because it is a matter that we have reviewed, that staff are doing a lot of work on and that we have discussed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is the role of wage growth and the role of profit margins as two key drivers of inflation, which are gradually eliminating the external causes that were prevalent before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The wage increases are definitely playing an increasing role as a driver of inflation and so have profit margins.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the profit margins front, we are seeing a slight decline in the first quarter of 2023 and as you may remember, our projection is also predicated on the fact that profit margins are wide enough to accommodate the squeeze that will be needed in order to allow for wage increases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if we look at inflation expectations, if we look at how wages and profit margins are evolving, we are not seeing a second-round effect and for the moment at least, nothing suggests the risk of strengthening any second-round effects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are really monitoring that very carefully because, as you know, service inflation is the sort of hard nut to crack in terms of inflation, given that on goods it's going down, energy is coming out and it's negative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, we are focusing on services that are labour-intensive and that are also not as sensitive to interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are looking at that very carefully and will continue to look at that extremely carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Do you mind me asking you to repeat what you said about the unemployment rate in Spain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll start with that one, your question about Spain, because it demonstrates the beauty of Europe and the heterogeneity that we have among the 20 countries that are members of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously, the numbers that we see now for Spain, with inflation trending towards 2% and hopefully sustainably so, plus unemployment numbers that are as low as they have ever been, is a good set of numbers for the country and for the economy at large.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not the same for all Member States and there are Member States where inflation is still very high and has been high and is expected to remain high for longer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to be very attentive to the aggregate numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those are the ones that are driving our inflation outlook, helping us determine our policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we also have to look at each Member State and the characteristics of each Member State.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the hope that we have is that inflation will come down to 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, we don't have a dual mandate, unlike the Fed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we can do that with unemployment at the lowest level and staying there, that could be very good.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's funny because you ask the question of a lawyer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The issue of the burden of proof is very often a lawyer's issue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the burden of proof is going to be on the data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because we are determined to bring inflation back to target, but we are also going to be in the hands of data and the assessment of data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the burden of proof is going to be on data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are working on and what staff is trying to be as detail-specific and conclusive about is the impact of our monetary policy on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is really what is the focus and what is driving us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What impact our interest rate hikes have produced, produce, and will produce on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously, the exercise of producing the inflation outlook that will be conducted in September by ECB staff will be very informative for the Governing Council to determine how much has been transmitted and what is expected to continue to be transmitted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said earlier on, in the financing leg, a lot has been transmitted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And your second question is totally hypothetical, and I understand why you would want me to answer that question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are so many data and so much to take on in terms of the projection that will be produced in September, that I cannot answer your question in advance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our key tool, our key instrument in the current circumstances, given the level of inflation that we have at the moment, is interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there will be no trade-off between either interest rates or QT.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Interest rates are the main tool and the most efficient one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is the one that we will be using.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is the possibility of a hike, there is the possibility of a pause.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But don't expect me to go one way or the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, the burden of proof is going to be the data and the ultimate point that we are determined to reach is the 2% inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we would be doing too much and promising too much.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Look, doing too much is certainly not something that we are considering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are committed to delivering 2% headline, medium term, on a sustainable basis, in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I look at headline numbers, when I look at core inflation numbers, when I look at all the many measures of underlying inflation, trying to really isolate the most robust element, and removing the most volatile part of it, we are seeing inflation that is still too high and that we project to remain too high for too long.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to do what we have to do, which is currently to hike.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that we are getting closer, but we also know the options that are on the table: to continue to hike or to hold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we also know that it will vary meeting by meeting because we want to be determined by the data and the analysis, and the assessment we make of the data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not surprising that it is transmitting to the financing channel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not surprising that there is less investment in housing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not surprising that there is less investment altogether.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is the intended impact of the monetary policy stance that we have determined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is precisely what will return inflation to target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have promised in our strategy review and subsequent decision, we have promised to be Paris Agreement-aligned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously, as noted by all of you and as noticed by Greenpeace as well, we stopped any asset purchases under the Asset Purchase Programme, because we are no longer reinvesting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So as a result of that under the CSPP, we are not reinvesting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have decided is that we will stick to our commitment to be Paris Agreement-aligned, and we will in the course of 2023 elaborate the means and the ways by which we will be Paris-aligned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just want to remind you, and this is not just to distract me for a second from the fight against inflation, but I just want to call your attention to the massive amount of work that is being done in the supervision arm of the ECB in order to really raise the level of awareness and the level of concern by banks and through banks by their clients.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously we will be looking at all inflation data, starting with headline, we will have two readings before our September monetary policy Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will look at core inflation, but we will go deeper into underlying inflation numbers to really appreciate and understand what is moving and what is steadily, sustainably moving.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that some indicators are showing, particularly in goods, it's pretty obvious, you look at producer prices, it's pretty obvious.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But when you start looking into services in particular, you have to really dissect those that are energy intensive, those that are interest sensitive, what share of labour there is in various segments of services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have to look into all that to understand whether the action that we have determined in the last year-and-a-half now, is really having a long-standing impact that will take inflation back to 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Don't forget also that we will be looking at the inflation outlook that will be produced by the ECB, which will give us again the expected path of inflation, and the readings for 2024 and 2025 will obviously be very informative for us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will look at labour numbers, we will look at investment numbers, we will look at just every single parameter of the whole economy of the euro area that we can look at in order to inform ourselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know it would be helpful for those who are using the same models, that are playing the same exercise, to understand from us that there is one particular specific indicator, one particular set of data that prevails over the others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking at all of it and expectations are part of the picture as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The institution that I used to lead, the IMF, has updated its real April numbers and I don't think that any of its terribly talented staff would argue with me that inflation in the United States and inflation in Europe are two different beasts, that are fueled by different drivers and in a context that is vastly different, both in terms of fiscal, in terms of labour market, in terms of energy and that certainly has something to do with explaining why figures are where they are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know that better than anyone else, the Fed started a little bit earlier than the ECB and started from a base that was not negative interest rates either.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point in time, I wouldn't say so because as I said, the data we just discussed, and the assessment of data, will actually tell us whether and how much ground we have to cover in September and at subsequent meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said in the early part of this press conference, it may vary from one month to the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think the good news for European compatriots is that inflation is declining.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know we had a reading of 10.6% in October, we are now at 5.5%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a target which is medium term 2% sustainable and we want to get there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'm sure that people when they do their shopping, when they fill up their tank, when they pay the gas bill, they see that the increase is not quite the same as six, seven months ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, we want to go to the end of the game.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The bank lending survey, yes, we looked at it carefully, it was debated with governors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if you look at the monetary policy statement in the last paragraph that we have, it's very significantly described.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The annual growth rate of lending continued to decrease in June falling to 3% for firms and 1.7% for households, with annualised growth rate of 0%, completely flat, and -0.2% in the second quarter, respectively.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So not only are we seeing it very mildly grow year on year, but we are seeing a decline in the last quarter and the same holds for both corporates and households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So yes, of course, this is one of the elements of transmission that we have seen discussed and the fall in demand is also obvious, particularly on the part of corporates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A bit less so for households, but on the part of corporates, absolutely, absolutely yes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had a lot of data, a lot of analysis done by staff and obviously this was a projection meeting and the projections were prepared by ECB staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to give you an example, we spent hours and hours yesterday, morning and afternoon, with the usual presentation by staff in the morning and by the Chief Economist and the member of the Executive Board responsible for markets to have as much intelligence, numbers and analysis as possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm pleased to say that at the end of this morning session, we came to the conclusion that we shared the analysis that was conducted, on GDP, on inflation, on anticipation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously some members did not draw the same conclusion and some governors would have preferred to pause and reserve future decisions once more certainty, more intelligence would have resulted from the passing of time and the impact of our many previous decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can tell you that there was a solid majority of the governors to agree with the decision that we have made and that I have just read to you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So yes, there are a few members in the Governing Council who would have preferred a pause and we had to rely, as I told you, on a solid majority.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not the practice to give numbers of who did what and when, but suffice to say that the majority was solid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want you to believe that we had an antagonistic adversarial discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We really went deep into the numbers and the analysis, and tried to really take into account the sensitivity analysis, the scenarios that were provided by staff and we really discussed the baseline and the impact of our measures in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I am happy to go through the process that we followed in terms of reasoning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, is the door open or is the door closed?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, there was a beautiful theatre play by De Marivaux, who said that a door has to be either opened or closed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have decided is actually reflected in that key paragraph, which I have read twice because it is in the body of the text which was released to you earlier and also in the conclusion of the text.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it is based on all the data, the numbers, the analysis, the assessment, the projections and any other information that we have available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We considered that "the key ECB interest rates have reached levels" - note, levels - "that, maintained for a sufficiently long duration" - so there is the time element that comes up - "will make a substantial contribution" - substantial contribution, those are heavy words - "to the timely return of inflation to the target".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The whole paragraph is important and needs to be read in symbiosis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the next sentence says that "our future decisions will ensure that the key ECB interest rates will be set at - one - "sufficiently restrictive levels" - two - "as long as necessary".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those are really two parameters that are going to guide us very much.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not that we are forgetting about the three components that have guided our reasoning so far.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue to follow a data-dependent approach to determining the appropriate level and duration of restrictions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In particular, our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment - and I repeat there, it's in the in the text - of number 1, inflation outlook in the light of the incoming economic and financial data, number 2, the dynamics of underlying inflation, number 3, the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, that addresses your question and I think that the exercises that no doubt some of you will conduct in relation to "substantial contribution" and how that substantial contribution contributes from "significant level maintained for as long as necessary, based on current assessment", gives you the answer to your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, we regard interest rates as the key tool in the work that we are doing in order to reach our 2% medium term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have not discussed the PEPP programme, the reinvestment and the forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: PEPP is our flexibility instrument, as you know, and is the first line of defence if we want to defend a proper transmission of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not discussed any kind of APP outright sales.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You are correct that the GDP has been revised significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We moved from 0.9% to 0.7% in 2023 and more importantly we moved from 1.5% to 1.0% in 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me just take a moment to explain to you what seems like the biggest revision, which is 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Most of it, actually three quarters of that revision of 0.5, is attributable to carry over from 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are going through a period of about five quarters of very, very sluggish growth and, based on our projection, we are coming to the end of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The pickup according to the same calendar, the same quarter calendar that we have had in the June projections, picks up again in 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The downgrade from 1.5% to 1%, as I said, is a carry-over from 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In 2025, we have a small revision and we move from 1.6% to 1.5%, which is really a minimal revision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In essence, the recovery we had projected for the second half of 2023 is actually pushed out into time for various reasons that I'm happy to expand upon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not going to annoy you with the rereading but you obviously all picked up the "level".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our two key determinations are "levels sufficiently restrictive" for long enough, so that we are confident that we are reaching the 2% medium term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And, as indicated in that paragraph that I have read, under current assessment, we believe that the interest rates that we decide will provide a substantial contribution to that target, but with the two elements: sufficiently restrictive and for long enough.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now your real question is, did you discuss the "long enough"?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to that is no, because we are also saying in the same breath that we will be data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what we want to do is continue to be data dependent and test our assessment that I have just described for you against future projections and subsequent assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is what we are tasked to do with the determination to reach the 2% medium term target in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I stand by what I said and I wrote in Sintra.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not saying either that we are now at peak.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the sentence that I read is really the critical one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: With today's decision, we have made sufficient contributions, under current assessment, to returning inflation to target in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said, both elements matter, the level sufficiently restrictive and the duration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's obvious that the focus is probably going to move a bit more to the duration.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we can't say that now we are at that peak.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know it is complicated, because the "as long as necessary" cannot be actually pinned down and the "substantial contribution" cannot be pinned down either, because we have to conduct an assessment every time against the data, against the analysis, against the various information that we derive from experts, and against the projections and what our staff offers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the credibility of a central bank, I know that the experts will probably give you probably a lot of measurements and surveys and indicators to determine whether the central bank, ours or any other central bank, is credible, is losing credibility or is gaining credibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I know is that the ECB is on a positive path directionally.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But my definition of credibility is that we deliver on our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our credibility on the line is to reach the 2% medium term in a timely manner and we will do everything we have to do in order to deliver on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the stability and strength of banks I refer here to our Vice President.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: 15 years after Lehman, the situation of the banking industry in Europe is totally different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The capital levels, the quality and the level of liquidity are not comparable to the situation 15 years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that we have a very good example what happened in March in the US and with Credit Suisse.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This kind of events did not have any impact on the European banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: After that, we had our stress test exercise that indicated that the European banks are resilient, that they can withstand even a very severe scenario.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think this is proof that the situation has changed quite a lot for the better.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Perhaps now the attention is much more on the non-banks, the non-bank part of the financial system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that in terms of financial stability, we have identified many more vulnerabilities now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the focus of our attention now in terms of financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will dispose of the second question first because I think it is going to be a fast response to the point about whether the likelihood or possibility of national central banks or the ECB to make a loss impacts on the decision-making process and our decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is because, and it also addresses the first questions, the objective that we have and the mandate that we were given is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is to procure price stability within the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I would observe that the fight that we are leading against inflation - we are not the only ones - is making progress and what we are doing today is trying to reinforce that progress.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are down to 5.3% now, so it's been divided by two.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, because our projection expects it to still remain too high and for too long.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But inflation has declined and we want it to continue to decline and to reinforce that process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are doing that, not because we want to force a recession but because we want price stability to be there for people who are taking the brunt of inflation and high prices, and predominantly for those who are not the most privileged people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This [rate cut] is not even a word that we have pronounced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, the data dependency applies to both the determination of the sufficiently restrictive level as well as the length of time where it has to stay at that level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we don't see any contradiction in having the two components in the same sentence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is certainly an area, whether you're looking at residential real-estate, which affects, obviously, at the end of the day households and people, or whether you look at commercial real-estate.This is a sector that is clearly responding very much to the current circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The level of interest rates and the financing tightening that we are conducting to bring inflation down is one of the factors that caused this overall real-estate sector to be in a difficult situation at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said earlier on, we're not driven to sustain and support a particular sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are driven by the imperative of delivering on our mandate, which is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the transmission channel, there is evidence that the current hiking cycle is transmitting to financing conditions faster than previous ones.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will remember that we use three criteria, three elements in our assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is the inflation outlook, the second one is underlying inflation and the third one is the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the third one, I think we all shared the same view in the room earlier today, that this channel of transmission is strong and stronger than we have seen in previous cycles.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So when you look at how fast it transmits to various rates, whether it is overnight or whether it is longer term, it's extremely rapid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is reflected in the lending rates for corporates, in the lending rates for households, which I think are mentioned as 3.8 in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a transmission and it is having a constraining impact that is visible when you look at M3, when you look at the volume of loans and when you look at the interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is clearly a fact that transmission is effective and more so than in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
