text: With regard to the second question: one of the bright spots that we have in terms of activity in the euro area is the labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The labour market is still going strongly, the employees' wages are growing, the employee remuneration is still increasing at 5.5% and the participation has increased by 0.2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are beginning to see some signs of weakening in the volume of hires and notably in some sectors, particularly in the services sector that is related to manufacturing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But overall, when I look at my numbers today it's employee remuneration: plus 5.5%; employee participation in the economy: 0.2% plus; and the lowest unemployment rates we have ever had.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking very, very carefully at that, because it is having a serious impact on inflation, particularly inflation in the service sector, which is typically much more labour intensive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now what are we seeing in in terms of profit?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at profit unit cost and its growth, it is still growing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that growth is, for the first time, having an inflection downwards.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that would comfort the assumption that we have made throughout - we made that at the June projection and we are making it yet again - it comforts the projection that gradually profits will squeeze in order to allow for the wage increases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we want to be confident that that is a lasting component.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It should normally be so because as demand is dampened, this should normally be the reaction in the corporate world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will take you through the reasoning that we adopted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had indicated and we are bound by that intellectual reasoning that we would approach the assessment using three key criteria - inflation outlook, underlying inflation, strength of the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said earlier on regarding the third criterion, there is no question in anybody's mind around the Governing Council table, if you want to propel yourself into that room.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was shared analysis of that, with little variations on the margin.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first item, which is the inflation outlook, we looked at the projections that were given to us by ECB staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you look at the projections, and notwithstanding the GDP revision, we have a revision upward of headline inflation in both 2023 and 2024 and a 0.1 revision downward for 2025, which is hallowed with uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because the further out you go into the projection, the less certain it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the core inflation which we look at as well - not the only one, but we also look at core inflation - core inflation is maintained in 2023 and revised by 0.1 in 2024 and 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But overall, we are not at target in 2025 on headline inflation and we are almost on target on core and we only hit around 2% in the fourth quarter of 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So when we look at that, we ask ourselves "how does the inflation outlook compare with our commitments and our target?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said, it's the key sentence in that monetary policy statement, under current assessment with this decision of a 25 basis point hike, we believe that we are making a substantial contribution etc.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So those are the elements that we take into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The real purpose of what we're doing here is not to be found in that sentence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's somewhere else in the beginning of the document that you have where we say "in order to reinforce progress towards our target, the Governing Council today decided to raise the three key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to be as timely as is possible and by doing that we support our projections with a higher degree of confidence and I think it will reinforce progress towards target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we're determined to get there to that 2% and we see that as the best way to accelerate the process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by the way: it also reinforces the anchoring of inflation expectations which are broadly at 2%, but which warrant monitoring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: De Guindos: As regards the question how much of a drag the property market is for the financial system, I will follow what the President has indicated before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the case of the residential market, what we have started to see is that there is a slowdown in the evolution of prices in residential property, whereas in the case of commercial property, commercial real-estate, the situation is different because we identified a decline in prices even before the tightening cycle of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was related to the situation of COVID, teleworking and these kinds of things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have made a lot of analysis about the potential impact that the commercial property might have in the financial system and we have identified some channels, some links between commercial property, commercial real-estate, and mutual funds that could reinforce the comment that I have made before about non-banks as a potential source of vulnerability for the financial system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is the element that we are trying to analyse.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are real-estate funds, property funds, that have a lot of investments and a lot of great exposure to the commercial property.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is something that we have to look at and monitor very closely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, I think it's in all countries that economic activity depends on financing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in Europe it's largely banks, but it's not something that is peculiar to Italy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Banks in Europe play a critical role in financing the economic activity both for corporates and for households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are going through a phase of very sluggish growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We move from -0.1 to revised 0.1 to revised 0.1 and we see also very weak signs whether you look at PMI, or the gap between manufacturing and services that is now being reduced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are clearly in a period of slow and sluggish growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, the revision that we're making for the next year, where we're moving from 1.5% to 1% of growth, is for three quarters attributable to the sluggish growth that we are going through at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the difficult times are now and the recovery that we had anticipated is pushed out into 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And when you look at the September projection that we have on a quarter-by-quarter basis, it is the same as the one that we had in June, which shows that we are confident that growth will pick up in 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course, we need to succeed, we need to bring inflation down and wages have to be sustained and labour has to hold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those are some of the assumptions that we make in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first one, as I said, the food inflation has come down but it is still at 10% at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it is still hard for people because food is obviously a component of the basket which matters a lot and which matters more for those who earn less.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we hope that food will continue to go down but it's one of the components that is still very high.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would maybe enlarge your question to the price of commodities in general because we are seeing movements, whether it is on grains, and obviously the Black Sea Agreement denunciation by Russia is flying in the face of stability, if anything.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But whether it's grain, oil, gas, we're looking at all those components very, very carefully because some of them are volatile, some of them are on their way up and they will have consequences on prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we will have to assess on a projection-by-projection basis to really appreciate what impact it has in view of activity around the world as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had a good scenario analysis produced by staff about China and the role that China's growth or deceleration of growth would have on our own GDP and our inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That, combined with the price of oil is obviously something that we need to be attentive to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the compliance with the Paris agreement, as you know, because of the tilting programme that we've put in place since last October, that we have improved and modified.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can tell you very seriously that until the end of 2023, we are Paris-compliant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can also tell you that we need to look at other measures and more measures in order to make sure going forward that we will remain Paris-compliant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: given the fact that we have gradually phased out any reinvestment under the APP and under the PEPP, the volume of corporate bonds is extremely limited.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will be looking at that and there will be work done by staff to propose options in order to remain Paris compliant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Neither of these two questions, neither the PEPP, nor the remuneration of required reserves have been discussed at this meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You ask me about the current geopolitical environment and how that has weighed on our decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we repeat two or three times in the context of this monetary policy statement the risks posed by the geopolitical environment and these aggravated risks as we see them unfold and develop.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And of course, you have a special sentence in the monetary policy statement (MPS) that refers specifically, in addition to the totally unjustified war of Russia against Ukraine, to the tragic developments as a result of the terrorist attack on Israel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are very attentive to the economic consequences that that could have, whether in terms of direct or indirect impact on energy prices, or the level of confidence that economic actors will continue to display.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously, we refer to "timely manner", "sufficiently long", but in the same breath I say we shall be data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At this point of our fight against inflation and after ten successive hikes, now is not the time for forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now is the time to really stick to our data dependency 'knitting' if I may say and we shall do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have acknowledged on the occasion of this meeting that our assessment is confirmed, the assessment that we had in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All numbers, if anything, have reinforced our assessment of the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have applied the three criteria that you all know well; the inflation outlook, duly informed by any information that we have, the underlying inflation in all its compositions and the strength of the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we will continue to be data dependent.Your second question was essentially when and at what level do you cut?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was not discussed at all, and the debate would be absolutely premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have acknowledged in our review of the macroeconomic situation back in September and yet again this time around, and we all know, and you know, that labour cost, wages, profit units - the analysis of that - is critically important to determine the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On labour, for instance, we are going to have a wealth of numbers and data, and intelligence, when collective bargaining agreements and annual negotiations in 2024 will be completed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even having a discussion on a cut is totally premature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment, what we are saying is that we have to be steady, we have to hold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are holding.Your third question had to do with this sort of external tightening, which is not directly relevant to the fundamentals of the euro area economy, but which are tightening elements nonetheless because they directly impact long-term yields and long-term rates as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That definitely is a spill over that we take into account and that is compounded with other elements that clearly are bringing inflation down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll start with your second one, which is essentially have we learned anything from the last energy crisis, the impact it has on inflation directly and indirectly, and would we apply the same approach?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is work that is ongoing and that we will continue to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is clear to us that it applies to a completely different economy today and an economy which has had an episode of very high inflation, an economy where the interest rates (on the deposit facility) are at a very high level of 4%, and an economy that has strong employment and which is weakening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to take all these factors into account to see how possible higher costs of energy would actually affect both GDP and inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it is in the context of that assessment that we would respond accordingly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But be under no doubt, our determination is intact and our determination to bring inflation to 2% in the medium term is absolutely the same if not reinforced by the proximity of the destination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question: what we are seeing is a very strong transmission of our monetary policy in the banking sector in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the financing of the economy as a result is directly affected, which in turn plays on to the reduction of inflation and the dampening of demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am sure you have seen the bank lending survey - those numbers are very striking in terms of both volume and rate transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So as is often the case with monetary policy, there is this transmission lag time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The assessment by our staff is that there is still more in the pipeline and more to come to affect the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the assumption is that it will continue to unfold throughout the end of 2023 and first quarter of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One might argue that it's going to last longer but we have already seen a significant transmission to the financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More is to come and if you look at, for instance, the housing sector, it is pretty obvious that there is transmission to the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the volume of capital expenditure, of investment by corporates, there is a reduction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not just the banks telling us that they will be more attentive to the risk and that they are reducing their flow of credit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is also the corporates that are putting a brake on their investment because of the level of interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That clearly results from the various corporate telephone surveys that we conduct and from the bank lending survey as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, both in the housing sector and in investment numbers that we have, it is transmitting to the real economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me turn to Greece first and remind you that we only have one active purchase programme that is operating at the moment and that is the reinvestments that we conduct under the PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Under APP, we don't do any reinvestment anymore, so there is no question as to which country is eligible or not eligible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So Greece was eligible to PEPP under a special waiver that had been decided at the time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Greek instruments are eligible to PEPP without any exceptions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Greece is now back to a pre-COVID situation and I speak under the control of my colleague and friend Governor Stournaras.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But Greece is actually higher than the level where it was just pre-COVID.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not going to comment any further on who is better because I don't want to comment on countries' specific situations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are here in Greece and Greece has demonstrated phenomenal recovery capacity and it is, if I recall, 10% above the pre-COVID level at this point in time now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I don't know what is normal or abnormal, but I have to say that it's a stellar performance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yannis Stournaras: I fully agree President with what you have said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On activity, we are about 10% higher than the pre-COVID situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: GDP growth is much higher than the average of the eurozone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, all in all, it's a success story as the President said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I do not deny that there is still a lot to be done until we get back to a rating of A+ as you said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So on the first part of your intervention, let me remind you what we do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have defined it in our strategy review as inflation at 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The best tools that we can use to return inflation to 2% are our interest rates, and this is what we are using.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I just want to mention that the fact that we are holding doesn't mean to say that we will never hike again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, at this point in time, on the basis of the data that we have, we are confident that the deposit facility rate at 4% - or the three rates at the level they are - contribute substantially to bringing us back to 2% in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second point is that, in addition to our stance, we also have to make sure that there is proper transmission of our monetary policy throughout the whole euro area and to all countries in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we have all the adequate tools in order to make sure that that happens.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, I will not go into the specifics of each and every national central banks because they are all in a different situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of them are publicly-quoted institutions, others are not and there is no one-size-fits-all for the situation they're in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I know is that, as the Eurosystem and as ECB, we have one mission and that is price stability and we do not have as a purpose toshow profits or to cover losses and it would be actually wrong if our decisions were guided by our P&L accounts rather than for pure monetary policy purposes in order to bring inflation back to 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point, as I said earlier, we have not discussed PEPP on the occasion of this meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm tempted to give you an appointment for our next monetary policy meeting because obviously in December we will have a whole range of new projections, new numbers and, as is often the case, we revisit either up or down depending on the situation and once again, we're going to be purely data-dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we know for a fact is that growth has weakened and if we look at PMI numbers for instance, they are not indicative of a very vigorous growth, which is why I have clearly indicated in the monetary policy statement that growth continues to be weak.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can only repeat what we say and we actually repeat in the monetary policy statement which is that we believe that the three rates where they are, if kept for a sufficiently long period of time, will actually make the contribution that is needed, the substantial contribution that is needed, to return inflation to 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we did on the occasion of this monetary policy meeting was to compare the projections that we had in September when we made our decision, to the new data that came in including the inflation number, headline and core inflation, including the bank lending survey, notably, and the various flash estimates and PMI numbers to confirm the assessment that we had previously.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's not forget our mission is to return inflation to 2% to make sure that inflation does not cut into purchasing power of people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm going to share your question with the Vice President because he is the real expert on this panel on financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I just want to again remind you of what I said about the rising bond yields.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is a movement that originated outside the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not directly related to the fundamentals of the euro area and it is different but we are facing the same circumstances that we feared back in March at the time of the various regional banks and Silicon Valley banks and Signature and First Republic collapses where again there was spillover and the fear of more of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is something that clearly impacts our own rates and we take that into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Luis de Guindos: In a couple of weeks, we are going to release our Financial Stability Review (FSR).

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The FSR is the document where we indicate the main financial stability risks that we have here in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The increases in yields is something that we are looking at very carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because the main risk that we have identified in the past, and continue to identify in the near future, is very high valuations of different kinds of assets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we have seen that when you look at these valuations, not only of financial assets as the President indicated before, we refer as well to the real estate market, the increase in yields can give rise to an important correction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is something that we are taking into consideration very, very closely and simultaneously all the factors such as the higher yields can have an impact mainly on the non-bank financial intermediaries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There we have seen that there is a concentration of potential vulnerabilities in terms of liquidity risks or liquidity mismatches in terms of credit risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And these situations that you have, an important and pervasive increase in yields, can give rise to additional problems for this part of the financial system that is not totally isolated from the rest of the financial system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the increase in yields is something that we are considering very closely and we will make a lot of comments with that respect in our Financial Stability Review about the potential impact that this might have in terms of financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first one, I'm tempted to tell you that I don't want to deal with the hypotheticals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in a process of fighting inflation, of bringing it to 2% using predominantly the interest rates, and ancillary, additional components that come as a complement such as the gradual reduction of the balance sheet as we have seen as a result of TLTRO reimbursements as a result of non-reinvestment of APP but I'm not going to have the hypotheticals about "what if" after tightening...Suffice to say that Greece is today eligible to the PEPP without any waiver, so it's pari passu, everyone in the group, the 20 Member States are in the same situation from that perspective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me about the rates and the obvious gap between the lending rates by banks to corporates and to households and the remuneration of deposits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our job at the ECB and at national central banks is to set the rates at which banks and other institutions finance themselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our job is not to set the rates at which they lend - we hope that they transmit that properly because that's part of the transmission mechanism - nor the rate at which they remunerate deposits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is an issue that occurs in several euro area countries to which solutions are brought by either the authorities or by the power of consumers themselves or by the competition authorities, but this is not an area where the ECB or the national central banks can take action.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for your personal question and rest assured that I have no regret.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know what happened today: one of our members after 12 years of loyal and good services finished his term on the Governing Council, and it was his very last Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The level of warmth, of emotion, of acknowledgement that was demonstrated to him and his response reminded all of us around the table that sometimes we disagree.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, we had an unanimous decision on this occasion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While we disagree on occasion, because there is this common drive for delivering on the mission, we have a quality of debates, of exchanges, of different views, we try to convince each other on occasions, and we sometimes manage; that is something that is to be cherished and, in a world where, for dissenting opinions, people go into totally unconsensual and irrational directions, it's a gem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Luis de Guindos: our assessment on bank taxes is well known.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have always said that these kinds of levies, these kinds of taxes should not impair lending, should not impair credit growth, and should not damage the solvency of the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was the recipe included in our opinions for taxes that were approved in the case of Lithuania, Spain, and Italy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the case of Italy, we had different versions [of the Decree Law] and the final one was more reasonable in that terms because they indicated that if they increase the capital buffers then the tax will be reduced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't know what's going to happen with the Spanish case, whether it's going to be extended or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the principle of our assessment with respect to this kind of taxation is quite clear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Typically when you reach by unanimous consent a decision, you don't have a widening of the differences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Together with colleagues who have been participating in all these hours of discussions here in Athens, I can assure you that there was a general well-shared assessment of the current situation, the judgement that we have made and the monetary policy decision we took which, after 10 different hikes over the last 15 months, is for the first time a hold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Sometimes inaction is action and a decision to hold is actually meaningful and was taken by total agreement of all governors and members of the Governing Council this morning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If any of you wanted to add to that, but I think you have either misinterpretation or strange information from inside our discussion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We were inside the rooms and I can assure you that it was strong.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as to your question on peak, I'm not going to pass a judgement to say that we are at peak.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are data dependent and we are going to meeting after meeting after meeting, assess on the basis of the three criteria of the inflation outlook, of the underlying inflation and the strength of our monetary policy transmission, whether or not our interest rates are delivering sufficiently in order to help us reach the 2% medium term inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And let me take you into the Governing Council room.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you remember, we have defined the three key criteria of our monetary policy stance, namely inflation outlook, underlying inflation, transmission - strength of the transmission of our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it is against those three criteria that we determine whether enough progress has been made and whether our monetary policy is working.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And clearly, when we look at our inflation outlook, at the projections produced by staff and the entire Eurosystem on the occasion of the December meeting, our new projections see inflation at 2.1% in 2025, not 2026, which is included, but in 2025 we see headline at 2.1%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the path to get there is flatter than it was before, which lowers the risks of inflation expectations risking de-anchoring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On underlying inflation, the monetary policy statement says quite specifically that a lot of indicators are showing that underlying inflation comes in below expectations, with a decline across all components.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at transmission, we are clearly seeing a strong transmission to the financing of the economy and strong transmission at large, particularly if we look at the volume of loans to both corporates and the households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one is that our inflation outlook, which is one of the three criteria, is conditioned on the interest rate path that was embedded in market data at the time when our cut-off date was determined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The cut-off date, as you will see in the publication, was November 23rd.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Point number two: when we look at all the measurements of underlying inflation, there is one particular measurement which is hardly budging.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's declining a little bit, but not much, and that is domestic inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need more data, we need to understand better what happens there and why is domestic inflation resisting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is going to be measured in multiple ways.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have really as wide an area of indicators for that; the wage tracker, the number of job offers, the vacancies that turn around, plenty of them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That of course determines how tight the market is and therefore how wages will behave in the next few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at the data that we have now, it is not declining.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Compensation per employee has declined from Q2 to Q3, that's true.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we need to have a lot more data in that regard.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the second element, which is critical given the way we have constructed our projections, the way staff has constructed projections, we need more information about unit profits as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because our projection is predicated on the assumption that a lot of the catch-up wage growth will actually be absorbed in the markup of enterprises and corporates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we need to have these two on a more sustainable basis, demonstrating that domestic inflation too is going to head down towards our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have a lot more data in the course of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will be particularly rich in the first half, but we will need that in order to determine whether it is actually sustainable or not.Now you had a second question, which had to do with PEPP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just tell you how I regard the decision that we made on PEPP and that was shared by a very, very large majority of the governors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Everybody was fine with stopping the reinvestments at the end of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some would have liked a slightly different tapering, starting a little earlier, starting later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we ended up with that 100% reinvestment until the end of June, 50% reinvestment from July until the end of December, no reinvestment from January 2025 onwards.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Markets have absorbed a decline in asset purchase programme (APP) reinvestment as we had done it in a very similar fashion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we think that it is really on a standalone basis and it will continue to operate on the back burner if you will, without, we hope, being significant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's totally unrelated to "If they do that with PEPP, then maybe they're planning this on rates".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, rates are the primary tool and we're going to use that independently of what happens on the PEPP side, which as I said is on the back burner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think everybody in the room takes the view that between hike and cut, there's a whole plateau, a whole beach of hold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's like solid, liquid and gas: you don't go from solid to gas without going through the liquid phase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think going forward, we are going to continue to be data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are going to continue to determine meeting by meeting what we see on the totality of data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But obviously, given a certain resistance of domestic inflation and the risk of second-round effects that we absolutely want to avoid, we're going to be very attentive to that category of data that I have just described.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your latter question, we don't have any particular country in mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we have the principle in mind that the fiscal support, particularly the discretionary support that was granted to compensate for the high prices of energy, that should absolutely be withdrawn.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you look at how fast the price of energy has gone down, both on the oil and gas front, it's just totally unjustified and probably unjustifiable to continue to have those fiscal measures in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we make the point in that same paragraph that we strongly encourage the reduction of the sovereign debt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We make the point that fiscal measures must be rolled back and that sovereign debt must be reduced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we make another point, which as you will have noted because you're a regular of these monetary policy statements: we have changed the language on structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we have done that because we perceive and we fear a level of procrastination in reaching agreement in closing on some of the technical files, which have been pending for way too long and which would be critical in order to support the competitiveness of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will see when we publish the data that competitiveness is really weakening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And whether it's capital markets union, whether it's banking union or the whole market union and free movement of goods and services, a lot of progress needs to be made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Vice President is a very strong supporter of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there were many voices on the Governing Council to say in the presence of Valdis Dombrovsky, who is working on those issues, that it has to happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question: it is true that we will receive a lot of data in the first half of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it will be data rich, particularly on the employment front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just consider that about 50% of the employees that we cover under our wage tracker will see their collective bargaining agreement renegotiated and new terms of employment and possibly new wages agreed upon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in the same vein in the corporate world whether it's for goods or services, terms and conditions and price lists are also often revised in the first few months of any calendar year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that's not to say that this will be it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will remain attentive to a whole host of data that will come in in the course of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question: Who wants to hang on for too long?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But equally what we are saying today, on the basis of the forecast that we have, which has been produced by the Eurosystem staff, is that we don't think that it's time to lower our guard, and we believe that there is still work to be done and that can very much take the form of holding.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think in our monetary policy statement, what we essentially say and have said before is: based on our current assessment, we consider that the key ECB interest rates are at levels that, maintained for a sufficiently long duration, will make a substantial contribution to our goal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we continue with: our future decisions will ensure that our policy rates will be set at sufficiently restrictive levels for as long as necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you combine that with our data dependency, and the fact that we are not narrowing the focus of what we look at, but we know that some data, and a combination of data and the mechanics between these two, wages and profit in particular, are going to play a significant role, and we will be particularly attentive to those.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have another bank lending survey, we will have a corporate telephone survey coming in, and we will take that into account to determine when we can lower the guard.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am of course not going to address your second question directly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will simply say that we will be looking at our three criteria.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be identifying, on the basis of staff forecasts, on the basis of our measurements and of underlying inflation, and on the basis of the strong transmission of our monetary policy, where we are regarding this medium term target that we have set ourselves, of reaching the 2% target at the end of our projection.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are probably a little bit more severe with ourselves because the end of our projection or the end of the projection horizon would take us to 2026, where we have 1.9%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are probably going to look very carefully at the end of 2025, where I think we are at 2.1%, and we will arrive on a more sliding basis to that 2.1%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The projections that we have now are conditioned on the interest rate path that was embedded in market data before the cut-off date of 23rdNovember.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, let me say that we do not have a recession in our baseline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course I'm not looking at specific countries, we are looking collectively at the euro area at large.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our mandate is to reach the medium-term target of 2%, which we have defined as price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To do that, we know that we're going to have to continue with financing, which will be triggered by the interest rates that we set.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We take all the macroeconomic data and the whole situation into account, but we are driven by delivering on our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On PEPP: first of all, don't forget that as long as we reinvest - by which I mean 100% of redemption coming to maturity - we still have that flexibility.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that flexibility applies to the 100% reinvestment until the end of June, and then to 50% of the reinvestment until the end of the 2024 calendar year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was intended for the pandemic, it was an emergency programme.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Despite stupid Covid-19 coming to hit you now and again - as it hit me - the pandemic is over.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously it's a normalisation of the balance sheet that is welcome at a time when we don't actually currently see a risk of fragmentation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there were such risks, we also have tools that are available, that we would not hesitate to use for a second, because proper transmission is actually part of the mission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The announcement from the German coalition about the decision came yesterday.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not included those numbers and their forecast into our current projections, and obviously we will do so and we will try to understand exactly what impact it would have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Germany is a big country, it represents roughly 25% of the euro area and fiscal measures that would be taken need to be accounted for and the impact on inflation determined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for finishing with the wage and profit question, because it's something that staff - both here at the ECB but also in the national central banks - looks at very, very carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what we have seen is a contribution from unit profits to inflation declining over the course of 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From memory, the contribution was at about 2.4% and it's now down to 1.4%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, it's a big "if" and we need to really understand and make sure that this is sustainable, but if that is confirmed, it would mean that the hypotheticals that we had in our previous forecast and that we have for this forecast in December - which was that markups would be reduced in order to absorb increased wages by way of catch-up or otherwise - that that is actually taking place, which would be really good news for inflation purposes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we don't have enough on the table to really determine that this is what is going to happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, the consensus around the table of the Governing Council was that it was premature to discuss rate cuts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In addition to that, I typically stand by my comments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the comments I made to your television channel, Bloomberg, I certainly stand by them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not sure that I would exactly characterise them as you have, but I stand by what I have said, not what others have commented that I have said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One other thing which was very much the consensus around the table was that we had to continue to be data-dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So rather than being fixated on any kind of particular calendar, which would be being date-dependent, we reaffirmed our data dependency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I have flagged in the course of the monetary policy statement some of the areas that we will be particularly attentive to in the course of the next few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would be maybe a bit cautious about the use of supply bottlenecks because it was very much associated with the consequences of COVID and the multifaceted bottlenecks that we observed both in shipping, in port handling, in dispatching of containers, which was really a very sizeable disruption in the whole logistics chain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are observing very carefully because we are seeing what you are all observing, which is that shipping costs are increasing, delivery delays are increasing and, while we all know that there is more shipping capacity than there was in 2020 and 2021, we also know that costs and fees are increasing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, I think most observers agree to say that it has a moderate impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The percentage of the water transport costs is a little north of 1.5% of total input costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are being very careful and looking attentively to the developments, and it's pretty clear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think whether you look at the IMF, the OECD, or other commentators, if the conflict in that region was to develop further, clearly that would be an additional risk, whether it's a question of the disruption of shipping that we alluded to or the price of energy and commodities at large.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for your question on wages because, as you have noted, it is an item that we're going to look at and that we have looked at very carefully, as we are also looking very carefully at profit unit and the link between labour unit and profit unit, which was one of the key assumptions we had under our baseline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll remind you that the baseline we had was that wage increases would gradually over the course of time be absorbed by a gradual reduction of profit unit, and that's exactly what we are seeing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's often said that wage indicators are backward-looking, and yes there is a whole battery of backward-looking indicators.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For instance, the latest - I think it's the compensation per employee data - that is available dates back to October.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what we have in addition to that is indices that we have built over the course of time, one of which actually originates from Ireland.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our chief economist, Philip Lane, was at the origin of that one, which is the wage tracker.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This receives almost live any change to negotiated agreements in particular, and we receive that on a constant basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other indicator, which also is important not so much in relation to wages but in relation to the tightness of the labour market, is Indeed, which gathers all the vacancies advertised, particularly on the internet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That informs about the tension of the labour market and of course is telling us a little bit where we are heading in terms of that tightness, which itself results in a position of strength in the negotiation for one party or the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are also seeing on the wage tracker is stabilisation, which explains the comments included in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in Indeed we are seeing also a slight reduction of the volume of vacancies that are advertised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we take all these data at face value, and we try to constantly corroborate them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do that with the national central banks, observers, and economists to make sure that we really canvas the 20 Member States as accurately as possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not elusive because really, we're trying to pin it down, but it requires that we look at it from multiple angles to make sure that we are as accurate and as up to date as we can be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But just to give you an idea, I think it's 40% of the employees covered by our wage tracker which have had their employment contract renewed without new terms of salary levels in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the 40% include those whose terms and conditions have expired and must be renewed at the end of December and those for which the same will happen in the first three months of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you have 40% of the workforce of whom salaries, wages, one-off payments are yet to be determined and will be tracked by our wage tracker.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This information will come in the course of the next few months, which will be of course really rich in information to help us better understand exactly where we are on wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, we are data-dependent, and we make decisions one meeting at a time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have done in the course of this meeting today is that we have confirmed our inflation outlook and we consider that the information that we have received in the last few weeks since our December meeting showed that the medium-term inflation outlook is broadly following the path that we had projected in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Point number two, we look also very carefully at data concerning underlying inflation and here we are seeing a decline across the board of pretty much all our indicators.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those were a few weeks which were rich in information, where we have seen that both the market-based and the survey-based inflation expectations are also, both in the short term and for some of them also for the medium term, really coming in at around our 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And of course, we look at the latest inflation numbers, and you will have seen all of you that the December number was 0.5pp north of the November number, which was this 2.4.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we had expected that upside, which was caused by base effects largely attributable to German measures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was weaker than we had anticipated but it was totally predicted, and it does not detract from the view that we have that the disinflation process is at work.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And - I should have mentioned that because I mentioned the inflation outlook and the underlying inflation - of course we look very carefully at the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And here again we had some good data and information, notably from the bank lending survey.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All I can say is that the consensus around the table of the Governing Council this morning was that it was premature to discuss rate cuts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You had another point on wages and the publication of wage numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have a lot of information coming in the next few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's a big set of information that will clearly inform on the inflation outlook and which will lead us to assess whether we are on path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will receive two monthly inflation data for January and February before our March meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then we will continue to receive additional data and, you're right, some of those wage data will come in later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are clearly interested in wages because it's a significant component of services, and services is that section in the breaking down of inflation which is still quite resistant and stayed at 4% from December to November.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the only item that has actually stayed at the same level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On wage growth, I think whether you look at past wage numbers, whether you dissect that in compensation per employee, in negotiated wages, taking on or excluding the one-off payments, we are seeing a slight decline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To your question about should it stabilise or should it decline, it's already declining.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, our hope is that the wage increases - because we are still seeing an increase, whether you look at 5.2% or 3.4% depending on what measurement item you take - are sufficiently absorbed by the profit unit, as we are seeing happening at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that it does not go into fuelling inflation, which would create the risk of a second-round effect, which we are not seeing for the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the hypothesis that we had when we built the baseline of December, which was that the profit unit would eventually come down as a result of dampened demand as a result of our monetary policy stance, is actually happening, and there is a phenomenon of catching up for employees.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also one of the reasons why we see growth coming up and the recovery beginning in the course of 2024; because of rising wages while inflation comes down, which will free up some purchasing power, which hopefully will stimulate consumption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, I'm not going to answer it because the real answer is that I'm not so sure, and it's the honest answer to you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I could play a game of telling you that maybe it's a little higher, but we're not going to know until we get to that point of the neutral interest rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as policymakers, I think it's our responsibility not to predicate, not to anticipate, but to make the right policy decisions in due course to make sure that we reach our medium-term target of 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in January and the first quarter of 2024 is going to end in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think it is totally premature to anticipate what exactly will be the growth projections at our next meeting in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will come to that projection when we produce our projections in March.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other question, I think in terms of an overall evaluation of our policy trajectory, which many of you are after, we need to be further along in the disinflation process before we can be sufficiently confident that inflation will actually hit the target in a timely manner and in a sustainable way at target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is working but we need to be more advanced and we need to be further along in that process to be confident that inflation will be at target sustainably so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm giving you a little indication about what I call the trajectory, but it's not forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's trying to give you the mechanics that we will apply in our considerations when we look at data in the next few weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the issue of omission here or there, I think you should not be overly focused on what is deleted, what stays in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are some segments in the monetary policy statements that we are very keen to keep because they indicate the principles on which we lay our monetary policy stance and that are the backbone of our discussions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But a word here or a word there, I would not give it too much weight as such.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You may have noticed that we are trying to be a little more simple in our expression, to use fewer words, to be more normal, in a way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that sometimes implies that we change a sentence, the order of a paragraph versus another one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So don't pay too much attention to the deletion of one word or the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, when you see sentences or block of key points that are repeated on a regular basis, that means something.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the ECB, we have many surveys and we actually conduct surveys in a very technically-proof way that we can trust.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in the surveys that the ECB conducts, we typically ask staff whether they are happy to work at the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those surveys are responded to at a rate of about 60%, north of 60%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To that question, are you happy to work at the ECB?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The overwhelming majority, namely 80%, say yes, I'm happy to work at the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question that we ask also is would you recommend to a friend to work at the ECB?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is an overwhelming majority again, north of 75%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And a question that is often asked as well, is do you feel a mission associated to your work?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now we ask lots of other questions about satisfaction, dissatisfaction, compensation, dignity at work and all the rest of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we pay great attention to these technically sound responses and we act upon them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, what keeps me going is those answers and I'm extremely proud of the staff of the ECB, and I'm very proud and honoured to lead the institution, because we are driven by a mission, delivering price stability but serving the Europeans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those are the surveys that I'm particularly attentive to and keen to constantly improve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know it's inherent to the euro area that we have heterogeneity, that we have divergences, and it does not escape any topic or any field that there is heterogeneity and differences and divergences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is the case for the type of lending terms that are offered to Europeans, whether you have a loan in Portugal or Spain or whether you have a loan in France.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you're a household, you're going to have different terms applying to you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's what we have inherited from the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I can assure you that around the table, all governors come both in their respective category, having in mind their country, but also having in mind the whole euro area and determining the policy for the whole euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are lots of explanations as to why, for instance, inflation was much higher in the Baltic states than it was in France, for example.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we obviously have to decide for the whole of the euro area and the governors are riveted to that as their area of competence as far as they are concerned.Spreads is one indication of transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And of course, we look at those carefully, but I'm not going to pass any other judgement in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you very much for asking for the update on the operational framework.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what I can tell you is that work is advancing at a very fast pace.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a technical, difficult issue which has many ramifications and of course there are different options.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we are narrowing down to what will be optimal from the perspective of our market, which, as we just discussed, has heterogeneity and large differences between the Member States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will most likely, you know I have to take some precautions because work is underway, but we'll most likely be done by the end of spring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not necessarily, because we start from a balance sheet size, which will not require that the operational framework principles that we will decide collectively at the Governing Council level will have an impact in the very short term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on emergency lines and the risk that we see - you are talking about the US market here.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't want to pass judgement and I have full trust in my colleagues at the Fed and at the SEC and otherwise to actually supervise very carefully what is going on at the regional banks' levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't know exactly what PMI numbers you're referring to because the most recent PMI numbers are actually a little indication that things are coming in place for recovery in 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if you have other PMI numbers that I'm not aware of, then let me know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But you know, when I look at the composite PMI output, it's higher than it was the month before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I look at PMI future output, it's north of 50.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Politico is usually very, very insightful in all sorts of things.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But for us, these PMI numbers are a small signal that, having stabilised or stabilising, we have the conditions for recovery that are coming into place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not suggesting that it's going to pick up radically, but it's coming into place from what we see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I said that at the opening of the Monetary Policy Statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we recognise the weakness of growth, and that weakness obviously applies to Q4.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now you know there are multiple ways to define what is a recession.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The technical terminology of two quarters in a row that are negative is one way to look at it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I remember discussing that with my colleague and friend Janet Yellen, where the US had two quarters in a row that were negative.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And when I said, well Janet, you must be in a recession and she said, "what with those employment numbers, forget it, we are not in recession."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think we have to be attentive to all sorts of data signals and understanding of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as I'm concerned, I am irrelevant as long as I deliver on leading this institution of talented people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Not just economists, but talented people who are driven to do their job and to deliver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in terms of activity, what we are seeing is hard data that is weak.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, you look at industrial production, it continued to decline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we try to look at PMI numbers in particular, as I just said, we are seeing some encouraging numbers, whether it indicates stabilisation or slight uptick.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: People can challenge PMI numbers and they do, but at least we are seeing numbers that are either to the upside or are stable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your other question, as I said, we are looking at all sorts of data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking at wages a lot for the reasons that I have explained, and because there is a catch-up process that is underway and that should run its course this year, probably next year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would not draw any conclusion from a date of publication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have to appreciate that yes, we are data-dependent, but we look at multiple data, wages being a key one of course, profit unit being extremely important as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They've been taking us up and down and they are volatile and moving almost as we speak at the moment, given the geopolitical developments that we see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are commitments on the part of Member States' governments that they will be withdrawing the energy support.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be very attentive to that, and we will see how much fiscal consolidation there is relative to the budgets that have been submitted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's all this data that we will be looking at and you are correct about the date of publication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you very much for your question and allow me to preface my response to your question with something that we discussed this morning, which is a little bit unrelated to monetary policy, which has to do with the topic of concern to many European institutions, which is the capital markets union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As some of you will remember, the Governing Council had taken a view on the capital markets union back in 2020, when the Commission had published its action plan at the time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And given the momentum and the special efforts deployed by the euro area, deployed by the Commission, to progress the capital market union, we have decided to update significantly that statement and we have unanimously agreed on a new statement which is more specific, which sets out the imperative of moving fast and making progress.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That statement will be available before close of business today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will come after all the monetary policy documents are made available, so that we don't mix the two of them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was a decision that we made after a good discussion on the matter yesterday and a little bit this morning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On inflation, first of all, I would observe that we are on this disinflationary process, and we are making progress.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We came from 2.9% in December, 2.8% in January, 2.6% in February.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a definite decline which is under way, and we are making good progress towards our inflation target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are not sufficiently confident, and we clearly need more evidence, more data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that this data will come in the next few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will know a little more in April, but we will know a lot more in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, this is what we have determined during our discussion this morning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as usual, we have proceeded with a review of the three criteria, which you know is the inflation outlook which, as you will have noted in the monetary policy statement, has been slightly revised, a bit more for 2024 for headline [inflation], but slightly, both for headline and core [inflation] in the next two years, 2025 and 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second element that we look at, as you know, is the underlying inflation and on that front as well we are seeing a narrowing of the range between the various measures that we use.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are also seeing a general moderation, with one exception.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have looked carefully at the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those are the three components that we are very keen to check carefully and to monitor meeting-by-meeting to see what information it delivers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's clearly a positive signal, but certainly not enough of a series of signals to make us confident enough yet at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was general broad agreement about the fact that we will get a lot more data and a lot more information in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was also a very broad agreement around the fact that we will not change our views on one single data [point].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what we are seeing in the data at the moment is indicating certain movements that are directionally good, but it is not strong enough and durable enough, for the moment, to give us sufficient confidence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that was a generally accepted sentiment around the room and the decision that we made was a unanimous decision, by the way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You are correct that while we continue to look at the three components of the reaction function; the inflation outlook, the underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy, there are two components that we are particularly vigilant about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And those two components are the wages evolution as well as the profits evolution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Unit labour costs, unit profits are two items that we will be particularly attentive to and will continue to be attentive to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mentioned that in the underlying inflation measurements there is one which is not moving in the same direction as the others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The others are generally declining and the range between the various instruments is narrowing as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is one that is not declining and that is domestic inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Domestic inflation is largely informed by services, which itself is for most services labour-intensive, and therefore very sensitive to wage evolution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So those are the two components that we will particularly zero in and try to be laser focused on to see whether there is confirmation or not of this beginning of moderation that we are seeing on the wage front, and confirmation of what has been observed on the profits, as to whether or not profits absorb and act as a buffer for the wage increases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have the Q4 numbers for CPE, for compensation per employee, tomorrow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our assessment for the moment is: [the CPE was] declining, relative to the third quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's a conservative assessment given the various other elements that we try to look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at some backward-looking elements, but we also try to be as forward-looking as we can by really following very carefully all the new agreements that are signed and how terms and conditions will apply going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't say that underlying inflation is the only figure that is above 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We tried to look at the inflation outlook, which includes of course the headline inflation, which is the one that under our strategy review we have agreed is the compass that we're using.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're also looking at the inflation without energy and food, otherwise called core inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at other measurements of underlying inflation to try to remove the noise from the signals and try to really measure each and every time what is going to be the best indicator to give us the measurements of what is to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even on headline inflation, we are still projecting 2.3%, which is a revision from what we had before.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we're still at 2.3% in 2024 and we are at 2% in 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Core inflation is at 2.6% in 2024 and then moving to 2.1% in 2025 and finally reaching 2% in 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not saying here that we will wait until we are at 2% and that we see 2% to take a decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in terms of projections, both headline and core, this is what we are seeing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are all looking forward to the two Italian reports, if I may say, because there will be a report by Enrico Letta on the single market which, if fully implemented, would certainly deliver more growth than we have at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we're very much looking forward to the report of President Draghi on the competitiveness of Europe, which is obviously a major topic going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm sure he will be making recommendations and I will wait until we have the report to react to his proposals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have a mandate, we have a mission, we are determined to reaching our 2% inflation target in the medium term and we will be riveted to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've tried in the past to refrain from passing judgement and commenting specifically on market expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I just note that it seems to be converging better, but everyone has to do their job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at the three elements, we look at our projections, we try to anticipate the impact of our monetary policy and that's how we make decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In terms of the operational framework, we have had a discussion, short of course because the main agenda yesterday and today was monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we had a discussion yesterday morning on the operational framework to narrow areas of discussions and arrive at a platform that hopefully will be a consensus between the governors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My strong expectation is that it will be completed on the occasion of our meeting on March 13, and it will then be released, published, explained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our communications department has some ideas as to how to best do it because it is a highly technical matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of you are fully versed in the sophistication and the delicacies of the operational framework, but it warrants a good review, a good explanation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I hope that March 13 will be the date when we will go out with the operational framework.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, I would use the analogy of seasons and episodes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will move to the restrictiveness season, that will take a while.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And once that season is over, we will move into a normalisation season.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if that's the definition of gradual, so be it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I would not commit to any kind of pace, rhythm, magnitude, because we will continue to be data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue to observe how the economy evolves, how the labour market moves, how wages moderate, and the impact of tightening on the financing of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All these factors will be taken into account to determine future moves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, it's a matter which is under discussion at the European Commission level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a matter which is highly debated within the G7, which is a complicated issue which has legal ramifications.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And while there is no doubt in anybody's mind that Ukraine will need significant financing for its completely legitimate reparation programme, as a result of this aggressive and unjustified war by Russia against Ukraine.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The financing, the sources of financing, the terms under which it is deployed by those who will support Ukraine, need to be agreed and need to respect the international legal environment in which we operate and be particularly attentive to the international monetary order and the rule of law which has been enforced for decades.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They are interesting propositions that are being reviewed concerning the interest generated by the proceeds, such interest belonging actually to Euroclear, which could possibly prosper.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that's clearly work in progress on which we have no final say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will be for the leaders to decide what happens.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the mandate that we have - the mission that we have - the ECB acts independently and we will do what we have to do when we have to do it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously we are mindful of the international environment in which we operate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if the conditions are satisfied, if our diagnosis is that we have been restrictive for long enough to be sufficiently confident that we will reach our 2% target, we will make our decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know there are writings here and there and views about the order and the sequence and reference to previous episodes, but I really think that we have to act in accordance with our mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second question, if I may, dear Vice President, I will pass on to you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not that I don't want to answer, but you're far more qualified than me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Commercial real estate, as you perfectly know, is something that we have reiterated as one of the main risks for financial stability in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have seen an important reduction in the volumes of transactions in commercial real estate, even before starting the tightening of monetary policy, and we have seen a decline in prices as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I can say with respect to commercial real estate that I think is relevant is first that the exposure of the European banks to commercial real estate is quite limited.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
