text: If you look at the figures, commercial real estate credit amounts to something close to 5% of the total assets of the European banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The problem - and this happens quite often in economics - is the disparity around the average.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are some banks that have higher exposure and a higher concentration of commercial real estate in their portfolios and in their balance sheets.This is something that we have been monitoring very closely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So far, we have not seen any sort of widespread contagion because of the evolution of commercial real estate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have indicated several times that the exposure of the non-banks is much larger than the exposure of the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to repeat, this is something that we have been looking at very carefully and it's one of the main risks for financial stability at present.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I would just remind you that, in our projection, while aiming at reaching our target timely and in a sustainable manner, as our projections indicate, we also project recovery during the second-half of 2024 and more importantly, in 2025 and 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our projection is 1.5% in 2025 and 1.6% in 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we are really seeing is a slight delay in a process that we had anticipated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Maybe you have observed that recently we have reduced our errors in our projections significantly and they certainly make us feel more confident, not sufficiently confident yet, but more confident that we will reach the target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question was about the unit labour costs and you suggested that unit profits would absorb, or were absorbing all the labour costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is not quite the case yet and we have seen some encouraging numbers in the late part of 2023 and earlier part of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is really one of the hypotheses that we made for our projections, and our projections are predicated on that precisely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want to see that movement confirmed by both moderation of wages, as we anticipate, but also by the squeezing of profit margins so that the unit profits absorb part of the unit labour costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So first of all, we have not discussed rate cuts at this meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we have done is that we have just begun discussing the dialling back of our restrictive stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course we need a lot more information coming in in the next few months to be sufficiently confident.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, when you look at what will be published and what data we will have, in terms of activity, wages and profits, we will have a little in April, and we will have a lot more of that for our June meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It matters, because we are data dependent, and we are adamant that we will be data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I addressed this earlier on when I said that the ECB is an independent central bank and will act independently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will decide on the basis of the three criteria that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the basis of the measurements that we have, the projections that we have, and the additional data that we need, we will determine what action we need to take, and that will be done independently from what my colleague at the Fed decides to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As to whether or not investors are reasonable or not, that's not for me to say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I hope we can do is being attentive and monitor carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Once the data confirms that we are sufficiently confident to reach our 2% target in the medium term and make sure that it will be sustainable, we will act.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the way, I didn't say that there was no rush.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said that we did not discuss cuts for this meeting, but we are just beginning to discuss the dialling back of our restrictive stance, provided that we have enough and certainly more information to be sufficiently confident.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be looking at all of that, because we continue to look at the three key components: the inflation outlook, which tells us what we should expect on the basis of the projections that are prepared by staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That indicates clearly that we are in this disinflationary process - that inflation is declining.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we also look at the underlying inflation and what feeds some of this underlying inflation, including wages in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at that because we want to be stable on three accounts: inflation outlook, underlying inflation and strength of transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Regarding the latter, I think we're seeing a good and solid transmission to the financing sector and then further down the road to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, you are asking the first question, but you seem to be covering quite a bit of ground that maybe others wanted to cover as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'll try to respond briefly to give others a chance as well to ask similar questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you heard me loud and clear, indicating that new sentence which is prominent in our monetary policy statement - and I'll read it again - that if our updated assessment of the inflation outlook, the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission were to further increase our confidence that inflation is converging to our target in a sustained manner, it would be appropriate to reduce the current level of monetary policy restriction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's an important sentence because it really describes the mechanics and it better clarifies our reaction function and the process through which we are engaging.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have said previously that in April we get some information and some data, and we looked at all that, but in June we know that we will get a lot more data and a lot more information and we will also have new projections, which will incorporate and be informed by all that will be published before the projection is completed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be looking at all this information, all this data and the projection results that will be produced by the entire Eurosystem, not just the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we will determine whether all of that confirms our hope that inflation returns to target in a sustained manner, and if as a result, our confidence is sufficiently reinforced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is really the mechanics that we will adopt, that we have resolved to adopt and that we will follow in the coming meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you asked me whether everybody was exactly on the same page.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Truth be told, a few members felt sufficiently confident on the basis of the limited data that we received in April and agreed to rally to the consensus of a very large majority of the governors, who were comfortable with the need to reinforce confidence when receiving a lot more data in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your third question: you asked whether the US CPI number received yesterday had any bearing on the subsequent market development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have said in the past that we are data dependent, we are not Fed dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those numbers were not from the Fed, they were from CPI, and obviously anything that happens matters to us and will in due course be embedded in the projection that will be prepared and released in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The United States is a very large market, a very sizeable economy, as well as a major financial centre, so all that finds its way into our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all I would not speculate what other central banks are or are not going to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that, as I just responded to the previous questions, consequences in terms of impact on price stability, impact on inflation - whether it is imported inflation or otherwise - all that of course needs to be taken into account and is monitored very carefully and finds its way into our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all of that will be included, embedded, monitored and taken into account in our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we don't target exchange rates, and we don't comment on exchange rates, and I'm not going to go any further than that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would simply mention that there are multiple channels through which influence can be exercised, it's not just through exchange rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The size of our balance sheet has quite significantly reduced already and I'm sure you have followed that very carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The entire, very large TLTRO repayment that was coming due in March has been entirely repayed of course and an additional amount over EUR 30 billion has also been added to the repayment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In addition to that, given the APP gradual runoff, we also reduce our balance sheet by an average of about EUR 30 billion per month.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That process is ongoing and will continue to happen as anticipated, as predicted and as determined by the maturity of those bonds that come to runoff, and then we will move to the reduction of the PEPP reinvestment, from the 1stof July until the end of December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the plan, but there is no further discussion on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for picking up on the Watchers speech - I think the one you are referring to is the one in which I tried to describe as accurately as possible the sequences that we went through: the hiking cycle, the holding cycle and the prospect of the dialing down cycle.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that most, if not all that I have said in that speech still holds to this day.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I described, I think in very specific terms, what the confidence level should be and on what basis we're going to nurture that confidence and reinforce it over the course of time in that process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'm not going to comment on whether I'm more or less confident - I think that what we are saying in the monetary policy statement (MPS) today is that if -- and I'm not going to bore you with repeating it - but if the updated assessment of the inflation outlook, the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission were to further increase our confidence that inflation is sustainably at 2% as we anticipate, then it would be appropriate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That very much stands and is completely the continuation of the Watchers speech that I gave about 20 days ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me about the distinction that we should or should not draw between euro area inflation and US inflation, and why would we not be entirely US inflation dependent in a way, or US CPI dependent, and should we take our cue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are operating in the euro area with the euro area economy for the benefit of the Europeans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our objective is price stability, and we have to determine our monetary policy decisions on the basis of the data that are produced by the euro area, on the basis of the global environment - and that includes obviously the United States, but it also includes China, which matters, it also includes Japan, which matters, and a lot of emerging market economies that also have a bearing - but we focus predominantly on the territory for which we have responsibility for monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you know, and as I'm sure all of you in the room know, the nature of inflation in the euro area was different from the nature of inflation in the United States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Notably, the drivers of it were different, the fiscal response was different, the consumption by US consumers is of a different nature, investments were different, so I don't think that we can draw conclusions based on an assumption that the two inflations are the same.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a result of that, we have to focus on what we have jurisdiction for, which is the euro area, taking into account what happens in the rest of the world, but not assuming that what happens in the euro area will be the mirror of what happens in the United States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In many ways you've answered the first question or you at least gave me the elements of my answer to your questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will operate meeting by meeting, and we will take into account all the data that actually matter and how they unfold and develop and affect our economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a result of that I cannot pre-commit to any route, to easing more or easing less, unless and until we have the data and we can analyse the data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that will take its course as the events unfold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, I'm not going to speculate on the monetary policy stance and decisions of another central bank.On the energy market: there is one particular segment in the monetary policy statement that I wouldn't want to let go unnoticed because I think it's important, particularly in relation to energy prices, and that's the portion that relates to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll read it again for you: inflation is expected to fluctuate around current levels in the coming months and to then decline to our target next year, owing to weaker growth in labour costs, the unfolding effect of our restrictive monetary policy, and the fading impact of the energy crisis and the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A lot of those fluctuations that we refer to in that particular paragraph will actually be associated with the very low energy cost that we had in two episodes over the course of 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously the price of energy as we see it unfolding in the weeks and months to come will have a bearing related to that base to which prices are compared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So declines in inflation, which we have observed so far, are not going to be linear, and we will have fluctuations around the current level, based on our projections, until it declines to our target in mid-2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The ECB is a bank of all seasons, and I don't think that we can be tied to any particular season.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be data-dependent, and if the data continue to move in the direction of the disinflationary path that we see, then progress will be continued as well in the path that we adopt.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this is going to be data-dependent, and that is the reason why we state very clearly in the monetary policy statement that we are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The direction is rather clear, but there is no pre-commitment to any particular path and it will all depend on the data that come about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your TPI question, there is a very clear press release that we have posted and that stands, which I'm not going to comment upon yet again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the excessive deficit procedure is one of the four components that we assess when we determine eligibility, and it's an alternative condition that is indicated in that particular segment, which will be taken into account by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On fiscal affairs, I'm going to limit myself to the comments that we included in the monetary policy statement, where we indicate that governments should continue to roll back energy-related support measures so that disinflation can proceed sustainably.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, we then say that implementing the EU's revised economic governance framework fully and without delay will help governments bring down budget deficits and debt ratios on a sustained basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had the privilege of Valdis Dombrovskis being with us during the Governing Council meeting this morning, and I think all governors were very pleased to hear him confirm that the revised economic governance framework will be put to a vote to the European Parliament before the end of their session, which I think has another two weeks to go.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, this is good news to the extent that there will be a framework within which governments are expected to operate and which will be guiding principles and helpful from our monetary policy standpoint.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, you are right, and I think we point out very clearly in the monetary policy statement that services inflation is still holding at high levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has been at 4% for the last five months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Domestic inflation, which comprises a lot of services as well, is at 4.5% and has been there for the last three months, if I recall.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is a segment, and those are numbers and indicators, that we're going to monitor very carefully and that we will look at very carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The momentum is also something that we will be very attentive to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we're not going to wait until everything goes back to 2% to make the decisions that will be necessary in order to make sure that inflation returns to 2% sustainably, at target, in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that, for instance, if you look at the disaggregation of items, goods have gone down from 1.6% in February to 1.1%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it's inevitable that some items and some segments will be at higher levels, and we will look at all of them to make our determination and to decide whether on the basis of that assessment we are confident enough.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the balance of risk, I know one or two governors are keen on this balance of risk concerning inflation, but we've always tried to stay away from that in relation to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Historically, we have determined whether it was to the upside, to the downside or broadly balanced in relation to activity, not in relation to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what we prefer to do, as a matter of principle, is identify those components that will bring an upside to the risk and those that will bring a downside to the risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we have done repeatedly in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do that yet again, and when you look at the level of uncertainty around, it's probably the right approach to do so in relation to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On oil prices, they have increased, as was said by one of your colleagues, by roughly 10% in recent weeks, and this is obviously an item which matters a lot.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have learned from the recent shocks that energy costs play a significant role, and we are very attentive to those evolutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are largely informing our assessment on the basis of futures.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not just the price of the barrel of Brent that we look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not perfect, but we try to use futures as an indicator of where the markets are seeing prices of oil for the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, the bank lending survey is always informative, but it's a survey.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It indicates what the banks assess, assume and expect from their customers - both corporate customers and households, or people.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Predominantly mortgages and a bit on consumption, but predominantly mortgages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we also have the hard data, which is interest rates that are offered to those customers, and the volume of loans on an annual basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, if you only look at the bank lending survey, what you see is the anticipation by banks that demand will be slightly lower on the corporate side while it will be slightly higher on the household side.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at volume, there is a slight - not a major - uptick in the volume of loans to corporates and a slight - stable compared with the last month - uptick in the volume of loans offered to households.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as a final point, on both corporate loans and loans to households we have a slight decline in the interest rate that is offered to borrowers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, you can deduct from that that the financial sector is expecting that financing costs are likely to be smaller in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In many of those numbers and data indicators that we have, we see positive developments, but it's the beginning of developments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said earlier, we want to reinforce that confidence that things are going in the right direction, both in terms of growth but more importantly in terms of inflation decline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, we know that there will be fluctuation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's the reason why we put it in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that there's not going to be a linear decline of inflation over the course of the next months or quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what our projections are telling us is that we will have those bumps on the road, if you will, but we will reach the target in mid-2025, so a return to 2% in mid-2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Between now and 2025, there will be ups and downs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And, as I said, a lot of that is related to the base effects that result from the two significant changes in energy prices in the course of 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have embedded in our projection of last March those bumps on the road.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we need to see is how far away from those bumps embedded in the baseline we are likely to go if we are facing supply shocks, as you suggested.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will take stock of that in June as well and update our projections at that point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, without being triumphant and without celebrating anything yet, what we are observing is a decline in inflation and a disinflationary process that is in progress and that is comforting us that the monetary policy that we have adopted so far has contributed significantly to this.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will continue to operate on the basis of the three criteria that I have mentioned several times, which are in the monetary policy statement: being particularly attentive to wages and the evolution of wages, which constitute a large contributor to services; paying close attention to profits, to make sure that unit profits actually absorb as much as possible of the wage increases; and continuing to be very attentive to productivity, which is also something that we expect will improve in the course of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me take this opportunity to give you bit of an opening answer and tell you what we did this morning and what happened as a preamble to this morning's decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me first tell you that we started our meeting this morning by paying tribute to the many men and women who sacrificed their lives on the beach of Normandy today, which is the 80th anniversary of D-Day.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we paid tribute to those sacrifices and those of many others because it enabled us to build what we have built, to disagree in a very civilised way and to have very harmonious and congenial decisions amongst 20 different nationals representing their respective national central banks amongst our Governing Council[1].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it was perfectly appropriate and fitting to do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we decided to cut, and we did so because overall our confidence in the path ahead, because we have to be forward-looking, has been increasing over the last months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So let me explain to you why our confidence has increased in the path ahead.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I will take you back a little bit because this is, after all, the first time in many years that we make that kind of decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'll take you back a little bit to our monetary policy cycle, to remind you that we have had two successive phases and we have made that decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the first phase, as you will remember, was a phase of very robust and rapid tightening.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We tightened by 450 basis points between July 2022 and September 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then we moved into a phase of holding from September 2023 up until today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if we look back at those phases, during each of those phases we divided inflation by half.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if you look at the peak of inflation, in October 2022, we were at 10.6% - double-digit inflation on average.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now fast forward to September 2023, we were at 5.2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So at each and every step of the way, when we reassess and decided to move in a different direction, we had halved inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the second element that we took very much into account was the reliability and the strength of our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there is one particular line of projections which to many of us was relevant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at Q4 2025 projections - you look at September, you look at December, you look at March, you look at June - there's a variation between those projections of 0.10 percentage points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's either 2 or 1.9 or 2 or 1.9 or 2.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's on the basis of this reliability and solidity and robustness of those projections that we have made that decision to actually cut.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm sure that you will be asking "What about next time?"

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: and I will invariably tell you the same thing, which is what is included in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We shall be data-dependent and we shall decide meeting by meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And how we collect data matters, but what is also more important is how we analyse the data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm not only specifically pointing at one set of data, but all the data that we get.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're looking at it under the prism of our three criteria.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will have noticed that I have repeated three times, I think, in this monetary policy statement the three criteria, which are the inflation outlook on the basis of the financial and economic data that we collect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the underlying inflation, and it's the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's under the prism of these three criteria that we analyse all the data that we have available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need to have enough of those data to make a relevant and appropriate analysis that took us this time around to this decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, markets do what markets have to do, and we do what we have to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You are correct that there is no perfect synchronization between our meetings and our decisions and the publication of particular data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm thinking of one particular data that will come for publication tomorrow, which is the compensation per employee (CPE) for Q1, which obviously is relevant because we look very carefully at wages from all possible angles of analysis and CPE is a relevant point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Wages are an important field of data that we need to analyse, but CPE is one of them and it's only being published tomorrow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what we try to do, just to take you a little bit behind the scenes, is we collect as much data as are available.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And at the moment we have about 15 countries or so and a very large portion of the euro area economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we calculate what is the likelihood of that number to better assess and test our resolve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we have to do, and there is no perfect synchronization between the dates of publication, which are set, and the dates of our monetary policy meetings, which are also set.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You also asked what kind of data we are talking about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, it is enough data so that the analysis that we conduct under the three criteria that I have mentioned can actually be relevant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'm not going to tell you today, nor at any point in time until much later on in the summer, whether we do this now or we do something else at another point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The only thing I'm telling you is that we need sufficient data, and data comes in gradually over the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need sufficient data to actually corroborate the view that we have that the disinflationary path is being confirmed and warrants further decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, thank you for reading my speech or for having been in the room.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was the Watchers speech, in which in a sort of prospective but also vaguely academic way I tentatively analysed the phases that we had gone through and anticipated what could come next.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because, as I said, we are making a decision on the basis of the confidence that we have that we are on a path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But at each and every point in time in the course of the next few months, we will need data and more data and analysis of those data to constantly confirm that we are on this disinflationary path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know the volume of multiple data that we should be receiving, and that will accumulate and corroborate hopefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I cannot confirm that it is the dialling-back process that is underway.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's a strong likelihood, but it will be data-dependent and what is very uncertain is the speed at which we travel and the time that it will take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again, this will be determined by the data that we receive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are currently restrictive, even after this 25 basis point cut, as you well know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are today more restrictive in real interest rate terms than we were back in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what we're doing here, as indicated by our chief economist Philip Lane, is removing a degree of restriction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm sure that you will hear some of my excellent colleagues take their view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will take such time, or it will move at such speed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would caution against any such conclusion for one simple reason.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know the path we are on, but we also know that there will be other bumps on the road.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I said last time when we were together that we were travelling that journey on a road that was downward towards the 2%, but that there would be bumps on the road.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are bumps that we can more or less predict and that we can anticipate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are bumps on the road that can come as a surprise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are bumps on the road that we can anticipate, but the magnitude of which we are not totally confident about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Depending on which country you look at or depending on what collective agreement you look at, there can be a massive amount of catching up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There could be a front-loaded agreement to increase wages and then it fades away.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So all these things have idiosyncratic characteristics that will actually either increase, reduce or deliver the same level of bumps that that we are considering.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we know it's going to be a bumpy road.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's face it, the next few months will continue to be bumpy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again, what we wanted before making that decision was collectively to increase our confidence level that the path ahead was on its disinflationary rhythm that we needed in order to make our decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to do that we looked back at the last time we decided to hike, which was in September, and we assessed the journey from September 2023 up until now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I just said in the previous answer, there are bumps on this road that we are travelling with more confidence that the disinflationary path is actually materialising.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be looking at multiple data, not only wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But you're quite right to take me back to wages, because wages matter enormously in a tight labour market when it comes to services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we know that services are an important element of the items in the index, which have been rising.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The last service, our number that we had was 3.7.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It went up to 4.1 in May after a series of fours in March, February and January before that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what's at the root of this increase in service prices is predominantly wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what happened to wages in the last few months?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we really looked under the bonnet of wages and we looked under the bonnet of countries because some of the decisions that were made were country-specific.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In Germany, most of those collective agreements are negotiated every two to three years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to give you a more specific example, a public service agreement actually happened in 2024 and has now compensated for the lost purchasing power since 2021, which is when the last agreement was reached in the public service.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you can imagine that an agreement that is cut in 2024 and that covers [lost purchasing power in] 2021, 2022 and 2023 is obviously going to be very sizeable, and it was - in the 12% range.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have exactly the same story for the retail sector, which is quite significant, where again an agreement has been reached now, which is an ovation compared with three years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not too clear in the public service, but it's very clear in the retail sector agreement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that leads us to assume that wages will continue to remain elevated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at negotiated wages, in the first quarter they were at 4.7%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at compensation per employee based on what we can calculate on the basis of 15 countries, it was 4.7%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Compared with 4.5% in Q4 [2023] for negotiated wages in the fourth quarter, 4.7% is the same stabilisation on the compensation per employee in the fourth quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have elevated levels, tentative stabilisation and then we look at our third indicator, which is the wage tracker, which includes seven euro area countries, including the largest ones.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we cover a very large chunk of European economic activity and labour markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what that wage tracker tells us is that while the stock of agreements and various accords that are recorded by the wage tracker is still elevated, when we look at the flow [since last year] - what is coming in now - we are seeing a decline in wage growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Wages are not an easy matter, because they are peculiar as they include lots and lots of elements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have catching up, you have social security contributions, you have what we call wage drift, which includes a lot of very specific items, including overtime, including differential between low-paid and high-paid employees and all the rest of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we try to really combine and confront all this data and all this information to analyse it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that leads to the conclusion that while still elevated - no question about that - we are seeing those wages on a declining path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that will particularly be the case in 2025 because the 12% decided in 2024 are not going to be producing the same impact in 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is, I think, even comforted by the fact that this particular projection exercise is checked and cross-checked and produced jointly by the staff of the ECB and the staff of the national central banks, which really have their fingers on the pulse of those collective agreements and compensation per employees.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second part of your question was how long it will take or how much more you see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are going to look at data as they come in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will have to test our assumption of declining wages towards the end of 2024 and seriously less elevated wages in 2025 in the course of the next few weeks and months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can't go more than two, but OK, I'll take the three.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'll leave it to your sagacity to identify who it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Were we divided as far as the path ahead is concerned, we were all absolutely united to agree that our path would be data-dependent, that we would decide meeting by meeting and there was absolutely no dissent on that front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also confirmed that our criteria, the three that I have mentioned, inflation outlook, underlying inflation, strength of monetary policy transmission, will continue to drive our analysis of data going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Regarding your first question, first of all, those are not our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's obvious that projections produced by staff on a regular basis are very informative, go deep into the data that we receive, analyse at length, produce scenarios, analysis, sensitivity analysis, and that this is very helpful for us to make decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that doesn't mean to say, and I would not say that now, that we would only decide at the time of projection meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But obviously, we have more data when we have projection meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can assure you that we take the fight against inflation extremely seriously.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there is one thing that I have learned in this job is that we have to be persistent, we have to be determined, we have to be data-dependent, but we cannot give up on the objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And our objective is to tame inflation and to bring inflation back to 2% in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So let there be no doubt about our determination to tame inflation and to restore price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I will mention three numbers for you, because I think that in my sleepless nights I try to have that in the back of my mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there's that little voice that says, "Carry on, carry on".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In October 2022 inflation on average in the euro area was 10.6%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In September 2023, less than a year later, inflation was 5.2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was the reading of August, because we made the decision in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Each and every step of the way we divided inflation by two.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't want to divide the next inflation by two, because if we divide 2.6 by two, we have 1.3.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't want to go there, but as is very clearly stated in the monetary policy statement, we are moderating our restrictive stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will continue to be restrictive as long as necessary to bring inflation to 2% in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Vice-President Luis de Guindos: I think that we have been crystal clear with respect to them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do not elaborate or comment on transactions and deals that have not been finalised yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will make an assessment about any kind of transaction that implies mergers and the purchase of stakes in banks, but this assessment will be based on prudential and solvency issues.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer to that question is no, because that's the privacy of the deliberations to the extent that they relate to one particular person.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'm sure you will identify that person quickly and will be able to get that information from him.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: More seriously, on the neutral rate, you know that I have refrained systematically from erring towards a particular number or identifying a neutral rate or a range around the neutral rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will simply say this: if it has increased compared with where it was before the coronavirus (COVID-19), we also know that we are far away from the neutral rate now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by moving from 4% to 3.75% on the DFR, we are not close to the neutral rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, welcome to this circle, and we're very happy that Croatia has joined and has extended the circle to 20.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your question is similar to the ones that we had when some of the Baltic States in particular were cruising at much higher inflation rates than the average in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's the whole issue of divergences that we have amongst ourselves because we have different fundamentals, because we have different heritage, because of different structural rigidities as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From an ECB standpoint, we have to look at euro area data and we cannot go down into the specificities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be mindful of the divergences and we do publish - we will be publishing soon actually - a convergence report that will identify these divergences and how close countries are getting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We very much believe that inflation will come down and we will continue this disinflationary process and that that will apply to all Member States.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But again, the pace and consistency between countries is always going to be an issue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously having growth and strong demand has its disadvantages as well as benefits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At the ECB we have a very clear mandate, and that mandate is enshrined in the Treaty and that mandate is a focus on delivering price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that that price stability mandate provides solid guideposts and boundaries for our monetary policy strategy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't see a need nor do we have the capacity or the competence to change that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would also observe that providing price stability and giving predictability to sustainable investment is certainly one of the various contributions that we can make in relation to the fight against climate change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have different sets of actions, from risk management to better modelling and including climate change risks and mitigation measures in our work.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But providing price stability is certainly a good way to tell those investors in sustainable projects you have price stability and the ECB will be here to guarantee that prices are stable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's nothing like waves of inflation to discourage investments that require a long-term perspective and a later return on investment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The dot plot mechanism is an interesting concept, and I think I would leave it at that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: See also: ECB Code of Conduct for the Members of the Governing Council (2002/C 123/06)3.2 The members of the Governing Council shall act in the general interest of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For decisions to be taken in accordance with Article 10.3 of the Statute of the ESCB, Governors may also take into account the interest of their respective national central bank as shareholder.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me start with the second one and I'm going to repeat for you a paragraph that we discussed and that we slightly modified, but which essentially remains intact with a bit more force probably, which is that "national fiscal and structural policies should aim at making the economy more productive and competitive, which would help to raise potential growth and reduce price pressure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: An effective, speedy and full implementation of the Next Generation EU programme, progress towards the Capital Markets Union and the completion of the Banking Union, as well as the strengthening of the Single Markets, are key factors that would help foster innovation and increase investment in the green and digital transitions."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That could probably echo some of the things that you heard probably this morning, when President von der Leyen presented her proposals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is really important about the fiscal aspect is the following sentence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "We welcome the European Commission's recent guidance calling for EU member states to strengthen fiscal sustainability and the Eurogroup's statement on the fiscal stance for the euro area in 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Implementing the EU's revised economic governance framework fully and without delay will help governments bring down budget deficits and debt ratios on a sustained basis."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was discussed and we believe that it's a very strong endorsement of the principle of discipline, so that all Member States who have adhered and agreed to a set of rules under the fiscal governance framework will actually apply those rules and principles.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's a process that is underway that will take them to submit the multi-annual proposals that will be then reviewed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this is certainly the set of rules that have to be implemented and respected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, and you give me an opening because you said what was actively discussed in the Governing Council over the course of the last two days and specifically this morning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I see very much the discussions we had this morning as a story of on the one hand, on the other hand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you're only asking me a question on the other hand, which has to do with the services inflation, which is obviously well exemplified by the domestic prices that you referred to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the domestic prices are clearly high, have slightly increased compared even with the May reading.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we believe they are largely determined by what I call the WPP, which for me is the wage, the profit and the productivity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we spent a lot of time actually looking under the hood of wages, profit and productivity on the basis of rather limited information because we don't have a lot of specificity at this juncture, and we will have a lot more of that in the coming weeks and months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But suffice to say that the wages, whether you are measuring them with reference to compensation per employee, compensation per employee on an hourly basis, the wage trackers that we use and various other instruments, including Indeed for instance, point us in the direction of rather elevated wages, which were embedded and totally taken into account in our June projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this does not come as a surprise to us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a very large component of catching up with inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So nominal wages increase significantly this year in order to compensate the loss of purchasing power that has been experienced by workers over the last couple of years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is very interesting, because we debated that, including with representatives of the national central banks, is that while it [wage increases] will remain elevated this year, many surveys and the corporate telephone survey, in particular, the SAFE survey that is published, indicate that this trend of elevated wages will decline significantly in the course of 2025 and even more so 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So directionally, that's the direction that it is heading for.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On productivity, there is a limited element of recovery at very low levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is a little bit of progress, but certainly not what we would like to see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our expectation is that with consumption picking up with more demand, the recovery will strengthen and that will raise productivity as hoarded employees will be asked to respond to the demand that is addressed to the goods production and service supplying sectors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So on that front, a slight improvement in the month of June and we hope to see more of that as demand picks up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the third component - profits, it has reversed compared to what we observed in the last quarter of 2023, meaning that unit profits are now down to negative territory when they were actually in positive territory in the last quarter of 2023.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there has been absorption of the additional labour costs that resulted from the catch up and from the drift in labour costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But clearly they are high and are a component of prices that we try to observe very carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that leads me to one word that you used.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And for those of you who care to listen or to read the speech that I gave in Sintra, I specifically referred to data dependency, which is something that was unanimously endorsed by the Governing Council today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I also made very clear that data dependency did not mean data point dependency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we applied that to wages, to other elements that we measured very carefully in the last weeks and that we looked at together in the last two days.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The decision that was taken this morning was a unanimous decision, but what was equally unanimously determined was the fact that we were determined to be data dependent to decide meeting by meeting and not to have any predetermined rate path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the question of September and what we do in September is wide open and will be determined on the basis of all the data that we will be receiving.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously, our projection from June will be a point of reference, but the projection of September plus all the other elements that we will be receiving will be taken into account to decide what we do in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is no predetermined path and that was very strongly endorsed by the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The issue of tariffs that you mentioned, that's an important aspect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will have internal discussions within the Governing Council about the risk resulting from segmentation, fragmentation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously the tariff increases that are flagged, either as to be maintained or to be increased, come into the picture.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is particularly important given that export is one of the engines of the recovery as we flagged it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's consumption first and foremost, driven by the increased purchasing power resulting from nominal salary increases and reduced inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's also an increase in trade as a result of which exports out of Europe to the rest of the world would matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is an area where we will be attentive to whatever political decisions are made by whoever in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, you all know how the Governing Council works.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do a lot of debate and discussion and we present views in the course of Wednesday.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on Thursday morning, a proposal is put forward by our chief economist Philip Lane.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Then each and every Governing Council member says whether he supports or doesn't support the proposal by our chief economist, Philip Lane.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on this occasion, everyone was supportive of the decision proposed by Philip Lane.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said, it encompasses the three key rates unchanged and the meeting-by-meeting data dependency and no predetermined rate path going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You pointed to the issue of confidence and we were not the only central bank in the world to have referred to the need to be sufficiently confident about the inflation path and the disinflationary process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we are at the stage where with additional data - data, not data points - additional data that will take multiple avenues and forms, and that we will dissect in great detail in the weeks and months to come; so with additional data, if that data actually confirms the disinflationary process that is at work at the moment, it will reinforce our confidence and we shall see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it will encompass a whole range of data and indications.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on each and every review of those components, we will still continue to apply our threefold approach, which will focus on inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Therefore, it gives us a way in which we can look forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will also look at underlying inflation, into all its decomposition, and we will look at the transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue to review those three components in the same way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In my old synchronised swimming days, the coach used to say you have the choice: you swim or you sink.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The difference will be in the hard work that you put in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are a few things from synchronised swimming that I still have loud and clear in my head.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not going to comment on the policy avenues that have been flagged by President von der Leyen because the speech was at 11:00 this morning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that all I can do at this point in time is offer my congratulations for the re-election by such a margin.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But, of course, we will look very attentively at what the proposals are at the European level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment, we are also very fixated on the April fiscal governance framework that has been decided and which is obviously vetted by the Eurogroup, and of which we will see implementation in the early weeks of September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me about our staff and I would just like to say that, number one, a very significant majority, if not 80 to 90% of our staff, is highly motivated by the mission of working at the European Central Bank and for the benefit of European compatriots.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would also say that a lot of people are working very hard in this institution and I think that all Europeans should appreciate that this work that translates into a few recommendations, into a few numbers and into a few policy matters are substantiated by a massive amount of work that is itself supported by what we call the shared services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm extremely grateful to them for the work that they do and I'm extremely privileged to lead this institution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not saying that because those would be my speaking points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, because we have to be mindful of the very large amount of work that is discharged by many of them, we of course have programmes in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a lot of means and tools that are available for members of staff who feel under pressure, who feel that they're not getting the right opportunities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Just to give you an example, since I started as President of the ECB, we've put in place a whistle-blowing procedure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We've installed a mediator who started his work earlier this year.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have numbers of workshops for the leadership in the institution to understand the ramification of leadership and how it is important to not only motivate but also encourage members of staff who work in the various divisions of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue the dialogue with all staff and certainly with staff representatives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we conduct our own surveys as well to corroborate or understand better what is at stake.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I take huge strength from the motivation of our staff and the determination that they all have to do a good job for the Europeans.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question, I'm not going to speculate on political development, particularly as election processes are underway and sometimes under dramatic circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, we have to take into account the consequences of, for instance, the increase in tariffs or policies that are determined outside of the euro area by any country with which we have either strong trade or financial links.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously, given the size of the US financial markets in particular, the developments taking place in the United States will be very carefully assessed to see what consequences it might have on the European Union and on the euro area in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the magnitude of - I guess you're referring to interest rates - movement that would be needed if the wages [wage growth] were not to decline as expected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's obviously a domain where we dig and we research and we try to find as much evidence, surveys, assessments as possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we do that with all national central banks, but we do that also on the basis of our corporate telephone survey, on the basis of all the numbers that are reported by Eurostat, on the basis of the wage trackers and - honestly -- on the basis of everything that we see, the direction in '25 and in '26 is downwards.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's not basic, because none of that is basic, and a lot of developments have not had a lot of historical previous examples.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there was a period of two years of very high inflation because of the way in which employment relationships are organised in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And because of the staggered determination of collective bargaining agreements, annual, biannual, triannual negotiations, the deferred impact of inflation is taking place now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The highest numbers that you have are in '24, whether you look at wholesale, retail, public sector, private sector: it's in '24 that the impact is the heaviest.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the catch up, once completed, will return the employment relationship and the collective bargaining agreement process to a more normal path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I'm to believe what our national central banks see in their respective numbers in the 20 member states, they see a return to numbers that are perfectly compatible with our target of 2% in the course of '25 and even more so in the first part of '26.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'm not going to entertain the hypothesis where all that would be wrong because there's too much corroboration of our assumptions and too much by way of both model-driven but also empirically determined understanding of what is going to happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if we are wrong, we will do what we normally do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We reassess on the basis of the data and we take the decision and we continue to be restrictive - more restrictive if it was necessary - so that we can return to our target in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is the invariable in any of our reasoning: return to target 2% in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, that's what we say very clearly in the monetary policy statement: that we will stay in restrictive territory as long as it's necessary to reach our 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are not at target and there's time to be had before we get to target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your first question, what should you look at, which means also what should we look at, to confirm or reinforce our confidence that we are on that disinflationary path and that it remains broadly on track and pointing in the right direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We must look at all components of data, all measurements, all indicators that will be coming in, in the next weeks and months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not suggesting that we're going to stop in September and, and not look and continue to look further.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's clear that between now and September, we will be receiving a lot of information, whether it's GDP, whether it's inflation reading, whether it is wage and profit decomposition.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know I'm overly simplistic in that enumeration, but that's what we will be looking at, to see whether or not it confirms the path that we are seeing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'm afraid that it's going to be a bit of a busy summer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me a second question, you asked me about the bank lending survey.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Allow me to distinguish in terms of credit, because there's a slight difference between corporates on the one hand, households on the other one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's at 5.1%, which is 8 basis points lower than where it was.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But on the other hand, the credit demand has been extremely low on the part of corporates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And when you decompose their demand, it's largely for the short term and there is redemption for longer term credits by the corporates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other hand, when you look at mortgages, the rate is the same, at 3.8%, and that's the first time in many months, but there is an increase in the mortgage demand as indicated by the bank lending survey.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a bit of a story of two sides and obviously we would like to see a bit more on the corporate side because that would mean more investment, which is obviously a prelude to continued recovery going forwards.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, in your first question of the strong likelihood of dialling back, we clearly dialled back in June and that's when we decided the 25 basis points rate cut.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you have noted on the occasion of this monetary policy Governing Council, we decided to hold the three rates because of the reason that I've mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While we are on that disinflationary track, at the same time, the domestic price pressures remain high and the interconnection between wage, profit and productivity can really constitute uncertainty around that path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a story of "on the one hand, on the other hand", which leads us to not make any decision on the occasion of this meeting and for future meetings it will be a matter of observing the data, analysing the data and determining whether or not we are reinforced in our confidence that we are on the path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Mr Vice President, you have the rest of the question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, today the Bank of Espana was represented by the deputy Governor of the Banco de Espana, Margarita Delgado.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I would even say well represented by Margarita Delgado; she made her points and it was part of the unanimous decision that the President referred to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: With respect to the future, well the election of the Governor of Banco de Espana is the prerogative of the Spanish government.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And they have indicated very clearly that before the next meeting they will appoint someone there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Hopefully, I hope that we will have a new governor of Banco de Espana before our next meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The only thing that we recommend to all the governors is that they have to be knowledgeable, in terms of economics, finance, banking, and I hope that will be the case again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you so much to take care of my summer reading.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I might do a lot of reading stories during the summer for my grandchildren rather than diving into very substantive reading as you suggested, but I'll come to that question later.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So growth is obviously something that we look at carefully and we certainly observe that we have recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a recovery that is led by services supported by what we call the "virtuous circle", between high employment in services and consumption of services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I remind you that service production was up 0.7% above Q1 level, that was the number in April.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The service PMI remains expansionary, a tad lower than where it was, but still very expansionary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the total employment in services has also significantly contributed to the increase of employment in Q1.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's clear that on the manufacturing side it's not the case and manufacturing has actually declined in the last few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the other aspect which we are also looking at very carefully, because it helps to have a forward-looking vision, is the level of investment, and investment remains weak, driven also by the tight financing conditions and by the uncertainty experienced by the corporates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have recovery and we will continue to observe carefully where it is coming from.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Suffice to say at this point that it is service driven, not manufacturing driven and that investment could certainly be stronger going forwards.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other element which I pointed to earlier on is this issue of exports.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think that this is also a domain that we will look very carefully at to see how the numbers are faring going forwards, and in particular, what is the competitive position of the European Union and the euro area relative to other other economic nations, in particular China.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to come back to your question, which is really "what are you going to do with the strategy review?".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The strategy review that we conducted back in 2020-2021 was a massive exercise, that we conducted after, 18 years, of no strategy and no strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it required that, as I said at the time, we turned every stone and we looked at everything that we use, that we decide, how we decided, how we communicate it, and we will assess what has been achieved, where we have been short, where we can improve, and that will not be the lengthy process that we had, but a shorter process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will start reasonably soon and you should expect the outcome in the second-half of '25.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have deliberately excluded any discussion concerning the symmetric 2% medium term, so the inflation target will not be debated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It can be debated in the future by a future President of the ECB, but not on my watch.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other item that we will also exclude is the discussion of the dot plots, given the experience that some of my colleagues have had of this element.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the beauty of Europe, but particularly the euro area because we are a monetary union and we are 20 different fiscal jurisdictions, as a result of which we have discrepancy or disparity if you will between some countries and others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was the case exactly in the other direction at the time when inflation ran very high, where you had Nordic countries or Baltic countries where inflation was hitting in the 20% plus, when the average was much lower and the peak on a euro-consolidated basis was 10.6%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is the reality that we have and we have to deal with it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have to tell you that each and every governor when he or she walks in the Governing Council room is a member of the Governing Council and not the representative of his or her country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not suggesting that it's not in the back of their mind because of course they come from there, they return there and they are very much aware of the reality of their economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But they also know that we are making decisions for the Euro area at large and we cannot make specific decisions that would be nationally and member-state based.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your question about our decision, we decided to cut the deposit facility rate by 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We proceeded as we normally do and have very clearly indicated by obviously looking at data and looking in particular at data through the prism of our three key criteria.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So when you look at the incoming information, it confirms our previous projections and it comforts us in our confidence that we are heading towards our target in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: During the course of 2025 in particular, inflation will decline towards our 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we thought that given the gradual disinflationary process, it was perfectly appropriate to moderate the degree of monetary policy restriction by cutting our deposit facility rate, which I will call the DFR if you don't mind from now on, by 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I said that we looked at all the information that we get on the occasion of a projection exercise through our three prisms, I'm referring obviously to the inflation outlook, I'm referring to the underlying inflation and I'm referring to the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the inflation outlook, when we receive the projections of our staff for September, it's virtually unchanged relative to June for the inflation outlook.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it continues to see a return to 2% at the end of 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is, by the way, the fifth consecutive projection exercise pointing to that 2% at the end of 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because it certainly reinforces our confidence in the solidity and robustness of those projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the underlying inflation on the other hand, we look at the various indicators that we have from domestic inflation to PCCI [Permanent and Common Component of Inflation].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And here we see one particular indicator, the domestic indicator, which is abating a little bit because it moved from 4.5% to 4.4% between June and July, and it is not satisfactory.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is the reason why we have to be resilient in our approach and very attentive to the various components of core inflation as measured by those various indicators.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on that front, we all observe that the financing conditions continue to be restrictive and the footprint of our monetary policy in the real economy has been visible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the basis of that review of incoming data, staff analysis, consistency of the projections for the fifth exercise in a row, that decision to cut by 25 basis points was perfectly legitimate and, as I said, unanimously decided.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am tempted to quote the Spanish Que sera sera because we have consistently said, and we repeat again, that we shall remain data-dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is particularly justified in view of the uncertainty that abounds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And our path, of which the direction is pretty obviously a declining path, is not predetermined neither in terms of sequence nor in terms of volume.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I would like to add one thing which I have already said before, which is still true, which is that data dependency does not mean data point dependency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're not going to be fixated on one single number.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm saying that in particular because September will certainly deliver a low reading of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We expect, because of the base effect, particularly on energy, our inflation numbers to be up in the fourth quarter, so the last three months of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're looking at a whole range of data that we receive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, we can all count: it is five weeks before 17 October, which is a relatively short period of time compared with other intervals that we've had in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not giving you any commitment of any kind as far as that particular date is concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other matter that you referred to, typically we do not comment on individual institutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as you know well, we have a clear procedure which involves our supervision authority, the SSM [Single Supervisory Mechanism], which at certain thresholds of equity ownership or transfer of shares, if you will, has to be consulted and has to authorise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And of course I'm confident that the authorities of these institutions concerned, namely UniCredit and Commerzbank, will be perfectly aware of their regulatory requirements and will comply with such requirements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The SSM will do what it has to do in full independence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, cross-border mergers have been hoped for by many authorities, and it will be very interesting to see that process unfold in the weeks to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm going to spend a bit more time on your second question because on the first one - how long are we going to be sufficiently restrictive?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Becausewhat we want is to achieve the goal of returning inflation to target in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, for the fifth projection exercise we have inflation at target during the second half of 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is on the basis of the baseline that we have in our projection.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
