text: And we're going to observe how that baseline evolves over the course of time as data come in to decide for how long we have to continue cutting rates and at what point we have been sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'm not going to give you any idea as to where r* is because this is an unobservable concept anyway.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as we get closer to it, we will know certainly better.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you probably know, the staff have produced a very good paper on r*, which indicates that it's probably a tad higher than where it used to be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, as we get closer to it, we will know better whether we are there, and there are multiple factors that are going to have an impact on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question of whether this 25-basis-point cut is going to be a boost for our economy given that so much is structural.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know I'm preaching to the converted here, but obviously there is a lag between the time when we make a decision and when the impact is actually felt and can be observed in the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we're still observing at the moment is the impact of our tightening decisions from more than a year ago - almost two years ago now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We believe that the peak has been reached in relation to GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there will be continued, although downward sloping, effects of those decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will have the same kind of lag applying to the decision that we are making now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The passing of time does not satisfy the instantaneous satisfaction that we would have to see the results coming out of our decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is the reality of monetary policy and the functioning of our economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second part of my answer to your question, because you refer to structural causes, gives me a chance to actually comment on the Draghi report.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Neither has anyone for that matter, because it's sufficiently substantive and material enough to require more time and special attention.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's a formidable report in that it poses a diagnosis which is severe, but which is just in our view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it also points to structural reforms and practical proposals to achieve such structural reforms that could be extremely helpful for Europe to be stronger, but also for us as the central bank to achieve better results in our monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If productivity can rise as a result of the structural reforms, for instance, that would be very good news for us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the capital markets union can be implemented and more financing be made available in order to finance innovation, that is good news for us as well when it comes to inflation, price stability and the components that underlie this work that we do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you will appreciate, I'm not going to give you an answer that is country-specific because we work on a euro area basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But obviously it's a risk that we have to be attentive to, which is why we are targeting that 2% sustainably, has to be as symmetric in the medium term as we have anticipated in our in our strategy review, which remains completely valid.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Energy has been one of the key factors that took prices up directly and indirectly through all sorts of channels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in the same vein as it took prices up, it is helping to move prices down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is an exogenous matter, and it is one that can move again and that we have to be prepared for.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I have partially responded to your second question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of the proposals in the Draghi report as well as in the Letta report, by the way - because achieving the single market and improving competitiveness in our view can be very complementary - touch directly on what we are specifically concerned about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the Capital Markets Union is one in particular on which the Governing Council has had a strong view and issued a special opinion upon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the same vein, the financing of innovation, the increase of productivity and competitiveness in relation to its external position, all of that matters when it comes to the work that we have to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I didn't see in Mario Draghi's report any suggestion that the mandate of the ECB should be modified.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a single mandate, as you know, which is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We comply with the treaty and with the mandate that was given by the founding fathers of Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And whatever is suggested by Mario Draghi has a lot more to do with structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I very much hope that the executive authorities in charge will actually take it to heart and we'll see a path towards those structural reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for pointing to this services inflation because that is clearly the component of prices that requires very attentive understanding and monitoring.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But suffice to say that it went up from 4.0% to 4.2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whereas so many other components are on the declining path, that particular segment is increasing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we've tried to decompose what is behind it and it's a combination of holiday packages, insurance and - I'm trying to remember what the third one is, I'm sure it will come back - but it's predominantly these two.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking attentively to the nexus of three elements: number one, wages, number two, profits, number three, productivity, and services is particularly sensitive to wage increases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, our expectation is that services inflation will decline over the course of 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because what staff had anticipated, which is moderation of wage growth, buffering of wage costs by slightly declining profit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And increase of productivity is actually being demonstrated by numbers, by observations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at wages, whether you look at compensation per employee, whether you look at negotiated wages, whether you look at unit labour cost - growth in all of these is going down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And our expectation is that it will continue to go down in the course of 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On negotiated wages, we will still have relatively high numbers and we know that some are in the making at the moment, the auto workers' unions, the IGMetall request and in various other countries, but with some heterogeneity, will continue to move wages higher in the first half of 2025, but then it's definitely on a declining path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The growth is already on a declining path, but it will pick up again in the latter part of 2024 and very early in 2025, and then it will continue to decline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On profits, we are now observing from high numbers that we had at the end of 2020 up until the end of 2023, we are seeing declining numbers on profits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As a result of that, you can obviously deduct that profits are actually buffering and absorbing some of these labour cost increases.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On productivity, it is on an increasing path, as considered and envisaged by staff, a little less than what they had projected, but it's also heading in the right direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that really confirms the views that they had taken initially, and that has given us confidence that services inflation will move downward as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That wages growing moderately and more moderately now, profit absorbing more wages and productivity increasing a little bit by virtue of cyclicality will lead us to having services inflation less than where they are at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's obviously a sector that is resistant and to which we have to be very attentive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Mario Draghi's report includes so many important structural reforms that are going to be the responsibility of governments, that will require the leadership of the Commission and the leadership of those leaders in Europe who are determined to strengthen Europe to give it more sovereignty and to give it more capacity in the current geopolitical circumstances, that I'm really certain that monetary policy will do what it has to do, which is to provide price stability and to deliver on its mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: While structural reforms are not the responsibility of a central bank, they are the responsibility of the governments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our staff provides projections, goes into real in-depth analysis of the situation of every country and receives the feedback of the national central banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They don't provide projections and they don't provide analysis in the vacuum of the wonderful main building and Eurotower of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do reach out and we do work together on a Eurosystem basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The slowdown of the German economy was certainly anticipated by the Bundesbank, certainly the ECB as well, and shared on a Eurosystem basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's embedded and included in the projection that we have and we analysed that very carefully with members of the Governing Council in the last couple of days because there is clearly heterogeneity amongst various countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you look at countries separately as they come together to form the system, you see for instance that at the moment, Spain and the Netherlands are delivering strong GDP numbers, while at the other end Germany is on the other side.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your other question about pan-European banks: I think there are quite a few pan-European banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What you're talking about here is more a cross-border merger between two large national institutions, and that is something which, as I said, will be reviewed from a regulatory standpoint and which certainly will satisfy many of those who have expected cross-border mergers to result from banking union when it is achieved.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had extensive discussions on all the data that we received, all the analysis that was produced by staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we tested the rationale behind the current recovery, which is moderate, and the pick-up in recovery that we expect in 2025 and 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think we were convinced that while private consumption is low and has actually weakened, it should economically result from the combination of higher net income, fading monetary policy impact and low inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It should necessarily result from those forces that consumption and investment actually pick up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we tested all that and we discussed, and some tend to be a bit more pessimistic, some are more optimistic, but we really discussed in depth the rationale behind those outlook numbers that we have for 2024, for 2025, for 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the reason why we revised down by 0.1 percentage points only is really a combination of reduced net export numbers, given the uncertainty and the geopolitical risk that we have going forward, and a carryover of the situation that we have now, which is reduced activity because consumption has been lower than we had anticipated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, we are going to assess all the data that come in each and every time along the way and see that we continue to reach our target in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You are correct that our projection numbers for HICP, which is the headline inflation, have not changed a bit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The one that we have slightly revised is core inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have revised core, which takes out energy and food, by 0.1 percentage points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: By the fact that energy prices have significantly impacted downward and have benefited the headline inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fact that food has slightly increased, but very little.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as a result of these two components, there's a bit of a trade-off and a net-off, if you will, with other prices, notably services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have revised downwards the outlook for growth, because the consumption that we had anticipated for now, essentially, because net income has begun to increase, inflation has gone down significantly and we were expecting consumption to pick up, has not picked up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think that we will be looking at that carefully when we produce our next growth and GDP numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: José Luis Escrivá has joined the circle of governors and we have welcomed him in the circle of governors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Like other governors, he has made some very useful contributions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I hope, like any other governor, he will continue to not only give his personal views, which might be inspired in part by the Spanish situation, but he will have this European dimension that other governors also have when they sit around the table of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a process and it's a journey that I hope will be productive and pleasant, both for him and for the group of governors around the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can assure you that he was welcomed and he was contributing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decided to cut all our rates by 25 basis points because we believe that the disinflationary process is well on track and all the information that we received in the last five weeks since our last monetary policy decision was heading in the same direction - lower!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether you looked at inflation numbers, headline core, whether you looked at PMI numbers, all categories, composite manufacturing, services, employment - are heading downwards as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we look at all the surveys that are in the works at the moment, of which the specific numbers and data will be available soon, it is the same story.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether it is the corporate telephone survey or other surveys that we have available, it's all heading in the same direction - downwards!

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That really confirmed for us the confidence that we have that the disinflationary process is well on track.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is what has caused us to make the decision to cut our three rates by 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have also reiterated that we will continue to be data dependent and honestly, this decision is a case in point of us being data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have all the available data all heading in the same direction, the largest countries all also moving in negative territories in PMI numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those are really strong elements - and because of their synchronisation and the similar direction - we have to take into account those data and make the decision that we have made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are going to continue doing exactly the same thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's clear that between this meeting and the next meeting we have in December, we will be receiving more data - some of it soft, some of it hard - and more readings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All of that will help us decide, as I have said, "meeting by meeting," what monetary policy stance we should decide at that time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think there were no variations in that respect from the decision that we made in the past, in terms of methodology.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the same steer, the same stance, the three-pronged approach and the meeting-by-meeting data dependency, no predetermined path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other point you raised: Trade is obviously an important element and as part of the drivers of activity going forward, we obviously have consumption and investment, but we also have trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Any restriction, any uncertainty, any obstacles to trade matter for an economy like the European economy, which is very open.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Trade within itself, of course, but trade also with the rest of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Any hardening of the barriers, the tariffs, the additional obstacles to that possibility to trade with the rest of the world is obviously a downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a fact that the economic activity has come in, on the basis of the elements that we have and the indicators that are available, a bit below what we had anticipated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in between two projection exercises, and clearly December will be another opportunity for us to run all the data and all the information through our models and to apply the three-pronged approach to our stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What was on the table and what was debated and proposed by our Chief Economist Philip Lane was a 25 basis point cut.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had discussions and debates and rationales and narratives, and all of that is part of the debate and the legitimate discussions that we have within the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But at the end of the day, there was a unanimous decision to cut rates by 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It may have been the Slovenian great atmosphere that precipitated this more than consensus.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was a unanimous decision to cut by 25 basis points and we thought that it was the appropriate decision to make in view of the moment, in view of the indicators that we have and our assessment of this disinflationary process that is really under way and well on track.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the risk of undershooting or overshooting, we can debate ad nauseam on this particular matter and you will find views on both sides of the equation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is clear to all is that we still have risks on both sides of our forecast, upside and downside, probably a bit more on one than the other, probably more downside risk than upside risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'm talking here about our forecast for inflation and that's what we are looking at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, we don't recalibrate, we calibrate, and this is really the process through which we go.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As laborious as it is, we believe in our three-pronged approach.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I won't bore you with the repetition of it all, but it is inflation outlook, underlying inflation and transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we calibrate our monetary policy on the basis of all the data that are available and applying that three-pronged approach.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's obvious that the state of the economy and the activity has a bearing on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to that extent, of course, we take that into account in order to assess inflation and its return in a timely manner to our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that's the extent of our consideration: the bearing of activity on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because our job is price stability and our mission is to return inflation back to the 2% target in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is a fact that at each projection exercise, we receive more data and in particular more updated projections of course, and typically, given that between now and the December meeting there will be more than six weeks, we will also receive more data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, I did not open the door to anything.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I repeated that at each and every meeting we will look at the data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Hence we will be data dependent, not data point dependent, nor anything else.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will determine what is the best rate, what is the best speed, how far and how deep we have to go in order to return inflation to its 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is what we will do in December, and I would not give any other commitment, nor make any other statement in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said in the monetary policy statement that I read earlier on, we are not pre-committing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again, I think that the decision that we're making today is a perfect example of how we can be data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One coupled with obviously a major conflict and horrifying one that is taking place in the Middle East.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We of course are concerned beyond the humanitarian approach, beyond the conflict aspects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking at the economic consequences and we are looking in particular at the impact that this conflict could have on trade, because that part of the world is very much open to trade and the passing of ships of all sorts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are also very attentive to the price of oil that can be impacted, and this oil price is a good segue into your question about China.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What will happen in China, what kind of stimulus will be activated, with all full details as is expected at some stage, will also be an indication of the demand addressed by China to the oil market and the impact that it will have on the price of such a commodity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are looking at all those components and obviously focusing on the economic consequences and the impact that they could have on inflation, and obviously activity to the extent that it impacts inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the issue of economic growth, are we still on a soft landing expectation?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The answer is: on the basis of the information that we have, we certainly do not see a recession.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The euro area, on the basis of what we have, is not heading for a recession, and we are still looking at that soft landing that you have just mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me whether we are more concerned about growth than we are about inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would say that we are concerned about growth to the extent that it has an impact on inflation, and we have to be particularly attentive to both because of the impact that it has on inflation, which is our main focus and our key objective, as you know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is, and you pointed to it, that sentence which is sort of the magic language.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm sure that you will be very attentive if and when that magic language changes a bit.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We still say that "we will keep policy rates sufficiently restrictive for as long as necessary to achieve this aim", which refers to the previous sentence, which is that "we are determined to ensure that inflation returns to our 2% medium-term target in a timely manner".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is no question in our mind that we are currently restrictive, hence that sentence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is also no question in our mind that we are not yet at this 2% medium-term target in a timely manner, and this has to be sustainable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So even if it could well be as markets anticipate, but they are not always right, that the time at which we reach that 2% sustainably has advanced a bit, it is not yet now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will have to wait further in order to make sure that we are at that 2% sustainable medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If anything, I would say that what the numbers are showing at the moment is that our monetary policy is working.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the fact that we've managed to bring inflation down as we have so far, not to a complete victory, but to have brought it down so much is an indication that our monetary policy is actually working.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not the only thing that is operating in that respect, but it is certainly part of the elements to explain that we have moved from very high inflation numbers to much lower [inflation] and hopefully soon to target on a sustainable basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our assessment of inflation as we stand now is really based on all the numbers that are available, and that leads us to assess and take a view on inflation now and the potential impact going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But that will be done in a strict, rigorous, published way when we have our December projection exercise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you will be obviously not privy because it will be public, but you will be on the receiving end of this very clear updating.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the meantime, we are not blind to what happens.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And when we receive inflation by way of HICP at 1.7%, when we see core at 2.7%, when we see services moving down to 3.9% and when we look at the three-month-over-three-month services moving significantly from August to September, all of that put together leads us to believe that inflation is definitely on that disinflationary track that I was referring to earlier.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the forecast, again we had a forecast in September.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Between September and December, a lot of data, a lot of numbers, a lot of indicators and a lot of surveys will come into play and will be integrated in the work that we do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will have a forecast that will be, by the way, extended to 2027 because the December forecast always takes one further year into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We shall see whether there is a move and in which direction in terms of inflation and in terms of activity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in between projection exercises, as I said as a case in point, that data matters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at everything that we have available, and if it is appropriate to take us closer to this timely reaching of our target of 2% medium-term symmetric, we make the decision, as we have today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is a little bit irritating sometimes is the lapse of time between meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in those five weeks we received quite a lot of information, some of it by way of hard numbers and readings that were actually updated downwards a little bit today, and some of it by way of PMIs, which are a bit softer than hard data, but all synchronised and moving in the same direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not sure that we had anticipated that 1.7% [inflation], nor did anyone else for that matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because if I look at analysts and if I look at those whose job it is to project and to forecast, or markets, I think we were all a little bit surprised by the acceleration that is being demonstrated by that number.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's certainly raised our confidence that the disinflationary process is well on track.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's the beauty of the English language: data are either singular or plural, but it's the same word.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not because HICP came out at 1.7% or core at 2.7% that we made that decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And, by the way, we also know for instance, based on the work that has been done and that was already mentioned during the previous press conference in September, on the basis of projections, that the next three months will not have this linear low and below-target inflation number.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that it will be higher than that because of obvious base effects that we know of already.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we shouldn't be surprised by that, and we should not be jumping to any kind of conclusions either.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for bringing Slovenia back into the picture, because there is a lot to be learned from Slovenia.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I was in the market in Ljubljana a couple of days ago to check on prices, because I come to Ljubljana on a regular basis if I can.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Food prices are still growing at 2.4% on average in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are clearly still above target, and it's one area, together with energy prices, to which consumers are highly sensitive, which has a bearing on what they do, whether they consume, whether they save, which matters a lot.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that food prices in particular are very sensitive, and we know that we are not at target yet on that front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, I think that the key messages that I wanted to make yesterday, using the beautiful example of Slovenia, is that in times of uncertainty, you have two options.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can either resign yourself and suffer, or you can get a grip of yourself and take uncertainty as an opportunity, which is exactly what Slovenia did when it became independent, when it fought inflation and when it really bounced back in terms of its economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second lesson, which is interesting and which I mentioned yesterday as well, is that when there is that expansion and when there is prosperity, it needs to be widely shared.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is particularly the case in times of the risk of a digital divide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's a very good case in point where digitalisation has been widely spread and where the Gini coefficient of Slovenia is in the top two of all the OECD countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think the lessons we can learn is that when it's hard, we have to get a grip of ourselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And from our perspective as a central bank, if anything, it should push us in the direction of the capital markets union, of the banking union and making sure that capital flows can actually fuel innovation in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I cannot tell you today what our December outlook will be and what the projections will say.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to be attentive to the data that we get and work on the basis of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the issue of being restrictive, I made the point that we are restrictive at the moment, at the current rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even with the 25 basis point cut, we will continue to be restrictive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we believe that it is necessary and would have to continue to be so until we are confident that we are reaching the 2% target in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That will come in due course, but we're not there yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Even with one of the Member States, however large it is, facing difficult circumstances on the basis of what they themselves are producing, it does not necessarily imply that the whole of the euro area is going to be affected in the same way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And based on the information that we have at the moment, we do not, we do not see a recession in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, we have to be attentive to particular sectors of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as we stand here in Slovenia, which is a country that participates in the supply chain of the automotive sector in particular, of course many countries will be paying attention to these sectoral developments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But to your specific question of whether we see a recession, the answer is no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On fiscal consolidation, we now have a fiscal governance framework that identifies the right equilibrium and balance between fiscal consolidation that is needed in many countries and the necessary investment in growth-enhancing reforms.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think it is that balancing act which is the virtue and the value of this revised governance framework for fiscal purposes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's associated with a timeframe of four or seven years depending on the level and degree of reforms that the Member States will propose and will implement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if those rail guards are followed and observed by Member States, we believe that it's the right environment within which to develop activity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And for our part, while the fiscal authorities will do what they have to do in fiscal terms and while the authorities will do what they have to do in structural reforms, we will do our part by maintaining price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course we are interested in what they do, because everyone has to play their part.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your bank consolidation question, I have said this last time around, our view is that for bank mergers, to the extent that they strengthen the banking system and on the basis of the cost-benefit analysis that the shareholders and the stakeholders conduct, which is not to say that we are directly involved other than through the supervision authorities that we apply to the requests and applications that are filed with us, it is for them to decide how to progress those projects.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm not referring to any particular project, as you know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had a Governing Council meeting that was the last of 2024 and which really led us to acknowledge, not yet the victory against inflation, not yet "mission accomplished", but certainly it led us to acknowledge that inflation was really on track, in terms of reaching our 2% target in the medium-term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that gave us a level of confidence to actually decide to cut and to decide the appropriate cut, which is, in our view, 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That proposal was agreed by all members of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There were some discussions, with some proposals to consider possibly 50 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the overall agreement to which everybody rallied was that 25 basis points was actually the right decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think it was predicated on three key elements.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first element is that inflation in our projections has converged towards 2% for six projection exercises in a row.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, you probably have forgotten, as I wish I had, the days when everybody was considering that maybe we would slip into 2026 and we would not reach 2% in 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, as I said, six times in a row, our projections are telling us that we will be at 2% target in the course of 2025 and if anything, it has moved a little bit forward in the course of 2025, but suffices to say that in 2025 we shall be at 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is, you know, clearly reflected in the projections that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the second element is that the fading of past shocks has pushed underlying inflation down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If I look, for instance, at wages, if I look at profits, and you remember the discussion that we had many times about the buffer that profits could exercise to absorb additional labour costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are actually seeing that reality unfolding and the projection for compensation, whether we look at the wage tracker, whether we look at compensation per employee, whether we look at the vacancy ratio, all of that is pointing in the direction of wages gradually, in the course of 2025 reaching a percentage increase that is compatible with our 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in terms of profits, we are also observing the same movement, of growth in profits having declined and being in a position to absorb some of this labour costs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Productivity: we are beginning to see also some a little bit more promising numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So those three components: wages, profit, productivity, also heading in the right direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think the third element that we took into consideration, and that led us to this decision, is that risk to inflation is now two sided, clearly, and that led us to making the decision that we've made, but also removing the reference to restrictiveness that you have mentioned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And by that, I'm also addressing your second question by the same token.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But having said all that, we still have service inflation, which is running high.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if we look in particular at domestic inflation, we are still at 4.2% and service inflation has hedged down a little bit from 4 to 3.9, but it is still resistant, and we would really want to see a change in the composition of inflation to feel totally confident that we are really almost at target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, the risks to inflation are clearly stated in our monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I have said, they are more two sided than they were before, and that's really the analysis that we have about risk to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: No, I don't really think about that, but I would simply observe that that was the case also a few weeks ago, and things change over the course of time, depending on data, depending on assessment of the situation, and this is exactly what we are going to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will continue to not have a pre-committed path downward, but it will be again based on the three criteria that we have flagged and that I have repeated at least three times in this monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we will do, and we are not anticipating X or Y for the next monetary policy decision that that we will take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A lot is going to be clarified, we hope, in the next few months, not in the next few weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If there is one thing that we discussed in the last two days, it's the level of uncertainty that we are facing, and whether it's uncertainty resulting from political situations in some of the member states, whether it's uncertainty resulting from the outcome in terms of policies of the US elections, all of that is largely a question mark, because there is a distance between the words and the action taken.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I would really recommend is that you go back to this publication that we had approximately one year ago, which really discusses the tools and the methods that we all try to apply in order to determine something that cannot be determined with great precision, particularly in advance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And those methods are based on either the inflation, financing, savings, economies, and this is what is done by our staff, very ably.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But have we discussed the neutral rate in the last couple of days?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one about trade - I've given my views very extensively in a recent Financial Times interview, and I continue to think that restrictions on trade, protectionist measures, are not conducive to growth and ultimately have an impact on inflation that is largely uncertain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the short term, it's probably net inflationary, probably, but the overall impact on inflation is uncertain, because it is going to depend on the scope of the measures, on the retaliation that is decided, on the rerouting of trade traffic from other parts of the world, and that is a very complex situation with movable parts, which we will determine if and when they come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, I'm tempted to suggest that you put it to somebody else, because our focus is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is our mandate, and that's the best we can do to help economic actors to make their decisions and to create growth and create value.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Member states in Europe and in the euro area in particular have to comply and respect the fiscal governance framework that they have established for themselves, and that includes a combination of fiscal consolidation and growth-enhancing measures at the same time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if other measures which are expected by the economic operators are delivered, then I don't see any reason why demand would not be stimulated as a result.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The central bank cannot be the jack of all trades.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to do our job, which is to procure price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question about restrictiveness, we are currently restrictive, and it's stated very clearly in the monetary policy statement, in the fourth paragraph, if I recall, where we say very clearly that - I want to give you the exact reference so that we don't make any mistake.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is in the fourth paragraph; we talk about the financing conditions and we say "but they continue to be tight because our monetary policy remains restrictive".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The pace at which it happens, the data that will determine it, the method that we will apply, the meeting by meeting, all of that is quite clear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But, you know, obviously, a lot of ground has been covered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have already cut interest rates four times, a total of 100 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are now, as a result of this decision, today, at 3% for the DFR [Deposit facility rate], and we are in a completely different environment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said earlier, our projections for six times in a row indicate convergence towards 2% in 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, the macroeconomic landscape in which we make our decisions is vastly different from the days when we were at very high inflation, we had a lot of ground to cover, and risk to inflation was one sided.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So as a result of that, it was completely legitimate and natural to remove that reference to being restrictive for long enough, to arrive at target in a timely manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is the other word which, as you may have noticed, has disappeared from our monetary policy statement, timely.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You said, what about if staff projections are on the optimist side.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, I think that they do those projections in with a great sense of integrity and loyalty to the facts, to what is unquestionable, and they apply the best judgment that they can in the work that they do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The element which has changed and which has been reinforced, as you will have noted also in the monetary policy statement, is the downside risk, particularly downside risk to growth, which is more elaborate in the wording of the monetary policy statement, and I think that that's a way to indicate that, given the uncertainty that we have in abundance, it is also the right approach to beef up the risk measurement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You are correct that PEPP is coming to the end of its active life, because we will stop any reinvestment as of the 17th of December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This will be the last reinvestment phase, and it has proven an incredibly efficient tool in order to fight the pandemic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was also an extraordinary tool in that it was associated with flexibility, with no reference to the capital keys, if you remember, which was also quite a breakthrough and quite an exceptional tool for exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the last time we used the flexibility was in July 2023[1].

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think we will continue to have publications, I think on a monthly basis, actually, as opposed to the bi-monthly, which was every other month in the past, just to indicate what is the maturity of those bonds that are coming to maturity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if you're interested in the conditions and the terms and the publication and the modalities, there's a great press release which is out there and which includes all of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, the uncertainty that I referred to, stemming from the policies that could be decided by the next US administration, is not incorporated in the baseline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Except, I think from memory, the extension of the tax reductions that were, in a way, committed by both candidates to the presidency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has a fiscal dimension to it, but the trade dimension is only incorporated indirectly, as you said, through using the yield curve and other market determined elements, which are only part of the many assumptions or data that are taken into consideration by staff when they do their projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, the trade uncertainty is captured in the Risk Assessment section, and we have taken the precaution to add a full sentence at the end of the risk paragraph to relate to the friction in relation to trade.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said to your colleague earlier on, it's a risk and of itself it's not good for growth at large.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It produces uncertain inflation impact in the euro area, at least - I would not pass judgment on what it impacted would have on the on the US - but it's very tentative and it's very uncertain, and you really have to dig into it to appreciate what the impact will be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think you should appreciate that we are on a path, currently, that leads us to reach our 2% target medium-term, and that our monetary policy stance, each and every step of the way, at each meeting will be determined by the data that we that we have, by the projection that is proposed by our staff, and will be based on those three criteria that you know well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, to assume anything in particular at any point in time, I think, is not the right approach, because we are going to continue to be data dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We simply indicate by removing the reference to restrictiveness that we have come a long way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are much closer to a target which we are seeing much more closely now and as a result of that, we want to remain appropriate in our determination of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you want to compare apples and apples, it's "restrictiveness" goes, "appropriate determination" replaces it, because we are getting closer, but we're not done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's face it, when you still have 4.2% domestic inflation and wages of which the growth is slowing down, you have to be very cautious.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I was simply referring, and I'll refer again in response to your question, to the uncertainty that is stemming from the lack of budget submission by several member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you ask me the list, I will be happy to procure it, but there are at least four of them that are either operating on the basis of an old budget from 2024 or 2023 or that simply do not have it yet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, uncertainty about budget, which makes the fiscal projection a little bit complicated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Uncertainty about the actual political evolution, depending on elections, appointments or whatever, in several member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is self-inflicted uncertainty that we have nothing to do with, but which is caused by the current political situations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Things will, again, probably come to resolution, and we will see better the economic consequences of those decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, there are elections coming up in the first quarter of 2025 and hopefully decisions being made much earlier than that for other member states.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, on your latter question, I'm off to Vilnius on Sunday night, and I will give a speech on those issues in particular, on Monday.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, I strongly encourage you to look at that speech.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know you do, so I feel very comfortable referring you to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it really dissects and in great detail this issue of how restrictive and the sort of the direction forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the exchange rate, you gave half the answer by saying that we do not target exchange rate, and I repeat that gladly, and obviously, exchange rate and variations have an impact on inflation, and we are attentive to that, and we will continue to be attentive to that in the next few weeks and months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the European Union was founded by the founding member states, one of which was Germany, and it came on the step of a horrible period of time when member states, currently sitting at the same table were at each other's throat, and that caused the killing and the dying of many, many, many Europeans, and I would very much hope that this history, which is at the root of the construction, stays very clear on the mind of everyone.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, I think this issue of the neutral rate is one that we will probably debate more and further, as we get closer to where it eventually is, and we will probably apply the various tools and methodologies that are suggested by staff in that work that was published about a year ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the conventional wisdom around the table is that it is probably a little higher than where it was before, for multiple reasons, and that we will debate in due course.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's premature to do that at the moment, and the numbers, if I recall, that were flagged by staff in that report, varied from 1.75 to 2.5 and you know, this is the range that is a result of the calculation and the methodologies that they have suggested.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we get there, I'm sure that we will be debating that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, I just want to remind you that by lowering by 25 basis points today our three interest rates, particularly the DFR, we have now cut by 125 basis points relative to the high level where we were.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Secondly, there was no discussion as to whether this decision was appropriate or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was a unanimous decision, so all governors supported the decision that was articulated by Philip Lane this morning of cutting by 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will have seen in the monetary policy statement, clearly stated, that at this point in time we are still in restrictive territory, and we have not had a discussion, because it would be premature at this point in time about the point where we have to stop.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: At which pace, with what sequence, what magnitude will be informed by the data that we will collect in the coming weeks and months, and by the analysis that our staff will conduct.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are lucky that for our next monetary policy meeting in March, we will receive a projection prepared by staff, which will be informed by the economic environment as it unfolds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will have in the meantime two additional readings on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those are data points, granted, but a series of inflation readings are informing those decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the r-star - natural interest rate - you will be pleased to see in eight days, on 7 February, a publication by staff on the revision of the natural interest rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a range, and it's a range that does not give a guideline or a destination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's an indication and in many ways a conceptual principle that is elaborated by a number of models.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is what staff will publish and will comment upon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you will have plenty of it to elaborate upon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can reassure you right away, we did not even utter the two numbers 5, 0.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So 50 basis points was not in the debate at all.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, there was rallying support unanimously by all members of the Governing Council for 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We took the precaution in the monetary policy statement to refer to exports as a potential engine for growth, not the main one, but an additional one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we took the precaution to say that this is provided there is no trade or additional trade friction, something along those lines.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then we talk about exports yet again in the risk section.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we clearly analyse the trade environment, the framework within which trade takes place and the uncertainty associated with it as a potential risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But obviously there are rumours, there are statements, there are assumptions, but we don't have anything that is clear and tangible, and that can be inserted into the analytical work that staff does.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will be looking very carefully at the numbers that come in, at the information that consolidates, and obviously staff will incorporate all that in the work that they are going to do for the March projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not sure that there will be by March enough certainty to actually be very confident.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we will still be plagued by uncertainty in that respect, and there will be more to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as it comes, we will be taking that into account.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Yes, we are confident that headline inflation will reach our target in the course of 2025 and that's the 2% medium-term target, sustainably so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you are right that there is one particular item which is still resisting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you look at goods, when you look at non-energy industrial goods, when you look at subsets of all that, they are definitely moving down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have said in previous press conferences that when goods are going down to 0.5%, we are not going to expect services to be at 2%, because we would be clearly undershooting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But services, and in particular if we look at the various underlying measurements, the domestic one that strips out anything that has to do with exports is still resisting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it has actually gone up a little bit, because on services we were at 3.9% in November, we moved to 4% in December.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not data point-dependent but we look carefully at services, and we know that those services are largely labour-intensive, with or without contract.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We used to have that distinction in the time of COVID.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have less of it at the moment but it is largely labour-intensive and, as a result, wage-sensitive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We try to measure and to understand wages as much as possible because they are so relevant for services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All the indicators that we have at the moment are heading downward and are confirming our confidence that wages in 2025 will be going down.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Whether you look at compensation per employee, which is quite a useful and relevant indicator, whether you look at the wage tracker that we have, whether we look at Indeed, whether we look at the ratios of vacancies to unemployment, all of those indicators are heading in the same direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not celebrating that, but we are taking note and acknowledging the impact that it will have on services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of you will remember that I, and we, have also focused on the distinction between the newcomers and the latecomers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We carried out, for instance, a particular review and tried to get a better and deep understanding of those latecomers that waited for a period of time until they decided to hike prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is clearly the case for insurance companies, for instance, that do not increase their prices on a monthly or quarterly basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Rather, they generally wait until the expiry of a contract and then hike prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be very attentive to how the latecomers that hiked prices in January to March 2024, and whether this process under which they caught up with inflation is going to be duplicated this year again.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We conduct a corporate telephone survey, the result of which you will see tomorrow, because we publish tomorrow.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our understanding from the corporate telephone survey as well, because we asked them how do you see negotiations taking place and when do you expect increases, is that all of this is heading in that direction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It gives us the confidence that wages are on their way down and therefore will impact the price of services, and that we will see a declining movement in the course of 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We say in the monetary policy statement that the next couple of readings will still be resistant, if you will, largely because of base effects on energy prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But from there on, we see this declining path in the course of 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But once again, we don't look at one data point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not just compensation per employee; it's not just negotiated wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a combination of it all because it's a complex matter, depending on Member States, depending on collective bargaining agreements and their renewal; all of that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On this matter that you referred to and whether central bank reserves should or could include bitcoins, I think there is a view around the table of the Governing Council, and most likely the General Council as well, that reserves have to be liquid, that reserves have to be secure, that they have to be safe, that they should not be plagued by the suspicion of money laundering or other criminal activities.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as a result, I am confident that bitcoin will not enter the reserves of any of the central banks of the General Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I had a good conversation with my colleague from the Czech Republic, and I leave it to him to make whatever announcement he wants to make.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I am confident that he is convinced, as we all are, of the necessity to have liquid, secure and safe reserves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are comfortable with one thing, which is to reach our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We want that 2% medium-term sustainable inflation and we will do everything that is required in order to reach that goal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said to another colleague of yours earlier on, under the baseline that we have and with the data that we have received, we can comfortably indicate that we are directionally on this downward slope, the pace and sequence of which will be determined by data and will be decided on a meeting-by-meeting basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And for those who would like to have this solid forward guidance, it would be totally unrealistic to do anything of that nature, simply because we are facing significant and probably rising uncertainty at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we continue to be guided by this sort of threefold analysis, which includes the inflation outlook, the underlying inflation and the transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said earlier on, for the moment there is nothing that we can actually capture in terms of policy determination, in terms of numbers, in terms of scope or in terms of custom line items to understand exactly what is considered.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When that happens, then of course it will enter into our assessment and into the macroeconomic analysis that is produced by our staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's far more complicated than "it's this way or this way" or "it's inflationary or deflationary", depending on whether there is one set of decisions with variable rates around the world, rerouting of trade, whether there is retaliation or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All we know for sure it that is that it will have a global negative impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that's the first thing that we have to keep at the front of our mind.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We went from a very low 2023 to almost double the growth in 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Granted, it is not at potential yet, but it's certainly a recovery.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And given the job market and given the real income increase, we have good reasons to believe that consumption will pick up and will continue to support this recovery process that we expect to continue.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fourth quarter was stagnation of growth, but it's one quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the whole year, it's a different story.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, it's a process that is ongoing and that has been quite something in the course of 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the yield increase, whether you look at the short end or the long end of the curve, yes, it has increased, and it's a global process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has been predominantly in the United States, but it has spilled over across the world, and the euro area has not been spared of those spillovers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's largely attributable to spillovers from the United States - not only - partly because of energy prices, but also for other reasons.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is probably less of a downside risk expectation concerning inflation on the part of the markets, which probably explains partly this yield increase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it doesn't stop our monetary policy from transmitting quite materially.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I look at the decline of interest rates for corporates, the decline of interest rates to households for mortgages, it is really channelling through into the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And when I look, for instance, at the consumer survey and the intention to invest, there is clearly an added demand on the housing sector, for instance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So more to be seen on that front, particularly fuelled by lower interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we get closer to that, we will operate on the basis of a staff research paper, on the basis of the analysis provided by staff, and then that will help us determine how close we are and what our monetary policy stance should be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you're asking me today whether we should go below the neutral rate in order to stimulate the economy, I cannot tell you that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decide meeting by meeting on the basis of data, and we are not pre-committing to any particular pace.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So how could I tell you if and when we arrive at this conceptual principle of the neutral rate and what we will do afterwards?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is going to depend on the data that we receive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know staff are going to work very hard on models, but we will be looking at all sorts of information and intelligence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know the famous reference to looking out of the window.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President von der Leyen honoured us with her presence at dinner on Tuesday.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: She was not the first one to attend what I very immodestly call the "Presidents' dinners".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Paschal Donohoe, the President of the Eurogroup, had also attended one of our dinners, and it was a very rich experience which all Governors felt could be repeated with other guests from around Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I was particularly grateful to the President that she came, despite the crazy agenda that she has.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's face it: this week is particularly heavy for her, and she managed to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It gave us a chance to understand better from her exposé and her remarks what exactly the Commission was going to focus on in terms of competitiveness, in terms of simplification and in terms of keeping the goals but being flexible on the approach.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think that she was herself - but she can speak for herself better than me - pleased with the exchange that we had because it took the form of her explaining the policies considered by the Commission in order to restore competitiveness, in order to incentivise innovation, in order to eliminate some of the red tape and so on and so forth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it was also a chance for her to hear from the Governors what their concerns were and to check facts and policy recommendations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it was in that respect really an interesting dinner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there will be more of those, as I have other guests up my sleeve, which I'm not going to disclose at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me a question about the withdrawal from the NGFS.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The NGFS includes, I think, around 150 members around the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We actually provide the scenarios that are used by the NGFS and most members.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we see huge value in this multilateral comparing of notes, comparing of scenarios, comparing of risks and comparing of policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think, in this day and age, having a multilateral setting where these issues can be debated and analysed is of great value.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in many Member States there has been a complete catch-up with pre-pandemic levels.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What has been different from pre-pandemic levels is the level of savings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has varied over the course of time, but in net terms it has increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we very much hope that if confidence can be restored, particularly in view of a degree of anxiety and uncertainty about European political developments, for instance, consumers and investors will restore their previous pattern of consumption and investment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On Bulgaria, there is a convergence process that is well advanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are marginally involved in the process because we do not pass judgement on anything else than convergence towards inflation, and we look at the fiscal position and the sustainability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But on those fronts and from what I have seen and the discussions that I have had with the Bulgarian authorities, I'm confident that this process is going well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the special convergence report that has been asked* by the Bulgarian authorities will, I suppose - it's not my decision - be determined by the Commission and will proceed so that there can be a review of all the criteria - not just inflation - that Bulgaria has to satisfy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm only giving you a partial answer because the rest can only be given by the Commission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: *While the Bulgarian authorities may submit a request for an ad-hoc convergence assessment, they have not yet done so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In your first question, you very well noted that we have changed the wording of the fourth paragraph of our monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So let me try to explain what it means because it's not just an innocuous little change, it's a change that has a certain meaning.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we had previously was that we would keep our restrictive monetary policy as long as was necessary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that was very much a static assessment of what was needed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are now moving -- by having "our monetary policy is becoming meaningfully less restrictive" -- to a more evolutionary approach.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in other words, we take account of the journey that we have travelled - 150 basis points since we started cutting - and we acknowledge the fact that, as a result, it is becoming meaningfully less restrictive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We add to that, in the same paragraph, the two forces that we are seeing operating on our financing conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I used a comparison a few weeks ago, when we were at the G20 in South Africa, of the Cape of Good Hope, where you have warm water from the Indian Ocean and the cold water from the Atlantic - and this is really where the position is at the moment, where we have the impact of the current monetary policy decisions that we take, and have been taking, which is to cut rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But at the same time, we still have the cold water of the Atlantic, meaning the remaining effects of decisions that we have taken over the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's really where we are at the moment, and that has led us to acknowledge the fact that our monetary policy is becoming meaningfully less restrictive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you asked me the second question, which has to do with the most recent development.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I have to say that we have not been spared recent developments in the last few hours and and days.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the one that you're referring to is the announcement by the European Commission, on the one hand, of this 800 billion comprising the 150 borrowing facility and the 650 space within which member states can borrow for defence purposes, on the one hand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on the other hand, the announcement by the German authorities of a two-fold programme, in a way: one which is the big infrastructure financing of 500 billion over a period of 10 years, and a special measure that relates to defence expenditure that would be decided in the years to come.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So two observations: One is that this is work in progress, and we have to be attentive, vigilant; we have to understand how this is going to work, what the timing will be, what the financing will be, so that we can then draw the conclusions and appreciate how much it will contribute to growth and what impact it would have eventually on inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So for that part of the work, we have not yet of course determined the conclusion, but one thing that around the table of the Governing Council was clear is that on both accounts that would be supportive to European growth at large and would be a boost to the European economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now everything is going to be a factor of the details: where will the purchases take place, what will the timing be, what will the financing be?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And all of those are obviously political decisions that are not within the remit of the central bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are very attentive to what will come out of today's meeting in Brussels and any further development on the German political sceneto appreciate the economic consequences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our assessment - based on the bank lending survey, the numbers that we receive, and the corporate survey that we hold; and comparing the current situation with the last few quarters, and this month versus last month as well - indicate that lending is actually increasing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Lending to households in terms of mortgages is up by 1.3%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now this is not yet bringing us to the strong, solid, robust levels of borrowing by economic actors, but it is definitely on the way up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you have two phenomena: You have interest rates that we see going down, both for corporate and households - not phenomenally yet; we hope that process will continue -- and we are seeing, at the same time, the volume of lending going up as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, on those two accounts, it's one of the elements that we use to determine whether or not - and how much we are or not - still restrictive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we're not really passing judgement, because I think that particular point is not necessarily the most relevant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said, we take into account all the work that has been done and we assess the process that we are in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That gives me a chance to to explain to you where we are.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think there is a particular sentence in the monetary policy statement which refers to the particularly high uncertainty under which we operate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because clearly we have three phenomena that we have debated over the course of this Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some people have used the adjective "phenomenal" uncertainty, and we debated as to whether it was high, high and rising, but suffice to say that it is all over - so we have risks all over, uncertainty all over.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So under those circumstances, our determination is obviously to reach the destination, but we will do sowithoutpre-committing to any particular path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you have seen that sentence in in our monetary policy statement in the past; I think it is even more relevant at the moment, given the level of uncertainty that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you might have some governors who will say "I believe that…".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is their individual views -- I can assure you that the collective view around the table is that we do not pre-commit to a path, and we will be - as ever and probably more so - data-dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if the data indicate to us that, in order to reach the destination, the appropriate monetary policy should be to cut, we shall do so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if, on the other hand, the data indicate that it is not the case, then we shall not cut and we will pause.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's really where we are: not pre-committing, being data-dependent as ever, and deciding on a meeting-by-meeting basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I know some will find it frustrating, but I'm terribly sorry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the circumstances we're facing at the moment, anything more would would not be very responsible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From one day to the other, the situation changes dramatically, and our projection, the measure of underlying inflation, the price of energy, you name it: risks are all over the place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This gives me a chance to tell you how the decision was made, and it was made as a result of substantive discussion all around the table on the state of the economy, on our projections, and on the risks that we are facing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the decision was a consensus, and no one opposed that decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Or you might have ä different source of information, but I was sitting in the room, and no one opposed the decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One governor - specifically Governor Holzmann, for whom I have great respect - abstained.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
