text: On the Russian assets, I think we have made our position quite clear in the sense that those frozen assets, as you know, are being used in order to guarantee 50 billion in loans granted under the ERA by the various members of the G7.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This process is underway, and there are political debates that are vastly broadcasted around the fact that we should maybe move from freezing to seizing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is not for the European Central Bank to debate, but I would certainly submit that the international law basis on which any decision is made will matter as far as other investors are concerned.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it is, I'm sure, an element that will be taken into account by those whose job it is to make those ultimate decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I have tried to explain in the previous answer to the question that the situation that we face at the moment is predicated by this disinflationary process that is on track and confirms broadly the estimates that staff has made over the course of time, and without much error most recently.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And three - and that's probably the most important in relation to the question that you've pointed at me - the landscape that we have at the moment is clouded with uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And more than ever before, it will require that we be vigilant to all governors, all the national central banks, all the economies that are scrutinising the developments and the work that is conducted in each of the national central banks as well as at the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Each of them will continue to scrutinise, and we will all have to be extremely vigilant.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will have to be agile to respond to the data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said, if the data indicates that the most appropriate monetary policy stance is a cut, it will be a cut.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If, on the other hand, the data indicates that the most appropriate decision is not to cut, then it will be a pause.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think I have been as clear as I could be on that one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You asked me a second question which had to do with the markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at all market developments, and we are very attentive to what's happening and we try to understand the reaction function of markets.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And clearly there has been a lot of reaction, particularly in the last 12 hours - 24 hours, including yesterday.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are not going to be changing a policy stance as a result of a market determination of the last 24 hours.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Equally, when we look at the spread, there has been very limited spread variation despite the massive change in the yields.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that gives us an answer concerning the solidity of transmission and the solidity of the sovereigns around Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now on your second question, I know you all want to move faster than light and certainly faster than our brain power collectively can determine.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, those announcement dates from yesterday and honestly in 24 hours, our staff, despite the great work that they do and despite the agility that they demonstrate, particularly in those times, are not in a position to identify how much it will contribute to growth and to European GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Nor are they in a position to identify how it will impact inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Intuitively, all of us around the table, the governors believe that if all that works, and that's a big if, because it needs to be decided, it needs to go through the parliamentary channels, it needs to then be implemented -- if all that works, it will boost growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is more to come, frankly, and I think that we need to be attentive to the coming days and weeks, and then try to anticipate the economic consequences that it would have and how it would be distributed as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first point, the reason I gave earlier quite an elaborate answer is because the situation is not as straightforward, black and white, we go here, we go there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is not what we are facing at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said, repeatedly, we are not pre-committing to any particular rate path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be data dependent more than ever and we will decide meeting by meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One thing that is really clear for me, because you asked me my view, is that we have to reach our destination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And let me just mention one thing, because some of you might be attentive to when we reach that target of 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the projection of staff, you will see it's very early in 2026 and not in late 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Staff have considered that on the basis of the cut-off date that they have, which was quite a few days ago, it was legitimate, on the basis of future prices both on oil and gas, to probably increase the inflation projection by 0.2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at energy prices today, whether it's oil or gas, the impact would be seriously different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that gives us the dimension of uncertainty that we have and the many risks that we have to look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's energy prices, it's trade policy, it's potential retaliation, it's massive investment programmes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are a lot of variables that we have to be attentive to, that we have to be vigilant about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there are certain things that are solid and stable, and actually fall in line with the projections and anticipation of staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look, for instance, at wages, if you look at the labour markets; they are really moving in line with what we had expected.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Those of you who were here last time and at the monetary policy meeting we had before, you will remember I said I am particularly attentive to the price of services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is heading in the direction that we had anticipated, which is comforting given the work that we've been doing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the first one, as I said, it's work in progress.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if the proposal by the Commission for massive borrowing programmes and exemption under the escape clause, and the two proposals identified by future Chancellor Merz, if all that was to work, it would certainly have a fiscal impact, which itself would have an impact on demand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we will have to take that into account and factor that in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I don't see that as related to our monetary policy because our monetary policy, provided under the mandate that we have in Article 127 of the Treaty, is price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we're going to really adhere strictly to our mandate of price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are attentive to transmission, we are attentive to underlying inflation, we are attentive to the inflation outlook and all of that is informed by a large amount of data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if your question is intended to ask whether we would participate in a financing effort, this is not the purpose of the ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a European Investment Bank, there are multiple institutions whose actual purpose it is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Geopolitical risks on the one hand, determination by policy makers on the other hand, it is really something that is in their hands, because it will contribute to boosting the European economy, because hopefully it will be a source of innovation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Typically, investments in defence are a source of innovation and therefore will improve productivity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are very attentive to that and we are hoping that it will have those impacts on the European economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is it a "whatever it takes" moment for the German economy?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is for the political leaders to appropriate that expression.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You are perfectly correct in that we stopped reinvesting quite a while ago now under the APP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We stopped reinvesting gradually over the course of time under the pandemic emergency purchase programme and all TLTRO reimbursements have now been refunded.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But this is a process which has taken place very smoothly, which has been absorbed by markets in a very innocuous way over the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't regard that as a component of our monetary policy, primarily.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It is operating on the back burner, if you will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have anticipated and communicated to markets so that it happens in a very smooth and gradual manner, which is what we are seeing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The main monetary policy instrument that we have used recently and that will be the driving force is interest rate, not QT or otherwise such financing programmes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we do calculate, we do try to work with counterfactuals.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you well know that my colleague Piero Cipollone has tried to assess exactly how much it contributes or not, and you know this is something that he has had calculated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is not our key instrument and it's really not perceived as having a significant impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second point, I tend to share your views.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We started working on the digital euro way back, actually when I started my term 5 1/2 years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I am not claiming parentality on the digital euro because my colleague Benoit Coeuré had already committed a speech on this matter before I arrived, but I certainly carried on with that project.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Subsequently, Fabio Panetta on the Board and then Piero Cipollone, who has replaced Fabio, have taken the lead together with a very good team, which is focused on accelerating the pace and hopefully campaigning enough with all the stakeholders - meaning the European Parliament, European Council, European Commission - so that we can eventually, not put to bed, but put to reality this digital euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The deadline for us is going to be October 2025 and we are getting ready for that deadline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we will not be able to move unless the other parties, the stakeholders as I call them - Commission, Council and Parliament - actually complete the legislative process, without which we will not be able to move.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it is critically important, and for the agnostics or the sceptics, it now seems more relevant and more imperative than ever before, both on the wholesale and on the retail level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My personal view is that you have to negotiate from a position of strength.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So one thing leads to the other and that is the hope that I can formulate because we know that tariffs, and particularly if there is retaliation, are not good at all and are net negative on pretty much all accounts.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Although I think around the table of the Governing Council, we all agreed that it was net negative when it happens and it's even negative before it happens because of the uncertainty that is generated, and the undermined confidence that results from just the threat of those tariff increases, and potential retaliations are putting a brake on investment, on consumption decisions, on employment hiring and all the rest of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I don't think that we can draw a line between the short term and the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The developments that we are seeing at the moment, because of how they will transform the outlook, because of the impact that they will have on our societies as well as our economies, both in terms of growth and in terms of inflation and in terms of employment and in terms of transformation of Europe -- those are significant changes, essential changes that we are witnessing and for which we have to account to help make the best and the most appropriate monetary policy decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can confirm to you that the decision to cut rates by 25 basis points was a unanimous decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Options were debated, but there was no one to argue in favour of a 50-basis-point cut, for instance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So 25 basis points was definitely the rate cut on which all in the room agreed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will happily address the issue of why we actually cut rates, because I think it's a twofold rationale, but looking at today and the tariffs debate that is going on, as well as the tariff impact that is actually happening, we know that it's a negative demand shock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can anticipate that it will have some impact on growth, but the net impact on inflation will only become clearer over the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there are diverging views as to the short-term and the longer-term impact of the development of circumstances, because let's be clear: we have a lot of uncertainty still today, and there will be many decisions and many implementations that will take place over the course of the next few weeks and months that will be decisive to err in one direction or the other.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think the net impact of inflation will become clearer over the course of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your first question, I think, is very relevant because we did remove from the monetary policy statement a sentence that referred to the restrictiveness and, in particular as lately qualified, the "meaningful restrictiveness" or not.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And while that assessment of the restrictiveness was meaningful or made sense to the extent that we were very far away from destination, it is meaningless at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Meaningless because assessing restrictiveness relies heavily on the comparison between the policy rates and the neutral rate, and I think I had the opportunity in front of this esteemed group to give you my views and, I think, the views that are shared by many of us on the Governing Council concerning the neutral rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our view - my view certainly - is that the neutral rate, apart from the measurement issues associated with it, is a concept that works for a shock-free world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And anybody in this room who thinks that we are in a shock-free world would, I suggest, maybe raise their hand or have their head examined.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that assessment of the restrictiveness is not operative anymore.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what we need to do is to determine the appropriate monetary policy stance that will actually take us to our destination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I will not comment on the direction of travel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will comment on the destination that, as you know, is our 2% target in a sustained manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think given the cloud of uncertainty that we have and the multiple decisions that are expected, or lack of it, in the next few weeks and months, our stance will have to be determined by two key attributes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We must be attentive to all the developments, and in particular the development of those new shocks, and be able to make the appropriate determination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Given the speed at which we see developments, the impact they have and the spillovers that we can analyse, it's not going to be a question of rushing to a particular stance, but it will be a question of agility in the face of what we are seeing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that will require a cohesive approach that will be based more than ever on the analysis of data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, as I have said repeatedly, we need to be data-dependent and we need to decide meeting-by-meeting, and we do not have a predetermined path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know this has been annoying for some, because there's nothing like having a bit more certainty and anticipating where it's going.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But more than ever now, we need to be data-dependent, and we need to rely on safe, reliable data.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are going to be particularly attentive to all that at the moment, and we will decide meeting-by-meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What is certain is the destination, and we are determined to take whatever measures will be appropriate and to use whatever instruments will be appropriate to arrive at that destination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We always debate, and we debate on all sides of the decision that we ultimately arrive at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In total candour with you, there were a number of governors who a few weeks ago would have argued in favour of a skip.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: "Uncertainty and the halo of fog around our navigation call for a skip, and then we will decide when we have more data and the projection exercise that is built with the central bank and the national central banks together".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that was on one side of the debate, if you will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there were some who said "Well, it might warrant a 50, but at the end of the day, this is not what I'm arguing for".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I say "debated", but there was not any single argument in favour of arriving at 50 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it was a very strong 25 rally by everybody.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we debate, and we hypothetically try to figure out "what it would have been if" or "what it would imply if".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm sure that you will all do your homework to find out who said what and all the rest of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can assure you that it was a unanimous rally of about 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your first question had to do with whether or not I quantify the current situation relative to the previous assessment of the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will characterise it as follows: we are in the presence of a negative demand shock - no question about that - but this is not in and of itself.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And let me be clear on that: when I say we are in the presence of a negative demand shock, some of the tariffs are already in place, and from an average tariff of less than 3%, we are now in the presence of around 13% in terms of customs duties on goods.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's what we face now, but we also have the prospect of something that could be far more impactful, number one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Number two, there is a series of potential responses on the part of the Commission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know one or two or three of them, depending on the tactic that is adopted.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the most obvious one, which has been commented and actually put on the table, is the zero-for-zero tariff offer that has been made.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, there will likely be - and that really falls in the category of our risk assessment - some redirection and rerouting of goods that will be supplied by markets that are subject to much higher tariffs, even as we speak now, and possibly other destinations from which those goods could be rerouted to Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And third, there are other policies that are also in play and being discussed, including in particular in Germany.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So fiscal policies that would see significant investments and significant fiscal impulse that would be given.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you have a combination of either policies or threats of policies of different categories that will obviously have an impact on the situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Added to which, and you alluded to it, and we actually refer to it in the risk statement, there is the appreciation of the euro, which we mentioned specifically in the Monetary Policy Statement, and there has been a significant decline in the price of commodities and particularly the price of energy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So you have to combine all that and anticipate that there will be development, which will lead me to not actually give you a specific quantification of the impact.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Suffice to say that there will be a negative impact on growth, possibly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And, as I said, the impact on inflation and the net impact on inflation is less than clear at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is so much ongoing, some of which will probably settle a bit by our June meeting, but given that the 90 days will only elapse around 9 July and 14 July - Bastille Day - we will know more on that front and on the fiscal front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Clearly, the incoming of new governments in various countries, including in Germany, will also take us to more clarification on exactly where the situation will evolve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But, as I said earlier, there is no better time to be data-dependent.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is no better time to rely on very strong and solid analysis by all our staff, and I'm glad that the June projections are going to be a combined exercise of the ECB and the national central banks, who will be confronting their respective viewpoints and analyses to arrive at something that will be really consolidated around our three key analytical underpinnings, which are the inflation outlook, underlying inflation and transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just say very squarely that I have a lot of respect for my esteemed colleague and friend, Jay Powell.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that that relationship is decisive in order to have a solid financial infrastructure to make sure that there is financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have demonstrated in the past that we could actually operate on that basis of consultation and understanding of the financial risk, and we will continue doing so in an undeterred and unchanged manner, I'm sure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is a nice African saying which goes "you never swim twice in the same water".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think for economic players, investors, consumers, employers, employees and all categories, confidence, predictability and a reasonable level of certainty are important factors for them to make decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In the mandate that we have of procuring and maintaining price stability, we will certainly make sure that we respect those principles.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Predictability, confidence, all based on access to the data, the right data, the safe data, and in as much transparency as is possible with all of you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the issue of stablecoins, you know that we have regulation in place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's currently under review and consultation for possible improvements, and I'm delighted that this is the case because we are facing a constant evolution of those digital payments, of those cross-border payments, of those stablecoins - which I would put in a very separate category within cryptoassets - so the stablecoins are a different animal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And clearly having a good, solid regulation that constitutes the framework within which they can operate is paramount and has been understood by the European Union, by the Commission, by various authorities in charge of those matters, and will be reviewed in order to make sure that it procures a safe harbour for those initiatives.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But let me take the opportunity here to acknowledge that, for the first time in our Monetary Policy Statement, we refer to the digital euro, and that should be a clear signal that not only do we stand ready and do the hard work that is incumbent upon us, but it also acknowledges the fact that other European authorities are hopefully going to accelerate the pace at which we can deliver.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We did not discuss the matter of stimulation and we certainly rallied around the statement that is in the monetary policy overall statement that we will take the appropriate monetary policy stance and decisions in order to make sure that we deliver on our commitment to reach our medium-term target of 2% in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So obviously the degree of appropriateness will be measured and exercised through these two principles - readiness and agility - in the face of the uncertainty and the multiple decision points, which are external factors, and which for some of them constitute new shocks that are facing the European economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your latter point concerning the independence, you know that within the euro area and within Europe, it is particularly important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's actually one of the criteria used in the convergence assessment that applicant new members have to go through.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if a new member who applies to join the euro area does not evidence the independence of their central bank, both in its legislative foundation and in its operations, that's an obstacle to joining the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, for us here, independence of central banks is fundamental.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first point, we will determine our monetary policy stance on the basis of what is appropriate in order to reach our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will do that demonstrating effectiveness and agility: analysing the nature of the shock, the kind of responses that it requires, and doing so in a prompt manner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at the paragraph I read for you earlier on, the downside risks are clearly identified in relation to growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will be a factor of how decisions are made, which decisions are made, what trade measures will be taken, what countermeasures will be adopted, whether there is an escalation as a result.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I addressed earlier: What kind of rerouting will we be seeing?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What measures will be taken to prevent this massive rerouting if necessary?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What national and European fiscal decisions will be made over what period of time?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When you inject €800 billion in the economy, or near €1 trillion, it's not a small feat.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a serious impulse and it has a serious effect, certainly on growth, and to be seen on inflation, but this will be for later analysis when we have more information and more data on these particular matters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not going to characterise what's happening at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that the commentators, the top-notch economists who specialise in trade matters, all agree that it will have downside consequences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The consequences will differ depending on which part of the world you stand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that really justifies the fact that monetary policy decisions are not going to be the same the world over.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I cannot tell you whether we are at the peak of uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Proposals have been made, at least on one side, but all of that could change.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's a degree of unpredictability, which adds to the uncertainty, and if you add to that the incredulity that we've had, certainly in the first phase where it was difficult to assess and understand, because it was such a break from previous conventional wisdom as to how trade relationships are organised, as was discussed by the WTO yesterday, that I don't know whether we are at the peak.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I know for a fact is that the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem, in our monetary policy decisions, we have to stand ready for the unpredictable, which is why I think it makes a lot of sense to be ready, to be agile, to work on reliable data, and to operate on a meeting-by-meeting basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Think about the number of changes that have taken place in the last six weeks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There could be more changes in the next six weeks, but that's in the nature of our job: to stay focused on our mandate, to analyse what is coming at us, and to draw conclusions in order to make the appropriate monetary policy decision that will take us to target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's what we will do, and we're not going to move away from that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we do mention, in the risk assessment in the second paragraph, we say "increasing global trade disruptions are adding more uncertainty to the outlook for euro area inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Falling global energy prices", that's one, "and an appreciation of the euro could put downward pressure on inflation".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we do mention it because of the occurrence, the magnitude, and we try to account for it in the assessment that we make for our monetary policy decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a methodology to take into account developments, and the level of scrutiny is high, whether it is completely legislated or so certain in its outcome that we can actually take it into our exercise and the analysis that we do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we are not too sure, we constantly do some scenario analysis to assess and estimate what the impact would be of such or such other decisions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that exercise will be intense in the next few weeks and will give rise to some very serious results at our June projection meeting, as I said, thanks to the consolidated exercise between NCBs and ECB.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But currently, if you ask me about the countermeasures, they are not included in the baseline that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Obviously, we look at the entire trade balance, we look at goods, we look at services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We cannot look only at goods or only at services, so I do pay attention to services, but I look at goods as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The two are intrinsically the outcome of the economy and the trade movements that we have with other parts of the world, so I look at both.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think each central bank in the world does its job in good conscience on the basis of its mandate and on the basis of the currency that it is in charge of and the territory in which it has competence.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that leads us to look at the euro area not in isolated form because we are open to the rest of the world and more open than many other economies, including the United States for that matter, but we look at that, we are focused on the euro and we are focused on our price stability mandate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The other central banks in the world have a different mandate, they have a dual mandate for some of them, and clearly their macroeconomic situation is different and they will be on the receiving end of a different nature of shocks than the shocks that we will be receiving.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wanted to mention something that nobody asked me about.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I want to call your attention to one particular segment of our monetary policy statement that you will see, which we have debated and which actually is a clear message from us, the central bank, to the other European institutions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is the paragraph which sometimes is considered as business as usual.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This time around, we do specifically mention, with a special timetable associated with it and the swift implementation that we expect, that there are three categories of structural efforts on the part of Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is the Competitiveness Compass, which is a derivative of the Draghi report.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Number two is the savings and investments union, which I've repeatedly called the capital markets union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think we've taken the view that this is a moment for Europe to not only be solid on its monetary policy, and not just for us to deliver on price stability, but for the Europeans altogether and the European institutions to actually focus on what opportunities there are, what changes need to take place, and at which accelerated pace this should happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's a strong message from us to colleagues, friends, and other decision-makers in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'll start with the first question, which is really the order of business and the main topic today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And with today's cut, at the current level of interest rates, we believe that we are in a good position to navigate the uncertain conditions that will be coming up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can also tell you that it was an almost unanimous decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was one Governing Council member who did not support the decision, but other than that it was virtually unanimous.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would call it either very broad consensus or virtually unanimous support for the decision to cut by 25 basis points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously we analysed the situation in the light of the three criteria that you know well because they are repeated several times in the monetary policy statement and have not varied for a number of meetings now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But under those three criteria, really the situation points towards inflation settling at our 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We can come back to the path, but this is what we are seeing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that is what has predicated the cut that we made today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you asked me about my future, which is far less important than the future of the economy and the future of our monetary policy, rest assured.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I can very firmly tell you that I have always been and I'm fully determined to deliver on my mission and I'm determined to complete my term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I regret to tell you that you're not about to see the back of me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The only year we have slightly revised is 2026 and by -0.1 percentage points.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we have confirmed our projected growth rate as per our projection of last March at 0.9% for 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that was certainly reinforced by the number we had for the first quarter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mentioned the 0.3 first quarter number, which was, as you know, revised from an initial 0.4.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would not exclude that there be further revision of that number on the upside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's improved consumption, it's improved investment, but more importantly it's the build-up of inventory or anticipated purchases and therefore sales in fear and anticipation of the tariffs.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that first quarter is of course very particular and is clearly giving momentum to the growth that we are seeing and anticipating for 2025.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But again, I would not exclude that that number of 0.3 be revised upward given the volume that we are seeing being traded out of some countries in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are not revising 2027 and we are very marginally revising 2026 because there is a carryover - number one - and because we believe that the impact of tariffs, if and when they materialise, on the export that we have towards the United States, which I remind you is only 17% of our total exports outside from the euro area and European countries, will impact predominantly 2026 and will then be significantly offset by the expected investment in both military equipment and construction or infrastructure, if you will, particularly out of some countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So our assessment is that that will have a bearing on 2027 predominantly - some on 2026, but predominantly on 2027.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, I think we are well-positioned after that 25-basis-point rate cut, and with the rate path as it is, we are in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do not know what the outcome of the negotiations will be between the various partners.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We don't know the level of retaliation that might be decided, which incidentally is not included in our baseline, as you will see published later on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as a result, we have to be prepared and we will be assessing, meeting-by-meeting, data as they come in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said again, we are well-positioned at the moment and the path of inflation that we see certainly returns to 2% in 2027.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we start from a place where we have inflation for 2025 at 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It goes below target in 2026 for reasons that have predominantly to do with the price of energy and the value of the euro because, as you know, it's based on our current assumption of those prices now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are in a good position on the basis of the current rate path and with the 25-basis-point cut that we decided, so that we can face the uncertainties that are coming our way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as you have heard in the monetary policy statement, we will decide meeting-by -meeting on the basis of data and we will assess, as and when data come in, whether or not that position is secure in order to deliver on our 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I'm saying today is that we are in that good position.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have not discussed this wonderful concept of the neutral rate on the occasion of this meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think that we all know well that as we are getting closer to that zone, we need to be particularly attentive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We need to be confident in our resolve to deliver with the appropriate monetary policy our medium-term 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have not discussed that neutral rate, and I alluded to that at our last press conference.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The neutral rate is predicated on the absence of shock: great equilibrium, no shock.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wish there was no shock, but we have just nearly concluded a cycle of monetary policy that dealt with a series of shocks - pandemic, war in Ukraine, energy crisis - and I think we have done that decently well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And those elements that I told you repeatedly over the few last press conferences were of concern to us, namely inflation on services, evolution of wages, evolution of profit, are coming really in line with what our projections were in order to deliver on our 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You will read in the monetary policy statement: I think we quote uncertainty nine or ten times.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is plenty of that, and clearly we are trying to improve our game as much as we can in order to anticipate, measure and calibrate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's the reason you will be not only receiving our projection exercise, but also the scenarios which encapsulate some of the channels of transmission to growth and inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In particular, I would mention one that we discussed quite extensively during the Governing Council, which is the disruption of the supply chain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, I would like to congratulate Bulgaria, the Bulgarian people and welcome them.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is not yet a completed decision-making process because, as you know, while the Commission and we have validated under the convergence report that the criteria are met, the European Council still has to approve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I don't want to prejudge what the European Council will decide, but there is a very strong likelihood that Bulgaria will become our 21st member around the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will be looking forward to the Bulgarian contributions, both in terms of intellectual input, economic analysis, monetary policy determination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as soon as the decision is final with the European Council, as you probably know, we will welcome for several meetings before 1 January the Bulgarian representative at the table of the Governing Council in order to facilitate and do the onboarding properly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And so that we can also get to know a new colleague.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I also hope that the Bulgarian people will value the solidity of the euro area and the solidity of the currency that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Some of you have probably noticed that the supportive judgement of the Europeans has gone up and is now at 83% in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So 83% of Europeans, based on the survey that is done on a regular basis, actually value and appreciate the euro as their currency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I hope we can together do everything we can so that Bulgarians can also appreciate the value and the shield impact that the euro constitute for new members.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Victory laps are always nice, but there is always another battle.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, I think that with today's cut and the current level of interest rates, number one, I think we are getting to the end of a monetary policy cycle that was responding to compounded shocks, including COVID, the illegitimate war in Ukraine and the energy crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But of course we are now into a different time with different players, with different partners, with different policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will continue to analyse and assess and measure and make sure that we deliver on our 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is, in a way, the thing that is certain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You should not doubt for a second our determination to deliver with the appropriate monetary policy the 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What we're seeing currently with this 2% projected inflation for 2025, 2% for 2027 and 1.6% in 2026, caused predominantly with our current assumption on the price of energy and the value of the euro, is that we have a good path to this target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we'll make sure that it will be close navigation around our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's where we have to be and want to be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, the reason I use the direction of travel concept was when we were really at a distance from our medium-term 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to talk about the direction of travel when we have our medium-term 2% target in sight - sustainably so - and when underlying inflation is not budging.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For those in doubt, headline inflation in 2026 is clearly oil and gas and the value of the euro, which we assess at the time when we cut off the period when the staff does its assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Underlying inflation or core inflation is hardly moving and it's at around our target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there's no point talking about the direction of travel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What I'm saying is that we will be determined to deliver that 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will be looking at all data that come in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will constantly assess and reassess how we are delivering on this 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As to your second question, I will repeat what I have said.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I have always been driven by my mandate and I'm determined to complete my term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, while I appreciate that some of you would like to hear me talk about pause, hold or whatever, I just can repeat myself that we are currently well-positioned to navigate the uncertainties of the next months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think the risk of inconsistency of QT associated with interest rate policy, which is our main tool, is probably less critical in the event - which I'm not confirming here now - of a pause than it is in the event of a cut.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I don't see that, but neither do I say anything about future decisions, which would only be predicated on major shocks that we are not seeing at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the role of the euro, I highly regard the speech that was given by my colleague and friend, Governor Panetta.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I happen to be very much on the same page as he is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I gave a speech in Berlin about ten days ago now at the Hertie School of the Jacques Delors Institute, in which I tried to identify the key pillars that would need to be consolidated and further developed if the euro was to play a critical role as an international reserve currency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And my conclusion is that there is an opportunity, which is opening now, to strengthen the role of the euro as an international currency as to take it further towards possibly the international reserve currency of choice.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But my conclusion is that it is not going to be granted to us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It should not be taken as a given, and it will require in particular that Member States, the Commission and the European Council make very substantive decisions that will have to do with consolidating the economic and geopolitical role of Europe, that will simplify, streamline and develop the role of the capital markets union in particular - the savings and investments union, if you will, but particularly the capital markets union.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we'll have to continue to sustain the effort of making Europe a place where the rule of law is respected and where a contract is a contract so that there is certainty on the part of the investors and of the economic actors that Europe is actually a reliable place of business.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think it's not a question that can be responded to with yes or no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a fairly thorough and deep debate that we have touched on during the Governing Council meeting in the last two days, where we strongly feel that we have done our part and will continue to do our part.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we also strongly advocate in the monetary policy statement the role that authorities have to play if we want to develop in that direction, which is a window of opportunity now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I hope you don't mind if I ask my colleague, Vice-President and friend Luis de Guindos to address the latter part.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I will turn the floor over to you and I'll come back to you afterwards.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Vice-President: As you have said, we produced our report and we released our report.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And now the antitrust authorities in Spain have given their opinion and the remedies that they have imposed for the deal.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: According to Spanish law, the government has the possibility to analyse the conditions imposed and, according to the general interest, to modify these conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We should wait until we have a definitive opinion from the Spanish government.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Otherwise what we would be making is a sort of speculation, which I think doesn't make much sense in this moment of time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: President: And on your first question, I just want to remind you that our forecast is 2% inflation in 2025, 1.6% in 2026 and 2% in 2027.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And our core inflation is even more stable than that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, you think 1.6% in 2026, but that's exactly part of the assessment that has been produced by staff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if you look at what other institutions have forecasted, it's at the very low end of the range for 2027.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's also because they take into account the most recent data available, not including the first quarter, because I think the first quarter will give us some surprises.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But if you compare headline inflation and core inflation, you can see exactly where the difference lies, and that is energy prices and the value of the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also have inflation - both headline and core - returning to 2%, or 1.9% for core in 2027, and the 25-basis-point cut of today is deliberately taking care of that inflation path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are confident of the analysis of our staff on that basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as I said, we will do what is necessary in order to make sure that that inflation stays at our 2% target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When I look around and reflect on the work that we have done in the last six years, we have a very solid labour market, where participation has - including most recently - increased, where we have been at a rock bottom unemployment rate ever since the euro was created and where the fears of recession that abounded only about a year ago have not materialised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are forecasting 0.9, 1.1, 1.3 percentage points with very limited revision to growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The output gap closes at the end of our projection horizon.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Wages have increased over the course of those years, particularly with a view to catching up with the lost purchasing power that citizens had suffered as a result of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is now decelerating, just in line and in time, I would say, to deliver on our 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The monetary policy is transmitting quite smoothly to the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It could be further and higher up, but credit is up.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I would say that the economy is responding quite well to our monetary policy and is delivering on that front.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would add, as I did in response to one of your colleagues earlier, that more needs to be done.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what we have seen - the Vice-President and I - when participating in the finance ministers meetings in Brussels, whether it's Ecofin or Eurogroup or on the occasion of Paschal Donohoe, the President of the Eurogroup, when he had dinner with us a couple of nights ago, is that we perceive a serious momentum to improve, to change, to simplify, to streamline and to encourage and welcome capital into Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The reverse Yankee bonds significant increase that we have seen in the last few weeks is a clear indication that there is trust in our system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The capital flow that we are seeing as well, whether it is European investment returning to Europe or a bit of non-European investment coming to Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: All that is an indication that at least market forces and investors - those who move real money around - actually see value and have confidence in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, I'm not sure what you meant by higher for longer, because I think I have gone out of my way to say that we are in a good place and we are well-positioned now and that we will be assessing, meeting-by-meeting on the basis of data, what, if anything, needs to be done in terms of appropriate monetary policy to return us to the 2% medium-term target.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that really brings together the discussions that we've had over the last two days.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me just tell you that in relation to exchange rates, we do not target any exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, we monitor exchange rates indeed because exchange rates matter for our inflation forecast.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm here quoting my dear friend and colleague, the Vice-President, who said recently, "we take into account exchange rates to forecast inflation."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are exactly on the same page in terms of our message regarding exchange rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question had to do with conjecture as to what the outcome will be of ongoing trade negotiations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I know that there was a newspaper yesterday that sort of hinted that we were at a particular closure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was a closing in, not a closure, and required very careful reading.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are operating on the basis of the work that we do to forecast and to anticipate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a baseline on which we are basing our decision of today, which is our June baseline, which holds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That baseline is generally confirmed by all the recent data that we have received.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We decide meeting-by-meeting, but we take news one day at a time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And for the moment we are relying on our baseline and relying on the scenario that we have done back in June, which we have published, which you all have had a chance to look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But one thing I will add to that is that the sooner this trade uncertainty is resolved - I think we use the word "resolved swiftly" - so the sooner it is resolved, the less uncertainty we will have to deal with, and that would be welcomed by any economic actors, including ourselves.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had a strategy review that we concluded in 2021.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had committed to review that strategy on the basis of new economic developments and certainly in view of the process through which we had gone, namely facing those incredible shocks and going full cycle in many ways.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We did that, and as a result of that strategy assessment, it was determined that we had to amplify, enhance and probably give a slightly higher focus to risk assessment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously scenarios, sensitivity analysis are part of that exercise that is conducted on a regular basis - that is published occasionally but conducted on a regular basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is certainly very opportune that this focus on enhanced risk assessment is agreed at a time when we have a higher level of uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have the usual risk assessment section in our monetary policy statement, which focuses on growth and inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we thought it was appropriate, given the enhanced focus that we want to give to the measurement of risk and the assessment of risk, to actually have that element included in the first part of our monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm going to repeat myself: we are in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are in a good place because inflation is at 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And our target is the medium-term inflation, which is at 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'm saying that we are in a good place because our projections point to inflation stabilising at target in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As you will remember, I have often mentioned the importance of wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Wages are heading in the right direction and are showing this downward trend that we were expecting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The unit profit is continuing to buffer in a little bit of that wage increase, which is the natural result of an element of catching up and adjusting to the development of the economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we have seen, and I'm coming now to the specific point of your question, we have seen growth developing in a relatively favourable way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, if you look at the first quarter in particular - we will have the second quarter in a week's time - but if we look at the numbers we have, the first quarter was a surprising 0.6%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course, because we like to look under the hood, 0.6% is partly attributable to Ireland.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And then if you look at what was actually driving this growth increase, it's partly frontloading because economic operators anticipated the rising of tariffs and decided to frontload.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's also increased consumption and increased investment and not only attributable to Ireland, which is often an outlier for all sorts of intellectual property reasons and what have you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So growth is developing mostly in line with, if not a little better than, our expectations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said last time around, we are now confident that the inflationary shock of the past few years is now behind us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And our job now is to look at what's coming and to try to, first of all, wait because there are a lot of elements that will pan out in the next few months and see what impact it will have on our economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Concerning the risk of undershooting, I just want to remind you and colleagues that we are at 2% according to the latest reading, but more importantly because that's what we have to look at.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is actually a forecast of undershooting in 2026 for all sorts of base effects, reasons and consequences that we are forecasting today.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But, as has been mentioned by some of my colleagues in their various speeches, we are not going to be moved away by some minor deviation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are looking at the medium-term targets that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will proceed on the basis of those three elements to determine our monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is the result of our strategic assessment, but it's also the approach that we are taking inside the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, you will always find two or three governors who are very concerned about undershooting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what I say to you is that undershooting is actually in our projections, in the staff June projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what matters is our medium-term target because this is the objective that we have reaffirmed in our strategy and which is definitely 2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And when I look at inflation expectations, it is strongly anchored around 2% in the short term but also in the longer term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And, as you know, we have this rosy scenario where everything is at zero and it's perfectly symmetric and reciprocated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have the baseline, which is at 10%[tariff rate], which is the current rate that the economy is taking in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we have the 20%, which is the severe scenario.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think that as we observe the interesting negotiations and what leaks out in various forms, retaliation is optional, doesn't seem to be a definite element.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the ultimate net result in terms of inflationary forces or disinflationary forces cannot be determined at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because it's a very complicated set of factors that we will have to analyse and take into account to determine what the impact will be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have some sectoral rates as well that apply to either the automotive industry or the steel and aluminium industry.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And to add to that complexity, you also have the indirect impact on our economy of tariffs that are decided in relation to other countries that will induce some redirecting or rerouting, which itself will have an impact on our economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment, we assume that this impact will be disinflationary and staff have worked on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But equally - and this is very difficult to assess for the moment - there will probably be some bottleneck issues as a result of the trade disruption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will probably be, just as there will be some rerouting and redirecting, there will be some supply chain significant changes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that will also have an impact on inflation - more likely to be inflationary than disinflationary.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's not just trade one way and retaliation in response, but it's also the rerouting, the redirecting, the supply chain disruption and the bottlenecks that will all come together to impact prices.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, the next question you have to ask yourself as well - and that we are asking ourselves and will be asking - is: is that going to be a level effect?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Is that going to be an ongoing consequence of a new paradigm?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are going to monitor, factor in and model as much as we can.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But at this point in time, a conclusion is not, in my view, definite as to which of those forces will prevail.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it's a good expression that my colleague and friend and esteemed central banker has used to refer to being on hold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We ourselves at the ECB have left our rates unchanged, and you could argue that we are on hold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in this wait-and-watch situation, and any monetary policy decision will for the future be decided on the basis of data, will be decided meeting-by-meeting, is not predetermined by any particular path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think that the jury is out as to how quickly the uncertainty will be cleared under present circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A large part of that uncertainty is itself caused by trade and tariffs, as well as non-tariff barriers by the way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The uncertainty in and of itself is also playing a role in relation to the level of risk that we see.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's trade-related, caused by tariffs and non-tariff fears or expectations - depending on how you look at it - and it's the overall uncertainty about the outcome, which obviously induces different behaviour on the part of consumers and investors.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the GENIUS Act, the first point I would make is that having a legal framework helps understand what the risks, benefits and prospects are for these instruments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, I think that it's a little bit early in the process to really have a clear and good understanding of what the consequences will be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Third, we have to be focused on what we do here at home in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have to make sure that we are strong in terms of currency issuance and protection.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are the curator of the euro and we are ultimately focused on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Of course, we are mindful of what's happening elsewhere and what the dangers could be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we have to make sure that at home we take all the necessary measures to protect and preserve our currency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in that respect, we are very decisively focused on developing the digital euro and doing everything that we can to be on time and prepared to make this digital form of sovereign money available in the shortest possible time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Which doesn't mean that it's going to be tomorrow, rest assured.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Cash will always be there, and banks will be part of the game and will be an intermediary in the process.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But our duty is to make sure that as Europeans' preferences evolve over the course of time, the digital euro is a possible reality.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Each and every Executive Board member and each and every governor has their preference and their views.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think it is the beauty of this institution to allow for diversity of viewpoints and allow for the expression of those viewpoints.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: My job as President of the ECB is to harness all the views of the Governing Council members and, on the basis of our staff work, projections and proposals, to elicit as large a majority view as is possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So what I can tell you as far as today is concerned is that the decision to keep interest rates unchanged was a unanimous decision.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I can also tell you that the risk assessment, which is nicely spelt out in the monetary policy statement, was broadly shared by members of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As to the future path, I think it's also widely shared by members of the Governing Council that we have to work on the basis of the data as they come in, that we have to decide meeting-by-meeting and that to predetermine a path or preset the level or the material and significant development that would trigger one thing or the other is prospective and not part of the job that I do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If trade tensions are resolved in short order, it will clear some of the uncertainty that we have weighing on the decision-making of consumers, investors and enterprises.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it will of course help us as well anticipate and model what the outcome of those tariffs will be.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I suppose you're talking about liquidity and the volume of liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, there is still plenty of liquidity in the system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The volume has reduced over the course of time and it has reduced as a result of the reimbursement of TLTRO, which is now completed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has reduced as a result of the discontinuation of reinvestment under the APP first, and under the PEPP second.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But despite that and the fact that our balance sheet reduces on a monthly basis regularly and predictably, the volume of liquidity in the system is still north of €2 trillion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to talk about limited liquidity in the system, I think, is not the appropriate characterisation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Added to which, there is probably more liquidity in the system than we had anticipated because there has been less demand for banknotes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there are other technical reasons caused by the fact that governments eventually moved their own reserves away from the central bank to put them to better use somewhere else, which has, as a result, increased the volume of liquidity out there.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The latter question I'm not going to address actually because you are jumping ahead.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have a review of the operational framework that will come in due course in 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let us just see how things work, draw conclusions from that and then we shall see when we reassess in due course and in due time, that is in 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, I have a pretty simple understanding of what the digital euro is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And for me this is the digital expression of cash.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I like cash, whether it takes the form of coins or banknotes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is cash and this is central bank money, if you will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as technologies evolve over the course of time and as the preference for payment evolves as a result, we need to respond to the demand of our European compatriots.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I see the digital euro as the digital expression of cash.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can argue at the margin that in terms of absolute privacy, we're not exactly on the same page.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You could argue that the cost of cash is higher.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So to argue that digital cash is a nuclear bomb, I think, is a little bit over the top.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We're not holding nuclear bombs in our pockets, as far as I know.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Markets do what they have to do, and we do what we have to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are well-positioned to deal with turbulent waters and to deal with the risks that will develop over the course of the next few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm here referring particularly but not only to the risks related to tariffs, but you can include geopolitical risks as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You can include a vast uncertainty which might partly clear as a result of whatever tariff certainty we receive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have essentially closed that disinflationary cycle that we battled over the last months and which has led us to move from 400 basis points to 200 basis points with eight cuts in a matter of nine meetings.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are in a good place now to hold and to watch how these risks develop over the course of the next few months.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And later on, we will reassess at each monetary policy meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do projections and we publish them on a quarterly basis, but we do that on a regular basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will continue to do that in September, in October, in December and on and on.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's on the basis of that work that the Governing Council will decide what is the appropriate monetary policy stance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I cannot tell you much more than that because it's been repeated twice in the Monetary Policy Statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've tried to avoid repeating it too much, but our collective determination is (1) keep inflation at our 2% medium-term target, (2) operate on a meeting-by-meeting basis, and (3) be data-dependent - and there will be plenty of that in the coming months - and not have any kind of predetermined rate path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I understand that markets would like to have more anticipation of that possible rate path.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let me say this: the disinflationary process is over, and I'm referring here to the causes for inflation that we have experienced in the last few quarters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, in anticipation of the possible questions, are we still in a good place?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The domestic economy is showing resilience, the labour market is solid, and risks are more balanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But when I say that we are and continue to be in a good place, am I saying that we are on a predetermined path?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because in the same breath of air, I say that we decide meeting-by-meeting, that we are data-dependent and that we will decide accordingly in order to make sure that we stay in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I hope I'm making myself clear in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We continue to be in a good place, but we are not on a predetermined path and we will take stock, meeting-by-meeting, to look at all the data - the outlook, the projections - that we receive in order to make sure that we stay in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I never want to overstretch the general agreement in the room, but we had a unanimous decision by the Governing Council today to leave all three interest rates unchanged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We discussed the risks, but I think that what I have just formulated for you is something that was agreed unanimously around the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, which deals with the risks to inflation, we don't actually narrow down the risks to inflation exclusively.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's where we say in our statement that risks are more balanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we don't nail down a risk diagnosis on inflation in isolation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'd be happy to come back to why we are more balanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have to go back to where we were back in June, where we do the assessment of risk on the basis of the projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if you walk back to June, we had a highly uncertain situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was post-April 9, sure, but it was pre-July and certainly pre-August 21 when a deal was agreed and documented, however it was documented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And as a result of that, I think that two things have clearly moved out of our radar screen when it comes to downside risks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That was factored into our June projection and that was considered as one of the risks in a trade war, as we had it at the time in terms of fear.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second thing is the uncertainty, what we call trade uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That has clearly diminished, and we can see that in the instruments that we use to measure uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It has not gone back yet to where it was pre-COVID.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not the normal level, and maybe there will not be a normal level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's something that we really have to consider and take into account for future determination.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It could well be that there was a reset in uncertainty around the world because of the trade situation and because of the geopolitical environment in which we operate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the trade uncertainty has abated since June, when we had our last projection.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's really what is at the root of this more balanced indication.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not to say that we are short of challenges.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be new challenges, which really anchor our determination to work meeting-by-meeting and to assess each and every time what the situation is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are post our new strategy, and you will remember that one of the innovations in our new strategy is that we not only look at the baseline but we look at and discuss the risks around the baseline on the basis of work that is sometimes published, sometimes not necessarily published.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are certain things that we keep to ourselves, yes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And sometimes we do publish the scenarios, for instance, sometimes we don't because we don't think it's absolutely relevant or helpful, but at least it informs our judgement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, I'm not going to comment on individual countries.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I avoid that because we are the European Central Bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are not narrowing our judgement on a particular country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I would say that I'm confident that the policymakers, that those who make decisions, will take it to heart in that period of uncertainty to reduce uncertainty as much as possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is also a set of rules - that is the fiscal governance, the fiscal framework, the internal rules of the European countries - and the Member States have to adhere to it and to deliver against it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm sure that all governments, wherever located, will want to operate on the basis of that fiscal framework.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
