text: Let's go to the inflation projections, if you will, because that's your first question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For 2025 and 2026, we have increased by 0.1 percentage point our projection.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So for 2025, our projection is now 2.1%, and we've increased it by 0.1 percentage point.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And, first of all, it's a big 1.9%, I hasten to add.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's really on account of the exchange rate impact with the lag effect that it usually has, and this is factored into our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have indicated very clearly in our strategy that minimal deviations - if they remain minimal and not long-lasting - will not necessarily justify any particular movement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the second question that you asked me, and this relates to France I suppose, I'm going to tell you the same thing.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But suffice to say that we always monitor market developments, and euro area sovereign bond markets are orderly and are functioning smoothly with good liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our focus is, as you know, price stability, but we need financial stability for that, and it requires a well-functioning monetary policy transmission mechanism.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we believe that we have all the necessary tools, if needed, should that transmission not prove efficient throughout the entire euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, in the situation where we are of this disinflationary process and having increased rates from minus 50 basis points to 400 basis points, the most efficient and primary tool that we use for monetary policy stance is the interest rates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we have cut interest rates by 200 basis points over the last 12 months or so.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The fact that we are not reinvesting and that we are letting our portfolio on a run-off mode is proceeding smoothly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was anticipated, it was predictable, and I think that everyone who cares about those issues knows exactly how this proceeds and what very limited impact it has.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That's a resolution that that we have made, that we have explained very clearly to markets and it is proceeding accordingly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, we are always monitoring financial market developments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said as well, euro area sovereign bond markets are orderly and are functioning smoothly with good liquidity.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you observe the spreads, they have considerably tightened over the course of the last two years, and the spreads relative to bonds have a rather limited width between the other Member States relative to German bonds.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You give me a chance to say something that I wanted to say in the first place, which is that on the occasion of this Governing Council meeting, we had a chance to welcome two new members around the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first one was the new governor of Austria, Martin Kocher, who has joined us to replace Mr Holzmann, and the other person that we greeted at the table was indeed Dimitar Radev, the governor of the national central bank of Bulgaria.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would like to welcome those of you from Bulgaria, because I know that there are a number of you who are present in the room, and I hope your colleagues will welcome you, but I certainly welcome you and I know that you are spending a little bit of time with us and it's very, very welcome because it's wonderful to accept and to include a new member around the table of the Governing Council and to have Bulgaria join the euro area and share our currency, which is now yours, as of 1 January.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Having said that, you bring me back to more than a couple of decades ago, when all of us moving into the euro from wherever we were - the Deutsche Mark, the franc, the lira, the peseta.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The surprise was to the upside, I can assure you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It removed this nightmare of having to change from your local currency to another currency if you wanted to either travel, transact or conduct any kind of business with other members of the European Union that are part of the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that's really the core mandate of the ECB: to provide price stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the fact that inflation is very precisely targeted for the medium term and that our monetary policy is aiming and taking all the necessary steps in order to deliver on our commitment to target is something that all Member States benefit from.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It requires on the part of those in charge of monetary policy to participate in the discussion, so Bulgaria has a view and can express it, and I trust Governor Radev to do so; Bulgaria has a voice, so you can comment on any monetary policy decisions and any decisions by the European Central Bank, which is becoming yours and part of your fabric; and Bulgaria has a vote.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Every member around the table - each of the 21 members - has a voice which is regarded, considered and respected exactly as the voice of the other ones, no matter how small or big the country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I can assure you that in chairing those meetings and organising the consultations, I respect that principle to the letter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You are already part of the supervision mechanism that we have under the SSM, so you know about the stability of the financial system that is supervised by the SSM, but I think the cooperation and the collaboration will be even closer as of 1 January.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There's one point that I would like to make, and that happens regularly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Upon joining, everybody has to convert from lev to euro, as we had to convert from Deutsche Mark, franc, lira, etc.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Sometimes, at the time of conversion, some shopkeepers and retail merchants take the opportunity of that conversion to increase a little bit the price that is charged for the same service.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think you have tools, because my understanding is that since August you have a converter and the necessary flagging of the price in lev and the price in euro, and therefore consumers can check whether the conversion is correct.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if there is some discretion on the part of the shopkeepers and the retailers to add on, then certainly it's for the authorities to enforce the rule of strict conversion.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I very much hope that the authorities do that because it's the rule and it needs to be enforced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And don't forget: being part of this market of 350 million people, your destination, whether it's for vacation or whether it is for investment, has a different face.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As to whether the burden of proof is here or there to justify up or down or hold.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think there were many governors around the table who, after a good discussion on the inflation outlook, the underlying inflation, the strength of transmission and the risks - there was a good discussion on risks - said "Look, let us not over-engineer, please."

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You give me a chance to actually make another point, which is slightly different.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are very lucky so far - and I hope that stays the same - to have data whose integrity is not challenged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think the integrity of the data that we receive from the statistics offices of the Member States and that are compiled by Eurostat - despite the trauma that we have seen a few years ago out of Greece, which I think has been a lesson for all of us - is very high, and this is valued by all of us.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We take all of that - the data that exist, the projections that we receive, the detailed analysis, the granular details in which we go down to understand underlying inflation, the assumptions that we make on the price of oil, on the price of gas, on the price of commodities, the exchange rate - and we factor all that in.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's on the basis of that mass of data that we try to organise as best as we can to see how it impacts inflation and how it helps us transmit our monetary policy stance that we decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that I would betray my governors on the Governing Council if I was to enter with you in that rather circumvoluted discussion about the burden of proof, which I was very familiar with in my legal days, which were of a slightly different nature.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Let's look at all of them when they come, decide on a meeting-by-meeting basis and make sure that we can continue to be in a good place with the decisions that we need to make at each meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your second question, you're very familiar with TPI and we have given a host of details and terms and conditions under which it operates.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's to be found in the press release that we issued back more than three years ago at the time when it came out.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And you have to remember always that there is a set of criteria, there is a market assessment and then there is the decision of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not a straightjacket, and the discretion of the Governing Council always exists.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, having said that, this is an explanation about TPI, because TPI was not discussed at all in the course of our Governing Council meeting.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: That is three questions, so I will discount your third one.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I just said, particularly because we have now agreed on the strategy review and that one of the changes that we have all agreed on is to discuss around the baseline the risks, we had that good discussion of risks: risks to growth, risks to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do not ever settle on risks to inflation as to whether it is to the upside or to the downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We mention a number of factors that constitute risks to the upside and risks to the downside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is all highly technical and subtle, because depending on where you are and where you want to be, those risks to inflation to the downside or to the upside are either good or bad.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we do have those discussions, and we did have it yesterday and this morning, and it resulted in the risk paragraph that you have in the monetary policy statement, which starts with - and I will quote it for you- "risks to economic growth have become more balanced".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I tried to explain why we came to this conclusion as compared with risks to the downside, which was incorporated in our June monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It relates predominantly to the trade situation and the risk level resulting from no agreement, an agreement, possible retaliation and no retaliation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This was clearly a trigger to say that it is more balanced.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm sure that you will hear people say "Well, it's more balanced but a bit to the downside".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And there are reasons to fear and there are reasons to hope.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what we're saying here is that it is more balanced now than it was back in June.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I've lost sight of your second question, but I think you said I was interpreted as being hawkish.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I remind you that I'm neither a hawk nor a dove, I'm an owl.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For our Bulgarian colleagues, when I first took this job, I was instantly asked as to whether or not I was a hawk, the hard liner, or a dove, the softer liner.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I said neither, I'm an owl, because I want, number one, to see everything that happens around me.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not 360 degrees, but it's a pretty large diameter that I can look at, and I want to come to my conclusions having heard all colleagues around the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think that during my July communication, I expressed exactly what was felt by a very large majority of the governors around the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think I've repeatedly said that we continue to be in a good place, which does not mean that we are on a predetermined path because we have to decide meeting-by-meeting, because we are data-dependent and because we have to face the risks and challenges that are coming.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Thank you for your fidelity in attending and in remembering the words that I've used in the past.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You are right to refer to the resilience of the euro economy, and as an example of that the fact that we had over the first half of 2025 0.7% growth is quite indicative of that resilience.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, some would argue "No, you had a big frontloading in the first quarter and a big payback in the second".

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I would submit that this is not actually the case.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was frontloading, but the unexpectedly high number that we had during the first quarter was partly frontloading but was also partly investment and consumption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if you look at the second quarter, which is higher than we had anticipated, if you take out Ireland - we tend to take out Ireland not because we don't like Ireland, but because sometimes it's a bit of an outlier for reasons that many of you understand - the contribution of consumption and investment to growth was 0.2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We know that there are headwinds and there will continue to be headwinds to growth, but I remind you that we have revised upward our growth projection for the whole of 2025 from 0.9% to 1.2%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a 30% increase, when you think about it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there will be headwinds, and that is reflected in the slight adjustment that we made for 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We revised down growth for 2026 by 0.1 percentage point and we left 2027 unchanged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we believe that there will be positives for growth that result from the real disposable income that people have and will continue to have from a very strong labour market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We project the labour market to have a 6.1% unemployment rate in 2027, for instance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We also believe that for savings, which are still very high at about 15% - this is not a given - there is a likelihood that those savings decline and will therefore help with additional consumption.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Added to which there will be significant investment, and public investment in particular, on the part of those countries that want to increase their military spending and increase their infrastructure spending.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The Recovery and Resilience Fund will continue to be disbursed until the end of 2026, and the military expenses will pick up the baton from there - probably a little earlier than that actually - and will contribute to growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So those are essentially the reasons that we see on the upside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As I said, there will be headwinds, no question about that, and you can include in that more trepidation in trade, the strength of the exchange rate and what have you.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this is factored into our projections, by the way.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not going to characterise it as pause, hold, direction of travel.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think all of that is swept away by the principles that we have agreed, which is to be data-dependent, to decide meeting-by-meeting, to not have a predetermined path and to really look at the inflation outlook, meaning baseline plus associated risks, underlying inflation and the strength of transmission.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is our mechanism, this is our framework and this is how we try to think and to anticipate our monetary policy stance going forward to continue to be in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think that markets do what they have to do, and we do, as the central bank, what we have to do.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, of course, as I said, we monitor markets always and, as you know, also as part of our projections, we account for market positions at a certain point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, in a way, we also factor into our assumptions a particular situation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I'm not going to repeat one more time what I have said about where we are, where we continue to be, where we want to continue to be, which will require that each and every time we take stock, we look at data and we determine what monetary policy stance is appropriate to continue to be in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, we have discussed the situation of the global economy and global growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously we look at the United States, we look at China, we look at Japan, the rest of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think on the United States, there are two stories.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have the stories of the slight decline, possible more decline, but you also have the story of productivity, of artificial intelligence, of the Magnificent Seven.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that we need to bring all of it together and see what spillovers there will be to our economies as a result.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the key focus at the moment as far as the United States-Europe relationship is concerned is really on trade and how much more we are going to learn of this trade situation and the repercussions that it will have, taking into account the overall spread of the tariff changes that have taken place and will continue to take place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would observe that thanks to the hospitality of Banca d'Italia, we are in a magnificent place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: From a monetary policy point of view, we are in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we will do whatever is needed to make sure that we stay in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I would observe that with growth of 0.2% for Q3, which is a tad more than what was expected by the consensus - and including Ireland a little more than what we had expected, not by much - I would not complain too much about growth at this point in time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I observe that there is quite a bit of investment underlying this number, certainly in respect of France, which publishes breakdown.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So turning to your other question, which has to do with artificial intelligence: what we are hearing from the corporate telephone survey in particular that we conduct on a regular basis, is that corporates are really moving ahead with investment, and the transition to a more digital world is obviously on their mind, and it's also drawing on the investment that they are committing now.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is a process, and the impact it will have on labour will probably take time.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There will be job creation, there will be job destruction.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: How exactly that will impact our economies, depending on the sectors, depending on the classes of age, depending on the training, depending on the educational background of workforce in Europe, which which tends to be quite high, I think is to be seen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, I have said that we are in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I continue to say that we are in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I repeat that we will take the necessary measures and steps on the basis of data, meeting by meeting, to make sure that we stay in a good place.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I also want to remind you that we have very clearly defined our objective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that objective, because you asked me the question about symmetry, our target is symmetric 2% medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we will abide by that objective that we have discussed extensively in 2021, reiterated in our 2021 strategy review, and reiterated again in 2025 when we took stock of our strategy implementation and the stocktaking exercise.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the risks, you are right, because when you go to the section of our monetary policy statement, we list as exhaustively - and yet as principally as is possible - the number of risks on the downside and on the upside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But what is a little bit different this time around is that our paragraph on risk assessment begins with indicating some of the risks which have faded or have been alleviated in the last few weeks, and the impact that it has had in particular.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we start with the EU-US trade deal reached over the summer.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We follow with the recently announced ceasefire in the Middle East.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we continue with the announcement today, this morning actually, of progress in the US-China trade negotiations.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we continue with: these components have mitigated some of the downside risks to economic growth.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So if you remember last time in September, I said that the risk to growth was more balanced, and the range had narrowed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think this time around we acknowledged that some of the downside risks to growth have abated, and we specifically mentioned these three.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I would not necessarily draw the same conclusion for inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think on that front, it's a more balanced picture that we paint, and we go through the upside and the downside risks to inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I would suggest that we remain attentive to the occurrence, or the risk of occurrence, of any of these risks that can weigh on our inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, we are in a period of still great uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And many of those risks are resulting from policies and implementation of policies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think that's the best that I can give you in terms of explaining to you why we do not draw a line on it being one way or the other, and prefer to list those risks carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the impact, no, it will not have any financial stability implications.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We will not have financial instability because of the tax.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The banks are highly profitable, and the tax is a limited percentage of their profits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the specific characteristics of the tax, I will comment when I will see the final text of the legislation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So in our mind, and certainly in my mind, central bank money has to remain an active part of the system that people can actually trust.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you think of digital euro, it's the digital form of a banknote.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Maybe in 10 years' time there will be fewer of those banknotes in circulation, but they will still need to have the certainty that a euro is a euro is a euro, just like a rose is a rose is a rose.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And for me it is our mission to make sure that money remains that public good that is available to our compatriots.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are working for the Europeans in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, when I hear that it's a project in search of a cause, I think of money as a public good, the sovereignty of the European authorities at large over their currency, and the way in which money stands: this is not a project in search of a cause.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It embodies the capacity of Europe to defend itself and to transact with a currency that is its own.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are many other reasons why the digital euro is perfectly legitimate, valid, and will be cheaper, user-friendly, good for transactions throughout Europe and not just in various countries on a national basis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But the key points for me is: money is a public good; central banks are the custodian of that public good; and central money issued by central banks has to have its digital form, because we're moving into a different era where not everybody will want necessarily to have banknotes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the costs, I think it would be unwise to discuss costs before discussing the benefits.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Currently, euro area banks only represent one third of total activity on digital payments in the euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Two thirds of digital payments in the euro area are intermediated by non-European companies, both for digital payments at the point of sale and digital payments online.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now the reason why this is so is that European banks did not agree until now on ways to provide their services to the entire euro area.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They don't have what is called in technical terms a rail, the infrastructure to provide, to offer their digital payment services to all European citizens.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of the main benefits for banks - there are many benefits for consumers, there are benefits for the stability of the financial system - but one of the main benefits for the banks in the euro area is that once the digital euro infrastructure will be built, they will be able, by using this so-called open standard infrastructure, to use that rail and compete at a European level, thus generating additional business, additional revenues, and there will be many implications in terms of sovereignty for the euro area, in terms of control of the information that travels with your payments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, there are estimates on the cost of adoption, because the construction of the digital euro will be paid by the Eurosystem.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The costs, I don't know if the estimates which are available are correct, discuss numbers of about 6 billion euros for four years.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now if you think that we have 2,000 banks in the euro area, for four years, this means that the cost of adoption is a few hundred thousand euros per year per bank.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now even forgetting the benefits I just mentioned, the costs of adoption are not so high.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They represent overall about 3% of total yearly IT costs for the banks.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, it depends on the competition on the payment market.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If the digital euro would be introduced, competition would be higher, and the banks would not be able to transfer those costs to consumers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it would be limited, there would be additional revenues, and then the cost would be allocated depending on competition, and competition will improve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's always more fashionable to make negative comments whenever you have good news, that I understand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But when we have some good news, we have to also acknowledge and draw the consequences and see what impact it has.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Because as I said repeatedly we are determined, we are driven by data, we take into account all data, and we measure the impact that it has in terms of outlook, underlying inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I come to you, the first part of your question, because as you know, we maintain this three-pronged approach that we have had to take into account inflation outlook, underlying inflation, and transmission of monetary policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I would add to that, you know, since our strategy review, in addition to pure inflation outlook and the identification of our baseline, we also try to identify and measure risks to the baseline, risk to the upside, risk to the downside, and we use different tools in order to do so, including scenario analysis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Everything that we see in terms of transmission leads us to believe that transmission is effective, is very much on time, and the numbers that we see in terms of interest rates charged to corporates, interest rates charged to mortgages, lead us to believe that that transmission is not impaired at all, but is functioning well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have seen two things in the bank lending survey.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One is that there has been a slight tightening of the credit terms by the banks, which was unexpected, and that is in our view and on the basis of their response to our survey caused by the more attentive measurement of risk of their customers, particularly in the corporate sector.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the second, which is twofold, but it's in relation to households, that interest rate has not budged.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And on the other hand, the volume of loan to households has itself increased.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But again, we observe on the part of the banks, based on the bank lending survey, a more cautious attitude probably in order to better measure the risks that they have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I'm happy to say that on the occasion of this meeting in Firenze, there was absolute unanimity on the part of all members of the Governing Council to arrive at the decision that I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, let me mention a few elements that we discussed or that we are attentive to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One risk that we have not yet seen materialise and could be a risk to the upside, so we will continue to be attentive to that, is the risk that would result from potential bottlenecks and disruption in the supply chain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are still to understand exactly what the outcome of the discussions between the US authorities and the Chinese authorities will deliver in terms of rare earth in particular - which is, as you know, a very material segment of the supply chains in quite a few sectors, including the automotive sector, but the energy sector as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's not a big amount in terms of actual value, but it's critical at the juncture where it is situated in the production chain.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are in this sort of wait-and-watch or wait-and-see mode in relation to that specific risk.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are two other areas that we are attentive to, and that is the composition of inflation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And in that respect, the way in which the labour market evolves, the way in which wages evolve and the impact that it will have to service inflation are elements that we are also monitoring to understand the impact that it will have going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I wouldn't call it a risk, so to speak, you don't find it in the risk section.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I just want to mention these two because they are ingredients that feed into services inflation, which in September has picked up by 0.1%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And they of course also have an impact on underlying inflation, particularly domestic.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, the numbers which we got today on GDP - GDP was flat - are largely expected and they do not materially change the projections we have just published.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In order to have a better assessment, we need more information on the composition, because the composition matters.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Was the deceleration in GDP growth due to investment, consumption, inventories or foreign demand?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Investment and foreign demand have performed very well in the past so it is important to understand what is the source.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think we should broaden the horizon and look at the conditions of the Italian economy from a broader perspective.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: In recent years, the Italian economy continued to grow, although at a moderate pace, in spite of a number of shocks that have hit, like many other economies, the Italian economy and others.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The geopolitical tensions, the tightening cycle of the ECB, tariffs, appreciation of the euro, the weakening of the traditional export markets of Italy, the weakening of the German economy is a big headwind for the Italian economy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But overall, the economy has been much more resilient than many would have predicted only two, three years ago.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I think we should look at the structural underlying conditions of the Italian economy, which have improved significantly.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you look at public finance, the deficit shot up to above 9% during the pandemic crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now it is at 3%, we'll go even lower than that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The debt-to-GDP ratio, which increased significantly during the pandemic phase, now is back to the pre-pandemic level.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And what went largely unnoticed in recent years is the change which took place in Italy's net financial international position.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We have now a persistent surplus of the balance of payments.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And if only 10 years ago the net financial international position of Italy was negative for more than 20 percentage points of GDP, today we have a positive international financial net position.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So from minus 20 plus percent to around 8, 9 percentage points of GDP.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And this happened - a very rare case - without a crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Without a forced restructuring due to an enormous shock which then evolves into a crisis.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This has gone largely unnoticed, but just to emphasize this concept, now Italy is a net creditor country.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Every year we give some of our savings, unfortunately, to foreign countries and our position is positive vis-a-vis the rest of the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, thank you so much for asking these two questions and thank you for helping me to clarify what I mean.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I did not repeat that sentence on purpose or to convey any particular message.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If you read carefully our statement, which I know you do, you will see that in the second paragraph of our monetary policy statement, we say we are determined to ensure that inflation stabilises at our 2% target in the medium term.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So this is all there is to be read about it, and it's a determination of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We continue to be in a good place, and we are determined to ensure that inflation stabilises at that 2% medium-term target, which is the result of our strategy review.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is nothing else or nothing more to read about me having repeated two sentences.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So the EU Emissions Trading System 2 (ETS2), first of all, has been in our projection since it was on the table, and has been in there since 2024.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think I would read too much, again, into an expected delay of the implementation of ETS2.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And when I speak to colleagues at the European Commission, they are still strongly of the view that ETS2, which is committed, must proceed, and the deadline for implementation is still 2027.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: What, on the other hand, is being discussed and has been put on the table by Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra, is a slight smoothing in the implementation of ETS2, which means that the impact might be spread a little bit more over time, possibly a bit less in 2027 and a bit more in 2028.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So overall, you know, as with many other data, we will be attentive.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And the December projection exercise will certainly take that into account, that smoothing over a slightly longer period in order to make sure that ETS2, which is so important for climate change purposes, will actually be implemented.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: First of all, I would like to insist on the fact that we at the ECB, in the Eurosystem, are very attentive to innovation, and we are very supportive of innovation.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The digital euro, the different options that we're exploring, the way in which we reach out to suppliers, merchants, banks, which stand to benefit from this system, is a clear indication that we want innovation into money and into this public good for which we are responsible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So for those who would like to argue that we are trying to stifle innovation, terribly sorry, but no.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Innovation is definitely part of us and part of the DNA of central bankers in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Second, we are also attentive to the regulatory framework in which private forms of money, certain financial instruments that I would not call currencies, and I'm here referring to cryptos, equivalent of currencies as they present themselves, but which are private form of money such as stablecoins, are launched, are reserved against, are made secure.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And that was under the MiCAR, which was the European regulation that was issued in order to establish the protection of consumers, enough financial stability, and rules by which some of those issuers were supervised.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I observed, by the way, that in spite of the executive decision that was made back in January, the GENIUS Act, which was issued by Congress in the United States is also attempting to put together a framework which has a lot of overlap with MiCAR.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are some discrepancies and there are areas for which we have to be attentive not to create financial stability risk or arbitrage risks that would be detrimental to Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is our job and we will continue to do that job and to have a dialogue with the Commission which is in charge of establishing the rules of the game, if you will.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as I said earlier, what we are doing, putting money as a public good on the map and making sure that the anchor is alive and digital as well as cash, is our duty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it does not stop private issuers from doing what they think is their business.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: They're into penetration of certain spheres of either payment or transactions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are going to continue doing that, notwithstanding initiatives that some of those issuers will take.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it certainly does not preclude European-based issuance that would be in compliance with the regulatory framework that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So it's a vibrant domain, but one where we have to make sure that we do not expose our compatriots or our economy to financial instability risk that would certainly be a recurrence of what we observed back in 1890 in the United States, for instance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On interest rate, we reconfirmed that we are in a good place, which does not mean that we are static.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There was a unanimous decision that was taken today concerning the rates that we decided to hold, but there was also a unanimous view that all optionalities should remain on the table and that we would stick to the meeting-by-meeting, data-dependent approach, with no rate path set and no set date for any move, and it was a unanimous view around the table.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Your second question is, always an interesting question from you, but it's an interesting question because it raises issues that we will probably review in deeper detail at our February meeting[1], because we will also be looking at the surveillance report that we produce, we will be looking at the fiscal policy note, we might look also at the supply side review to go a bit deeper in some of the facts that would answer your question.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We think that there is some change taking place in our economies, and if you look in particular at the drivers and what has surprised us on the upside, it's characteristically investment, and it's not just spending by the public sector, which there is.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it's also the private sector, the corporate sector, both large corporates but also SMEs as well.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And their investment, based on the data that we collect, based on the surveys that we conduct, is largely attributable to the development of AI.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And AI takes multi-facets, but certainly computer capacity, telecommunication, additional investment in intangible -more than tangible - CapEx is really characteristic of what we are seeing at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that is something that we can already analyse, but I think we will be able to go a bit deeper in February, as we will see a bit of a longer interval to determine whether that's a long-lasting fact that is characteristic of this new growth, but that is clearly in play.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The second one, which came as a bit of a surprise to us, is the contribution of exports.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We had anticipated that exports - particularly out of the chemical industry, and out of Ireland notably, but not only - would really correspond to a build-up of inventory and to a front-loading in the early months after the decision to increase tariff or pre-decision to increase tariff.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Well, that has been sustainable, and the contribution of exports has surprised us on the upside.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, we don't know whether it's entirely attributable to the weight-losing drugs that are largely exported or to other phenomena, but the contribution of export has surprised on the upside, when in fact we believe that trade is more likely, as a result of tariffs, to be a drag on growth going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's also something that we will be attentive to.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You know, certain things have changed and others have not changed.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, when we look at activity, we have upgraded our projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: When we look at inflation, we've also increased our inflation projection for 2026 and we have taken into account the movement from 2027 to 2028.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there are lots of things that have moved in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One thing that has not changed much at all and which, if anything, may have actually worsened is uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I think we all suffer from that degree of lack of comfort.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And we are all attentive to uncertainty: how it pans out, whether it's uncertainty related to geopolitics, whether it's uncertainty related to the movement of trade from countries with overcapacity in particular, what happens at the borders of Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there are lots of factors that are in play and that will evolve over the course of 2026 that are generating uncertainty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: As far as the future is concerned, as I told your colleague just earlier on, there was unanimous agreement around the table about the fact that all optionalities should be on the table and that we should stick to the meeting-by-meeting approach, to the data dependency - and we will be looking at all sorts of data in the field of wages, salaries, the decomposition of it; we will be particularly attentive because it plays a significant role in relation to services - and we do not have a set path for our rates going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know everybody would like some forward guidance, but in the current situation, with the degree of uncertainty that we are facing, we simply cannot offer forward guidance.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Now, your second question related to government spending, public investment: we take into account the documents that are filed by the various Member States with the Commission to review the path of investments going forward, and we have an impact on growth for certain countries - Germany being obviously one - in 2026, in 2027 and still a bit in 2028, and so much can change in the meantime.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it does have an impact, and it is a driver of growth in the investment section that I was describing earlier.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't have any favourite candidate, and I did not say that Klaas Knot wasthegood candidate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There are plenty of very good candidates, and Isabel is one of them, but there are plenty of them, and I'm sure that there will be more in the future.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I find it terribly satisfactory, in a way, that so many people want to have my job.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's a great job, and it's one where you feel that you can actually matter and affect the life of people and try to deliver for the European Union and for our currency, the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But as to who it is, what nationality, I'll have nothing to say about that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It will be for the European Council, and the decision will be made outside this beautiful institution, so whatever they decide.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You have still a long time to ask all those questions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I might give you the answer that you expect, which is that we do not target exchange rate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We do refer to exchange rate in the risk section of our monetary policy statement, if I recall, when we refer to a possible higher exchange rate, an appreciation of the euro.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So I'll refer you to that section in the risk segment of the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously it is something that we look at carefully as we look at the way in which currencies are positioned around the world.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And obviously the current situation of the renminbi is one that we pay attention to, yes.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question, thank you for focusing on inflation on services because it's clearly one domain that we will be attentive to, going forward.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It went from 3.2% in September to 3.4% to 3.5%.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So there is a trend that we look at carefully.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: A lot of that is related, based on the staff study, to wages.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we look at compensation per employee, for instance, we are at 4%, which is more than had been anticipated in particular in the September projections.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So with wages having increased more than anticipated, and being a strong contributor to most activities of services - not all of them, but most activities of services - it's hardly surprising that services inflation is higher than anticipated and contributing to the current inflation number that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's balanced out by goods, as you will have seen in the monetary policy statement.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Goods go down, services increase, and we anticipate two things in relation to that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Number one, that wages will follow a slightly declining trend, going forward, and we have wages slightly below 3% at the end of 2026, and that is based on measurement instruments that we have: whether it's the wage tracker, which incorporates all the collective bargaining agreements that are negotiated, and which roll out in either one or two or three years, depending on the countries, and under which we cover now eight countries with quite a large number of employees, workers, or whether it is the surveys and the corporate telephone survey that we conduct asking corporates, you know, where do you see salaries, where do you see wages, how are the negotiations going?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, on the basis of all that, we believe that this compensation per employee should decline in the course of 2026.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But we are attentive because while we believe that a lot of the catch-up, for instance, has taken place, a lot of the one-off specific payments have occurred, we were surprised, between September and December in our projection, and that is reflected in our numbers.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So we are humble, we look at as many details and data, and we look at the vacancy, of course, to see what's likely to happen.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We look at PMI numbers, but that's where we are, and it's a big contributor to services.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: This is one that we really debated quite a bit and that we looked into, and staff is working really hard to get to the bottom of it.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Services is a big package, you have lots of things in there - you have accommodation, transportation, telecom, IT, financial services - there is a lot in there, and some of those subsectors of services are labor-intensive, are wage-intensive, others less so, so we have to sort of balance out and distribute the wage increases that we expect in between all that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But there is really solid work done in that respect.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, your question is: Can a sitting member of the Executive Board be eligible for another board position or the position of President?

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was looked at when Christian Noyer, the then Vice-President of the ECB, was possibly considered for Presidency.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It was looked at for Benoît Cœuré, who was then an Executive Board member, and who was also considered possibly for the replacement of Mario Draghi.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think in both those instances, the determination by the jurists, the lawyers of various corners of Europe was that it was not possible.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But I think the matter needs to be looked at again in order to ascertain what is possible, what is not possible, what are the conditions.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And it's not for me to pass a judgment on that.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I think it needs to be cleared so that everyone knows where to stand.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I know these are important moments for the digital euro because we have done our work, we have carried the water, but it's now for the European Council and certainly later on for the European Parliament to identify whether the Commission proposal is satisfactory, how it can be transformed into a piece of legislation or amended.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our ambition is to make sure that in the digital age, there is a currency that is the anchor of stability for the financial system.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: For the moment, that anchor is central bank money, which essentially has material form: it's the banknotes that you have in your wallet.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But in the digital age, it has to be a digital expression of that sovereignty and a digital anchor for the purpose of the financial system that we have.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So that's what we're pursuing, in addition to making sure that it is user-friendly, not costly, fast, efficient, private, that it can work online, offline.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I mean, I could go on and on, because you know that I've followed that very carefully with my Italian colleagues, and both Luis and myself are very strong supporters of this initiative, and we place great hopes in the work that will be done in Parliament, once the Council has determined its views.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On the other topic that you raised, I'm not going to expand on this matter, because it's something that is under review, that is under work at the moment, which is of the competence of the European leaders and which is the expression of foreign policy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, it's not for a central bank to have either political views or central banks' choice as to what is appropriate or not appropriate.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Our job, and we are trying to do it as much and as well as we can at the odd hours of the day or the weekend, is to respond to the requests that are put upon us to determine that whatever choice is made by the leaders is going to respect the treaty, is going to respect the international rule of law, and will not damage financial stability.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are lucky in Europe to have something that is called MiCAR.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's the legal framework within which instruments like stablecoins can work and can be supervised and can be regarded as safe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So our view is that an instrument that is in compliance with MiCAR is an alternative form of payment, which might have its benefit, might have a business case for those that issue the stablecoins.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: To the extent that it conforms to MiCAR, that it is properly organised, that it has the right one-to-one guarantee for the users, I don't need to have a view.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Supervisors need to have a view, those who control that there is actually the reserve.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Where I have a concern is when you have (something that is getting a bit technical now, if we go there) the situation of multi-issuance currency for stablecoins, because without going into the details of how it is structured, it exposes the reserves, the resolution mechanisms and the redemption mechanism in Europe, as is organised under MiCAR, to other currencies under which the stablecoin would be issued and which could be a threat and a drain on the provisions of MiCAR that apply in Europe.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So on that particular area, I think that we need to be extremely attentive to what the potential risks are for the system itself and for the holders of stablecoins.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: On your first question: Look, I'm not going to agonise over the issue of where and how is the r-star and the rate which is ideal because it neither stimulates nor restricts our economies.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: If we draw a lot of productivity out of artificial intelligence, it will impact it, but there are multiple other factors as well that will impact r-star.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: One of the characteristics of r-star is that you can only sort of identify it, eventually, in completely stable circumstances.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: I don't think that we can call the current circumstances perfectly stable and predictable.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: There is, as I said earlier, too much uncertainty, too much risk, and too many shocks, under the spell of which we still are, to actually identify r-star and have a view as to whether it's going to increase.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: So, as I said, it's not observable, so to speak, and I think it's a very good debate to have, but I'm not sure that this is the one that has caught the attention of the Governing Council.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It's certainly not one that we debated today, or yesterday for that matter.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: The first question: There is work going on at the moment.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: Again, it's not our remit, it's for the leaders to decide, and given the importance of the matter, given what is at stake, I am fully confident that they will find a solution.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: It might be in the usual European way, you know, going in circles and being time-consuming and giving rise to a lot of speculation as to whether it will work, it will not work, there will be one camp or the other, but I'm confident that they will find a solution, because it's too important.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: We are an area of the world which prides itself for respecting the rule of law, and this is one of the characteristics of our democracy.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: And I'm sure that there are solutions that can be debated and discussed, and there are constructions that can be elaborated.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: But it is not for the Central Bank to actually encourage or support a mechanism under which we would be called upon and scheduled to breach Article 123 of the Treaty.

speaker: Christine Lagarde
text: You cannot expect me to validate ex ante a mechanism under which there would be monetary financing.
